Some crude expressions, sexual humor and innuendo, cartoonish witchcraft elements and partial blurred nudity make this best for adults and perhaps older adolescents

title: Beyond and Back
synopsis: The movie presents itself as a serious, scientific examination of certain alleged happenings that seem to indicate that there is life after death. The result, however, proves to be utterly uncritical in its treatment of data and many of its conclusions are not merely absurd but at variance with some traditional religious beliefs. Its realistic depiction of death experiences may be too strong for the very young

title: Beyond Bombasa
synopsis: Tepid African adventure follows a rugged American (Cornel Wilde) and his guides (Donna Reed, Leo Genn and Christopher Lee) through the jungle to a mysterious mine discovered by his murdered brother. Filmed largely in Kenya by director George Marshall, the action is colorful but the clumsy, far-fetched plot hinges on a religious murder cult and a mad humanitarian. African stereotypes and some stylized but nasty violence are unsuitable for young imaginations

title: Beyond Borders
synopsis: Hollow melodrama about a sheltered American (Angelina Jolie) living in London with her socialite husband (Linus Roache), who has her eyes opened to the suffering of the wider world when she becomes romantically involved with a renegade doctor (Clive Owen) passionately committed to relief efforts in war-torn countries. Despite the sincerity of its humanitarian message, the film, directed by Martin Campbell, suffers from severe narrative malnutrition with characters less fleshed out than the famine victims they champion, and a story that seesaws awkwardly between a globetrotting soap-opera romance and a UNICEF travelogue. Some war violence, several disturbing images of famine and disease-ravaged victims, an implied sexual encounter, recurring rough and crude language and profanity

title: Beyond Control
synopsis: German import in which a pair of young men and their girl friends rob banks during the 1930s supposedly as a form of anti-Nazi protest is not only suffocatingly inept but made thoroughly offensive as well by splicing in some sex exploitation footage (shot entirely from the neck down)

title: Beyond Love and Evil
synopsis: French sex exploitation movie directed by Jacques Scandelari about the woodland villa of an evil count where a seemingly endless parade of perversity and cruelty take place

title: Beyond Rangoon
synopsis: Stranded in 1988 Burma when her U.S. passport is lost during student demonstrations against the military dictatorship, a newly widowed doctor (Patricia Arquette) and her elderly Burmese guide (U Aung Ko) struggle to evade murderous soldiers as they join the flood of desperate dissidents fleeing to the safety of the Thai border. Though director John Boorman's political thriller is overly contrived in developing the American woman's plight, it succeeds in calling attention to human rights violations in that beleaguered country. Intermittent scenes of military attacks on unarmed civilians

title: Beyond Silence
synopsis: Lyric family drama in which the young daughter (Tatjana Trieb) of deaf parents (Howie Seago and Emmanuelle Laborit) learns to play the clarinet, proves musically gifted and, as a young woman (Sylvie Testud), enrolls in a conservatory, leaving her father deeply hurt by what he considers his daughter's rejection. Directed by Caroline Link, the German production puts across the warm, though sometimes painful, story of a hearing child being raised by loving parents whose inability to hear leads to occasional misunderstandings and conflicting emotions. Subtitles. Some intense domestic confrontations, several sexual situations, a toilet scene and a crude expression

title: Beyond the Door
synopsis: Cheap horror movie directed by Oliver Hellman is an inept, tasteless attempt to combine "Rosemary's Baby" and "The Exorcist."

title: Beyond the Gates
synopsis: Gripping dramatization about the 1994 siege of a Rwandan secondary school at the height of the genocide, as a dedicated Catholic priest (John Hurt) and an idealistic young British teacher (Hugh Dancy) -- both fictional characters -- attempt to protect some 2,500 Tutsi citizens from the machete-wielding Hutus hovering just outside the school gates. Director Michael Caton-Jones has filmed this powerful film at the actual locations of the horrific events with survivors among the cast and crew. This important film is acceptable for mature teens. Much disturbing if discreetly handled violence, description of atrocities, images of dead and wounded, some rough language and mild profanity uttered under duress, a childbirth scene

title: Beyond the Last Frontier
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Howard Bretherton in which an undercover Texas Ranger (Eddie Dew) joins a band of outlaws whose leader (Harry Woods) sends one of his men (Robert "Bob" Mitchum) to join the Rangers, resulting in confusion on both sides. Stylized violence

title: Beyond the Law
synopsis: Novelist Norman Mailer's self-indulgent home movie about brutality in a New York City police station is offensive in its almost jocular use of violence and its coarse and obscene language

title: Beyond the Limit
synopsis: Director John Mackenzie's screen version of the Graham Greene novel, "The Honorary Consul," is a plodding, uninspired effort given some merit only by Michael Caine's performance as the hapless diplomat in an Argentine backwater, whom an inept band of revolutionaries kidnap by mistake. Another mistake is Richard Gere as Greene's introspective protagonist. Extensive nudity in the context of an adulterous affair

title: Beyond the Mat
synopsis: Because of intermittent wrestling violence with some gore, minimal profanity and some rough language,

title: Beyond the Poseidon Adventure
synopsis: Tugboat captain Michael Caine (aided and abetted by Karl Malden and Sally Field) try to salvage the Poseidon, moments after the climactic rescue of the previous disaster film. Producer-director Irwin Allen supplies only vacuous plot, dialogue and resolution in a boring adventure yarn

title: Beyond Therapy
synopsis: Based on the Christopher Durang play, Robert Altman's emotionally anemic romance tries to find humor in the failures of modern psychoanalysis and in the flaws of a sexually confused cast (Jeff Goldblum, Julie Hagerty, Glenda Jackson, Tom Conti and Christopher Guest). Shallow insights pervade the movie which relies totally upon sexual innuendo, negative stereotypes and some vulgar language for interest

title: Beyond the Reef
synopsis: This is a South Pacific idyll about a Polynesian lad and his pet shark who helps him win the love of a rich man's daughter, despite interference from her greedy brother and unscruplous land developers. Directed by Frank C. Clark, it's an amateurish little movie, save for some remarkable underwater photography and a school of apparently trained sharks. Some partial nudity and permissive attitude toward the lovers' affair

title: Beyond the Rocks
synopsis: > Superb restoration of a film thought lost for 80 years, starring two of the silent era's biggest stars, Rudolph Valentino and Gloria Swanson. In England, the daughter (Swanson) of a retired guardsman (Alec Francis) is pressured into marrying a wealthy older man (Robert Bolder) to help her impoverished father and stepsisters. She dutifully complies, but falls in love with a handsome earl (Valentino) who had earlier rescued her from drowning. The couple endeavor to do the right thing and not act on their feelings. Directed by Sam Wood, the story traverses the Swiss Alps, London, and Paris, and the two stars radiate a "rare, almost spiritual intensity," according to Martin Scorsese who introduces the film. The handsome DVD - some imperfections in the original damaged print aside - contains bountiful extras: Valentino's 1919 film "The Delicious Little Devil" costarring Mae Murray; an 85-minute audio recording of Swanson's reminiscences; Valentino trailers; featurettes on the film's discovery and reconstruction by the Nederlands Filmmuseum, the recording of a new orchestral score by Henny Vrienten. As if that weren't enough, the DVD-ROM features include the original Elinor Glyn novel (196 pages), the continuity script, original press clippings, and much more. A-II (nr) (Milestone) 1922

title: Beyond the Sea
synopsis: Entertaining -- if dramatically uneven -- biopic about Bobby Darin (Kevin Spacey, who also directed) which traces the singer's life from sickly child in the Bronx, where his bout with rheumatic fever had doctors predicting he wouldn't make it to his 15th birthday, through his early rise to fame, marriage to actress Sandra Dee, and triumphs in nightclubs, film and recording. He did all this while racing the clock with a bad heart, a condition that would fell him at the young age of 36, and coping with a devastating revelation about his parentage. Spacey's singing of the Darin hits is phenomenally good, and even if he looks a mite mature for the role, he pulls it off, and though the flashback framing device is initially awkward, once the story gets going the film is absorbing with several touching scenes. Some rough and profane language and one nonexplicit sexual encounter

title: Beyond the Valley of the Dolls
synopsis: Director Russ Meyers' unfunny spoof of Hollywood lacks story, stars and appeal. Boring as it may be, it abounds in unhealthy fantasies of sex, with some nudity, and violence

title: Beyond Tomorrow
synopsis: Dated Depression fantasy in which three aging business partners (Harry Carey, C. Aubrey Smith and Charles Winninger) share the Christmas holidays with two needy New Yorkers (Richard Carlson and Jean Parker), but after the three die in a plane crash, the spirit of one of them lingers on earth to insure the young couple wed. Directed by A. Edward Sutherland, the sentimental melodrama has plenty of heartfelt warmth and a bit of soul-searching as the dead partners face eternity. Romantic complications involving a gold digger

title: Bicentennial Man
synopsis: Because of mild sexual innuendo and references, as well as occasional profanity,

title: The Bicycle Thieves
synopsis: Bicycle Thieves (see: " The Bicycle Thief ")

title: Big Bully
synopsis: Comedy clunker in which an author (Rick Moranis) returns to his hometown as a grade-school teacher, then learns the bully (Tom Arnold) who had made his life miserable as a child is on the faculty. Directed by Steve Miner, the unamusing situation has the two resume their childhood antagonism with grown-up intensity, while their boys do their own bully-victim routines. Much unfunny violence, some life-threatening situations, sexist humor and occasional coarse language

title: Big Business
synopsis: Two sets of identical twin girls are mismatched at birth -- one set ends up at the helm of a New York-based conglomerate, the other set is raised by a poor, rural couple in West Virginia. Director Jim Abrahams keeps the farce fast and funny in showing how the real twins (both sets are played by Bette Midler and Lily Tomlin) are reunited in New York City's Plaza Hotel, but not before confounding husbands, lovers and all manner of co-workers and hotel employees. Much humor with sexual connotations and some rough language

title: Big Eden
synopsis: A romantic comedy in which a gay, thirty-something artist (Ayre Gross) returns to his small hometown and wrestles with lingering feelings for a high school friend (Tim DeKay) while his presence sparks interest from the local male shop keeper (Eric Schweig). Although the townsfolk's respect and sensitivity toward gays is commendable, writer-director Thomas Bezucha's unconvincing narrative condones the homosexual lifestyle without considering the moral aspects. Sympathetic depiction of gay lifestyle with a few same-sex kisses and instance of profanity

title: Big Enough and Old Enough
synopsis: Family of Mexican migrant workers runs afoul of a motorcycle gang in this wretched movie directed by Joseph Prieto. Rape, mental and physical violence, sexually suggestive dialogue and visuals and coarse language. O 1968

title: Big Fat Liar
synopsis: Lame comedy in which a grade-school boy (Frankie Muniz) writes a school essay that ends up in the hands of a egomaniacal Hollywood producer (Paul Giamatti) who refuses to admit he stole it until he is forced to do so. Director Shawn Levy's unfunny fantasy about a teen-ager getting revenge ends up mocking truth instead of championing it, while the plodding story line, caricatured characters and mean-spirited escapades become increasingly disagreeable. A few crude expressions

title: Big Fish
synopsis: Enchanting fable about an estranged son (Billy Crudup) who returns home to reconnect with his dying father (Albert Finney), a compulsive storyteller, and discovers that the tall tales he was told as a youngster hold the key to unlocking his father's elusive past. Blending fantasy and reality, director Tim Burton's delightful fish story is sure to reel viewers in by suggesting that life is not a problem to be solved but an adventure and a mystery to be embraced with a childlike sense of wonder. Brief violence, an instance of rear nudity and minimal mildly crude humor and language

title: Bigger Than Life
synopsis: When a mild-mannered, underpaid and overworked elementary school teacher (James Mason) falls ill, the drug used in his treatment has disastrous psychological aftereffects that make him a threat to his wife (Barbara Rush) and young son. Directed by Nicholas Ray, the well-meaning but slow-moving lesson in the pitfalls of becoming addicted to prescribed drugs is less than convincing

title: Big House, U.S.A.
synopsis: Brutal crime picture in which the callous kidnapper (Ralph Meeker) of a schoolboy buries the ransom money in Colorado's Royal Gorge Park before being arrested and sent to prison, but his cellmates (led by Broderick Crawford) force him to join them in an escape to retrieve the loot. Directed by Howard W. Koch, the formula proceedings are paced by cruel action scenes including the death of the kidnapped boy and the use of a hammer and blow-torch to destroy a dead convict's identity. Considerable brutality

title: Big Jake
synopsis: John Wayne Western in which he and his two grown sons (Patrick Wayne and Christopher Mitchum) trail the gang who kidnapped his grandson, with occasional pauses for bloodshed, to a Mexican village where they take on villain Richard Boone and his band of eight cutthroats. Directed by George Sherman, it's a rather old-fashioned kind of shoot-em-up, except some of the violence is overdone

title: Big Jim McLain
synopsis: Dated patriotic melodrama in which the title character (John Wayne) and his associate (James Arness) are investigators for the House Un-American Activities Committee and while ferreting out Red subversives in Hawaii, McLain finds romance with a loyal citizen (Nancy Olson). Directed by Edward Ludwig, the story plods along with more lectures than action, though the result may interest students of Cold War politics. Some stylized violence

title: Big Mommas: Like Father, Like Son
synopsis: Warm but somewhat bland third installment in the "Big Momma" franchise, with Martin Lawrence again in the title role. Director John Whitesell and screenwriter Matthew Fogel put Momma through her paces as a housemother at an Atlanta girls school while Lawrence's real persona, an FBI agent -- with the help of Brandon T. Jackson as his son -- searches for a flash drive that will convict a group of mobsters. Some gun violence, fleeting crude and crass language and a partial rear view of a body suit

title: Big Momma's House
synopsis: Because of brief violence, an implied sexual encounter and sporadic innuendo, fleeting rear nudity, crude toilet humor and recurring crass language,

title: Big Momma House 2
synopsis: Stale sequel to the 2000 comedy in which FBI agent Malcolm Turner (Martin Lawrence), while posing as a plus-size nanny to investigate a software designer tagged with compromising national security, winds up bringing the suspected man's family closer together. Directed by John Whitesell, this only fitfully funny and unnecessarily crude second helping rehashes much of the original's forced slapstick humor, with the perfunctory plot an afterthought to Lawrence' sassy shtick. Comic violence, some gun waving and an implied shooting, some crude and sexual humor and innuendo, a brief drug reference, age-inappropriate suggestive dance moves involving young children, scattered crass expressions

title: Big Night
synopsis: Two Italian immigrants in the 1950s -- a perfectionist chef (Tony Shalhoub) and his more pragmatic brother (Stanley Tucci) -- risk bankruptcy by putting on a lavish banquet for celebrity Louis Prima in hopes the resulting publicity will attract business to their restaurant. As co-directed by Tucci and Campbell Scott, the bittersweet story is a warm-hearted celebration of family, community and the fragile relationships that give life its flavor. Implied sexual affair, sporadic rough language and minimal profanity

title: Big Red
synopsis: French-Canadian orphan (Gilles Payant) taken in by a wealthy dog breeder (Walter Pidgeon) devotes himself to raising a beautiful Irish setter who later saves his master's life. Director Norman Tokar's rather flat Disney production has plenty of picturesque scenery of the Quebec countryside and youngsters will fancy the boy-dog story

title: Big Shots
synopsis: Two fatherless youngsters -- a streetwise inner-city black and a naive suburban white -- help each other through a series of dangerous mishaps while trying to locate one boy's father and the other's watch. Director Robert Mandel unnecessarily emphasizes the boys' recklessly anti-social antics, foul street talk and some violence in what disappointingly amounts to no more than a conventional chase picture

title: Big Time
synopsis: Theatrical concert film directed in contrived, artsy fashion by Chris Blum showcasing the eccentric talents of singer-songwriter-poet Tom Waits. Best for Waits' fans. Some vulgar comic banter

title: Big Top Pee-wee
synopsis: Zany child-man Pee-wee Herman (Paul Reubens) matures as a gentleman farmer with a talking pig, a hotdog tree, a school teacher fiancee (Penelope Ann Miller) and his first screen kiss with her rival, a trapeze artist (Valeria Golino). Directed by Randal Kleiser, its colorful circus activity and gorgeous production values are marred by hackneyed images implying Pee-wee's sexual blossoming and loss of virginity

title: Big Town After Dark
synopsis: Low-budget programmer directed by William C. Thomas and based on a radio series about a crusading newspaper editor (Philip Reed) and the woman (Hillary Brooke) who's his top reporter as they put aside their bickering long enough to expose a local gambling ring. Stylized violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Big Trouble
synopsis: A zany pair of con artists (Peter Falk and Beverly D'Angelo) force a broker (Alan Arkin) to become their unwilling accomplice in an insurance fraud until a detective (Charles Durning) nails the pair. Director Jobn Cassavetes elicits amiable performances in this witty but slight farce. Some rough language and brief nudity

title: Big Trouble
synopsis: Unfunny ensemble comedy involves, among others, a hit man (Dennis Farina), his target (Stanley Tucci), the wife (Rene Russo), a divorced dad (Tim Allen), a dumb ex-con (Tom Sizemore) and a cop (Janeane Garofalo) all chasing each other and culminating with a nuclear bomb allowed onto a commercial jet. Director Barry Sonnenfeld fails badly with witless characters both shrill and flat in scenarios contrived and clunky. Much profanity, some violence, brief sexual situations, rear nudity, double entendres and crass expressions

title: Big Trouble in Little China
synopsis: Kurt Russell reveals a comic flair for mock heroics in an action-fantasy about a 2000-year-old Chinese wizard who is determined to kidnap and marry the green-eyed girl friend of one of Russell's pals. John Carpenter directs this martial-arts frolic in a movie teeming with special effects. Much profanity and sadistic violence

title: Big Wednesday
synopsis: Three young surfer fanatics spend their time boozing, fighting and womanizing in director John Milius' vulgar glorification of the male bond, arrested in the adolescence of the beach-bum culture of the past, offering viewers little save scenes of nature's grandeur

title: Biker Boyz
synopsis: High-octane foray into the world of Southern California's underground motorcycle scene. Despite action-packed race sequences and a solid cast, director Reggie Rock Blythewood's contrived story about an aging street racer (Laurence Fishburne) and a brash contender (Derek Luke) gunning for his title, hits more than a few narrative speed bumps, never kicking into second gear. Brief violence, much peril, occasional sexist stereotypes and some crude expressions

title: Bikini Beach
synopsis: Sun-baked youth comedy in which the owner (Keenan Wynn) of a seaside retirement home tries to rid the area of boisterous surfers whose leader (Frankie Avalon) is more concerned that his girlfriend (Annette Funicello) is falling for a British pop singer (also Avalon). Directed by William Asher, the banal plot adds drag-racing to the formula mix of song, dance, surfing and brawling. Slapstick violence, sexual situations and much sexual innuendo

title: Bill and Coo
synopsis: Canaries and parakeets are the main performers in this live-action fantasy about a feathered utopia being saved from a marauding crow by a bird named Bill. Directed by Dean Riesner and narrated by producer Ken Murray, the cast features George Burton's Love Birds in anthropomorphic proceedings which may amuse youngsters, though others are more likely to find it little more than a curiosity piece. Mild menace

title: Bill & Ted's Bogus Journey
synopsis: In this moronic sequel to their 1989 clunker, the two young oafs (Keanu Reeves and Alex White) are murdered by robot look-alikes and, after sampling heaven and hell, force the Grim Reaper to return them to Earth to rescue their girlfriends. Peter Hewitt directs a lame fantasy whose lack of intelligence is no laughing matter. Some mock violence and minimal gutter talk

title: Bill & Ted's Excellent Adventure
synopsis: Two spacey teenagers (Keanu Reeves and Alex Winter) are saved from sure flunk-out with the help of a futuristic genie (George Carlin) whose magical phone booth enables them to nab some historic figures (Napolean, Sigmund Freud, Billy the Kid, etc.) as show 'n' tell for a crucial oral history project. Director Stephen Herek's cheesy putdown of modern adolescent sensibilities includes moronic depictions of education and parenting. Some gratuitous vulgar references laced with sexual innuendo

title: Billion Dollar Brain
synopsis: Filmed on location in Finland, the third in the British spy-with-horn-rimmed-glasses series starring Michael Caine as Harry Palmer goes gimmicky, humorless and even offensive with some graphic love-making. Almost nothing of the original Palmer character is recognizable but the glasses, as Caine stumbles stolid1y through acres of snow on a mission involving bio-warfare and a Texas millionaire's giant computer. Director Ken Russell's elaborate satire on obsessive anti-Communist types is clear enough, but that's about all that is in this brainless film. Violence and sexual scenes. O 1967

title: Billy Bathgate
synopsis: Sluggish 1930s gangster movie about a Bronx youth (Loren Dean) learning the ropes under his idol Dutch Schultz (Dustin Hoffman) while juggling a dangerous relationship with the mobster's seductive girlfriend (Nicole Kidman). Director Robert Benton's less-than-compelling guys-and-molls flick has more vapid valleys than high spots. Sporadic violence, a brief bedroom scene, momentary nudity, a homosexual reference and some rough language

title: Billy Budd
synopsis: Engrossing version of Herman Melville's story contrasting justice and the letter of the law when the seaman of the title (Terence Stamp) faces hanging aboard a British man-of-war in 1797 for striking an officer (Robert Ryan) who has falsely accused him of fomenting mutiny. Director Peter Ustinov (who also plays the vessel's vacillating captain) effectively evokes the twisted malevolence of the bullying master-at-arms who cannot abide the simple innocence of the stammering seaman. Stylized violence and moral dilemmas

title: Billy Elliot
synopsis: Stirring tale about a coal miner's young son (Jamie Bell) who rises above the tough macho culture that surrounds him to follow his dream of becoming a ballet dancer. Though debut director Stephen Daldry's coming-of-age story is by-the-numbers, effective character development, an engaging narrative and well-placed dance sequences create a pleasurable experience. Some homosexual innuendo and fleeting profanity with recurring rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Billy Jack
synopsis: Simple-minded story of the conflict between a redneck town and a school for runaway teenagers located on an Arizona Indian reservation where the title hero (Tom Laughlin who also directed) champions the area's oppressed Indians, Mexicans, blacks and school's youngsters by fighting violence with violence. Besides the violent proceedings are a rape, brief nudity and rough language

title: Billy Liar
synopsis: Satiric British tale in which a bright young clerk (Tom Courtenay) tries to make his drab ordinary life more bearable by inventing a fantasy world but this leads him to lies and deceptions that only complicate his life. Directed by John Schlesinger from Keith Waterhouse's novel, much of the humor comes from visualizing the lad's over-active imagination but these tend to be overlong and overdone. Comic violence and sexual situations

title: Billy Madison
synopsis: Dimwitted comedy in which a retiring billionaire (Darren McGavin) decides to leave control of his hotel empire to his loutish 27-year-old son (Adam Sandler) provided he graduates grades 1-12 in six months, or else it all goes to the billionaire's scheming assistant (Bradley Whitford). Director Tamra Davis' dismal attempt to fashion a vehicle for Sandler's limited comic talents never rises above dumb toilet jokes and moronic situations. Occasional sexual innuendo and alcohol abuse, brief violence played for laughs, some crude bathroom humor and an instance of rough language

title: Billy Rose's Jumbo
synopsis: Bright but overlong turn-of-the-century musical about a failing circus whose owner (Jimmy Durante) relies on his daughter (Doris Day) to keep things going but she falls for a helpful stranger (Stephen Boyd) who's out to get their prize elephant for a rival circus. Directed by Charles Waters, the soggy Day-Boyd romance is a distinct handicap but the comic byplay between Durante and Martha Raye as his longsuffering fiancee, the Rodgers and Hart musical numbers and the colorful circus acts offer something for everybody

title: Billy the Kid
synopsis: After switching sides in a range war between a conniving landgrabber (Gene Lockhart) and a straightarrow English rancher (Ian Hunter), the hard-bitten gunman of the title (Robert Taylor) becomes a peaceable cowboy until the Englishman's murder causes him to seek vengeance on the killers, despite the warnings of his boyhood friend (Brian Donlevy) who is now the marshal. Directed by David Miller, the Western action is colorful but flawed by a romanticized plot and Taylor's wooden performance. Frontier violence with some sense of its tragedy and pain

title: Billy the Kid vs. Dracula
synopsis: Director William Beaudine's low-budget attempt to graft the Western and horror movie strains results in a silly hybred that youngsters might possibly sit through but anyone of the age of reason will find beyond endurance

title: Billy Two Hats
synopsis: Two smalltime bank robbers (Gregory Peck and Desi Arnaz Jr.) are on the run from a racist, Indian-hating marshall (Jack Warden) and his deputy (David Huddleston). Directed by Ted Kotcheff, the two friends in crime become symbolic reference points for the death of the Old West with the passing of the buffalo and the advent of the railroad. One very violent sequence

title: Biloxi Blues
synopsis: Coming-of-age comedy adapted by Neil Simon from his autobiographical play about a New York would-be writer (Matthew Broderick) in a Mississippi boot camp at the close of World War II who is constantly in hot water with his brain-damaged sergeant (Christopher Walken) and some of his company's more macho men. Tight direction by Mike Nichols enhances Simon's perceptive reflections on the milestones and meatheads one is forced to confront in such close quarters during wartime. Much rough language and a sexual situation involving a prostitute

title: Bingo
synopsis: Contrived fantasy in which an amazingly clever little mutt saves a half-drowned boy (Robert J. Steinmiller, Jr.), then tails him cross country to become part of his family. Director Matthew Robbins' scrappy comedy is no more than a series of cutesy dog tricks in search of a movie. Some slapstick violence, menace to a child and frequent toilet humor

title: Bio-Dome
synopsis: Mindless comedy directed by Jason Bloom in which the obnoxious antics of untalented comics Pauly Shore and Stephen Baldwin wreck an expensive environmental habitat, then put it back together for a bogus feel-good ending. Comic crudities, sexist humor, sophomoric sexual references, coarse expressions and an instance of rough language

title: Birch Interval
synopsis: Charming and affecting movie produced by Robert B. Radnitz, about a pre-teen New York City girl (Susan McClung) who in 1947 confronts the emerging complexities of adult life when she is sent to stay with her grandfather (Eddie Albert) and uncle (Rip Torn) in a tranquil Amish community in Pennsylvania. Director Delbert Mann treats the marital problems of the uncle delicately while depicting in close detail Amish country life. Episodic and a little slow-moving, the movie nonetheless is a refreshing view of family matters that parents and their teenagers might benefit from discussing

title: Bird
synopsis: Biography of troubled jazz saxophonist Charlie "Bird" Parker (Forest Whitaker), who died in 1955 at age 34 after ravaging his body with years of heroin and alcohol addiction, follows his last years on the road and with his common-law wife (Diane Venora). Directed by Clint Eastwood, there's not a false note in this expressionistic, moody look at the jazz subculture of the 1950s. Realistic view of the consequences of Parker's addiction, a graphic suicide attempt, sexual promiscuity and an offhanded acceptance of out-of-wedlock pregnancy

title: Birdman of Alcatraz
synopsis: Fact-based prison saga of Robert Stroud (Burt Lancaster) whose death sentence for killing a guard in Leavenworth prison was commuted in 1916 to life in solitary confinement which he spent becoming an eminent authority on birds before transfer in 1942 to Alcatraz where he was deprived of anything to do with birds until transferred out in 1959. In showing Stroud's transformation from a vicious criminal to a dedicated ornithologist over 43 years in solitary, director John Frankenheimer probes the man's rehabilitation in relation to his mother (Thelma Ritter), wife (Betty Field), a sympathetic guard (Neville Brand) and a punitive prison warden (Karl Malden). Stylized violence and justice questions

title: Bird of Paradise
synopsis: Exotic romance on a remote South Sea island where an American sailor (Joel McCrea) falls in love with the king's daughter (Delores Del Rio) who's destined to be sacrificed to save her people from the island's angry volcano. Directed by King Vidor, the couple's romantic idyll is picturesque but as emotionally hollow as the phony melodramatics of the contrived story. Sexual situations and fleeting nudity

title: Bird on a Wire
synopsis: Classy slam-bang chase thriller in which a former government witness (Mel Gibson) and his one-time sweetheart (Goldie Hawn) are on the run from vengeful drug dealers (David Carradine and Bill Duke) as well as assorted police agencies. Director John Badham maintains an air of romantic comedy throughout the desperate proceedings, mixing the screwball characterizations of the couple with some spectacular action stunts, notably in a jungle zoo. Much menace and demolition-derby violence, a bedroom scene and some sexually suggestive dialogue

title: Birds Do It
synopsis: Harmless comedy directed by Andrew Marton in which Tab Hunter plays a secret agent trying to get from Soupy Sales, who he mistakes for a scientist, a secret ionizer that enables people to fly. Innocuous story which young children may find amusing

title: Birds Do It, Bees Do It
synopsis: Documentary focuses on how living things make other living things from the world of microbes to that of human beings. Very graphic in depicting the mating of birds, bees, and just about everything else. For adults and older teens

title: Birds in Peru
synopsis: French melodrama written and directed by Romain Gary in which a nymphomaniac (Jean Seberg) spends the night with four lovers on a Peruvian beach where each year flocks of birds come to die. Graphic treatment of sex scenes

title: Birdy
synopsis: Vietnam vet (Matthew Modine) left virtually catatonic by a battlefield wound dreams about his past and his boyhood desire to be a bird while a friend (Nicolas Cage) tries to bring him back to reality in the grim confines of an Army hospital. Director Alan Parker gets lost in sketchy characterizations and great globs of tedious monologues that seem pointless, especially recollections of youthful sexual encounters with graphic nudity

title: Birth
synopsis: Unconventional love story about a New York widow (Nicole Kidman) who comes to believe that her dead husband has been reincarnated as a 10-year-old boy (Cameron Bright), much to the dismay of her new fiance (Danny Huston). Director Jonathan Glazer has crafted an elegiac meditation on love, loss and mortality, buttressed by exceptional performances from the assembled ensemble, hauntingly evocative visuals and a disquietingly plaintive score, but the film contains several controversial scenes between Kidman and Bright -- including one in a bathtub -- that many viewers may find extremely troubling. Suggestive situations involving an adult and a minor, and an explicit sexual encounter between adults with nudity

title: Birthday Girl
synopsis: Adequate thriller about a lonely British bank teller (Ben Chaplin) who orders a Russian mail-order bride (Nicole Kidman) over the Internet, but is in for a surprise when the bride's fiendish cousins (Mathieu Kassovitz and Vincent Cassel) show up on her birthday. Initial quirkiness abruptly gives way to menace in director Jez Butterworth's film, which becomes increasingly formulaic before ending on a falsely upbeat note that allows the protagonists to escape the consequences of their criminal actions. Some subtitles. A few sexual situations with fleeting nudity, brief violence and minimal profanity and rough language

title: Bite the Bullet
synopsis: Muddled Western directed by Richard Brooks dealing with a 700-mile horse race shortly after the turn of the century. Its hero (Gene Hackman) gives a coolly reasoned critique of the cruel stupidity of the race and its win-at-all-costs spirit but not long afterwards, he himself joins in and submits his horse to the brutal ordeal. Stylized violence

title: Bitter Creek
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Thomas Carr in which a Texas cowboy (Wild Bill Elliott) arrives in the title Montana town to search out the killer of his rancher brother, then saves a woman (Beverly Garland) from marrying the villain responsible. Numerous shootouts and justice questions

title: Bitter Moon
synopsis: Repelling shipboard melodrama in which a paralysed American (Peter Coyote) and his sultry French wife (Emanuelle Seigner) lure a conventional British couple (Hugh Grant and Kristin Scott-Thomas) into joining them in deadly sadomasochistic sex games. Director Roman Polanski's darkly perverse look at extreme sexual obsession thoroughly dehumanizes its characters and despairs of any normal loving relationships. Brief graphic violence, numerous bedroom scenes with nudity and much rough language

title: Bitter Sugar
synopsis: The pro-Castro beliefs of a young Cuban student (Rene Lavan) are shaken to the core when he discovers his fiancee (Mayte Vilan) has taken to prostitution to survive and his rebellious brother (Larry Villanueva) has deliberately injected himself with AIDS-tainted blood in protest against the repressive regime. Director Leon Ichaso's melodramatic political tract blends doomed romance and family crises into a scathing portrait of a beleaguered island whose economy caters to tourists at the expense of its own people. Subtitles. Brief spurts of violence, a discreet sexual encounter and some rough language

title: Bittersweet Love
synopsis: A couple (Meredith Baxter Birney and Scott Hylands) fall in love but only after getting married and her pregnancy is well advanced do they discover that they have the same father (Robert Lansing). Director David Miller takes a glossy soap-opera approach to the theme of incest in a cloying and tedious film that raises issues about abortion and divorce without much insight. A- III (PG) 1977

title: Bitter Victory
synopsis: Muddled World War II picture of a British commando raid behind German lines in the North African desert led by a gutless professional soldier (Curt Jurgens) and a cynical civilian recruit (Richard Burton) familiar with the area. Director Nicholas Ray focuses on the officers' prior conflict over a woman (Ruth Roman), then over Jurgens' fear Burton will report him for an act of cowardice in the raid, with tragic results that underline war's inhumanity. Combat violence, including the killing of a wounded soldier

title: B.J.Lang Presents
synopsis: B.J. Lang Presents -- Only Mickey Rooney's hardiest fans may be able to endure a picture in which their idol rants and rages mercilessly as a movie director driven insane by fantasies of former glory. Director Yabo Yablonsky revels in flashy camera tricks, strobe lighting and sound effects in a pointless exercise in horror

title: Black and White
synopsis: Because of an explicit menage � trois, brief nudity and violence, intermittent recreational drug abuse, and recurring rough language,

title: Black and White in Color
synopsis: Extremely subtle and probing French comedy set in West Africa at the start of World War I, it tells the story of what happens when a small French settlement decides to attack a nearby German post. In looking at the human factors that lead to war, director Jean-Jacques Annaud avoids sentiment entirely, spares no one in this cast of characters and delivers an outrageous challenging and extremely funny anti-war film. Wartime violence and brief, incidental nudity

title: Black Angel
synopsis: Dark crime story from the Cornell Woolrich novel in which the wife (June Vincent) of a man convicted of murder joins forces with the victim's estranged husband (Dan Duryea) to find the real killer whom they suspect is a shady nightclub owner (Peter Lorre). Director Roy William Neill goes for atmosphere rather than action, with plodding results and an unsurprising twist ending. More menace than violence and an alcoholic central character

title: The Black Balloon
synopsis: Moving Australian film about a teenager (Rhys Wakefield) settling into a new neighborhood with his pregnant mother (Toni Collette) and army officer father (Erik Thomson) and caring for his autistic brother (Luke Ward) with the help of a sympathetic girlfriend (Gemma Ward). First-time feature director Elissa Down's semiautobiographical story is well-acted and conveys a strong pro-family message and compassionate view of the disabled. Some crass expressions, brief domestic violence, a few expletives including a single use of profanity and of the F-word, mild sexual elements with innuendo and a birth control reference, and some scatological elements; acceptable for older teens

title: Black Bart
synopsis: Fanciful Western in which the title's smooth outlaw (Dan Duryea) throws in with a crooked banker (John McIntire) to rob Wells Fargo gold shipments, then is forced to take in a shifty ex-partner (Jeffrey Lynn) who gums up the works and both end in a hail of bullets. Directed by George Sherman, the tale is embroidered with a visit by Lola Montez (Yvonne De Carlo) who falls for the dashing outlaw in a brief interlude adding a wistful note to the otherwise tough-minded proceedings. Stylized violence and mild romance

title: Blackbeard's Ghost
synopsis: Disney comedy in which some elderly New England ladies are saved from eviction through the invisible machinations of pirate Blackbeard (Peter Ustinov) who helps the inept local school track team win a meet and lots of money. Director Robert Stevenson's simple-minded slapstick and special effects provide laughs, but the team's coach (Dean Jones), after being thoroughly ridiculed for objecting to Blackbeard's tactics, gets into the act himself. Children may get the impression that cheating is O.K. if you can't win honest1y

title: Blackbeard the Pirate
synopsis: With grimaces, guffaws and rolling eyes, Robert Newton hams his way through the title role as the 17th-century scourge of the Spanish Main in a muddled story involving buried treasure, a dead pirate's daughter (Linda Darnell), a captive surgeon (Keith Andes) and Blackbeard's arch-enemy, Sir Henry Morgan (Torin Thatcher). Director Raoul Walsh plays the disjointed script mainly for laughs, relying on the occasional swashbuckling action to hold interest. It doesn't. Much stylized violence, considerable brutality and some sexual innuendo

title: Black Beauty
synopsis: British version of the classic tale of a boy (Mark Lester) and his horse comes to the screen under the direction of James Hill. It is lovely to look at but is unfortunately flawed by stilted scripting and wooden performances which, one hopes, will not spoil it for younger audiences

title: Black Beauty
synopsis: Richly pictorial version of Anna Sewell's 1877 children's classic in which the spirited horse of the title recounts (voice of Alan Cumming) his life under good masters (Sean Bean, Jim Carter and David Thewlis) and bad (Eleanor Bron, Peter Cook and Alun Armstrong) until, old and broken, he's given a home by the former stable boy who had grown to love him. Scripted by director Caroline Thompson, the movie captures the beauty of the animal world and the picturesque nature of the Victorian era, though the woes seem to outweigh the joys in this episodic chronicle teaching youngsters the responsibility of caring for animals. Scenes of the horse's mistreatment and endangerment by sickness, fire and flood may distress the very young

title: Black Belt Jones
synopsis: Black kung-fu movie with Jim Kelly and Gloria Hendry fighting to keep their school of self-defense in the Watts area of L.A. from falling into the hands of the Mafia. Director Robert Clouse goes in for a lot of clowning and sight gags leading to a sudsy climax in a car-wash gone berserk, an approach which makes the movie fairly tolerable despite its deep-down mindlessness and brutality

title: Black Book
synopsis: Glossy, well-acted World War II saga set in Holland about a Jewish singer (a compelling Carice van Houten) who, after her family is gunned down by the Nazis, joins the Dutch Resistance who ask her to romance and spy on the local Gestapo chief (Sebastian Koch) with whom she then genuinely falls in love. Director Paul Verhoeven has made essentially an old-style Hollywood espionage story but with a good deal of present-day permissiveness, and though the film has some serious intent, it registers mainly as escapist entertainment, even if inspired by true events. In Dutch, German, English and Hebrew, with subtitles. Strong rough and crude language and profanity, sexual encounters, full male and female nudity, innuendo, wartime violence including shootings and beatings, vigilante justice

title: Black Caesar
synopsis: Black crime movie in which Fred Williamson takes over a Harlem-South Bronx crime syndicate by acquiring pay-off ledgers incriminating New York politicians. Written, produced and directed by Larry Cohen, it trades exclusively in ruthless violence, sex and street language

title: Black Christmas
synopsis: Nasty Canadian horror movie directed by Bob Clark follows the exploits of a maniac who terrorizes a sorority house over the Christmas holidays. The incoherent script attempts to bridge the gap between the gruesome murder of coeds with obscene telephone calls that are disgusting

title: Black Dragons
synopsis: Wartime clunker directed by William Nigh concerns an Axis spy ring using a Nazi plastic surgeon (Bela Lugosi) to transform Japanese espionage agents into bogus American businessmen. Period anti-Japanese stereotypes

title: Black Eye
synopsis: Black private eye Fred Williamson is searching Los Angeles for an antique cane stuffed with heroin and for a missing girl who is reportedly being held in a commune of Jesus freaks. Jack Arnold's direction is fast-paced, but muddying the waters is a sub-plot involving a bisexual relationship between our hero, his girl friend (Teresa Graves) and her girl friend (Rosemary Forsyth). Routine violence

title: Black Girl
synopsis: Uneven drama of a black American family, portrays the tensions and conflicts, the misplaced love and bitterness, that stem from a kind of collective familial sense of inferiority. Directed by Ossie Davis, the movie seems largely aimed against its own members, particularly those who attempt to break the mold and escape the family's self-imposed cultural limitations

title: Black Gold
synopsis: An Indian rancher (Anthony Quinn) and his wife (Katherine DeMille) adopt an orphaned Chinese boy, become millionaires when oil is discovered on their land and enter a horse they've raised from a colt in the Kentucky Derby. Despite a rambling narrative with predictable plot complications, director Phil Karlson holds it together by focusing on the rancher's mare and her colt, abetted by warm performances from the human principals. An animal story with heart and some social consciousness

title: Black Gunn
synopsis: Black crime movie features Jim Brown as a posh nightclub owner drawn into a confrontation with the mob when they kill his younger brother for knocking off a numbers parlor. Directed by Robert Hartford-Davis, the story provides ample opportunities for violence of every description, some casual sex and coarse language

title: Black Hand
synopsis: After his father is murdered by the criminal society of the title, a young Italian American (Gene Kelly) determines to drive the gang from his turn-of-the-century New York neighborhood, getting help along the way from a dedicated city detective (J. Carrol Naish). Directed by Richard Thorpe, the formula story is told with vigor, plenty of period atmosphere and strong performances from the two leads. Stylized violence and much menace

title: Black Hawk Down
synopsis: Intense war drama about the 1993 United States raid on Somalia in which an elite American squad of soldiers (including Josh Hartnett, Ewan McGregor and Sam Shepard) is sent to abduct two warlords, but the mission goes woefully awry. The relentless, raw combat scenes in director Ridley Scott's true story are strikingly realistic, evoking a deep revulsion for war, but it comes at the expense of character development with the soldiers barely distinguishable from one another. Fierce, graphic war violence, several gory images and intermittent rough language with some profanity

title: Black Hills
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Ray Taylor in which a singing cowboy (Eddie Dean) and his sidekick (Roscoe Ates) stop a gang of crooks from taking over a ranch they alone know is rich in gold. Stylized violence

title: Blackjack Ketchum, Desperado
synopsis: Formula Western directed by Earl Bellamy in which a retired gunman (Howard Duff) pins on a badge to rid his valley of a local badman (Victor Jory) and his gang. Frontier violence

title: Black Jesus
synopsis: Awkward Italian production about a black African revolutionary (Woody Strode) who tries to maintain a peaceful course in the midst of leading an energetic revolution. Director Valerio Zurlini's narrative suffers from interminable, badly-dubbed dialogue, an agonizingly slow pace and a mechanical plot devise drawing rather simplistic and superficial parallels to the passion of Jesus. Some brutal violence

title: Black Like Me
synopsis: Uneven dramatization of John Howard Griffin's book about a Texas journalist (James Whitmore) who uses chemicals to darken his white skin, then passes for black to write a series of articles on "what it's like to be a Negro in the South." Director Carl Lerner leans on melodrama in depicting the writer's experiences, especially with various forms of white oppression and sexual racial myths but, despite its flaws, the picture was deemed strong fare in its day and serves as a reminder of how far we've come since then. Racial injustices, menacing situations, sexual references and coarse language

title: Blackmail
synopsis: Intriguing crime thriller in which the girlfriend (Anny Ondra) of a jaunty Scotland Yard detective (John Longden) kills an overly amorous artist (Cyril Ritchard), then is blackmailed by a petty crook (Donald Calthrop) whom the police mistakenly link to the crime and chase into the British Museum for a smashing climax. Directed by Alfred Hitchcock, the first British talkie may seem fairly creaky today, though the unsentimental treatment of the characters and the visual flair of the action scenes still hold interest. Stylized violence, a sexual situation and much tension

title: Black Mama
synopsis: A black woman raising her child in a Los Angeles ghetto is gradually radicalized by her experiences in just trying to survive. Although director Haile Gerima uses an impressionistic style, alternating between objective reality and subjective fantasy, its message is clear that the dehumanizing conditions of poverty and racism are intolerable

title: Black Mama, White Mama
synopsis: Philippine story of two women (Pam Grier and Margaret Markhov) who escape from a prison camp handcuffed together. Director Eddie Romero, no stranger to this kind of thing, features lots of whipping, stripping and degradation

title: Black Mask
synopsis: Routine Hong Kong martial-arts flick in which a genetically enhanced human (Jet Li) joins forces with a cop (Lau Ching Wan) to battle an elite group of supersoldiers intent on world domination. Directed by Daniel Lee, the threadbare story is merely an excuse to demonstrate myriad ways to maim and slaughter opponents. Excessive violence with gore, a rough-sex encounter, much rough language and an instance of profanity

title: Black Moon
synopsis: French surrealistic fantasy in which a young girl (Cathryn Harrison), fleeing a bloody civil war between men and women combatants, finds refuge in an isolated country house in which live a bedridden old woman (Therese Gieshe), a brother and sister (Joe Dallesandro and Alexandra Stewart) and a band of children. While battles rage round the estate, the girl is preoccupied with her bizarre surroundings which include a talking unicorn, crying flowers, and an enormous rat named Humphrey. Director Louis Malle is less concerned with the theme of innocence than with the modern preoccupation with death and sex. Mature themes

title: Black Moon Rising
synopsis: Seething raw sexuality and toughness, Tommy Lee Jones slithers through this implausible drama from director Harley Cokliss as a thief hired to obtain some tax court evidence. He hides his findings in a prototype racing car which is then stolen. The casual sex, brutal beatings and hair-raising stunts he puts up with to retrieve the data are not worth the viewing time

title: Black Narcissus
synopsis: Engrossing British adaptation of Rumer Godden's novel about the difficulties confronting an Anglican community of nuns (headed by Deborah Kerr) in a remote area of northern India where a native student (Jean Simmons) and an English administrator (David Farrar) upset their spiritual peace. Directed by Michael Powell and Emeric Pressburger, the community's religious mission in an exotic alien environment is handled with sensitivity, with most of the dramatic conflict stemming from the human foibles of the characters. Sexual situations and innuendo

title: Black on White
synopsis: Exploitation movie directed by Tinto Brass about the sex fantasies of a white woman pursued through London by a black man. Much nudity and graphic sex

title: Black Orpheus
synopsis: Vibrant intercultural feast updating the Greek myth to Rio de Janeiro where trolley driver Orpheus (Breno Mello) accidentally kills his beloved Eurydice (Marpessa Dawn) while trying to protect her from a stalker costumed as Death and, after a religious cult fails to revive her, he sets out with her body for burial until another fatal accident intervenes. Directed by Marcel Camus, the appealing leads are supported by a spirited cast who play out the mythic tragedy amidst the gaiety of Rio's Carnival with its colorful parades of dancing bands, backed by a haunting music score and spectacular views of Rio's picturesque locales. Subtitles. Stylized violence, sexual situations and innuendo

title: Black Patch
synopsis: Western misfire about a one-eyed marshal (George Montgomery) and a mixed-up widow (Diane Brewster) in a one-street town whose nasty boss (Sebastian Cabot) sends an alienated youngster (Tom Pittman) to kill the lawman. Writer-director Allen H. Miner never gets beyond the bogus motivations of one-dimensional characters in a convoluted but pointless plot. Heavy-handed stylized violence, sordid atmosphere and sexual inferences

title: Black Peter
synopsis: Czechoslovakian movie of a 17-year-old boy (Ladislav Jakim) growing up with all the anguished diffidence of adolescence in his dealings with parents and friends, his first job and his shy curiosity about girls. The first feature of director Milos Forman, made in 1964, it is a string of small gems crystallizing the final, wonderfully hazy days of uncommitted youth the world over

title: Black Peter
synopsis: Black Rain -- Glossy crime thriller celebrates the hard-edged cynicism of an American cop (Michael Douglas) who bludgeons his way through Japan in pursuit of an escaped criminal but ultimately is taught a lesson in honor by a self-effacing Japanese detective (Ken Takakura). Director Ridley Scott devotes his energies to endless chase scenes in an exotic foreign culture but is unable to work up any sympathy for the foul-mouthed, small-minded anti-hero portrayed by Douglas. Much excessive violence and incessant rough language

title: Black Robe
synopsis: After arriving in 17th-century New France, a Jesuit missionary (Lothaire Bluteau), guided by Algonquins, endures both a dangerous journey through the Canadian wilderness and an Iroquois attack to reach a distant Huron mission. Towards the end director Bruce Beresford manages to put the cultural clash between the humorless priest and the unbelieving Native-Americans in a moving spiritual context. Some brief but graphic violence and several shadowy sexual encounters with momentary nudity. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Black Rodeo
synopsis: Documentary about a contingent of black cowboys who bring a Wild West show to New York which serves to make people aware of the black contribution to the heritage of the American West. Directed by Jeff Kanew and narrated by Woody Strode, the result has some expert slow-motion photography and a soundtrack full of pop songs commenting ironically on the action in the arena

title: Black Samson
synopsis: Familiar story of black versus white in the struggle over inner-city turf, though the hero this time is a rather whimsical ghetto bar owner (Rockne Tarkington) who wants to keep his Los Angeles neighborhood drug-and-crime-free. Directed by Charles Bail, it wastes its potential by taking the predictable, brutal path leading to the inevitable bloodbath climax. Violence, rough language and numerous glimpses of the casual nudity in a topless bar

title: Black Sheep
synopsis: Inept comedy in which a well-meaning oaf (Chris Farley) nearly ruins his brother's chances to be elected governor, despite the efforts of a campaign staffer (David Spade) to keep the bumbler out of the public eye. A limp script and tepid physical comedy make director Penelope Spheeris' movie look more like an extended TV sitcom. Some slapstick violence, brief substance abuse, minor sexual innuendo, intermittent profanity and an instance of rough language

title: Black Snake Moan
synopsis: Extremely lurid, but ultimately redemptive, melodrama set in rural Tennessee about an aging blues singer (Samuel L. Jackson) who nurses a badly beaten nymphomaniac (Christina Ricci) back to health, and gets her to overcome her drug and sexual addictions, conquering his own inner demons in the process. Writer-director Craig Brewer pulls out the stops with an intentionally florid style, while the impressive performances of the leads -- as well as those of John Cothran as a benevolent preacher, S. Epatha Merkerson as an empathetic friend and Justin Timberlake as an emotionally damaged soldier who loves the young woman -- overcome the more outrageous plot elements, The high quotient of sex, violence and foul language -- which walks the finest of lines between morally objectionable and dramatically valid -- will seriously limit the film's appeal to audiences, Catholic and otherwise. Pervasive rough and crude language and profanity, racial epithets, strong sexuality including a couple of graphic encounters without nudity, premarital situations, upper female nudity elsewhere, violence and drug use

title: Black Starlet
synopsis: A serious topic, the exploitation of women, is handled ineptly and is not above incorporating a bit of what it pretends to decry

title: Black Sunday
synopsis: Palestinian extremist group plots to commit a terrorist atrocity at the Super Bowl while Israeli agent (Robert Shaw) tries frantically to avert it. Director John Frankenheimer's thriller is exciting enough but it unfortunately exploits some larger issues for the sake of entertainment. Some intense violence

title: Black Swan
synopsis: At the behest of her ballet company's artistic director (Vincent Cassel), a shy, inhibited dancer (Natalie Portman) rebels against her overprotective mother (Barbara Hershey) and seeks to imitate a passionate rival (Mila Kunis) by embracing a hedonistic lifestyle in order to fit her for the major role in Tchaikovsky's "Swan Lake," an onstage embodiment of guile and sensuality. Though Portman turns in a striking performance, director Darren Aronofsky's nightmarish, morally muddled drama plays on the extremes of sexual repression and debauched license and, whether read as insisting on the necessity of indiscriminate experience or as a cautionary tale, presents its heroine's experimentation with voyeuristic excess. Strong sexual content, including graphic lesbian and nonmarital heterosexual activity, as well as masturbation, drug use, a few instances of profanity, much rough and some crude language and numerous sexual references

title: Black Thursday
synopsis: On July 16, 1942, Paris police rounded up 13,000 Jews for deportation to Nazi concentration camps, from which all but 30 failed to return after the war. Director Michael Mitrani has reconstructed in semi-documentary style that terrible Black Thursday, using as his script the account of a young student who attempted to save those he could

title: Black Widow
synopsis: Debra Winger and Theresa Russell square off in a confrontation of cunning and guile when a Justice Department data analyst (Winger) tries to put an end to the series of seductions and murders of wealthy men by a mysterious and deadly woman (Russell). The double-bluff conclusion is as flawed as the sensually toned melodrama which has a brief instance of nudity and a decidedly adult treatment by director Bob Rafelson

title: Blacula
synopsis: African prince (William Marshall), seeking Dracula's signature on a petition abolishing slavery is instead bitten by the Transylvanian count, entombed in the cellar and liberated two centuries later by a pair of swishy interior decorators whereupon he begins teething on the town. Director Bill Crain provides a few genuine thrills on the horror side but, for the most part, the movie tries to have some simple fun with its horror premise

title: Blade
synopsis: Ultraviolent horror fantasy adapted from a comic strip about the battle between a city full of vampires (led by Stephen Dorff) and three armed-to-the-teeth humans (Wesley Snipes, Kris Kristofferson, N'Bushe Wright) bent on exterminating them. Director Stephen Norrington's gory, stomach-turning tale of hatred and murder wallows in constant scenes of brutality, butchery and bloodshed. Excessive violence, much profanity and constant rough language

title: Blade II
synopsis: Gory and boring horror-action sequel about a half-human, half-vampire warrior (Wesley Snipes), out to save the human race from blood-suckers, who is compelled to team up with the very creatures he hates to fight off an uber-vampire that kills mortals and monsters alike. Based on the Marvel Comics character, director Guillermo del Toro's tedious bloodfest follows a ridiculous story line where pretentious characters engage in brutal acts while spluttering absurd dialogue. Nonstop violence, excessively brutal and gruesome imagery and recurring rough language with some profanity

title: Blade Runner
synopsis: Science fiction thriller about a private eye (Harrison Ford) whose job is to hunt down and dispose of out-of-control humanoids. His work gets complicated when he falls in love with an advanced prototype who doesn't know she's not human (Sean Young). Director Ridley Scott's moody atmosphere and futuristic sets evoke an ecologically fouled and spiritually demoralized metropolis, but the disappointing script meanders listlessly. Excessive violence and partial nudity

title: Blades of Glory
synopsis: Fitfully amusing buddy comedy about rival skating champions -- a macho ladies' man (Will Ferrell) and a former child prodigy (Jon Heder) -- banned from the world championships after fighting on the ice, who reluctantly become a team when they learn it's the only way they'll be allowed back to compete, while a jealous brother-sister act (Will Arnett and Amy Poehler) attempt to sabotage the duo. Will Speck and Josh Gordon direct the sophomoric proceedings capably, the skating stunts are well handled, the leads are well paired, and there are apt satirical barbs at the skating industry. The pervasive low humor and vulgarity preclude the younger viewers who would most appreciate the humor, even as predictable affirmations of friendship and good sportsmanship eventually prevail. Crude language, crass expressions, mild profanity, a couple of brief nongraphic sexual encounters, innuendo, comic violence and mayhem, including a decapitation, brief comic suggestion of incest and drug use

title: Blade: Trinity
synopsis: Violent and vacuous fantasy action sequel, based on the titular Marvel Comics' character, a brooding half-mortal, half-vampire slayer (Wesley Snipes), who in this third go-round must join forces with a team of vampire-hunters (Jessica Biel and Ryan Reynolds) and battle an army of bloodsuckers (led by Parker Posey) bent on resurrecting the granddaddy of all undead, Dracula (Dominic Purcell) -- here re-imagined as an ancient Sumerian demon -- to spawn a vampiric master race. Directed by David S. Goyer, this bloodfest dishes out the same tedious gore and cheesy dialogue as the first two installments, and hopefully this one will drive a stake through any future films in this forgettable franchise. Excessive violence, much profanity and rough language

title: Blame It on Rio
synopsis: Businessman (Michael Caine) yields to the seduction of the daughter of his best friend (Joseph Bologna) who is depending upon him to help trap the daughter's lover. Director Stanley Donen's misguided celebration of male sexual fantasies tries to milk humor from a promiscuous situation and its use of partial nudity

title: Blame It on the Bellboy
synopsis: Screwball complications abound when a bellboy (Bronson Pinchot) in a Venice hotel misdelivers messages intended for a meek English worker (Dudley Moore), a philandering Mayor (Richard Griffiths) and a hitman (Bryan Brown). Writer-director Mark Herman concocts a lively, fast-paced comedy whose silly antics make for innocuous escapist entertainment. Some stylized violence and ethnic stereotyping played for laughs, a fleeting bedroom scene and many double entendres

title: Blank Check
synopsis: After taking a blank check from a gangster (Miguel Ferrer) in return for his damaged bike, a resourceful 11-year-old (Brian Bonsall) fills it out to the tune of one million dollars, successfully cashes it and goes on a spending spree, with three buffoonish crooks and an undercover FBI agent (Karen Duffy) in hot pursuit. Director Rupert Wainwright's silly comedy looks like a commercial for oversize toys and computer gadgets, with plotting and characterizations tossed in as an afterthought. Some violence played for laughs and a child's greedy excesses

title: Blankman
synopsis: Dopey comedy in which a wacky inventor (Damon Wayans) turns into a masked crimefighter whose ineptitudes require frequent rescues by an exasperated older brother (David Alan Grier). Director Mike Binder's dumb, cartoon-like comedy downplays plot and characterization in favor of goofy gadgets and gizmos that enable the would-be superhero to defeat villains and get the girl (Robin Givens). Comic violence, vulgar humor and occasional profanities

title: Blaze
synopsis: Failed dramatization of the love affair between a striptease performer (Lolita Davidovitch) and Louisiana Governor Earl Long (Paul Newman). Written and directed by Ron Shelton, the movie offers little insight into the characters or the era of the 1950s. Sympathetic treatment of adultery and several extended sex scenes

title: Blaze of Noon
synopsis: The dangers of early aviation plague barnstorming brothers (William Holden, Sonny Tuffs, Sterling Hayden and Johnny Sands) when they turn airmail pilots in the 1920s, with tragic results. Director John Farrow gets suitable tension from the flight sequences but can't hold interest in the earthbound romance between Holden and nurse Anne Baxter. Restrained treatment of air calamities

title: Blazing Saddles
synopsis: Vulgar and broad satire on Westerns has not so much a plot as a series of wacky situations and comic stereotypes, including black sheriff Cleavon Little, rail baron Harvey Korman and bar room singer Madeline Kahn. Directed by Mel Brooks, it offers some funny moments but the overall tone of its humor runs solidly toward the coarse, the smutty and the scatological

title: Bless the Beasts and Children
synopsis: Failed melodrama about a handful of adolescent misfits at an Arizona dude ranch who decide to free a herd of captive buffalo. Directed by Stanley Kramer, the obvious aim was to deal with the mistreatment of wildlife and youth but the result is a heavy-handed succession of mini-soap operas that wrench the emotions without compensating insights. Killing of animals and some harsh language

title: Bless the Child
synopsis: Absorbing thriller in which a psychiatric nurse (Kim Basinger) suspects that her six-year-old niece (Holliston Coleman) is being targeted by members of a Satanic sect planning to misuse the child's extraordinary powers to fulfill a Biblical prophecy. As directed by Chuck Russell, the familiar good versus evil premise has a convincingly spooky edge with a refreshing emphasis on the selflessness of love, but is marred by a cheesy ending. Recurring violence with some gore, occult theme, brief drug use and minimal rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Blind Date
synopsis: Bruce Willis goes on a blind date with Kim Basinger but forgets to keep her away from alcohol. The consequences are traditional slapstick sequences of reckless abandon and funny sight gags in this romance from director Blake Edwards. Jealous ex-boy friend John Larroquette supplies most of the genuine humor, but Basinger shows some flare for the zany. Brief nudity, casual treatment of alcoholism and some rough language are adult fare

title: Blindfold
synopsis: Complicated espionage story directed by Philip Dunne starts in Central Park where a psychiatrist (Rock Hudson) is approached by a G-man and asked to treat a top government scientist but when he does, enemy agents and the patient's sister (Claudia Cardinale) get on his trail. Moderately entertaining with some mildly romantic interludes

title: Blind Fury
synopsis: Blind Vietnam vet (Rutger Hauer) uses a samurai sword to skewer a farflung network of gun-happy criminals. Director Philip Noyce's inept rip-off of the Japanese "Zatoichi" series about a blind swordsman in medieval Japan proves a bloody exercise in the ludicrous with blade pitted against bullets in a modern American setting. Excessive violence and occasional rough language

title: Blindman
synopsis: Italian Western in which the hobo hero of the title (Tony Anthony) is robbed of the 50 women he is delivering to a Texas mining camp by two hairy bandits (Ringo Starr and Lloyd Batista) who have other plans for them. Time and again senseless slaughter follows sadistic torture as blindman and badmen match wits under Ferdinando Baldi's routine direction. Most objectionable is its presentation of women as objects to be abused

title: Blink
synopsis: When a blind musician (Madeleine Stowe) whose sight is gradually returning after an operation glimpses a serial killer, she becomes involved in a steamy affair with the detective (Aidan Quinn) assigned to find the killer before she becomes his next victim. Director Michael Apted's formula cop-and-endangered-female thriller moves slickly along to an unconvincing climax amid a persistent atmosphere of casual promiscuity. Some violence, several bedroom scenes, recurring nudity and much rough language

title: Bliss
synopsis: An advertising executive (Barry Otto) dreams that he has died and gone to hell but, when shocked out of this nightmare, he tries to change his alreedy hellish and misdirected life. Directed by Ray Lawrence, this Australian import has difficulty finding a balance between social commentary and sex farce. Nudity and some profanity

title: Bliss
synopsis: Ludicrous exploitation piece in which a husband (Craig Sheffer) goes to a quirky sex therapist (Terence Stamp) to learn how to satisfy his frigid wife (Sheryl Lee) whose problems stem from having been sexually abused as a child. Writer-director Lance Young's dramatically unconvincing story is a dreary mix of Western psychobabble, Eastern sexual lore and simulated sex scenes which, of course, are the whole point of this bogus enterprise. Exploitative sex scenes and sexually graphic dialogue

title: Blithe Spirit
synopsis: Noel Coward's witty comedy about spectral complications after the late wife (Constance Cummings) of a happily remarried writer (Rex Harrison) returns from "the other side" during a seance conducted by an enthusiastic but inept medium (Margaret Rutherford). Director David Lean has fun with the unexpected twists in the silly proceedings and their wry jabs at middle-class pretensions, but does best with Rutherford's zesty performance as a good-natured eccentric. Marital misunderstandings, satiric treatment of infidelity and supernatural hokum

title: Blonde Crazy
synopsis: Snappy period piece about a calculating hotel bellhop (James Cagney) and the blonde chambermaid (Joan Blondell) whom he ditches along the way for supposedly easy money with a veteran swindler (Louis Calhern), then wins back years later after her embezzling husband (Ray Milland) double-crosses him. Director Roy Del Ruth presents the rise and downfall of a wise guy in zestful, if dated, fashion, but it's Cagney's performance as a likeable heel that's worth watching. Benign view of crime and sexual innuendo

title: Blonde Dynamite
synopsis: Formula slapstick comedy directed by William Beaudine in which the Bowery Boys (Leo Gorcey, Huntz Hall and the rest) open a male escort service, then help a pal (Gabriel Dell) out of a jam involving a gang of bank robbers. Comic violence and sexual innuendo

title: Blondie Brings Up Baby
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed by Frank Strayer in which Baby Dumpling (Larry Simms) starts school, then becomes the object of a frantic search when he wanders off looking his pooch, Daisy, but both are found with a rich man's daughter who has discarded her wheelchair to play with them

title: Blondie for Victory
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed by Frank R. Strayer in which Dagwood (Arthur Lake) pretends to join the Army in an attempt to make Blondie (Penny Singleton) realize that looking after the Bumstead household is more important to the war effort than working as a volunteer in the homefront activities of the Housewives of America (a fictional patriotic organization)

title: Blondie Goes Latin
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed by Frank R. Strayer exports the Bumstead's domestic complications south of the border on a cruise ship where Dagwood (Arthur Lake) tries his best as the drummer in a conga band and Blondie (Penny Singleton) gets to warble a few songs

title: Blondie Goes to College
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed by Frank R. Strayer in which the Bumsteads put Baby Dumpling in a military school while they go back to college enrolled as singles, with Blondie (Penny Singleton) being courted by the campus hero (Larry Parks) and Dagwood (Arthur Lake) befriended by a rich co-ed (Janet Blair) until he loses the big crew boat race

title: Blondie Has Servant Trouble
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed Frank R. Strayer has some fun with the Bumsteads (Arthur Lake, Penny Singleton and Larry Sims) moving into a reputed haunted house with strange servants (Arthur Hohl and Ester Dale) and even stranger goings-on, none which have anything to do with spooks. Mild racial stereotyping

title: Blondie Hits the Jackpot
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed by Edward Bernds has Dagwood (Arthur Lake) send son Alexander (Larry Simms) to a birthday party for a client's spoiled daughter who manages to get Dagwood fired, but he becomes a hero when he spots structural flaws on a construction job just before Blondie (Penny Singleton) wins a radio contest

title: Blondie in Society
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed by Frank R. Strayer has Dagwood (Arthur Lake) getting into trouble with his boss (Jonathan Hale), a dog owner (William Frawley) and a kennel manager (Arthur Kennedy) over a pedigreed Great Dane which Blondie (Penny Singleton) turns into a prizewinner at a dog show

title: Blondie in the Dough
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed by Abby Berlin starts with Dagwood (Arthur Lake) getting fired and Blondie (Penny Singleton) turning breadwinner by selling home-made cookies which are tasty enough for a baking manufacturer (Hugh Herbert) to buy the recipe

title: Blondie Knows Best
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed by Abby Berlin with predictable complications as Mr. Dithers (Jonathan Hale) tries to get a construction contract from a man (Jerome Cowan) he's insulted by switching places with Dagwood (Arthur Lake) who's on the run from a near-sighted process server (Shemp Howard)

title: Blondie Meets the Boss
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed by Frank R. Strayer in which Blondie (Penny Singleton) goes to work for Mr. Dithers (Jonathan Hale) while Dagwood (Arthur Lake) does the household chores until Blondie mistakenly suspects he's involved with another woman

title: Blondie of the Follies
synopsis: Creaky period romance in which a showgirl (Billie Dove) helps her working-class pal (Marion Davies) succeed in the chorus, then fears losing her rich boyfriend (Robert Montgomery) to the newcomer and causes her to break a leg in an "accident," with predictable results. Director Edmund Goulding doesn't let the contrived rags-to-riches plot get in the way of the colorful backstage action and parties with philandering millionaires, until the hokey moral ending. Implicit affairs and sexual innuendo

title: Blondie on a Budget
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed by Frank Strayer in which Dagwood (Arthur Lake) is visited by an old sweetheart (Rita Hayworth) whom Blondie (Penny Singleton) suspects is up to no good

title: Blondie Plays Cupid
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed by Frank R. Strayer has Blondie (Penny Singleton) take the family on a visit to her aunt in the country where they meet a nice young couple (Glenn Ford and Luana Walters), then help them elope

title: Blondie's Anniversary
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed by Abby Berlin in which Dagwood (Arthur Lake) celebrates his 15th wedding anniversary by getting fired after Blondie (Penny Singleton) thinks he's given her a $300 watch belonging to his boss (Jerome Cowen), then compounds the mix-up by buying a cheap replacement with money borrowed from a loan shark (William Frawley)

title: Blondie's Big Deal
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed by Edward Bernds in which Dagwood (Arthur Lake) invents a fire-repellent paint, then burns down the summer home of his boss (Jerome Cowen) after rivals for a construction contract switch the paint, leaving it up to Blondie (Penny Singleton) to save the day by getting proof of the theft

title: Blondie's Big Moment
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed by Abby Berlin in which Dagwood is fired by his new boss (Jerome Cowan) after letting his son's classmates visit his office, but he gets his job back when one of the youngsters proves to be the key to buying a tract of land needed by the firm

title: Blondie's Blessed Event
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed by Frank R. Strayer has Dagwood (Arthur Lake) off at a convention in Chicago when Blondie (Penny Singleton) gives birth to their second child, Cookie, then he returns home with a penniless playwright (Hans Conried) who settles in with them until Blondie lays down the law. Comic treatment of pregnancy and birth

title: Blondie's Hero
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed by Edward Bernds has Dagwood (Arthur Lake) join the Army reserve and on his first weekend of training is visited by Blondie (Penny Singleton) who spends the day chasing Daisy around the firing range and taking a hair-raising spin in a tank before the Bumsteads return home to find it has been sold by a swindler (William Frawley)

title: Blondie's Holiday
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed by Abby Berlin in which Dagwood (Arthur Lake) plays the big shot by insisting on paying the tab for Blondie's high school reunion dinner, then gets fired because of a stodgy banker (Grant Mitchell) and winds up in jail after trying to raise the money at a betting parlor

title: Blondie's Lucky Day
