Stylized violence and justice questions

title: Caged Men Plus One Woman
synopsis: The various manifestations of homosexuality in prison provide sensational subject matter for Edward J. Forsyth's movie about an incredibly ignorant victim (Ross Stephanson) who just as incredibly wreaks bloody revenge on his tormentors inside as well as on the girl friend outside who had betrayed him

title: Cahill, U.S. Marshal
synopsis: John Wayne stars in a contemporary Western about an overworked peace officer whose two neglected sons are involved in a robbery he is investigating. When Wayne decides to make his pursuit of the criminals into an object lesson for his sons, director Andrew V. McLaglen's movie seems to condone the use of guns in the hands of the young. Worse than the violence is what youngsters may make of the story's muddled morality

title: Cain and Mabel
synopsis: Flimsy romantic comedy in which a prizefighter (Clark Gable) and a showgirl (Marion Davies) decide to quit their careers and get married, despite efforts by their agents to break up the planned nuptials. Director Lloyd Bacon shortchanges the comedy for elaborate production numbers that pad out the contrived plot. Romantic complications and stylized fight scenes

title: Cal
synopsis: Set against the background of the present conflict in Northern Ireland is the story of a doomed love affair between the widow (Helen Mirren) of a slain policeman and a shy, sensitive young man (John Lynch) who was inadvertently involved in her husband's death. Director Pat O'Connor has fashioned a nuanced morality tale of human beings caught in a divided world but there is some use of nudity and a fairly graphic love scene

title: Calamity Jane
synopsis: Agreeable Western musical in which the title character (Doris Day) forsakes her rough cowboy ways to learn feminine demeanor from a novice showgirl (Allyn McLerie), then sets her bonnet on an Army officer (Phil Carey) but winds up instead in the arms of her friendly rival, Wild Bill Hickok (Howard Keel). Director David Butler paces the romance with plenty of comic action and a bushel of tunes, notably "Deadwood Stage," "A Woman's Touch" and "Secret Love."

title: Calamity Jane and Sam Bass
synopsis: Routine Western in which Hoosier tenderfoot Bass (Howard Duff) comes to Texas, meets a good woman (Dorothy Hart) and plans to buy a ranch, then gets swindled in a horse race and becomes an outlaw with the help of Calamity (Yvonne De Carlo). Directed by George Sherman, the story of a good man who goes bad starts well, then bogs down in formula proceedings. Stylized violence and muddled justice questions

title: Calendar Girl
synopsis: Formula musical directed by Allan Dwan mixes romance with comedy as the daughter (Jane Frazee) of a New York fireman (Victor McLaglen) is torn between a poor songwriter (William Marshall) and the playboy artist who makes her the Calendar Girl of 1901. Unpretentious fun for those in the mood

title: Calendar Girl
synopsis: Witless comedy about three 18-year-olds (Jason Priestley, Gabriel Olds, Jerry O'Connell) driving to Hollywood in the summer of 1962 hoping to have a date with movie goddess Marilyn Monroe. Director John Whitesell panders to adolescent male fantasies in a boringly inept, woefully unfunny movie. A sexist view of women, some nudity, fleeting bedroom scene, brief violence and minimal rough language

title: Calendar Girls
synopsis: Amusing comedy in which a group of prim-and-proper English matrons (including Helen Mirren and Julie Walters) pose naked for a calendar to raise money for medical research after the husband of one of the women dies of leukemia. Although the anemic premise is stretched to its limit, Nigel Cole's mostly forgettable film does have a few entertaining moments and likable characters, with a healthy dose of the maxim to accept one's body throughout the natural aging process. A flash of nudity with several scenes suggestive of nudity, a few instances of crass language and brief drug content

title: California
synopsis: Disappointing Western in which an Army deserter (Ray Milland), a willful adventuress (Barbara Stanwyck) and a feisty farmer (Barry Fitzgerald) arrive in Monterey during the 1849 gold rush, then get involved in a scheme to seize the territory led by a lunatic sea captain (George Coulouris). Director John Farrow makes the most of the colorful situations but the disjointed story flounders in a tangle of personal ambitions that end badly. Stylized violence and muddled motivations

title: California Conquest
synopsis: While a group of California dons in the 1830s seek to end Mexican rule by joining the U.S., a Russian plot to annex the territory is foiled when one of them (Cornel Wilde) gets help from an American sharpshooter (Teresa Wright) in stopping the head conspirator (John Dehner) and his bandit chief (Alfonso Bedoya). Directed by Lew Landers, the muddled plot has some furious battles and a lot of empty heroics but none of it is very convincing. Frontier violence

title: California Passage
synopsis: Formula Western directed by Joseph Kane in which a honest gambler (Forrest Tucker) has a showdown with his dishonest partner (Jim Davis) whom he suspects is behind a series of gold robberies and, even worse, has evil designs on a good woman (Adele Mora). Frontier violence

title: California Split
synopsis: Magazine writer (George Segal) befriends a small-time hustler (Elliott Gould) whose wild antics intrigue but this leads him deeper and deeper into the gambling underworld of dumb call girls, tough losers, impatient bookies, sleazy bars, and hole-in-the-wall games. Director Robert Altman's off-beat comedy ends with Segal's realization that he, unlike Gould, doesn't really care about winning, suggesting that with this knowledge, his obsession to gamble has been exorcised. Questionable attitude toward casual sex

title: California Suite
synopsis: Screen version of Neil Simon's play integrates the original's four one-acters into a single narrative with a good cast, including Jane Fonda, Alan Alda, Maggie Smith and Michael Caine. Although not a completely successful adaptation from the stage, director Herbert Ross's movie is good fun for the most part and sometimes unexpectedly moving. Mature themes

title: Caligula
synopsis: The R-rated version of the X-rated original is no less a dreary exploitation movie awash with sex and violence. Directed by Tinto Brass, it brings not a trace of insight to the historical figures of the Roman Empire or to this period of history

title: Callas Forever
synopsis: Fictitious but true-in-spirit story of self-obsessed opera diva Maria Callas' lonely last years in Paris after she had lost her voice, wherein a gay former manager (Jeremy Irons) persuades her she can have a second career by making film versions of her most notable operas while lip-syncing to her old recordings. French accent notwithstanding, Fanny Ardant succeeds to a remarkable degree in capturing the Greek-American soprano's temperament and physical appearance, while director Franco Zeffirelli -- a close friend and colleague of Callas -- directs with the expected authority and brings special flair to the "Carmen" sequences, though the specialized subject matter will be of most interest to Callas fans and opera buffs. A few instances of rough and crude language and a couple of mild sexual situations

title: Call Her Savage
synopsis: Melodramatic claptrap about a Texas millionaire's headstrong daughter (Clara Bow) who marries a bounder, loses her infant son in a tragic fire, falls for a man who rejects her, then learns from her dying mother her father was an Indian. Directed by John Francis Dillon, the florid storyline is as dizzy as the ending, with unflattering results for silent screen star Bow. Some sexual situations and much sexual innuendo

title: Calling Wild Bill Elliott
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Spencer Bennet in which a cowboy (Bill Elliott) and his sidekick (George "Gabby" Hayes) get the goods on a corrupt governor. Stylized violence

title: Call Me
synopsis: Basically soft porn all fancied up with an inane plot about hoods on the trail of a woman (Patricia Charbonneau) who inadvertently witnesses a murder and who enjoys trading phone turn-ons with an obscene caller. Director Sollace Mitchell offers an abundance of gory violence, much profanity and rough language of an explicit sexual nature and a total insensitivity to the offensiveness of real obscene phone calls

title: Call Me Bwana
synopsis: Generally funny but mindless Bob Hope comedy about a space scientist (Hope) who is easily distracted by the feminine wiles of a foreign agent (Anita Ekberg) from his mission of retrieving a space capsule that has landed in the African jungle. Directed by Gordon Douglas, it consists of typical Hope one-liners and double-entendres

title: Call Me Mister
synopsis: Musical romance set in post-war Japan where an infantry sergeant (Dan Dailey) tries to win back his estranged wife (Betty Grable) by going AWOL to take part in a musical revue she's staging for the troops. Directed by Lloyd Bacon, the thin plot is stitched together with period songs, weak dance numbers and dated comic skits of service life. Romantic complications and sexual innuendo

title: Call Northside 777
synopsis: Fact-based story in which a Chicago newspaper reporter (James Stewart) digs into the case of a convicted cop-killer (Richard Conte) and finds evidence of his innocence. Filming on Chicago locations, director Henry Hathaway gets the flavor of the city's ethnic neighborhoods and sustains the credibility of the reporter's dogged leg work in following leads until the convict's ultimate release in a downbeat ending emphasizing his lost years in prison and ruined marriage. Sobering justice theme

title: Call of the Forest
synopsis: Routine outdoor adventure directed by John F. Link in which a young boy (Charlie Hughes) gentles a wild black stallion, then is saved by the horse from the villain (Robert Lowery) who killed his father (Ken Curtis). Enjoyable wildlife scenes, especially those with a bear cub and a family of skunks

title: Call of the Prairie
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Howard Bretherton in which Hopalong Cassidy (William Boyd) tangles with a gang of badmen (notably Alan Bridge and George Hayes) who have framed a Bar 20 rider (Jimmy Ellison) for a hold-up. Frontier violence

title: Call of the Rockies
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Lesley Selander in which a cowboy (Smiley Burnett) masquerades as a French engineer to help some miners save their claims from a crooked contractor (Harry Woods), though he gets some help from another cowboy (Sonny "Sunset" Carson) along the way. Frontier violence

title: Call of the Yukon
synopsis: Adventure programmer in which a hunter (Richard Arlen) rescues a writer (Beverly Roberts) from a deserted Eskimo village besieged by ravenous wolves and wild dogs. Directed by B. Reaves Eason, the rugged location photography gives credibility to the couple's dangerous trek through the icy wastes before turning to romance in the melodramatic ending. Romantic complications and menacing situations

title: Camelot
synopsis: Director Josh Logan's screen version of the Broadway musical on the King Arthur legend offers the charming Lerner and Loewe score and lyrics, luxurious fantasy settings and a grand cast (Richard Harris, Vanessa Redgrave, Franco Nero and David Hemmings). Emphasizing the human implications of the legend rather than its romanticism, the musical shows that power is not strength and that compassion is not weakness. Never has adultery carried so high a price -- the downfall of Camelot

title: Camila
synopsis: The daughter of a wealthy family in 19th-century Argentina falls in love with a Jesuit priest in this tragic love story with modern political implications. In this Argentinian production, director Maria Luisa Bemberg deals with difficult historical matters as well as the sacrilegious character of the 1ove affair. Powerful but problematic, with one brief but excessively graphic love scene

title: Camille
synopsis: Cast includes Greta Garbo, and Robert Taylor. Directed by George Cukor. A-III (nr) 1936

title: Camille 2000
synopsis: In updating Dumas' tubercular heroine, director Radley Metzger has changed the flighty and unstable Camille into an amoral jet-setter who fills her days with hip slang, liquor, drugs and sex. The plot is no more than a flimsy structure for scenes replete with nudity, joyless orgies and 20th-century guilt-ridden anxieties

title: Camille Claudel
synopsis: Bittersweet story of French sculptress (Isabelle Adjani) whose troubled life (1864-1943) as a trailblazer in a male-dominated field ended in a mental asylum after an emotionally devastating May-December affair with her mentor, sculptor Auguste Rodin (Gerard Depardieu). Directed by Bruno Nuytten, it's powerfully acted but confusing as to chronology and characters. Unmarried sexual liaisons and nude models in studio scenes

title: Camouflage
synopsis: Meditative essay on the corruptive nature of any bureaucratic system and the destructive games peop1e play in seeming to conform to what is expected of them. The Polish production's success lies in an intelligent script and perceptive direction by Krzysztof Zanussi. Several sexua1 situations

title: Camp Nowhere
synopsis: Nitwit comedy in which a bunch of adolescents (led by Jonathan Jackson and Andrew Keegan) hire an unemployed drama teacher (Christopher Lloyd) to impersonate a responsible camp owner in order to dupe their parents into sending them to an abandoned campsite for a summer of unsupervised fun. There's nothing funny about director Jonathan Prince's lame attempt at innocent hi-jinks, with the youngsters eventually confessing all to parents who appear to be less bright than their inventive offspring. Mild sexual innuendo and a few profanities

title: Canadian Bacon
synopsis: Limp political satire in which a U.S. president (Alan Alda) determines to boost his popularity by uniting the country against a foreign enemy, but all his aides (Rip Torn and Kevin Pollak) can come up with is a media campaign charging a Canadian plot to take over North America. Writer-director Michael Moore's comic premise is too thin to support a feature, though his scattershot spoof of political, military and business leaders yield some smiles and a few laughs. Some profanity and crude language

title: Can-Can
synopsis: Colorful if disappointing adaptation of composer Cole Porter�s Broadway hit, set in 1896 Paris where a young magistrate (Louis Jourdan) falls for a cafe owner (Shirley MacLaine) who agrees to marry him until her attorney boyfriend (Frank Sinatra) figures out how to win her back. Directed by Walter Lang, the film has a thin plot, stereotyped characters, stage-bound production numbers, and only so-so performances of the show�s hits like "I Love Paris" and �C�est Magnifique� and interpolations of other Porter evergreens like "Just One of Those Things" and �Let�s Do It (Let�s Fall in Love).� Innuendo and a benign view of unmarried relationships. Once again, Fox has done an outstanding job of packaging, and the generous two-disc set includes substantive featurettes on the making of the show and subsequent film, Porter himself, and Broadway book writer Abe Burrows, plus a copious stills gallery. There�s a nice option to listen to music scoring sans dialogue and voices. Knowledgeable commentators include musical historians Robert Kimball and Miles Krueger and film historian Scott McIsaac who don�t gloss over the film�s shortcomings. A-III (nr) (20th Century Fox Home Entertainment) 1960

title: Cancel My Reservations
synopsis: Bob Hope plays the henpecked half of a husband-wife TV talk-show team who falls victim to a gang of murderous Arizona land-grabbers. Wife Eva Marie Saint races to Hope's rescue and ultimately learns that a woman's place is in the home. Director Paul Bogart strikes out with tired gags and dated topical humor

title: Candidate for a Killing
synopsis: Itinerant sportsman (John Richardson) is used by a businessman (Fernando Rey) in a scheme to extort gold from the Congo and becomes a target for assassins as he races around Europe accompanied by a questionable ally (Anita Ekberg). Director Sidney Pink pads his picture with silly conversations and irrelevant interludes, many of them of a teasing sexual nature

title: Candleshoe
synopsis: Jodie Foster plays a Los Angeles juvenile delinquent whom confidence man Leo McKern uses to hoodwink wealthy Helen Hayes into thinking is her long-lost granddaughter. Standard Disney fare from director Norman Tokar that tends towards slapstick rather than anything more gentle and satisfying

title: Candy
synopsis: Screen version of the Southern-Hoffenberg novel about the travail of a threatened virgin (Ewa Aulin) is no more than a gross sex farce that reinforces all the behavioral patterns it supposedly satirizes. Christian Marquand directs a big-name cast with a sensitivity only for the vulgar remark, the suggestive sequence and the explicitly titillating

title: Candyman
synopsis: Idiotic horror story relates the problems of a skeptical graduate student (Virginia Madsen) after she conjures up a 19th-century hook-handed ghoul (Tony Todd) who goes on a murderous rampage. Writer-director Bernard Rose's badly scripted tale of brutal mayhem in a gang-ravaged Chicago ghetto slowly drowns in its own gore. Excessive violence, continuing deadly menace to an infant and occasional nudity

title: Candyman: Farewell to the Flesh
synopsis: Repellent slasher sequel in which a horribly mutilated black man (Tony Todd), killed for impregnating his white lover in the 1890s, returns to life in present-day New Orleans, wreaking murderous revenge on the family whose ancestors betrayed him and anyone else who gets in his way. Employing strictly one-dimensional characters, director Bill Condon exploits violence and hateful racial animosities in a dreary series of grisly killings. Excessive violence and gore, fleeting shots of simulated sex and occasional profanities and rough language

title: Can Hieronymus Merkin Ever Forget Mercy Humppe and Find True Happiness??
synopsis: Can Hieronymus Merkin Ever Forget Mercy Humppe and Find True Happiness? -- Writer-director Anthony Newley plays a star entertainer making a movie about his career and using fragmented and surrealistic techniques both for the film and the film-within-the-film. Apparently an attempt to make a statement about the artist's quest for identity, the result is an incoherent failure, floundering in excesses of explicit sexual adventures and moral relativism that leave viewers with little to share other than the character's lack of self-knowledge and the director's lack of ability to control his material

title: Cannibal Attack
synopsis: Jungle adventure directed by Lee Sholem in which an American denizen of the African wilderness (Johnny Weissmuller) saves a cobalt mine from being exploited by foreign agents whose cannibal allies surprise their victims by dressing up as crocodiles. Hokey violence

title: Cannibal Girls
synopsis: The title refers to three beauties in a remote Canadian town whose diner serves beefy portions of male travelers whom they have seduced and slaughtered. Director Ivan Reitman's low-budget movie romps in sex and gore to no entertaining end

title: Cannonball Run II
synopsis: Sequel with Burt Reynolds and friends is a sort of cinematic People magazine-on-whee1s. Stuntman Hal Needham's direction of this demolition-derby comedy is geared toward dangerous auto stunts and off-color jokes

title: Cannon for Cordoba
synopsis: George Peppard, leader of a undisciplined platoon in Pershing's Mexican expedition, is responsible for the loss of cannon and supplies, and subsequently must re-capture or destroy them. Directed by Paul Wendkos, the far-fetched adventure is seasoned with torture and violence, in ludicrous fashion

title: Can't Buy Me Love
synopsis: Suburban nerd (Patrick Dempsey) pays a popular cheerleader (Amanda Peterson) to date him for a month in director Steve Rash's comic exploration of teen mores which condemns in-crowd conformism and self-deception but passively conveys a permissive attitude toward adolescent sex

title: Can't Help Singing
synopsis: Flat musical romance in which a U.S. Senator's daughter (Deanna Durbin) runs off to join an Army officer posted to California during the Gold Rush of 1849, then falls in love with a gambler (Robert Paige) she meets along the way. Directed by Frank Ryan with music by Jerome Kern and lyrics by E.Y Harburg, the weak script makes disappointing use of the colorful era, the comic relief (Akim Tamiroff and Leonid Kinsky) fizzles and the songs are mostly forgettable. Frontier violence and romantic complications

title: Can't Stop the Music
synopsis: This vehicle for The Village People, a disco singing group, is a high-energy, low-IQ, 100-percent synthetic product. Directed by Nancy Walker, the silly comedy about the music publishing and recording business is marked by sexual situations and jokes as well as a homosexual sheen coloring most of the production numbers

title: Canyon Passage
synopsis: Tangled Western in which a rugged individualist (Dana Andrews) pioneers a delivery service in 1856 Oregon, though distracted by a woman (Susan Hayward) engaged to a crooked banker (Brian Donlevy) and an Indian uprising incited by the banker's lustful henchman (Ward Bond). Directed by Jacques Tourneur, the contrived plot gains interest from the wilderness setting and colorful characters, including Hoagy Carmichael as a frontier minstrel. Stylized violence, including an off-screen rape

title: Canyon River
synopsis: On a cattle drive from Oregon to Wyoming, a rancher (George Montgomery) hires ex-outlaws (led by Alan Hale, Jr.) to get the herd past rustlers in cahoots with his best friend (Peter Graves). Standard outdoor shoot-'em-up directed by Harmon Jones. Stylized violence

title: Cape Fear
synopsis: Stomach-churning suspense thriller in which a vengeful ex-convict (Robert Mitchum) sets out to brutalize the wife (Polly Bergen) of the lawyer (Gregory Peck) he blames for his imprisonment. Director J. Lee Thompson's picture of an ordinary decent citizen pitted against a cunning sadistic criminal builds the tension to the breaking point on a boat in a lonely North Carolina bayou. Well-crafted exercise in terror, not for the nervous or faint-of-heart

title: Cape Fear
synopsis: Violent remake of the 1962 thriller has a Bible-spouting psychopath (Robert De Niro) imprisoned for viciously violating a woman returning to terrorize his former lawyer (Nick Nolte) and to rape the man's wife and teenage daughter (Jessica Lange and Juliette Lewis). Director Martin Scorsese loses the atmospheric terror of the original in favor of graphic brutality and a relentlessly ugly vision of the law as powerless to protect the innocent. Excessive violence, perverse sexual innuendo, adult endorsement of teen drug abuse and minimal rough language

title: Capitalism: A Love Story
synopsis: Hard-hitting but at times overly simplistic documentary in which filmmaker Michael Moore highlights numerous dysfunctional aspects of the capitalist system in the U.S. and their negative effects on working people, who are thrown into unemployment or have their homes seized in foreclosure, ultimately calling for an economic revolution that would bring democracy to the workplace. Though Moore interviews two Catholic priests and Auxiliary Bishop emeritus Thomas Gumbleton of Detroit, who are unanimous in condemning capitalism as inherently sinful, this is not the teaching of the full magisterium, which instead recognizes both the efficiencies of the free market system and its need to be prudently regulated, while upholding the human dignity of workers, particularly their right to unionize. At least three uses of the F-word, a couple of crude terms

title: Capone
synopsis: The rise of Al Capone (Ben Gazzara) from Brooklyn street mug to Chicago's top mobster is depicted with excessive resort to violence and sexual displays. Directed by Steve Carver, the movie is a sleazy, slapdash effort

title: Capote
synopsis: Gripping chronicle of writer Truman Capote (a superb Philip Seymour Hoffman) getting the inspiration to write his acclaimed "nonfiction novel," "In Cold Blood," after a Kansas farm family is brutally murdered, and his probing interviews with the townspeople and the killers, which walk a fine line between calculation and compassion. Director Bennett Miller's sobering film masterfully recreates the early 1960s as Capote travels back and forth from the superficial New York social scene to the bleak aura of death row at Leavenworth, with fine performances by Catherine Keener, Clifton Collins Jr., Chris Cooper and Amy Ryan. Brief violent images, an implied homosexual relationship, scattered profanity and rough language, crude expressions, a vulgar anecdote, sexual reference, and a hanging

title: Caprice
synopsis: Spy spoof misfires badly as an undercover agent (Doris Day) for a cosmetics firm tries to steal a water repellant hairspray from a rival company, then falls for a quirky double agent (Richard Harris) and winds up solving the murder of her Interpol father years before. Directed by Frank Tashlin, the slapdash proceedings don't make much sense and the treatment swings erratically from slapstick to suspense with tiresome results. Stylized violence, menacing situtions and sexual innuendo

title: Capricious Summer
synopsis: In this Czechoslovakian production set in a small country village between the world wars, three aging friends make fools of themselves over a young woman in a traveling circus and, by summer's end, they realize that their courting days are over. Director Jiri Menzel captures the elegaic mood of period and character with a tolerance of human foibles. Adult situations

title: Capricorn One
synopsis: Three astronauts are persuaded by a NASA official (Hal Holbrook) to fake a landing on Mars to save the threatened space program but a hot-shot reporter (Elliott Gould) eventually saves the day. Director Peter Hyams has come up with a solid if unspectacular entertainment with some clever twists

title: Captain Apache
synopsis: Poor Western about an Indian scout for the U.S. Cavalry who becomes the unwilling victim of a plot to fake an uprising that will see the Indians cruelly exiled to uninhabitable territory. Director Alexander Singer's message of brotherhood is as subtle as his battle sequences. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Captain Blood
synopsis: Swashbuckling adventure begins in 1685 England as an Irish doctor (Errol Flynn) is unjustly arrested with a band of rebels against King James II, then condemned to slavery in Jamaica under a brutal commander (Lionel Atwill) until the plucky doctor organizes their escape by sea to become pirates. Directed by Michael Curtiz, the lively proceedings include well-staged sea battles, the doctor's romance with the commander's niece (Olivia de Havilland) after rescuing her from a French buccaneer (Basil Rathbone) and justice for the rebels from the new English monarch, William of Orange. Assorted period violence

title: Captain Blood, Fugitive
synopsis: (see: " Captain Pirate ")

title: Captain Carey, U.S.A.
synopsis: Former OSS officer (Alan Ladd) returns to northern Italy after World War II to search out the traitor who betrayed his underground unit to the Gestapo. Director Mitchell Leisen makes the foreign locales more interesting than the captain's murky, slow-paced quest to avenge his dead comrades. Stylized violence

title: Captain Corelli's Mandolin
synopsis: Visually alluring World War II drama set during the Italian occupation of Greece in which an Italian officer (Nicolas Cage) falls in love with a Grecian beauty (Penelope Cruz), forcing him to decide between allegiance and love. Aside from its majestic presentation, director John Madden's mildly engaging romance strikes too many false notes to have real emotional resonance. Several rather graphic battle scenes, a sexual encounter, some nudity and fleeting rough language

title: Captain from Castile
synopsis: Plodding historical adventure begins in 1518 Spain with a don's son (Tyrone Power) escaping arrest by a corrupt agent of the Inquisition (John Sutton) to flee to the New World where he joins Cortez (Cesar Romero) in his expedition into Mexico, with dramatically hollow results. Directed by Henry King, the long hand of the Inquisition is the real villain here, though there's a muddled romantic subplot featuring Jean Peters and some colorful encounters with Aztec emissaries before the picture ends as Cortez sets off to conquer Montezuma's capital. Stylized violence and an implicit sexual relationship

title: Captain Horatio Hornblower
synopsis: Fanciful sea yarn with C.S. Forester's title character (Gregory Peck) commanding a British man-of-war battling the Spanish allies of Napoleon off the Central American coast, then the French fleet in their home waters, escaping capture to return home a hero, with the Duke of Wellington's sister (Virginia Mayo) as his prize. Director Raoul Walsh packs in a fair amount of colorful action and some humor but the far-fetched plot is meandering at best. Stylized sea battles and romantic complications

title: Captain January
synopsis: Formula sudser with loveable orphan Shirley Temple cared for by lighthouse keeper Guy Kibbee until the loss of his job forces him to seek out the child's rich relatives. Director David Butler covers the bases with occasional song-and-dance numbers, some playful humor and a capable supporting cast (Slim Summerville, Buddy Ebsen and Jane Darwell). Easy-going, unpretentious family fare

title: Captain John Smith and Pocahontas
synopsis: Dull low-budget programmer directed by Lew Landers plods through the story of how Smith (Anthony Dexter) and Jamestown are saved by the daughter (Jody Lawrance) of Algonquian Chief Powhatan (Douglass Dumbrille). Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Captain Kidd
synopsis: Tepid swashbuckler directed by Rowland V. Lee is set in 1699 when the title pirate (a subdued Charles Laughton except for his unkempt hair) bamboozles William III into sending him to escort a British treasure ship from India, making easy plunder for his henchman (John Carradine, Gilbert Roland and Sheldon Leonard), until confronted by the son (Randolph Scott) of one of their previous victims. Stylized violence

title: Captain Kronos: Vampire Hunter
synopsis: Classy British horror import in which the itinerant Kronos (Horst Janson) is called to a rid a village of a vampire who has been putting the bite on local maidens which he accomplishes with his able hunchback assistant (John Cater). Director Brian Clemens maintains the proper chilling atmosphere for hair-raising encounters with the hooded fiend who comes to a grisly end. Stylized violence and sexual implications

title: Captain Lightfoot
synopsis: Colorful but artificial blather about the rebel hero of the title (miscast Rock Hudson) whose adventures in 1815 Ireland consist mainly of falling in and out of the hands of British dragoons and local traitors. Directed by Douglas Sirk, the color comes mainly from the costumes and the Irish locations, but the contrived story is hammy and the acting is wurst. Stylized violence and menace

title: Captain Nemo and the Underwater City
synopsis: Jules Verne's Nemo (Robert Ryan) rescues a group of landlubbers (Nanette Newman, Bill Fraser, Kenneth Connor and Chuck Connors) on condition that they not attempt an escape from his self-sufficient city 20,000 leagues under the sea. Directed by James Hill, the special effects, the underwater city and the dramatic complications are intriguing enough to engross a child's imagination in this generally pleasing utopian, anti-war fantasy

title: Captain Newman, M.D.
synopsis: World War II comedy-drama set in an Army Air Force psychiatric ward where the title's dedicated officer (Gregory Peck) labors to help deeply troubled patients, notably a suicidal colonel (Eddie Albert), a guilt-ridden survivor (Bobby Darin) and an autistic pilot (Robert Duvall). Directed by David Miller from Leo Rosten's novel, the result is an uneasy blend of serious psychological problems, the doctor's sarcastic wit and the zany antics of ward attendants Tony Curtis and Larry Storch. Stylized violence, menacing situations and sexual references

title: Captain Pirate
synopsis: Mediocre swashbuckler about a reformed pirate (Louis Hayward) who once again hoists the Jolly Roger in order to stop a Caribbean buccaneer using his name. Directed by Ralph Murphy, this sequel to "Captain Blood" (1935) meanders aimlessly in search of compelling adventure but only comes up with some colorful action scenes. Stylized violence

title: Captain Ron
synopsis: Inept comedy about a Chicago family (headed by Martin Short and Mary Kay Place) who take a Caribbean dream cruise on an inherited sailboat whose disreputable captain (Kurt Russell) involves them with guerrillas and pirates. Director Thom Eberhardt's waterlogged plot soon sinks under the weight of its contrived situations and leaden script. Brief shadowy nudity, some sexual innuendo, stylized violence and an instance of rough language

title: Captain Scarlett
synopsis: Humdrum swashbuckler directed by Thomas H. Carr in which the French hero of the title (Richard Greene) rights the wrongs done by villainous royalists back in power after Napoleon's defeat. Routine swordplay and romantic complications

title: Captains Courageous
synopsis: Spencer Tracy won an Oscar for his performance as Manuel, the simple Portuguese fisherman in Rudyard Kipling's story of a spoiled rich boy (Freddie Bartholomew) rescued at sea and turned into a good shipmate by the kind-hearted veteran sailor. Director Victor Fleming provides a gruff but appealing picture of life aboard the fishing boat backed by some memorable sea scenes and the unsentimental transformation of the youth's character under Manuel's manly yet compassionate influence. Youngsters may get teary-eyed at Manuel's death but all is emotionally resolved in the lad's homecoming

title: Captain Sinbad
synopsis: Silly Arabian Nights fantasy pits the title hero (Guy Williams) against a dastardly magician-ruler (Pedro Armendariz) who's abducted a lovely princess (Heidi Bruhl). Directed by Byron Haskin, the European co-production limps along with a weak storyline but some passable special effects. A few hideous creatures and grizzly fight scenes may scare the very young

title: Captains of the Clouds
synopsis: Happy-go-lucky but bored Yank aviator (James Cagney) joins the Royal Canadian Air Force before U.S. entry in World War II, rebels against military discipline, then comes through in heroic action against the Luftwaffe. Director Michael Curtiz's patriotic melodrama has plenty of human interest with a good cast (Alan Hale, Dennis Morgan, George Tobias as well as RCAF veterans). Stylized violence and a marriage in name only

title: Captive
synopsis: (see: " Two ")

title: Captive Girl
synopsis: Adventure programmer directed by William Berke in which Jungle Jim (Johnny Weissmuller) saves a wild jungle woman (Anita Lhoest) from capture by the witch doctor (John Dehner) who had murdered her anthropologist parents years before and now seeks to dispose of Jim with help from a greedy treasure hunter (Buster Crabbe) until a thundering swarm of gibbons comes to the rescue. Stylized violence

title: Captives
synopsis: Angry and confused over her divorce from an unfaithful husband, a woman (Julia Ormond) begins working as a dentist in a London prison, then falls into a passionate affair with a lonely inmate (Tim Roth) who can't protect her when she's blackmailed by a fellow prisoner. Director Angela Pope sets up the situation credibly enough, but has trouble sustaining the risky romance which follows, then turns the ending into a conventional thriller. Some nasty violence, a fairly graphic sex scene and occasional rough language

title: Captivity
synopsis: Nasty tale about a model (Elisha Cuthbert) abducted and subjected to unrelenting torture by a masked figure. Director Roland Joffe's film eventually comes up with some interesting elements and plot twists, but by then it is too late, demonstrating he has come a long way from earlier and loftier achievements such as "The Killing Fields" and "The Mission." Graphic sex, violence, sadism and torture

title: Capturing the Friedmans
synopsis: Unusual documentary chronicling the destruction of a Long Island family in the late 1980s after the teacher-father and his teen-age son are accused of child molestation and the mother and two other sons take sides. Filmmaker Andrew Jarecki interviews law enforcement personnel and surviving family members but it is the Friedmans' own obsessive taping of their furious arguments at the time that speaks volumes about this intensely dysfunctional family and their wavering versions of the truth. Sexual references, specifically pedophilia, and much rough language

title: Car 54, Where Are You?
synopsis: Trigger-happy movie version of the 1960's TV series teams a rookie Brooklyn patrolman (John McGinley) with a bumbling veteran (David Johansen) on the tail of a mob don (Daniel Baldwin) who is trying to rub out a government witness (Jeremy Piven). Director Bill Fishman has trouble stringing together assorted witless sketches which fail to capture the amiable kookiness of the original sitcom. Recurring violence played for laughs, some sexual innuendo and occasional toilet humor

title: Caravans
synopsis: A young State Department official (Michael Sarrazin) in 1948 Iran is ordered to locate a missing American (Jennifer O'Neill) reportedly in the mountainous domain of a nomad chief (Anthony Quinn). Directed by James Faro, the effort is a silly misfire, with rambling and unfocused plot line, atrocious dialogue and leadfooted pacing. A bloody execution as well as a sequence involving a homosexual dancer make it mature fare

title: Carbine Williams
synopsis: Gritty fact-based story of a North Carolina moonshiner (James Stewart) who gets 30 years for his part in the death of a revenue agent, then is pardoned after the prison warden (Wendall Corey) allows him to perfect a light-weight rifle which the Army adopts for use in World War II as the M1 carbine. Directed by Richard Thorpe, the story is awkwardly told in flashbacks, much of them devoted to his mistreatment on a chain gang and at the prison farm, with the rest providing a sentimental before-and-after picture of his relations with his large farm family, as well as supportive wife (Jean Hagen) and puzzled son. Stylized violence, justice questions and contemplation of divorce

title: Carbon Copy
synopsis: Successful business man (George Segal) marries the boss' shrewish daughter (Susan St. James) but finds his snug, affluent nest disrupted when a black youth (Denzel Washington) shows up one day claiming to be his illegitimate son. Director Michael Schultz's crude and heavyhanded comedy attempts to get laughs by some cheap shots at religion, not excluding a dose of male chauvinism. Strong language and two rather distasteful bedroom scenes

title: Career Girls
synopsis: British drama of a woman (Lynda Steadman) renewing her friendship with a former college roommate (Katrin Cartlidge) on a weekend visit which recalls their frenetic, uncertain lives as undergraduates and how much each has changed in the six years since then. Written and directed by Mike Leigh, the impressionistic narrative is loosely assembled from scenes of past and present, relying mainly on improvisational performances but the result is too disjointed to add up to more than a tentative understanding of how much progress the two have made in their lives since college. Sexual encounter with brief nudity, sexual situations, recurring rough language and occasional profanity

title: Career Opportunities
synopsis: A novice janitor (Frank Whaley) and a lonely shoplifter (Jennifer Connelly), locked overnight in a department store, become friends while warding off a pair of dimwitted thieves. Writer John Hughes and director Bryan Gordon bomb out with a terminally dumb comedy of humorless stick figures and glaringly bad plotting. Mock comic violence and very suggestive double entendres

title: Carefree
synopsis: Wacky musical comedy about a psychiatrist (Fred Astaire) whose best friend (Ralph Bellamy) asks him to treat his marriage-shy girlfriend (Ginger Rogers) but matters get complicated when the patient falls for the doctor. Directed by Mark Sandrich, the thin plot takes some very giddy turns, with the added bonus of appealing Irving Berlin tunes, including "I Used to Be Color Blind" danced in slow motion by Rogers and Astaire as well as Astaire's stand-out syncopated solo on the golf links. Silly romantic complications

title: Careful He Might Hear You
synopsis: Sensitive, extremely well-acted Australian movie about a 1930's custody fight between two sisters over the six-year-old son of a third sister who died in childbirth. Director Carl Schultz has done well with showing the effect of all this upon the boy, partly in a less-than-wholesome attraction of a woman for a young child

title: Careless Lady
synopsis: Uneven romantic comedy in which an inexperienced young suburbanite (Joan Bennett) pretends to be a married socialite while on an unchaperoned trip to Paris, but matters turn serious when her supposed "husband" (John Boles) turns up and promptly falls in love with her. Directed by Kenneth MacKenna from Guy Bolton's script, the plot makes little sense though it generates some amusing misunderstandings along the way to a trite conclusion about true love having nothing to do with prior experience. Romantic complications, sexual situations and innuendo

title: Caribbean
synopsis: Convoluted swashbuckler in which an 18th-century English pirate (Cedric Hardwicke) sends an agent (John Payne) to lead a slave uprising on the island plantation of his foe (Francis L. Sullivan) whose daughter (Arlene Dahl) is the cause of their enmity. Directed by Edward Ludwig, the implausible narrative has a hard-working cast and exotic settings but the muddled plot falters with cardboard characters, aimless action and throwaway ending. Stylized violence

title: Carlito's Way
synopsis: Planning to leave crime and New York City gangsters behind for a new life in the Bahamas with his girlfriend (Penelope Ann Miller), a newly released convict (Al Pacino) pays a high price for his friendship with the corrupt lawyer (Sean Penn) who got him out of jail on a technicality. Director Brian De Palma overstuffs his bleak crime drama with a profusion of morally bankrupt characters who glibly rationalize their murderous acts. Much violence, incessant rough language, some drug abuse, ethnic slurs, topless dancers and brief sexual encounters

title: Carmen
synopsis: During the rehearsals for a dance version of Bizet's opera about the gypsy temptress whose infidelities end in murder, the choreographer (Antonio Gades) falls in love with the young woman (Laura del Sol) in the title role and their affair offstage follows the same scenario as that enacted onstage. Carlos Saura directs the Spanish production which is filled with stunning flamenco dance numbers and its story of life imitating art is intriguing at first but gradually bogs down in operatic melodrama. Subtitles. Mature theme and treatment

title: Carmen Jones
synopsis: Bizet's tragic opera is updated to World War II when a soldier (Harry Belafonte) falls for a pretty worker (Dorothy Dandridge) in a southern parachute factory, then goes AWOL to follow her to Chicago where he strangles her after she dumps him for a prizefighter. Directed by Otto Preminger, the strong period Americana and fine African-American cast can't overcome the disappointment of the movie's flatly dubbed singing and stiffly staged musical numbers. Sexual situations and innunedo

title: Carmen Miranda: Bananas is My Business
synopsis: Brought to Hollywood in 1940, the popular Brazilian samba singer was quickly typecast as a comic figure who wore bizarre hats and spoke mangled English in a career increasingly ridiculed by her countrymen and American moviegoers. Directed and narrated by Helena Solberg, the documentary presents a sobering account of the unhappy personal life and tragically early death of a performer whose vivacious talents were misused by Hollywood resulting in a career sadly lost between two cultures. Discreet treatment of sexual affairs

title: Carnal Knowledge
synopsis: Producer-director Mike Nichols and screenwriter Jules Feiffer collaborate on a movie with three episodes spanning two decades (late 1940s to late 1960s) in the lives of two men (Jack Nicholson and Art Garfunkel), tracing their non-maturation from sex-starved college students to sex-saturated, middle-aged men in professional life. It is a feeble morality play which preaches once again, with pathetic exploitation, that the wages of sin is impotence. Brief nudity and rough language

title: Carnival of Souls
synopsis: Low-budget but effective horror tale directed by Herk Harvey follows the eerie experiences of a church organist (Candace Hilligoss) after she emerges from a car crash in a Kansas river until her reunion weeks later with others who died in the same accident. Sinister, unsettling atmosphere and sexual situations

title: Carnival Story
synopsis: Shabby melodrama directed by Kurt Neumann in which an impoverished German woman (Anne Baxter) finds work with a touring American carnival, then is torn between an amorous but brutal barker (Steve Cochran) and the caring high diver (Lyle Bettger) whom she marries with disastrous results. An off-screen murder and tawdry sexual situations

title: Carny
synopsis: Set against the background of a traveling carnival is a triangle theme involving a teenage runaway (Jody Foster), a clown (Gary Busey) and his best friend (Robbie Robertson). The theme, however, is undeveloped because director Robert Kaylor is more interested in documenting carnival life, especially its seamy side with generous amounts of violence, sex and rough language

title: Caroline and the Rebels
synopsis: Vapid French melodrama directed by Jean Devaivre follows the romantic misadventures of a Spanish noble (Jean-Claude Pascal) who goes off to fight the French during the Napoleonic Wars, then finds proof he was an adopted child and is free to marry his loving sister (Bridget Bardot). Dubbed. Stylized violence and sexual situations

title: Carousel
synopsis: Rodgers and Hammerstein musical from Ferenc Molnar's tragic romance in which a macho carnival worker (Gordon MacRae) dies in a robbery trying to provide for his pregnant wife (Shirley Jones), then gets a chance to come back in spirit to set things right for his still-grieving widow and teen daughter. Directed by Henry King, the dramatic portions seem stilted and out of place in the lovely 19th-century New England setting, though the production numbers are eye-filling and the songs memorable, notably "If I Loved You" and "You'll Never Walk Alone." Romantic complications

title: Carpool
synopsis: Taking hostage a workaholic dad (David Paymer) and five schoolkids in a minivan, a bumbling but goodhearted robber (Tom Arnold) gradually turns them into accomplices as they elude pursuing police cars. Director Arthur Hiller's witless chase movie frequently stalls out, thanks to its tired, lowest-common-denominator brand of humor. Indulgent treatment of kidnapping and theft, comically intended violence and brief toilet humor

title: Carrie
synopsis: Elaborate sudser from the Theodore Dreiser novel about a country girl (Jennifer Jones) who gets a job in turn-of-the-century Chicago, is seduced by a salesman (Eddie Albert), then runs off with a married man (Laurence Olivier) to New York where she leaves him flat while finding fame on the stage. Director William Wyler's studied period piece arouses little interest in the characters and their woes, though Olivier's descent into penury gains some sympathy. Mature theme and treatment

title: Carrie
synopsis: A repressed high school student (Sissy Spacek) discovers that she has telekinetic powers which she uses at the senior prom to wreak a bloody revenge on taunting classmates and her religious fanatic mother. Director Brian De Palma's horror movie is too ludicrous and overdrawn to scare, but succeeds in the shock value of its callous, unhealthy mix of nudity and violence

title: Carried Away
synopsis: Pretentious tale of a middle-aged country schoolteacher (Dennis Hopper) who throws himself into a passionate affair with a 17-year-old student (Amy Locane) to the consternation of his friends and the widow (Amy Irving) who wants to marry him. Director Bruno Barreto captures the gritty reality of the rural Texas setting and characters but turns the story into romanticized claptrap portraying the teacher's affair with a dangerously mixed-up teenager as a minor indiscretion which supposedly reawakens his passion for the widow. Graphic sex scenes, frontal nudity and occasional profanity and rough language

title: Carrington
synopsis: Fact-based story of the live-in relationship between homosexual author Lytton Strachey (Jonathan Pryce) and painter Dora Carrington (Emma Thompson) who remain devoted to one another while carrying on a series of affairs with other men. Writer-director Christopher Hampton establishes the pair's deep mutual affection while indulging their sexual appetites with others, but leaves their part in the British cultural scene between the world wars a disappointing blank. Uncritical treatment of sexual promiscuity, brief bedroom scenes with fleeting nudity, an off-screen suicide and a few instances of rough language

title: Carry It On
synopsis: Documentary on an anti-Vietnam draft resister, David Harris, sentenced to a three-year term in federal prison focuses on his last meeting with his wife, folk singer Joan Baez, and then on her activities with the anti-war movement. Robert Jones, Christopher Knight and James Coyne have assembled a very moving and effective statement against war

title: Carry On Camping
synopsis: Rude British send-up of summer campers employs such familiar funsters as Sidney James, Kenneth Williams and Joan Sims. Director Gerald Thomas has assembled a grab-bag of comic skits but too often strains for double entendres and vulgar sexual shenanigans to carry the day

title: Carry On Cleo
synopsis: Thin British farce directed by Gerald Thomas follows enslaved English rustics in ancient Rome where their bumbling antics help save Caesar (Kenneth Connor) from a plot concocted by Marc Antony (Sidney James) and Cleopatra (Amanda Barrie). Slapstick violence and bawdy humor

title: Carry On Cruising
synopsis: Slack British farce from director Gerald Thomas follows a two-week Mediterranean cruise aboard a ship whose dour captain (Sidney James) bullies inept crew replacements (notably Kenneth Williams and Kenneth Connor) on the prowl for romantic passengers (Liz Fraser and Dilys Laye). Broad sexual innuendo and slapstick vulgarity

title: Carry On Doctor
synopsis: Director Gerald Thomas commits his comic cronies (Sidney James, Frankie Howerd, Kenneth Williams, Hattie Jacques, Barbara Windsor and Jim Dale) to hospital, but the operation results in the same old monkey business. There is a generous share of double entendres, but the ribaldry is fairly tame

title: Carry On Henry VIII
synopsis: The latest offering in this series from director Gerald Thomas concerns two previously undiscovered wives of King Henry and their topsy-turvy effect on the beleaguered monarch and his court. Coarse language and blatant double entendres

title: Carry On Jack
synopsis: Thin British farce directed by Gerald Thomas in which a barmaid (Juliet Mills) gets aboard a Navy frigate in the uniform of a midshipman (Bernard Cribbins), then the two become heroes in the Napoleonic Wars by saving the ship from mutiny, pirates and Spanish galleons. Slapstick swashbuckler with broad sexual innuendo

title: Carry On Nurse
synopsis: Feeble British farce in which director Gerald Thomas finds few laughs as hospital patients (Kenneth Connor, Charles Hawtrey, Wilfrid Hyde-White and others) suffer various indignities while engaging in hijinks at the expense of haughty administrators (led by Hattie Jacques), befuddled attendants (notably Shirley Eaton) and each other. Sexual innuendo and vulgar situations

title: Cars
synopsis: Delightful computer-animated movie set in a world of anthropomorphic autos about a cocky racecar (voiced by Owen Wilson) which, while en route cross-country to compete in a prestigious championship, is unexpectedly detained in a neglected desert town, where his growing friendship with the town's four-wheeled residents (voiced by Paul Newman, Bonnie Hunt and Larry the Cable Guy, among others) effects a change of heart regarding fame in the fast lane. Co-directed by John Lasseter and Joe Ranft, the film has a full tank of humor and emotions -- not to mention bar-raising visuals -- while its solid storytelling imparts a charming message about taking the time to appreciate what really matters in life

title: Carson City
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Andre de Toth in which a determined engineer (Randolph Scott) builds a railroad line by tunneling through the mountainous terrain between Carson City and Virginia City, despite a gang of outlaws (led by Raymond Massey) out to stop it. Frontier violence

title: Carson City Cyclone
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Howard Bretherton in which a frontier judge (Noah Berry) is murdered by a gang of bank robbers and his lawyer son (Don "Red" Barry) straps on his six-guns to bring them to justice. Frontier violence

title: Carson City Kid
synopsis: Routine Roy Rogers Western in which he gets help from sheriff Gabby Hayes and gold miner Noah Berry, Jr., in tracking down the gambler who killed his brother. Mild chases, brawls and gunplay

title: Cartouche
synopsis: Stilted adventure in 18th-century France as a hunted nobleman (Richard Basehart) tries to find the culprit who committed the murder for which he has been blamed, getting help along the way from an actress (Patricia Roc) with a traveling troupe of players. Directed by Steve Sekely, the period story is flat and the action has less flair than the picture's colorful costumes and ornate settings. Stylized violence and muted sexual innuendo

title: Car Wash
synopsis: Director Michael Schultz's touching, sometimes extremely funny movie follows the course of a day at an inner city car wash where the employees keep a jive rhythm to their work and to their joking. Richard Pryor, Ivan Dixon, the Pointer Sisters and George Carlin supply the wit and energy in this comic tale of streetwise surviva1. Some rough language, sexual innuendo and casual acceptance of drug use

title: Casablanca
synopsis: Classic romantic melodrama set in the refugee crossroads of French North Africa where an American expatriate (Humphrey Bogart) helps the woman who broke his heart (Ingrid Bergman) and her husband (Paul Henreid), an underground leader, escape the Nazi dragnet. Directed by Michael Curtiz, the story is replete with World War II intrigue, sardonic humor, punchy dialogue ("Here's looking at you, kid!") and a great cast, including Claude Rains as a sauve Vichy police officer and Dooley Wilson's rendition of "As Time Goes By." Time stands still for this one, though the wartime atmosphere may be too menacing for the children

title: Casa de Los Babys
synopsis: Poignant drama about six American women (including Daryl Hannah, Marcia Gay Harden and Lili Taylor) entrenched in a South American motel waiting out government bureaucracy to adopt children from a local orphanage. Though weighed down at times by a talky script, the film, directed by John Sayles, poses important questions about the thorny cultural and political issues involved in foreign adoptions, painting a bittersweet portrait of maternity which ultimately celebrates the joy of motherhood. Sporadic rough and crude language, as well as an instance of drug abuse involving young children

title: Casanova
synopsis: Handsome but leisurely paced period piece about history's most famous lover (Heath Ledger), focusing on a fictitious "secret" episode in his life: his incognito love affair with an 18th-century Venetian beauty (Sienna Miller) who writes feminist tracts under a male nom de plume. On the plus side, Lasse Hallstrom's film is well acted, farcical without overdoing the slapstick, remarkably restrained in sexual matters, and even has a reasonably moral ending, but there's a surfeit of troublesome Inquisition-era jibes at the Catholic Church (including a comically villainous bishop played by Jeremy Irons), and an episode involving seduction of a novice. Brief sexual episodes without nudity, innuendo, some crude expressions, pervasive anti-clerical view and a mild torture scene

title: Casanova Brown
synopsis: Disappointing romantic comedy about a college professor (Gary Cooper) whose marriage is over almost before it starts, then learns months later that his ex-wife (Teresa Wright) has become a mother. Except for an hilarious house-burning sequence, director Sam Wood treats the situation with such deadly coyness that all involved appear to be congenital idiots. Sophomoric treatment of marriage and parenthood

title: Casanova's Big Night
synopsis: Mistaken for the notorious lover Casanova (Vincent Price), a tailor's apprentice (Bob Hope) escapes imprisonment by the doge of Venice (Arnold Moss) to save a woman (Audrey Dalton) from dishonor and win the heart of his true love (Joan Fontaine). Director Norman Z. McLeod's listless comedy wastes a good cast in a leaden 18th-century period piece from which Hope wrings only a few smiles. Mild sexist humor

title: Case 39
synopsis: Turgid self-parody of a horror film in which a social worker (Renee Zellweger) finds she has a demon-possessed child (Jodelle Ferland) on her hands. Director Christian Alvart and screenwriter Ray Wright scoop deeply from the cliches of demon-seed-children flicks to clumsy effect. Fleeting crude language, a scene of non-sexual child abuse, brief but intense bloody violence

title: Casey's Shadow
synopsis: An irascible but basically good-hearted Cajun horse trainer (Walter Matthau) has to make an agonizing decision whether or not to run a horse with an injured leg in a race that could mean fame and fortune for him and his three sons. Director Martin Ritt captures the colorfu1 world of quarter-horse racing in the Southwest but the movie's benign attitude toward the trainer's moral failings and the frequent use of profanity make it mature fare

title: Cash McCall
synopsis: Low-powered romantic drama in which a shrewd corporate raider (James Garner) buys a stagnant company in order to woo the daughter (Natalie Wood) of its owner (Dean Jagger), but things get complicated when the deal produces millions in unexpected profits. In tracking the devious turns of the business world, director Joseph Pevney generates little interest in the characters and even less in their personal problems. Romantic situations and sexual innuendo

title: Casino
synopsis: Increasingly violent story of the rise and fall of a mob-backed Las Vegas casino manager (Robert de Niro), married to a money-obsessed drug addict (Sharon Stone) who seduces her husband's best friend (Joe Pesci), a murderous gangster she hopes will kill the husband she despises. Director Martin Scorcese spins a well-acted, compelling yarn ultimately ruined by an excess of sadistic violence. Much graphic violence, adulterous affairs, fleeting nudity, substance abuse and incessant rough language

title: Casper
synopsis: A lonely 13-year-old (Christina Ricci) is befriended by the cuddly ghost of the title when her widowed therapist dad (Bill Pullman) is hired to coax some menacing spirits out of a mansion rumored to be hiding buried treasure. Director Brad Silberling pumps up the cuteness factor, but there is not much of a story or little else to engage audiences beyond a few novel special effects. Some comic violence, a couple of profanities and a crude expression

title: Casper, A Spirited Beginning
synopsis: Casper, A Sprited Beginning -- Made-for-video sequel to the 1995 feature shows how Casper became a friendly ghost after missing out on ghost training and winding up in a small town where he's befriended by a lonely 10-year-old (Brendon Ryan Barrett) who introduces him to a trio of ghosts haunting a mansion scheduled for demolition by the boy's father (Steve Guttenberg). Directed by Sean McNamara, the formula story developes at a pedestrian pace with the live-action proceedings of less interest than the animated ghosts and their special-effects antics. Slapstick violence, some bathroom humor and occasional coarse language

title: Cassandra's Dream
synopsis: Fairly interesting but ultimately unconvincing London-based drama about two financially needy brothers (Ewan McGregor and Colin Farrell) asked by their rich uncle (Tom Wilkinson) to kill a business associate for pay. The two leads are excellent, but writer-director Woody Allen's Hitchcockian script fails to avoid a sense of contrivance, and Allen's nihilistic worldview, as espoused here by McGregor's character, is beginning to grow tiresome. An off-screen murder, brief violence, much conversational profanity, drug references, some brief sexual banter and nonmarital relationships

title: Cassidy of Bar 20
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Lesley Selander in which Hopalong (William Boyd) and his pards (Russell Hayden and Frank Darien) save a former Bar 20 rider from being driven off the range by a vicious landgrabber (Robert Fiske). Frontier violence

title: Cast a Dark Shadow
synopsis: British thriller in which a ruthless charmer (Dirk Bogarde) murders his rich wife (Mona Washbourne), then marries a well-off widow (Margaret Lockwood) until sidetracked by a new prospect (Kay Walsh) who is not what she seems. Directed by Lewis Gilbert, the sinister proceedings prove less intriguing than the interesting ensemble of characters made credible by a fine cast. Stylized violence, menacing situations and sexual innuendo

title: Cast a Giant Shadow
synopsis: Standard Hollywood biography of David (Mickey) Marcus, New York lawyer and World War II hero, who helped whip the young Israeli army into shape. Written and directed by Melville Shavelson, the dramatization is at times painfully stilted but for the most part human and likeab1e. Extramarital attachment and wartime violence

title: Castle Deep
synopsis: Screen version of novelist William Eastlake's surrealistic satire on the absurdity of war is set in a Gothic chateau with its priceless art treasures where an American major (Burt Lancaster) and a company of infantrymen prepare to make a stand against the German army's offensive at Bastogne. Regrettably, director Sydney Pollack fails to incorporate a convincing human and moral dimension to counterbalance the senseless heroics and casual sexual relationships that result

title: Castle in the Desert
synopsis: Playful murder mystery with Charlie Chan (Sidney Toler) on the job in a spooky 16th-century castle built in the Mojave Desert by a reclusive millionaire (Douglass Dumbrille) whose wife is suspected of poisoning a visitor. Directed by Harry Lachman, there's a fortune at stake in a twisty story involving real and bogus murders, almost as many red herrings as suspects (notably Richard Derr, Henry Daniell, Steve Geray and Ethel Griffies) and some comic relief from Chan's Number Two Son (Victor Sen Yung). Menacing situations

title: Castle Keep
synopsis: Screen version of novelist William Eastlake's surrealistic satire on the absurdity of war is set in a Gothic chateau with its priceless art treasures where an American major (Burt Lancaster) and a company of infantrymen prepare to make a stand against the German army's offensive at Bastogne. Regrettably, director Sydney Pollack fails to incorporate a convincing human and moral dimension to counter-balance the senseless heroics and casual sexual relationships that result

title: Casual Sex
synopsis: Unfunny comedy about two young single women (Lea Thompson and Victoria Jackson) who, in search of a healthy way to meet Mr. Right, sign on for a vacation at a singles health spa. Director Genevieve Robert uses humor to portray contemporary issues of sexuality and the AIDS epidemic in a frank if non-cerebral manner. Much blunt sex talk and a non-sexual nude beach sequence

title: Casualties of War
synopsis: Fact-based story of an atrocity committed by an American patrol during the Vietnam War centers on the moral dilemma of a soldier (Michael J. Fox) who tries to prevent his unit (led by Sean Penn) from gang raping and murdering a Vietnamese woman. Director Brian DePalma's treatment of the atrocity and the war's violence is extremely graphic. Intense violence and much foul language

title: Cat and Mouse
synopsis: German adaptation of the Gunter Grass novel about a young man's groping for maturity under the Nazi regime, and his subjective way of facing reality and his own handicaps. Directed with precision and style by Hansjurgen Pohland, it is of interest for what it shows of the period but also has some insights for those working with adolescents

title: Cat and Mouse
synopsis: Unorthodox police inspector (Serge Reggiani) is baffled by what appears to be a millionaire's murder and theft of his art collection but as the case progresses nothing is quite what it seems and the viewer is never exactly sure where the abundance of clues will lead. Written and directed by Claude Lelouch, the mystery comedy is both intelligent and playful, especially with its offbeat cast of characters acted with style by the likes of Michele Morgan and Philippe Leotard

title: Cat Ballou
synopsis: Wild romp out West as the daughter (Jane Fonda) of a murdered rancher (John Marley) seeks justice by enlisting the aid of an over-the-hill gunfighter (Lee Marvin), an Indian ranch hand (Tom Nardini) and a pair of con men (Michael Callan and Dwayne Hickman). Director Elliot Silverstein's frontier spoof has comic flair, droll performances (Marvin also doubles as the chief villain) and musical commentary by balladeers Nat King Cole and Stubby Kaye. Comic violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Catch 22
synopsis: Screen version of Joseph Heller's black comedy about a bomber squadron in Italy during World War II and its troubled airman, Yossarian (Alan Arkin). Although skillfully done under Mike Nichols' direction, it is more pretentious than profound in its statement that war is madness. Brief nudity and some graphic depiction of wartime casualties

title: Catch a Fire
synopsis: Intelligent if unevenly compelling drama set in apartheid-era South Africa that tells the real-life story of Patrick Chamusso (Derek Luke), a husband and father who abandons his apolitical stance and becomes a militant rebel fighter after he and his wife (Bonnie Henna) are wrongfully arrested and tortured by white police investigators (headed by Tim Robbins) in connection with an explosion at the oil refinery where he works. Despite all the right ingredients -- a solid cast, a worthy story, taut pacing and an accomplished director in Phillip Noyce -- the tale never ignites from an emotional standpoint. However, in exploring themes of racism and the timely issue of using violence as a means of political protest, the film ultimately advocates forgiveness as imperative in healing the wounds caused by hatred. Some violence, images of torture, an instance of rough language and a few crude expressions and racial slurs

title: Catch and Release
synopsis: Dour, slow-moving romantic comedy about a woman (Jennifer Garner) whose fiancee is killed shortly before their wedding who learns that he fathered a child with an out-of-town massage therapist (Juliette Lewis) who eventually comes to town with the child in tow moving in with her and her fiance's buddies (Kevin Smith, Sam Jaeger and Timothy Olyphant) with ensuing romantic complications. Writer-director Susannah Grant's formulaic chick flick strains for credibility, the acting is bland (especially Olyphant as her principal love interest), and is unredeemed by the overall message of forgiveness and a reasonably moral wrap-up. Permissive sexual mores, intimate encounters (one intense but fully clothed, the other gauzily photographed with no actual nudity), sexual banter and innuendo, some crude language and expressions and profanity, a suicide attempt and drug use

title: Catch Me If You Can
synopsis: Fact-based breezy comedy in which a runaway teen (Leonardo DiCaprio) successfully poses as a pilot, a doctor and a lawyer and cashes fraudulent checks over several years as a dogged FBI agent (Tom Hanks) methodically chases his slippery prey. Director Steven Spielberg turns in a high-style cat-and-mouse tale made interesting by the agent's determination not only to catch the youthful culprit but to rehabilitate him as well. Light-hearted treatment of crime, implied sexual encounters, abortion reference, occasional profanity and an instance of rough language

title: Catch My Soul
synopsis: Uneven rock opera version of Shakespeare's "Othello" turns the wicked Iago (Lance Le Gault) into the devil incarnate dressed as a hippie and the noble Moor (Richie Havens) is now a pacifist preacher who heads a hippie commune. The score by Havens and Tony Joe White is quite good but Jack Good's script ranges from the sublime to the ridiculous in its mixture of Shakespearean imagery, Biblical diction and contemporary argot. Directed by Patrick McGoohan and photographed by Conrad Hall, the New Mexico locations are an impressive backdrop for the opera but the contemporary rarely meshes smoothly with the classic

title: Catch That Kid
synopsis: Cleverly conceived but morally misguided kiddie caper about a 12-year-old girl (Kristen Stewart) and her two best friends, rival suitors (Max Thieriot and Corbin Bleu) who decide to break into a high-security bank in order to steal enough money to pay for her dad's costly, life-saving surgery. Despite a smart script and a fresh-faced cast that gives the flick's shopworn heist plot a youthful twist, director Bart Freundlich uses an end-justifies-the-means attitude to rationalize his improbable premise, which, though ultimately discredited, makes it difficult to wholeheartedly applaud this otherwise entertaining movie. An ambiguous attitude toward larceny, minimal mildly-crude humor and some action violence

title: Catch That Kid/Like Mike Set
synopsis: "Catch That Kid" (2004). Cleverly conceived but morally misguided kiddie caper about a 12-year-old girl (Kristen Stewart) and her two best friends, rival suitors (Max Thieriot and Corbin Bleu), who decide to break into a high-security bank in order to steal enough money to pay for her dad's costly, life-saving surgery. Despite a smart script and a fresh-faced cast that gives the film's shopworn heist plot a youthful twist, director Bart Freundlich uses an end-justifies-the-means attitude to rationalize his improbable premise, which, though ultimately discredited, makes it difficult to wholeheartedly applaud this otherwise entertaining movie. An ambiguous attitude toward larceny, minimal mildly crude humor and some action violence

title: Catfish in a Black Bean Sauce
synopsis: Mediocre effort about a Vietnamese man (Chi Muoi Lo) reared by an African-American couple (Paul Winfield, Mary Alice), who goes through an identity crisis when his biological mother (Kieu Chinh) suddenly arrives. Director Lo's offbeat comedy has several humorous high points, but peters out with amateurish scenes and forced dialogue. Intermittent crass language, fleeting profanity, an instance of rough language and a mild homosexual innuendo. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Catherine the Great
synopsis: Historical drama centers on the troubled marriage of German princess Catherine (Elisabeth Bergner) to Russia's Grand Duke Peter (Douglas Fairbanks, Jr.) who becomes Czar after the death of the Empress (Flora Robson), but his unstable personality and despotic rule lead to his murder and Catherine being acclaimed Empress. Directed by Paul Czinner, the British production has elaborate sets, endless court intrigues, Peter's mad antics and Catherine's triumphant smile. Implied sexual affairs

title: Catlow
synopsis: Flip outlaw (Yul Brynner) shoots his way across the Southwest and part of Mexico with a quixotic marshal (Richard Crenna) in hot pursuit. Directed by Sam Wanamaker, action rather than plot is all this meandering, serio-comic Western shoot-'em-up has to offer. Stylized violence

title: Cat People
synopsis: Effectively understated horror movie in which a husband (Kent Smith) tries to help his bride (Simone Simon) conquer her fear of an old Serbian legend about humans cursed with the power to turn into deadly panthers. In their first effort to wring suspense from low-budget melodramas, producer Val Lewton and director Jacques Tourneur create a sinister atmosphere and some scary scenes --notably in a hotel swimming pool -- but are less successful with the weak plot. Much menace and a broken marriage

title: Cat People
synopsis: Very loosely based on Val Lewton's 1942 horror classic, this one is tediously explicit in showing the tribulations of a brother and sister (Malco1m McDowell and Nastassia Kinski) who turn into black panthers at odd moments and must kill to regain their human form. Paul Schrader's direction offers clumsy, heavyhanded doses of blood and gore, graphic sex and nudity

title: Cats & Dogs: The Revenge of Kitty Galore
synopsis: Cats & Dogs: The Revenge of Kitty Galore Entertaining and inventive 3-D spy adventure -- seamless blending live action, puppetry, and computer animation -- in which rogue feline agent Kitty Galore (voice of Bette Midler) threatens to make the world her "personal scratching post" by unleashing the "Call of the Wild," a screech that serves as a weapon of mass destruction. Led by Diggs (voice of James Marsden), a police K-9 German shepherd who hates cats, and Catherine (voice of Christina Applegate), a feline agent who puts her nine lives on the line, the covert pet intelligence agencies DOG and MEOWS must put differences aside and work together to bring Kitty down. Plenty of excitement, gizmos, and cute-as-a-button moments will charm and enthrall the youngsters, while their parents will enjoy the inside jokes referencing James Bond films

title: Cats
synopsis: Filmed version of the Andrew Lloyd Webber stage musical based on T.S. Eliot's delightfully whimsical "Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats" about a nighttime gathering of flamboyant junkyard cats. Fluid camerawork lessens the film's stagebound appearance, zeroing in on the artful costumes, extravagant make-up and sheer theatricality of the performances. A few mildly suggestive dance numbers

title: Cats and Dogs
synopsis: Fitfully amusing action comedy in which a young pup (voiced by Toby Maguire) and his canine crew must protect man from a frisky feline (voiced by Sean Hayes) who plans to destroy a new vaccine for dog allergies and dominate the world. Director Larry Guterman makes clever use of the age-old battle between cats and dogs and the computer-generated effects are exceptional, but the soft narrative disappoints. Some mild action violence

title: Cat's Eye
synopsis: Three episodes that are an unstable blend of suspense, violence and black humor linked together tenuously by the presence of the same cat in each. Directed by Lewis Teague from a screenplay by horror writer Stephen King, these are moderately entertaining with relatively restrained violence

title: Cattle Annie and Little Britches
synopsis: Two teenage girls (Amanda Plummer and Diane Lane) join a once famous outlaw gang (led by Burt Lancaster) and inspire its aging members to live up to their reputation. Director Lamont Johnson's contrived Western does not measure up to its whimsical intentions and takes a benign view of immorality of various sorts, including sexual

title: Cattle Drive
synopsis: Western adventure in which the spoiled teenage son (Dean Stockwell) of a railroad owner (Leon Ames) gets lost in the wilds and is rescued by a cowboy (Joel McCrea) who teaches him the value of work and self-discipline while driving a herd of cattle to Santa Fe. Directed by Kurt Neumann, it's "Captains Courageous" on horseback with an agreeable cast and colorful outdoor vistas

title: Cattle King
synopsis: Tired formula Western about an 1880's Wyoming range war between a big rancher (Robert Taylor) and the hired guns of a city boss (Robert Middleton). Directed by Tay Garnett, there's nothing new here, though it does touch on the question of government land policy. Stylized shoot-outs and fisticuffs

title: Cattle Queen of Montana
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Allan Dwan has an undercover government agent (Ronald Reagan) give some needed assistance to the title character (Barbara Stanwyck) in the fight to save her ranch from an ambitious land-grabber (Gene Evans) and his Indian allies. Stylized violence

title: Caught
synopsis: Slow-paced drama of the close friendship that develops between a Jersey City fishmonger (Edward James Olmos) and the young drifter (Arie Verveen) he takes into his home, but things turn nasty when the fishmonger's wife (Maria Conchita Alonso) takes a fancy to the boarder and they begin an affair. Directed by Robert M. Young, the picture develops its working-class environment and characters in credible fashion, then gets swept away in the torrid depiction of an increasingly passionate affair whose tragic ending falls flat. Simulated sex scenes with nudity and occasional profanity and rough language

title: Caught
synopsis: Charm school graduate (Barbara Bel Geddes) marries a manic millionaire (Robert Ryan) whose abusive behavior drives her unaware she's pregnant, then takes a job with an idealistic doctor (James Mason) and a messy triangle results. Director Max Ophuls tries to impart some psychological depth to the characters, but the picture is undone by a soapy plot and some unconvincing melodramatics. Threatening situations and romantic complications resolved by divorce

title: Caught Up
synopsis: Formula thriller set in L.A.'s South Central 'hood where an ex-con (Bokeem Woodbine) falls for a woman (Cynda Williams) who gets him involved with the loot from a big jewel heist, then finds he's been set up to take the fall for the crime. Writer-director Darin Scott offers a slick but uneven reworking of the old story of an innocent man caught up in a web of desperate doings which he must unravel at the risk of his life. Gory violence, a sexual encounter with brief nudity, numerous sexual references and much rough language

title: Cauldron of Blood
synopsis: Far-fetched, unscary would-be chiller about a mad housewife (Viveca Lindfors) who won't tell her blind sculptor-hubby (Boris Karloff) the source of the skeletons she supplies for him to use as models for his lifelike statues. A bubbly vat of acid has the title role. Directed by Edward Mann, it is pure hokum, but innocuous enough for hardy, undemanding adults

title: Cause for Alarm
synopsis: Gimmicky suspense thriller directed by Tay Garnett follows a panicky housewife (Loretta Young) as she tries to retrieve a letter written by her demented husband (Barry Sullivan) just before his death charging that she and his doctor (Bruce Cowling) are lovers plotting his murder.
