Directed by Sam Wood, the setting is an air base in England where the necessity of launching a series of risky attacks is questioned by the general's fellow officers (Walter Pidgeon, Brian Donlevy, Ray Collins and John McIntire), a Congressman (Edward Arnold) and a war correspondent (Charles Bickford). Conflicting views of patriotism and its cost

title: Commandments
synopsis: Blaming God for his pregnant wife's drowning and other personal tragedies, a distraught widower (Aidan Quinn) vows to break all ten commandments, in the process falling for his late wife's sister (Courteney Cox) whose mariage to a womanizer (Anthony La Paglia) is on the rocks. Writer-director Daniel Taplitz treats the protagonist's heartfelt loss of faith in jarringly comic terms that become sappy and ultimately ludicrous. Fleeting sexual encounters, brief violence, intermittent rough language and some profanity

title: Commando
synopsis: When the daughter of a retired Army martial arts expert (Arnold Schwarzenegger) is kidnapped by a Latin American strongman to force him to assassinate a political rival, he turns, instead, to assassinating the kidnapper's entire army. Mark Lester's direction has a certain leavening of comic book humor, but it won't seem especially funny unless you happen to think there is something intrinsically amusing about sudden death. Unrelenting celebration of violence

title: Commandos Strike at Dawn, The
synopsis: After the German Army occupies Norway in 1940, a fisherman (Paul Muni) assassinates the German commandant of his village, then spots a camouflaged enemy airbase, escapes to Britain and returns with a commando unit to destroy it. Director John Farrow's wartime morale booster is quite effective in its depiction of innocent villagers (Lillian Gish, Ray Collins and others) brutalized by a cruel enemy and the bravery of Norwegian patriots in league with their British allies. Wartime violence and much menace

title: Command, The
synopsis: Pale Western in which a doctor (Guy Madison) is the only officer left to command the cavalry squadron escorting a wagon train through hostile Indian country. Directed by David Butler, the hokey proceedings include an outbreak of chicken pox and the doctor's unorthodox military tactics which include dressing some troopers in women's outfits. Frontier violence

title: Commissar
synopsis: In a small Ukrainian village after the Bolshevik Revolution, a pregnant commissar (Nonna Mordukova) is given shelter by a poor Jewish family. Russian director Aleksandr Askoldov's 1967 movie shows compassion for the family whose lives are threatened by local anti-Semites and by political enemies of the commissar. Subtitles. Some rough language, an intense childbirth scene and a harrowing anti-Semitic children's game

title: Commitments, The
synopsis: Soul music, 1960's-style, resurfaces in of all places, Dublin, when an unemployed Irish youth (Robert Arkins) fashions a band out of an experienced trumpeter (Johnny Murphy) and 9 cheeky working-class youngsters. Director Alan Parker's vibrant, gritty movie ultimately goes over the top but not before it has energetically celebrated hope amidst poverty, the vitality of youth and the power of music. Much rough language, intermittent sexual innuendo and minimal violence

title: Committee, The
synopsis: Stage revue featuring the antics of eight young West Coast comics was videotaped during a performance and the results were then transferred to color fi1m. Produced and directed by Del Jack, the program consists of 18 sometimes lively skits, often spiked with adult language, that concentrate on exposing the foibles of everyday life, especially of young couples, married and unmarried. Though there are some good laughs, it's for those who appreciate satire even when it misses

title: Common Clay
synopsis: Period tearjerker in which an arrested speakeasy hostess (Constance Bennett) seeks reformation by becoming a maid in a wealthy household but is seduced by the family's son (Lew Ayres), then abandoned when she becomes pregnant. Directed by Victor Fleming, matters are resolved in a trial whose wildly sentimental contrivances may evoke laughter today, though the picture's condemnation of womanizers is as valid now as then. Implicit sexual affairs and innuendo

title: Companeros
synopsis: Italian-Spanish-German production shot mostly in English and set in turn-of-the-century Mexico finds Franco Nero running guns during the revolution. Director Sergio Corbucci clutters the story with plenty of loudly-staged massacres, a fair share of unusual tortures and a bit of sexual innuendo

title: Company Man
synopsis: Intermittently amusing comedy about a hen-pecked school teacher (Douglas McGrath) who, fed up the relentless nagging from his social climbing wife (Sigourney Weaver), ends up in the middle of the Bay of Pigs invasion pretending to be a secret CIA agent. As written and directed by Douglas McGrath and Peter Askin, the ensemble cast in the zany farce is just going through the motions despite terrific rapid-fire one-liners and fun madcap mayhem. Several sexual references, fleeting rear nudity, brief drug content and an instance of crass language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Company of Killers
synopsis: Van Johnson heads a special police squad trained for unusual assignments, while Ray Milland sets the wheels in motion for a murder to help his financial designs. Routine crime melodrama directed by Jerry Thorpe contains mild doses of violence, sex and some ambiguous religious themes

title: Competition, The
synopsis: Rival concert pianists (Richard Dreyfuss and Amy Irving) fall in love but have problems because of his sense of insecurity in a romantic melodrama written and directed by Joel Oliansky. Despite good performances, it is but mediocre entertainment marred by crude sexual references and a graphic bedroom scene

title: Compromising Positions
synopsis: A former journalist (Susan Sarandon), caught up in the investigation into the murder of a womanizing dentist (Joe Mantegna), does some snooping on her own and comes into conflict with the detective in charge (Raul Julia). Director Frank Perry's shallow, contrived and unpleasant comedy-mystery leans heavily on crude, sexually oriented humor

title: Compulsion
synopsis: Fictionalized account of the Leopold-and-Loeb murder case in 1924 Chicago where the prosecutor (E.G. Marshall) demands the death penalty for two university students (Dean Stockwell and Bradford Dillman) in a thrill killing until their attorney (Orson Welles) makes the case for sentencing them to life imprisonment, Directed by Richard Fleischer, the dramatization is quite effective in its portrayal of the students, the police work which led to their arrest and the tense courtroom proceedings which end by putting capital punishment on trial. Verbal descriptions of an off-screen murder, a sexual encounter and arguments for and against the death penalty

title: Computer Wore Tennis Shoes, The
synopsis: Typical Disney comedy in which none-too-bright college student (Kurt Russell) accidentally has his brain computerized and becomes an intellectual phenomenon who by chance threatens the operations of a racketeer (Cesar Romero). Director Robert Butler's movie is a zany, very superficial comedy intended to amuse youngsters

title: Comrade X
synopsis: Wacky romantic comedy set in Moscow where an American reporter (Clark Gable) woos a patriotic streetcar conductor (Hedy Lamarr) while trying to keep track of Kremlin intrigues. Director King Vidor's dated spoof of life in the Soviet Union has some very funny moments but not enough to sustain interest in the slapstick plot and belabored East-West romance. Comic political menace and romantic complications

title: Conan the Barbarian
synopsis: Based on a pulp hero's violent exploits in savage prehistoric times, the movie's preliterate narrative ponderously details how the slow-witted Conan (Arno1d Schwarzenegger) revenges the slaughter of his parents. John Milius directs with heavy emphasis on brutality, violence and some graphic sex

title: Conan the Destroyer
synopsis: Director Richard Fleischer's sequel may be more polished and less gory than the original, but with Arnold Schwarzenegger again in the title role the result is still nothing more than a lead-footed, muscle-bound costume epic with an extremely high violence quotient

title: Concert for Bangladesh
synopsis: Saul Swimmer's documentary record of a landmark benefit concert in New York's Madison Square Gardens features the performances of Bob Dylan, Billy Preston, Eric Clapton, Leon Russell, Ravi Shankar and Ringo Star to name a few of those who appeared

title: Concorde -- Airport '79, The
synopsis: Another in the series of airport movies with the usual multitude of disasters and film stars (Alain Delon, Susan Blakely, Robert Wagner, et. al.) who can do nothing with the script's ineptness. Directed by David Lowell Rich, it contains harsh language and casual love affairs

title: Concrete Jungle, The
synopsis: Low-budget women-in-prison melodrama is directed by Tom De Simone as another exploitative sex-and-violence movie. Much nudity

title: Condemned Women
synopsis: Formula prison tale directed by Lew Landers focuses on an embittered inmate (Sally Eilers) who falls for the idealistic prison doctor (Louis Hayward), then thinking her love will bring him disgrace, joins a hardened con (Lee Patrick) in making a jail break. Stylized violence and penal injustices

title: Conduct Unbecoming
synopsis: Set on India's Northwest Frontier in 1878, the honor of the regiment is at stake when a flirtatious widow (Suzannah York) accuses a young subaltern (James Faulkner) of assaulting her. With an idealist (Michael York) appointed to defend him, the movie turns from larger issues of conflicting claims of duty and loyalty and becomes no more than a whodunit of only moderate ingenuity. Directed by Michael Anderson, the movie offers a very talented cast, magnificent locales and exotic costumes but only mediocre drama

title: Coneheads
synopsis: Having crash-landed on planet Earth, Mr. and Mrs. Conehead (Dan Aykroyd and Jane Curtin) pursue the American dream in their own weird ways while raising a precocious teenager (Michelle Burke) and avoiding immigration agents anxious to deport them back to the planet Remulak. Director Steve Barron stitches together a pleasantly daffy assemblage of episodic skits inspired by Akyroyd and Curtin's original 1970's Conehead sketches on TV's ``Saturday Night Live.'' Some mild sexual innuendo, fleeting rear nudity and occasional tasteless humor

title: Coney Island
synopsis: Standard musical romance directed by Walter Lang with a colorful 1890's honky-tonk background for a story of long-time competitors (George Montgomery and Cesar Romero) out-tricking each other over a popular singer (Betty Grable) who has a mind of her own. Duplicitous romantic complications and ethnic stereotypes

title: Confessions of a Dangerous Mind
synopsis: Unappealing tale based on the memoirs of Chuck Barris (Sam Rockwell), the crass TV producer of "The Dating Game" and "The Gong Show," who claims to have led a double life which included killing 33 people for the CIA. As stylishly directed by co-star George Clooney, the self-centered, sex-obsessed Barris flaunts his contempt for traditional values, seemingly learning nothing as the movie concludes on a smug, nihilistic note. Intermittent violence, promiscuous sexual encounters, crude sexual references, recurring rear nudity, some profanity and excessive rough language

title: Confessions of a Police Captain
synopsis: Italian story of corruption in high places features a police official Martin Balsam) who will use any method, including assassination, to get rid of crooks, and a young prosecutor (Franco Nero) who is an honest but ineffectual bureaucrat. Directed by Damiano Damiani, the result is little more than a pot boiler with considerable violence

title: Confessions of a Window Cleaner
synopsis: Infantile sex comedy with a pimply young apprentice window-washer (Robin Askwith) as he makes his predictable rounds of surburban London. Witless sniggering and leering sex

title: Confessions of Boston Blackie
synopsis: Solid series episode directed by Edward Dmytryk in which the reformed title jewel thief (Chester Morris) and his ex-con aide (George E. Stone) elude a New York cop (Richard Lane) while helping a dim millionaire (Lloyd Corrigan) who bought a fake statue unaware it contains the body of a murdered art dealer. Stylized violence, menacing situations and mild sexual innuendo

title: Confessions of Tom Harris
synopsis: The story of a tough mob enforcer (Don Murray) whose chance encounter with a woman (Linda Evans) led to his religious conversion at her father's commune for the spiritual and physical rehabilitation of alcoholics. Murray also wrote and produced, but neither he nor co-directors John Derek and David Nelson seem capable of capturing the spiritual malaise or, for that matter, the religious convictions of the characters in their drama. The result is a series of incidents, ranging all the way from a rape to a symbolic re-creation of the Last Supper, which convey little of human or religious significance

title: Confession, The
synopsis: Dramatic re-creation of the 1951 Czechoslavakian Purge Trials in which 14 dedicated Party members were convicted of high treason, to which all confessed though none were involved in any kind of political plot. Director Costa-Gavras focuses on one of them (Yves Montand), showing the process by which the man's idealistic faith in the Party was used against him in obtaining his confession

title: Confetti
synopsis: Three couples -- played by Martin Freeman and Jessica Stevenson, Stephen Mangan and Meredith MacNeill, and Robert Webb and Olivia Colman -- vie for "most original wedding in Britain" in a competition run by the executives at a British bridal magazine, and plan themes of Hollywood musicals, tennis and nudism for their ceremonies, respectively, under the guidance of a couple of campy wedding planners (Vincent Franklin and Jason Watkins). Director Debbie Isitt's largely improvised satire generates some laughs and contains truths about human relationships, but some may be put off by a fair amount of expletives and by the uninhibited -- if utterly nonsexual -- nudity of the naturalist pair. Conversational rough language and profanity, full male and female nudity, some innuendo, a brief hint of a gay marriage at end of film and a couple of rough brawls

title: Confidence
synopsis: Slick, shallow caper in which a tight-knit group of con men (led by Ed Burns) rips off a crime lord (Dustin Hoffman) so must agree to pull off a very dicey scam as repayment, despite a federal agent (Andy Garcia) closing in on them. Director James Foley's smug movie, with its crime-definitely-pays perspective, admires its brutal characters and seems most impressed with its own cleverness and cynical worldview. Some violence, brief nudity, seamy sexual situations, recurring profanities and constant rough language

title: Confidential Report
synopsis: ( see: "Mr. Arkadin" )

title: Confirm or Deny
synopsis: Hokey wartime romance between an American newspaperman (Don Ameche) and a British teletypist (Joan Bennett) bogs down in his attempt to get a scoop involving military secrets. Director Archie Mayo invests the trite tale with the tense atmosphere of London during the Blitz and good chunks of both comedy and pathos from the supporting cast (Roddy McDowall, Arthur Shields and Raymond Walburn). Wartime violence and romantic situations

title: Conformist, The
synopsis: Italian movie about a man (Jean-Louis Trintingnant) who joins the Fascist party and is eventually entrusted with a mission to kill one of his former university professors who is now causing trouble for the regime. Director Bernardo Bertolucci's portrait of a man who goes along with those in authority is frighteningly real and much more dangerous than any political fanatic. The central theme of the movie is a cautionary one for any politically threatened society though it has powerful scenes of violence and sexual inferences including that of homosexuality

title: Confrontation
synopsis: In 1936 a Jewish medical student assassinated the leader of the Nazi Party in Switzerland, an event and an era that this Swiss production has succeeded in re-creating with vivid force. Directed by Rolf Lyssy, the movie does not defend political murder but poses the kind of moral problems individuals must face in a time when injustice is an accepted national policy

title: Congo
synopsis: Love, greed and scientific pursuits bring together a zoologist (Dylan Walsh), a tough corporate executive (Laura Linney) and a bogus philanthropist (Tim Curry) who hire a savvy guide (Ernie Hudson) to get them into and out of a abandoned camp in wartorn Zaire where a fabled diamond mine and a previously unknown species of killer apes await them. Director Frank Marshall's visually impressive but contrived thriller pits high-tech humans against the forces of nature, but the campy performances and plastic dialogue have a lame comic-book effect. Brief bloody violence, much menace and a few profanities

title: Congo Crossing
synopsis: Wooden adventure tale directed by Joseph Pevney in which a surveyor (George Nader) finds a track of unclaimed land and helps a group of fugitives (Virginia Mayo, Peter Lorre, Rex Ingram and others) settle there. Stylized violence and sexual innunedo

title: Congo Maisie
synopsis: Wisecracking, man-savvy Maisie (Ann Sothern) turns up in darkest Africa to chastise a wolf (John Carroll), save a marriage (Rita Johnson and Shepperd Strudwick) and quell a native uprising. Directed by H.C. Potter, it's an early offering of the breezy comedy series featuring the likeable Southern in formula plots with thinbare budgets. Some racial stereotyping and mild sexual innuendo

title: Conjugal Bed, The
synopsis: Despairing melodrama set in contemporary Romania where a brutally abusive husband (Gheorghe Dinica), lusting after his mistress-turned-prostitute, determines to kill his pregnant wife, then hangs himself when she survives his hammering a nail into her brain. Director Mircea Daneliuc ineptly attempts to satirize a post-communist society by picturing its unstable economy as the principal reason virtually all of the characters act irrationally. Graphic spousal abuse, gory violence, mindless promiscuity, much nudity and frequent rough language

title: Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court, A
synopsis: Uneven musical fantasy derived from Mark Twain's tale of a blacksmith (Bing Crosby) hit on the head in turn-of-the-century New England, then awakened in sixth-century Camelot by a knight (William Bendix) of the Round Table. Directed by Tay Garnett, Crosby's bemused Sir Boss is entirely agreeable and Sir Cedric Hardwicke's Arthur is drolly dense, but the action rarely measures up to its comic potential and the forgettable songs add little to the entertainment. Brief stylized violence

title: Connie and Carla
synopsis: Breezy and brassy comedy about two struggling Chicago-based lounge singers (Nia Vardalos and Toni Collette), who, after witnessing a gangland execution, hightail it to Los Angeles to hide out, disguising themselves as drag queens who wind up becoming overnight sensations, headlining in a cross-dressing cabaret show. Director Michael Lembeck's film strikes a palatable though at times preachy tone, poking fun at the flamboyant female impersonators while stressing their humanity. A sympathetic portrayal of the gay lifestyle, recurring sexual humor, a sacrilegious comment, an instance of same-sex kissing, intermittent crude language and a few drug references

title: Conqueror, The
synopsis: Epic clunker about the early years of 12th-century Mongol leader Genghis Khan (John Wayne) who kills a powerful ally (Thomas Gomez) after his brothers (Pedro Armendariz and William Conrad) prove his treachery, then goes on to defeat the Tartar chief (Ted de Corsia) and wed his daughter (Susan Hayward). Directed by Dick Powell, there is plenty of bloody action in large-scale battles as well as individual combat, but the characters are cardboard primitives who happen to speak broken English. Much stylized gore and some sexual situations

title: Conqueror Worm, The
synopsis: Inept British horror movie about a 17th-century witchhunter (Vincent Price) who combines his delight in human suffering with the profits he makes out of his trade. Directed by Michael Reeves, it offers little more than a series of sadistic episodes

title: Conquest of Cochise
synopsis: The 1853 Gasden Purchase brings a U.S. cavalry unit (led by Robert Stack) to the former Mexican town of Tuscon where the title's Apache chief (John Hodiak) agrees to keep the peace despite American troublemakers. Directed by William Castle, the period is colorful with a rich mixture of Indians, Mexicans and gringos but the action is not in least credible. Frontier violence

title: Conquest of Space
synopsis: Ordered to pilot a rocket ship to Mars from the space station he's just constructed, a colonel (Walter Brooke) enroute developes religious scruples over tampering with the universe and tries to destroy craft and crew (Eric Fleming, Mickey Shaughnessy, Phil Foster and others). Produced by George Pal and directed by Byron Haskin, the heavy-handed plot and wooden acting are overshadowed by the special effects and novel notions of space flight. Menacing situations and occasional sexual innuendo

title: Conquest of the Planet of the Apes
synopsis: This fourth attempt at reworking the same material marks the fatal deterioration of a series that had some good moments. This time around all the apes on earth are abject slaves until a new Moses (Roddy McDowell) leads them in revolt against their cruel masters. Under J. Lee Thompson's direction there is too much violence for youngsters who might otherwise buy this stale stuff but it won't satisfy anyone else

title: Conrack
synopsis: Jon Voight gives a convincingly exuberant performance as the idealistic white teacher who comes to a remote sea island off the coast of South Carolina to teach the island's black children. The problems he encounters in adjusting to the island's timeless way of life, in reaching his students with useful knowledge and in dealing with suspicious adults and cranky school officials form the core of an unusual and often moving work. Director Martin Ritt does well with a movie that is enjoyable, funny, sad, poignant, full of hope and real feeling for people

title: Consenting Adults
synopsis: Sleazy thriller in which a musician (Kevin Kline) is framed for murdering the wife (Rebecca Miller) of his diabolical next-door neighbor (Kevin Spacey) who then takes up with the musician's wife (Mary Elizabeth Mastrantonio). Director Alan J. Pakula glosses over gaping plot implausibilities with a manipulative scenario glamorizing marital infidelity and making insurance fraud seem an easy solution to financial problems. Brief graphic violence, a titillating wife-swapping scene, many sexual references, occasional nudity and minimal rough language

title: Consolation Marriage
synopsis: Creaky romantic melodrama in which a wise-cracking reporter (Pat O'Brien) marries a shopkeeper (Irene Dunne) for a lark after both are jilted by their true loves (Myrna Loy and Leslie Vail), then face divorce when their former beaus resurface several years -- and a child -- later. Director Paul Sloane's sentimental sudser is helped considerably by a likeable cast, though its sappy treatment of the mating game turns heart-throbs into empty contrivances. Shallow view of marriage

title: Conspiracy of Silence
synopsis: Insipid thriller set in modern-day Ireland about a muckraking reporter (Jason Barry) who, while investigating the connections between two seemingly unrelated events -- the suicide of a local priest and the expulsion of a young, idealistic seminarian (Jonathan Forbes) -- uncovers a secret incriminating those in the highest ranks of the church. With little in the way of plausible suspense, director John Deery uses the film's slim story line as a rod on which to hang his grievances, including the church's stands on homosexuality and celibacy, employing caricature and distortion to position the hierarchy as one-dimensionally corrupt. A manipulative and sinister portrayal of the institutional church, including anti-clerical characterizations, a suicide, a sexual encounter with shadowy nudity, a shower scene with rear nudity, brief violence, and recurring rough and crude language

title: The Conspirator
synopsis: Engrossing historical drama, set in the final days of the Civil War, in which a Union Army officer-turned-lawyer (James McAvoy) is called upon to defend Mary Surratt (Robin Wright), the pro-Confederate widow in whose Washington boardinghouse John Wilkes Booth and his co-conspirators -- including her own son John (Johnny Simmons) -- plotted to kill Abraham Lincoln. Initially convinced of his client's guilt, the attorney's views shift as he witnesses the ruthless maneuvering of the prosecution team (led by Danny Huston) at her military tribunal. His new outlook leads to friendship with Mary's daughter Anna (Evan Rachel Wood) but alienates the powerful secretary of war (Kevin Kline) as well as the young barrister's socialite fiancee (Alexis Bledel). In recounting an episode with obvious implications for contemporary debates about the proper treatment of accused terrorists, director Robert Redford avoids heavy-handed politicking. Instead, his portrait of a protagonist admirably committed to the rule of law is made all the more effective by the fair assessment of those with other legitimate priorities. A similarly balanced approach characterizes the portrayal of Surratt's devout Catholic faith. Possibly acceptable for older teens. Some wartime gore, a realistic hanging, a couple of crude and crass terms

title: Constantine
synopsis: Intensely violent action film, based on the "Hellblazer" graphic novels, about a world-weary, chain-smoking exorcist (Keanu Reeves) fighting lung cancer and demonic forces with the help of a police detective (Rachel Weisz), whose twin sister either committed suicide or was murdered and is now consigned to the fires of hell. Though gussied up with all sorts of religious mumbo jumbo -- the powers of good versus the forces of evil, self-sacrifice, redemption, a Gabriel character (Tilda Swinton), and a "sword of destiny" (aka the weapon used to pierce Christ on the cross) -- Francis Lawrence's film is basically another formulaic action film -- think "The Exorcist," "Alien" and "The Matrix" rolled into one -- that's only fitfully interesting, when the gory bits aren't positively wince-inducing. Graphic violence with attendant gore, some rough and crude language, and some sacrilegious imagery

title: Constantine's Sword
synopsis: Earnest but unbalanced documentary, adapted from ex-priest James Carroll's "Constantine's Sword: The Church and the Jews -- A History," surveys the fraught history of Christian anti-Semitism, particularly as it plays out among American evangelicals today, and its roots dating back to the early days of the Roman Catholic Church, incorporating seminal episodes from his life story, including his sometimes conflicted relationship with his father, and his ultimate disillusionment with the institutional church. Director Oren Jacoby's film ignores some significant nuances in the historical record, as it broadly outlines the tragic conflict. Mature religious themes, one use of the f-word and occasional crude and crass language

title: Contest Girl, The
synopsis: Superficial British movie debunking beauty contests tells the story of a newspaper editor (Ian Hendry) teaching a nobody (Janette Scott) the tricks of the beauty game. Produced and directed by Val Guest, the movie and its moral are skin deep. Suggestive costuming and some sexual innuendo

title: Continental Divide
synopsis: A hotshot Chicago newspaperman (John Belushi) and an ornithologist who studies eagles in the Rockies (B1air Brown) fall in love, though both are lost outside of their chosen habitat. The attempt to resurrect a 1940's type of romantic comedy comes to grief because of Lawrence Kasdan's lackluster script and Michae1 Apted's uncertain direction. Winks at premarital sex and some brief nudity

title: Conversations With God
synopsis: Drama based on the successful series of spiritual self-help books by author Neale Donald Walsch (Henry Czerny), who, after losing his job and finding himself homeless, alleges that God, prompted by his questioning, began speaking to him directly, with their ongoing "conversation" resulting in his best-sellers. Earnestly directed by Stephen Simon, the film fluctuates between maudlin and genuinely moving, and while clearly containing ideas (a hodgepodge of gnosticism, pantheism and New Age mysticism) incompatible with Christian theology, nevertheless imparts a sincere message about God's unconditional love and abiding presence that should resonate with Catholic viewers. Questionable theological underpinnings, some mature themes and brief mild innuendo

title: Conversation, The
synopsis: Intricate story about the world of electronic eavesdropping in which a colorless professional bugger (Gene Hackman) is hired to spy on a young couple but then finds himself being spied upon. Directed by Francis Ford Coppola, it is beautifully acted, meticulously paced and of interest because it looks at some of the ambiguities and shades of responsibility in the subterranean area of electronic snooping as practiced by anonymous professionals for hire. Some violence

title: Convicted Woman
synopsis: Dated women-behind-bars story directed by Nick Grinde tells of an innocent inmate (Rochelle Hudson) who, aided by a sympathetic reporter (Glenn Ford), blows the whistle on prison abuses and helps turn the place into a model rehabilitation facility. Stylized violence, including an inmate's suicide

title: Convicts 4
synopsis: Fact-based story of a man (Ben Gazarra) whose 1931 death sentence is commuted to life imprisonment, then makes several attempts to escape until prodded by a reform-minded warden (Stuart Whitman) to develope his talents as an artist which gains his freedom in 1949. Writer-director Millard Kaufman presents an earnest, low-key account of events with a number of star cameos (Vincent Price, Broderick Crawford, Rod Steiger, Sammy Davis, Jr., and others), but the characters are one-dimensional and the results emotionally shallow. Stylized violence, oppressive prison atmosphere and domestic problems

title: Convoy
synopsis: Kris Kristofferson plays a free-spirited trucker who finds himself turned into a folk hero when he leads a group of fellow truckers across state lines in protest against police harassment. A1i MacGraw goes along for the ride. Director Sam Peckinpah lends some visual energy to an otherwise muddled, pretentious and often quite ludicrous movie displaying casual sex and a sophomoric disregard for the law

title: Coogan's Bluff
synopsis: Arizona deputy (Clint Eastwood) runs amok in Manhattan while tracking down an escaped prisoner. Action director Don Siegel emphasizes sex and sadism in a plot based on the premise that law enforcement should not be bound by constitutuiona1 restraints. Excessive violence and sex

title: Cookie
synopsis: Director Susan Seidelman tracks the comic transformation of an 18-year-old alienated adolescent (Emily Lloyd) into a street-smart Mafia princess who saves the life of her mobster father (Peter Falk) and unifies an offbeat family, including the mobster's wife (Brenda Vaccaro) and mistress (Dianne Wiest). Colorful performances, however, cannot make up for a far-fetched ending, a weak attempt at mob satire and an uninsightful look at an offbeat father-daughter relationship. Much profanity and a cavalier attitude toward murder and adultery

title: The Cookout
synopsis: Forgettable comedy about a young basketball player (Storm P) who, after striking it rich as the NBA's No. 1 draft pick, decides to throw a family barbeque at his palatial new home in an exclusive white suburban community, policed by an overzealous security guard (Queen Latifah). Mayhem ensues when the cookout turns into a tug-of-war between his eccentric relatives, who want to make sure that his newfound success doesn't go to his head, and his gold-digger girlfriend, (Meagan Good), who's just after his money. While imparting a message that family is more important than fame, much of Lance Rivera's unfunny directorial debut only serves to reinforce many of the African-American stereotypes it purports to discredit. Some crass sexual and racial humor, drug content and recurring crude language

title: Cook, the Thief, His Wife and Her Lover, The
synopsis: Boring when not repellent British production about a feral mobster (Michael Gambon) and his wife (Helen Mirren) who spend their evenings in a restaurant owned by the husband -- he gorging himself on delicacies prepared by a French chef (Richard Bohringer) while she makes love to a bookseller between courses in an affair that has dire, gruesome results. Written and directed by Peter Greenaway, it's a pointless exercise in moral decadence treated in tedious, pretentious fashion. Excessive violence, unremitting brutality, exploitative sex scenes and rough language

title: Cool Breeze
synopsis: Black exploitation movie traces the generally downhill course of a gang of thieves (Thalmus Rasulala, Raymond St. Jacques, Jim Watkins and Lincoln Kilpatrick). Written and directed by Barry Pollack, it has atrocious dialogue covering every racial stereotype and gripe in the book, flashy violence, gratuitous nudity and a particularly offensive attitutde toward black women

title: Cooley High
synopsis: Director Michael Schultz' story of young blacks, graduating seniors, in Chicago in the mid-1960s, has some good acting (Glynn Turman and Lawrence-Hilton Jacobs) and flashes of honesty and insight about ghetto life but its narrative is by turns clumsy and pretentious. More seriously, sexual promisicuity is either played largely for laughs, despite the hurt looks on the faces of the girls cast aside, or, in the case of its hero, given lyrical treatment hard to condone in a work aimed at a young audience

title: Cool Hand Luke
synopsis: Nonconformist loner (Paul Newman), sentenced to a brutal Southern prison farm, gains the respect of his fellow inmates for standing up to the guards's degrading treatment and cruel punishments. Director Stuart Rosenberg relieves the grim situation with some well-paced humor and Newman's memorable performance in the title role transforms Luke from a pathetic victim of an unjust system into a symbol of the rebellious spirit that refuses to accept the legitimacy of power. A few scenes of brutality that some might consider excessive

title: Cool Ones, The
synopsis: Once-popular singing idol (Gil Peterson) tries to stage a comeback but his struggles are complicated by a budding romance that his manager (Roddy McDowall) threatens to ruin. Director Gene Nelson contributes much ado about nothing

title: Cool Runnings
synopsis: Coached by a disgraced former Olympian (John Candy), four feisty Jamaicans (Leon, Doug E. Doug, Malik Yoba and Rawle D. Lewis) who had never even seen snow arrive in Calgary, Canada in hopes of representing their country in the 1988 Winter Olympics by qualifying as a bobsled team. Jon Turteltaub directs a high-spirited, loosely fact-based underdog story that never loses its sense of good, clean fun as the foursome practice on junkyard parts under a tropical sun, ignoring ridicule and impossible odds. Fleeting violence

title: Cool World
synopsis: Catapulted into his own two-dimensional comic strip world, a cartoonist (Gabriel Byrne) is seduced into helping one of his vampy creations (Kim Basinger) cross over to the real world where they are pursued by a hard-boiled detective (Brad Pitt) who knows their secret. Director Ralph Bakshi's manic mix of busy animation and live action produces an outlandishly uneven movie more adult in its sexual content than the juvenile story would suggest. Cartoon violence and suggestive sexual situations

title: Coonskin
synopsis: Ralph Bakshi's animated feature with some live action tells the story of three southern blacks (a rabbit, bear and fox) who go to Harlem, take over the rackets and vanquish a corrupt white policeman and a gross Mafia don's brood of murderous homosexual sons. Though it has some effective scenes of indignation at the squalor and hopelessness of ghetto life, the satire places heavy emphasis upon violent action, brutal caricature and a heavy-handed use of sex

title: Cop
synopsis: Exploitative crime thriller with James Woods as an obsessed Los Angeles detective who concocts a profile of a serial killer responsible for 15 years of unsolved murders of a young women. Written and directed by James B. Harris, the unpalatable, implausible cop melodrama features a detective whose blatant sexism and vigilante mentality are totally repugnant. Extreme violence, gratuitous sex, graphic shots of murder victims and profanity

title: Copacabana
synopsis: Lame musical comedy in which a jobless comic (Groucho Marx) persuades his former partner (Carmen Miranda) to audition for the title nightclub, first as a Brazilian singer, then a French one, and the club's unwitting owner (Steve Cochran) hires both. Directed by Alfred E. Green, the comic premise of one singer masquerading as two is frantic but tiresome, with Groucho limited to occasional one-liners, leaving the entertainment mostly in musical numbers featuring Miranda, Andy Russell and the club's showgirls. Romantic complications and mild sexual innuendo

title: Cop and a Half
synopsis: Cantankerous police detective (Burt Reynolds) humors an 8-year-old (Norman D. Golden II) by making him a member of the Tampa police force in order to get details of a murder the child witnessed, all the while have to protect the boy from the killers. Director Henry Winkler's one-joke comedy wears thin fast and may give children the wrong impression about the very real dangers inherent in police work. Menace to a child, frequent violence depicted comically and occasional toilet humor

title: Cop-Out
synopsis: Failed British murder mystery directed by Pierre Rouve has a generation-gap story of alcoholic lawyer (James Mason) whose neglect of his daughter (Geraldine Chaplin) leads to her joining the wrong crowd. Muddled story line fails to integrate several sexually suggestive sequences and a near rape

title: Copper Canyon
synopsis: Slack Western in which an ex-Confederate colonel (Ray Milland) saves some fellow Southerners from losing their Arizona copper mine to a villainous Northern lawman (Macdonald Carey). Directed by John Farrow, there's nothing new here, though Hedy Lamarr is pleasantly restrained as the romantic interest. Stylized violence

title: Copper Sky
synopsis: Small Western in which a hard-drinking drifter (Jeff Morrow) and a prim schoolmarm fresh from Boston (Coleen Gray) escape an Apache massacre and head for safety in a wagon, then on foot. Directed by Charles Marquis Warren, this variation on "The African Queen" makes some intelligent use of the Old West setting but the mismatched couple never becomes anything more interesting than stereotypes. Stylized violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Cops and Robbers
synopsis: Nifty comedy about two New York policemen (Joe Bologna and Cliff Gorman) who hatch the perfect crime in a scheme to steal and sell $10 million in bearer bonds to the Mafia. Director Aram Avakian breaks up the humor by building in some taut sequences showing the risks and demands of day-to-day police work in a big city environment, keeping the viewer from asking the sort of logical questions that might puncture the plot. Stylized violence

title: Cops and Robbersons
synopsis: Tepid comedy in which a crusty police detective (Jack Palance) sets up a stakeout in the home of a bumbling dad (Chevy Chase) who jeopardizes the operation by his unwanted, over-eager participation. Director Michael Ritchie allows Chase his familiar klutzy persona and Palance his wry snarls, but never does much with either in this unengaging one-joke comedy. Some violence, mostly of a comic nature, brief nudity with mild sexual innuendo and a sprinkling of profanity

title: Cop, The
synopsis: In order to avenge the death of a fellow policeman, an honest cop (Michel Bouquet) takes the law into his own hands, becoming as ruthless as the gangsters he hunts. Director Yves Boisset has made a fast-moving action film, hard-edged in violence, but with all elements completely integrated in expressing his theme of moral and social corruption

title: Copycat
synopsis: Twisted thriller in which a San Francisco homicide detective (Holly Hunter) tries to nab a cunning serial killer with the reluctant aid of an expert criminal psychologist (Sigourney Weaver) who's still traumatized by a murderous encounter with a patient. Directed by Jon Amiel, the plot has interest until disintegrating into a repelling horror show featuring the gruesome killer and his tortured victims. Excessive violence and gore, brief nudity and much rough language

title: Coraline
synopsis: Entrancing, though eerie, 3-D animated cautionary tale in which a bored girl (voice of Dakota Fanning) discovers an alternate world inhabited by more accommodating versions of her parents (voices of Teri Hatcher and John Hodgman) but finds herself imperiled when the doubles reveal sinister plans for her. Writer-director Henry Selick's vibrantly colorful stop-motion adaptation of Neil Gaiman's best-selling, award-winning 2002 young adult novel sees its heroine overcoming selfishness, learning to appreciate her blessings and drawing closer to family and friends. Brief partial nudity, frightening images and a few mildly bawdy lyrics

title: Cora Ashamed
synopsis: Cora Unashamed -- Compelling and complex drama set in a small southern town during the Depression about an African-American servant (Regina Taylor) who becomes the confidante and protector of the daughter (Ellen Muth) of her tyrannical, social driven employer (Cherry Jones) who forces the teen-ager to have an abortion. Director Deborah M. Pratt's fine production is a quietly powerful story with wonderful performances that presents the abortion issue from a negative perspective. An implied sexual relationship and an abortion

title: Corky
synopsis: Amateur hotshot speedster (Robert Blake) wants to make the big-time as a professional driver but from the very first scene, when he beats out another car at a stoplight, endangering wife, children, and best friend, it is obvious this is the story of a loser. Directed by Leonard Horn, the track footage has class, the Southern locales and people are evoked quite well and Blake's performance as a man whose delusions lead to inevitable self-destruction is first-rate

title: Corky Romano
synopsis: Mindless comedy about the goofy veterinarian son (Chris Kattan) of a Mafia boss (Peter Falk) who poses as an FBI agent to retrieve evidence the Feds have on his dad. Director Rob Pritts' tired fish-out-of-water premise garners a few chuckles from the silly circumstances and Kattan's shameless lunacy, but the comedy trudges along, feebly throwing in a lesson about family acceptance at the end. Recurring comically intended violence, some mild sexual humor including homosexual jokes, brief drug content and intermittent crass language with profanity

title: Cornbread, Earl and Me
synopsis: When a black youth (Keith Wilkes) is shot accidentally by two policemen, one black and one white, the city administration engages in a coverup but a lawyer (Moses Gunn), hired by the parents, clears their son's name. Directed by Joe Manduke, the movie deals well with the complexity of black-white relations and has a fine, convincing cast. Mature treatment

title: Cornered
synopsis: Tough thriller in which a Canadian airman (Dick Powell) tracks the Nazi agent responsible for his wife's death to Buenos Aires where he stumbles into a nest of escaped war criminals and their Argentinian collaborators (notably Walter Slezak). Director Edward Dmytryk keeps the tension high as the vengeful veteran blunders through the devious intrigues of fascist agents and counter-agents in quest of personal justice. Stylized violence, some of it quite nasty

title: Corn Is Green, The
synopsis: Fine adaptation of the Emlyn Williams play set in 1895 when a dedicated teacher (Bette Davis) wins over a Welsh mining town and the local lord (Nigel Bruce) through her perseverance in starting a school and preparing her prize student (John Dall) to take the entrance exam for Oxford. Directed by Irving Rapper, the performances and period setting convincingly demonstrate the value of universal education, though an unwed pregnancy seriously complicates matters

title: Coroner Creek
synopsis: Taut, no-frills Western about a cowboy (Randolph Scott) seeking to find the man (George Macready) who robbed a stagecoach and killed all its passengers. Directed by Ray Enright, the plot is anything but subtle yet holds sufficient interest until the final shootout. Stylized violence

title: Corpse Grinders, The
synopsis: Felines feeding on a new brand of cat food made from grain, exhumed corpses and freshly dispatched winos acquire a desire to attack their slovenly mistresses. Producer-director-editor Ted V. Mikels has made his dumb little movie in dim, closet-size settings which render transparent any horror that the disgusting plot and mangy characters might suggest

title: Corpse Vanishes, The
synopsis: Creaky chiller directed by Wallace Fox with Bela Lugosi as a mad botanist who has bred an orchid that emits a scent inducing a death-like paralysis in young women from whom he extracts a vital fluid needed for rejuvenating his aged wife (Elizabeth Russell). Horror hokum flavored with sinister atmosphere and dark sexual undertones

title: Corrina, Corrina
synopsis: Sentimental exercise in which a 7-year-old girl (Tina Majorino) is helped over the trauma of her mother's death by the take-charge housekeeper (Whoopi Goldberg) hired by her songwriter father (Ray Liotta) who slowly comes to appreciate how much the newcomer means to his daughter and, finally, to himself. Despite idealized characters and artifical situations, writer-director Jessie Nelson effectively manipulates viewers' deepfelt emotions about family, friends, romance and race in a story that has its heart in the right place. Some romantic complications and occasional racial epithets

title: Corruption
synopsis: Routine British thriller directed by Robert Hartford-Davis about a mad doctor (Peter Cushing) who murders women for their pitutary gland in a vain effort to restore the burned flesh of his beloved (Sue Lloyd). Graphic violence

title: Corvette K-225
synopsis: Patriotic World War II melodrama directed by Richard Rosson follows the captain (Randolph Scott) and crew (Barry Fitzgerald, Andy Devine and others) of the title Canadian warship in engagements with German submarines preying on a convoy they are escorting across the Atlantic. Wartime violence

title: Corvette Summer
synopsis: Innocent California high school senior (Mark Hamill) goes to Las Vegas to track down a car stolen from his shop class but things get very complicated once there. Boy meets aspiring hooker (Annie Potts), boy loses girl and regains his former ideals. Director Matthew Robbins' movie shows a much too benign acceptance of the affair between the two youngsters

title: Cosi
synopsis: Airy Australian comedy in which an easygoing college dropout (Ben Mendelsohn) is hired to stage an Italian opera in a mental institution using the unruly patients as the cast. Director Mark Joffe's well-acted ensemble piece is a warm-heartd look at the humanity of those with mental problems, demonstrating that creativity is not limited to the briliant. Fleeting violence, a live-in relationship and rough language

title: Cotton Club, The
synopsis: Big splashy celebration of the famous white-owned, black-talent nightclub that flourished in Harlem in the 1920s and 1930s has some entertaining moments, but it lacks emotional power and fails to mesh its two diverse elements: gangsters and show business. Directed by Francis Coppola with Richard Gere and Gregory Hines heading a good cast, the movie contains some very graphic violence and two restrained bedroom scenes

title: Cotton Comes to Harlem
synopsis: In a high-powered action story focusing on a big-time con game up in Harlem, two bumbling-but-uncanny detectives (Godfrey Cambridge and Raymond St. Jacques) unmask the fraud being worked by a back-to-Africa preacher (Calvin Lockhart). Directed by Ossie Davis, the dialogue and visuals are harsh and raunchy, with a lot of black racial humor and much gore to round things out

title: Cougar Country
synopsis: Semi-documentary on the life and hard times of a young cougar in the Great American Northwest makes a fine wildlife story, especially the earlier sequences showing the young animal learning to cope with life within its natural habitat. The going gets a little tougher when the grown cougar has to outwit human invaders of its domain. For the young and curious and all who enjoy the world of nature

title: Countdown
synopsis: Exciting visual exploration of the frantic behind-the-scenes activity surrounding a space launch. James Caan stars as the NASA astronaut whose life as a scientist spaceman is complicated by domestic troubles. Directed by Robert Altman, the location photography in the Houston ground control center and at Cape Kennedy overshadow the otherwise routine drama

title: Countdown at Kusini
synopsis: Directed by Ossie Davis and filmed in Nigeria, the movie's theme of struggle against neo-colonialism in Africa is never treated seriously and leads to no new insights into the old story of exploitation. Its muddled structure and melodramatic plot, however, wreck havoc with its credibility and do little to further the black image on the screen

title: Counter-Attack
synopsis: Soviet partisans (Paul Muni and Marguerite Chapman) hit a German command post to get vital information for an upcoming offensive, then spend most of the movie trapped in an underground bunker with their prisoners. Directed by Zoltan Korda, the patriotic paean to our World War II allies is short on both military as well as dramatic credibility. Stylized violence

title: Counterfeit Constable, The
synopsis: Droll British comedy directed by Robert Dhery about a Frenchman (Dhery) in England on the run from a publicity-seeking actress (Diana Dors), the police and his fiancee. Mild sexual innuendo

title: Counterfeit Killer
synopsis: Routine story of counterfeiters and treasury agents directed by Josef Leytes and with Jack Lord as the undercover man who infiltrates the gang and Shirley Knight as the waitress who falls in love with him. Fairly graphic violence

title: Counterpoint
synopsis: The fate of an entire symphony orchestra lies in the balance when a German general (Maximilian Shell) insists that they perform a concert and their conductor (Charlton Heston) refuses. Directed by Ralph Nelson, the World War II meldodrama's only merit is its classica1 music soundtrack. Wartime violence

title: Countess Dracula
synopsis: Aging countess (Ingrid Pitt) discovers quite by accident that her youth is revived by quick dips in virgin's blood. Directed by Peter Sasdy, the horror aspect is lost in a story line in which almost every relationship turns about the anticipation of a nude sexual encounter

title: Countess from Hong Kong, A
synopsis: The last movie directed by Charlie Chaplin is unfortunately an over-produced, heavy-handed romantic comedy about an impoverished countess (Sophia Loren) who tries to get into the U.S. by stowing away in the stateroom of an American diplomat (miscast Marlon Brando). The laughs are provided mainly by fellow passengers Margaret Rutherford and Patrick Cargill. Sexual situations and inferences

title: Count Five and Die
synopsis: Fact-based story of a World War II espionage unit (headed by Jeffrey Hunter and Nigel Patrick) whose mission is to convince German intelligence that the Allies plan to invade Holland rather than Normandy. Directed by Victor Vicas, the dramatic tension centers on neutralizing a double agent (Ann-Marie Duringer) within the London unit rather than on the morality of deliberately sacrificing members of the Dutch underground as part of the deception. Challenging fare

title: Count of Monte Cristo
synopsis: Rousing adaptation of Alexander Dumas' classic adventure tale about a sailor (Jim Caviezel) falsely imprisoned for treason who eventually escapes, reinvents himself as a count and wreaks revenge on the close friend (Guy Pearce) who framed him. As a deft visual storyteller, director Kevin Reynolds honors his source material by seamlessly interweaving themes of jealousy, betrayal and vengeance transformed into mercy and redemption in an opulent production, although it underplays the main character's spiritual struggles with God. An implied affair, fleeting sexuality and intermittent sword fights and gunplay

title: Country
synopsis: An Iowa family (Jessica Lange and Sam Shepard) trying to hold on to their farm while burdened with the interest due on massive governnent loans extended in more prosperous times. Nicely directed by Richard Pearce, it may be a little too predictable and its heroine a bit too courageous and noble, but it's an admirable achievement nevertheless. The only reservation for pre-teens is some humorous by-play occasioned by a contraceptive

title: Country Boy
synopsis: Randy Boone of TV's "The Virginian" stars in a story of grass roots patriotism. Scenario and catchy country-western songs by Paul Crabtree

title: Country Gentlemen
synopsis: Lame comedy directed by Ralph Staub in which a bumbling pair of swindlers (Ole Olsen and Chic Johnson) on the run from charges of selling phony gold mining stock arrive in a rural area where they start selling oil stock but, unsurprisingly, oil's well at movie's end. Comic dishonesty and muted sexual innuendo

title: Country Girl, The
synopsis: Uneven picture from Clifford Odets' play about an alcoholic singer-actor (Bing Crosby) trying for a Broadway come-back under a director (William Holden) who blames the former star's problems on his domineering wife (Grace Kelly), until he learns the truth. Writer-director George Seaton gets a fine performance from Crosby and an Oscar-winning one from Kelly, despite a heavily contrived back-stage story and all sorts of tangled motivations, especially the director's attempt to woo the wife. A child's off-screen death, romantic complications and a sobering scene of inebriation

title: Country Life
synopsis: After many years away, a pompous London-based theatre critic (Michael Blakemore) returns to 1919 Australia to visit an outback ranch whose owner (John Hargreaves) and the local doctor (Sam Neill) fall hopelessly in love with his young, bored wife (Greta Scacchi). Adapted from Chekov's "Uncle Vanya" by writer-director Blakemore, the slowly paced drama of unrequited romances has sprightly comic moments and stresses the humanity of its characters as they learn to accept life's disappointments with good grace. Momentary violence, fleeting nudity and romantic complications

title: Country Music
synopsis: Marty Robbins' company put together what is essentially a feature-length commercial for his kind of music. Directed by Robert Hinkle, the best that can be said for it as a movie is that there is a certain fascination in its naive artlessness as well as its unconscious humor

title: Country Music Daughter
synopsis: ( see: "New Girl in Town" )

title: Country Strong
synopsis: This music-filled drama about a troubled country singer (Gwyneth Paltrow) wears its mawkish cliches proudly on its flannel sleeves. Writer-director Shana Feste creates four one-dimensional characters -- besides the alcohol- and drug-addicted troubadour, there's her manipulative promoter-husband (Tim McGraw), her on-again-off-again lover (Garrett Hedlund) and a young, neurotic beauty queen-turned-crooner (Leighton Meester) -- then sends the quartet spinning like pinballs in a twangy, shopworn tale of substance abuse, adultery and the grim lifestyle played out on a tour bus. Scenes of implied adulterous and premarital sex, pervasive crude language and fleeting profanity

title: Count Three and Pray
synopsis: Muddled tale of a Civil War veteran (Van Heflin) whose experiences at Vicksburg transform him from hardened roughneck to self-styled preacher, but his backwoods community has trouble accepting his new role as pastor, especially when he takes in an orphaned adolescent (Joanne Woodward). Director George Sherman spends more energy in detailing the melodramatic conflicts between the characters than in probing the theme of a simple man's struggle to follow his conscience. Interesting but largely failed attempt to portray the power of faith

title: County Fair
synopsis: Low-budget adventure directed by Howard Bretherton in which a suspended jockey (John Arledge) battles racetrack crooks while helping a brother and sister enter their horse in a race at the local fair, despite the opposition of their puritanical father (J. Farrell McDonald). Criminal activities and romantic complications

title: Count Yorga, Vampire
synopsis: Fairly old-fashioned kind of horror movie with an involving, almost believable plot, underplayed stereotypes of good and innocent vs. evil and ghoulish, plus a very effective ending. Director Bob Kelljan suggests more than he shows of the story's sex, blood and violence

title: Coup de Grace
synopsis: Sober but rather dull German movie about the entangled passions of three German aristocrats set against the chaotic background of post-World War I Latvia. Starring Margarethe von Trotta and Matthias Habich, director Volker Schlondorff's tale of unrequited love and its wasteful consequences is for the patient and mature

title: Coup de Tete
synopsis: French comedy about a maverick soccer player (Patrick Dewaere) who wins the big match and becomes the hero of his home town which once scorned him as a feckless ne'er-do-well but which now is ready to believe that his conviction for rape was a miscarriage of justice. Though the acting is good and director Jean-Jacques Annaud's flair for satire occasionally hits home, the rape's central place in the plot makes for heavy going in a comedy

title: Coupe de Ville
synopsis: On orders from their father (Alan Arkin), three battling brothers drive a 1954 Cadillac Coupe de Ville from Detroit to Florida as a birthday gift for their mother but wreck the car along the way. This mildly entertaining coming-of-age comedy is directed in predictable fashion by Joe Roth, with appealing performances by Patrick Dempsey, Daniel Stern and Arye Gross as the brothers. Some locker-room language laced with sexual vulgarities and an incident of premarital sex

title: Couples Retreat
synopsis: Mostly dull, sexually wayward comedy in which a suburban couple (Jason Bateman and Kristen Bell) on the verge of divorce convince a group of their friends (most prominently Vince Vaughn and Malin Akerman) to join them at a South Pacific resort whose founder (Jean Reno) specializes in marriage therapy. While Peter Billingsley's directorial debut ultimately affirms marital fidelity, viewers have to endure waves of constantly suggestive, occasionally smutty humor and a tide of New Age psychobabble -- an obviously inadequate substitute for faith as a basis for lifelong commitment -- before reaching that safe shore. Strong sexual content, including brief but aberrant adulterous activity, fleeting nongraphic sexual activity within marriage, a flash of rear nudity, many sexually themed jokes, and some crude and much crass language

title: Courage Mountain
synopsis: Uninspired but wholesome story of 14-year-old Heidi (Juliette Caton) who is forced from an Italian boarding school into a rat-infested orphanage by the disruptions of World War I. Director Christopher Leitch strains credibility with some far-fetched action as Heidi and her friends escape across the Alps to Switzerland in the dead of winter. Children will enjoy hissing the despicable orphanage owners and young adolescents may be charmed by the hints of a blossoming romance between Heidi and her dashing soldier friend (Charlie Sheen). Some comic-book menace and minimal battlefield carnage

title: Courage of Lassie
synopsis: A lost, wounded pup is nursed back to health and raised as a sheepdog by a young girl (Elizabeth Taylor), then winds up as an heroic Army canine, shellshocked and ultimately vicious, until fate brings him back to his loving mistress and rehabilitation as a sweet-tempered companion. Directed by Fred Wilcox, Lassie goes through her appealing paces as Bill, the dog whose incredible adventures most youngsters will find irresistible, though their elders may be more interested in the story's post-war rehabilitation theme and the gorgeous Sierra locales. Brief wartime violence and some fairly intense scenes of menace

title: Courage of the North
synopsis: Formula outdoor adventure directed by Robert Emmet in which Sgt. Morton (John Preston) of the Canadian Mounted Police gets some help from his wonder horse Dynamite and his dog Captain in capturing a gang stealing pelts from the trap lines of fur traders. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Courageous Mr. Penn
synopsis: Earnest but plodding account of the religious persecution facing aristocrat William Penn (Clifford Evans) after joining the Quakers in 1667 London, his marriage to a good woman (Deborah Kerr), her death and his founding of Pennsylvania as a Quaker refuge in the American wilderness. Directed by Lance Comfort, the episodic script is dramatically weak and rather superficial in its treatment of the historical period and Penn's religious convictions. Heavy-going for children

title: Courage under Fire
synopsis: Returning from the Gulf War,an Army commander (Denzel Washington) feeling guilty over his part in a friendly fire incident doggedly pursues discrepancies in the recommendation of a posthumous medal of honor for a Medevac pilot (Meg Ryan). Director Edward Zwick blends the differing versions of the pilot's actions under fire with compelling character studies as a series of flashbacks gradually reveal how all concerned behaved under the stress of mortal combat. Intense battlefield violence, a suicide, substance abuse and frequent rough language as well as profanity

title: Courier, The
synopsis: Irish import with narrow appeal zeroing in on the victims of a notorious Dublin drug dealer (Gabriel Byrne) who'll stop at nothing to protect his criminal operation. Directed by Frank Deasy and Joe Lee, the movie's contrived romance and revenge plot are poorly focused and surprisingly uninvolving given its gritty subject and working-class setting. Some profanity, clumsy violence and implied heterosexual and homosexual promiscuity

title: Court Jester, The
synopsis: Delightful costume comedy with Danny Kaye in top form masquerading alternately as a clown and an assassin in order to help a band of rebels overthrow a corrupt king (Cecil Parker) and his treacherous ally (Basil Rathbone) while saving a damsel in distress (Glynis Johns). Written and directed by Norman Panama and Melvin Frank, the silly court intrigues and mistaken identities are clever nonsense, there are some pleasant songs and Kaye delivers the laughs stylishly, especially in his patter routine with Mildred Natwick about "the brew that is true." Enjoyable romp for the family

title: Courtney Affair, The
synopsis: ( see: "The Courtneys" )

title: Courtneys of Curzon Street, The
synopsis: ( see: "The Courtneys" )

title: Courtneys, The
synopsis: Plodding British saga of an aristocratic family from 1900 when the Courtney heir (Michael Wilding) weds his mother's Irish maid (Anna Nagle), through their ups and downs over the years until ending in 1945 with the engagement of their grandson to a working-class girl. Producer-director Herbert Wilcox details the changes in British society from the Boer War to World War II in grand soap opera fashion which still holds appeal for undemanding romantics

title: Courtship of Andy Hardy, The
synopsis: Judge Hardy (Lewis Stone) asks son Andy (Mickey Rooney) to squire the neglected daughter (Donna Reed) of a custody case but he does such a good job, she wants to marry him. George B. Seitz directs an episode whose sub-plots include mechanic Andy's troubles with the FBI and sister Marian (Cecilia Parker) taking up with a playboy

title: Courtship of Eddie's Father, The
synopsis: Treacly romantic comedy about a widower (Glenn Ford) with a precocious six-year-old (Ronny Howard) who nixes his father's wooing of a bubble-headed drummer (Stella Stevens) and a ritzy fashion consultant (Dina Merrill) in favor of a wholesome divorcee (Shirley Jones). Director Vincente Minnelli can do little with the contrived plot's artificial situations and the result is an embarrassment for all concerned. Sticky romantic complications

title: Cousin Angelica
synopsis: A middle-aged man (Jose Luis Lopez Vazquez) returns to the village where he had been a boy during the Spanish Civil War and his recollections help explain his alienation as an adult. Carlos Saura directs the Spanish production with controlled intensity, making the individual's story credible but also using it to show the Spanish character and culture at war with itself

title: Cousin Bette
synopsis: Strained black comedy set in 1840's Paris where a wily spinster (Jessica Lange) exacts revenge on her selfish relatives and a young sculptor (Aden Young) she had saved from starvation. Based on the Honore de Balzac novel, director Des McAnuff's period piece is only fitfully amusing in conveying the simmering fury of a woman long taken for granted. Fleeting sexual encounter, intermittent nudity, brief violence and a comic theme of vengeance

title: Cousin Bobby
synopsis: Affirmative documentary profile of Episcopal Father Robert Castle, the white rector of a mostly black parish in Harlem, chronicling his decades of social activism in championing minority rights despite countless arrests since the 1960s. Director Jonathan Demme's portrait of his activist cousin is in part an easygoing home movie, but the pastor's undiminished idealism and involvement with his parishioners shines through his own laid-back commentary. Minimal street language

title: Cousin, Cousine
synopsis: A married man and a married woman (Victor Lanoux and Marie-Christine Barrault) meet at their relative's wedding that makes them cousins and are immediately drawn to each other. The story of marital infidelity that results is an amusing, malicious trifle which has more to do with wish fulfillment than reality. Under the good-humored surface of this French production directed by Jean-Charles Tachella is a pervading acceptance of adultery. Some nudity

title: Cousins
synopsis: Remake of the 1976 French satire, "Cousin, Cousine," centers in the adulterous liaisons between the partners of two unhappily married couples related by marriage (Isabella Rossellini, William Petersen, Ted Danson and Sean Young). Director Joel Schumacher features some delightful ethnic family weddings, but the film's romanticization of adultery and premarital sex are morally objectionable. Discreet nudity and rough language laced with sexual vulgarities

title: Covenant with Death, A
synopsis: Suspenseful drama about an innocent man (Earl Holliman), wrongfully convicted of a crime and sentenced to death, whose fight for his life results in the death of another and a dilemma for a small-town judge (George Maharis). Director Lamont Johnson's lackluster production lets an intriguing moral-ethical-legal premise get lost in side issues. Casual love affair condoning seduction

title: Covered Wagon Raid
synopsis: Western programmer directed by R.G. Springsteen in which an insurance investigator (Allan "Rocky" Lane) finds the gang behind a series of robberies just in time to save a wagon train of settlers. Frontier violence

title: Cover Girl
synopsis: Mediocre musical with Rita Hayworth as a nightclub dancer catapulted into stardom after being put on the cover of a magazine whose publisher (Otto Kruger) had wooed her grandmother, but she's torn between wedding a Broadway impresario (Lee Bowman) or returning to the nightclub owner (Gene Kelly) who loves her. Directed by Charles Vidor, Hayworth looks good in the part but is outshone by Kelly's performance as a song-and-dance man in a flimsy plot bolstered by comic relief from Eve Arden and Phil Silvers. Romantic complications and sexual innuendo

title: Cover Me Babe
synopsis: Bad movie about a student filmmaker (Robert Forster) whose wrongheaded ideas about moviemaking alienate his co-workers, girlfriend (Sondra Locke) and department instructor (Robert Fields). Directed by Noel Black, the movie suffers many of the faults it seems to be criticizing, including an exploitative emphasis on sex

title: Cowards
synopsis: Draft-age youth (John Ross), pondering the alternatives to imminent induction, moves in with his girlfriend (Susan Sparling) and takes part in a raid to destroy draft files. Writer-producer-director Simon Nuchtern makes light of the moral issues, preferring instead to anchor his hero in absolute confrontations with an overloaded anti-war tract disseminated by supporting characters

title: Cowboy
synopsis: Rawhide coming-of-age story from the Frank Harris novel in which a callow Chicago hotel clerk (Jack Lemmon) learns from a hardened cattle herder (Glenn Ford) that cow-punching is hard work but, as the youth's character toughens on the trail, that of his mentor mellows. Director Delmer Daves get some modest enjoyment out of the tenderfoot's education but it is Ford's performance as the veteran cowman that dominates the picture. Dangers of the trail from snakebite to a brush with Comanches, some mild romance, rough humor and an off-screen suicide

title: Cowboy and the Girl, The
synopsis: ( see: "A Lady Takes a Chance" )

title: Cowboy and the Lady, The
synopsis: Romantic comedy in which a presidential candidate's daughter (Merle Oberon) falls for a rodeo rider (Gary Cooper) who mistakes her for a maid, then after they marry, the bride has to square matters with him and her wealthy family. Directed by H.C. Potter, the contrived plot premise provides some dizzy amusement with a fine supporting cast (notably Walter Brennan, Patsy Kelly and Harry Davenport) until the artificial egalitarian ending

title: Cowboys, The
synopsis: When the local cowpokes join the Gold Rush to California, a tough old rancher (John Wayne) resorts to hiring some schoolboys (ages 9 to 15) to drive his cattle to the railhead, teaching them the dangerous craft of cow-punching along the trail. In a traditionally violent finale, the young adolescents slaughter a gang of cattle rustlers who have brutally murdered the rancher (one of the rare roles in which Wayne is not invincible). Well directed by Mark Rydell but definitely not for the youngsters or the squeamish

title: Cowboy Way, The
synopsis: Witless comic adventure of two rodeo stars (Woody Harrelson and Kiefer Sutherland) in New York City on the trail of the vicious killer (Dylan McDermott) who has murdered their buddy and kidnapped his daughter. Director Gregg Champion's slack handling of the chases and shootouts in the derivative plot is made worse by Harrelson's clumsy overacting. Intermittent violence, brief bedroom scene with rear nudity and an instance of rough language

title: Cow Country
synopsis: Routine low-budget Western directed by Lesley Selander has a group of Texas ranchers (led by Edmond O'Brien) fighting to save their land from the local banker (Barton MacLane) and his gang of gunmen. Stylized violence and a false romance

title: Coyote Ugly
synopsis: Forgettable romantic drama in which a young New Jersey woman (Piper Perabo) moves to New York City with songwriting aspirations, but is distracted by the attention she receives from her ``day'' job as a sexy barmaid in the city's hottest watering hole. Pitifully trite dialogue and a formulaic narrative mark director David McNally's tiresome film which lacks dramatic credibility and noteworthy characters. Sexual promiscuity, brief crass language and mild bar brawling violence. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: CQ
synopsis: Quirky but flat story about a young American filmmaker (Jeremy Davies) in 1969 Paris who is asked to direct a floundering sci-fi movie set in the year 2000 and saddled with all sorts of problems. Director Roman Coppola's tribute to the 60's passion for cinema remains grounded and fractured, with uninspired characters who, despite all the action going on around them, aren't able to stir up much interest. Frontal nudity, a sexual encounter, brief rough language and an instance of profanity. A-III � adults (R) 2002 Full Review A young American filmmaker in Paris gets a chance to make his mark by directing a low-budget sci-fi flick in the quirky but flat "CQ" (MGM). Director Roman Coppola, son of Francis Ford Coppola, makes his directorial debut in "CQ" much like Paul (Jeremy Davies), the low-key American filmmaker in 1969 Paris does in Coppola's film. While editing "Dragonfly," a "Barbarella"-like sci-fi actioner, Paul is asked to take over the project when the temperamental director, Andrzej (Gerard Depardieu), can't find an ending for the movie. Andrzej's judgment has also been clouded by his infatuation with the film's star, Valentine (Angela Lindvall), who plays Dragonfly, the kittenish secret agent dressed in skin-tight pink leather. So, the demanding Italian producer Enzo (an excellent Giancarlo Giannini) fires Andrzej and hires Paul. Though Paul tries hard to make "Dragonfly" work, he remains more concerned with his own project, which he believes shows the truth in cinema. A collection of shots of coffee mugs, tea kettles, his pouty French girlfriend Marlene (Elodie Bouchez) in various states of undress and, finally, long rambling lectures made by Paul from his throne on the toilet comprise his supposedly edgy black-and-white piece. Paul's personal work might be interpreted as a pointed jab by Coppola at the pretensions of cinema and filmmakers, but instead it never gets off the ground. This movie-within-a-movie is Coppola's tribute to the passion for cinema that was so fervent in Europe during the 1960s. But despite the eventful narrative and the Paris and Rome settings, the film remains grounded with uninspired characterizations. Paul, who takes the art of cinema very seriously and is obsessed with making an honest film about his own life -- no matter how boring it may turn out to be -- is a dullard. Throughout the film he wears the same world-weary expression behind his shaggy hair and black suit, white shirt and thin black tie. Depardieu spices things up during the limited screen time he has, but can't lift the film entirely. And Jason Schwartzman makes an even briefer appearance as an eccentric and talentless director whom Enzo hires before committing to Paul. However, Schwartzman is flamboyant and fun, adding a little pizzazz to an otherwise drab story. Coppola, who wrote the screenplay as well, has trouble bringing all the loose ends together coherently. At various points it seems as if several different subplots may come together to form an interesting point or revelation. But this never happens. "CQ" alternately pokes fun at or reveres the cinema of the intoxicating days of the 1960s, but when everything is pieced together, it doesn't create enough momentum to transport the viewer. Due to frontal nudity, a sexual encounter and brief rough language and an instance of profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops

title: Crackers
synopsis: Donald Sutherland plays the ringleader of an inept band of San Francisco characters who devise an elaborate plot to break into their loca1 pawnshop and repay its cranky owner (Jack Warden) by cracking open his safe. Director Louis Malle spends more time trying to find some new angles on the old caper formula than on character development, a miscalculation that results in a flat, lackluster comedy with some sexual situations and a benign view of petty crime

title: Crack in the World
synopsis: Doomsday scenario unleashes widening series of earthquakes caused when a scientist (Dana Andrews) explodes a nuclear bomb to tap the energy at the earth's core. Director Andrew Marton gets some frightening moments in an otherwise sluggish script ending with the earth's getting a second moon. Stylized violence and a menacing premise

title: Crack-Up
synopsis: Intriguing mystery thriller opens with an art specialist (Pat O'Brien) found raving about a train wreck that police establish never occurred but which eventually leads to evidence of forged masterpieces. Director Irving Reis invests the puzzling proceedings with suitably sinister atmosphere, taut suspense and a solid cast of suspicious characters (Claire Trevor, Herbert Marshall, Ray Collins and Wallace Ford). Stylized violence

title: Cradle 2 the Grave
synopsis: Brutal action film in which a thief (DMX) whose little daughter has been kidnapped must retrieve stolen black diamonds as ransom and so reluctantly teams with a Taiwanese cop (Jet Li) who has his own reasons for finding the black ice. Director Andrzek Bartkowiak orchestrates a noisy, chaotic tale of murder and revenge where fatherly affection seems to negate felonious crimes. Excessive violence, a sexually suggestive scene and sexual references, much rough language, racist remarks and a few instances of profanity

title: Cradle Will Rock
synopsis: Ambitious political drama set in 1936 New York City follows a struggling, federally funded theatre group under Congressional investigation as being communist-influenced while rich industrialists plot to profit on the coming war. Writer-director Tim Robbins' fact-based story of greed, and artistic integrity at the mercy of government censorship, is a well-acted ensemble effort but one whose numerous characters and story strands nearly overwhelm the choppy narrative. Brief violence, discreet sexual situations and some profanity and rough language

title: Craft, The
synopsis: Cliche-ridden horror clunker in which four Catholic high school girls-turned-witches (led by Fairuza Balk) cast evil spells on classmates until one of the quartet (Robin Tunney) tries to stop them from doing further harm. Directed by Andrew Fleming, the occult nonsense employs thousands of snakes and maggots, though some of the spells have deadly results. Stylized violence, brief sexual innuendo, several crude expressions and an instance of rough language as well as a profanity

title: Crank
synopsis: Noisy and endlessly unpleasant action film about a Los Angeles hit man (Jason Statham) who must keep in perpetual motion after he finds out that a rival thug (Jose Pablo Cantillo) has poisoned him with a substance designed to kill him within seconds if his heart rate drops. Co-writers and directors Mark Neveldine and Brian Taylor load on the bloody video-game-style action in an empty, mindless and unrelentingly ugly exercise. Excessive and graphic violence and gore, lewd sexual content, vulgar humor, recurring partial nudity, drug use and pervasive rough and crude language and profanity

title: Crash
