synopsis: Convoluted crime thriller about a media-savvy police detective (Robert DeNiro) who teams with an arson investigator (Edward Burns) on a homicide investigation only to become a murder target himself by killers seeking their own fifteen minutes of fame. The dark social commentary made by writer-director John Herzfeld about exploitative tabloid TV journalism and the desire for notoriety is eventually lost amidst the film's nonsensical plot and excessive brutality. Much gory violence, brief nudity and recurring rough language with some profanity. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: 40 Days and 40 Nights
synopsis: Crude romantic comedy about a young bachelor (Josh Hartnett) who swears off sex for Lent after his girlfriend (Vinessa Shaw) breaks up with him, but complications ensue as soon as he meets the girl (SS) of his dreams. Snickering at the Catholic Church's teaching on pre-marital sex, director Michael Lehmann's one-joke film exploits the holy season of Lent as a cynical pretext for abstinence. Misuse of the sacrament of penance, sexual encounters, recurring nudity, intermittent rough language, crass sexual expressions and profanity

title: 40 Guns to Apache Pass
synopsis: Routine Western about a U.S. Cavalry captain (Audie Murphy) saving an Arizona outpost from marauding Apaches and a treacherous white man (Kenneth Tobey) by getting through with a shipment of repeating rifles. Directed by William Whitney, the formula action scenes are held together by a cliched narration. Stylized violence

title: 40 Pounds of Trouble
synopsis: Predictable comedy in which a Nevada casino manager (Tony Curtis) finds a five-year-old girl left on the premises, then dodges a detective over alimony owed his ex-wife by taking the child and a casino singer (Suzanne Pleshette) to Disneyland. Directed by Norman Jewison, the sentimental proceedings rework the plot of "Little Miss Marker," with the updated casino setting and sprawling theme park adding some visual zest. Romantic complications

title: 48 Hours
synopsis: ( see: "Went the Day Well?" )

title: 48 Hrs.
synopsis: San Francisco police detective (Nick Nolte) springs a convict (Eddie Murphy) on a 48-hour pass in order to get his help tracking down some vicious killers. Directed by Walter Hill's slam-bang action thriller is filled with entirely disagreeable characters who indulge in extreme violence, crude sights gags and rough language
Spurious Swedish movie uses a rehabilitation program for incorrigible boys as an excuse for a parade of sadism, violence, vandalism and sexual perversity

title: 49th Man, The
synopsis: Cold War potboiler directed by Fred F. Sears in which a federal agent (John Ireland) tries to save San Francisco from annihilation by a Soviet spy ring which has smuggled a portable nuclear bomb into the country. Pulp menace

title: 4 Clowns
synopsis: Robert Youngson's compilation deals with the art of visual comedy as shown in the work of four of its leading buffoons: Charley Chase, Buster Keaton, Stan Laurel and Oliver Hardy. The selection of excerpts is fine, the narration is helpful and the silent comedy is timeless

title: 4D Man
synopsis: Halting sci-fi tale in which a dose of radiation from a lab project enables a scientist (Robert Lansing) to dissolve his body's molecular structure and pass through solid matter such as walls, but the process ages him rapidly and can be reversed only by draining the life out of others. Directed by Irvin S. Yeaworth, Jr., the special effects showing Lansing melting through material objects are simple but effective, though the formula story bogs down in a subplot of the scientist's fiancee (Lee Meriwether) falling for his troubled younger brother (James Congdon). Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: 4 for Texas
synopsis: Bloated comic Western in which rival sharpsters (Frank Sinatra and Dean Martin) fight for control of a Galvaston gambling boat, then unite against a crooked banker (Victor Buono), with help from a couple of shady ladies (Anita Ekberg and Ursula Andress). Producer-director Robert Aldrich gets little comic mileage out of his two leads who are more at home with double entendres than six-shooters. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: 4 Little Girls
synopsis: Moving documentary revisits Birmingham, Alabama, where on a Sunday morning in 1963, four young girls were murdered in the racially motivated bombing of a Southern Baptist Church. Director Spike Lee interviews relatives of the victims to put human faces on the tragedy as well as examines how these cruel killings served to focus public condemnation of white extremists and increased support for the civil rights movement. Some grisly photos of corpses and news footage of police brutality

title: 52 Minutes to Midnight
synopsis: ( See: "Hot Rods to Hell" )

title: 52 Pick-up
synopsis: A wealthy industrialist and unfaithful husband (Roy Scheider), who dabbles in the sleazy underworld of drugs and sex, is taped in a liaison with a young girl that implicates him in her subsequent murder. The demand for b1ackmail motivates him to use his money to set the killers against themselves. The nasty peep-show ambiance of the proceedings, directed by John Frankenheimer, wallows in brutish violence, nudity, drugs and profanity

Empty retelling of the rise and demise of Studio 54, New York City's wildest disco in the late 1970s, as seen through the eyes of a pleasure-seeking bartender (Ryan Phillippe). Written and directed by Mark Christopher, the movie proves a lifeless assemblage of decadent disco scenes in search of a story and the result offers no lessons to be learned from life in the fast lane. Uncritical portrayal of substance abuse, promiscuity and theft, as well as brief nudity and much rough language

title: 55 Days at Peking
synopsis: With the encouragement of the Manchu dowager empress (Flora Robson), the forces of the 1900 Boxer Rebellion lay siege to the walled compound in the Chinese capital where the foreign community tries to hold out until an international relief force arrives. Director Nicholas Ray's widescreen spectacular has impressive sets and energetic action scenes but the cast (U.S. Marine officer Charlton Heston, British diplomat David Niven, Russian baroness Ava Gardner and the rest) are cardboard characters adding little human dimension to a script of limited historical proportion. Stylized violence and romantic interludes

title: 5 Against the House
synopsis: Bored with college studies, three Korean War veterans (Brian Keith, Alvy Moore and Kerwin Matthews) concoct a "fool-proof" plan to rob a Reno gambling casino but need another vet (Guy Madison) and his girlfriend (Kim Novak) to pull it off. Director Phil Karlson's routine crime caper takes a long time getting away from the phony campus setting and some soggy romance before heading for Reno and a heist complicated by one of the vets being an ex-psychiatric case. Criminal situations and mild sexual innuendo

title: 5 Fingers
synopsis: Fact-based dramatization of World War II espionage in neutral Turkey where the British ambassador's valet (James Mason) finances early retirement by selling top-secret embassy documents to the Germans, only to be double-crossed by a Polish countess (Danielle Darrieux) and his Nazi paymasters. Director Jospeh L. Mankiewicz does best with Mason's coolly intelligent portrayal as the enterprising spy code-named Cicero, but dampens the effect with sporadic wry humor while comic Nazi stereotypes undercut the irony of German agents discarding the plans for the Normandy invasion because they feared Cicero was a double agent. Wartime dangers and mild romance

title: 5 Fingers of Death
synopsis: Hong Kong martial arts movie directed by Cheng Chang Ho shows the training of a young disciple of a kung fu master and their problems with thugs from a rival school. The atrocious dubbing of this thin effort makes the action seem at first to be played for laughs but it proves, unfortunately, to be deadly serious. Acrobatic violence

title: 5th Musketeer, The
synopsis: Uninspired Austrian remake of the 1939 American movie, "The Man in the Iron Mask," stars a miscast Beau Bridges in the dual role of Louis XIV and his twin brother, with aged musketeers Jose Ferrer, Cornel Wilde, Alan Hale Jr. and Lloyd Bridges assuring that the good twin ascends the throne. Director Ken Annakin's lackluster adventure includes some adult situations

title: 5X2
synopsis: Finely acted, perceptive story of the disintegration of a contemporary relationship, told in five sequences in reverse order from divorce to first romantic meeting. Francois Ozon's measuredly paced "scenes from a marriage" is quite fascinating, as it reveals layer by layer the over-the-years affection, betrayals, foibles, and idiosyncracies of the couple played impeccably by Valeria Bruni-Tedeschi and Stephane Freiss. Subtitles. A graphic sex scene with female frontal nudity, gay subplot, frank sexual talk, premarital and postmarital sexual situations, discussion of artificial insemination, and rough and crude language

title: Fabulous Baker Boys, The
synopsis: Demoralized piano-playing brother team (Jeff and Beau Bridges) on the Seattle cocktail-lounge circuit briefly revitalize their stale act with a sultry female singer (Michelle Pfeiffer) who catalyzes the men to face some hard, personal realities. The acting of the principals is fine and writer-director Steve Kloves has a feel for these fringe performers and the poignant unravelling of family ties. Some profanity laced with sexual vulgarities and brief sexual situations with a flash of nudity

title: Fabulous Dorseys, The
synopsis: The Dorsey brothers play themselves in this screen biography as trombonist Tommy and saxophonist Jimmy leave Pennsylvania to take their jazz band on the road in the 1920s, then quarrel and go their separate ways to fame and fortune with their own dance bands. Directed by Alfred E. Green, the routine dramatization overplays the bickering brothers' rivalry, though the main attraction here is the movie's showcase of pop standards performed by the Dorseys, Paul Whiteman and other period bands

title: Face in the Crowd, A
synopsis: Cautionary tale about an Arkansas drifter (Andy Griffith) whose homespun appeal is discovered by a local radio producer (Patricia Neal), then goes on to become a national television star but his ambitious ego and nasty disposition ultimately make him a dangerous political force. Directed by Elia Kazan from Budd Schulberg's savvy script, the result takes a close look at the media's power to influence and manipulate, a theme given credibility by Griffith's chilling two-faced performance, but the story itself grows increasingly contrived and predictable. Sexual situations and innuendo

title: Face of a Fugitive
synopsis: Clumsy Western in which a man (Fred MacMurray) on the run from a false charge of murder arrives in a town where he's unknown, then risks discovery by staying on to help its citizens, including the sheriff. Director Paul Wendkos can do little with a contrived plot, talky script and wooden acting. Stylized violence

title: Faces
synopsis: Director John Cassavetes' intense study of the marital crisis of a middle-aged, middle-class couple (Gena Rowlands and John Marley) who discover that divorce isn't the answer to their personal emptiness and despairing search for meaning in life. Troubling, sardonic, somewhat depressing treatment of a mature theme that is part of so many contemporary relationships. Some rough language, sexual innuendo and a suicide attempt

title: Faces of Love
synopsis: A movie director (Jean-Louis Trintignant) tries to win back his ex-wife (Delphine Seyrig) by starring her in an adaptation of Chekhov's "The Three Sisters" (with Lea Massari and Valerie Mairesse as the other leads). Swiss director Michael Soutter wastes a talented cast with what is in effect a shallow exercise in psychodrama

title: Face to Face
synopsis: Stockholm psychiatrist (Liv Ullmann) discovers that she must heal herself when she suffers from a nervous breakdown in director Ingmar Bergman's clinical investigation into the realm of the feminine psyche. Ullmann's magnificent performance conveys the failure of psychiatry as a remedy to the disappointments and contradictions of her guilt-ridden life. The movie includes some harrowing scenes, including an attempted rape, but the emphasis is on the interior journey to peace of soul

title: Facing the Giants
synopsis: Evangelical sports drama about a losing football coach (Alex Kendrick, who also directs) at a Christian high school in Georgia, who, experiencing personal and professional adversity, revives his team's season by turning to his faith. The earnest performances from the nonprofessional cast are surprisingly competent and the movie's look is reasonably polished, but while the film's heart is in the right place, its positive message about putting one's trust in God is undermined by a prosaic script that tends toward the preachy. Some mature thematic elements, including discussions about infertility

title: Factory Girl
synopsis: The sad, sordid rise and fall of socialite Edie Sedgwick (Sienna Miller), who shone briefly in the spotlight as part of Andy Warhol's (Guy Pearce) artistic center, the Factory, in the 1960s, appearing in his underground movies until the pop artist tired of her, showing how the over-the-top lifestyle led to her eventual burnout despite a nurturing interlude with a legendary singer (Hayden Christensen). Director George Hickenlooper's film takes an episodic approach in telling the story as Sedgwick, near the end of her short life (which ended at 28 from a drug overdose), relates her experiences to a psychiatrist. The milieu is downbeat and often seamy, but presented with relative restraint, and Miller is immensely appealing in her sensitive portrait of the trusting, vulnerable waif. Nongraphic premarital sexual encounters, upper female and partial nudity, brief sexual banter and innuendo, drug use, some rough and crude language, gay references, references to child abuse and suicide

title: Factotum
synopsis: Bleak adaptation of novelist-poet Charles Bukowski's 1975 novel (his second) about a heavy-drinking, often brutish, aspiring writer (a superb Matt Dillon), drifting from one menial job to another, and his relationships with a couple of equally self-destructive losers (Lili Taylor and Marisa Tomei). Writer-director Bent Hamer captures the desolate world of the writer (Bukowski's alter ego) with uncompromising exactitude, and the performances are perfectly realized, but the unrelenting ugliness of the story and language, strong sexual elements and overall amoral behavior of its protagonists -- despite the film's literary pedigree -- will seriously limit its appeal. Pervasive rough and crude language and profanity, rear male and partial female nudity, premarital sexual encounters, gambling, heavy drinking and occasional violence

title: Faculty, The
synopsis: Inept sci-fi horror tale in which a malevolent alien force from outer space begins taking over the teachers, then the students of a decrepit high school until a diverse group of students (led by Elijah Wood as the school nerd) go into action. Directed by Robert Rodriguez, the derivative plot has some scary effects but little suspense, with the slack taken up by the teenagers' preoccupation with sex and drugs. Gory violence, sexual references and innuendo, the use of narcotics as a plot device, recurring rough language and occasional profanity

title: Fade to Black
synopsis: Muddled, unsavory tale directed by Vernon Zimmerman centers on a frustrated young man (Dennis Christopher) who escapes the rigors of reality by living in a dream world nourished by murderous fantasies derived from movies. Excessive violence and sordid atmosphere

title: Fahrenheit 451
synopsis: A fireman (Oskar Werner) reforms his book-burning ways in this adaptation of Ray Bradbury's science fiction novel about a society that forbids the printed word. First rate performances by Julie Christie in a dual role as two women in the fireman's life and Cyril Cusack as a smiling fanatic help sustain the dream-like reality of director Francois Truffaut's allegorical fantasy. Menacing atmosphere

title: Fahrenheit 9/11
synopsis: Scathing indictment of President Bush's domestic and international policies leading up to and following the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, which attempts to link his family with prominent Saudi moneymen, including members of the bin Laden clan, and which contends that his administration capitalized on the climate of fear following World Trade Center tragedy in order to hoodwink the American public into an immoral war with Iraq. Director Michael Moore walks a perilous line between documentary filmmaking and partisan propaganda, which, though by turns compellingly sobering and engagingly entertaining, presents an unfairly one-sided blame-Bush-for-everything case that fails to take into account wider geopolitical realities, resulting in a manipulative and at times misleading interpretation of facts

title: Fail Safe
synopsis: A mechanical failure makes impossible the recall of nuclear bombers headed for Russia in a movie questioning the ability of humans to control their inventions. Sidney Lumet directs Henry Fonda, Dan O'Herlihy and various machines with mounting suspense

title: Failure to Launch
synopsis: Uneven but oddly likable comedy about professional "intervention" consultant (Sarah Jessica Parker) hired by the parents (Kathy Bates and Terry Bradshaw) of a 35-year-old, still-living-at-home jock (Matthew McConaughey) in the hopes of making him independent enough to move out, with predictable romantic complications. Director Tom Dey maintains a spirited pace, there are some pleasing performances, the sylvan and aquatic settings are easy on the eyes, and the ending is morally sound, outweighing too many conversational expletives and a permissive view of premarital sex. Profanity, rough and crude language and expressions, implied sexual situations and banter, and a comic instance of rear male nudity

title: Fair Game
synopsis: Senseless thriller about a Miami cop (William Baldwin) protecting a confused lawyer (Cindy Crawford) from a hit squad of ex-Soviet agents on a computer fraud caper. Directed by Andrew Sipes, the hammy performances match the cheesy marathon of violent special effects and bloody shootouts which pass for the plot. Excessive violence, a shadowy sexual encounter, flashes of nudity and much rough language

title: Fair Wind to Java
synopsis: Fair adventure tale of a Yankee sea captain (Fred MacMurray) fighting pirates in the Dutch East Indies while getting some help from a native dancer (Vera Ralston) in locating a treasure in diamonds hidden on the volcanic island of Krakatoa just before it explodes in 1883. Directed by Joseph Kane, the action is slowed by various conspiracies aboard ship and ashore, but the ending is suitably suspenseful and the volcano's eruption is quite spectacular even by today's standards. Stylized violence including a torture scene and a woman assaulted by a drunken sailor

title: Fairy Tale: A True Story
synopsis: Romanticized account of the controversy stirred in 1917 England by two little girls whose photographs of what they said were tiny fairies frolicking in their garden aroused the skepticism of Harry Houdini (Harvey Keitel), though were proclaimed genuine by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle (Peter O'Toole). Director Charles Sturridge spins an enchanting tale of childhood innocence in a sweet family film marred by a few rude words. Serious argumentation over the existence of fairies and fleeting mild language

title: Faithful
synopsis: Nasty black comedy in which a depressed wife (Cher) turns the tables on her philandering husband (Ryan O'Neal) and the hitman (Chazz Palminteri) he has hired to kill her on their 20th wedding anniversary. The laughs are hollow in director Paul Mazursky's talky and mean-spirited look at marital infidelity. Off-screen murders, many adulterous references, minimal profanity and constant rough language

title: Faithless
synopsis: Disturbing Swedish drama about a happily married woman (Lena Endre) who impetuously enters into an affair with her husband's friend (Krister Henriksson), irreparably damaging not only her marriage, but her 9-year-old daughter (Michelle Gylemo) as well. As directed by Liv Ullmann from Ingmar Bergman's autobiographical screenplay, the film's remorseful tone exposes the destructive effects of thoughtless sexual misbehavior and the results of living a selfish life void of morality. Subtitles. A few sexual encounters, brief frontal nudity, an abortion, a suicide and some rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Falcon and the Co-eds, The
synopsis: Creaky murder mystery directed by William Clemens in which the suave private eye (Tom Conway) of this detective series investigates several deaths connected with a girl's school. Stylized violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Falcon and the Snowman, The
synopsis: Some boyhood friends, now young men (Timothy Hutton and Sean Penn), sell secret data to the Soviets. How all this happened and why is an engrossing and very well-acted story but director John Schlesinger has left too many loose ends and tends to sentimentalize these treasonous actions as mistaken idealism. Brief nudity, some drug use and ambivalent treatment of a complex subject

title: Falcon in Danger, The
synopsis: Intriguing mystery directed by William Clemens with series hero (Tom Conway) cracking a case involving a pilotless plane, a kidnapped industrialist, blackmailers and murder. Some stylized violence and threatening situations

title: Falcon in San Francisco, The
synopsis: Thin series entry directed by Joseph H. Lewis in which the title sleuth (Tom Conway) and his assistant (Edward Brophy) interrupt their Frisco vacation to help a distressed child (Sharyn Moffett) overcome problems caused by a bickering gang of murderous smugglers. Stylized violence and veiled sexual innuendo

title: Falcon Out West, The
synopsis: Change of pace for this mystery series as director William Clemens takes the dapper crimebuster (Tom Conway) from his usual Manhattan haunts to find a murderer on a Texas ranch complete with cowboys and Indians. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Falcon's Adventure, The
synopsis: Tired formula mystery directed by William Berke with series hero (Tom Conway) and comic sidekick (Edward Brophy) in Miami thwarting a gang after a formula for making synthetic diamonds. Minimal stylized violence

title: Falcon's Alibi, The
synopsis: Routine mystery directed by Ray McCarey in which the suave private eye (Tom Conway) nabs a murderer after locating some missing pearls in a case involving, among other, a radio disk jockey (Elisha Cook, Jr.) and his two-timing wife (Jane Greer). Some stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Falcon's Brother, The
synopsis: Routine murder case directed by Stanley Logan leads to the smashing of an Axis spy ring but the plot is most notable for killing off the series dapper sleuth, Gaylord Lawrence (George Sanders), and replacing him with his brother Tom (Tom Conway, Sanders real-life brother). Stylized violence

title: Falcon Strikes Back, The
synopsis: Formula mystery directed by Edward Dmytryk with the series sleuth (Tom Conway) and his wise-cracking aide (Cliff Edwards) suspected of stealing war bonds in a caper whose suspects include a resort manager (Harriet Hilliard) and a veteran puppeteer (Edgar Kennedy). Minimal violence and romantic byplay

title: Fallen
synopsis: Silly supernatural chiller in which a homicide detective (Denzel Washington) realizes he is being framed for murders committed by the demonic spirt of an executed serial killer. Directed by Gregory Hoblit, the ridiculous premise is more ludicrous than suspenseful in depicting the dead man's spirit making use of host bodies to commit evil deeds. Brief violence, menacing situations, much rough language and intermittent profanity

title: Fallen Angel
synopsis: Convoluted tale in which a con man (Dana Andrews) weds a small-town church organist (Alice Faye) planning to clean out her safety desposit box and skip town with a sultry waitress (Linda Darnell) who turns up murdered before he can get the money. Directed by Otto Preminger, the darkly contrived proceedings aren't very plausible, though the small-town setting has an interesting mix of eccentrics (Anne Revere, Percy Kilbride and John Carradine) as well as a sinister detective (Charles Bickford). Stylized violence, a feigned marriage and heavy sexual innuendo

title: Fallen Sparrow, The
synopsis: When a Spanish Civil War veteran (John Garfield) uncovers a nest of Nazi agents in 1940 New York, he goes after their leader (Walter Slezak) convinced he's found the limping man who tortured him in a Spanish prison. Directed by Richard Wallace, the result has plenty of period atmosphere and dark doings, but the meandering plot and surfeit of sinister characters fail to add up to more than a halting thriller. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Falling Down
synopsis: Pointless, ugly saga of a bitterly divorced, unemployed defense worker (Michael Douglas) who freaks out one day and goes on a one-man killing spree in L.A. while a persistent cop (Robert Duvall) doggedly tracks him down. Director Joel Schumacher presents a repulsive view of contemporary America where murderous behavior is seen as an inevitable response to mundane frustrations of modern urban life. Trivialization of deadly violence and much rough language, including racial and ethnic epithets

title: Falling from Grace
synopsis: Melancholy tale of a popular country singer (John Mellencamp) come home to rural Indiana where he cheats on his wife (Mariel Hemingway) with an old girlfriend (Kay Lenz) while considering how to proceed with the rest of his life. Also directed by Mellencamp, the ponderous story crawls along under the burden of static characters shuffling through midlife crises with little hint of resolution or personal growth. Discreet bedroom scene, references to adulterous affairs, fleeting violence and an instance of rough language

title: Falling in Love
synopsis: Two train commuters (Robert De Niro and Meryl Streep) fall in love, have a secret affair and part, never resolving their true feelings and their commitments to others. Although the story is essentially about adultery, the whole enterprise is so lacking in substance that moral principles hardly seem relevant. Director Ulu Grosbard fails to convey adequately the moral dilemma which was meant to be the core of the film's romantic theme

title: Falling in Love Again
synopsis: Elliott Gould plays the middle-aged owner of a Beverly Hills garment store who spends his time in nostalgic daydreams about his Bronx origins much to the chagrin of his wife (Susannah York) in this contrived and determinedly simple-minded little movie written and directed by Steven Paul. A bedroom sequence and a certain moral ambiguity makes this mature fare

title: Fall of the House of Usher, The
synopsis: ( see: "House of Usher" )

title: Fall of the Roman Empire, The
synopsis: In this lavish historical re-creation, Rome's wise old emperor Marcus Aurelius (Alec Guinness) is poisoned by his corrupt son (Christopher Plummer) whose savage policies against the barbarians brings the teetering empire to its ruin. Directed by Anthony Mann, the three-hour dramatization has an autumnal splendor that one can admire, yet find the spectacle unmoving on a human level. Stylized battle scenes and other assorted violence may frighten young children

title: Falstaff
synopsis: ( see: "Chimes at Midnight" )

title: Fame
synopsis: Ensemble drama with music follows a class of gifted students (most prominently Kay Panabaker, Asher Book, Naturi Naughton and Collins Pennie) and their dedicated teachers (among them Kelsey Grammer, Charles S. Dutton and Bebe Neuwirth) through four years at a New York City high school for the performing arts. Director Kevin Tancharoen's remake of Alan Parker's 1980 celebration of creative exuberance jettisons most of the original's objectionable elements but, some enjoyable musical numbers aside, the results are mostly tepid. A scene involving suicide, a sexual situation, underage drinking, at least one use of profanity, and a half-dozen crude and a few crass terms. The

title: Fame
synopsis: Irene Cara and several other talented youngsters from various ethnic and racial backgrounds learn the showbiz ropes studying in New York City's High School for the Performing Arts. Following them from audition to graduation, director Alan Parker's movie is a vibrant showcase for physical prowess not the least of which is demonstrated in some scenes involving nudity in a sexual context. Permissive sexual attitudes and irreverent treatment of religion overshadow the film's portrait of youngsters expressing their creativity and striving for professionalism

title: Family Affair, A
synopsis: Fine old-fashioned and full-blooded family melodrama in which Judge Hardy (Lionel Barrymore) rescues the town from an aqueduct scam while saving the marriage of his eldest daughter (Cecilia Parker). Directed by George B. Seitz, the picture's strong success spawned 15 sequels in a series that came to focus more on the judge's teenage son (Mickey Rooney) than the role of sage family patriarch created by Barrymore but thereafter played by Lewis Stone. In 1942 the series received a special Oscar for "representing the American way of life." The original is dated entertainment but still of interest for its idealistic view of family life

title: Family Business
synopsis: Muddled comedy-drama about a crooked grandfather (Sean Connery), his reformed son (Dustin Hoffman) and his bright grandson (Matthew Broderick) who join forces to commit the perfect theft in an improbable caper that proves self-destructive for the entire family. Directed by Sidney Lumet, there is much father-son business to resolve but the poor script and oddball casting only get in the way. Much profanity, some sexual innuendo and an unresolved moral perspective on crime as a career

title: Family Game, The
synopsis: Japanese director Yoshimitsu Morita fashions a gentle and noble comedy of family life and incisively chronicles their problems and how they resolve them. For those willing to read subtitles, the film will be an enjoyable as well as rewarding experience of the universality of family themes

title: Family Honor
synopsis: New York cop (Anthony Page) seeks revenge on the policemen who set up his father, also a member of the force, for opposing their taking payoffs from mobsters. Director Clark Worswick's crime movie is remarkable only in its consistent mediocrity which follows a predictable course of killings, drug traffic, warehouse confrontations and corruption in high places. Some Italian Americans may be offended by ethnic stereotyping

title: Family Jewels, The
synopsis: Sentimental slapstick comedy in which a 9-year-old orphan (Donna Butterworth) inherits her parents' millions, then ponders which of seven unlikely uncles (all Jerry Lewis) to choose as her guardian. Also produced and directed by Lewis, the self-indulgent proceedings offer little amusement for any but dedicated Lewis fans

title: Family Plot
synopsis: Director Alfred Hitchcock turns in a below-par thriller about the efforts of a not-quite-bogus medium (Barbara Harris) and her not-too-bright boy friend (Bruce Dern) to match wits with a pair of diabolically clever kidnappers (William Devane and Karen Black). The movie is peppered with profanity and unwitty double entendres, perhaps meant to inject some life into a slack picture

title: Family Prayers
synopsis: Melancholy tale set in 1969 as a sensitive Jewish boy (Tzvi Ratner-Stauber) prepares for his bar mitzvah while the marriage of his parents (Joe Mantegna and Anne Archer) unravels under the strain of his father;s compulsive gambling. Despite its heartfelt intentions, director Scott Rosenfelt's earnest drama is a familiar story marred by flat direction and weak scripting. Minor violence and an ongoing sense of menace from loansharks

title: Family, The
synopsis: Interesting Italian production recounting the lives of several generations of a family inhabiting an elegant apartment in Rome from the turn of the century to the present. Directed by Ettore Scola, the family portrait recalled by an aging man (Vittorio Gassman) is limited to the domestic life within the rooms of the apartment over the years. Many will find its fragmentary vignettes of personal drama surprisingly remote and lacking in emotional involvement. Some mature themes

title: Family Thing, A
synopsis: Suddenly learning he is half-black, an older Southerner (Robert Duvall) travels to Chicago to meet his half-brother, an African-American cop (James Earl Jones) who shuns him, but whose blind aunt insists he stay a few days and get to know the family. Directed by Richard Pearce, the plot may be contrived but Jones and Duvall give interesting performances in what proves a touching story of coping with life's surprises. Fleeting violence, mild sexual references and occasional epithets, profanity and rough language

title: Family Way, The
synopsis: The lives of a young married couple (Hywell Bennett and Hayley Mills) are frought with problems, including the groom's temporary inability to consummate their union. The groom's well-meaning but domineering father (John Mills) stands in his son's way but it is the strengths of family life that save the day. Directed by Roy Boulting with musical score by Paul McCartney

title: Famine Within, The
synopsis: Thought-provoking documentary about female obsession with body shape examines how, increasingly, young girls and women are suffering serious eating disorders as they define their worth by their weight. Writer- producer- director Katherine Gilday perceptively questions society's adulation of ultra-thin models and actresses in disturbing interviews with young female bulimics and anorectics. Brief shower room nudity

title: Fanatic
synopsis: ( see: "Die! Die! My Darling!" )

title: Fancy Pants
synopsis: Mistaken for an English butler, a jobless American actor (Bob Hope) is hired to bring some class to the household of a newly rich cattle baron whose sparky daughter (Lucille Ball) grows fond of the inept tenderfoot. Director George Marshall's enjoyable Western comedy -- a variation of "Ruggles of Red Gap" -- offers a winning pair of screen clowns at the top of their form and a script that has room for wit as well as pratfalls

title: Fandango
synopsis: It's May 1971, and five new-minted Texas college graduates go off on a car trip to the Mexican border in search of their lost youth -- fleeing Vietnam, marriage, regular jobs and other fearful spectres. Written and directed by Kevin Reynolds, the movie is sporadically amusing but more often sentimental, self-indulgent and tedious. Some brief nudity meant to be comic

title: Fando and Lis
synopsis: In an allegorical search for eternal happiness, Sergio Klainer and Diana Mariscal journey through a rocky, garbage-strewn landscape where a grotesque assortment of nightmarish characters confront them with sex and perversions. Scripted by Fernando Arrabal, directed by Alexandro Jodorowsky and filmed in Mexico, the bizarre narrative lacks coherence and is exploitative in its treatment of sex and violence

title: Fanny and Alexander
synopsis: Directed by Ingmar Bergman, this autobiographical mood piece set at Christmas in 1907 examines family ties through the eyes of a 10-year-old boy. Replete with the themes of earlier films, the period drama has none of the depth and perception of Bergman at his best but does offer the spectacle of a lavish re-creation. Scatological and sexually-derived humor and some brief nudity set the naturalistic tone of this decidedly mature tale of Swedish provincial life

title: Fanny Hill
synopsis: Swedish exploitation movie directed by Mac Ahlberg about an inexperienced country girl (Diana Kjaer) who comes to the big city to find a job. The situation is used as the premise for a series of crudely explicit sexual encounters

title: Fantasia
synopsis: Walt Disney's only excursion into the world of the fine arts presents eight selections of classical music, including Dukas' "Sorcerers Apprentice" with Mickey Mouse and a bucket brigade of brooms, Stravinsky's "Rite of Spring" with its massive, earth-bound images and the macabre vision of Musorgsky's "Night on Bald Mountain." Leopold Stokowski conducts the Philadelphia Orchestra as each piece of music is visualized in different animation styles and the imaginative result was not only Disney's most ambitious undertaking but it remains an enjoyably creative introduction to fine music, especially for youngsters

title: Fantasia 2000
synopsis: Follow-up movie in the super-size IMAX format presents animated images set to portions of classic compositions such as Gershwin's "Rhapsody in Blue," Elgar's "Pomp and Circumstance" and Stravinsky's 1919 "Firebird" suite, while keeping Stokowski's "The Sorcerer's Apprentice" from the original 1940 movie. State-of-the-art animation, backed by James Levine conducting the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, results in a felicitous wedding of beautiful sounds to colorful, sometimes whimsical images that may delight children and their parents

title: Fantastic Animation Festival
synopsis: Compilation consisting of 16 award-winning animated films. The majority are solidly entertaining, especially two featuring the clay figures of Will Vinton. For youngsters, it's a chance to view other approaches to the art of frame-by-frame moviemaking in contrast to Saturday morning cartoon fare

title: Fantastic Disappearing Man, The
synopsis: ( see: "The Return of Dracula" )

title: Fantastic Four
synopsis: Occasionally fun, but mostly unfantastic, superhero movie based on the Marvel comic-book series about four scientists endowed by cosmic rays with superpowers -- the elastic Mr. Fantastic (Ioan Gruffudd), Invisible Woman (Jessica Alba), self-combustible Human Torch (Chris Evans) and superstrong rocklike "Thing" (Michael Chiklis) -- who come together to stop the villainous Dr. Doom (Julian McMahon). Despite ham-fisted dialogue, bad acting, chintzy sets and, at times, cheesy special effects, director Tim Story's film has a goofy campiness but doesn't take itself too seriously, and manages to impart a positive message about teamwork and accepting those who are different. Intense comic-book action violence, some sexual innuendo and brief mildly crude language

title: Fantastic Four: Rise of the Silver Surfer
synopsis: The wedding of Mister Fantastic (Ioan Gruffudd) and Invisible Woman (Jessica Alba) is interrupted by a cosmic force set to destroy the planet, and the pair must join with the Human Torch (Chris Evans) and the Thing (Michael Chiklis) to avert disaster, trying to dissuade the evil force's emissary, a silver man (voice of Laurence Fishburne) on a flying surf board, from his dastardly mission, while contending with an overbearing army general (Andre Braugher) and duplicitous Dr. Doom (Julian McMahon). Apart from the elements listed below, director Tim Story's superior sequel -- with its personable leads, above-average special effects, and not-taking-itself-too-seriously tone -- makes for an engaging B-level adventure with a commendable message about making the right choices in life. Some mild innuendo and crass expressions, moderate action violence and implied nudity

title: Fantastic Mr. Fox
synopsis: Droll stop-motion animated adventure, set in the animal world of rural Britain, in which the titular vulpine creature (voice of George Clooney), now a respectable newspaper columnist with a wife (voice of Meryl Streep) and son (voice of Jason Schwartzman), tries to recapture his wild past as a chicken thief poaching on local farms, but his renewed raiding, abetted by his daring nephew (voice of Eric Anderson), enrages a trio of mean-spirited farmers whose escalating countermeasures endanger the whole burrowing community. A touch of menace and a fleeting joke about Mrs. Fox's youthful indiscretions aside, director and co-writer Wes Anderson's clever, lovingly crafted adaptation of Roald Dahl's 1970 children's book offers sophisticated family entertainment, with abundant fun for youngsters and a few insights into the tensions and paradoxes of human nature for adults

title: Fantastic Planet
synopsis: Lovely, haunting animated feature set in the far distant future where humans have become miniscule vermin in a world of purple reptilian giants who periodically exterminate the humans just as people today routinely exterminate rodents and roaches. For adults, this unusual picture, the creation of Rene Laloux and a Franco-Czech production team, can be a fascinating experience, heightened by its surrealistic imagery and eerie electronic soundtrack. Youngsters, however, might be disturbed by the occasional brutalities and the type of nudity associated with tribes living in a savage state

title: Fantastic Voyage
synopsis: The miniaturization of a medical team to the size of a molecule and their injection into a stroke patient's bloodstream is the only possible way to save the life of an important scientist. Director Richard Fleischer's incredible plot premise yields rich dividends in the form of exacting special effects re-creating the surreal world within the human body. Much suspense and some tense moments

title: Fan, The
synopsis: Young psychopath (Michael Biehn) stalks a glamorous star (Lauren Bacall) with whom he has become obsessed, striking with a razor at those whom he believes are preventing her from seeing him. Bacall is very good, but here she lends her presence and talent to a cheap, exploitative movie by director Ed Bianchi who seems obsessed with delivering brutal visual shocks. Extremely graphic violence

title: Fan, The
synopsis: Nasty thriller in which a psychotic baseball fan (Robert De Niro) kills a San Francisco Giants ballplayer and terrorizes another (Wesley Snipes). Directed by Tony Scott, the disturbing story concerns a troubled man's disintegration into insanity with murderous results. Some violence with gore, sporadic profanity and much rough language

title: Fantomas
synopsis: Gimmicky French-Italian superhero story about a master of disguise who battles all manner of Parisian criminals is directed by Andre Hanebelle in the melodramatic style of the old Saturday matinee adventure serials. Innocuous escapist fare

title: Far and Away
synopsis: Sprawling, brawling romantic adventure about the rebellious daughter (Nicole Kidman) of an Irish landowner and a scrappy tenant farmer (Tom Cruise) who wind up in Boston where they share quarters in order to save enough to get to the 1893 Oklahoma land rush. Director Ron Howard orchestrates rousing, feel-good entertainment whose romanticized predicaments detract little from the spirited performances of the two principals. Some sexual innuendo and bloody fisticuffs

title: Faraway, So Close
synopsis: Poetic fantasy of invisible guardian angels watching over the untidy affairs of people living in contemporary Berlin, until one of them (Otto Sander) becomes a mortal man in order to save a child's life, then suffers a series of misdaventures as a human. German director Wim Wenders' playfully creative but overlong journey is one of discovery in seeing modern life as experienced by a pure-hearted angel trying to cope with such things as alcohol, pornography and arms trafficking. Subtitles. Some stylized violence and sexual references

title: Far Country, The
synopsis: After taking a herd of cattle from Oregon to the gold camps of Alaska, a rancher (James Stewart) and aging sidekick (Walter Brennan) get in the way of a crooked judge (John McIntire) and his claim-jumping cohorts. Directed by Anthony Mann, the rugged setting appropriately frames the tough characters in an action picture that winds up with the usual shoot-out heroics. Some stylized violence and mild romance

title: Farewell My Concubine
synopsis: Long but colorful multi-leveled epic spanning the various political changes in China from 1925 to 1977 as seen in the lifelong friendship of two Peking Opera stars, one (Zhang Fengyi) famous for virile roles and the other (Leslie Cheung) for his performance of female leads, though the bond between them is strained after the former marries a prostitute (Gong Li). In intermixing the political with the personal, director Chen Kaige is particularly harsh on the excesses of the Cultural Revolution (1966-77), but his primary focus is on the world of the stage and those who make it their life. Subtitles. Some scenes of violence, sexual situations, including implications of homosexuality, and occasional rough language

title: Farewell, My Lovely
synopsis: Hulking ex-convict (Jack O'Halloran) hires private investigator Philip Marlowe (Robert Mitchum) to find his girl friend, though she hasn't bothered to write while he served a seven year sentence for bank robbery. Director Dick Richards' version of the Raymond Chandler mystery is skillfully crafted and Mitchum gives an outstanding performance. Some violence and incidental nudity

title: Farewell to Arms, A
synopsis: Disappointing version of the Hemingway novel about an American ambulance driver (miscast Rock Hudson) serving with the Italian Army during World War I and his ill-fated romance with a British nurse (Jennifer Jones). Director Charles Vidor portrays the swirl and confusion of events in a war zone with greater conviction than his wooden treatment of an intimate relationship which ends in a tragic pregnancy. Wartime violence and sexual situations

title: Farewell to the King
synopsis: Epic set in the jungles of Borneo during the final months of World War II where an American survivor of Corregidor (Nick Nolte) winds up as the adopted "king" of a tribe of headhunters whom he tries to protect from annihilation when they are forced to fight against the Japanese by a British Special Forces unit. Director John Milius leaves little doubt about who the true savages are in this uncomplicated, old-fashioned adventure movie. Intense battle carnage and minimal rough language

title: Farewell Uncle Tom
synopsis: Gualtiero Jacopetti and Franco Prosperi have been responsible for a long and dismayingly popular series of pseudo-documentaries but this time their subject is an historical one, slavery in the United States. Their voyeuristic treatment of the subject is simply vicarious flesh-peddling and the concluding section, specially prepared for the American version of this Italian film, can only deepen racial misunderstanding

title: Far From Heaven
synopsis: Poignant melodrama set in 1957 Connecticut where the prosperous life of a sweetly contented housewife (Julianne Moore) is completely upended when she discovers her husband (Dennis Quaid) in a homosexual embrace and she is scorned by the town for befriending her black gardener (Dennis Haysbert). Director Todd Haynes' lushly photographed period piece thoughtfully explores issues of racism, sexual identity and the role of women with delicacy, sensitivity and a focus on the humanity of all the characters. A brief homosexual kiss and implied affair, fleeting violence, alcohol abuse, some profanity and an instance of rough language. A-III � adults. (PG-13) 2002 Full Review The seemingly ideal life of an affluent housewife in 1957 Connecticut is shattered when she discovers her husband is attracted to other men in the sensitive melodrama "Far From Heaven" (Focus). Writer-director Todd Haynes pays homage to the films of Douglas Sirk, especially "All That Heaven Allows" and "Imitation of Life," by crafting an exquisite melodrama of the kind Sirk did best -- but bringing out themes that were not as openly addressed in the movies of a half-century ago. One might expect that Haynes would use a campy tone or turn the film into parody, but he does not. He respects his characters as they come up against societal barriers, and in focusing on their humanity has crafted a wistful, even poignant tale that lingers in the memory. The movie opens on a crisply glorious autumn day with Cathy Whitaker (Julianne Moore), the serenely gracious wife of successful executive Frank (Dennis Quaid), with her two young children at their beautiful Hartford home tended by a black maid (Viola Davis). Frank works long hours and when the police call her to pick him up after a fender-bender she isn't judgmental that he had been drinking. The next day, while being interviewed in her home for a photo society spread she is startled to see a black man on her property. She confronts Raymond (Dennis Haysbert) and apologizes when she learns that he is the new gardener. When she later sees widower Raymond at a modern art exposition she discusses the paintings with him, oblivious of her friends' highly disapproving stares. One evening when, as usual, Frank is delayed, she surprises him at his office with a hot dinner only to be shocked at finding him kissing another man. Horrified, he insists on going for therapy to end his homosexual urges and she keeps it secret, remaining supportive even as his increased drinking and emotional distance terrify her. Raymond, sensing her misery, tries to cheer her with a ride to pick up garden supplies and lunch in his part of town but that backfires enormously when a gossipy neighbor sees them and tells everyone. Scorned by all, a panicked Cathy promises her furious husband she will never speak to Raymond again. But further consequences are to follow, and Frank and Cathy's romantic holiday escape to Miami takes unexpected turns. Haynes delivers an insightful look at the tensions simmering below the facade of what would appear to be the ideal nuclear family. He treats his characters sympathetically: the husband struggling with his sexual orientation, the wife fearful of losing her husband and of her attraction to Raymond, who believes people can see beyond skin color -- until harsh reality deals him a glancing blow. Haysbert's performance as the gardener is quietly powerful but Moore carries the picture with her soft voice, earnest expressions and genteel movements perfectly conveying her character's sincerity and fragility. Cathy's essential sweetness shines through in a delicate, skilled portrayal. Nor do Moore or Haysbert need much dialogue to get across their doomed romantic yearning: a soulful glance, a feathery touch of hands says it all. Troubling as the subject is, the homosexual content is handled with extreme restraint. And not to be overlooked is the careful matching of technique to aesthetics. Some may say Haynes directed each frame to within an inch of its life but there is no denying that the autumn-hued, sun-dappled cinematography is quite beautiful, the production design meticulous and the period costumes remarkable. The mere rustle of Cathy's hoop skirts as she walks suggests the hushed community in which she lives where homophobia and racism simply are not acceptable topics. The filmmaker however allows us to look at that 1950s society not with condescension based on our more "sophisticated" contemporary perspective, but in a thoughtful way that prompts us to consider and hopefully reject our own prejudices. Because of a brief homosexual kiss and implied affair, fleeting violence, alcohol abuse, some profanity and an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops

title: Far from Home: The Adventures of Yellow Dog
synopsis: Bland family picture concerns a 14-year-old (Jesse Bradford) and his Labrador shipwrecked and stranded for weeks in the Pacific Northwest on a thickly forested, uninhabited island as his worried parents (Bruce Davison and Mimi Rogers) continue to hope they will be rescued. Writer-director Phillip Borsos presents a formula survival story, surprising only in its consistent predictability

title: Far from the Madding Crowd
synopsis: Excellent British screen version of Thomas Hardy's romantic melodrama of early Victorian country life with Julie Christie being pursued by Peter Finch, Terence Stamp and Alan Bates. Director John Schlesinger avoids the pitfalls of the formula blockbuster and comes up with a superbly realistic, atmospheric production filmed entirely on location in Hardy's Dorset

title: Fargo
synopsis: A debtridden Minnesota car dealer (William H. Macy) hires two thugs to kidnap his wife and split the hefty ransom her wealthy father would pay, but all goes horribly awry, resulting in several murders doggedly investigated by a small-town chief of police (Frances McDormand). Finding black comedy in this loosely fact-based tragedy, filmmakers Joel and Ethan Coen chillingly depict earnest small-towners caught up in shocking violence, although justice eventually prevails in the unlikely form of a folksy, very pregnant police officer. Recurring gory violence and much rough language

title: Far Horizons, The
synopsis: Colorful but wooden re-creation of the Lewis (Fred MacMurray) and Clark (Charlton Heston) expedition (1803-06) exploring the upper reaches of the Missouri River and across the Rockies to the Pacific Ocean. Directed by Rudolph Mate, the scenery is certainly picturesque but the adventure is too fanciful to be convincing, especially the hokey romance between Clark and the expedition's Indian guide, Sacajawea (a badly miscast Donna Reed). Some stylized violence and Native-American stereotypes

title: Farinelli
synopsis: Elaborate costume drama about the personal and artistic relationship between an acclaimed 18th-century castrato singer (Stefano Dionisi) and his ambitious composer brother (Enrico Lo Verso), who had had him castrated as a youth, focuses on their pact of sharing women until the singer's sexual frustrations jeopardize their relationship. Director Gerard Corbiau's visually lush production works primarily on the level of a passionately acted musical soap opera whose two main characters view sexual conquests as their artistic due, although the narrative also explores the psychological harm on those castrated in the name of art. Subtitles. A suicide, several bedroom scenes with nudity and a cavalier attitude toward sexual matters

title: Farmer & Chase
synopsis: Nasty crime drama in which a career criminal (Ben Gazzara) accepts his admiring son (Todd Field) as his new partner as well as the young man's gun-toting girlfriend (Lara Flynn Boyle), but their botched bank robbery ends in multiple deaths. Writer-director Michael Seitzman's drawn-out tale of mindless low-lifes who rob out of boredom or greed is emotionally uninvolving and dramatically uninsightful. A romanticized view of crime, several murders and beatings, fleeting drug use, brief sexual encounter, some profanity and constant rough language

title: Farmer's Daughter, The
synopsis: Enjoyable comedy about a Swedish-American country lass (Loretta Young) who wins the love of a bachelor congressman (Joseph Cotten) and the affection of his party boss mom (Ethel Barrymore) when she comes to work for them as a maid, but her wholesome virtues and honest candor lead to her nomination as the congressional candidate of the rival party. Directed by H.C. Potter, some fun is had with crooked politicans and a smear campaign that backfires, but the main attraction is Young's Oscar-winning performance as the country girl whose commonsense wisdom wins over the city slickers

title: Farmer's Wife, The
synopsis: Fine documentary follows three arduous years in the lives of a Nebraska couple with three daughters whose marriage is strained by crop failures and financial pressures as they struggle to avoid losing their farm. Director David Sutherland paints a moving portrait of rural Americans' love of the land as well as this Catholic family's faith as they endure through hard times. Serious treatment of marital discord

title: Farmer, The
synopsis: Revenge story of a World War II veteran (Gary Conway) has arty pretensions but not a spark of intelligence. Mechanically directed by David Berlatsky, it is excessively brutal and sexually degrading

title: Far Off Place, A
synopsis: Contemporary African adventure with a 14-year-old American girl (Reese Witherspoon) and young friend (Ethan Randall) fleeing murderous ivory poachers by trekking 1000 miles across the Kalahari desert with only an African Bushman (Sarel Bok) as guide. Director Mikael Salomon combines a lively story, delightful cast and exquisite cinematography for an old-fashioned outdoor adventure with modern environmental sensibilities. Brief violence, occasional profanity and continuing menace

title: Far Out Man
synopsis: Terminally revolting movie about the aimless wanderings of an aging, leftover hippie (Tommy Chong) who takes to the road to forget his longlost wife and son but accidentally chances upon them. Chong wrote, directed and stars (along with assorted relatives) in this warped tribute to the drug culture and sexual promiscuity. Much rough language, sexually suggestive scenes with nudity, promotion of drug abuse and a variety of gross, violent and vulgar acts

title: Fast Break
synopsis: Very funny movie about a new basketball coach (Gabe Kaplan) who recruits a motley collection of youths to give an obscure college a winning season. Directed by Jack Smight, it contains some rough language and several mildly suggestive sexual scenes

title: Fast Bullets
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Henri Samuels in which a Texas Ranger (Tom Tyler) gets the goods on the leader (Al Bridge) of an outlaw band with some help from a former gang member (Rex Lease) and a spunky barroom dancer (Margaret Nearing). Stylized violence

title: Fast Charlie...The Moonbeam Rider
synopsis: Failed period road comedy about a World War I vet (David Carradine) who enlists the aid of some of his old buddies to help him enter a transcontinental motorcycle race. Director Steve Carver's thin story is amiable but not very funny. Permissive attitude toward casual sex

title: Faster
synopsis: Sour revenge flick in which a paroled convict (Dwayne Johnson) hunts down and slays those responsible for his brother's death at the hands of a rival gang. On his trail are a scrofulous drug-addicted detective (Billy Bob Thornton) and a suave British assassin (Oliver Jackson-Cohen). Director George Tillman Jr. and screenwriters Tony and Joe Gayton assemble a series of foul cliches and then just let the actors rip. Multiple scenes of murderous revenge, slow-motion gun and knife violence, drug use, some profane and crude language

title: Fastest Gun Alive, The
synopsis: Contrived Western about a peaceful but fast-drawing storekeeper (Glenn Ford) who, after much soul-searching, saves his town from a crazed gunslinger (Broderick Crawford). Director Russell Rouse badly overplays the far-fetched situation, then muddles the hero's motivations in a coy conclusion that leaves viewers flat. Stylized violence

title: Fast Food Fast Women
synopsis: Pointless romantic comedy set in New York City which parallels the love stories of a single waitress (Anna Thomson) who falls for a novelist/taxi driver (Jamie Harris), and that of an aging, sexually insecure widower (Robert Modica) who begins to date again. As directed by Amos Kollek, the monotonous film is a compilation of contrived scenes that lurch between awkward and painfully predictable. A few sexual encounters, some nudity and intermittent rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Fast Food Nation
synopsis: Absorbing albeit bleak multiplotted expose excoriating the fast food industry for its dangerous, unsanitary and exploitative working conditions, from the perspective of a fictitious burger franchise's marketing executive (Greg Kinnear) who goes to Colorado to investigate conditions at their plant; a young cashier (Ashley Johnson) whose uncle (Ethan Hawke) urges her to improve her life, despite the complacency of her unmotivated mother (Patricia Arquette); and a young Mexican immigrant couple (Catalina Sandino Moreno and Wilmer Valderrama) struggling to build a better life. Director Richard Linklater's skillful dramatization of Eric Schlosser's nonfiction book (they co-wrote the script) is sometimes preachy and the ending intentionally inconclusive, but the issues raised are timely ones, while the cast (including Bruce Willis, Bobby Cannavale and Kris Kristofferson) offers solid, selfless performances. Partly subtitled. Rough and crude language, a couple of briefly intense, if nongraphic, sexual encounters, fleeting partial nudity, innuendo, some gruesome slaughterhouse shots and drug references

title: Fast Forward
synopsis: Some bright and talented teenagers from Sandusky, Ohio, go to New York to win a dance contest without bothering to inform their parents. The poor kids have to hang on for a month or so before they make it to the top. Mediocre entertainment, disappontingly directed by Sidney Poitier. Some vulgar language, nose-thumbing at parental authority and teenage drinking presented as humorous

title: Fast & Furious
synopsis: Overheated, morally swerving action sequel in which an ex-con (Vin Diesel) pursuing a vendetta and an undercover FBI agent (Paul Walker) renew their rivalry as they both use their driving skills to infiltrate a cross-border drug smuggling ring and identify its secretive leader. As directed by Justin Lin, the thin story is no more than an excuse for long sequences of reckless racing, while the characters move from one side of the law to the other as it suits them. Vigilantism, brief nongraphic sexual activity, partial nudity, cohabitation, occasional rough language and profanity

title: Fast Talking
synopsis: A modern artful dodger lies, cheats and steals his way out of high school and into the brave new wor1d of se1f-sufficiency in reaction to flawed family, alienated friends and a social order which offers little positive encouragement. But it's hard to accept the amiable, resourceful teenager as someone incapable of finding positive options. The film points to the mora1 and political inadequacies of adult society but in 1ess than contructive fashion

title: Fast Times at Ridgemont High
synopsis: Director Amy Heckerling's examination of teen mores in the suburban jungle of shopping malls, discos and the playing fields of Southern California has some insights. However, for the most part it is a crass, insensitive and superficial movie with an unsettling nastiness lurking just beneath its pleasant surface. Some extremely graphic nudity and a scene of adolescents discussing oral sex

title: Fatal Attraction
synopsis: Ambitious, hard-driving but happily-married lawyer (Michael Douglas) has a fling with a compulsive admirer (Glenn Close) and both suffer the dangerous consequences. Director Adrian Lyne's fatalistic romance begins as a moral tale and ends in a melodramatic bloodbath. Several graphic love-making scenes but violence and rough language dominate

title: Fat Albert
synopsis: Flat live-action comedy based on the characters of the long-running animated series created by Bill Cosby, in which the heavyset hero (Kenan Thompson) and his junkyard gang step out of their cartoon world in order to help a troubled teen (Kyla Pratt) believe in herself. While imparting the same sort of positive, family-value life lessons, director Joel Zwick's film lacks the intelligence, originality and fun of the groundbreaking Saturday morning show. Brief crude language

title: Fatal Instinct
synopsis: Strained send-up of movie thrillers in which Armand Assante is the thoroughly dense object of affection and /or extinction by his wandering wife (Kate Nelligan), simpering secretary (Sherilyn Fenn) and kooky client (Sean Young). The slapstick and sight gags in director Carl Reiner's weak, goofy parody are only fitfully funny and often crude. Some vulgar sexual innuendo, brief nudity and sporadic violence played for comic effect

title: Fata Morgana
synopsis: German director Werner Herzog's interior journey to Africa is a stunning portrait of the North African landscape where people are transformed into fragments of an alien, dreamlike world. For those adventurous enough to take a trip without the security of guideposts, it will most likely prove a consciousness-expanding experience

title: Fat City
synopsis: Complex character study of two boxers, one a has-been (Stacy Keach) and the other a youth of 19 (Jeff Bridges) whose prospects on the B-grade California boxing circuit are at best uncertain. Director John Huston's theme of wasted lives and loves and the hopes of youth for affluence and success (the ironic meaning of the title) are evocative but unsatisfying in terms of the dramatic whole. Well-staged, realistic fight sequences

title: Fate Is the Hunter
synopsis: Middling melodrama starts with a jetliner crash killing 53 people, including the pilot (Rod Taylor) whom an airline executive (Glenn Ford) spends the rest of the movie trying to clear of blame by interviewing those who knew him (notably Dorothy Malone, Nancy Kwan, Wally Cox and Mark Stevens). Director Ralph Nelson plods through numerous flashbacks of the pilot's free-wheeling life before a stewardess (Suzanne Pleshette) who survived the crash supplies the clue to its cause. Superficial treatment turns a serious subject into undemanding fare

title: Fateless
synopsis: Holocaust drama about a Hungarian Jewish boy's (Marcell Nagy) coming-of-age experiences in various concentration camps, where, through relationships with fellow prisoners, he struggles to make sense of the atrocities around him and gain deeper insights about himself. Directed by Lajos Koltai from a script by Imre Kertesz based on the latter's semiautobiographical novel, the film, despite its grim subject matter, is visually graceful, and the intimate story conveys universal themes, such as the resiliency of the human spirit and its ability to discern beauty in even the darkest situations. Disturbing Holocaust images, brief partial and full prison camp nudity, and some rough and crude language. Subtitles

title: Father Goose
synopsis: An unusually dishelved Cary Grant plays a beachcomber reformed by a prim but high-spirited French schoolmarm (Leslie Caron) and her seven girl pupils when they are stranded together on a Pacific island during World War II. Director Ralph Nelson handles the romantic comedy deftly enough, though the plot is entirely predictable as wartime dangers are overcome with affable, good-natured humor

title: Father of the Bride
synopsis: Delightful comedy from Edward Streeter's novel about a self-assured suburbanite (Spencer Tracy) suddenly thrust into the unfamiliar world of wedding preparations and financial obligations when his only daughter (Elizabeth Taylor) announces her engagement. Brightly directed by Vincente Minnelli, Tracy is superb as the caring but confused head of the household helped by patient wife Joan Bennett to come to terms with their daughter's vision of the perfect wedding. Amusing yet perceptive view of middle-class life and family values

title: Father of the Bride
synopsis: Trite remake of the 1950 Spencer Tracy-Elizabeth Taylor charmer this time has father Steve Martin battling the emotional loss of daughter Kimberly Williams while wife Diane Keaton tries to cushion the financial drain of a big wedding. A hilarious scene early on is outweighed by mawkish sentimentality in director Charles Shyer's drawn-out comedy. Fleeting sexual innuendo

title: Father of the Bride, Part II
synopsis: Warm-hearted sequel (and remake of the 1951 "Father's Little Dividend") in which good-natured dad (Steve Martin) copes with the pregnancies of both his daughter (Kimberly Williams) and wife (Diane Keaton) while feeling too young to be called gramps but too old to be pushing a baby buggy. Director Charles Shyer's sentimental domestic comedy is frequently funny in its wholesome depiction of family life. Mild sexual innuendo

title: Fathers and Sons
synopsis: Shallow drama of a widower (Jeff Goldblum) trying to help his teenage son (Rory Cochrane) confront the perils of contemporary urban life -- gangs, drugs, alcohol, sex, cults and street crazies. Written and directed by Paul Mones, the well-intended effort realistically portrays the youth's problems while mawkishly handling the father's inept attempts to communicate with his son until a contrived ending. Restrained depiction of moral problems requiring a mature perspective

title: Fathers' Day
synopsis: Needing help in searching for her 16-year-old runaway son (Charlie Hofheimer), a desperate mom (Nastassja Kinski) separately tells two former lovers (Robin Williams and Billy Crystal) that the boy is their biological son and the two join forces to find him. Director Ivan Reitman lets Williams and Crystal improvise in the style of Hope and Crosby in an amusing, though overly sentimental tale of unexpected bonding between strangers. Intermittent comic violence, several sexual references and humorous treatment of past sexual escapades

title: Father's Little Dividend
synopsis: "Father of the Bride" cast returns in a heavy-handed sequel turning good old dad (Spencer Tracy) into an unsympathetic grouch dismayed by the demands of impending grandfatherhood. Nor does director Vincente Minnelli find much humor in the predictable problems of expectant parents Elizabeth Taylor and Don Taylor in naming the baby, false labors and in-law competition over the heir apparent. Confusing situations for youngsters

title: Fathom
synopsis: Mindless spy intrigue with Raquel Welch being pursued by plane, by boat, by harpoonist and by bull (both figuratively and literally). Directed by Leslie Martinson, the star vehicle becomes tiresome long before the ending

title: Fat Man and Little Boy
synopsis: Fine production values and serviceable acting highlight this dramatization of the creation of the atomic bomb beginning in 1942 and focusing on the professional and personal agendas motivating the two key players, Gen. Leslie R. Groves (Paul Newman) and physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer (Dwight Schultz). Director Roland Joffe creates an air of scientific and historical accuracy together with a sense of visual tension and the result helps clarify the moral issues debated by those who made the bomb. An adulterous encounter with nudity, a grisly death from radiation and minimal rough language

title: Fat Man, The
synopsis: Weak murder mystery directed by William Castle has the rotund detective (J. Scott Smart) created for radio by Dashiell Hammett employing a dull assistant (Clinton Sundberg) in following the trail of a dentist's killer which leads along the way to an ex-con (Rock Hudson) and a circus clown (Emmett Kelly). The usual stylized violence and menace

title: Fatso
synopsis: Actress Anne Bancroft fails to convey much sincerity or intelligence in her directorial debut. Her comedy stars Dom DeLuise as a compulsive eater who is so shocked by the early death of an obese cousin that he determines to lose weight. The humor is weighted down, however, by foul language and silly sight-gags in a social satire which provides little insight into a serious malady

title: Faust
synopsis: Playfully absurd fantasy in which a man (Petr Cepek) finds himself in a Prague theater playing the role of Faust, sometimes on the stage or in a medieval setting but most often in a marionette version, all of which inevitably ends with Mephistopheles (again Cepek) claiming the man's soul. Writer-director Jan Svankmajer's Czech production is a surrealistic blend of live action, puppetry and clay animation but the traditional story gets lost in a welter of shifting scenes and bizarre images with Faust as a contemporary Everyman bumbling his way through a mythic world of good and evil. Sparse dubbed dialogue. A demonic incantation, some bawdy humor and sexual innuendo

title: Favor, the Watch and the Very Big Fish, The
synopsis: Strained comedy has an earnest photographer (Bob Hoskins) of religious tableaux and the model he uses for Jesus (Jeff Goldblum) falling for the same woman (Natasha Richardson). Writer-director Ben Lewin's mildly naughty black comedy is too self-conscious and contrived to inspire more than forced laughter from the wacky situations. Much sexual innuendo, brief nudity, comic violence and minimal rough language

title: F.B.I. Story, The
synopsis: The growth of the Federal Bureau of Investigation as seen in the career of one of its agents (James Stewart) from the early fight against Prohibition-era mobsters and Ku Klux Klan terrorists to combatting Nazi spies and communist agents. Directed by Mervyn Le Roy, the crimebusting episodes are interspersed with the agent's family life, especially the strains they cause his wife (Vera Miles), and the result is more idealistic than convincing. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Fear
synopsis: Manipulative thriller in which a psycho youth (Mark Wahlberg) seduces a 16-year-old girl (Reese Witherspoon), then goes on a murderous rampage when her father (William Peterson) interferes. Directed by James Foley, the premise is ridiculously contrived in escalating threatening situations into the frightful scares of its absurd climax. Excessive violence, intense menace, graphic sexual situations, occasional profanity and recurring rough language

title: Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas
synopsis: Repulsive tale in which a continually stoned journalist (Johnny Depp) and his menacing sidekick (Benicio Del Toro) lurch through a boozy, destructive Las Vegas weekend sampling every drug they can lay their hands on. Based on gonzo journalist Hunter S. Thompson's 1971 novel, director Terry Gilliam's salute to the acid-tripping subculture wallows in gleeful excess and gaudy nihilism. Constant substance abuse, brief nudity and non-stop profanity and rough language

title: Fear City
synopsis: Psychotic killer of New York City strippers is hunted by an ex-boxer (Tom Berenger) and his exhibitionist girlfriend (Melanie Griffith) in a sleazy exploitation feature directed by Abel Ferrara. Excessive violence, much nudity and recurring rough language

title: Fear Eats the Soul -- Ali
synopsis: German movie in which a 60-year-old cleaning woman meets a young Moroccan mechanic, and out of mutual loneliness and a desperate need for some special other person, they marry and encounter the same rejection and discrimination suffered by minorities everywhere. Directed by Rainer Werner Fassbinder, the story is simply told and yet is profoundly human and affecting in its picture of two ordinary people persecuted by a hypocritical society. Subtitles. Disquieting examples of the harm caused by prejudice

title: Fear in the Night
synopsis: Muddled but involving mystery in which a bank clerk (DeForest Kelley) awakens from a nightmare convinced he's murdered a man, gets his cop brother-in-law (Paul Kelly) to investigate and the clues eventually lead to a hypnotist. Directed by Maxwell Shane from a story by William Irish, the intriguing plot has some surreal visuals, including the multi-images reflected in an octagonal mirrored room, but the pacing is pedestrian and the solution is anti-climactic. Stylized violence, including an attempted suicide, menacing situations and infidelity as a plot element

title: Fear Is the Key
synopsis: Adaptation of Alistair MacLean thriller about an ex-salvage operator (Barry Newman) who, by reason of a wild and complex chain of events, finds himself in the palatial home of an oil heiress (Suzy Kendall) and given the task of dredging up a sunken treasure. Director Michael Tuchner's wildly improbable melodrama in which nothing is what it seems is moderately entertaining, mercifully short on sex and violence but awfully hard to swallow

title: Fearless
synopsis: In the months following a plane crash with many fatalities, a euphoric survivor (Jeff Bridges) feels disconnected from wife (Isabella Rossellini) and child, a situation aggravated by his determination to help a severely depressed survivor (Rosie Perez) adjust to the loss of her baby in the crash. Director Peter Weir realistically captures the spiritual anguish and psychological trauma of survivors trying to pull their lives together after a profound disaster completely changes their outlook on life. Violent aftermath of a crash with fleeting shots of the human carnage, minor sexual innuendo and occasional rough language

title: Fearless Frank
synopsis: The Second City gang have put together a super-spoof of crime movies with some digs at sex and religion. Jon Voight plays Frank, a Superman character flying through the air and fighting evil wherever it rears its ugly head. Director Philip Kaufman's campy, superficial adult comedy is of limited quality and appeal

title: Fearless Vampire Killers, The
synopsis: Offbeat horror spoof in which an old scholar of the occult (Jack McGowran) and his young assistant (Polanski) seek out a vampire's castle in the hills of Transylvania, using the tools of garlic, the cross and a wooden stake in their research but the vampires are released to spread throughout the world. Also directed by Polanski, it is imitation camp at best, all very short on humor, long on blood-drinking and sexual innuendo

title: Fear No Evil
synopsis: Bright but popular high school student is possessed by the devil in this inept horror film written and directed by Frank Laloggia. Excessive violence, nudity and exploitation of religious themes

title: Fear Strikes Out
synopsis: Fact-based story of Boston Red Sox baseball player Jimmy Piersall (Anthony Perkins) whose father (Karl Malden) raises him to be a star outfielder, but the pressure of making good brings on a nervous breakdown requiring psychiatric treatment before he's able to return to the club. Directed by Robert Mulligan, the movie presents a realistic picture of a youth trying to measure up to the high expectations of a well-meaning but ambitious father, with convincing performances from both Malden and Perkins. Brief but intense scenes of emotional instability

title: Fear, The
synopsis: Greek movie directed by Costas Manoussakis centers on a retarded youth's morbid preoccupation with sex and is offensive because of its explicit treatment of erotic activities

title: Feast of July
synopsis: Bittersweet romantic tragedy set in Victorian England where a woman (Embeth Davidtz) deserted by her lover is taken in by a kindly working-class family whose three grown sons compete for her affection. Directed by Chris Menaul, the handsome production presents the story in stately, understated fashion with a growing sense of doom for its ill-fated characters. Brief but intense violence and discreet bedroom encounters with fleeting nudity

title: Feast of Love
synopsis: Moving but excessively graphic examination of romantic love as experienced by a college professor (Morgan Freeman), his wife (Jane Alexander), the owner of a local cafe (Greg Kinnear), the two women for whom he sequentially falls (Selma Blair and Radha Mitchell), a hardened businessman (Billy Burke) and a young, Romeo and Juliet-like couple (Alexa Davalos and Toby Hemingway). The film, as directed by Robert Benton, is beautifully atmospheric and features some excellent performances, yet its script offers the audience a set of false choices, making an idol of erotic love and portraying that love with an intrusive frankness. Extensive frontal, rear and upper female nudity, sexual encounters, some of them graphic and adulterous, same-sex coupling, some rough language, occasional profanity, drug use and pornography

title: Feathered Serpent, The
