synopsis: Western programmer directed by Sam Newfield in which a government agent (Tim McCoy) tracks down the kidnappers of an inventor (Lloyd Ingraham) whose work with electrical impulses is being used to cause mail planes to crash, then be looted by the gang

title: Ghost Rider
synopsis: Lightweight supernatural action adventure based on the Marvel Comics� character about a motorcycle daredevil, Johnny Blaze (Nicolas Cage), who makes a deal with the devil (Peter Fonda) and is cursed with having to serve as his �bounty-hunter� � transforming into a flaming skeletal biker astride a fiery chopper by night � to escape damnation by stopping a renegade fallen angel (Wes Bentley) from unleashing hell on earth. Despite a dumb script and risible theology, the film never takes itself too seriously, and Cage�s campy but committed performance is laced with enough humor to make the hokey ride sufficiently diverting B-movie fare. Some parents may find the demonic elements problematic, but it�s little more than a comic book retelling of �Faust,� and, while, of greater concern, vengeance, not justice is meted out by Blaze, love is ultimately shown to be stronger than evil, with a recurring theme of redemption and second chances. Stylized violence, some horror images, a vulgar gesture, scattered crude language and couple of instances of profanity

title: Ghost Ship
synopsis: Gory tale about a salvage crew (led by Gabriel Byrne and Julianna Margulies) struggling to remove cases of gold bullion from a decrepit ocean liner inhabited by evil spirits. A pathetic script with preposterous developments should confine director Steve Beck's carnage-filled horror flick to Davy Jones' locker. Recurring violence with excessive gore, sexual innuendo with nudity, frequent profanity and much rough language

title: Ghosts Italian Style
synopsis: Italian romantic comedy about newlyweds trying to save their sputtering marriage by living rent-free in a decaying baroque mansion haunted by a womanizing Count. Sophia Loren and Vittorio Gassman turn social satire into farce as director Renato Castellani tries to make something out of a story about false impressions and mistaken identities

title: Ghosts of Girlfriends Past
synopsis: A heartless womanizing bachelor (Matthew McConaughey) is visited by the ghosts of his playboy uncle (Michael Douglas) and those of his jilted girlfriends (Emma Stone, Noureen DeWulf and Olga Maliouk) on the eve of the wedding of his brother (Breckin Meyer), and he comes to realize the depth of his feelings for his childhood sweetheart (Jennifer Garner). Though there's ultimately a wonderfully redemptive outcome and a strong affirmation of marriage and fidelity, along with a couple of superlative scenes for McConaughey, director Mark Waters' "A Christmas Carol" retread is marred by far too much crude and smutty humor before getting there. Crass sexual talk and innuendo, some crude language and fleeting profanity, premarital sexual situations and a drug reference

title: Ghosts of Mississippi
synopsis: Fact-based drama chronicles the struggle of a dedicated Mississippi prosecutor (Alec Baldwin), prompted by Medgar Evers' widow (Whoopi Goldberg), to retry and convict the white supremist (James Woods) guilty of the 1963 slaying of the civil rights leader nearly 30 years after two mistrials had left him a free man. Producer-director Rob Reiner's provides a straightforward though emotionally involving account of an infamous instance of institutionalized racism finally rectified. Scenes depicting the victim's bloody murder and a few instances of profanity

title: Ghosts on the Loose
synopsis: Formula comedy directed by William Beaudine with the East Side Kids (Leo Gorcey, Huntz Hall, Bobby Jordan, etc.) helping newlyweds (Ava Gardner and Rick Vallin) move into a supposedly haunted house which proves to be the hide-out of a Nazi spy ring (led by Bela Lugosi). Dated fun

title: Ghost Story
synopsis: Fred Astaire, Melvyn Douglas, Douglas Fairbanks Jr., John Houseman and Patricia Neal appear in director John Irvin's lavishly produced but intellectually impoverished film version of Peter Straub's novel about a vengeful spirit (an extremely fleshy spirit) stalking four old codgers who sent her to the bottom of a Vermont pond 50 years before. Ectoplasmic nudity and graphic spooky sexuality

title: Ghost World
synopsis: Poignant tale about two recent high school graduates (Thora Birch and Scarlett Johansson) at odds with the world around them whose friendship is jeopardized when one befriends an older jazz afficionado (Steve Buscemi). Director Terry Zwigoff captures teen angst and the alienation felt by characters who reject the sameness of and the corporate influence upon popular culture. Implied sexual encounter, brief violence, a few crude references and frequent profanity and rough language

title: Ghoulies
synopsis: Shameless, thoroughly inept ripoff of "Gremlins," it is directed by Luca Bercovici and has some brief partial nudity and gore but not too much in the way of real violence

title: Giant
synopsis: Sentimental but stylish adaptation of Edna Ferber's sprawling family saga of life and love in Texas oil country from the turn of the century to the early 1950s, with Dennis Hopper as the clean-cut, intense son of Texas patriarchs Elizabeth Taylor and Rock Hudson, while James Dean gives his most moving performance as the inarticulate cowhand who strikes it rich. Directed by George Stevens, the plot is less important than its themes of changing times, the generation gap, racial prejudice, the waste of war and marital incompatibility. Over three hours long, children may find it a taxing experience

title: Giant Behemoth, The
synopsis: Low-budget British monster movie directed by Eugene Lourie pits a marine biologist (Gene Evans) against a prehistoric sea creature that's been roused from the deep by A-bomb tests, then proceeds to ravage the coast of Cornwall in radioactive fury before heading up the Thames River to London. Scenes of destruction and radiation victims

title: Giant Claw, The
synopsis: Sci-fi timewaster directed by Fred F. Sears concerns a colossal bird from outer space attacking Earth with dime-store special effects until stopped by a cornball electronics engineer (Jeff Morrow). The crunching of unconvincing models is more silly than scary

title: Giant Gila Monster, The
synopsis: Low-budget horror directed by Ray Kellogg in which a Texas youth blows up a lizard blamed for the death of several motorists. Stylized violence, sexual innuendo and excessive drinking

title: Giant of Thunder Mountain, The
synopsis: When a little girl (winningly played by Noley Thornton) befriends a lonely, oversized woodsman (Richard Kiel) living on a nearby mountain, the villagers determine to drive him away but have a change of heart after he saves them from a gang of cutthroats. Written by Kiel and directed by James Roberson, the story of a child's ability to see the goodness in a man foolishly misjudged by her elders is ultimately heartwarming and certainly eye-filling in its tunr-of-the-century Western setting but suffers from a lumpy plot with too much violent action. Initial scenes of parents being killed by a grizzly bear, life-threatening situations involving children as well as adults and frightening scenes of vigilante justice

title: Giant Spider Invasion, The
synopsis: Sci-fi clunker directed by Bill Rebane involves a meteoric shower of space geodes on a farm near Gleason, Wis., which is soon overrun by a spider as big as a house until it's stopped by a pair of scientists (Steve Brodie and Barbara Hale) and the local sheriff (Alan Hale). Hokey violence and some sexual innuendo

title: G.I. Blues
synopsis: Formula romance in which an American soldier (Elvis Presley) stationed in West Germany bets he can get a local nightclub dancer (Juliet Prowse) to let him stay the night in her apartment, then falls in love with her and tries to call the bet off. Directed by Norman Taurog, the result is a thin mix of sexist leers, occasional Presley songs and some picturesque scenery of the Frankfort area. Sexual situations and innuendo, including an unwed mother

title: Gidget
synopsis: Dated coming-of-age story set in sunny California where a 16-year-old (Sandra Dee), whose nickname is a contraction of "girl midget," pals around with some would-be beach bums (led by beatnik Cliff Robertson) and learns about love from one of them (James Darren). Directed by Paul Wendkos, the slickly superficial proceedings feature the usual addled parents, empty-headed teenyboppers, partying young males and a free-spirited, clay-footed social dropout. Romantic complications, sexual innuendo and a sexual situation involving an adolescent

title: Gidget Goes Hawaiian
synopsis: Flimsy sequel with teenage Gidget (Deborah Walley) joining her parents on a Waikiki vacation after breaking up with her boyfriend (James Darren), though he shows up in time to help when she fears that her missing parents are off philandering. Director Paul Wendkos downplays the adolescent hormones in a contrived plot providing a simplistic lesson in trust and faith in others, no matter how guilty their actions may seem. Mild sexual innuendo and some excessive social drinking

title: Gidget Goes to Rome
synopsis: Tired sequel about the goofy misadventures and romantic mix-ups of 18-year-old Gidget (Cindy Carol) while touring the Eternal City with her boyfriend (James Darren), four of their chums and a dotty aunt (Jessie Royce Landis) going along as chaperon. Directed by Paul Wendkos, the lame plot is occasionally relieved by visits to Rome's ancient monuments, historic buildings and ritzy restaurants. Long sit for youngsters, though it may have nostalgic value for some of their elders

title: Gigi
synopsis: Soured Lerner-and-Loewe musical from the Colette story about a 1890's Parisian adolescent (Leslie Caron) who balks at her family's efforts to train her as a courtesan until she meets a charming young man (Louis Jourdan). Directed by Vincente Minnelli, the plush production makes good use of French locales and has a splendid cast but its theme, as enunciated in Maurice Chevalier's smirking rendition of "Thank Heaven for Little Girls," has lost the sense of sophisticated charm that was once considered amusing. Considerable sexual innuendo

title: Gigli
synopsis: Stale romantic comedy about a low-level leg-breaker (Ben Affleck) who falls for a beautiful lesbian mob enforcer (Jennifer Lopez) hired to assist him in kidnapping a federal prosecutor's mentally handicapped brother. Lopez and Affleck exhibit more fizzle than sizzle in this overhyped clunker written and directed by Martin Brest, full of forced lewd humor and fueled by a distorted suggestion that sexuality is a malleable social construct and a casual endorsement of homosexual activity. A sexual encounter, excessive sexually explicit and rough language, as well as profanity and brief strong violence

title: Gigot
synopsis: Seriocomic tale of a simple-minded French mute (Jackie Gleason) whose problems become increasingly serious after he gives shelter to a homeless woman and her child. Directed by Gene Kelly, the contrived plot provides an unlikely vehicle for a star whose sense of physical comedy and pathos of character in the role will not suit all tastes. Sentimental results that rarely touch the heart

title: G.I. Jane
synopsis: Hokey melodrama in which a woman naval officer (Demi Moore) undergoes the rigorous training program for the Navy's elite SEALS combat force, graduates despite various sexist obstacles and soon becomes a battlefield hero. Directed by Ridley Scott, the picture offers no real insights about women in the military, concentrating instead on the character's endurance of physical pain and emotional suffering to prove she's as tough as any man, but the result is hardly worth the effort. Much brutality, some violence, several sexual situations, a flash of nudity, occasional profanity and recurring rough language

title: G.I. Joe: The Rise of Cobra
synopsis: Futuristic combat fantasy in which two soldier buddies (Channing Tatum and Marlon Wayans) join an elite international force (led by Dennis Quaid) to thwart an evil arms dealer (Christopher Eccleston) bent on world domination. Special effects are expensive and the lives of the extras are cheap in director Stephen Sommers' slick but uninvolving action excursion, developed from a line of Hasbro toys. Pervasive action violence, brief gore, at least two uses of profanity and about a dozen crude or crass terms

title: Gilbert and Sullivan
synopsis: ( see: "The Story of Gilbert and Sullivan" )

title: Gilda Live
synopsis: Concert film by director Mike Nichols of comedienne Gilda Radner's Broadway stage show should appeal to fans of "Saturday Night Live," but leave others flat. Most of the amusing moments come from Don Novello as Father Guido Sarducci. Some rough language and Norvello's occasional (and highly original) ventures into theology make this mature fare

title: Gilded Lily, The
synopsis: Romantic comedy in which a New York secretary (Claudette Colbert) falls for a jobless charmer (Ray Milland) unaware he's a vacationing English aristocrat until put wise by the popcorn-chewing newspaper reporter (Fred MacMurray) who wants to marry her. Directed by Wesley Ruggles, the heavy-handed plot is kept afloat by Colbert's endearing performance, especially during the sequence in which she is unwillingly built into a celebrity by the reporter. Romantic complications

title: Gildersleeve on Broadway
synopsis: Feeble comedy directed by Gordon Douglas transports the small-town title bachelor (Harold Peary) to New York where he gets involved through a series of comic misunderstandings with a dizzy heiress (Billie Burke) as well as a brassy gold digger. The laborious romantic complications include female impersonation

title: Gildersleeve's Bad Day
synopsis: Formula comedy series entry directed by Gordon Douglas in which the pompous title character (Harold Peary) is called to jury duty on a robbery case which gets him involved with gangsters but the dizzy results are more exasperating than amusing

title: Gimme Shelter
synopsis: Straightforword documentary gives an honest picture of what it was like to tour America with the Rolling Stones rock group and their notorious Altamont Speedway free concert where a fan was beaten to death by a member of the Hell's Angels. Directed by David Maysles, Albert Maysles and Charlotte Zwerin, it is a disturbing picture of the dark side of the American Dream

title: Ginger
synopsis: Cheri Caffaro plays the female private eye of the title who has a yen for sadistic revenge. Her methods range from castration to outright murder as she disrobes and dispatches a nasty band of sex merchants. Directed by Don Schain, it is another tired sex and violence exploitation movie

title: Ginger and Fred
synopsis: Ginger (Giulietta Masina) and Fred (Marcello Mastroianni), a former vaudeville team who imitated Hollywood's Rogers and Astaire, are invited to perform in a Christmas television special. In this Italian production about the disappointments of old age and the commercialization of contemporary life, director Federico Fellini pays homage to performers important in his career, while at the same time indulging his penchant for visual cascades of freakish humanity. Some earthy proverbs about sex and several ambigious references to religion

title: Gingerbread Man, The
synopsis: Murky thriller from John Grisham's novel about a Savannah lawyer (Kenneth Branagh) whose attraction to a vulnerable client (Embeth Davidtz) who's being stalked by her unstable father ensnares him in a murderous plot that threatens the safety of his two young children. Directed by Robert Altman, the sinister proceedings are wrapped in a thick Southern Gothic atmosphere that fails to compensate for a less-than-credible script. Brief violence, an implied affair, fleeting nudity, occasional rough language and some profanity

title: Girl and the General, The
synopsis: Muddled Italian movie set in World War I in which an Austrian general (Rod Steiger) is captured by an Italian private (Umberto Orsini) and a peasant waif (Virna Lisi). Directed by Pasquale Festa Campanile, it has wartime violence and brief nudity

title: Girl Crazy
synopsis: Giddy musical in which a New York publisher sends his playboy son (Mickey Rooney) to a rugged, all-male college in the backlands of the Southwest where he falls for the dean's granddaughter (Judy Garland) and saves the school from financial ruin by making it co-educational. Directed by Norman Taurog, the thin storyline features buoyant lead performances, comic routines by Rags Ragland and Nancy Walker and, best of all, upbeat songs by George and Ira Gershwin, ending with Busby Berkeley's staging of the big production number, "I Got Rhythm."

title: Girl for Joe, A
synopsis: ( see: "Force of Arms" )

title: Girlfriends
synopsis: Director Claudia Weill's contrasting portrait of two New York women (Melanie Mayron and Anita Skinner) and the measures they take to find romance and commitment. Realistic treatment of sex and use of profanity override what little sensitivity and insight the film conveys

title: Girl from Petrovka, The
synopsis: Romance between a Russian woman (Goldie Hawn) and an American journalist (Hal Holbrook) based in Moscow blossoms into true love but she is picked up by the police while on an errand of mercy and sentenced to prison. Directed by Robert Ellis Miller, the story is thin and watery and treated in ponderously sentimental style. Some ludicrously inappropriate nudity

title: Girl-Getters, The
synopsis: British look at contemporary society through the eyes of young rebels (notably Oliver Reed) without goals. Michael Winner's direction of Peter Draper's episodic script captures something of the cynical innocence of its subject

title: Girl Happy
synopsis: Dim musical in which a band leader (Elvis Presley) secretly chaperones a gangster's daughter (Shelley Fabares) during the college spring break at Fort Lauderdale. Director Boris Sagal focuses on nubile co-eds and their sophomoric hijinks with largely mirthless results. Sexual situations

title: Girl Hunters, The
synopsis: Low-budget crime picture directed by Roy Rowland in which author Mickey Spillane plays his own fictional private eye, Mike Hammer, who sobers up long enough to help a federal agent (Lloyd Nolan) capture a team of Soviet assassins. Brutal violence, including a suspect held for the police by nailing his hand to the floor, and sexual innuendo

title: Girl in Blue, The
synopsis: David Selby crisscrosses pictureque Ontario looking for the blue-clad girl (Maud Adams) he encountered long ago. He also lives with his girl friend (Gay Rowan) just in case the girl in blue never materializes. Directed by George Kaczender, the hackneyed exercise in romantic sentimentality is so slight and silly that even the occasional expletive and glimpse of nudity seems innocuous

title: Girl in Pawn, The
synopsis: ( see: 1934's "Little Miss Marker" )

title: Girl, Interrupted
synopsis: When a half-hearted suicide attempt lands a spoiled late 1960's teen (Winona Ryder) in a private asylum her comaraderie with the more seriously disturbed, especially a charismatic sociopath (Angelina Jolie), allows her to gain some insight into her own problems. Director James Mangold's uneven adaptation of Susanna Kaysen's memoir is basically engrossing despite some melodramatics and sketchy characterizations. A suicide, implied sexual encounters and crude references, occasional profanity and much rough language

title: Girl in the Picture, The
synopsis: Slight romantic comedy about a young Glasgow commerical photographer (John Gordon-Sinclair) who ends his live-in relationship with an art student (Irina Brook), only to realize he loves her after she moves out. Writer-director Cary Parker developes the characters in warmly human fashion and makes good use of the photographer's trade, but the overly familiar plot has no surprises. Sexual situations and occasional coarse language

title: Girl Most Likely, The
synopsis: Musical remake of the 1941 comedy, "Tom, Dick and Harry," with Jane Powell in the Ginger Rogers' role as a woman torn between three suitors (rich Keith Andes, salesman Tommy Noonan and carefree Cliff Robertson). Director Mitchell Leisen gets some smiles from the daffy romantic complications but the song and dance numbers in the dream sequences add little zest to the lightweight proceedings

title: Girl Named Tamiko, A
synopsis: Unsavory sudser about an embittered Eurasian (Laurence Harvey) working as a photographer in Tokyo but trying to use a rich American (Martha Hyer) as his passport to the U.S. until falling for the lady of the title (France Nuyen). Directed by John Sturges, the only thing authentic about this ludicrous, anti-romantic account of a mean-spirited opportunist is the beautiful Japanese location photography. Implied sexual encounters

title: Girl of the Golden West, The
synopsis: Wildly fanciful Nelson Eddy-Jeanette MacDonald musical set in California pioneer days when a notorious bandit leader (Eddy) is reformed by the love of a good woman (MacDonald) who runs the saloon in a rough mining town whose sheriff (Walter Pigeon) wants to hang the bandit and marry her. Directed by Norman Z. Leonard, the creaky melodramatic plot is helped by a bizarre assortment of characters, though the Sigmund Rohmberg-Gus Kahn songs are entirely forgettable. Old-fashioned escapist fare with some well-intentioned ethnic stereotypes

title: Girl of the Year
synopsis: ( see: "The Petty Girl" )

title: Girl on a Motorcycle, The
synopsis: The woman of the title (Marianne Faithfull) relives her past as she speeds down the highway early one morning to meet her lover and her fate. Failing to come to grips with the motivation of the character's past actions, director Jack Cardiff understandably concentrates on the travelogue aspects of a ride through the beautiful French and German countryside. Frequent and explicit depictions of scenes of physical intimacy are dramatically as well as morally unjustified

title: Girl on the Bridge
synopsis: Enchanting French romantic comedy about a young woman (Vanessa Paradis) contemplating suicide on the railing of a Paris bridge when an itinerant professional knife thrower (Daniel Auteuil) recruits her to be his new human target. As directed by Patrice Leconte, the black and white film has exciting thriller elements with stylish camera work and an eclectic score, but the intriguing premise disappoints with an anti-climactic conclusion. Subtitles. Some sexual encounters, mild violence and a few instances of rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Girl Rush, The
synopsis: Romantic misfire in which a gambler's daughter (Rosalind Russell) inherits a dilapidated Las Vegas hotel, gets a rich man's son (Eddie Albert) to convert it into a plush casino and tries to run a suave competitor (Fernando Lamas) out of business. Directed by Robert Pirosh, the hard-working actors are trapped in a transparent plot paced by mediocre songs and weak production numbers, with disappointing results. Romantic complications and sexual innuendo

title: Girls Are for Loving
synopsis: In this latest chapter in the apparently ceaseless adventures of Ginger, our heroine breaks up a nasty extortion-kidnapping plot in high places and low. Once again Cheri Caffaro and writer-director Don Schain outdo themselves as the perfect husband-wife team of voyeur and exhibitionist working the sexploitation-action flick market

title: Girls Just Want to Have Fun
synopsis: Standard teen movie in which two plucky, clean-cut kids (Sarah Jessica Parker and Lee Montgomery) win a dance contest. Competent but mediocre light entertainment

title: Girls on the Beach, The
synopsis: Witless youth comedy in which some college co-eds try to pay off the mortgage on their sorority house by putting on a concert with the Beatles, then discover they've been hoaxed and have to substitute for them. Directed by William N. Witney, there's little going on here other than bikini-clad co-eds frolicking in the sand and cavorting to the music of the Beach Boys and other period performers. Considerable sexual innuendo

title: Girl Was Young, The
synopsis: ( see: "Young and Innocent" )

title: Girl Who Couldn't Say No, The
synopsis: Bland Italian comedy of a young surgeon (George Segal) who frequently falls in and out of love with an energetic Virna Lisi who's a soft touch for distressed persons. Directed by Franco Brusati, its permissive attitude toward sex is treated farcially but with excessive detail

title: Girl Who Dared, The
synopsis: Mystery programmer directed by Howard Bretherton is set on a stormy night in an isolated house where several people are murdered, with no way to contact the police until an insurance investigator (Peter Cookson) turns up to find the killer. Stylized violence, menace and family conflicts

title: Girl Who Knew Too Much, The
synopsis: Mystery story about a hired gun (Adam West) caught between the love for a slain crime boss' girl (Nancy Kwan) and his job of uncovering a Communist plot to take over the syndicate. Director Francis D. Lyon features a full-length strip-tease to enliven the dull, but brutally violent proceedings

title: Girl With a Pearl Earring
synopsis: Atmospheric drama in which renowned Dutch painter Johannes Vermeer (Colin Firth) grows obsessed with his young housemaid (Scarlett Johansson), who connects with him on an intellectual and artistic level, leading to the famed painting of the title that nearly tears his family apart. In visually adapting Tracy Chevalier's novel, director Peter Webber creates an evocative mood with color and light and recognizes the power of simmering passions kept in check, but the slack narrative and deliberate pacing prevent the film from making a commanding impression. A sexual encounter and brief violence

title: Girl with Green Eyes
synopsis: British coming-of-age drama about a naive young country girl (Rita Tushingham) who, on her first experience of living on her own away from home, becomes infatuated with a middle-aged writer (Peter Finch). Directed by Desmond Davis, the tale is slight but the acting is fine and the girl's problems quite convincing. Sexual situations

title: Girly
synopsis: ( see: "Mumsy, Nanny, Sonny and Girly" )

title: Give 'Em Hell, Harry
synopsis: James Whitmore gives his interpretation of Harry Truman in a film recording of his one-man performance in the Samuel Gallu play. Directed by Steve Binder, Whitmore brings a passion, a conviction and a dauntless energy that engenders some understanding for the man and his controversial political career. The language is sometimes rough, but it is in the service of honest emotions

title: Give Her the Moon
synopsis: Unpretentious French comedy in which an American industrialist is so determined to get a French maid (Marthe Keller) that he transports her entire village to New York where culture shock becomes amusingly apparent. Though there is some romance, director Philippe de Broca concentrates on the contrasting lifestyles with some gentle satire of both. Its an old-fashioned escapist movie that may be lost on the young

title: Give My Regards to Broadway
synopsis: When vaudeville flops in the 1920s, a juggler (Charles Winninger) awaits its return by taking a factory job while developing a family act with son (Dan Dailey) and two daughters who grow up to pursue more fruitful careers. Directed by Lloyd Bacon, the movie offers some entertaining stage routines, nostalgic songs and a sentimental but generally pleasing story of family solidarity despite changing times

title: Gizmo
synopsis: Howard Smith's delightfully zany little film uses newsreels from the 1920s and 1930s to chronicle the dogged if flawed ingenuity of a host of inventors whose creations did not become household words. Very entertaining

title: Glacier Fox, The
synopsis: Outstanding Japanese wildlife documentary, narrated by Arthur Hill, presents the story of a glacier fox, his mate and their five pups who live on the Okhotsk Sea coast of Hokkaido, a region blasted in winter by frigid winds that blow down from Siberia. Directed by Koreyoski Kurahara, the photography is stunning as it captures the intrinsic drama and humor in the life cycle of this fox family. Though it does not shy from some of the grimmer aspects of life in the wild, there are no visuals that might prove too strong for younger children, making it perfectly suited for the whole family

title: Gladiator
synopsis: Because of recurring stylized violence and a depiction of a character's incestuous longings,

title: Gladiator
synopsis: Routine prizefight picture in which a venal promoter (Brian Dennehy) pits a Chicago high schooler (James Marshall) against his best friend (Cuba Gooding, Jr.) in illegal boxing matches so the youth can pay off his father's gambling debts. Capitalizing on the popularity of the two young actors, director Rowdy Herrington goes down for the count with this strictly formula story. Brief teen bedroom scene, much graphic violence in the ring and intermittent rough language

title: Glass Bottom Boat, The
synopsis: A secretary (Doris Day) and a scientific genius (Rod Taylor) get involved with each other and assorted spies, gadgets and contrivances. The comedy has a number of good sight gags, some clever situations and a fine supporting cast. As put together by director Frank Tashlin, it adds up to a lot of fun

title: Glass Houses
synopsis: Broken family seeks self-revelation through group encounter therapy at a California spa. Director Alexander Singer's ill-conceived satire features Jennifer O'Neil as a mistress and Deirdre Lenihan as the daughter of a business type who contend for his sexual attention. Most viewers will experience a gagging sensation rather than a catharsis

title: The Glass House
synopsis: Thriller in which a suddenly orphaned brother and sister are sent to live with former neighbors (Stellan Skarsgard, Diane Lane) whom the sister (Leelee Sobieski) comes to suspect may have caused her parents' deaths. Directed by Daniel Sackheim, ominous visuals and fine performances add to the suspenseful narrative which only falters in a melodramatic final flourish. Some violence, a scene of drug addiction and minimal profanity

title: Glass Key, The
synopsis: Hard-boiled crime picture from the Dashiell Hammett novel about a machine politician (Brian Donlevy) saved from a murder rap by his right-hand man (Alan Ladd), despite various complications created by the victim's sister (Veronica Lake). Directed by Stuart Heisler, the murder mystery is less perplexing than the relationships between the principals and the efforts of the hoods (Joseph Calleia and William Bendix) to benefit from the situation. Stylized violence, some of it quite nasty, and romantic complications

title: Glass Menagerie, The
synopsis: Uneven adaptation of the Tennessee Williams play set in St. Louis where an aging Southern belle (Gertrude Lawrence) tries to get her shy lame daughter (Jane Wyman) interested in more than her collection of glass animals by having her son (Arthur Kennedy) invite his friend (Kirk Douglas) for a visit. Directed by Irving Rapper, the stagey proceedings are saved by Wyman's sensitive, convincing performance as the physically handicapped young woman who is more realistic about her situation than the others. Mild sexual innuendo

title: Glass Shield, The
synopsis: Idealistic African-American rookie (Michael Boatman) in a corrupt, all-white Los Angeles sheriff's unit joins another outcast, a Jewish female deputy (Lori Petty), in attempting to find evidence of police cover-ups of past and present crimes. Writer-director Charles Burnett centers on the rookie's moral conflicts in working with rogue cops in a drawn-out narrative downplaying violence in favor of exploring racialand justice issues. Some brief violence, a racial slur and an implied live-in relationship

title: Glass Slipper, The
synopsis: Pretty-looking but stilted rendering of the Cinderella story, this time with a waif (Leslie Caron) suffering under an ill-tempered stepmother (Elsa Lanchester) until the magic powers of a local eccentric (Estelle Winwood) help her win the love of a handsome prince (Michael Wilding). Director Charles Walters' slow-moving narrative is brightened by some elaborate fantasy numbers but there is little magic or humor in this version of the classic romance and the songs are strictly forgettable. For romantics of any age, though a long sit for children

title: Glass Sphinx
synopsis: Inept European production directed by Luigi Scattini about an archaeological expedition led by Robert Taylor in searching the Egyptian desert for a lost tomb containing the art treasure of the title. Some violence and sexual innunedo

title: Glass Web, The
synopsis: Muddled thriller directed by Jack Arnold in which a TV crime show's writer (John Forsythe) and his story consultant (Edward G. Robinson) become romantically involved with a blackmailing actress (Kathleen Hughes) whose unsolved murder becomes the subject of one of their shows and leads to the killer's apprehension. Minimal violence, some menace and an implied extramarital affair

title: Gleaming the Cube
synopsis: When an alienated teen (Christian Slater) decides to investigate the death of his adopted Vietnamese brother (Art Chudabala), he employs daredevil skateboard wizardry against the many meanies who get in his way. Set in a Southern California Vietnamese community, director Graeme Clifford's contrived murder mystery uses a lot of fancy footwork to divert attention from its flimsy plot. Mild rough language, some violence and comic-book menace

title: Glen and Randa
synopsis: After a thermonuclear apocalypse has destroyed contemporary civilization, two lost innocents (Steven Curry and Shelly Plimpton) live like primitive natives among the debris of Howard Johnson restaurants and deserted superhighways. Director Jim McBride's failed allegory about the primacy of animal passions becomes pretentious in execution and offensive in treatment, employing crude sex scenes and frontal nudity

title: Glengarry Glen Ross
synopsis: Screen version of David Mamet's play about four real estate salesmen (Jack Lemmon, Al Pacino, Ed Harris and Alan Arkin) who, under threat of being fired unless they close some deals within the week, commit desperate acts which ultimately backfire. James Foley's tautly directed movie delivers intense performances with blistering dialogue while depicting the characters' moral disintegration in a dehumanizing pressure-cooker where money is everything. Much rough language and some sexual references

title: Glenn Miller Story, The
synopsis: James Stewart gives an ingratiating performance as the trombone player who starts his own band, discovers the "sound" that makes it a national favorite, then dies in a World War II flight over the English Channel. Directed by Anthony Mann, the story's interesting and the acting good (June Allyson as his supportive wife) with plenty of examples of Miller's music and appearances by many of the era's musicians

title: Glimmer Man, The
synopsis: Mindless action thriller in which two Los Angeles homicide detectives (Steven Seagal and Keenan Ivory Wayans) break up a gang of international terrorists while after a serial killer who crucifies his victims. Directed by John Gray, the muddled plot alternates the search for a religious fanatic with hunting down the terrorist masterminds in numbingly dumb fashion. Numerous gruesome deaths, nudity, some rough language and occasional profanity

title: Glitter
synopsis: Pathetic musical drama set in the 1980s New York City club scene that tracks the rise of a young singer (Mariah Carey) from a childhood spent in foster homes to her discovery by a DJ (Max Beesley) and onto ultimate fame. Along with indistinguishable original songs, a pitiful narrative and contrived camera work, director Vondie Curtis Hall's leading lady has no charisma to pull off the vanity vehicle. An implied sexual encounter, brief violence and some crass language

title: Gloria
synopsis: Independent filmmaker John Cassavetes tries to transport a 1930's crime melodrama to the 1980 streets of New York in the story of a middle-aged gun moll (Gena Rowland), retired from the mob, suddenly finds herself responsible for a young boy marked for death by her old gang. The movie's strength lies in the extraordinary performance of Rowland, which more than makes up for some of the narrative's incoherence

title: Gloria
synopsis: Hollow crime tale in which a tough jailbird (Sharon Stone) tangles with her old gang when they try to rub out a 7-year-old boy who knows too much. Directed by Sidney Lumet, there are plenty of desperate chase scenes through gritty Manhattan locales, but the result lacks the emotional credibility of Gena Rowlands' title performance in the 1980 original. Some hard-edged violence, sexual references and innuendo, brief rear nudity, recurring rough language and some profanity

title: Glorifying the American Girl
synopsis: Interesting relic from the early talkies in which an ambitious shopgirl (Mary Eaton) joins a vaudeville song-and-dance act, then gains fame in a Ziegfeld musical revue while losing the beau she left behind (Edward Crandall) to a devoted co-worker (Olive Shea). Directed by Willard Webb, the storyline creaks and the sound quality is primitive but the result has historical interest as a record of Ziegfeld's florid production style, stage routines by Eddie Cantor, Helen Morgan and Rudy Vallee, glimpses of period personalities and lots of New York locations. Some sexual situations and double entendres

title: Glory
synopsis: Sentimental bluegrass tale directed by David Butler revolves around a penniless young Kentucky lass (Margaret O'Brien) who finds romance and the means to keep a cherished thoroughbred race horse with the help of her aunt (Charlotte Greenwood) and a longtime friend (Walter Brennan). Good-natured formula hokum

title: Glory
synopsis: The story of the 54th Regiment of Massachusetts Volunteer Infantry, the first black fighting unit raised during the Civil War, focuses on its enlightened white commander (Matthew Broderick) who molded field hands and runaway slaves into proud, heroic Union soldiers. Director Edward Zwick raises consciousness about the little-known regiment and re-creates some harrowing battle scenes but, unfortunately, gives shallow attention to the themes of racism and the obscenity of war. Stereotyping of key black characters, much grisly wartime violence and some profanity

title: Glory Boy
synopsis: World War II vet (Michael Moriarty) returns to the family farm with two of his buddies (William Devane and Mitchell Ryan) with the intention of proving to his patriotic father (Arthur Kennedy) that there is no glory on the battlefield but things get out of hand. Director Edwin Sherin's movie about the dehumanizing effects of war goes to excess in depicting rape and murder and its use of nudity and foul language

title: Glory Guys, The
synopsis: Formula Western in which a cavalry captain (Tom Tryon) and an Army scout (Harve Presnell) vie for the love of a widow (Senta Berger) before both go off to fight the Sioux in a campaign led by a glory-seeking general (Andrew Duggan). Directed by Arnold Laven, this variation on Custer's Last Stand grows tiresome with barrack hijinks and barroom brawls long before the main event finally gets underway, then abruptly finishes. Frontier violence and romantic complications

title: Glory Road
synopsis: Crowd pleaser based on the true story of an unproven, small-town basketball coach (Josh Lucas), who -- hired to turn around a Texas college's losing program -- bucks the color barrier by recruiting African-American athletes (including Derek Luke), molding his interracial underdogs into a unified team and leading them to an improbable and racially heated shot at the 1966 national title, where he starts five black players -- a first in college hoops -- against a top-seeded, all-white Kentucky squad. Directed by James Gartner, the feel-good, if formulaic, film rips a familiar page from the playbook of past inspirational sports movies, but has heart and a winning message about teamwork and racial equality that transcends sports. An instance of violence, some racial slurs and minimal crude language

title: Gnome-Mobile, The
synopsis: A lumber baron takes his two grandchildren to one of his forests, discovers some lonely gnomes and helps them find another gnome-infested forest. Walter Brennan is excellent in a dual role as the kindly grandfather and a waspish, irascible little old man. Robert Stevenson directs the colorful Walt Disney fantasy whose good humor and many finely executed special effects will divert just as many adults as children

title: Gnomeo & Juliet
synopsis: William Shakespeare's classic tragedy about star-crossed lovers morphs into a clever animated comedy as rival families of garden gnomes face off in a battle for backyard supremacy. It's love at first ceramic clink for Juliet Capulet (voice of Emily Blunt) and Gnomeo Montague (voice of James McAvoy), but differences in clan allegiance threaten to drive them apart. Until, that is, a wise pink flamingo (voice of Jim Cummings) assures them that love conquers all including, in this case, the Bard's original ending. Director Kelly Asbury's slightly warped but ultimately winning film offers good, clean, wholesome fun for the entire family

title: Go
synopsis: Smirky comedy divides its time between a smalltime drug deal gone awry with near deadly consequences and a gambling jaunt to Las Vegas by four pals also culminating in violence. Director Doug Liman's mindless comedy takes a benign view of drug abuse and treats dealing as a lucrative lark as long as no one actually dies. Recreational drug use, a menage a trois, some nudity, brief instances of violence, grand larceny, occasional profanity and much rough language

title: Goal!
synopsis: Good sports documentary highlights the skill and endurance of the champion soccer teams which vied for the 1966 World Cup in England. Octavio Senoret's production does well in showing the differences in the style of play of the 16 countries represented and Nigel Patrick's narration helps explain the worldwide popularity of a sport in which no substitutions are allowed during the game

title: Goal! The Dream Begins
synopsis: Familiar but satisfying sports drama about an undocumented Mexican migrant (Kuno Becker) who is given an opportunity to escape his father's (Tony Plana) hardscrabble fate and fulfill his dream of playing professional soccer when a former British scout (Stephen Dillane) visiting Los Angeles offers him a tryout with a top-tier English soccer team. Directed by Danny Cannon, the film's feel-good underdog theme coupled with Becker's appealing performance scores, despite a formulaic script, underdeveloped characters and an overlong length. A few crude expressions, suggested drunkenness and carousing, implied sexual situations and some sports roughness, limiting its appropriateness to older adolescents and up

title: Goat Horn, The
synopsis: Bulgarian folk tale set during the time of Turkish rule when a goatherd raises his daughter as if she were a boy so that she will never be the victim, as was her mother, of the lust of their despotic master. Though it all ends badly, director Metodi Andonov conveys the sense of powerlessness of a subject people, not through dialogue, but through small details showing the daily life of the period

title: Goat, The
synopsis: ( see: "La Chevre" )

title: Go-Between, The
synopsis: British period romance features Michael Redgrave reminiscing about his childhood role as the innocent messenger between lovers (Julie Christie and Alan Bates) who are separated by the gulf of social class. Director Joseph Losey handles with sensitivity the boy's growing awareness of the nature of the couple's relationship and how, on his 13th birthday, he is directly confronted with the physical realities of adult life

title: Gobots, Battle of the Rock Lords
synopsis: This animated action-adventure movie features constant combat between humanoids, robots and other silicon-based life forms, perpetuating the exploitation of the pre-teen market. Parents should consider the merits of further exposure of the very young to increased leve1s of hostility depicted in this movie

title: Goddess, The
synopsis: Episodic story follows the unhappy formative years of a young woman (Kim Stanley) who goes on to movie stardom, growing more self-destructive with each success. Scripted by Paddy Chayevsky and directed by John Cromwell, the period details of the 1930-50s provide a credible context for this psychological probe of a troubled woman driven by the need to be loved yet unable to believe that she deserves anyone's love. Mature themes and treatment

title: Godfather Part III, The
synopsis: Having shed all ties with the underworld, Michael Corleone (Al Pacino) seeks respectability and profits by investing in a Vatican holding company run by corrupt financiers whose business tactics include murder. Directed by Francis Ford Coppola, the narrative strives for tragedy but settles for melodrama after losing its way in the vague, shadowy world of international finance and the intrigues of certain church officials. Some scenes of intense violence, the twisted morality of criminal retribution, rough language and an unedifying ficitional depiction of some religious figures

title: Godfather, Part II, The
synopsis: Lacking the original's grace, majesty and energy, the sequel follows the rise to power of a crime boss (Robert De Niro) and the subsequent use of that power by his son (Al Pacino). Produced and directed by Francis Ford Coppola, the unmanageably complex scenario shifts interminably from Lake Tahoe to the Kefauver hearings, from the lower East Side to Florida base of a crime kingpin (Lee Strasberg). The effect is unsettling and there is much graphic violence

title: Godfather, The
synopsis: Blockbuster screen version of the Mario Puzo novel about a Mafia family's rise, decline and resurgence in the murderous world of New York racketeering. Marlon Brando plays the aging but indomitable Don with James Caan and Al Pacino as leading family members. Francis Ford Coppola's direction is a study in control and pacing with all the right touches in establishing the proper 1940's ambience. The murders are plentiful and gruesome, with little spared in detailing the intricacies of mob life

title: God Forgives, I Don't
synopsis: Professiona1 gambler (Terence Hill) tracks down a notorious outlaw for personal reasons rather then to bring him to justice. Directed by Giuseppe Colizzi, the tale of a personal vendetta has little action or sense, but maintains an atmosphere throughout of brutality and needless violence

title: God Gave Him a Dog
synopsis: ( see: 1940's "The Biscuit Eater" )

title: God Said, "Ha!"
synopsis: Filmed performance of comedian Julia Sweeney's one-woman show in which she gives a humorous account of putting her life on hold in her mid-30s to care for a brother dying of cancer, then facing further complications after her parents move in to help and she herself is shortly later diagnosed as having cervical cancer. Also directed by Sweeney, the monologue is mildly amusing in its self-deprecating anecdotes about the comedian's Irish-Catholic upbringing, her torturous but loving family relationship as well as her "amicable" divorce and expectations of single life, but the performance withers on the big screen and the thin material fails to sustain feature-length interest. Comic but never mean-spirited treatment of serious matters involving family, religion, sex and medical procedures as well as a reference to flatulence

title: Gods and Generals
synopsis: Epic 220-minute Civil War drama focuses on the convictions and strategies of Confederate Gens. Lee and Jackson (Robert Duvall and Stephen Lang) and the North's Gen. Hancock and Lt. Col. Chamberlain (Brian Mallon and Jeff Daniels) in the early war years of 1861-63. As directed by Ron Maxwell, battle scenes are impressive and the faith-filled generals can be inspirational, but their lengthy speeches and drawn-out scenes undercut dramatic conflict and themes of courage, duty and loyalty. Battlefield violence

title: Gods and Monsters
synopsis: Offbeat, fictionalized buddy movie set in 1957 Hollywood where terminally ill, openly gay horror film director James Whale (Ian McKellan) befriends his young, macho gardener (Brendan Fraser) who overcomes his revulsion of homosexuals to offer compassinonate, platonic friendship to the frail old man. Writer-director Bill Condon finds the humanity below the surface of the two very different men, as well as Whale's Catholic maid (Lynn Redgrave), in a subtle tale of manipulation and devotion. Fleeting violence, much homosexual innuendo, brief full frontal nudity, a shadowy sexual encounter, sporadic rough language and an instance of profanity

title: Gods and the Dead, The
synopsis: Brazilian turn-of-the-century drama about cocoa plantation owners who try to destroy each other with the ultimate survivor being a peasant who discovers that, just as he has been victimized by the owners, so too they were victimized by international business interests. Director Ruy Guerra's movie about the unequal distribution of wealth is filled with poetic imagery of the struggle for social justice

title: Godsend
synopsis: Cautionary psychological thriller about a grief-stricken couple (Rebecca Romijn-Stamos and Greg Kinnear) who agree to an offer made by a brilliant, but shadowy, scientist (Robert De Niro) to clone their 8-year-old son after the boy is killed in a tragic accident, only to find out later the chilling unforeseen consequences of their Faustian bargain. While the film, directed by Nick Hamm, raises thought-provoking questions involving bioethics and the morality of artificially creating human life, the story's philosophical pretensions quickly give way to spooky atmospherics and standard ghost-story devices which detract from the central moral dilemma posed. A sexual encounter, a problematic theme of cloning, recurring profanity, sporadic crude language and some scary sequences

title: Godsend, The
synopsis: Foundling with a nasty disposition knocks off, one by one, the natural children of her foster parents, who seem to be inordinately slow to get the drift. Director Gabrielle Beaumont's tepid British thriller has little to recommend it and, though all of its violence is off-camera, it creates a foreboding atmosphere and features a rather graphic birth scene

title: Gods Must Be Crazy II, The
synopsis: Mildly amusing but overly contrived sequel set in Africa's Kalahari Desert where three different sets of strangers (a pair of poachers, two soldiers from opposing sides and a couple whose plane has crashed) get lost but are helped periodically by a bemused bushman (N!xau) looking for his two missing children. Written and directed by Jamie Uys, the South African production has much broad visual comedy and some charming moments with the lost youngsters, but the endless predicaments of the strangers strain patience and credibility. Bare-bottomed Bushmen and several gags involving a woman's undergarments

title: Gods Must Be Crazy, The
synopsis: An African bushman discovers a discarded Coke bottle and, after it causes dissenion among his people, undertakes a trek to throw it off the edge of the world, but in the course of the journey he runs into some very peculiar civilized peop1e. Director Jamie Uys' simple comedy-adventure explores amiably the cultural differences between industrial society and ritualized tribal folkways. Some violence

title: Gods of the Plague
synopsis: German crime melodrama made in 1969 about a young gangster who teams up with a killer for another robbery but is betrayed by one his girl friends. Director Rainer Werner Fassbinder overdoes the murky underworld atmosphere, in which violence needs no motivation or justification, and the film has little point other than as an exercise in criminal brutality

title: Godson, The
synopsis: Chilling psychological study of a lonely criminal (Alain Delon) whose life is held in a delicate balance between the gang and the law. French director Jean-Pierre Melville unfolds this lone wolf's struggle to survive police pursuits, the distrust of his gangland associates and the false sympathy of a woman in a restrained and highly visual manner without the violent excesses associated with gangster films

title: Godspell
synopsis: Sparkling screen version of musical based loosely on the Gospel according to Matthew, featuring an off-Broadway cast with Victor Garber as the Christ figure and David Haskell as both John the Baptist and Judas. What makes the movie so high-spirited is director David Greene's turning the entire city of New York into a giant stage set, with its buildings, streets and parks all strikingly used for great effect. The parables are presented in imaginative skits, many of which serve as springboards for the irresistible tunes, such as "Day by Day" and "God Save the People!," that made the play so popular

title: Godzilla 1985
synopsis: You can't keep a good monster down and Japan's favorite has risen again, along with his old pal Raymond Burr, in a fair1y competent new version. Godzilla fans everywhere should have reason to be happy with the results, though all the crashing and banging might frighten young children

title: Godzilla
synopsis: Undistinguished monster movie in which New York City's landmarks and citizens are stomped upon by the giant beast whose hatching eggs prove an even greater threat, especially to a quartet (led by Matthew Broderick) in imminent danger. Director Roland Emmerich's special-effects thriller lacks the consistent excitement or goofy humor that would make it an escapist lark. Recurring fantasy violence with much mayhem and intermittent profanity

title: Godzilla 2000
synopsis: Sluggish Japanese monster film in which the famous giant reptile once again rises from the sea to terrify the populace while doing battle with a mysterious UFO and a mammoth alien beast. Lifeless characters and dopey plotting make director Takao Okawara's overlong creature feature lack even a campy sense of humor, although scattered special effects are impressive. Sci-fi violence. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Godzilla, King of the Monsters
synopsis: Japanese monster movie in which an American newsman (Raymond Burr) reports on a 30-story-high prehistoric reptile named Godzilla who rises from the Pacific after being revived by H-bomb tests, razes central Tokyo, then disappears back into the sea, apparently stopped by a scientist's "oxygen destroyer." In the dubbed American version, director Inoshiro Honda's thin storyline, bare-bones model work and rubber-suited monster provide little indication that this would spawn numerous sequels. Unconvincing special-effects violence and menace

title: Godzilla on Monster Island
synopsis: Dubbed Japanese monster movie directed by Jun Fukuda has alien cockroaches from a dying planet assume human form, then try to rule the world through space monsters Ghidrah and Gigan but, as they start destroying Tokyo, Godzilla and his pal Angillus come to the rescue. Much stylized violence and a few crude remarks

title: Godzilla's Revenge
synopsis: Young boy's conversation with Godzilla (who is in retirement on Monster Island) and also with his son teach him a few tricks which help thwart a pair of bank robbers who are hiding near his home. Director Ishiro Honda resurrects his collection of monsters for another round of campy adventures

title: Godzilla vs. Destroyah
synopsis: Dubbed Japanese monster movie directed by Takao Okawara in which Godzilla's nuclear-powered body overheats but before it explodes, he takes on a primordial monster which has emerged from Tokyo Bay. Much special-effects violence

title: Godzilla vs. Gigan
synopsis: ( see: "Godzilla on Monster Island" )

title: Godzilla vs. Mechagodzilla
synopsis: ( see: "Godzilla vs. the Cosmic Monster" )

title: Godzilla vs. Monster Zero
synopsis: ( see: "Monster Zero )

title: Godzilla vs. Mothra
synopsis: ( see: "Godzilla vs. the Thing" )

title: Godzilla vs. Spacegodzilla
synopsis: Dubbed Japanese monster movie directed by Kensho Yamashita in which Godzilla battles a mutated version of himself from outer space, with some help from a mechanical juggernaut originally built to destroy him. Much special-effects violence

title: Godzilla vs. the Cosmic Monster
synopsis: Dubbed Japanese monster movie directed by Jun Fukuda is centered in Okinawa where alien primates in human guise construct Mechagodzilla, a metal supermonster modeled on Godzilla, but their plans for world conquest hit a snag when the real thing turns up. Stylized violence, some gore and a few crude remarks

title: Godzilla vs. the Sea Monster
synopsis: Dubbed Japanese production has the sleeping Godzilla awaken halfway through the movie to do battle with a denizen of the deep and squash a secret island base producing nuclear weapons, with winged Mothra coming to the rescue of the islanders. Formula action plot with assorted stylized violence

title: Godzilla vs. the Smog Monster
synopsis: Godzilla tangles with a smog monster that bloats itself on factory and automobile wastes, and succeeds in frustrating its ambition to feed on the sacred fumes of Mt. Fuji. Wry social satire on pollution from director Yoshimitu Banno whose use of blurry, grainy, anemic color photography here is for once thematically motivated

title: Godzilla vs. the Thing
synopsis: Mild Japanese monster movie directed by Inoshiro Honda pits Godzilla, angered by an industrial development, against the dying Mothra, a colossal moth trying to protect its giant egg which, when hatched, proves Godzilla's undoing. Stylized fantasy menace

title: Go for Broke!
synopsis: Worthy, entertaining account of a World War II Japanese-American infantry unit and its exploits on the battlefields of Italy and France. Writer-director Robert Pirosh provides a convincing picture of the unit's perseverance not only against the German foe but also in the face of prejudice from fellow Americans, including one of their own officers (Van Johnson). Wartime violence

title: Goin' All the Way
synopsis: Shoddy exploitation movie about the sexual yearnings of some high school students, not one of whom looks a day under 25. Directed by Robert Freedman with crass vulgarity, abundant nudity and graphic sexuality

title: Goin' Down the Road
synopsis: Canadian movie in which two Nova Scotians come to Toronto in search of a better life but soon find themselves back on the highway, a little less likely of ever finding their place in the world. Directed by Donald Shebib, it is best in its celebration of the city and its environs, but its young people (Doug McGrath, Paul Bradley and Jane Eastwood) are so sincere and earnest in their idealism that they almost overcome the handicap of stereotyped roles

title: Going All the Way
synopsis: Satiric misfire about two Korean War vets returning to their Indianapolis homes to spend a summer pursuing women, the dim one (Ben Affleck) having effortless success while the other (Jeremy Davies) is an introverted clod suffers from his moralistic upbringing. Directed by Mark Pellingtoin from Dan Wakefield's 1970 novel, the movie's leering focus on sex makes it seem like a one-dimensional cartoon, made all the more off-putting by Davies' unlikeable portrayal of a borderline sociopath. Sexual encounters with nudity, sexual situations including masturbation, rough language and profanity

title: Going Ape!
synopsis: Three orangutans provide the madcap antics in director Jeremy Joe Kronsberg's inept and witless situation comedy about a young man (Tony Danza) who inherits a fortune with the requirement that he care for the apes. Danny De Vito helps him protect the beasts from a greedy zoological society that also tries to get the dough. Much vulgarity and frequent profanity

title: Going Berserk
synopsis: Collection of skits loosely joined together by the gimmick of having television comic John Candy handcuffed to an escaped convict. Written and directed by David Steinberg, the farce offer little other than much foul language and some gross sexually oriented humor

title: Going Hollywood
synopsis: Slight but bubbly musical romance in which a teacher (Marion Davies) falls for a radio crooner (Bing Crosby), follows him to Hollywood, then tangles with his tempermental French co-star (Fifi D'Orsay). Directed by Raoul Walsh, there's still some fun in its spoofing period radio shows and movie-making, with a good supporting cast (Ned Sparks, Stuart Erwin and Patsy Kelly) and bouncy production numbers, but the plot's hokey Cinderella romance has aged rather badly. Some sexual innuendo, an implied liaison and a comic blackface routine

title: Going Home
synopsis: Jan-Michael Vincent plays a man who as a young child saw his father (Robert Mitchum) kill his mother in a drunken rage and now seeks to avenge her by raping the paroled father's new bride-to-be (Brenda Vaccaro). Producer-director Herbert Leonard's failed drama deals in the cliches of abnormal psychology without any serious analysis of characters and their actions nor is there any meaningful resolution of its muddled plot. Some violence

title: Going in Style
synopsis: Three oldsters on pension (George Burns, Art Carney, and Lee Strasberg), fed up with feeding pigeons in a Queens park, decide to rob a Manhattan Bank. Only George Burns' fine performance makes director Martin Brest's flat and uninspired geriatric farce at all worth watching. Some rough language and its benign view of the crime

title: Going My Way
synopsis: Bing Crosby ambles amiably through the role of Father O'Malley, the crooning curate sent to assist the aging, crotchety pastor (Barry Fitzgerald) of a poor parish in need of change. Director Leo McCarey's sentimental story is well-paced with humor and songs such as "Swinging on a Star," but at its sugary center is the theme of new ways replacing the old as conveyed amusingly but with feeling by the two principals. The definitive Hollywood version of Catholic life in an age of innocence, the picture retains appeal today mainly as a well-crafted vehicle of popular entertainment

title: Going Places
synopsis: Pair of petty thieves (Gerard Depardieu and Patrick Dewaere) graduate to auto theft, kidnapping and assault as they wander aimlessly through the French countryside, with a sex encounter of some sort at every stop. Directed by Bertrand Blier, the movie's amoral view of life is conveyed in gross language and even grosser, ocassionally degrading. images

title: Going Upriver: The Long War of John Kerry
synopsis: Serious-minded feature-length documentary based on the book "Tour of Duty" profiling John Kerry's experiences as a Navy Swift boat commander during the Vietnam War and his subsequent anti-war activism, focusing on his leadership role during a 1971 veterans' protest in Washington. Directed by longtime Kerry friend George Butler, the film wrestles with questions about the meaning of patriotism, blending compelling archival footage and photographs with talking-head interviews with fellow veterans to create an emotional, if highly idealized, portrait of Kerry. Though temperate in tone, the film ultimately comes across as advocacy journalism, opinions of which will vary according to viewers' political stripes. Images of war violence and some crude language. USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting

title: Goin' South
synopsis: Jack Nicholson directs his own performance as a raffish outlaw who is saved from hanging when a young woman (Mary Steenburgen) agrees to marry him. Her sole interest is a hired hand to help her work a supposedly exhausted gold mine, but, naturally, romance blooms in the desert air. Moderately entertaining comedy Western with some sexually oriented humor

title: Go, Johnny, Go!
synopsis: Formula success story of a frustrated singer (Jimmy Clanton) who leaves an orphanage for New York where he's turned into overnight rock `n' roll star by disk jockey Alan Freed. Directed by Paul Landres, the simplistic tale is sandwiched between performances by such period music notables as Chuck Berry, Eddie Cochran, Ritchie Valens and Jackie Wilson. Attempted robbery

title: Gold
synopsis: Though its plot is a rather tiresome affair about the manipulations of an international gold syndicate, this large-scale disaster movie offers an exotic catastrophe (the flooding of an entire gold mining area), fresh South African locations and some gripping action sequences and spectacular special effects. Director Peter Hunt, however, fights a losing battle against an inept script. Some double entendres and an illicit romance make it inappropriate for youngsters

title: Goldbergs, The
synopsis: ( see: "Molly" )

title: Gold Diggers of 1933
synopsis: Frothy backstage musical about a Broadway producer (Ned Sparks) mounting a show with money from a novice songwriter (Dick Powell) whose Boston banking family threatens to disinherit him if he weds a showgirl (Ruby Keeler). Directed by Mervyn LeRoy, the creaky plot has stuffy family emissaries Warren William and Guy Kibbee falling for showgirls Joan Blondell and Aline MacMahon, but what still holds interest are Busby Berkeley's production numbers featuring "We're in the Money," "Petting in the Park," the illuminated violins in "Shadow Waltz" and the finale's Depression-themed "My Forgotten Man." Considerable sexual innuendo and alcoholic excess

title: Gold Diggers of 1935
synopsis: > Lame musical comedy in which a hotel clerk (Powell) agrees to chaperone the daughter (Gloria Stuart) of a rich dowager (Alice Brady) who hires a shifty producer (Adolphe Menjou) to put on a charity show with two big numbers -- "The Words Are in My Heart," staged with endless pianos, and Wini Shaw singing "Lullaby of Broadway," one of the most fascinating Berkeley stagings. Berkeley directed this one, and gets only weak smiles from the anemic plot. Romantic complications and mild sexual innuendo. A-II (nr) 1935

title: Gold Diggers: The Secret of Bear Mountain
synopsis: Formula adventure in which a vacationing city girl (Christina Ricci) pals around with a local tomboy (Anna Chlumsky) in the wilds of the Pacific Northwest where they foolishly risk their lives searching for a lost gold mine. Directed by Kevin James Dobson, the story is less about the gold escapade than the relationship between the two young teens and their widowed moms, one of whom has an abusive boyfriend. Life-threatening perils from nature and an evil human

title: Golden Blade, The
synopsis: Halting but colorful adventure set in ancient Bagdad where a desert nobleman (Rock Hudson) finds a magic sword enabling him to save the king's daughter (Piper Laurie) from marriage to the cruel son (Gene Evans) of her father's wicked vizier (George Macready). Directed by Nathan Juran, the formula story of right overcoming might has some good action sequences but the plot plods and the acting ranges from wooden to hammy. Stylized violence

title: Golden Boy
synopsis: Clifford Odets' romantic melodrama about a Depression youth (William Holden) who turns in his violin for boxing gloves, then falls for the girlfriend (Barbara Stanwyck) of his manager (Adolphe Menjou). Directed by Rouben Mamoulian, the ham-fisted story of material wealth versus human values is earnest but obvious, though its critical attitude towards prizefighting is quite effective. Stylized treatment of violence in the ring and romantic entanglements

title: Golden Calf, The
synopsis: The stratagems of a confidence man (Sergei Yursky) in the Soviet Union of the late 1920s backfire with slapstick regularity and when one of his schemes finally brings in a million rubles, he learns that money does not buy happiness and returns to his con games. Directed by Mikhail Shveitser, it is an amusing change of pace from the usual socialist realism of Soviet cinema

title: Golden Child, The
synopsis: A private detective (Eddie Murphy) is charged with rescuing from evil kidnappers a Tibetan toddler, revered by a cult as their sacred leader. A tiresome Murphy vehicle, more irreverent than funny, replete with some unwholesome seduction humor, many indecent expressions and other harsh language as well as much violent action and gruesome images

title: GoldenEye
synopsis: Action-packed escapist fare in which British agent 007 (Pierce Brosnan), abetted by a savvy computer programmer (Izabella Scorupco), is out to prevent Soviet-based villains (Sean Bean and Famke Janssen) from activating satellite weaponry set to destroy London. Martin Campbell directs a showy, explosive tale of death-defying stunts whose plotline almost vanishes among all of Bond's frenzied escapes and rescues. Much stylized mayhem, brief bedroom scenes and some sexual innuendo

title: Golden Eye, The
synopsis: Fairly enjoyable Charlie Chan mystery from director William Beaudine follows the Chinese-American detective (Roland Winters) from San Francisco to an Arizona gold mine to solve the murder of its owner with some help from No. 2 son (Victor Sen Yung) and his chauffeur (Mantan Moreland). Some eerie menace and a gun-toting bogus nun

title: Goldengirl
synopsis: Muddled potboiler about the merchandizing of an Olympic sprinter (Susan Anton) by a promoter (James Coburn) who discovers that her scientist father (Curt Jurgens) has been giving her periodic injections of a dangerous growth hormone. Directed by Joseph Sargent, the movie is against the commercialization of sports and the manipulation of human beings but compromises itself by attempting to merchandize an attractive model as an actress. A number of rather crude sexual references

title: Golden Hawk, The
synopsis: Slapdash 17th-century swashbuckler directed by Sidney Salkow features a womanizing French privateer (miscast Sterling Hayden) who's rebuffed by an attractive English pirate (Rhonda Fleming), then wins her love and aid in sacking the Spanish stronghold at Cartegana. Stylized violence, sexual situations and marital infidelity

title: Golden Horde, The
synopsis: Farfetched adventure from Harold Lamb's story about a band of English Crusaders (led by David Farrar) trying to save Samarkand and its princess (Ann Blyth) from Genghis Khan's Tatars in 1220 A.D. Directed by George Sherman, the swordplay is secondary to the bickering between knight and princess over whether to save the city by force of arms or feminine wiles. Stylized violence and feigned seduction

title: Golden Hour, The
synopsis: ( see: "Pot o' Gold" )

title: Golden Needles
synopsis: Fair adventure movie in which Elizabeth Ashley, acting for aging millionaire Burgess Meredith, hires Joe Don Baker to obtain an Oriental statuette whose seven gold needles are said to be able to restore youth and virility to its possessor. Directed by Robert Clouse, there are some generous helpings of kung fu and karate fights and enough love scenes to put it in the adult class, but otherwise it is an escapist movie that doesn't take itself seriously

title: Golden Raiders, The
synopsis: ( see: "Escape to Athena" )

title: Golden Seal, The
synopsis: Isolated by a storm, a lonely boy (Torquil Campbell) living on an island in the Aleutians befriends a mother seal and protects it from family and poachers. There is a lot of profanity, including some dark pearls from the mouth of our young hero, and a bit of violence

title: Golden Stallion, The
synopsis: Western programmer directed by William Witney in which singing cowboy Roy Rogers is wrongly sent to prison while his horse, Trigger, leads a herd of wild horses and sires a colt, until Rogers is paroled and smashes the gang using the herd to smuggle diamonds across the Mexican border. Stylized violence

title: Golden Voyage of Sinbad, The
synopsis: John Phillip Law as Sinbad sails off to find the Fountain of Destiny, harassed by a variety of demons and other nasty types conjured up by Ray Harryhausen's imaginative special effects which upstage the human cast. Director Gordon Hessler's lighthearted and entertaining adventure movie brings a treat for youngsters and those adults who wish to recapture some of the magic of childhood

title: Goldfinger
synopsis: British superagent James Bond (Sean Connery) is on the trail of international smuggler Goldfinger (Gert Frobe) and his chief henchman, Oddjob (Harold Sakata), and with a little help from the ladies (Shirley Easton and Honor Blackman), he thwarts their plan to rob Fort Knox. Directed by Guy Hamilton, the fast-paced plot contains the ususal assortment of gimmicky action and tongue-in-cheek sexual references but adults who enjoy escapist entertainment will find it harmless campy fun

title: Gold Rush, The
synopsis: Classic silent comedy with Charlie Chaplin as the Little Tramp searching for gold in the Klondike where he gets snowed in with a starving prospector (Mack Swain) and has a bittersweet romance with a dance hall girl (Georgia Hale). It's Chaplin at his best, with memorable comic highlights including a tilting cabin perched on the edge of a precipice, a Thanksgiving dinner made out of a boiled shoe and a charming dance performed by bread rolls. Delightful family fare

title: Goldwyn Follies, The
synopsis: Overblown, undernourished musical in which a failing Hollywood producer (Adolphe Menjou) hires an ordinary movie-goer (Andrea Leeds) to advise him on how to make his next picture a box-office hit. Directed by George Marshall, the script mixes high art (ballet's Vera Zorina) with low comedy (the Ritz Brothers) in an aimless grab-bag of indifferent skits featuring a Gershwin score, singer Kenny Baker and occasional mischief contributed by Charlie McCarthy and Edgar Bergen. Something for everybody adds up here to pleasing almost no one

title: Golem, The
synopsis: Classic silent fantasy set in 16th-century Prague where Rabbi Loew saves his people from expulsion by calling to life the clay monster (Paul Wegener) of the title whose Samson-like strength convinces the emperor to rescind his decree, but the monster, unwilling to return to clay, rampages through the ghetto until being disarmed by a little child. Also directed by Wegener, the mythic narrative is powerfully visualized with expressionistic sets, an ominous atmosphere and a memorable monster. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Go Naked in the World
synopsis: Trashy romantic clunker directed by Ranald MacDougall revolves around a young man (Tony Franciosa) being turned to mush after discovering that the woman he loves (Gina Lollabrigida) is a high-priced prostitute. Preposterous twaddle equating promiscuity with boredom and includes an off-screen suicide among its unconvincing contrivances

title: Gone Are the Days
synopsis: Good-natured satire about the withering of the Old South as Purlie Victorious (Ossie Davis) returns after 20 years to his family of Georgia sharecroppers, determined to end their exploitation by the local plantation owner (Sorrell Brooke). Directed by Nicholas Webster from a play by Davis, the story's farcical situations and comic misunderstandings ridicule a wide variety of racial stereotypes and, despite the movie's stagy production, the humor comes through in amusingly broad performances by a fine cast, including Ruby Dee, Beah Richards, Godfrey Cambridge and Alan Alda. Satiric treatment of racism

title: Gone Baby Gone
synopsis: Thought-provoking mystery about a private investigator (a superlative Casey Affleck) and his girlfriend-partner (Michelle Monaghan) hired to investigate the disappearance of the 4-year-old daughter of a drug addict (Amy Ryan) in the Boston area, with the reluctant cooperation of the police (Morgan Freeman and Ed Harris). Ben Affleck makes an auspicious directorial debut in this adaptation of Dennis Lehane's novel, and though the seedy environment, pervasive expletives and sporadic but graphic violence will not be to everyone's taste, mature viewers will find those elements and some morally troublesome actions handled with gravity and intelligence. Pervasive rough language, profanity, violence with blood, corpses, an impulsive vigilante-style killing, drug use, implied nonmarital relationships, and child abuse references

title: Gone Fishin'
synopsis: Inept comedy about two disaster-prone pals (Joe Pesci and Danny Glover) on a Florida fishing trip which turns into a tedious hunt for a nasty killer. Directed by Christopher Cain, the slow-paced, dim-witted proceedings are an unamusing mixture of large-scale comic destruction and pathetically dumb humor. Much slapstick violence, a menacing killer and coarse language

title: Gone to Earth
synopsis: ( see: "The Wild Heart" )

title: Gone with the Wind
synopsis: Epic romance spanning 20 years in the troubled lives of its ambitious southern heroine (Vivian Leigh), the man she loves (Leslie Howard) and the man she finally marries (Clark Gable). Produced by David O. Selznick and directed by Victor Fleming, the movie re-creates not the history but the myth of the Old South and its destruction in the Civil War and Reconstruction. Though blacks are treated in the stereotyped fashion of its time, the picture is sympathetic towards its main black characters, particularly Hattie McDaniel who received an Academy Award for her performance. Wartime violence, romantic complications and black stereotyping

title: Gong Show Movie, The
synopsis: Chuck Barris' television game show featuring out-takes too deplorable to show on television form the basis for this monument to bad taste and witless vulgarity

title: Go Now
synopsis: A young soccer-playing Scotsman (Robert Carlyle) working as a plasterer in Bristol, England, begins a serious love affair (with Juliet Aubrey) only to find himself facing life in a wheelchair when he is diagnosed with multiple sclerosis. Director Michael Winterbottom chronicles the effects of the insidious ailment on the athlete and his lover with unsentimental gravity that gives way to an uplifting climax. Sexual encounters, brief nudity, occasional profanities and frequent rough language

title: Good Boy!
synopsis: Family-friendly comedy about a timid young dog-walker (Liam Aiken) who, after adopting an extraterrestrial mutt (voiced by Matthew Broderick), discovers he understands doggie talk and must help convince his pooch's intergalactic boss that dogs -- not humans -- are in charge on Earth, lest all dogs be recalled to their home planet. Despite a formulaic premise and some syrupy moments, director John Hoffman's humorous spin on the old boy-and-his-dog theme imparts a sweet message about the importance of love, loyalty and friendship. Minimal mildly crude language and humor

title: Good Burger
synopsis: Weak comedy about the extremes to which two teen fast-food workers (Kel Mitchell and Kenan Thompson) go to keep a rival burger joint from stealing their secret sauce recipe which is saving their store from bankruptcy. Director Brian Robbins keeps up a peppy pace as the bumbling buddies are put in and out of an insane asylum in their quest to save their jobs. Some slapstick violence, mild sexual innuendo and a few crude expressions

title: Goodbye Again
