Some violence with a few gory images, brief nudity and much rough language

title: Jubal
synopsis: Dour Western directed by Delmer Daves is set on a Wyoming ranch whose straight-arrow foreman (Glenn Ford) gets into a heap of trouble because of an envious cowhand (Rod Steiger) and the unfaithful wife (Valerie French) of their boss (Ernest Borgnine). Stylized violence and sexual inferences. A-II (br) ( 1956 )

title: Jubilee Trail
synopsis: Sprawling Western romance in which a trader (John Russell) and his bride (Joan Leslie) befriend a singer (Vera Ralston) in 1845 New Orleans, then hit the trail for California where the husband is killed, leaving his widow and infant boy in the care of the singer and a frontier guide (Forrest Tucker). Directed by Joseph Inman Kane, the result is soap opera in Western dress, with much bathos and unconvincing melodramatics. Frontier violence, romantic complications and references to a premarital affair. A-II (br) ( 1954 )

title: Jude
synopsis: Grim adaptation of Thomas Hardy's bleak 1896 novel, "Jude the Obscure," in which a would-be scholar (Christopher Eccleston) runs off with his high-spirited cousin (Kate Winslet) to start a family despite each being married to another. Director Michael Winterbottom employs overly explicit visuals in depicting a harrowing story of star-crossed lovers suffering from their defiance of social mores. Graphic scenes of birth, death and sexual encounters with full nudity. A-IV (R) ( 1996 )

title: Judex
synopsis: French-Italian action melodrama about a daredevil champion of justice (Channing Pollack) who fights crime in the era just before World War I. Directed by Georges Franju, it will appeal to those who enjoy the innocent adventures of the superheroes of yesteryear. Stylized violence. A-II (br) ( 1966 )

title: Judge Dredd
synopsis: In a chaotic future society where magistrates have the power to execute felons on the spot, an uncompromising judge (Sylvester Stallone) is framed for murder by a homicidal maniac (Armand Assante) long thought dead. Director Danny Cannon's violent sci-fi action movie shows its comic-book roots in ludicrous plotting, one-dimensional characters, exaggerated campy performances and slick, cynical humor. Much mindless murder and mayhem, a twisted sense of law enforcement and a few instances of profanity. O (R) ( 1995 )

title: Judge Hardy and Son
synopsis: While the judge (Lewis Stone) saves an old woman (Maria Ouspenskaya) from losing her home, Mom Hardy (Fay Holden) battles pneumonia and Andy (Mickey Rooney) has his usual trouble with the girls. Directed by George B. Seitz, the point of the episode is that parents must be honored and listened to, as Andy does in one of the longest man-to-man talks in the series. A-I (br) ( 1939 )

title: Judge Hardy's Children
synopsis: Judge Hardy (Lewis Stone) takes son Andy (Mickey Rooney) and family to Washington, D.C., for a patriotic excursion in the Hardy series under the direction of George B. Seitz. A-I (br) ( 1938 )

title: Judge Priest
synopsis: Warmly sentimental tale derived from Irvin S. Cobb's stories about a wise small-town judge (Will Rogers) in 1890 Kentucky who saves an innocent man (David Landau) from prison by having the local parson (Henry B. Walthall) testify to the accused's bravery in fighting for the Confederacy. Directed by John Ford, the picture stereotypes the jury's nostalgia for the southern cause with as much good-natured humor as its depiction of the town's black characters (notably Stepin Fetchit and Hattie McDaniel). Stylized violence, veiled references to illegitimacy and comic period stereotypes. A-II (br) ( 1934 )

title: Judgment at Nuremberg
synopsis: Heavy dramatization in which four German justices (notably Burt Lancaster and Werner Klemperer) stand accused of war crimes in an American tribunal headed by a fair-minded judge (Spencer Tracy), prosecuted by a vengeful U.S. Army officer (Richard Widmark) and defended by a shrewd German lawyer (Maximilian Schell). Scripted by Abby Mann and directed by Stanley Kramer, the lengthy courtroom drama examines Nazi crimes against humanity, with emotion-laded testimony from victims (Judy Garland and Montgomery Clift) as well as sad remonstrances from a German officer's widow (Marlene Dietrich), but on trial are less the four judges than the German people and, indeed, the Western world. Important subject but turgid treatment. Some newsreel footage of Nazi atrocities. A-II (br) ( 1961 )

title: Judgment Night
synopsis: While taking a shortcut through a dark, deserted Chicago slum, four pals (Emilio Estevez, Cuba Gooding, Jr., Jeremy Piven, Stephen Dorff) happen to witness a murder and are pursued by the killer (Denis Leary) and his goons. Director Stephen Hopkins' edgy thriller tempers scenes of violence with fitful attempts to portray the positive nature of masculinity and the bonds of friendship. Much violence and rough language. A-III (R) ( 1993 )

title: Judith
synopsis: Sophia Loren plays a concentration camp refugee in Palestine after the war who joins an anti-Arab group in order get revenge on her ex-husband (Hans Verner), a former Nazi now working for the Arabs. Directed by Daniel Mann, it's melodramatic hokum, though some may enjoy its picturesque locales and a supporting cast including Peter Finch and Jack Hawkins. Restrained violence. A-II (br) ( 1966 )

title: Judo Saga
synopsis: Japanese movie about the moral discipline necessary for a student of judo to best the rival followers of jujitsu is set in 1882 when Japan was emerging from feudalism under the Meiji restoration and contrasts the changes of the period with the constant values of a moral code. Directed by Akira Kurosawa in 1943, his first movie already reveals the characteristic narrative style that so distinguishes his later, internationally popular works. A-I (nr) ( 1972 )

title: Ju Dou
synopsis: The setting is a Chinese village in the 1920s where a young bride (Gong Li), abused by her aged, impotent husband (Li Wei), finds refuge in the arms of his adopted nephew (Li Baotian) but the son they conceive brings disaster to all of them. As directed by Zhang Yimou, the melodrama is a beautifully shot, bittersweet love story condemning the feudal system that so regimented people's lives. Subtitles. Very discreet sexual encounters and some restrained violence. A-III (PG-13) ( 1991 )

title: Juggernaut
synopsis: Demolition expert Richard Harris tries to disarm seven bombs placed by a madman aboard Omar Sharif's luxury liner carrying some 1200 passengers. Director Richard Lester deftly turns a routine thriller into a grand, fast and suspenseful entertainment. A-II (PG) ( 1974 )

title: Juggler, The
synopsis: Arriving in a refugee camp in 1949 Haifa, a troubled Holocaust survivor (Kirk Douglas) runs away, injures a policeman and eventually takes refuge in a kibbutz. Directed by Edward Dmytryk, the uneven script doesn't do justice to the subject, though the movie's location photography in Israel and Douglas' game attempt to portray a professional juggler who appeals especially to children are worth seeing. Stylized violence, threatening situations and romantic complications. A-II (br) ( 1953 )

title: Juice
synopsis: Unrelentingly ugly story of four young Harlem thieves, one of whom (Tupac Shakur) relishes killing and turns with deadly force on his three friends (Omar Epps, Jermaine Hopkins and Khalil Kain). Director Ernest R. Dickerson presents a shrill movie where hatred, violence and drug use is the norm and has no moral implications. Mindless violence, momentary bedroom scene, some casual drug use and sexual references and constant rough language. O (R) ( 1992 )

title: Julia
synopsis: Recollections by writer Lillian Hellman (Jane Fonda) of her friendship with Julia (Vanessa Redgrave), an extraordinary Englishwoman whose struggle to help Jews and anti-Nazis flee Hitler's Germany ends in tragedy. Directed by Fred Zinnemann, it is rather slow-moving but its good acting and stress on human dignity in the face of inhumanity compensate for its dramatic flaws. A-II (PG) ( 1977 )

title: Julia and Julia
synopsis: Failed thriller about a young widow (Kathleen Turner) inexplicably reunited with her husband six years after his death and pulled unnervingly between two worlds, until finally pushed to murder and mental collapse. Despite its eerie Italian setting and Turner's valiant effort to reflect the terror felt by her character, director Peter Del Monte is unable to combine the psychological and supernatural in a plausible narrative. Considerable nudity, graphic sex and some violence. O (R) ( 1988 )

title: Julia Has Two Lovers
synopsis: A young man (David Duchovny) who gets his kicks sweet-talking strangers on the phone, then seducing them in their homes, falls for his latest victim (Daphna Kastner) just as she is about to marry her callous lover (David Charles). Director Bashar Shbib's low-budget movie traps the viewer into hearing details of the pathetic characters' perverse sexual encounters. Much sexual exploitation and recurring nudity. O (R) ( 1991 )

title: Julia Misbehaves
synopsis: Sentimental comedy set in 1936 as a struggling music hall performer (miscast Greer Garson) returns to the home of her wealthy husband (Walter Pidgeon) after a 20-years separation to attend the wedding of their daughter (Elizabeth Taylor). Directed by Jack Conway, the hokey story features a solid supporting cast (including Cesar Romero as an acrobat) but there's not much to smile about amidst all the cliches and Garson's vain attempts to put over her songs and comic routines. Romantic complications and much sexual innuendo. A-III (br) ( 1948 )

title: Julie
synopsis: Soapy thriller begins with Doris Day as an hysteric married to a psychopath (Louis Jourdan) whom she suspects murdered her first husband and fears will kill her. Writer-director Andrew L. Stone offers one implausible twist after another until a ludicrous climax with airline hostess Day at the controls of a pilotless passenger plane. Irrational violence and menacing situations are shaky fare for children. A-I (br) ( 1956 )

title: Julie & Julia
synopsis: Charming, frequently funny dramatization of passages in the lives of master chef Julia Child (a marvelous Meryl Streep) and Internet blogger Julie Powell (Amy Adams), who, 40 years after the publication of Child's 1961 blockbuster, "Mastering the Art of French Cooking," sets out to prepare every recipe in the extensive volume over the course of a year, aided by her supportive husband (Chris Messina) -- whose solicitude parallels that of Child's own spouse (Stanley Tucci) decades earlier. Writer-director Nora Ephron whips up a delicious melange of the two women's memoirs and, more significantly, details the ingredients, ranging from passion to patience, requisite for a successful marriage. Fleeting nongraphic sexual activity, a few sexual references, a suicide reference, at least one use of the F-word and about a dozen crude or crass terms

title: Juliet of the Spirits
synopsis: Federico Fellini's first movie in color centers on a middle-aged woman (Giulietta Masina) trying to take stock of her life by sorting through her problems, memories and illusions. Fellini's imaginative imagery and Masina's aging gamin make the reveries and evocations a delight to the eye and the spirit. Ambiguous treament of mature themes. A-IV (br) ( 1965 )

title: Juliette De Sade
synopsis: Sex exploitation movie about a young girl's desires to be initiated into a life of unrestricted sex and crime. The plot, dialogue and acting are of poor quality, with no other aim than titillation. O (R) ( 1970 )

title: Julius Caesar
synopsis: Lavish Hollywood version of Shakespeare's play in which the noble Brutus (James Mason) joins the conspiracy to assassinate Caesar (Louis Calhern) in order to preserve the Republic, but two years later his forces are crushed by Mark Antony (Marlon Brando) at Philippi in 42 B.C. Writer-director Joseph L. Mankiewicz has boiled down the play to its essentials and the fine cast does well with the Elizabethian language, but the drama is too static to be entirely satsifying. Period violence, including suicide. A-I (br) ( 1953 )

title: Julius Caesar
synopsis: Failed version of Shakespeare's tragedy directed by Stuart Burge with awkward staging, uniformly poor performances (Charlton Heston as Antony and Jason Robards as Brutus) and gauche Roman costuming right out of an Italian muscle movie. Even a desperate teacher, willing to try anything to motivate English students, had best beware this slack effort. A-II (PG) ( 1970 )

title: Jumanji
synopsis: Eye-popping fantasy adventure about a jungle wildlife board game which springs to life, threatening to destroy a whole town unless its players (notably Robin Williams) successfully complete the game. Director Joe Johnston provides some frightening thrills as spectacular special effects put humans at the mercy of rampaging animals and a deadly hunter. Frequent life-threatening menace and intermittent gunfire. A-II (PG) ( 1995 )

title: Jumbo
synopsis: ( see "Billy Rose's Jumbo" )

title: Jumper
synopsis: Chaotic science fiction thriller about a young man (Hayden Christensen) who learns he has the ability to transport himself instantly to any location around the globe, and how he teams with another Jumper (Jamie Bell) to fight an agent (Samuel Jackson) of the evil Paladin forces bent on their extermination. The premise is promising and there are some decent effects, but director Doug Liman, so adept in the action genre, can do little with a risible, underwritten script, dull plot and generally indifferent performances. Intense action violence, an instance of the f-word, crude language and profanity, implied nonmarital sexual relationship, murder and mayhem

title: Jumping Jacks
synopsis: Predictable but congenial service comedy directed by Norman Taurog as nightclub entertainers (Dean Martin and Jerry Lewis) manage to wind up together in the paratroopers clowning their way through boot camp under a blustery sergeant (Robert Strauss), with antic highlights by Lewis on field maneuvers and jumping without a parachute. A-I (br) ( 1952 )

title: Jumpin' Jack Flash
synopsis: Whoopi Goldberg plays a compassionate but fiercely independent computer operator who saves the life of a British intelligence agent trapped in an Iron Curtain country when she communicates with him via computer terminal. Director Penny Marshall's raucous but lighthearted spoof of the spy genre is chilled by an extraordinary amount of sexually derived expletives. A-III (R) ( 1986 )

title: Jump into Hell
synopsis: Hollywood account of the 1954 French defeat at Dienbienphu after a 56-day offensive by Vietnamese communist rebels which resulted in Indochina's partition. Directed by David Butler, the focus is on the brave actions of several French officers (notably Jacques Sernas, Kurt Kasznar and Peter Van Eyck) as well as flashbacks to their lives before the battle. Wartime violence and mild sexual innuendo. A-II (br) ( 1955 )

title: Jun
synopsis: Japanese movie about a maladjusted Tokyo worker who gives vent to his frustrations by molesting women on crowded commuter trains. Written and directed by Hiroto Yokoyama, its prretentious vision of urban alienation becomes a heavy-handed display of graphic sexual excesses. O (nr) ( 1980 )

title: June Bride
synopsis: Uneven romantic comedy in which the editor (Bette Davis) of a woman's magazine assigns an old beau (Robert Montgomery) to cover an Indiana wedding whose unexpected problems bring the two back together. Directed by Bretaigne Windust, the witty sparring between these veteran professionals is more amusing than the romantic guff of a story predicated on the male calling the shots. Sexual situations. A-III (br) ( 1948 )

title: Jungle 2 Jungle
synopsis: Workaholic Wall Street trader (Tim Allen) learns to bond with his visiting, newly discovered 13-year-old son (Sam Huntington) who was raised by his estranged wife in a Venezuelan rain forest. Director John Pasquin's clash-of-cultures comedy limps fitfully along, depending heavily on Allen's appeal as a TV sitcom star. Implied pre-marital relationship, comic violence and some coarse humor. A-III (PG) ( 1997 )

title: Jungle Book, The
synopsis: Uneven adaptation of the Rudyard Kipling story in which an infant boy (Sabu) is raised by wolves in the wilds of India, then protects an ancient treasure from a trio of greedy villagers (led by Joseph Calleia). Directed by Zoltan Korda, the jungle with its exotic animals has greater appeal than the village and its human tribe. Some graphic violence. A-II (br) ( 1942 )

title: Jungle Book, The
synopsis: Rudyard Kipling's adventure-filled story of Mowgli, a boy-child reared by obliging wolves in the jungles of India, has been freely but nicely adapted in this Disney animated feature directed by Wolfgang Reitherman. Using genial humor and the voices of Phil Harris as Baloo, a lovable bear, George Sanders as Shere Khan, a suave, menacing tiger and Sterling Holloway as an opportunistic python, the movie will amuse everyone in the household. A-I (G) ( 1967 )

title: Jungle Fever
synopsis: A married African-American architect (Wesley Snipes) becomes an outcast to his Harlem family as does his Italian Catholic girlfriend from Brooklyn (Annabella Sciorra) when their interracial affair is exposed. Written, produced and directed by co-star Spike Lee, the ugliness of racism is provocatively exposed and the human toll of drug addiction is harrowingly portrayed while religion comes off as something ineffectual or negative. An adulterous relationship, short outbursts of violence, brief partial nudity and much rough language. A-IV (R) ( 1991 )

title: Jungle Fighters
synopsis: British World War II tale set in Malaya where a patrol (led by Richard Todd) captures a Japanese soldier (Kenji Takaki), then find themselves cut off from base and quarrel over what to do with their prisoner before trying to fight their way out. Directed by Leslie Norman from Willis Hall's play, the picture focuses on the characters, especially the undisciplined private (Laurence Harvey) who tries to keep his mates from mistreating the frightened prisoner which hits home when the patrol faces capture or death. Wartime violence including menacing situations and a military atrocity. A-III (br) ( 1961 )

title: Jungle Jim
synopsis: Standard adventure directed by William Berke in which the title character (Johnny Weissmuller) guides a scientist (Virginia Grey) to a lost temple in quest of a cure for polio but a gold-hunting photographer (George Reeves) and hostile natives get in their way. Stylized violence and threatening situations. A-I (br) ( 1948 )

title: Jungle Jim in the Forbidden Land
synopsis: Adventure programmer directed by Lew Landers in which Jim (Johnny Weissmuller) fights a panther, a hippopotamus, ivory poachers and a fearsome tribe of giant people who stand in the way of rescuing an elephant herd trapped by a flood. Stylized violence. A-I (br) ( 1952 )

title: Jungle Man-Eaters
synopsis: Adventure programmer directed by Lee Sholem pits Jungle Jim (Johnny Weissmuller) against a renegade band of native warriors led by a French crook looking for a secret diamond mine. Stylized violence. A-I (br) ( 1954 )

title: Jungle Manhunt
synopsis: Formula adventure directed by Lew Landers in which Jungle Jim (Johnny Weissmuller) helps a reporter (Sheila Ryan) locate a missing millionaire war hero (football star Bob Waterfield), then frees natives forced to mine radioactive ore which a greedy scientist (Lyle Talbot) converts into synthetic diamonds. Stylized violence. A-I (br) ( 1951 )

title: Jungle Moon Men
synopsis: African adventure directed by Charles S. Gould in which jungle guide Johnny Weissmuller helps an intrepid author (Jean Byron) find the ruins of an ancient Egyptian city whose treasures are guarded by pygmy warriors under the command of a priestess (Helene Stanton) who alone knows the secret of eternal life. Stylized violence. A-I (br) ( 1955 )

title: Jungle Woman
synopsis: Horror clunker directed by Reginald LeBorg in which a doctor (J. Carrol Naish) comes to fear that one of his patients (Aquanetta) is really an ape that a mad scientist (John Carradine) has transformed into a woman. Stylized violence and hokey menace. A-II (br) ( 1944 )

title: Junior
synopsis: Low-brow comic fantasy in which a fertility specialist (Danny DeVito) tests an anti-miscarriage drug by injecting a fertilized egg into a willing male colleague (Arnold Schwarzenegger) who then refuses to end the experiment after the first trimester and goes to term with the pregnancy while romancing the woman (Emma Thompson) whose frozen egg was used without her knowledge. Director Ivan Reitman's one-joke premise of a pregnant man relys on common stereotypes of expectant women for its laughs while presenting fetal experimentation as all part of a nutty plotline that gets increasingly bizarre. Comic treatment of reproductive technology, references to casual sexual relations and an instance of profanity. A-III (PG-13) ( 1994 )

title: Junior Bonner
synopsis: Aging cowboy Steve McQueen has one big challenge left to meet in the form of a brahma bull that nearly killed him last time around. The film is stolen, however, by Robert Preston as Junior's wild Pa and Ida Lupino as his heartbroken, long-suffering but tough Ma in their superb and emotionally wrenching scenes together. Unlike some of his violent Westerns, director Sam Peckinpah has here devoted his talents to constructing a well-balanced, well-paced and well-acted rodeo movie. A-II (PG) ( 1972 )

title: Junk Mail
synopsis: Offbeat black comedy in which a grungy Oslo mailman (Robert Skjaerstad) becomes unwittingly involved with a suicidal woman (Andrine Saether) who is reluctantly holding stolen money for a criminal acquaintance. Director Pal Sletaune finds quirky romance in this wry Norwegian tale of alienated urban workers whose glum lives offer little hope of human fulfillment. Subtitles. Brief violence, full nudity, occasional profanity and an instance of rough language. A-III (nr) ( 1998 )

title: Juno
synopsis: Smart, funny and ultimately moving comedy-drama with a strong pro-life message about an unwed teen (an outstanding Ellen Page) who decides not to have an abortion, and promises the coming baby to a childless couple (Jason Bateman and Jennifer Garner) who long to adopt. The narrative has just the right moral wrap-up; performances are tops, including J.K. Simmons and Allison Janney as the girl's supportive parents and Michael Cera as the shy classmate responsible for her condition. Jason Reitman's direction strikes just the right piquant tone, though Diablo Cody's script contains a high expletive level for its appealing but sassy heroine. Crude language and at least one instance of the f-word, some crass expressions, an irreverent remark, a nongraphic premarital teen encounter with brief partial nudity, out-of-wedlock pregnancy, sexual talk and divorce. A-III adults. (PG-13) 2007 Full Review �Juno� (Fox Searchlight) is a smart, funny and ultimately moving comedy-drama with a strong pro-life message. The titular Juno is an unwed teen (a marvelous performance by young Ellen Page) who finds herself pregnant after, more or less, seducing her shy classmate Paulie (Michael Cera). When she gives herself a pregnancy test at the local drug store (there's a rather distasteful exchange with the smart-aleck pharmacist played by Rainn Wilson) and learns she's pregnant, she decides to have an abortion. But she's so turned off by the coldness of the abortion clinic that she resolutely decides not to have an abortion, and promises the coming baby to a childless upper-class couple, Mark (Jason Bateman) and Vanessa (Jennifer Garner), who long to adopt and have advertised in a local paper. Complications ensue as she learns that Mark and Vanessa's marriage is less than secure, and though Vanessa desperately wants a child, composer Mark -- with whom Juno finds herself platonically bonding over their mutual admiration for certain rock bands and horror films -- feels quite differently. Juno is horrified to learn Mark is considering divorcing Vanessa, and begs him not to do it. At the same time, Juno realizes that her feelings for Paulie are still strong. All of this leads to a somewhat surprising wrap-up that has just the right moral tone. Performances are tops, including J.K. Simmons and Allison Janney as the girl's supportive -- if surprisingly nonjudgmental -- father and stepmother. Garner's wonderment at hearing "her" baby kick for the first time, while she kneels and speaks to Juno's belly, is an especially magical moment. Unfortunately, Diablo Cody's wry, sardonic script contains a high expletive level for its appealing but sassy heroine, but the movie's sweet, sentimental core underneath the surface edginess wins the day. Jason Reitman's direction -- beautifully attuned to Cody's unique rhythms -- strikes just the right piquant tone

title: Jupiter Menace, The
synopsis: Narrated by George Kennedy with a straight face, this is one of those psuedo-scientific, quasi-religious documentaries which forecasts the end of the world. It may scare the wits out of those not inclined to take it all with several grains of salt, but then, fear is sometimes good for the soul. A-II (PG) ( 1983 )

title: Jurassic Park
synopsis: A bizarre theme park featuring genetically re-created dinosaurs becomes a potential deathtrap when the carnivorous monsters break loose, endangering some visiting scientists (Sam Neill, Laura Dern and Jeff Goldblum) and two very frightened young children (Joseph Mazzelo and Ariana Richards). Director Steven Spielberg's monster fantasy downplays plot and characterization in favor of spectacle and horrific special effects in which the realistic-looking creatures hunt down their human prey. Much intense menace to children and several stylized scenes of violent death. A-II (PG-13) ( 1993 )

title: Jurassic Park III
synopsis: New dino species are introduced to terrify paleontologist Sam Neill who is helping parents Tea Leoni and William B. Macy rescue their son (Trevor Morgan) from another island of rampaging, genetically re-created dinosaurs. Director Joe Johnston reduces dialogue and characterization to throwaway status but turns in an energetic sequel whose action sequences deliver the accustomed thrills and spills. Some intense fantasy violence

title: Juror, The
synopsis: Preposterous, dragged-out thriller involving the murder trial of a gang boss who unleashes a psychotic hitman to threaten a jury member and her child with death unless she convinces her fellow jurors to acquit the accused. Directed by Brian Gibson, the cat-and-mouse struggle of the woman to placate her twisted tormentor, then attempt to kill him has some nasty thrills but is too slow-moving and painfully contrived to hold attention. Sadistic threats, various murders, a sexual encounter with brief nudity, occasional profanity and some rough language. A-IV (R) ( 1996 )

title: Jury Duty
synopsis: Unamusing comedy in which a homeless juror (Pauly Shore) prolongs deliberations over the guilt of an alleged serial killer in order to enjoy free bed and board on a sequestered jury. Directed by John Fortenberry, Shore's dumb antics go from the inane to the obnoxious in a laughless timewaster. Some sleazy sexual innuendo, slapstick violence and several instances of profanity. A-III (PG-13) ( 1995 )

title: Just Another Girl on the I.R.T.
synopsis: Gritty cautionary tale of a bright but flip African-Amercian teen (Ariyan Johnson) who aims to go to college and become a doctor but falls for a jock with a jeep (Kevin Thigpen), gets pregnant and winds up a single mother enrolled in a community college. Writer-director Leslie Harris's low-budget account of coming of age in Brooklyn's public housing projects makes good use of the harsh urban landscape and blighted social conditions but fails to create much sympathy for the girl's character and provides little insight in her predicament. Some restrained bedroom scenes, explicit discussions of contraception and abortion, an intense birth scene, attempted infanticide and much rough language. A-IV (R) ( 1993 )

title: Just Around the Corner
synopsis: After her architect father (Charles Farrell) loses his job in the Depression, his little girl (Shirley Temple) helps him get it back by appealing to a millionaire (Claude Gillingwater) whom she mistakes for Uncle Sam. Director Irving Cummings pads out the formula plot with a little comic relief (Bert Lahr and Joan Davis) and some musical numbers with Shirley and Bill Robinson. Thin sentimental fare for the undemanding. A-I (G) ( 1938 )

title: Just Before Nightfall
synopsis: French psychological melodrama in which an ordinary man (Michel Bouquet) murders his mistress and then, overcome by guilt, decides to confess but his wife (Stephane Audran) takes steps to prevent him from disgracing the family name. Director Claude Chabrol tells his story of conscience and middle-class morality with one ironic twist after another, confronting viewers with an ambiguous conclusion that implicitly indicts the emptiness of materialistc values. Brief nudity. A-IV (PG) ( 1975 )

title: Just Between Friends
synopsis: Marital infidelity is the starting point for a seriocomic treatment of the relationship between a naive housewife and an independent career woman. When the man in their lives is killed in an accident, the wife (Mary Tyler Moore) discovers his affair with her friend (Christine Lahti) who is now pregnant with his child. The women ultimately find grounds for reconciliation and mutual support after the baby's birth. Directed by Allan Burns, the sitcom format and soap-opera characterizations offer little inspiration and less justification for a frivolous handling of a serious theme. A-III (PG-13) ( 1986 )

title: Just Cause
synopsis: Tawdry melodrama in which a Harvard law professor (Sean Connery) is persuaded by his lawyer wife (Kate Capeshaw) to make a last-ditch effort at overturning the murder conviction of a Florida death-row inmate (Blair Underwood) whose confession had been coerced by a brutal police detective (Laurence Fishburne). Director Arne Glimcher maintains moderate suspense through a darkly twisted plot abetted by some fine performances until the narrative goes haywire with a lurid, ludicrous ending. Some intense violence including grisly shots of corpses, fleeting shadowy nudity and recurring rough language

title: Just for You
synopsis: Routine musical in which a widowed Broadway producer (Bing Crosby) tries to woo a stage star (Jane Wyman) while coping with an adolescent son (Bob Arthur) who has a crush on her, and a daughter (Natalie Wood) who wants to enroll in a posh academy whose headmistress (Ethel Barrymore) proves uncommonly wise. Directed by Elliott Nugent, the narrative lumbers fitfully along, though matters brighten considerably whenever Barrymore is on screen in her small but pivotal role. Romantic complications. A-II (br) ( 1952 )

title: Just Friends
synopsis: Leaden romantic comedy about a former overweight "loser" (Ryan Reynolds) turned suave and successful ladies man, who, while waylaid in his New Jersey home town, pursues the affections of his high-school best friend and crush (Amy Smart), who back then only saw him through platonic eyes. Despite ending on an admirably sentimental note, director Roger Kumble's film is full of forced and witless humor that alternates between staggeringly unfunny and mean-spirited. Much cruel slapstick violence, some lewd sexual situations and humor, an erotic image, a crass sight gag, a brief same-sex kiss, an instance of rough language and some sexually crude remarks

title: Just Go With It
synopsis: Very loose -- and sloppy -- remake of the classic 1969 farce "Cactus Flower" weighed down by stale writing and a seemingly endless parade of potty jokes. Adam Sandler plays a philandering plastic surgeon who escapes commitment by telling his many girlfriends he's trapped in a bad marriage. So, once he decides to settle down with a schoolteacher (Brooklyn Decker), he needs to produce a "wife" he can divorce, the start of an increasingly complicated effort at deception in which he eventually enlists not only his sensible office assistant (Jennifer Aniston) but her two precocious kids (Bailee Madison and Griffin Gluck) as well. Director Dennis Dugan and screenwriters Allan Loeb and Timothy Dowling dumb down what was originally a sweet adult romance involving an escalating series of funny complications and a modest message about being true to one's self. The resulting comedy is not only frequently distasteful, but comatose almost from the start. An implied premarital situation, considerable scatological humor, sexual banter, fleeting crude language

title: Justin Bieber: Never Say Never
synopsis: This genial 3-D profile of teen pop singer and musician Justin Bieber showcases home movies of his childhood, footage documenting his rise to stardom via social media celebrity, backstage preparations for his sold-out concert at New York's Madison Square Garden as well as musical performances recorded there and at other venues. Director Jon M. Chu's portrait of a likable young man striving to resist the temptations of sudden-onset fame is not only perfectly acceptable for audiences of any age, it also highlights his close bonds with his mother and grandparents and the Christian faith he shares with them, typified onscreen by the prayers he and his entourage recite before each show

title: Justine
synopsis: The last days of the British involvement in Egypt frame this complicated story featuring Anouk Aimee as the somber, crafty medium of the title, Michael York as a spineless schoolmaster and Anna Karina as the tubercular dancer he comes to love. Director George Cukor uses the city of Alexandria to convey the social and moral decadence of the late 1930s. Graphic rendering of homosexuality and excessive use of nudity. O (R) ( 1969 )

title: Just Like at Home
synopsis: Hungarian director Marta Meszaros explores the relationship between a precocious 11-year-old girl (Zsuzsa Czinkoczy) and a rash and bedeviled man in his 30s. A flawed but nonetheless absorbing movie, it conveys the somber texture of life in contemporary Hungary. Mature themes. A-III (nr) ( 1979 )

title: Just Like Heaven
synopsis: Charming romantic fantasy about a dedicated young doctor (Reese Witherspoon), comatose after a near-fatal car accident, whose spirit "haunts" a grieving widower (Mark Ruffalo) who has rented her former apartment. Despite a somewhat formulaic setup and an uncertain start, director Mark Waters directs with just the appropriate gossamer touch, and the highly appealing leads play with the requisite delicacy. Some sexual innuendo and banter, mild profanity, a few crass expressions, brief rear hospital nudity, mild medical procedures including incisions, some occult thematic material, and an exorcism used for comic point make this best for adults (and older adolescents)

title: Just Married
synopsis: Insipid romantic comedy about an average working Joe (Ashton Kutcher) and his wealthy bride (Brittany Murphy) whose disastrous European honeymoon nearly ends their brief marriage. Director Shawn Levy pushes sappy, cutesy and teary scenes in which the self-absorbed couple sulk, pout and scream until they come to their senses. A live-in relationship and many sexual references, some comically intended violence, occasional crude humor and minimal profanity

title: Just My Luck
synopsis: Lightweight if likable romantic comedy set in New York about a girl (Lindsay Lohan) with uncanny luck and a guy (Chris Pine) with none, who magically swap fortunes through a chance encounter at a masquerade ball, winding up on polar ends of the luck spectrum and falling for each other, though neither realizes the other is the cause for the karmic reversal. Directed by Donald Petrie, the fairy tale's cute conceit has the bad luck of being wrapped in a limp and predictable script, though its sweet-natured message about valuing love over success is commendable. Some crude language and innuendo, a couple of crass sight gags, a sexual gesture and a situation involving a male "escort."

title: Just One of the Guys
synopsis: An ambitious high school girl (Joyce Hyser) who wants to be a journalist decides that no one takes her work seriously because she's too pretty and so she disguises herself as a boy. Director Lisa Gottlieb's plodding, mediocre comedy has a heavy emphasis on vulgarity and sexually oriented humor. Worse, outright promiscuity is portrayed as perfectly normal. O (PG-13) ( 1985 )

title: Just Tell Me What You Want
synopsis: Long-time mistress (Ali McGraw) of a greedy tycoon (Alan King) tries to break away by marrying a New York playwright (Peter Weller) and the tycoon's devious efforts to get her back provide the thrust for most of the plot in a sour and vulgar comedy directed by Sidney Lumet. Though it has a lot of action, it has little purpose and no heart. Condones immoral actions and features foul language. O (R) ( 1980 )

title: Just the Way You Are
synopsis: Crippled musician (Kristy McNichol) goes to bed with a succession of men at home and in the course of a vacation at a Swiss ski resort where she hides her affliction with a plaster cast. Directed by Edouard Molinaro, the dull and listless attempt at light romance takes an entirely benign view of the heroine's promiscuous behavior. O (PG) ( 1984 )

title: Just You and Me, Kid
synopsis: Retired comedian (George Burns) finds a teenage girl (Brooke Shields) in the trunk of his vintage Pierce-Arrow clad in nothing but an old inner tube. Neither the plot explanation nor the attempts at humor are convincing in director Leonard Stern's generation-gap bore which has some brief laughs from John Schuck and Andrea Howard as nosey neighbors. Some violence and strong language. A-II (PG) ( 1979 )

title: Juwanna Man
synopsis: Weak comedy in which a cocky professional basketball player (Miguel A. Nunez) is thrown out of the NBA for his repeated obnoxious antics on court, so he pretends to be a woman to play for the women’s league, where he develops a romantic crush on a fellow teammate (Vivica A. Fox). As directed by Jesse Vaughan, the film feebly inserts a message about teamwork, but the stale jokes don’t score and the sappy ending can’t compensate for the sexually suggestive poses, clothing and language. Several crude expressions and language and brief rear nudity.��

title: J.W. Coop
synopsis: Cliff Robertson plays a rugged rodeo champ fresh out of prison after serving 10 years for forging a check and raring to get back on the circuit to catch up with his life and the times. Also written, produced and directed by Robertson, the success story may be a bit long in the telling but its picture of a man who grits his teeth and gets on with the job of regaining a hold on life provides reasonably intelligent entertainment. Questionable romantic entanglement. A-III (GP/PG-13) ( 1972 )

title: The Jackals
synopsis: South African tale set in a 19th-century Transvaal ghost town where an old prospector (Vincent Price) and his granddaughter (Diana Evarson) are held captive by five bandits (led by Robert Gunner) certain they are hiding a fortune in gold. Directed by Robert D. Webb, the stark landscapes and local natives add some color to an otherwise flat adaptation of the 1948 Western, "The Yellow Sky." Frontier violence and sexual innuendo. A-III (br) ( 1967 )

title: The Jacket
synopsis: Dark and disjointed psychological thriller about an amnesiac Gulf War veteran (Adrien Brody) who is framed for the murder of a policeman and is sentenced to an asylum for the criminally insane where a psychiatrist (Kris Kristofferson) subjects him to mind-altering "treatment" -- involving being strapped into a straitjacket and locked in a morgue body drawer -- which enables him to see the future, including his own imminent death. Stylishly crafted by director John Maybury, the creepy atmospherics fail to conceal that, despite ending on a redemptive, life-affirming note, the formulaic film lacks any real emotion or logic

title: The Jungle Book 2
synopsis: Fun-filled sequel to the 1967 animated classic about Mowgli (voice of Haley Joel Osment), a boy raised in the wild who must choose between life in a "man-village" and his jungle friends, including the lovable bear, Baloo (voice of John Goodman). While the new film lacks the originality and enduring appeal of its precursor, director Steve Trenbirth combines cutting-edge animation and a jazzy score to create a charming tale of friendship and family

title: A Knight's Tale
synopsis: Rollicking action adventure story about a young squire (Heath Ledger) in 14th century France who assumes his deceased master's identity and works his way up the jousting circuit to foil a nasty villain (Rufus Sewell). Inspired by Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, director Brian Helgeland deftly blends contemporary attitudes, dialogue and rock music into an entertaining period piece although the movie's length is a bit indulgent. Intermittent action violence, some rear nudity and fleeting crass language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: K-19: The Widowmaker
synopsis: Fact-based, Cold-War submarine drama set in 1961 as the captain (a grim Harrison Ford) and Executive Officer (a convincing Liam Neeson) clash onboard a Russian sub whose malfunctioning core reactor could meltdown with catastrophic results. Directed by Kathryn Bigelow, the tense tale of honor, courage and human drama is marred by its sluggish pace and some blunt characterizations. Brief violence, images of injured seamen and fleeting rear nudity

title: K2
synopsis: The lifelong friendship of two amateur mountain climbers (Michael Biehn and Matt Craven) is put to the ultimate test in the Himalayas where they become stranded atop the world's most dangerous mountain peak. While the physical dangers in this adventure movie are predictable, director Franc Roddam enhances the spectacular action sequences with gripping character studies of the two men as they face impending death. Some sexual innuendo, rough language and a flash of nudity

title: K-9
synopsis: Lame story of a hotheaded San Diego narcotics cop (James Belushi) and his police dog partner. Director Rod Daniel tracks this unlikely cop team as they corner a slick drug czar (Kevin Tighe), but much of this comedy caper focuses on implausible macho heroics with intense comic-book violence, rough language and vulgar sexual innuendoes

title: Kafka
synopsis: Interesting excursion into the dark imagination of absurdist author Franz Kafka (Jeremy Irons) whose dull duties as an insurance clerk in 1919 Prague spark nightmare images of an oppressive regime secretly operating from the medieval castle overlooking the city. Directed by Steven Soderbergh, the narrative is by turns moody, bizarre and ironic but never quite achieves the dreamlike logic that would make it work as something more than an elaborate exercise of the emotions. Morosely unsettling atmosphere, some nasty stylized violence and a glimpse of a nude photo

title: Kagemusha
synopsis: Grand period spectacle set in 16th-century Japan when a thief (Tatsuya Nakadai) is trained to impersonate a dead warlord whose clan is fighting for its survival against a powerful rival. Director Akira Kurosawa's austere but powerful treatment of the historical material is filled with fierce martial pageantry, stirring action and poignant ironies as the story of a clan's downfall unfolds. Subtitles. Tragic theme and violent battle sequences

title: Kaleidoscope
synopsis: Sophisticated comedy-thriller involving the con games of a suave American gambler (miscast Warren Beatty) on the loose in London and on the Continent. Though the plot is overly complicated, the largely British cast (notably Susannah York, Clive Revill and Eric Porter) is excellent and director Jack Smight keeps matters diverting enough for those who like this kind of derring-do. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Kalifornia
synopsis: Violent road movie in which a cash-strapped couple (David Duchovny and Michelle Forbes) unwittingly share cross-country car ride expenses with another couple, a dimwitted innocent (Juliette Lewis) and her boyfriend (Brad Pitt), a cold-blooded murderer. Director Dominic Sena allows the drama to wallow in the vicious brutality of a callous killer and the conversion of a normal guy into a vengeful executor, depicting it all with flippant black humor. Excessive violence, positive portrayal of a revenge murder, rough sexual encounters, nude photos and occasional rough language

title: Kama Sutra
synopsis: Exploitation movie using the Hindu sexual manual as an excuse for graphic sex scenes and frequently ludicrous commentary

title: Kama Sutra: A Tale of Love
synopsis: Convoluted romantic melodrama set in 16th-century India where a king (Naveen Andrews) marries a princess (Sarita Choudhury) but is seduced by her envious servant (Indira Varma) who goes on to become a courtesan, falls in love with a sculptor (Ramon Tikaram) and ultimately incurs the king's wrath. Directed by Mira Nair, the exotic period setting is stylishly visualized but the story proves little more than a soap-opera saga of English-speaking cardboard characters and their shallow emotional lives. Several restrained sex scenes with nudity, some sexual references and brief violence

title: Kamouraska
synopsis: French-Canadian movie set in the early 19th century in which a passionate and headstrong young woman (Genevieve Bujold) marries the boorish master of a remote estate (Philippe Leotard), leaves him to return to civilization and has a romance with a doctor (Richard Jordan) that ends in murder. Directed by Claude Jutra, the movie captures a vanished era, has excellent acting and the beauty of its settings but its story of hot passion in a cold climate is heavily melodramatic. Some incidental nudity and scenes of questionable taste

title: Kandahar
synopsis: Impressive Iranian drama about a young Afghan woman (Nelofer Pazira) exiled in Canada trying to reach Kandahar from Iran to rescue her maimed sister who has threatened to commit suicide. Addressing the plight of women under Taliban rule and the accumulated misery of the Afghan people, director Mohsen Makhmalbaf's film is visually exotic yet emotionally grim as suffering and oppression are presented in inescapable terms. A few startling images of amputees. Some subtitles

title: Kangaroo Jack
synopsis: Passable comedy in which two Brooklyn buddies (Jerry O'Connell and Anthony Anderson) end up being pursued in the Australian Outback after a kangaroo hops off with the envelope of mob money they were supposed to deliver. The scenic setting, animal antics and the leads' easygoing rapport make director David McNally's goofy crime caper relatively innocuous entertainment. Mild sexual innuendo, occasional toilet humor and some menace with comic violence

title: Kansas City
synopsis: Dour crime story set in 1934 centers on the kidnapping of a politician's wife (Miranda Richardson) by a woman (Jennifer Jason Leigh) trying to free her husband (Dermot Mulroney) from a black gang leader (Harry Belafonte). Directed by Robert Altman, the tension of the kidnapping plot is dissipated by leisurely digressions into corrupt Missouri politics, lengthy monologues by the gang leader, asides on Hollywood movies and lively sessions in a jazz club. Considerable menace, hard-edged violence, sexual innuendo, drug abuse, racial epithets, profanity and rough language

title: Kansas City Bomber
synopsis: Raquel Welsh plays a top skater on the Roller Derby scene with Kevin McCarthy as the team owner trying to promote a bigger and better franchise. Burdened with some unconvincing, if decorative, performances, director Jerrold Freedman's inept and shallow melodrama manages to make the Roller Derby look boring. Some rough language

title: Kansas City Confidential
synopsis: Tough-minded tale of an ex-con (John Payne) who's wrongly implicated in an armored car robbery, then trails those who did it to Mexico for the final showdown. Directed by Phil Karlson, the gritty but contrived proceedings feature a gang (Jack Elam, Neville Brand and Lee Van Cleef) whose leader (Preston Foster) insists they all wear masks so none will know the identity of the others. Some deadly violence and intermittent brutality

title: Kansas Pacific
synopsis: Standard Western directed by Ray Nazarro tells how a Union officer (Sterling Hayden) built the title railroad while fighting off Quantrill's Raiders during the Civil War. Stylized violence

title: Kansas Raiders
synopsis: Muddled Western in which Jesse James (Audie Murphy), his brother Frank (Richard Long), Cole Younger (James Best) and Kit Dalton (Tony Curtis) join Confederate Col. William Clarke Quantrill (Brian Donlevy) to fight Yankees but wind up terrorizing Kansas citizens instead. Directed by Ray Enright, the contradictory plot tries to have it both ways as young Jesse protests atrocities while continuing to participate in them. Terrorist violence against civilians, much brutality and an implied sexual relationship

title: Kansas Terrors, The
synopsis: Western programmer directed by George Sherman in which a pair of cowboys (Bob Livingston and Raymond Hatton) deliver a shipment of horses to a Caribbean island where they help a rebel leader (Duncan Renaldo) overthrow the local dictator, then bring him back to Kansas where they become the Three Mesquiteers. Stylized violence

title: Kaos
synopsis: Comprised of four fables of Italian peasant life drawn from Luigi Pirandello's short stories, this Italian production by the Taviani brothers offers a range of sensitive characterizations expressing simple but profound truths. Each segment is a self-contained tale on a social, political or moral theme. Visually rich and dramatically provocative, the film's life-affirming narrative is well worth its running time of over three hours. A brief shot of partial nudity and a gruesome shot of a decapitated head punctuate an otherwise pastoral vision

title: Karado, the Hong Kong Cat
synopsis: Martial arts champion returns to the island of his birth and finds himself between two opposing factions. Non-stop violent encounters in which everything from chain whips to revolvers come into play, as well as some sex scenes

title: Karate Kid Part III, The
synopsis: Against the wishes of his karate mentor (Noriyuki "Pat" Morita), young Daniel (Ralph Macchio) is coerced by sleazy martial artists into defending his championship title. Director John G. Avildsen puts more emphasis on the smirking heavies and grisly brutality than on the anti-violence values of the earlier series. The exploitative nature of the violence is unsuitable for preteens or impressionable younger adolescents

title: Karate Kid Part II, The
synopsis: Repeating his role in the sequel, Pat Morita gives a winning performance as the martial arts teacher who brings his young student (Ralph Macchio) to Okinawa in a gentle story re-affirming the importance of devotion, loyalty and the sweet-and-sour of life as seen from the perspective of old age. Unabashedly moralistic without being didactic, it is high-spirited, engaging entertainment

title: Karate Kid, The
synopsis: High school student (Ralph Macchio) learns about life, friendship and the martial arts from a kindly Japanese-American gardener (Pat Morita) who shows him how to deal with the bullies tormenting him. Directed by John G. Avildsen, the movie is made extremely appealing by the performances of the two principals despite its message that violence solves all ills. Parents should be sure that their youngsters realize karate is considerably more lethal than depicted here

title: Kate and Leopold
synopsis: Sweet time-travel romance in which a 19th century duke (Hugh Jackman) is accidentally brought to the present time where he falls for a hard-edged executive (Meg Ryan) whose cynical view of love is tested by his gallantry. With a mixture of old-fashioned romance, fish-out-of-water chuckles and a good dose of star power, director James Mangold's fluffy romance is a sprightly piece, albeit a conventional one with few surprises. Sporadic crass language and some profanity

title: Katerina Izmailova
synopsis: Russian production of Shostakovich's opera features the performance of Galina Vishnevskaya, first soprana of the Bolshoi. Director Mikhail Shapiro provides a fluid rendering of tragic lovers who resort to murder to preserve their relationship but imprisoned in Siberia, love gradually turns, through mutual recriminations and the man's infidelity, into hatred. Dreary moral tale in Russian with English subtitles

title: Kathy's Love Affair
synopsis: ( see: "The Courtneys" )

title: Kaya, I'll Kill You
synopsis: Yugoslavian import conveys the simplicity of life in a pre-war Croatian village and the terror which is unleashed by the emergence of its own home-town fascists inebriated by power. Symbolic narrative set in exotic locales and directed by Vatroslav Mimica makes obscure points about the nature of violence and militarism

title: Kazaam
synopsis: Trashy comic fantasy in which a 12-year-old brat (Francis Capra) and a 5,000-year-old genie (Shaquille O'Neal) tangle with some nasty thugs in a rap-music racket, after which the boy reconciles with a father he hasn't seen in 10 years as well as the man his divorced mom plans to marry. Directed by Paul Michael Glazer, the witless proceedings are noisy, the characters are generally unlikable and there's nothing magical about the clumsy special effects. Stylized violence, menacing situations, domestic tensions, coarse language and a profanity

title: Kazablan
synopsis: Israeli musical pits the Sephardim against Ashkenazim in the Jaffa slums of Tel Aviv, telling the story of two lovers from different sides of the ethnic gap. Director Menahen Golan's economy-sized extravaganza of dancing and singing has some natural charm and its salty taunting and gesture is submerged in its theme of finding one's heart by relaxing one's prejudices

title: Keane
synopsis: A schizophrenic and sometimes violent man (Damian Lewis) wanders a New York bus terminal looking for the daughter he claims was abducted, and later befriends a troubled mother (Amy Ryan) and her 7-year-old daughter (Abigail Breslin) at a transient motel. Writer-director Lodge Kerrigan's grainy, cinema-verite-style film has an ugly milieu, sordid situations and tedious stretches in its first half, though the ending is intensely moving and redemptive. Lewis' performance is a tour de force, with first-class support by Ryan, Breslin and Tina Holmes. Profanity and rough language, a violent episode, an unrestrained sexual encounter, and alcohol and drug use

title: Keeper of the Flame
synopsis: Contrived melodrama in which a journalist (Spencer Tracy) sets out to gather material for a tribute to a late public leader, falls for his widow (Katharine Hepburn), then discovers the truth about the man's death and secret subversive plans. Director George Cukor's woolly tale of home-grown fascism starts slowly and grows increasingly portentous until ending in typical period flagwaving. Muddled attempt to justify murder

title: Keeper, The
synopsis: Gritty drama in which an idealistic Brooklyn prison guard (Giancarlo Esposito) tries to help a Haitian immigrant (Isaach de Bankole) he believes is wrongly accused of rape by paying his bail and taking him home, then turns on him when he imagines the man is after his wife (Regina Taylor). Writer-director Joe Brewster probes the psychological effects of the prison environment on its workers with some insight before opting for an overly melodramatic ending. Brief violence, several racial slurs and constant rough language

title: Keeping the Faith
synopsis: Problematic yet witty comedy about two dynamic young men of faith, one a rabbi (Ben Stiller) and the other a Catholic priest (Edward Norton) whose friendship is threatened when their childhood friend (Jenna Elfman) returns to New York, and both fall for her. Director Edward Norton's portrayal of a conflicted priest is occasionally off-putting, but his vow of celibacy and his accompanying doubts are dealt with in an earnest manner that does not undermine his priestly commitment. Questioning of priestly vows, the rabbi's affair, fleeting crass language and an instance of profanity

title: Keep On Rockin'
synopsis: Documentary of the 1969 Toronto Rock and Roll Revival features performances by Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis and Bo Didley. Made by D.A. Pennebaker, the film captures the infectious energy of the performers, and the drive of their music

title: Keep, The
synopsis: Nazi unit guarding an ancient fortress in Romania runs into some odd events in this arty, pretentious and thoroughly muddled drama of the supernatural written and directed by Michael Mann, and starring Scott Glenn and Ian McKellan. Vicious rape scene and some graphic sex

title: Keetje Tippel
synopsis: Dutch drama about a 19th-century woman, forced by her mother into prostitution to support the family, who learns from a middle-class lover how to act and dress like a lady, and eventually marries a wealthy social reformer. Director Paul Verhoeven's masterful depiction of the terrible poverty of the working class and their first stirrings of revolt are overshadowed by obsessive detailing and graphic treatment of sexual encounters

title: Kelly and Me
synopsis: Flat melodrama directed by Robert Z. Leonard tells of an ambitious vaudeville hoofer (Van Johnson) who breaks into the movies in 1930, thanks to his befriending a dog whose screen talents prove more valuable to the studio than those of his master. Formula fare of little appeal, save for those who appreciate canine antics

title: Kelly's Heroes
synopsis: Clint Eastwood and Telly Salvalas lead a group of U.S. soldiers (including Don Rickles and Donald Sutherland) 30 miles behind German lines to pull off a gold heist. Directed by Brian Hutton, the movie's premise is that all Germans are stupid, that American pragmatism is invincible and that the realities and deadly rituals of warfare make engrossing entertainment

title: Kennel Murder Case, The
synopsis: Twisty murder mystery in which S.S. Van Dine's gentleman sleuth, Philo Vance (William Powell), proves that a dead man in a room locked from the inside is no suicide, then uses a dog to trick the killer into making a confession. Directed by Michael Curtiz, the mystery is intelligently plotted and unfolds in witty fashion, with Eugene Pallette's bungling cop especially amusing. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Kentuckian, The
synopsis: Rough-hewn but unconvincing frontier tale of an 1820's backwoodsman (Burt Lancaster) torn between starting a new life in Texas with a servant girl he's rescued (Dianne Foster) or settling down in a small Kentucky town with a schooteacher (Diana Lynn). Also directed by Lancaster, the plot is a haphazard series of complications delaying the predictable choice between frontier and civilization until the final scene. Assorted violence, some of it quite nasty, and romantic complications

title: Kentucky Fried Movie, The
synopsis: Unfunny collection of sketches spoofing television and movies, especially movie trailers. Director John Landis finds vulgarity a proper source of humor but even on a simple slapstick level his satire is often tasteless and sexually exploitive

title: Kentucky Rifle
synopsis: Formula Western directed by Carl K. Hittleman has Kentucky frontiersmen (Lance Fuller and Chill Wills) save a wagon loaded with settlers and long rifles from being captured by Comanche raiders. Frontier violence

title: Kes
synopsis: British movie set in a small, drab Yorkshire coal mining town tells the story of a lonely, sullen boy (David Bradley) whose life is momentarily given meaning by his experience in raising and training a baby kestrel, a European falcon. Directed by Ken Loach, the movie is a compassionate study of the blighted conditions and brutalizing life of this youth which in its final scenes indicates the possibility of his rising above his environment. Fine experience for adults and older adolescents

title: Key Exchange
synopsis: Young novelist (Ben Masters), unsure of his feelings about a young woman (Brooke Adams), joins a friend (Dan Jenny), whose wife deserted him, in prowling the singles bar jungle before the inevitable happy ending. A very slight sex farce with little wit or charm, directed by Barnet Kellman. Nudity, graphic depiction of sex, benign view of adultery and fornication

title: Keyhole, The
synopsis: Convoluted romantic melodrama in which a cynical private detective (George Brent) is hired to shadow a rich man's wife (Kay Francis) on a trip to Cuba where, after trying some romantic ploys to test her fidelity, he falls in love with her himself. Director Michael Curtiz can't hide the holes in a plot involving a blackmailer (Monroe Owsley) threatening to expose the wife's invalid marriage, though the two principals carry off the romantic angle convincingly, with some good comic relief from Allen Jenkins and Glenda Farrell as each tries to con the other. Romantic situations and sexual innuendo

title: Key Largo
synopsis: High tension melodrama from Maxwell Anderson's play in which a hardened war veteran (Humphrey Bogart) arrives at a Florida Keys hotel to find its owner (Lionel Barrymore) and his daughter (Lauren Bacall) being held prisoner by gangsters (headed by Edward G. Robinson), then is forced to take them to Cuba by boat after a hurricane leaves them stranded. Directed by John Huston, the desperate proceedings are given conviction by a fine cast, including Claire Trevor's aging gun moll, with the outcome hinged on the veteran's regained idealism in the riveting climax. Stylized violence, menacing situations and muted sexual innuendo

title: Keys of the Kingdom, The
synopsis: Underrated adaptation of A.J. Cronin's novel about a Scottish priest (Gregory Peck) sent to China at the end of the 19th century where he rebuilds a ruined mission, endures misunderstanding, war and disease but perseveres through humility and cheerful service to win many converts and friends until retirement in Scotland fishing for supper rather than souls. Directed by John Stahl, the narrative is interestingly contrived and Peck's characterization is entirely likeable and sincere though, like so many vintage Hollywood pictures about religion, lacking much spiritual depth

title: Key, The
synopsis: Curious World War II tale in which an American skipper (William Holden) joins a squadron of British tugboats used to rescue torpedoed ships, is befriended by a veteran captain (Trevor Howard) and given a duplicate key to the apartment of a woman (Sophia Loren) who has given lodging to a succession of tugboat captains after her fiance died on a rescue mission. When his friend is killed, the American must decide whether to move in, throw away the key or pass it on to another. Director Carol Reed crafts the wartime action scenes with satisfying conviction but never quite gets a handle on the character of the sad, lonely woman who comes with the key. Wartime violence and implied cohabitation

title: Khartoum
synopsis: Exciting action adventure with modern overtones about the British involvement in the Sudan during the 19th-century pits the Empire's most famous general (Charlton Heston) against the ferocious leader of the desert tribes (Laurence Olivier). Directed by Basil Dearden, the movie has the sweep of history and some good characterizations. Stylized violence

title: Kick-Ass
synopsis: Intentionally outrageous but deeply perverse action comedy in which an ordinary high school student (Aaron Johnson) attempts to transform himself into a crusading superhero but instead becomes caught up in a feud pitting a deranged ex-police officer (Nicolas Cage) and the tween daughter (Chloe Grace Moretz) he has home-schooled as an assassin against a mob boss (Mark Strong) and his son (Christopher Mintz-Plasse), with all but the gangster assuming masked alter egos. Director and co-writer Matthew Vaughn's adaptation of Mark Millar and John S. Romita Jr.'s series of comic books fills the screen with bloody mayhem and the mouth of Moretz's blithely murderous character with cringe-inducing vulgarity. Much gory violence including torture and dismemberment, brief graphic nonmarital sexual activity and offscreen masturbation, upper female nudity, drug use, a few instances of profanity and pervasive rough and crude language

title: Kickboxer
synopsis: Belgian martial-arts whiz Jean-Claude Van Damme is pitted against a deadly Thai kickboxing champ (Tong Po) who crippled his brother in the ring. Featuring some amateurish acting, melodramatic scripting and heavy-handed direction by David Worth and Mark DiSalle, the movie is entertaining when it focuses on Van Damme's strict training sessions with a mysterious Thai mentor (Dennis Chan) but the kickboxing fight scenes are brutal. Intense ring violence and profanity

title: Kicking and Screaming
synopsis: Mostly funny, if formulaic, comedy about a timid suburban soccer dad (Will Ferrell), who seeks to redeem his unathletic childhood by coaching his 10-year-old son's last-place team and finds himself in the championship game going head-to-head with his own supercompetitive father (Robert Duvall), who coaches the league's best squad. Directed by Jesse Dylan and dominated by Ferrell's manic presence, this farce inspired by "Bad News Bears" imparts a humorous critique of our hypercompetitive culture, but deserves a penalty flag for a crass running gag which makes it questionable fare for very young viewers. Some comic violence, a minor same-sex parent theme, as well as mildly crude language and humor, including some ethnically insensitive remarks

title: Kicking and Screaming
synopsis: Self-indulgent picture of four college men who hang around campus months after graduation to mull their future while chasing co-eds, with intermittent flash-backs as one (Josh Hamilton) moons over a lost love (Olivia d'Abo). Writer-director Noah Baumbach's comic treatment of the narcissism of aimless youths shirking adult responsibilities is too superficial to be truly amusing or insightful. Sexual situations and innuendo with much mindless rough language

title: Kickin' It Old Skool
synopsis: During a school dance contest in 1986, a 5-year-old break dancer does a wrong move, ends up in a coma, and 20 years later, he wakes up as a man (Jamie Kennedy) still thinking he is a child. Harv Glazer directs with an inconsistent tone, going from sentimental to silly slapstick in a flash, and all the actors mug shamelessly, save for the dry wit of Michael Rosenbaum. Suggestive dancing, drinking, brief male rear nudity, a comic scene of cross-dressing, numerous scatological gags, a brief reference to Internet pornography, one use of the f-word, frequent crude and crass language, an instance of profanity and mild sexual banter

title: Kid Blue
synopsis: Petty outlaw (Dennis Hopper) gives up on crime to make his way honestly in the little Texas town of Dime Box, whose single industry is a ceramic novelty factory, finds honesty hard work and decides to rob the factory pay-roll. James Frawley's direction makes the most of the comic potential of an uneven script which stretches to make contemporary references to everything from the drug culture to the plight of the American Indian. Brief but explicit seduction scene

title: Kid Dynamite
synopsis: East Side Kids caper directed by Wallace Fox has bullying Muggs (Leo Gorcey) trying to outdo mild Danny (Bobby Jordan) in the boxing ring, then in a jitterbug contest, but the hapless Danny gets tired of being pushed around and joins the Army in a patriotic finish. Slapstick violence

title: Kid for Two Farthings, A
synopsis: Uneven British fable set among the residents of London's Petticoat Lane market where a boy (Jonathan Ashmore) buys a small goat with one horn, convinced it's a unicorn whose magical powers will help his friends and bring his father back from South Africa. Directed by Carol Reed from Wolf Mankowitz's novel, the narrative tries to parallel the boy's power of imagination with the changing fortunes of others (notably seamstress Diana Dors who wants her beau, bodybuilder Joe Robinson, to earn some money wrestling veteran Primo Carnera), but what works best is the tender relationship between the lad and a wise tailor (David Kosoff). Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Kid from Brooklyn, The
synopsis: Uneven musical comedy in which a meek milkman (Danny Kaye) is made to believe he's a prizefighter by a manager (Walter Abel) who pays his opponents to take a dive until left on his own in a title fight with the middleweight champ (Steve Cochran). Directed by Norman Z. McLeod, this remake of Harold Lloyd's "The Milky Way" adds some big production numbers featuring the milkman's girlfriend (Virginia Mayo) and his sister (Vera-Ellen) but the result is less funny than the original and Kaye's performance proves more irritating than amusing. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Kid from Cleveland, The
synopsis: Bumpy baseball yarn in which a troubled youth (Rusty Tamblyn) is befriended by the radio announcer (George Brent) for the Cleveland Indians who gets the team behind his efforts to keep the lad from becoming a delinquent. Directed by Herbert Kline, the contrived story often borders on the ridiculous, though what still holds interest are scenes featuring Indians' owner Bill Veeck and players Lou Boudreau, Bob Feller, Hank Greenberg, Satchel Paige and others. Stylized violence and domestic tensions

title: Kid from Left Field, The
synopsis: Corny sports fun directed by Harmon Jones in which the 9-year-old son (Billy Chapin) of a former baseball player (Dan Dailey) goes from bat boy to manager of a faltering major league club, bringing it out of the cellar and into pennant contention. Just the right speed for little leaguers, with enough heart for older members of the family willing to suspend their disbelief

title: Kid from Spain, The
synopsis: After being expelled from college for a prank in the women's dorm, an over-aged zany (Eddie Cantor) winds up in Mexico helping a friend (Robert Young) by masquerading as the son of a famous bullfighter. Director Leo McCarey wrings some laughs from predictable situations, aided by a good cast and inventive Busby Berkeley production numbers. Some sexual innuendo and comic menace

title: Kid from Texas, The
synopsis: Routine account of Billy the Kid (Audie Murphy) begins in 1879 Lincoln, New Mexico, where he's hired as a ranch hand by an Englishman (Sheppherd Strudwick) who's murdered in a range war leaving Billy a hunted man until killed at age 21 by Sheriff Pat Garrett (Frank Wilcox). Director Kurt Neumann's shoot-'em-up fails to work up much sympathy for this vengeful, hot-tempered youth who died with 21 notches in his gun. Numerous shoot-outs and muted sexual innuendo

title: Kid Galahad
synopsis: In this remake of the 1936 original, a young auto mechanic (Elvis Presley) is turned into a prizefighter by a needy promoter (Gig Young), then falls for the man's sister (Joan Blackman). Directed by Phil Karlson, Presley is unconvincing as a boxer but is otherwise likeable as an earnest fellow who wants to make enough money to wed and open his own auto shop. Mild fight scenes and romantic complications

title: Kid in King Arthur's Court, A
synopsis: Magically transported from his Southern California baseball field to 12th-century Camelot, a timid teenager (Thomas Ian Nicholas) finds the inner resources to rescue King Arthur's daughters (Paloma Baeza and Kate Winslet) from a villainous usurper (Art Malik). Director Michael Gottlieb's unimaginative fantasy-adventure strings together a sluggish series of routine obstacles for the lad to overcome, often with 20th-century gizmos from his backpack. Minor violence

title: Kid Millions
synopsis: Vintage Eddie Cantor musical follows him to Egypt to claim a fortune left by his archeologist father, but along the way he has to fend off an assortment of other claimants (Ethel Merman, Warren Hymer, Ann Sothern and George Murphy). Directed by Roy Del Ruth, the plot is sappy and the songs forgettable but it's a lot of silly fun, including the final reel with Eddie's ice cream factory in Technicolor. Some stylized violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Kidnapped
synopsis: Melodramatic adaptation of Robert Louis Stevenson's tale of an 18th-century orphaned youth (Freddie Bartholomew) befriended by a Scottish rebel (Warner Baxter) who tries to help the lad gain his stolen inheritance while fighting the English. Director Alfred L. Werker's good vintage cast (John Carradine, C. Aubrey Smith, Nigel Bruce and Reginald Owen) keep the adventure exciting, if not quite what Stevenson had mind. Stylized violence

title: Kidnapped
synopsis: Low-budget version of Robert Louis Stevenson's classic adventure in 18th-century Scotland with William Beaudine directing Roddy McDowall as the wronged youth and Dan O'Herlihy as the anti-English rebel in a generally lackluster production. Stylized violence

title: Kidnapped
synopsis: Disney version of the Robert Louis Stevenson adventure classic about a 18th-century Scottish youth (James MacArthur) done out of his inheritance and sold into servitude as a cabin boy by his treacherous uncle, then rescued by a dashing Jacobite rebel (Peter Finch) during the course of his battles with the English. Director Robert Stevenson is faithful the spirit of the original, though some of the action may be a bit too intense for the pre-teen crowd. Stylized violence

title: Kidnapping of the President, The
synopsis: South American terrorist (Miguel Fernandes), laden with dynamite, handcuffs himself to the President of the United States (Hal Holbrook) but the villains are no match for the head of the Secret Service (William Shatner). Canadian director George Mendeluk's routine suspense thriller features unnecessarily graphic violence in the opening sequence

title: Kid Rodelo
synopsis: Passable melodrama about a drifter (Don Murray) who is forced to protect a young woman (Janet Leigh) from a rough band of former convicts who are looking for gold. Director Richard Carlson moderates the violence in favor of the action adventure

title: Kids
synopsis: A day in the so-called life of a group of feral inner-city youths shows them to be aimless dropouts from home, school and the human race as they pass the time in pursuit of sex, drugs, cheap booze, petty larceny and outbursts of violence. Director Larry Clark uses a lot of hand-held camera shots in filming a cast of adolescent non-actors in New York locations but manages to bring no sense of reality, let alone insight or perspective, to tawdry situations which never develop beyond surface sensationalism. Exploitative treatment of sex, violence, substance abuse and rough language

title: Kids Are Alright, The
synopsis: Performance and interview film featuring the antics and music of the British rock group, The Who. Director Jeff Stein's poorly organized documentary is marked by very little revelation, some vulgar language and sexual references

title: Kids in the Hall Brain Candy
synopsis: Canadian comedy troupe brings its TV antics to the big screen in a half-baked spoof of a pharmaceutical firm rushing an anti-depression pill to market before testing its side effects. Directed by Kelly Makin, the result is a hodgepodge of weak skits relying on males in drag, ludicrous situations and frequent bad taste. Sexual innuendo, rear nudity, occasional profanity and recurring rough language

title: Kika
synopsis: Strained sex farce about a ditzy hairdresser (Veronica Forque), her lovers, a rapist, a talk show host (Victoria Abril) and a serial killer. Director Pedro Almodovar never strays far from the sexual eccentricities of his surreal characters in this tiresome, unamusing send-up of rape and mass murder. Subtitles. Some graphic sexual encounters, flippant treatment of rape, much nudity, several gory murders and rough language

title: Kill a Dragon
synopsis: Run-of-the-mill action adventure movie set in the Orient with contrived plot and unbelievable scenes of bravado. Directed by Michael Moore, it follows a predictable course of sex and violence

title: Kill and Kill Again
synopsis: Martial arts master (James Ryan) is hired to rescue a scientist from the clutches of a villain who wants to control the world in this slapdash, simple-minded melodrama produced in South Africa. Directed by Ivan Hall, the movie's violence is far less fierce than the accompanying grunts and groans

title: Kill Bill Vol. 1
synopsis: Ultraviolent tale about a female former assassin (Uma Thurman) gunned down and left for dead on her wedding day, who wakes up from a four-year coma revved up to exact revenge on her would-be killers -- the same hit squad which had previously employed her services. Buckets of blood flow in this first installment of Quentin Tarantino's mayhem-mired two-part opus, a film which, despite its slick pulp-noir veneer, is fueled by a sadistic killing-is-cool mentality that packages gratuitous gore as entertainment. Excessive graphic violence, twisted sexual references, as well as much rough and crude language and profanity

title: Kill Bill Vol. 2
synopsis: Violent and vapid continuation of director Quentin Tarantino's sanguinary saga about a former female assassin (Uma Thurman) gunned down at her wedding rehearsal and left for dead by the assassin circle she had once been a member of, led by her former boss-lover, Bill (David Carradine). She has already dispatched two of her former hit squad associates in the first film; the second installment follows her on a roaring rampage of revenge as she slices and dices her way through her two remaining would-be killers, working her way up the chain of command in order to -- what else? -- kill Bill. While the more dialogue-driven "Vol. 2" is not as bloody as its much gorier predecessor, the superficiality of its hip, highly stylized savagery promotes a video-game attitude toward violence which seems to say killing is cool and, despite its pulp cinema references and flashes of visual brilliance, is fueled by a revenge-driven theme incompatible with the Christian understanding of forgiveness. Recurring gratuitous scenes of violence, much rough and crude language and drug content

title: Killer Ape
synopsis: Formula jungle adventure directed by Spencer G. Bennet in which Jungle Jim (Johnny Weissmuller) gets some help from a wild apeman (Ray Corrigan) in stopping foreign agents (led by Nestor Paiva) from using animals to experiment on a drug that destroys "the will to resist." Stylized violence

title: Killer Bats
synopsis: ( see: "The Devil Bat" )

title: Killer Elite, The
synopsis: James Caan and Robert Duvall give fine performances as professional assassins working for a secret government agency in a suspense drama directed by Sam Peckinpah. Though flawed and lapsing into melodrama at times, the film raises questions of undercover agencies. Some brutal violence

title: Killer Force
synopsis: Peter Fonda plays the leader of a raid on the vaults of a diamond mine in South Africa and after much muddlement escapes with the loot. Directed by Val Guest, the plot twists in this movie are so arbitrary that they are not worth following. Excessive gory violence

title: Killer Grizzly
synopsis: ( see: "Grizzly" )

title: Killer Klowns from Outer Space
