synopsis: Pop concert documentary with Mick Jagger and crew at their slightly satanic but self-parodying best. Directed by former ad man Rollin Binzer, it is bright, swift and irresistable for adult rock fans

title: Ladies' Day
synopsis: Lightweight comedy about a baseball pitcher (Eddie Albert) who's no good on the mound after marrying an impulsive movie star (Lupe Velez) in the middle of a pennant race, forcing teammates and their wives (notably Patsy Kelly and Iris Adrian) to take bizarre measures in keeping the newlyweds apart until after the world series. Director Leslie Goodwins tries for the daffy tone of a Ring Lardner story but the mildly comic proceedings are strictly slapstick. Brief violence and romantic situations

title: Ladies' Man, The
synopsis: Uneven farce with Jerry Lewis playing a klutzy handyman in a mansion which its owner (opera singer Helen Traubel) has turned into a women's school for aspiring performers. Also directed and co-written by Lewis, the self-indulgent exercise juggles an erratic mix of sightgags, pratfalls, spoofs and double-takes, but Lewis' tiresome mugging gets fewer laughs than Kathleen Freeman's cheerful performance as the mansion's dizzy maid. For Lewis fans

title: Ladies of Leisure
synopsis: Pedestrian tearjerker in which a gold digger (Barbara Stanwyck) is reformed by a love-struck artist (Ralph Graves) whose rich family persuades her to give him up, then fate takes a hand. Directed by Frank R. Capra, the creaky plot is strictly formula fare, but the breezy characters add some period vitality and Stanwyck manages to make the most of her role as a hustler redeemed by love. Sexual situations, drunken parties and a suicide attempt

title: Ladies of the Chorus
synopsis: Lame sudser in which an aging burlesque queen (Adele Jergens) turns her daughter (Marilyn Monroe) into the show's star, then warns her against marrying a wealthy admirer (Rand Brooks) because she knows from bitter experience that burlesque and high society don't mix. Directed by Phil Karlson, the pedestrian plot is drearily predictable in a picture notable only as Monroe's first starring role. Sour view of marriage and considerable sexual innuendo

title: Ladies They Talk About
synopsis: Prison melodrama in which a gang moll (Barbara Stanwyck) winds up in San Quentin because of a reformer (Preston Foster) who's sweet on her, then gets out determined to kill him but love conquers all. Directed by Howard Bretherton, the romantic angle is pure hokum but what still holds interest is its seriocomic depiction of life in a women's prison whose inmates include singer Lillian Roth and wisecracking Ruth Donnelly among the guards. Benign view of criminal activities, off-screen violence and romantic complications

title: La Discrete
synopsis: A wily publisher (Maurice Garrel) convinces a self-important writer (Fabrice Luchini) to select a woman at random, make her (Judith Henry) fall in love with him, at which point he will seduce and abandon her, turning over the intimate details for publication. French director Christian Vincent's mildly comic movie is a sluggish, talky affair peppered with small charms along the way, primarily in Ms. Henry's gently dignified performance. Subtitles. An unmarried sexual relationship and several promiscuous references

title: La Dolce Vita
synopsis: Lengthy episodic Italian drama about a troubled journalist (Marcello Mastroianni) who mingles in the circles of Rome's high society (including Anita Ekberg, Anouk Aimee and Alain Cuny), alternately fascinated, bemused and repelled by what he observes. Director Federico Fellini's crowded picture of the moral ills as well as the human foibles and positive values of various segments of Italian soicety mixes realism with satire and a tragic sense of wasted lives. Subtitles. Critical treatment of immoral situations

title: Lady and the Tramp
synopsis: Walt Disney's animated feature about a cute little cocker spaniel in a Victorian family who loses her place in the couple's affections with the birth of their first child but who is reinstated through the efforts of a freedom-loving mongrel. The cast of lovable dog characters and some delightful songs by Peggy Lee still appeal to youngsters

title: Lady at Midnight
synopsis: Lackluster mystery directed by Sherman Scott in which a couple (Richard Denning and Frances Rafferty) discovers someone wants to get custody of their adopted daughter and is willing to kill anyone who interferes. tylized violence and sexual implications

title: Lady Beware
synopsis: A window dresser (Diane Lane), with a penchant for the erotic, decides to turn the tables on a psychotic admirer who terrifies her. Director Karen Arthur's clumsy chiller relies heavily on male and female nudity rather than developing any feminist insights

title: Ladybird Ladybird
synopsis: Blistering portrait of a loving but violent-tempered unwed mother of four (Crissy Rock) whose children are taken from her when British authorities deem her an unfit parent, only to do the same when she has two children by a caring foreigner (Vladimir Vega) who has taken her in. Director Ken Loach's superbly acted, fact-based examination of a flawed bureaucratic system compounded by a woman who is her own worst enemy is emotionally heart-rending and intellectually challenging, though the narrative lacks any insight into why she fails to learn from past mistakes. Troubling theme of unwed motherhood, brief but intense violence and constant rough language

title: Ladybugs
synopsis: A salesman (Rodney Dangerfield) whose promotion depends on successfully coaching his company-sponsored all-girls soccer team gets his fiancee's son (Jonathan Brandis) to play disguised as a girl in order to ensure a winning season. Sidney J. Furie directs a genial sports comedy peppered with Dangerfield's snappy one-liners. Mild sexual innuendo and double entendres

title: Lady Caroline Lamb
synopsis: Robert Bolt wrote and directed this vehicle for Sarah Miles about a high-born but promiscuous lady who consorts with poets and other male playthings during the early 19th century. Miles' non-acting is complemented by Richard Chamberlain's non-limping parody of Byron, and the sincere efforts of Jon Finch as her stoical husband Willie cannot offset the movie's overall absurdity. Brief nudity

title: Lady Chatterley's Lover
synopsis: French director Just Jaeckin's skin-deep adaptation of the D.H. Lawrence novel, with Sylvia Kristel and Nicholas Clay, is a dulling exercise in commercial eroticism. Graphic sex

title: Lady Eve, The
synopsis: Playful romantic comedy in which a con artist (Barbara Stanwyck) falls for a millionaire's guileless son (Henry Fonda) but when he breaks with her, she seeks revenge by visiting his father's Long Island estate masquerading as a British aristocrat's daughter. Writer-director Preston Sturges centers the comedy on the attraction of opposites as the socially inept Fonda is hopelessly confused by the sophisticated Stanwyck in a series of ridiculous situations held together by a splendid supporting cast (Charles Coburn, Eugene Pallette, William Demerest and Eric Blore). Romantic complications with some sexual situations

title: Lady for a Day
synopsis: Cheerfully sentimental comedy from the Damon Runyon story about an aging Broadway apple seller (May Robson) who gets help from a dapper crook (Warren William) and a phony judge (Guy Kibbee) in masquerading as a wealthy socialite when her convent-educated daughter (Jean Parker) arrives from Spain with her fiance. Director Frank Capra mixes the pathos of the Depression-era situation with plenty of comic zest provided by an odd assortment of New York types ranging from underworld thugs to high society swells as the improbable proceedings turn big-city cynics into fancy do-gooders. An elaborate deception and mild sexual innuendo

title: Lady Frankenstein
synopsis: When her fanatic father (Joseph Cotten) dies at the hands of the demented creature he created, his daughter (Sara Bey) vows to create a perfect superman to destroy her father's murderer. Unfortunately in this Italian penny-dreadful directed by Mel Welles, she has to seduce her subjects for surgery and graphic sex sequences only detract from the blood-drenched horror fantasy

title: Lady from Cheyenne, The
synopsis: Uneven romantic comedy set in Wyoming after the Civil War when a schoolteacher (Loretta Young), infuriated by her town's corrupt boss (Edward Arnold), tricks the new legislature into giving women the right to vote. Directed by Frank Lloyd, the unlikely tale involves the schoolmarm's love-hate relationship with the smooth lawyer (Robert Preston) fronting for the villain, though the movie undercuts the theme of women's rights by ending with the heroine vowing to become a meek housewife. Frontier violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Lady from Louisiana, The
synopsis: Routine melodrama directed by Bernard Vorhaus in which a crusading lawyer (John Wayne) is brought to pre-Civil War New Orleans to battle the wealthy group controlling the city's popular lottery, then falls for the daughter (Ona Munson) of one of them. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Lady Gambles, The
synopsis: Hokey cautionary tale directed by Michael Gordon recounts the downward spiral of the troubled wife (Barbara Stanwyck) of a Chicago newspaperman (Preston Foster) after a visit to Las Vegas turns her into a compulsive gambler who gets mixed up with a big-time operator (Stephen McNally), then hits the skids. Psychological tension and domestic misunderstandings

title: Lady Godiva
synopsis: Historical charade set in 11th-century England where a Saxon earl (George Nader) is imprisoned for battling Norman intriguers in the court of Edward the Confessor (Eduard Franz), but is freed when wife Godiva (Maureen O'Hara) proves Saxon fidelity by taking her famed bare-but-for-her-hair ride through the streets of Coventry. Director Arthur Lubin's shallow costume melodrama is a frivolous exercise in popular history. Period violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Lady Godiva of Coventry
synopsis: ( see: "Lady Godiva" )

title: Lady Hamilton
synopsis: ( see: "That Hamilton Woman" )

title: Ladyhawke
synopsis: Medieval sword-and-sorcery epic looks beautiful but tells a silly story of a curse which changes two true 1overs into a hawk (Michelle Pfeiffer) and a wolf (Rutger Hauer). Directed by Richard Donner, it is rife with bad dialogue, bad acting and anachronisms. Aside from some violent swordplay, it is innocuous

title: Lady Ice
synopsis: Middling diamond heist caper in which an insurance investigator (Donald Sutherland) gets involved with a diamond fence (Jennifer O'Neill) and a hard-bitten U.S. Justice Department agent (Robert Duvall) who adds a bit of class but his scenes get lost in the shuffle. Directed by Tom Gries, the complex, and at times, confusing plot doesn't add up to much

title: Lady in a Cage
synopsis: Sadistic exercise in urban violence opens with an ailing widow (Olivia de Havilland) spending the July 4th week-end alone until an electrical outage traps her in the house elevator while her wealthy home is robbed by street people (Jeff Corey and Ann Sothern) and her life threatened by a trio of punks (led by James Caan). Directed by Walter Grauman, the menace escalates in nastiness until the woman's struggle for survival becomes as barbaric as the acts of her attackers. Cynical treatment undermines its pretensions as social commentary

title: Lady in Cement
synopsis: Hard-boiled private detective (Frank Sinatra) gets involved in the murder of a woman in the title but director Gordon Douglas provides neither credibility nor atmosphere in the rambling, loosely plotted proceedings that create an ersatz excitement only by resorting to brutal violence and some sleazy sexual distractions

title: Lady in Question, The
synopsis: Muddled tale set in France where a shopkeeper (Brian Aherne) called to serve on a murder case convinces his fellow jurors that the accused (Rita Hayworth) is innocent, then gives her a job in his shop, but comes to believe the worst when his son (Glenn Ford) falls for her. Directed by Charles Vidor, the sketchy characters and ambiguous situations fail to achieve the comic pathos intended and the sunny ending is particularly flat. Sexual innuendo

title: Lady in the Car with Glasses and a Gun, The
synopsis: Failed mystery thriller in which Samantha Eggar takes a holiday drive in the South of France and, after a number of puzzling incidents happen to her, she discovers a body in the trunk of the car she got from her boss (sinister Oliver Reed). Director Anatole Litvak goes overboard trying to create some suspense but the result of all his efforts is no more than pure cleverness and empty contrivance. Some adult mayhem

title: Lady in the Dark
synopsis: Lame screen version of the Moss Hart musical about a fashion magazine editor (Ginger Rogers) who gets help from a psychoanalyst (Barry Sullivan) in resolving her troubled relations with a married man (Warner Baxter), a movie star (Jon Hall) and an irritating associate (Ray Milland). Directed by Mitchell Leisen, the halting proceedings are short on wit and imagination, with charmless production numbers and a couple of Kurt Weill-Ira Gerschwin songs which don't help matters much. Sexual situations and innuendo

title: Lady in the Lake
synopsis: Hard-boiled private eye Philip Marlowe (Robert Montgomery) is hired to find the missing wife of a publisher (Leon Ames) in a twisty case involving the man's business associate (Audrey Totter), a devious cop (Lloyd Nolan) and a mystery woman (Jayne Meadows). Also directed by Montgomery from the Raymond Chandler novel, the picture is memorable for the camera taking Marlowe's place, filming events as if seen through his eyes, with the actor seen only in mirror shots, but the result isn't helped by a confusing plot, the Christmas setting and phony cynical tone. Stylized violence, menacing situations and veiled sexual innuendo

title: Lady in the Water
synopsis: Atmospheric but unconvincing fairy tale about members of a suburban Philadelphia housing complex (Paul Giamatti, Jeffrey Wright, Bill Irwin, Bob Balaban) who -- harking back to mythic times when humans and water creatures were friends -- attempt to return a nymph (Bryce Dallas Howard) to the sea, while pursued by wolf-like beasts. Director-writer M. Night Shyamalan provides some trademark scary moments with admirably little overt violence, and the universal brotherhood theme is unarguably a noble one, but this aquatic "E.T." retread isn't terribly compelling despite skillful direction and solid performances. Some scenes of intense peril, suggested nudity

title: Lady in White
synopsis: Supernatural thriller about a small-town boy (Lukas Haas) who comes face to face with the ghost of a girl murdered 10 years before as well as with her murderer. With breathtaking special effects and cinematography, director Frank LaLoggia's unique fantasy attains wonderful interplay between the boy, his family and the ghosts in a lovely re-creation of life in 1962. Graphic violence directed toward children and some particularly chilling supernatural occurrences

title: Lady Jane
synopsis: The innocence and altruism of youth are contrasted with the deceit and treachery of the adult world in this period drama about the religious power struggle following the reign of King Henry VIII. Its romantic treatment of adult themes contains a brief scene of nudity and a brutal scene of f1ogging

title: Ladykillers, The
synopsis: Droll British comedy in which a daffy gang of crooks (Alec Guinness, Cecil Parker, Herbert Lom, Peter Sellers and Danny Green) take a London flat as their hideout while planning a big heist until their sweet old landlady (Katie Johnson) innocently gums up the works. Director Alexander Mackendrick rings in the comic changes adroitly, going from whimsical to black comedy as the bumbling thieves try to murder the old woman but wind up killing each other instead, then topping it off with a wryly innocent conclusion. Comic treatment of violence and criminal activities

title: Lady L
synopsis: Tasteless British comedy set in 1920's Europe stars Sophia Loren and under Peter Ustinov's direction is excessive in its sexual emphasis

title: Lady Liberty
synopsis: When Sophia Loren flies into JFK Airport to rejoin her fiance, she has a 20-pound mortadella sausage under her arm and the crisis this causes at Customs promises one of those coarse peasant comedies the Italians do so well. Unfortunately, director Mario Monticelli presents a freak show of grisly New York stereotypes in a cynical blend of contempt, distrust and generally low opinion of humanity

title: Lady of Burlesque
synopsis: Tepid Hollywood cheesecake is mixed with corny jokes as a not-very-exotic dancer (Barbara Stanwyck) teams with a not-very-funny comic (Michael O'Shea) to solve two backstage murders in a ramshackle burlesque theater. Directed by William A. Wellman from Gypsy Rose Lee's novel, "The G-String Murders," the search for the killer plays second fiddle to the picture's sentimental hokum about good-hearted strippers. Some stylized violence and much sexual innuendo

title: Lady of Monza, The
synopsis: Sordid Italian melodrama supposedly based on a 17th-century incident in which the lover of a Spanish nun was beheaded and she was walled up alive. Directed by Eriprando Visconti, the movie's production values are as minimal as its ludicrous nude love scenes

title: Lady on the Tracks, The
synopsis: Czechoslovakian musical fantasy about a lady streetcar driver in Prague (Jirina Bohdalova) who mounts a campaign for women's rights when she discovers her husband's love affair. Directed by Ladislav Rychman, its musical numbers are done in 1930's Hollywood style and the result is a warm and humorous tale of one woman's dreams of glory

title: Lady Says No, The
synopsis: Comedy clunker in which a feminist author (Joan Caulfield) repudiates her anti-male best-seller after she falls for a suave photographer (David Niven) who ridicules her lack of romantic experience. Directed by Frank Ross, the clumsy script gets few laughs from heavy-handed plot twists transforming the prim author into a calculating vamp. Sexist humor

title: Lady Scarface
synopsis: Routine crime melodrama directed by Frank Woodruff in which a Chicago cop (Dennis O'Keefe) trails a gang of robbers (notably Arthur Shields and Marc Lawrence) to New York City, then nabs its notorious boss (Judith Anderson) with the aid of a photographer (Frances Neal). Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Lady Sings the Blues
synopsis: Diana Ross stars as Billie Holiday in a screen biography that reduces the famous singer's life to a series of cliches and soap opera theatrics. A very good performance by Ross can't save director Sidney J. Furie's failed movie. Rough language and sordid situations

title: Lady Takes a Chance, A
synopsis: Breezy romantic comedy in which a New York tourist (Jean Arthur) falls for a genial rodeo cowboy (John Wayne), then pursues him despite his avowed intention to remain a bachelor, with amusingly predictable results. Director William A. Seiter gets good-natured performances from the two leads as they mix romantic situations with rough-and-tumble comedy, helped along the way by a good supporting cast (especially Charles Winninger and Phil Silvers). Comic violence and romantic complications

title: Lady Takes a Flyer, The
synopsis: Predictably bumpy romance directed by Jack Arnold in which a lady aviator (Lana Turner) marries a hotshot pilot (Jeff Chandler) who gets so wrapped up in trying to build his own airline that he neglects wife and child, with predictable results. Domestic tensions and sexual situations

title: Lady Vanishes, The
synopsis: Mystery classic in which a kind old lady (Dame May Whitty) abruptly disappears from a train traveling through Central Europe without anyone noticing until a frantic search by fellow passengers (Margaret Lockwood and Michael Redgrave) uncovers a ring of secret agents (led by Paul Lukas). Director Alfred Hitchcock leavens the mystery's suspense with some keen humor (notably Basil Radford and Naunton Wayne as woolly English travelers) and rich characterizations by a fine British cast (not least of which is Catherine Lacey as a counterfeit nun). Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Lady with the Dog, The
synopsis: Russian production of Anton Chekhov's short story about a married Moscow banker (Alexei Batalov) vacationing in Yalta where he has a brief affair with an unhappily married woman (Iya Savinna), then can't forget her after returning home to wife and children, but when they meet again in Moscow, both realize their future prospects are doomed. Director Josef Heifits charts the course of infidelity from passionate yearnings to anguished aftermath without any bedroom scenes, relying instead on depicting the characters' inner turmoil underscored by evocative photography of period locales and the dreary emptiness of middle-class life. Discreet treatment of an adulterous relationship

title: Lady Yakuza
synopsis: Japanese gangster movie in which a young woman (Junko Fuji) takes over the leadership of a gang after her father's murder and ultimately is able to avenge his death. Directed by Kosaku Yamashita, there is plenty of violence but used within a context of group loyalty and personal friendship

title: Lafayette Escadrille
synopsis: In this lame tribute to Americans who flew for France during World War I, a troublesome rich enlistee (Tab Hunter) escapes imprisonment after slugging a French officer, then is hidden by his lover (Etchika Choureau) until the U.S. enters the war and he joins the American air force. Directed by former Escadrille pilot William A. Wellman, the result is disappointingly thin on action and characterization, with only the final sequence providing a full-scale re-creation of biplanes in aerial combat. Wartime violence and sexual situations

title: La Femme Infidele
synopsis: French director Claude Chabrol manages to generate suspense with many layers of tension, ambiguity and passion seething under a placid surface. Here he examines the apparently happy suburban marriage of insurance man Michel Bouquet and wife Stephane Audran but the husband's growing suspicions of his wife's infidelity are confirmed and he confronts and kills the other man (Maurice Ronet). Though Chabrol's style is coolly detached, viewers will be caught up in an inquiry into the human potential for evil

title: La Femme Nikita
synopsis: A convicted killer (Anne Parillaud) working as an assassin for the French government wants out when she falls for an innocent store clerk (Jean-Hughes Anglade). Writer-director Luc Besson's sleek action thriller goes somewhat overboard on violence during the protaganist's journey to redemption via the healing power of love. Subtitles. Some grisly violence, a live-in relationship, flash of nudity and occasional rough language

title: La Fuga
synopsis: Italian dramatization of the psychiatric treatment of a disturbed 27-year-old wife whose marital problems are related to latent lesbian tendencies. Directed by Paolo Spinola, the effort is well-intentioned but the graphic treatment of several sexual scenes is excessively explicit

title: La Grande Illusion
synopsis: ( see: "Grand Illusion" )

title: La Grande Vadrouille
synopsis: ( see: 1969's "Don't Look Now" )

title: Lair of the White Worm, The
synopsis: Director Ken Russell's update of a 1911 Bram Stoker novel has a vampire (Amanda Donohoe) lure humans into the lair of an ancient serpent still living in an English town with two sisters (Catherine Oxenberg and Sammi Davis) as key targets. The satiric elements are diluted by Russell's fascination with sexual debauch, involving dream sequences of the blood-splattered rape of nuns by pagan soldiers in front of a serpent-draped cross. Explicit sexual seduction, fleeting nudity and intense vampire attacks

title: Lake City
synopsis: Atmospheric family drama in which a young man (Troy Garity) targeted by a criminal (Dave Matthews) escapes to his rural childhood home with his girlfriend's son (Colin Ford) and reconnects with his estranged mother (Sissy Spacek). Though their script contains considerable salty dialogue and deals with some gritty subjects, co-writers and directors Hunter Hill and Perry Moore craft a hopeful tale of reconciliation and rediscovered values further enhanced by skillful performances. Beatings, moderate gun violence, drug theme, implied cohabitation, a character born out of wedlock, much rough and crude language, and a few uses of profanity

title: Lake Placid
synopsis: Lame horror-comedy in which a big-city paleontologist (Bridget Fonda), a wealthy eccentric (Oliver Platt) and an earnest game warden (Bill Pullman) insist on helping a skeptical rural sheriff (Brendan Gleeson) catch a huge crocodile that has devoured a few locals. Directed by Steve Miner from David E. Kelley's contrived script, the movie offers sparse spurts of comic mileage with suspense equally absent. Some predatory violence with decapitations, sex references, occasional profanity and intermittent rough language

title: La Lectrice
synopsis: French literary comedy in which a woman (Miou-Miou) fantasizes that she is the heroine of a novel about a woman who makes a living as a professional reader. Directed by Michel Deville, the dual role leads to some delightful vignettes about the woman's interaction with her eccentric clients and the literary works she deems suitable for each. The charm wears off, however, when she becomes both reader and sex surrogate to a frustrated client. Several gratuitous sexual encounters

title: La Mandragola
synopsis: Italian adaptation of a Machiavellian satire whose theme is adultery and whose treatment is steeped in prurience and cynicism is unrelieved by any redeeming qualities

title: Lamb
synopsis: Distraught over his father's death and the punitive atmosphere at the Irish school for troubled boys where he teaches, a Christian Brother (Liam Neeson) flees to England with a 10-year-old student (Hugh O' Conor) he wants to help, but is unprepared to deal with the boy's debilitating epileptic seizures. Director Colin Gregg's frail story summons up much sympathy for the vulnerable boy and the plight of the well-intended brother whose initial mistake of kidnapping the child ultimately has tragic consequences. Brief violence borne of despair and some rough language

title: Lambada
synopsis: High school math teacher (J. Eddie Peck) moonlights in an East Los Angeles barrio disco where he dances and educates young Latinos so they can pass their high school equivalency exams. Director Joel Silberg plays up the gyrations of the scantily clad female dancers as well as a student's lust for her teacher in this cut-and-paste exploitation of adolescent male sexual fantasies. Much sexual innuendo and vulgar language

title: Lamerica
synopsis: Eager to make a fortune in post-communist Albania, an Italian con man (Enrico Lo Verso) sets up a phony scheme involving a confused old man (Carmelo Di Mazzarelli) who spent 50 years as a political prisoner, then becomes ashamed of exploiting the elderly man's simple love and trust. Director Gianni Amelio's moving human drama strikes a universal chord both in its small-scale story of the two men and in the larger picture of impoverished Albanians desperate for a better life abroad. Subtitles. Occasional rough language

title: L'Amour
synopsis: Andy Warhol's counterculture denizens flutter around Paris in this generally vapid put-on which Warhol co-directed with Paul Morrissey. In tune with Warhol's philosophy, the camerawork is grainy, the color is anemic and the parade of verbal and visual vulgarities is constant

title: Lancelot of the Lake
synopsis: French director Robert Bresson takes the Arthurian legend and interprets it in austere realistic fashion, focusing on the decline of the Knights of the Round Table after their failure in the quest of the Grail. His treatment purges the legend of its magic and romance, searching for some historical substance which for some will have more interest than the story. Subtitles. Some realistic violence

title: Lancer Spy
synopsis: World War I tale of a British agent (George Sanders) arriving in Berlin in the place of a lookalike captured German spy and using a beautiful woman (Delores Del Rio) as an unwitting accomplice in ferreting out war secrets. Director Gregory Ratoff builds the cat-and-mouse suspense as the agent arouses the growing suspicions of the German military (Peter Lorre, Joseph Schildkraut and others). Implausible but diverting enough espionage thriller

title: Land and Freedom
synopsis: Joining the communist-backed republican forces in their fight against Franco's fascist-backed army in the 1936 Spanish Civil War, an idealistic young Brit (Ian Hart) becomes disllusioned by the violent in-fighting among the Stalinists and their peasant allies. Director Ken Loach re-creates the struggle with documentary-like intensity, dramatizing the view that political treachery by the communists undermined the republican cause. Battlefield violence, sexual references and much rough language

title: Land Before Time, The
synopsis: Delightful animated feature about the exploits of five young dinosaurs of differing species who band together for survival. Plagued by hunger and threats from meat-eating dinos, the leaf-eating tykes make their way to the Great Valley for food. Director Don Bluth offers some cute little characters, quality animation and a lovely message of solidarity and courage. A brief, nicely handled sequence of a mother dino's death

title: Landlord, The
synopsis: Rich young man (Beau Bridges) becomes a ghetto landlord in some vague hope that by renovating a decaying Brooklyn brownstone, tenanted by justly suspicious blacks, he can rebuild his empty life. Directed by Hal Ashby, the seriocomic drama has some good performances (Diana Sands and Lou Gossett) and lyric photography but lacks depth and coherence. Interesting failure with some mature themes

title: Land of the Blind
synopsis: Disappointing and sadly misguided political satire about jailed playwright turned terrorist (Donald Sutherland), who upon release from prison assassinates the petty tyrant (Tom Hollander) of the unnamed country, and then imposes a repressive regime of his own, turning on even the idealistic military man (Ralph Fiennes) who helped pull off the coup. Writer-director Robert Edwards attempts to leaven the grim tale with some sardonic humor, and Fiennes delivers his accustomed superlative performance, but the cautionary points about the corrupting of power, with no doubt several contemporary parallels in mind, are fairly standard beneath some cinematic flash, while the nonstop expletives and occasional sexual elements seem gratuitous. Pervasive rough language and crude expressions, some profanity and irreligiosity, sexual situations and partial nudity, violence and brutality, and gratuitous scatological elements

title: Land of the Dead
synopsis: Repulsively violent fourth (and let's hope final) chapter in director George A. Romero's pulp zombie saga set in an apocalyptic near-future where what is left of humanity is holed up in a in a class-divided, fortified city lorded over by a ruthless opportunist (Dennis Hopper) and besieged by an army of newly sentient undead, with only a band of mercenaries (Simon Baker and John Leguizamo) standing between survival and total zombification. While the zombies have "evolved," the campy horror franchise remains a smor-gores-bord of stomach-churning mayhem, despite pretensions of social satire. Pervasive bloody violence and gore, including graphic dismemberment and cannibalism, some sexual content with brief partial nudity, some drug content, a same-sex kiss, recurring rough and crude language, as well as some profanity

title: Land of the Pharaohs
synopsis: Uneven tale in which a ruler of ancient Egypt (Jack Hawkins) forces a captive architect (James Robertson Justice) to build a great pyramid housing a tomb that proves spacious enough not only for the pharaoh but also for his greedy, treacherous second wife (Joan Collins). Director Howard Hawks turns in an historical spectacle on a scale far grander than required for the soap opera antics of a conniving royal golddigger. Stylized violence and sexual situations

title: Land Raiders
synopsis: Telly Savalas plays a loud, overbearing rancher who stirs up trouble with a local Indian tribe, is discovered to have killed his brother's girl and gets his just desserts when the Indians go on the warpath. Directed by Nathan Juran, it's a poorly done Western with some gory violence and sexual references

title: Landscape after Battle
synopsis: Polish drama directed by Andrzej Wajda is a compilation of short stories by Tadeusz Borowski, survivor of Auschwitz and suicide victim. Some brief nudity, but the somberness of the theme makes this a movie for mature viewers

title: Landscape in the Mist
synopsis: Two runaways, a girl (Tania Palaiologou) and her little brother (Michalis Zeke) hitchhike and sneak onboard trains all across Greece in a pitiful attempt to reach Germany where they seek the father they have never seen. Director Theo Angelopoulos' film is rich in striking imagery and symbolism but its ponderous pace and theme of innocents set adrift in a world of mostly hostile adults is a decidedly downbeat experience. Greek production with English subtitles. Offscreen rape of the girl

title: Land That Time Forgot, The
synopsis: Doug McClure, John McEnery and Susan Penhaligon are among the survivors of a World War I U-boat attack who find themselves in a strange land filled with prehistoric beasts. Routine British fantasy adventure directed by Kevin Connor. Restrained violence

title: Land Unknown, The
synopsis: When a Navy helicopter crash-lands in a fog-enshrouded valley in Antarctica, its commander (Jock Mahoney), two crew members and a woman reporter (Shawn Smith) find themselves in a volcanic hothouse threatened by giant prehistoric animals and the mad survivor (Henry Brandon) of a previous expedition. Director Virgil Vogel's tame adventure fantasy features bargain-basement sets and monsters, though the formula plot takes some intriguing twists along the way. Stylized violence, contrived thrills and mild sexual innuedo

title: Language of Love
synopsis: Swedish exploitation import is a crudely done series of demonstrations of sexual techniques that will offend any who consider sex a private human expression of love rather than a perfectable mechanical task

title: Lantana
synopsis: Intriguing psychological drama that follows four couples (including Barbara Hershey, Anthony LaPaglia, and Geoffrey Rush) caught up in a police investigation of a missing person. Confronting unpleasant truths about relationships, marital infidelity and human foibles, director Ray Lawrence incisively probes the psyches of the realistically depicted characters in an intelligent film with strong performances. A few sexual encounters including extra-marital affairs and intermittent rough language with some profanity

title: La Passion de Notre Seigneur Jesus-Christ
synopsis: Though better known for one-reel crime melodramas, movie pioneer Ferdinand Zecca (1863-1947) also produced this two-reel (c. 30 minutes) dramatization of Christ's Passion. Distributed by Pathe, France's leading motion picture company, it was reportedly quite popular in its time and was notable, according to film historian Georges Sadoul, for its "rudimentary" camera movements. (No ratings) ( 1905 )

title: La Peau Douce
synopsis: ( see: "The Soft Skin" )

title: La Prisonniere
synopsis: French import about a woman who finds herself first intrigued by, and then hopelessly attracted to an art dealer (Laurent Terzieff) who proves to be a sadistic voyeur incapable of love. Director Henri-Georges Clouzot affects a detached, noncommital attitude toward his subject, forcing viewers to share the voyeurism which his characters are experiencing

title: La Promesse
synopsis: Belgian drama in which a venal contractor (Olivier Gourmet) lets one of his illegal alien employees die rather than hospitalize him, resulting in his teenage son (Jeremie Renier) attempting to help the dead man's wife and infant without turning in his dad to the authorities. Directed by Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne, the movie probes the good and dark sides of its characters while creating a powerful portrait of desperate immigrants and those who callously exploit them. Subtitles. Brief violence and a few instances of rough language

title: Lara Croft: Tomb Raider
synopsis: Unexceptional action flick based on the video game in which buxom archeologist adventurer Lara Croft (Angelina Jolie) races to beat an evil secret society from finding a mysterious artifact which gives power over time. Jolie exhibits a certain charm, but it can't compensate for the slim story line in director Simon West's derivative film, which is engulfed by big, loud, repetitive action sequences. Much action violence and an instance of crass language. The U.S. Catholic Conference

title: Lara Croft: Tomb Raider: Cradle of Life
synopsis: Entertaining action film about globetrotting archeologist and adventurer Lara Croft (Angelina Jolie), who must find Pandora's Box before a maniacal scientist (Ciaran Hinds) can unleash its power and destroy the world. Though Jolie shines, director Jan De Bont's roller-coaster sequel, while a marked upgrade from the 2001 original, deviates little from its predecessor's recipe of repetitive action sequences at the expense of story and character. Much action violence, brief sensuality and some profanity

title: Laramie Trail, The
synopsis: Western programmer directed by John English in which a cowboy (Bob Livingston) and his pal (Smiley Burnette) catch a murderer while on the trail of a payroll robber. Stylized violence

title: Larger than Life
synopsis: Feeble comedy in which a hapless chap (Bill Murray) inherits his father's performing elephant, then struggles to personally escort the unruly pachyderm across the country to an impatient buyer. Directed by Howard Franklin, the comic proceedings are pleasant enough, though they never venture far beyond its limited odd-couple premise. Fleeting profanity and brief menace

title: Larry the Cable Guy: Health Inspector
synopsis: Witless and virtually unwatchable comedy about a redneck health inspector ("Blue Collar" comedian Larry the Cable Guy) who must crack a string of mysterious food poisonings at upscale eateries in the days leading up to a big culinary competition, zeroing in on the town's sleazy mayor (Joe Pantoliano) and a duplicitous restaurateur (Joanna Cassidy). Director Trent Cooper serves up an insufferably juvenile stream of gross jokes that are unfunny no matter what color your collar, making the film's PG-13 rating misleading. Pervasive crass and sexual humor, recurring scatological sight gags, innuendo, fleeting partial rear nudity, and much crude and bawdy language, as well as profanity

title: Lars and the Real Girl
synopsis: Poignant story of emotionally fragile delusional man (a brilliant Ryan Gosling) who -- unable to make human connection -- buys a life-size female doll whom he presents as his girlfriend, and how his brother and sister-in-law (Paul Schneider and Emily Mortimer), his office mates, fellow churchgoers and townspeople accept "her" as human out of love and compassion for him. Though suspension of disbelief is essential, director Craig Gillespie, working from Nancy Oliver's delicate script, makes this improbable tale utterly believable, while the themes of family, community, religion, forgiveness, redemption and a strong affirmation of human decency override those very few elements that might preclude younger teens. Two nonexplicit images of a porn site, mild innuendo, discreet sexual references and brief profanity

title: La Rupture
synopsis: Contrived French mystery about a woman (Stephane Audran) seeking a divorce from her deranged husband in order to protect herself and her child without realizing that her rich father-in-law (Michel Bouquet) will stop at nothing to get custody of his grandson. Director Claude Chabrol has used the theme of social decadence and moral corruption to better effect in other movies but this one is little more than an interesting exercise in the modern gothic imagination

title: La Salamandre
synopsis: Engrossing Swiss drama about the collaboration between a journalist and a fiction writer on a television play based on a recent case of a young woman's shooting of a relative but when they finally meet her (Bulle Ogier) she is too chameleon-like for them to continue the project. Director Alain Tanner's story seems on the surface an amusing anecdote about whether imagination or fact reveals the truth better but underneath is the question of survival in a destructive post-industrial society where by movie's end it is clear that the woman has made the most progress toward self-liberation. Mature themes and treatment

title: La Scorta
synopsis: Compelling Italian drama focusing on four government bodyguards (led by Enrico Lo Verso) assigned to protect a crusading judge (Carlo Cecchi) from the bullets of Mafia hitmen while he investigates a case that implicates corrupt officials in his own department who will stop at nothing to have him silenced. Director Ricky Tognazzi puts in human terms the price being paid by brave individuals in the arduous effort to crush generations of mob-related activities in Sicily. Subtitles. Brief violence, much menace and intermittent rough language

title: Lassie
synopsis: Handsome adaptation of Eric Knight's original novel, "Lassie Come Home," about an impoverished Yorkshire mining family (Samantha Morton, John Lynch and Jonathan Mason) in World War II that reluctantly sells its beloved dog to a rich nobleman (Peter O'Toole) who takes the dog to Scotland where the collie escapes and attempts the impossibly long trek back home. Writer-director Charles Sturridge has assembled a fine, mostly English cast, including Edward Fox, Kelly MacDonald and Jemma Redgrave, and two appealing youngsters, Mason and Hester Odgers. The scenic vistas are breathtaking and the story appealing, making this fine family viewing, though discerning adults may be bothered by a disjointed narrative, some plot turns that defy credulity, and an awkwardness in both script and direction that places it several notches below the classic 1943 MGM version. A brief sequence of Lassie being beaten with a belt, a nongraphic scene where the miners urinate to throw some hunting dogs off the scent of an escaping fox, some mildly crass language, some mild violence and the death of a dog

title: Lassie
synopsis: A stray collie befriends a lonely boy (Thomas Guiry) adjusting to life in Virginia's Shenandoah Valley where his Baltimore parents (Helen Shaver and Jon Tenney) are attempting to make a go of a sheep ranch despite stiff competition from an unprincipled neighbor (Frederic Forrest). Director Daniel Petrie delivers a postcard-pretty, very sentimental boy-and-his-dog story in which the brave collie predictably helps save the ranch and brings the family closer together. Fleeting violence and brief menace to children

title: Lassie Come Home
synopsis: Before television, the faithful collie got her start in this story of a poor English family who have to sell their dog, Lassie, but the canny canine crosses the Scottish highlands, despite the elements and all manner of hazards, to return to the little boy (Roddy McDowall) who loves her. Directed by Fred M. Wilcox, the movie's charm holds up quite well as family entertainment, especially for youngsters enthralled by Lassie's intelligence and perseverance

title: Lassiter
synopsis: Tom Selleck stars as a womanizing detective forced to become a spy in this espionage thriller directed by Roger Young and set in London just before World War II. Lauren Hutton is the German Mata Hari with a kinky appetite for blood, sex and brutality. Violence and nudity

title: Last Action Hero
synopsis: Overproduced parody of action movies follows an 11-year-old boy (Austin O'Brien) as he magically enters the movie he's watching to join his hero, a trigger-happy cop (Arnold Schwarzenegger), in countless chases and shootouts. Director John McTiernan does little but stitch together the mindless mayhem wrought by assorted weapons and the pyrotechnics engineered by the special effects unit for a clunky and uninvolving pastiche that glamorizes violence and equates heroism with macho posturing and big guns. Much mean-spirited comic violence, positive treatment of phony male heroics, sexist images of women and an instance of rough language

title: Last Adventure, The
synopsis: Episodic French movie about the comradeship between two men (Alain Delon and Lino Ventura) and a young woman (Joanna Shimkus) with the trio winding up on a dangerous search for sunken treasure. Directed by Robert Enrico, the emphasis is less on their adventures than on the qualities of loyalty and respect that keep the three together

title: The Last Airbender
synopsis: Strained 3-D fantasy adventure, set in an alternate world where some human beings have the power to "bend," that is, control, one of the basic elements of fire, earth, air and water, and where a brother and sister (Jackson Rathbone and Nicola Peltz) assist a child (Noah Ringer) who is the latest incarnation of a global peace-giver in his quest to restore order to society by ending the oppressive rule of a warlike, imperialist nation (led by Cliff Curtis and Aasif Mandvi). Though free of objectionable language or behavior, writer-director M. Night Shyamalan's live-action adaptation of an animated TV series -- which also features Dev Patel as a disgraced prince out to prove his mettle by capturing the boy wonder -- fails to gain dramatic traction, bogging down in stilted dialogue and endless explanations of its back story, some aspects of which suggest pantheism or nonscriptural beliefs. Potentially confusing religious themes and much nongraphic martial arts and combat violence

title: Last American Hero, The
synopsis: Story of champion stock-car driver Junior Johnson (Jeff Bridges) who evolved from running corn whiskey over the backroads of North Carolina to earning $100,000 a year racing cars. Directed by Lamont Johnson, the movie's gritty atmosphere is evoked beautifully, supported by a fine cast (Art Lund, Geraldine Fitzgerald, Gary Busey and Ned Beatty)

title: Last Bandit, The
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Joseph Kane in which a railroad express agent (William Elliott) in 1870 Nevada has to stop his outlaw brother (Forrest Tucker) from stealing a million-dollar gold shipment. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Last Big Thing, The
synopsis: Ineffective satire in which a man (Dan Zukovic) obsessed with the lack of creativity in modern popular culture seeks out pop performers to ridicule and insult while a troubled follower (Susan Heimbinder) chronicles his bizarre exploits. Also written and directed by Zukovic, the comic concept is too thin to be sustained as a feature, though its wacky jabs at pop culture icons provide some amusement along the way. Sexual situations and references, dark pranks, outrageous deceptions and occasional rough language

title: Last Blitzkrieg, The
synopsis: Uneven World War II tale in which an English-speaking German officer (Van Johnson) heads a group of saboteurs dressed in American uniforms during the Battle of the Bulge. Directed by Arthur Dreifuss, the story's conflict of loyalties to nation and to common humanity is well-intended but muddled. Wartime violence and an attempted sexual assault

title: Last Boy Scout, The
synopsis: A former Secret Service agent (Bruce Willis) and a drug-addicted ex-football player (Damon Wayans) constantly court death while atempting to stop the assassination of a corrupt Senator. Director Tony Scott's sleazy bloodbath is an affront to human sensibilities disguised as slick action entertainment. Excessive violence, incessant rough language and brief nudity

title: Last Chance Harvey
synopsis: Delicate romantic comedy about an isolated New York jingle composer (Dustin Hoffman) who travels to London for his estranged daughter's (Liane Balaban) wedding and falls for a lonely airport employee (Emma Thompson). While somewhat predictable, writer-director Joel Hopkins' skillfully wrought valentine to midlife romance -- which also features Eileen Atkins as Thompson's mother -- draws masterful performances to touching effect and shows the lingering negative consequences of both divorce and abortion as it portrays a mutually generous relationship untainted by irresponsible sexuality. Some sexual references and humor, occasional crude words, the acceptability of divorce and an abortion reference

title: Last Command, The
synopsis: Historical dramatization centers on the exploits of Jim Bowie (Sterling Hayden) with the Texicans led by William Travis (Richard Carlson) and some Tennessee volunteers under Davy Crockett (Arthur Hunnicutt) at the 1836 Battle of the Alamo against the Mexican forces of Santa Anna (J. Carrol Naish). Directed by Frank Lloyd, the movie sets the scene with some sequences helping define the characters as well as the political issues leading to the battle which is reenacted with convincing gusto. Battlefield violence

title: Last Dance
synopsis: Flawed drama in which a novice lawyer (Rob Morrow) is stymied by the legal system and back-room politics in struggling to gain clemency for a young woman (Sharon Stone) sentenced to death for a brutal double slaying. Director Bruce Beresford focuses on the humanity of a death-row inmate in a simplistic story questioning the state's right to take human life. Brief gory shots of murder victims, fleeting sexual innuendo and recurring profanity as well as rough language

title: Last Days of Disco, The
synopsis: Wryly observed tale, set in early 1980's New York City, follows the fluctuating social lives and fledgling careers of a half-dozen recent college grads who frequent a trendy disco over the course of a year. Writer-director Whit Stillman's talky comedy serves as a cautionary tale in exploring opinionated characters who discover there are consequences to sexual permissiveness. Momentary violence, a fleeting sexual encounter and nudity, implied affairs, a character's substance abuse and a few instances of profanity

title: Last Days of Dolwyn, The
synopsis: Stodgy British production about a village in 19th-century Wales which must be abandoned before its valley is turned into a reservoir, until a widow (Edith Evans) rejects any compensation from the project's agent (Emlyn Williams) and refuses to leave. Also written and directed by Williams, the Welsh setting is quite appealing, but the story grows increasingly melodramatic until a heavy-handed ironic ending. Stylized violence, including an accidental death by fire

title: Last Days of Man on Earth, The
synopsis: Failed British satire set against the background of a post-nuclear disaster in which a group of scientists led by a ruthless woman (Jenny Runacre) force a brilliant young man to help them in an attempt to create a new breed of superhumans. Directed by Robert Fuest, the exotic settings are far more interesting than the action occuring in them. Excessive nudity

title: Last Days of Pompeii, The
synopsis: Creaky but colorful tale in which a happy Pompeii blacksmith (Preston Foster) turns dour seeking wealth as a gladiator, then finds it as a trader in Judea where his boy is cured by the miracle worker later crucified by Pontius Pilate (Basil Rathbone). But back home, the unworldliness of his now-Christian son puzzles the rich old man, then inspires him to save others in the volcanic eruption of Vesuvius. Directed by Ernest B. Schoedsack, the episodic story of a good man changing into a greedy one, then shedding selfishness in the face of disaster plods fitfully along until the spectacular effects depicting the city's destruction. Stylized violence

title: Last Detail, The
synopsis: Career sailors (Jack Nicholson and Otis Young), assigned to escort a young seaman (Randy Quaid) to the Marine brig, stop off along the way to give him a last fling, which proves to be his first. Directed by Hal Ashby, it is fairly consistent but very coarse adult entertainment. Brothel scene with brief nudity and unrelenting flow of rough language are part of the movie's apparent definition of manliness

title: Last Dragon, The
synopsis: A kind of black Kung Fu movie that doesn't take itself too seriously. Although it has a banal story line about a good martial arts expert vanquishing a nasty one, director Michael Schultz is helped out by lively high-spirited performers. Some restrained violence and vulgar language

title: Last Embrace
synopsis: Florid melodrama directed by Jonathan Demme about a government agent (Roy Scheider) who has a mental breakdown after his wife is killed in a shootout in which he inadvertently involved her. A mysterious graduate student (Janet Margolin) is somehow involved in a flimsy plot loaded with red herrings. Generous doses of brutality and sexual scenes

title: Last Emperor, The
synopsis: Sweeping historical saga of Pu Yi (1906-67) who, after being crowned emperor at age 3 of the fading Manchurian dynasty, becomes a passive pawn amidst political power plays until ending his life as a humble gardener under Chinese Communist rule. Italian director Bernardo Bertolucci's movie boasts exquisite historical detail, beautiful costumes, extraordinary location sets in the Forbidden City and breathtaking pageantry, but oddly lacks dramatic punch. Some scenes of violence, sex and opium smoking, though brief and integral to the cultural context

title: Last Escape, The
synopsis: Stuart Whitman leads an Allied operation in the final months of World War II to smuggle a leading rocket scientist out of war-scarred Germany while the Russians are attempting to do the same. Director Walter Grauman compensates for an obvious script and wooden acting by a lot of wartime action scenes with remarkably little bloodshed

title: Last Exit to Brooklyn
synopsis: Repugnant view of working-class life during a 1952 shipping strike in a waterfront neigborhood where thugs amuse themselves terrorizing passersby, the local union strike leader (Stephen Lang) destroys himself in a homosexual affair and an aspiring hooker (Jennifer Jason Leigh) winds up the victim of a stand-in-line gang rape. Director Uli Edel's dark picture of human degradation makes several feeble gestures affirming the values of family and union solidarity but they ring hollow and fail to add any significance to the dehumanized proceedings. Excessive violence and sexual exploitation

title: The Last Exorcism
synopsis: Middling fright fest about an evangelical minister and self-confessed charlatan (Patrick Fabian) who brings a film crew (led by Iris Bahr) along to document his final faked exorcism. But he gets more than he bargained for when the Louisiana farm girl (Ashley Bell) whose father (Louis Herthum) summoned him shows signs of genuine possession. While the gore factor is kept comparatively low in director Daniel Stamm's gothic outing -- which toys cleverly with the modern presumption that all phenomena can be explained scientifically -- the preacher's corrosive cynicism and the occult atmosphere by which he unexpectedly finds himself surrounded make this inappropriate for all but well-grounded and judicious adult viewers. Complex treatment of religion, sacrilegious activity, some gruesome images, at least two uses of profanity, brief sexual talk, and references to incest and homosexuality

title: Last Flight of Noah's Ark
synopsis: Elliott Gould agrees to fly missionary Genevieve Bujold and a menagerie of domestic animals to a South Pacific island but, when the plane crash lands, they discover two child stowaways (Ricky Schroder and Tammy Lauren). Directed by Charles Jarrott, the Disney production is disarming and has a lighthearted grace that is irresistible. Appealing fare for young and old

title: Last Flight Out
synopsis: Evangelical-flavored action parable about a cynical pilot (Richard Tyson) who finds faith while evacuating a village -- including the medical missionary (Bobbie Phillips) he was hired to rescue -- under the heel of a ruthless Colombian-cartel drug lord. Produced by Billy Graham's World Wide Pictures, the well-intentioned film's strong Gospel message is handicapped by amateurish performances and a B-movie script full of heavy-handed homiletics with a view to proselytize at the expense of plot. Some gun violence, including two shootings, a scene of child peril, drug references and several explosions

title: Last Frontier, The
synopsis: Standard Western in which a fur trapper (Victor Mature) becomes an Army scout during a Sioux uprising, then saves the fort after its deranged commander (Robert Preston) is killed in a futile attack, with his widow (Anne Bancroft) showing interest in the scout. Directed by Anthony Mann, the formula plot has a boisterous performance by Mature as the hard-drinking, free-spirited trapper whose antics are colorful but not very credible. Frontier violence and romantic complications

title: Last Grenade, The
synopsis: British agent Stanley Baker tramps up and down the hills bordering Hong Kong in pursuit of Alex Cord, a grinning sadist working for the other side. Director Gordon Flemyng's chase story, in which an adulterous affair plays a part, doesn't make much sense and the movie is a dud

title: Last Hard Men, The
synopsis: Ugly, distasteful Western about an escaped convict (James Coburn) who is determined to get revenge upon the retired sheriff (Charlton Heston) who put him in jail. Coburn manages to be interesting and Michael Parks contributes a few bright moments, but all director Andrew V. McLaglen's movie really has on its mind is the usual rape and other brutalities that go with simple-minded debasements of the Western myth

title: Last Holiday
synopsis: Touching if improbable tale of dowdy spinster (Queen Latifah), who upon learning she has only a few weeks to live takes her life savings and goes to Europe where she gets a makeover and learns to live life more fully, changing the lives of a corrupt businessman (Timothy Hutton) and less-than-altruistic politicians. Wayne Wang's remake of a 1950 Alec Guinness movie which had a script by august English writer J.B. Priestley is marred by some silly slapstick, but mostly, though predictable and contrived, it's a feel-good film with the marvelously empathetic Latifah and a positive message about recognizing life's possibilities and having the courage to follow through on them. A few instances of crude language, some frank sexual talk and innuendo, and an adulterous situation in an otherwise admirably wholesome film

title: Last House on the Left, The
synopsis: Two teenagers (Lucy Grantham and Sandra Cassel) are kidnapped, tormented, raped and slaughtered while a foolish sheriff bungles his investigation and the parents of one girl take their own brutal revenge. Written and directed by Wes Craven, this lurid movie indulges in gore, sex and profanity

title: Last Hunt, The
synopsis: In the 1880s, with the last of the great buffalo herds nearing extinction, a cynical gunman (Robert Taylor) persuades a veteran hunter (Stewart Granger) to join him in going after buffalo hides, with predictably disastrous results. Director Richard Brooks reduces the plot to a simplistic contrast between the noble hunter and the cold-blooded gunman who not only kills people as wantonly as buffalo but also brutalizes an Indian woman (Debra Paget) he has taken captive. Much stylized violence and sexual situations

title: Last Hurrah, The
synopsis: Uneven screen version of Edwin O'Connor's novel about the end of a colorful era in urban machine politics as seen in the final campaign of fictional Boston Mayor Frank Skeffington (Spencer Tracy). Directed by John Ford, the story's contrast between the old and the new TV breed of politicians is less interesting than its nostalgia for a more human, if much flawed American past as evoked by a cast of veteran character actors (Pat O'Brien, Frank McHugh, James Gleason) as well as some of Ford's own stock company (Donald Crisp, Jane Darwell, John Carradine) who balance the thick sentimentality with broad humor. Lingering demise of the main character

title: Last Man on Earth, The
synopsis: Halting horror tale in which the sole survivor (Vincent Price) of a world-wide plague whose victims become vampires manages to fend off their attacks for three years, then is suddenly confronted by a group of mutants who fear him more than they do the vampires. Directed by Sidney Salkow from a story by Richard Matheson, the picture is thinly plotted and unevenly acted, though Price's performance more than holds interest until the muddled ending in a church sanctuary. Stylized violence and considerable menace

title: Last Man Standing
synopsis: Arriving in a Texas border town overrun by rival Prohibition-era bootleggers, a trigger-happy tough guy (Bruce Willis) hires himself out to both sides, then systematically kills them all. Willis smirks his way through one boring shootout after another in an empty story of violence from writer-director Walter Hill. Heroic treatment of a brutal murderer, excessive violence, a sexual encounter and much profanity

title: Last Married Couple in America, The
synopsis: George Segal and Natalie Wood begin to doubt the validity of their own relationship when the marriages of all their friends shatter around them. Directed by Gilbert Cates, it is a clumsy, shapeless affair, poorly scripted and badly acted. Some nudity and a great deal of foul language

title: Last Metro, The
synopsis: Uninvolving wartime melodrama directed by Francois Truffaut about a harried actress-theater manager (Catherine Deneuve) who tries to keep her theater open and her Jewish husband (Heinz Bennent) hidden during the German Occupation of Paris. It is a romantic and sophisticated production lacking depth and passion. Subtitles. Adultery figures in the plot

title: Last Mile, The
synopsis: Awaiting execution, a vicious murderer (Preston Foster) takes control of death row in an attempt to exchange a hostage for freedom. Directed by Sam Bischoff from John Wexley's play, the action is stagey but viscerally effective as the tension mounts within the cell block and among the prison guards surrounding it. Stylized violence in a desperate situation

title: Last Mile, The
synopsis: Remake of the 1932 original with Mickey Rooney giving a hard-edged performance as a condemned killer leading seven prisoners in an ill-fated take-over of death row. Director Howard W. Koch sets a somber scene with a Catholic chaplain preparing an inmate to face execution but the brutal action in taking over the ward is nasty and conscienceless. Realistic violence

title: Last Movie, The
synopsis: Failed story about the bizarre and tragic effects a movie company has on a community of primitive Peruvian Indians whose village they use as a location. Directed by Dennis Hopper, who also stars, the movie's concept is an intriguing one that, unfortunately, is not realized in a work totally out of control with incredible lapses of logic and jumbled time sequences. Graphic scenes of sexual encounters and a demeaning attitude toward Indian culture and religious beliefs

title: Last Musketeer, The
synopsis: Western programmer directed by William Witney in which cowboy Rex Allen saves settlers from being forced out of a valley whose only source of water is owned by a ruthless landgrabber, with some comic relief from bumbling water finder Slim Pickens. Stylized violence

title: Last of His Tribe, The
synopsis: Stolid human drama based on the book by anthropologist Alfred Kroeber (Jon Voight) about his 1911 discovery of Ishi (Graham Greene), the last survivor of the Yahi, an Indian tribe long thought extinct, and his work in trying to preserve its language and culture. Director Harry Hook gives a rather flat account of an aboriginal man's learning to live in the 20th century and Kroeber's attempts to reconstruct the lost Yahi way of life. Some heart-rending scenes of violence and a restrained sexual episode

title: Last of Sheila, The
synopsis: Film producer (James Coburn) invites some friends (Richard Benjamin, Joan Hackett, Dyan Cannon, James Mason, Raquel Welch and Ian McShane) for a week's cruise in the Mediterranean celebrating the first anniversary of the hit-and-run killing of his wife, whose name graces both the yacht and the movie's title. Director Herbert Ross is so busy being slick and clever in his parody of Hollywood types, that he creates an elaborate hoax rather than a plausible whodunit

title: Last of the Comanches
synopsis: After Comanches massacre a troop of U.S. Cavalry, six survivors (led by Broderick Crawford) along with several civilians (including Barbara Hale) take refuge in an abandoned mission and hold off waves of attackers until reinforcements arrive. Directed by Andre de Toth, the result is little more than standard action fare ending in a tribute to the bravery of the fallen. Frontier violence

title: Last of the Dogmen
synopsis: Tall tale comes up short in telling how a bounty hunter (Tom Berenger) and an anthropologist (Barbara Hershey) discover a tribe of Cheyenne Indians who have managed to stay undetected for 128 years in a Montana valley hidden behind a waterfall. Writer-director Tab Murphy has the makings of a robust Western yarn but wastes the opportunity on a pedestrian treatment of cliched characters and sentimental situations. Some brutal violence and needless profanity

title: Last of the Fast Guns, The
synopsis: Convoluted Western in which a gunfighter (Jock Mahoney) hired to find an American missing in Mexico teams with a local adventurer (Gilbert Roland) who has his own reasons for joining in the search. Directed by George Sherman, the contrived plot has some colorful characters, notably a backcountry padre (Eduard Franz), but the quest becomes tiresome long before its improbable ending. Stylized violence

title: Last of the Finest, The
synopsis: Suspended veteran Los Angeles cop (Brian Dennehy) and his three young cronies bust a bigtime drug and money laundering racket tied to Central American gunrunners. Directed in plodding, unimaginative fashion by John MacKenzie, this implausible cop adventure justifies vigilantism as patriotism. Some profanity, sexual expletives, bathroom humor and explosive comic-book violence

title: Last of the Mobile Hot-Shots
synopsis: Failed screen version of a play by Tennessee Williams presents a muddled and superficially symbolic story of Southern racial attitudes involving James Coburn, Robert Hooks and Lynn Redgrave. Directed by Sidney Lumet, this talky affair has an excess of crude dialogue and several unnecessarily explicit sex scenes in the flashbacks

title: Last of the Mohicans, The
synopsis: When the French and Indian War erupts on New York's colonial frontier, heroic woodsman Hawkeye (Daniel Day-Lewis) cannot save a British force from being massacred in the wilderness but at least he's able to rescue its commander's daughter (Madeleine Stowe) from a wicked Huron warrior (Wes Studi). In adapting the James Fenimore Cooper classic to the screen, director Michael Mann updates its romanticized version of pioneer life amidst noble woodland savages by dwelling in realistic detail on the inhuman cruelties of hand-to-hand combat. Many graphic depictions of deadly violence and bloodshed

title: Last of the Red Hot Lovers
synopsis: Failed screen version of the Neil Simon comedy about a man (Alan Arkin) who uses his unsuspecting mother's apartment for sex in the afternoon. Directed by Gene Saks, it tries deserately to be amusing but, except for the occasional one-liner, it is boring when it's not irritating in its search for euphemisms for sin

title: Last of the Renegades
synopsis: Routine European-made Western directed by Harald Rinl is an old-fashioned cowboy and Indian movie with Lex Barker and Anthony Steel trying to avert an Indian war while both pursue the same Indian maiden (Karin Dor). Stylized violence

title: Last Orders
synopsis: Slow-moving drama in which a group of old friends (including Bob Hoskins, David Hemmings and Ray Winstone) get together to honor the last wishes of their close friend (Michael Caine) who wanted them to spread his ashes across the sea. As directed by Fred Schepisi, the sentimental script has many flaws but the superb ensemble cast picks up the slack, giving the deliberately paced film about death, painful memories and new beginnings some vitality. A few sexual encounters, an extra-marital affair, brief nudity and sporadic rough language with profanity

title: L.A. Story
synopsis: A TV weatherman (Steve Martin) is chased by a bouncy blonde (Sarah Jessica Parker) while he, with a little help from a magical freeway sign, pursues a reserved English journalist (Victoria Tennant). Directed by Mick Jackson from Martin's script, the result takes a wry view of the trendy populace of Los Angeles which proves more diverting than the fairly bland fantasy-romance storyline. Causual attitude toward premarital sex and minimal rough language

title: Last Outlaw, The
synopsis: Unpretentious Western in which an aged bank robber (Harry Carey) is released after 25 years in prison, then takes on some Detroit gangsters with the help of an oldtime lawman (Henry B. Walthall) and a young rancher (Hoot Gibson). Directed by Christy Cabanne from a story by John Ford, Carey is in fine form portraying the old badman's bemusement at the changes in the modern West as well as his disdain at seeing a movie with singing cowboys. Shootout to free a woman held hostage by the gangsters

title: Last Outpost, The
synopsis: Raiding Union supply lines along the Santa Fe Trail, a Confederate officer (Ronald Reagan) comes across his brother (Bruce Bennett), who happens to be a Yankee officer, and the two join forces to stop an Apache uprising. Director Lewis R. Foster, treats the far-fetched yarn as if it were a Rover Boys adventure in blue and gray. Stylized violence

title: Last Picture Show, The
synopsis: Bleak picture of life in a dust-stricken and culturally depressed little town in 1951 Texas. Director Peter Bogdanovich captures brilliantly the banal details of time and place but portrays the town's inhabitants (Timothy Bottoms, Jeff Bridges, Cybill Shepherd Ellen Burstyn, Cloris Leachman and Ben Johonson) as a hopeless lot whose only interests are sexual experimentation and watching TV soap operas and quiz shows. There's more to life than that, even in a small town. Brief nudity

title: La Strada
synopsis: Two-bit strongman (Anthony Quinn) adds a simple-minded peasant (Giulietta Masina) to his circus act, treating her badly until a tragic encounter with a bantering acrobat (Richard Basehart) who tries to help her. Italian director Federico Fellini's somber picture of lost souls on the backroads of life has its emotional center in Masina's Chaplinesque performance as the poor waif struggling to keep her spirit from being crushed by the brute she serves. Subtitles. Some stylized violence and brutalizing conditions of life

title: Last Rebel, The
synopsis: Joe Namath smirks his way through a puerile Western as an ex-Confederate adventurer who shoots up a few rivals, hustles some local pool sharks and makes merry with ladies high and low. Director Denys McCoy's movie has crude language, stylized violence and brief nudity, but its major offense is being so witless and dull that an adult will find it hard to sit through

title: Last Remake of Beau Geste, The
synopsis: Witless and boring spoof of a classic adventure movie stars Ann-Margret and Michael York who are less embarrassing to watch than the struggle of a cast of comedians in the clutches of a dreary script. Director Marty Feldman relies almost solely on vulgar sight gags and crude humor to keep the French Foreign Legion afloat

title: Last Resort
synopsis: Charles Grodin takes his movie family on an island resort vacation in this failed satire about the crude excesses of the travel business. The sex maniacs who run the resort manage to corrupt the middle-class values of mom, dad and the kids in this unfunny farce obsessed with crude sexual innuendo and sight gags, the drug-and-booze culture and profanity

title: Last Rites
synopsis: Donald P. Bellisario directs a trashy, twisted tale of a New York priest (Tom Berenger) who falls in love with a woman (Daphne Zuniga) seeking to protect him from a Mafia gang headed by the priest's father (Dane Clark). Several simulated sex scenes, some bloody violence and occasional rough language

title: Last Romantic Lover, The
synopsis: French sex farce begins with a male beauty contest sponsored by a women's magazine and ends with the runner-up romancing the supposedly liberated woman editor with such old-fashioned techniques as tenderness. The movie is directed by Just Jaeklin with all the gloss and glamour that he learned as a fashion photographer. Except for some partial nudity, it is a throwback to an earlier age of sexual comedy that feminists may find more objectionable than moralists

title: Last Run, The
synopsis: George C. Scott plays an old-time professional getaway driver hired to break-out a young convict (Tony Musante) and he handles all the ensuing ambushes, chases and double-crosses with credible assurance. Directed by Richard Fleischer, the flawed narrative is of less interest than Scott's bravura performance. Some violence and sexual references

title: Last Safari, The
synopsis: Mediocre British adventure directed by Henry Hathaway with Stewart Granger as a safari guide. The original version featured extensive nudity which was edited out of the American release

title: Last Seduction, The
synopsis: After stealing the proceeds of a drug deal from her hapless husband (Bill Pullman), a manipulative woman (Linda Fiorentino) hides out in a small town until she ensnares a lovestruck chump (Peter Berg), hoping to get him in the clear by having him kill her spouse. Director John Dahl's cynical crime thriller twists its way through a hard-edged narrative of greed and lust perpetrated by colorful if despicable characters. Brief sexual encounters with partial nudity, crude sexual references, fleeting violence and much rough language

title: Last Shot You Hear, The
synopsis: Unintriguing thriller dealing with a renowned marriage counselor (Hugh Marlowe) who, after refusing to give his wife a divorce, is murdered by her lover. Director Gordon Hessler's movie concludes fatuously attempting to elicit sympathy for the murderers

title: Last Starfighter, The
synopsis: High school senior (Lance Guest), a whiz at electronic games, finds himself defending the frontiers of the universe against ruthless space invaders in a touching, romantic, humorous fantasy from director Nick Castle. Some of the violence might be too much for younger viewers

title: Last Summer
synopsis: Suntanned teenagers (Richard Thomas, Bruce Davison and Barbara Hershey) exploring adolescent limits of mutual trust and confidence and the tragic destruction of a self-possessed young girl (Kathy Burns) form the background and structure of the movie. Director Frank Perry's vision of upper-class youths contending with their curiosity about each other's physique and psyche features a terrifying rape sequence in which the antics and silliness in the first part of the film turn to dread. Though its use of nudity is questionable, this journey of sorts into self-discovery is a provocative examination of physical and spiritual maturation

title: Last Summer in the Hamptons
synopsis: Talky comedy in which a theatrical family's matriarch (Viveca Lindfors), who has put on Chekovian dramas at her summer estate for years, gathers the clan and a young Hollywood star (Victoria Foyt) to stage their swan-song production before the property is sold. Director Henry Jaglom's rambling look at several generations beset by romantic and professional longings has occasional scenes of wry dialogue sprinkled throughout its rather drawn-out gabfest. Numerous sexual references, an attempted suicide and intermittent rough language

title: Last Sunset, The
synopsis: Western clunker in which a U.S. lawman (Rock Hudson) trails a killer (Kirk Douglas) to Mexico, then both help a rancher (Joseph Cotten) on a cattle drive to Texas where they finally shoot it out. Directed by Robert Aldrich, the inert script focuses on the outlaw's relationship with the rancher's wife (Dorothy Malone) and teen daughter (Carol Lynley), with incest as a plot gimmick. Superficial treatment of mature themes

title: Last Supper, The
synopsis: Empty satire in which idle graduate students invite those they regard as less enlightened, e.g., pro-lifers, anti-Semites and homophobes, to dinner each week, then poison them until the tables are turned one night by a pragmatic TV commentator (Ron Perlman). Directed by Stacy Title, the ludicrous premise gives license to outrageous political and social stereotypes in static proceedings that are witless, pointless and lacking in moral perspective. Callous murders, racist rhetoric, sexual innunedo, much rough language and occasional profanity

title: Last Tango in Paris
synopsis: Middle-aged man (Marlon Brando), numb with despair at the suicide of his wife, happens upon a woman (Maria Schneider) inspecting a vacant apartment, and they immediately engage in sex. She returns again and again to the apartment for further encounters but when he eventually proposes marriage, she runs away and in pursuing her he is killed. Directed by Bernardo Bertolucci, the romantic twaddle about tortured, alienated people adds up to very little and the sex scenes, while not pornographic are needlessly extended and explicit

title: Last Time I Committed Suicide, The
synopsis: Weak dramatization of the Denver youth of Neal Cassady (Thomas Jane), one of the 1950's Beat literary group, follows his affairs with a suicidal secretary (Claire Forlani) and a wild teen-ager (Gretchen Mol) as well as drinking bouts with a pool-hall buddy (Keanu Reeves). Writer-director Stephen Kay's hectic narrative is a chaotic series of vignettes picturing a shiftless young man more interested in fun than art. Sexual situations, some rough language and occasional profanity

title: Last Time I Saw Paris, The
synopsis: Sentimental tearjerker in which an American in Paris at the end of World War II marries a lovely woman (Elizabeth Taylor), becomes a reporter, inherits some money, turns into an alcoholic, then sobers up to return to wife and child. Directed by Richard Brooks from F. Scott Fitzgerald's updated story, the result is a glossy but unconvincing sudser. Romantic complications and alcohol abuse

title: Last Train from Gun Hill
synopsis: Uneven Western in which a marshal (Kirk Douglas) tracks down a killer (Earl Holliman) whose victim was the lawman's Indian wife, then has to get him out of a town loyal to the culprit's father (Anthony Quinn). Despite an overly contrived plot and muddled relationships, director John Sturges effectively depicts the consequences of racial prejudice while wringing considerable suspense out of the lawman's predicament. Stylized violence and justice questions

title: Last Tycoon, The
