synopsis: Ludicrously serious prehistoric adventure tale about three warriors (Everett McGill, Ron Perlman and Nameer Eli-Kadi) whose search for fire when that of their clan has been extinguished by a marauding band of Neanderthals leads to a humanizing encounter with a more culturally advanced girl (Rae Dawn Chong) who helps them learn to laugh and even fall in love. Directed by Jean-Jacques Annaud who co-scripted with Gerard Brach, its attempts at authenticity are made even more ludicrous by brutal sex scenes, violent combat and other assorted caveman antics

title: Quest, The
synopsis: While a skilled streetfighter (Jean-Claude Van Damme) competes in a martial-arts championship in 1928 Tibet, his suave con-artist manager (Roger Moore) plots to steal the first-prize -- a solid-gold dragon. Also directed by Van Damme, the result is little more than a series of bone-crunching bouts surrounded by a flimsy plot with one-dimensional characters. Recurring martial-arts violence and an instance of profanity

title: Quick and the Dead, The
synopsis: Revenge-themed Western in which a female gunslinger (Sharon Stone) arrives in town to compete in a quick-draw, shoot-to-the-death contest, intent on gunning down the sadistic town tyrant (Gene Hackman) who had her lawman father lynched years earlier. Director Sam Raimi's flashy but cynically ludicrous shoot-'em-up amounts to nothing more than redundant stagings of stylized shootouts that greatly glamorize guns and killing. Justification of murderous revenge, numerous deadly gunfights, some sexual innuendo and fleeting partial nudity

title: Quick, Before It Melts
synopsis: Witless comedy directed by Delbert Mann in which a magazine reporter (Robert Morse) and photographer (George Maharis) doing a story on U.S. operations in Antarctica inveigle the commander into allowing a planeful of women to tour the ice-bound base. Comic violence and heavy-handed sexual situations

title: Quick Change
synopsis: Disguised as a clown, Bill Murray and accomplices Geena Davis and Randy Quaid pull off an ingenious million-dollar bank robbery in the Big Apple, only to find that their complicated caper was a breeze compared to getting to the airport. Co-directed by Murray and Howard Franklin, the result is a sporadically funny attempt at screwball comedy with the madness of New York City serving as a backdrop for understated performances by Murray and Davis, abetted by Quaid's slapstick goofiness. Some rough language, references to an unmarried sexual relationship and crime treated as a lark

title: Quick Gun, The
synopsis: A reformed gunslinger (Audie Murphy) is treated as an outcast in his home town until he saves it from a band of desperados (led by Ted de Corsia). Director Sidney Salkow's slack Western has no particular merit or interest. Stylized violence

title: Quicksand
synopsis: Small but effective thriller in which a cocky garage mechanic (Mickey Rooney) dumps a nice girl (Barbara Bates) for a sharp cookie with a shady past (Jeanne Cagney), then hits the skids after she gets him to rob a penny arcade owner (Peter Lorre). Directed by Irving Pichel, Rooney holds attention as the two-bit tough guy who gets deeper and deeper in trouble until an unexpected conclusion. Stylized violence, sexual innuendo and an escalating series of crimes

title: Quicksilver
synopsis: Ill-conceived youth movie in which a young stockbroker (Kevin Bacon) has a run of bad luck, quits the market to become a bicycle courier and saves his new working-class friends from dope pushers, loan sharks and dead-end jobs. Directed by Tom Donnelly, it is a phony picture of a teenage hero demonstrating that immaturity and juvenile behavior can lead to success

title: Quiet Cool
synopsis: When a gang of dope addicts brutally murder a peaceful family, they themselves are hunted down and killed in an extraordinarily violent and sadistic manner. The crude and bloody story encourages vigilantism

title: Quiet Days in Clichy
synopsis: Screen version of a Henry Miller novel about the dehumanized sexual adventures of two writers down and out in Paris. The result is human debasement, made all the worse by an irrelevant scatological music-lyric soundtrack supplied by Country Joe McDonald

title: Quiet Earth, The
synopsis: New Zealand scientist (Bruno Lawrence) awakes one morning to discover that he is the last man alive after a U.S. celestial experiment goes haywire. Director Geoff Murphy's quaint science fiction mystery has some suspense and a warning against tampering with the laws of nature. Several scenes with nudity

title: Quiet Gun, The
synopsis: Sluggish Western directed by William F. Claxton in which a sheriff (Forrest Tucker) arrests the men who lynched a rancher, then goes after the nasty cowboy (Lee Van Cleef) who instigated the lynching in order to get the rancher's land. Frontier violence and implied adultery

title: Quiet Man, The
synopsis: When a retired Irish-American boxer (John Wayne) buys a plot of Irish land and courts a lovely colleen (Maureen O'Hara) to go with it, his stubborn bride insists he collect her dowry from her mean-spirited brother (Victor McLaglen). Director John Ford's grand celebration of all-too-familiar Irish stereotypes, ranging from a fondness for spirits to the love of a good fight, is delivered with much broad humor but the movie's universal appeal lies in the robust romance at the heart of the good-natured, old-fashioned story. Comic violence

title: Quiet Place in the Country, A
synopsis: When a troubled abstract-expressionist artist (Franco Nero) is placed in an institution (a nice quiet place in the country) by his mistress (Vanessa Redgrave), his madness crystalizes into an object of tediousness rather than of possible interest. Director Elio Petri choses to use tricky nude shots and violent erotic dreams to hold attention, but the movie crumbles as it goes all out for slick sensationalism

title: Quiet Room, The
synopsis: Australian drama in which a 7-year-old girl (Chloe Ferguson) stops speaking as a response to her battling parents' imminent separation. Writer-director Rolf de Heer has the child voice her thoughts to the audience, offering insights into the fear, anger and stress felt by a youngster when divorce looms, although the uncompromising nature of the film is not for those seeking bouyant entertainment. Serious treatment of marital discord and an instance of profanity

title: Quigley Down Under
synopsis: An American cowboy (Tom Selleck), hired as a sharpshooter in the 1860's Australian Outback, turns against his villainous boss (Alan Rickman) in defense of the native aborigines and a slightly mad young woman (Laura San Giacomo). Director Simon Wincer gives a fresh spin to the traditional Western and backs it with interesting plot developments, credible performances and breathtaking Australian locales. Intermittent violent shootouts, occasional menace and shots with tribal nudity

title: Quiller Memorandum, The
synopsis: Resurgence of Nazism in post-war Germany is the background for this spy story with George Segal, Max von Sydow, Senta Berger and Alec Guinness in a cameo. Director Michael Anderson gets some suspenseful moments in a convoluted thriller that is spun out beyond its limits

title: Quills
synopsis: Sordid drama set in 1807 Paris recounting the final years of infamous author and sexual deviant the Marquis De Sade (Geoffrey Rush) in an insane asylum where he is helped by a laundress (Kate Winslet) to smuggle out his manuscripts for publication and befriended by the asylum's priest-director (Joaquin Phoenix). Despite engaging performances and a somewhat complex narrative, director Philip Kaufman's fictionalized account of the grotesque De Sade repulses the sensibilities with explicit images and language. Much anti-religious sentiment, several sexual encounters including a menage a trois, intermittent violence, base sexual dialogue, some profanity and sporadic rough language

title: Quinceañera
synopsis: Beautifully crafted coming-of-age drama about good-hearted Los Angeles teenager (Emily Rios) who finds herself unaccountably pregnant, and her sexually confused cousin (Jesse Garcia) who are taken in by their gentle uncle (Chalo Gonzalez) after their families reject them. Writer-directors Richard Glatzer and Wash Westmoreland's colorful Sundance Film Festival winner with its moving themes of tolerance, redemption and forgiveness overcomes some plot elements that may not be to every taste. Brief violence, some rough and crude language, sexual banter, premarital sex, a couple of nongraphic homosexual encounters, and drug use

title: Quintet
synopsis: Director Robert Altman's failed futuristic fable about six citizens of an ice-bound, dying world engaged in a lethal cat and mouse game of survival that gives the movie its title. Paul Newman, Bibi Andersson, Fernando Rey, and Vittorio Gassman head the fur-swathed cast of an ambitious but hapless attempt to philosphize about the meaning of life. Graphic depiction of brutal killings

title: Quiz Show
synopsis: Fact-based retelling of the late 1950's television scandal in which quiz contestants are fed answers beforehand until a disgruntled loser (John Turturro) spills the beans to a Congressional investigator (Rob Morrow) about the show's corrupt producer (David Paymer) and a much-admired winner (Ralph Fiennes) who reluctantly confess betraying the public trust while the network and sponsor escape official blame. Producer-director Robert Redford dramatically captures the contrasting personalities involved and the manner in which basic ethical considerations got shoved aside in favor of personal and corporate greed. Questions of moral integrity and minimal rough language

title: Quo Vadis
synopsis: After a Roman general (Robert Taylor) falls in love with a Christian maid (Deborah Kerr), the situation is complicated by the looney emperor deciding to burn Rome and blame the Christians. In director Mervyn LeRoy's version of the Henryk Sienkiewicz novel, the epic production overpowers the pallid love story and is less interested in the conflict between Christianity and paganism than that between the mad Nero (Peter Ustinov) and his rationalist advisor (Leo Genn). A mixed bag of religious fervor and pagan frolics, there's a lengthy suicide scene, some sexual innuendo and stylized violence

title: The Queen
synopsis: Absorbing British drama about the days following the death of Princess Diana, as new Prime Minister Tony Blair (Michael Sheen) tries to convince Queen Elizabeth (Helen Mirren) to express public remorse about her former daughter-in-law, as public grief reaches fever proportions. Stephen Frears directs beautifully, and even if Peter Morgan's script is mostly speculative, what we see on-screen plays convincingly, with a fine cast (including Alex Jennings, Helen McCrory and Roger Allam) and Mirren whose crusty yet vulnerable impersonation softens the anti-monarchist tone of the screenplay. A couple of instances of mild profanity and a few crass expressions

title: The Quiet American
synopsis: Atmospheric adaptation of the Graham Greene novel set in 1952 Vietnam where a veteran British reporter (Michael Caine) fears losing his beautiful local mistress to a newcomer Yank (Brendan Fraser) whom he begins to suspect is involved in deadly political treachery. Aided by Caine and Fraser's nuanced performances, director Phillip Noyce observes the romantic triangle against the larger backdrop of the waning days of French colonial rule and the beginnings of U.S. involvement in Vietnam. Wartime bombings and a stabbing, an implied affair, fleeting opium abuse, occasional profanity and an instance of rough language

title: A Rumor of Angels
synopsis: Honeyed melodrama set in Maine in which a 12-year-old boy (Trevor Morgan), still grieving the death of his mother two years before, befriends an eccentric old woman (Vanessa Redgrave) who tells him that the dead communicate with the living by Morse code. Despite some fine performances, director Peter O'Fallon's film is predictable in its sentiment and story line and the shallow spiritual mumbo-jumbo strains believability without offering insights into coping with the loss of a loved one. Confusing message about what happens after death, brief drug references and a smattering of crass language

title: Rabbit-Proof Fence
synopsis: Fact-based drama set in 1931 Australia where three aboriginal girls, ages 14, 10 and 8, forcibly taken from their mothers under the law and sent to an institution for "half-castes" 1,200 miles away, escape and begin their long walk home while evading the pursuing authorities. As directed by Philip Noyce and enhanced by the three novice child actors and Kenneth Branagh as the rigid bureaucrat in charge, the heart-wrenching tale of institutionalized racism resonates deeply. Some menacing scenes and a theme of racial bias against indigenous peoples

title: Rabbit, Run
synopsis: Failed screen version of John Updike's dark and brooding novel probing the shadowed corners of the mind of an irresponsible young man (James Caan) who persists in chasing illusions and women with equal fervor, resulting in a ruined marriage and shattered dreams. Director Jack Smight dissipates the novel's passionate intensity by concentrating on the surface level of the action. Graphic sexual depictions

title: Rabbit Test
synopsis: Failed sex farce about the world's first pregnant man is comedienne Joan Rivers' debut as a director. Posing a feminist satire, the effort lacks the wit and satiric nuance that might have saved it from being ploddingly tasteless and offensive. Unfunny jokes about religious beliefs are scattered throughout this indelicate comedy

title: Rabid
synopsis: Canadian production about a young woman (porno star Marilyn Chambers) who undergoes plastic surgery only to find herself turned into a vampire who soon has a good portion of the population of Montreal going green in the face, frothing at the mouth and biting one another. Directed by David Cronenberg, it's a nauseating, gory piece of trash

title: Race for Your Life, Charlie Brown
synopsis: Feature cartoon based on the Charles M. Schulz comic strip which tells of the adventures and perils that the Peanuts characters encounter while spending the summer at a wilderness camp out West. Though little of the subtlety of Schulz at his best is represented, the movie will entertain younger children

title: Race Street
synopsis: Routine crime story directed by Edwin L. Marin in which a San Francisco gambler (George Raft), about to retire and wed (Marilyn Maxwell), gets some unwanted help from a friendly cop (William Bendix) when a protection racket (headed by Frank Faylen) moves in and kills his best friend (Henry Morgan). Underworld violence and treachery

title: Race to Witch Mountain
synopsis: Engaging sci-fi adventure about a Las Vegas cab driver (Dwayne Johnson) and a UFO expert (Carla Gugino) who try to help two alien children (AnnaSophia Robb and Alexander Ludwig) find their spaceship and return home to head off an alien invasion of earth, while relentlessly pursued by a federal UFO investigator (Ciaran Hinds). Director Andy Fickman's reimagining of the 1975 "Escape to Witch Mountain" moves at a fast clip with likable lead performances and elaborate special effects making this recommendable family fare for all but young children who might be bothered by some scary moments. Generally mild action violence with explosions and gunshots

title: Race with the Devil
synopsis: Businessmen (Warren Oates and Peter Fonda) on a vacation trip with their wives inadvertently come upon some Satanists at their rituals and then are pursued across Texas by the vengeful cultists. Directed by Jack Starrett, the silly horror movie has a bad script, a few scares and some bloodshed

title: Rachel and the Stranger
synopsis: A widower (William Holden) raising a son on the Kentucky frontier marries a bondswoman (Loretta Young) but only appreciates her when his best friend (Robert Mitchum) tries to win her affections. Directed by Norman Foster, the odd triangle leads Young to reject both men as wanting a servant rather than a wife but a Shawnee attack resolves the dilemma. Quasi-feminist theme with conventional romantic ending

title: Rachel, Rachel
synopsis: Joanne Woodward plays a painfully lonely, somewhat repressed school teacher in a small midwestern town where she fears becoming a dowdy spinster. When an old school chum (James Olson) visits, she falls hopelessly in love and has a brief, intense affair that ends harshly and with bitterness. Director Paul Newman receives excellent performances from a fine cast in a story that is touchingly poignant and deeply human. Mature theme

title: Racing Stripes
synopsis: Delightful family comedy about an underdog zebra (voiced by Frankie Muniz) who grows up believing that he is a racehorse and proves he has the heart of a champion by finding his inner thoroughbred and -- with a little help from a former horse trainer (Bruce Greenwood), his young daughter (Hayden Panettierre) and some barnyard buddies (voiced by Whoopi Goldberg and Dustin Hoffman, among others) -- competing for top racing honors in a prestigious derby. Directed by Frederik Du Chau, this lively crowd-pleaser combines live action and computer-generated talking animal effects -- think "Seabiscuit" meets "Babe" -- and imparts a charming feel-good message about acceptance and overcoming challenges by believing in yourself. Ethnic stereotyping and some mildly crude language and humor

title: Racing with the Moon
synopsis: Likable teenager (Sean Penn), finishing high school during World War II, falls for a winsome California beauty (Elizabeth McGovern) and both try to get money for a friend's abortion. Nostalgic romance from director Richard Benjamin captures the atmosphere and the mood of the period but concentrates too heavily on the sexual nature of youthful relationships. Some nudity and a benign view of premarital sex

title: Racket, The
synopsis: Tired crime melodrama in which an honest cop (Robert Mitchum) and a cynical racketeer (Robert Ryan) try to knock each other off, despite having been boyhood friends and sharing a common enemy in the syndicate now running the town. Directed by John Cromwell, the proceedings are earnest but predictable with an unsurprising pat ending. Some nasty violence

title: Rack, The
synopsis: Back from a North Korean prisoner-of-war camp, an Army officer (Paul Newman) refuses to defend himself when put on trial for collaborating with the enemy, despite the anguish of his career officer father (Walter Pidgeon) and the endeavors of a discerning military lawyer (Edmond O'Brien). Adapted from Rod Serling's TV drama and directed by Arnold Laven, the treatment is slick and melodramatic, save for Newman's powerful performance as the tormented, withdrawn soldier. Demanding fare for children

title: Rad
synopsis: Talia Shire stars in her own production of a story about a teenage bike enthusiast who overcomes an unscrupulous businessman's plot to keep him from winning a national championship race. Directed by Hal Needham, it is a pretentious and simplistic tale and its execution is graceless and unrewarding. Several obscene gestures by Ray Walston in a cameo role and some rough language by a litt1e girl seem quite unnecessary

title: Radio
synopsis: Moving portrait of a friendship which develops between a respected high school football coach (Ed Harris) and a mentally challenged young man (Cuba Gooding Jr.) that changes their lives and transforms their small Southern town. Director Mike Tollin's touching film, set in 1976, emphasizes the great impact one person can make by extending himself for the good of another. Yet despite fine performances and an inspiring story, the narrative flags, idling until its predictable ending. A scene of menace and some crass words

title: Radioactive Dreams
synopsis: Two youths leave their bomb shelters after 15 years to explore the post-nuclear world outside. Passing through a desolate and bleak landscape, they encounter a vile assortment of mutants and perverted road life. Many visual effects are used by director Albert Pyun simply to frame violence, brutality, nudity and profanity

title: Radio City Revels
synopsis: Thin comedy directed by Ben Stoloff in which a songwriter from the hills of Arkansas (Bob Burns) comes to the big city in hopes of finding success, but instead is taken in by a second-rate composer (Jack Oakie) who copies the songs the yokel sings in his sleep and sells them under his own name

title: Radio Days
synopsis: Writer-director Woody Allen celebrates the positive impact of radio on the lives of a New York family in the story of two women (Dianne Wiest and Mia Farrow) seeking romance via different paths. This nostalgic look at the 1940s indicates that the values of that era have been lost and even the fond memories are fading

title: Radio Flyer
synopsis: Sensitive but jumbled drama about two kid brothers (Elijah Wood and Joseph Mazello) who build a wagon that can fly so the younger boy can escape their brutally abusive, alcoholic stepfather (Adam Baldwin). Director Richard Donner mixes a serious story about child abuse with elements of magical fantasy that don't successfully mesh. Continual menace to children and momentary graphic violence

title: Radioland Murders
synopsis: Opening night in 1939 Chicago for a new radio network proves wildly eventful when the head writer (Brian Benben) frantically struggles to keep the on-microphone actors supplied with dialogue while trying to reconcile with his estranged wife (Mary Stuart Masterson) and elude police after him for a series of murders that begin in the station after it signs on the air. Director Mel Smith's chaotic comedy is a case of overkill with a script too stuffed with incident and an immense cast that is largely wasted in scrambled comic misfires. Several murders played for laughs, some sexual innuendo and a flash of partial nudity

title: Ra Expeditions, The
synopsis: Documentary record of anthropologist Thor Heyerdahl's voyage from Africa to the Americas in a papyrus reed boat called the Ra, the name of an Egyptian god. Using a reed craft of early Mediterranean design, Heyerdahl set out to demonstrate that such a ship could stand the long voyage between hemispheres, and does on a second try. Produced and directed by Lennart Ehrenberg, the documentary enables a vicarious sharing of adventure on high seas

title: Rafferty and the Gold Dust Twins
synopsis: Bumbling Los Angeles driving-test examiner (Alan Arkin) is kidnapped by roving hippies (Sally Kellerman and Mackenzie Phillips) and forced at gunpoint to drive them to New Orleans. Directed by Dick Richards, everything about this predictable heart-tug road movie is bogus, including the realistic language and frequently sordid situations

title: Raffles
synopsis: Ronald Colman turns on the charm as the gentleman thief who steals a valuable necklace to help a needy pal, then has to outwit Scotland Yard's bulldog sleuth (David Torrence). Directed by Harry D'Arrast and George Fitzmaurice, the picture of an honorable crook is dated and its treatment creaky, but still fun for all that

title: Raffles
synopsis: Playful gentleman thief (David Niven) steals a jeweled necklace from under the nose of a Scotland Yard inspector (Dudley Digges) and the chase is on. Directed by Sam Wood, Niven's bright performance as the lightfingered Raffles sparkles in its stuffy British society setting but the period plot fairly creaks and the action is disappointingly slack. Justice prevails implicitly

title: Raga
synopsis: American documentary provides an historical introduction to the musical heritage of India and Ravi Shankar's part in introducing it to Western audiences. Produced and directed by Howard Worth, the account is filled with insights about the individual and the cultural diffusion engendered by modern world communications

title: Rage
synopsis: Muddled melodrama set in a remote area of Mexico where an alcoholic doctor (Glenn Ford) is bitten by a dog with rabies, then delivers a poor woman's baby before racing the clock to get the serum needed to save his life. Directed by Gilberto Gazcon, the dubbed Mexican production is hardly credible, especially with Stella Stevens' role as the doctor's would-be girlfriend. Much menace, a complicated childbirth and some sexual innuendo

title: Rage
synopsis: After camping out with his boy one night, an Arizona sheep farmer (George C. Scott) wakes to the horror of finding his son and flock dying in convulsions. When he finally learns that a secret military test of nerve gas is responsible, he goes beserk and sets out to destroy those he considers responsible. The story of a decent man crushed by a technocracy unconcerned with the individual is told by Scott in his debut as a director in purely melodramatic terms with two-dimensional figures and plot contrivances. Yet it is close enough to reality to trouble any viewer's complacency, though its violent conclusion undercuts the meaning of what precedes these scenes of destruction

title: Rage at Dawn
synopsis: Slack Western directed by Tim Whelan has an undercover lawman (Randolph Scott) join an outlaw band of brothers (led by Forrest Tucker) in order to get the goods on corrupt officials in 1866 Indiana. Stylized violence, including a lynching

title: Rage: Carrie 2, The
synopsis: Nasty horror film in which callous high schoolers taunt an emotionally fragile classmate (Emily Bergl) who eventually turns her telekinetic powers on them with murderous ferocity. Director Katt Shea's sequel exploits teen angst, peer pressure and sexist attitudes to deliver a bloodbath of cheap thrills. Gory multiple killings, a sexual encounter, much implied promiscuity, brief nudity, some rough language and a few instances of profanity

title: Rage in Harlem, A
synopsis: Toting a trunkful of stolen gold, a scheming sexpot (Robin Givens) hooks up with a gullible chump (Forest Whitaker) but is tracked down by her furious ex-lover and partner in crime (Badja Djola). Bill Duke directs an overproduced potboiler awash in brutal characterizations and sleazy situations. Excessive, gory violence, some promiscuity and nudity and much rough language

title: Rage in Heaven
synopsis: Labored adaptation of the James Hilton novel in which a cracked millionaire (Robert Montgomery) kills himself so that it appears he has been murdered by a friend (George Sanders) he suspects is in love with his wife (Ingrid Bergman). Directed by W.S. Van Dyke II, the fine cast seems hopelessly adrift in this static, unconvincing melodrama. Unsettling atmosphere and a suicide

title: Rage of Paris, The
synopsis: Flimsy romantic comedy directed by Henry Koster in which a Frenchwoman (Danielle Darrieux) stranded in New York agrees to trick a millionaire (Louis Hayward) into marryiage, then falls for his even wealthier friend (Douglas Fairbanks, Jr.). Romantic situations and some sexual innuendo

title: Raggedy Ann and Andy
synopsis: Feature-length musical cartoon inspired by the long-time childhood favorites is, unfortunately, distinguished more by the technical excellence of Richard Williams' animation than by any real creative verve or even sense of imagination. The songs are mostly forgettable and there is no story line of any significance to keep children's attention

title: Raggedy Man
synopsis: A young divorcee (Sissy Spacek) in a small Texas town during the Second World War has a brief romance with a sailor passing through (Eric Roberts) and fends off the unwelcome attentions of two local louts who threaten her and her two boys. Director Jack Fisk fails badly in the attempt to mix childlike whimsey, light romance and Gothic terror. Some violence and premarital sex are central to the plot

title: Raging Bull
synopsis: Hard-edged, uncompromising portrait of former middleweight boxing champ, Jake La Motta (Robert De Niro in an outstanding performance) and his agonizing relationship with his second wife (Cathy Moriarity) and his brother (Joe Pesci). Director Martin Scorsese's stark black-and-white treatment conveys La Motta's often grim, violently hostile personality, which, the film suggests was born of sexual problems. Brutal fight scenes, a graphic bedroom sequence and rough language

title: Raging Tide, The
synopsis: Uneven crime melodrama in which a San Francisco hood (Richard Conte) escapes a pusuing police detective (Stephen McNally) by hiding out on a fishing trawler whose captain (Charles Bickford) treats him like a son. Directed by George Sherman, the situation is redemptive but the characters remain largely undeveloped and the plotting overly contrived. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Ragman's Daughter, The
synopsis: British bittersweet romance between a young tough who steals out of need and his hopelessly middle-class girl friend who does it for kicks. Scripted by Alan Sillitoe and directed by Harold Becker, the predictable plot lacks energy and drive as well as credibility

title: Ragtime
synopsis: Loose, sporadically effective adaptation of the E.L. Doctorow patchwork novel about some representative Americans at the turn of the century. Notable among them are James Cagney as the police commissioner of New York City and a black piano player (Harold E. Rollins, Jr.) who turns into a revolutionary combating social injustice. Directed by Milos Forman, it succeeds as a lavish historical re-creation but gets low grades in the matter of credible characterization. An excessively extended sequence involving partial nudity and some rough language

title: Raiders of the Lost Ark
synopsis: Tongue-in-cheek action melodrama about Indiana Jones, an archeologist-adventurer (Harrison Ford), and his feisty girlfriend (Karen Allen) who save the biblical Ark of the Covenant for the good old U.S.A. despite the worst efforts of a clutch of Nazi villains. Director Steven Spielberg's attempt to recapture the excitement of the old movie serials becomes tiresome and repetitious in its reliance upon constant action. Intense violence, gruesome special effects and a questionable use of something as sacred as the Ark as a source of destructive power

title: Raiders of the Range
synopsis: Western programmer directed by John English in which the Three Mesquiteers (Bob Steele, Tom Tyler and Rufe Davis) are hired to stop the acts of violence which are keeping oil workers from drilling a new well. Stylized violence

title: Raiders, The
synopsis: Muddled Western directed by Herschel Daugherty in which Wild Bill Hickok (Robert Culp) and Buffalo Bill Cody (James McMullan) try to help desperate Texas ranchers (led by Brian Keith) avoid bloodshed on a cattle drive through hostile country to the railhead in Abilene, Kansas. Frontier violence and justice questions

title: Raid on Rommel
synopsis: World War II adventure gasps along with Richard Burton's commandos as they fight Rommel's Afrika Korps across the Sahara and through Tobruk to an awaiting rescue unit, leaving a path of mayhem and devastation in their wake. Directed by Henry Hathaway, the action sequences are made up of stock footage and darkened sequences lifted from the 1966 "Tobruk." Ludicrous desert action histrionics

title: Raid, The
synopsis: Fact-based Civil War account of how the Vermont border town of St. Albans was sacked in 1864 by Confederate soldiers who mounted the attack from Canada after escaping from Union prison camps. Directed by Hugo Fregonese, the story centers on the Reb officer (Van Heflin) who spends some days reconnoitering the town disguised as a Canadian, then leads the raid despite having been befriended by many of the townspeople. Wartime violence and the conflict between military duty and human compassion

title: Railroad Man, The
synopsis: Series of misfortunes plague a working-class family in Italy after World War II. The sincerity of the characterizations more than outweigh the contrivances of the plot. Pietro Germi both directs and stars as the head of the family but it is a child actor (Eduardo Nevola) who will steal the affection of even the most cynical viewer

title: Rails & Ties
synopsis: Intimate, moving drama in which a terminally ill woman (Marcia Gay Harden) and her emotionally repressed railroad engineer husband (Kevin Bacon) find their failing relationship revived when they surreptitiously shelter a boy (Miles Heizer) whose mentally ill single mother (Bonnie Root) committed suicide by parking in front of the husband's train. Director Alison Eastwood, in her first feature, balances a plot that tugs shamelessly at every heartstring with an understated approach that generally forestalls sentimentality. Problematic religious elements, upper female nudity, tense accident scene, one use of the f-word, two crude words, one crass term and one use of profanity. Acceptable for older teens

title: Rails into Laramie
synopsis: Standard Western in which an Army troubleshooter (John Payne) is sent to clean up the corruption that has halted the building of the transcontinental railroad in 1869 Wyoming. Directed by Jesse Hibbs, the story pits noble troubleshooter against devious troublemaker (Dan Duryea) who eludes justice until tried by the first all-woman jury in U.S. history. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Railway Children, The
synopsis: Three children (Jenny Agutter, Sally Thomsett and Gary Warren) and their mother (Dinah Sheridan) are forced to move from their comfy Victorian mansion to an austere cottage in the country along the railway tracks while they wait expectantly for their Daddy to be cleared of false charges. Directed by Lionel Jeffries, the entire production is colored with an instinctive, childlike innocence and loyalty providing viewers of all ages with a warming and reassuring conviction that even in the most adverse times hope and love can, indeed must, exist

title: Rain
synopsis: Stilted but still powerful version of Somerset Maugham's South Seas story of Sadie Thompson (Joan Crawford), a hard-as-nails prostitute waiting out a monsoon on Pago Pago where she attracts both a U.S. Marine (William Gargan) and a missionary (Walter Huston) whose efforts to reform her lead to his own terrible downfall. Director Lewis Milestone generates the story's sexual tension through suggestion rather than overt action, with the confrontations between Crawford and Huston deeply charged with emotion. Sexual situations and references as well as an offscreen suicide

title: Rainbow Brite and the Star Stealer
synopsis: In her film debut, Rainbow Brite, the creation of toy manufacturers, must save the universe from destruction. Not strong on imagination or substance but lots of color and action designed to sell dolls to the toddler crowd. A- I (G) ( 1985 )

title: Rainbow, The
synopsis: British adaptation of the 1915 D.H. Lawrence novel about the sexual and political awakening of an adolescent girl (Sammi Davis) occasioned by her maverick swimming instructor (Amanda Donohoe). Despite writer-director Ken Russell's uncharacteristically restrained treatment of the material, there are several needlessly explicit depictions of heterosexual and lesbian encounters

title: Rain for a Dusty Summer
synopsis: Humberto Almazan, a popular Mexican actor who retired from the screen at the age of 35 to become a missionary priest, returns to portray Father Miguel Pro, a Mexican priest whose ministry during a time of religious oppression in the 1920s made him a folk hero and, ultimately, a martyr. Unfortunately, Arthur Lubin's heavy-handed direction of an oversimplified, melodramatic script makes the religious theme appear absurd and prevents a talented cast (including Ernest Borgnine as the dictator) from developing any but superficial characterizations, especially with the flat, expressionless dubbing of the mostly Spanish-speaking cast. Restrained violence

title: Raining Stones
synopsis: Gritty British social drama about an unemployed Catholic (Bruce Jones) who's determined to buy his daughter a First Communion dress but, unable to find enough odd jobs to pay for it, borrows the money from a loan shark who terrorizes his family when he can't repay it. Director Ken Loach explores working-class life in semi-documentary fashion, finding universal appeal in the story of a good but muddled family man whose struggles to find work are often humorous, though they have serious consequences reflecting social justice issues. Passing sexual references, occasional profanity and assorted rough language

title: Rainmaker, The
synopsis: Static melodrama in which a 1913 con man (Burt Lancaster) promises to bring rain to a drought-stricken farm family (headed by Cameron Prud'homme), then comes to realize his flamboyant flim-flam has inspired the farmer's lonely daughter (miscast Katharine Hepburn) with hope of finding a husband. Directed by Joseph Anthony, the feel-good story of realizing one's dreams relies more on the dialogue than the action, with unconvincing results despite game performances from most of the cast. Brief stylized violence and sexual situations

title: Rainmaker, The
synopsis: ( see: "John Grisham's The Rainmaker" )

title: Rain Man
synopsis: A shady Los Angeles car dealer (Tom Cruise) loses the family inheritance to an older brother (Dustin Hoffman) who suffers from irreversible autistic savant syndrome and has been institutionalized most of his life. On a cross-country auto journey, the younger brother drops his plans for a custody battle when he learns to love his brother despite his disability. Under Barry Levinson's direction, the brothers' intense and sometimes comical interaction during the life-affirming journey is wonderful but the rest of the movie is less satisfying and detracts from the character study. Much profanity, a few intense but brief emotionally unhinged outbursts by the autistic protangonist and a fleeting off-camera sex scene

title: Rain or Shine
synopsis: Sentimental comedy in which the young owner (Louise Fazenda) of a failing circus depends upon a savvy manager (Joe Cook) to keep it running -- even putting on a show almost by himself when the performers strike over unpaid salaries. Director Frank R. Capra builds the movie around the multi-talented Cook who flawlessly performs a variety of circus acts while proving equally adept in nonsensical dialogues with comic Tom Howard and pantomimes with clown Dave Chasen. Some crude humor and a bit of sexual innuendo

title: Rain People, The
synopsis: Shirley Knight plays a pregnant woman fleeing husband and home to come to terms with her womanhood and incomplete sense of fulfillment. Written and directed by Francis Ford Coppola, the movie's theme of flight from responsibility is treated with poetic intensity and subtle nuance. Some violence and sexual references

title: Rains Came, The
synopsis: Soggy romantic melodrama set in a remote Indian principality where some Western visitors endure monsoon, earthquake and cholera, resulting in the moral transformation of a dissolute painter (George Brent) helped by the love of a missionary's daughter (Brenda Joyce) and of a cynical socialite (Mryna Loy) inspired by a noble Indian physician (Tyrone Power). Director Clarence Brown uses the exotic setting to make the stock characters almost as interesting as the spectacular catastrophes they face, though the script's dated colonial attitudes may put some viewers' teeth on edge. Romantic situations and ethnic stereotyping

title: Rains of Ranchipur, The
synopsis: Romantic clunker set in modern India where the rich American wife (Lana Turner) of an English lord (Michael Rennie) wins the love of an idealistic Hindu doctor (Richard Burton) until an earthquake makes her realize she can't compete with his dedication to helping those in need. Directed by Jean Negulesco, this updated version of "The Rains Came" flounders in pedestrian action, unconvincing characters and shallow emotions, with even the scenes of devastation wrought by earthquake and flood rousing little interest. Natural disasters and romantic complications

title: Raintree County
synopsis: Epic misfire about a Hoosier youth (Montgomery Clift), his hometown sweetheart (Eva Maria Saint) and the troubled Southern belle (Elizabeth Taylor) he marries on the eve of the Civil War. Directed by Edward Dmytryk, the tragic romance unfolds in a muddled, overlong narrative which, despite lyric interludes and interesting period detail, flounders in its focus on the unbalanced wife's lethal obsessions with race. Wartime violence and suicide in the plot resolution

title: Rain Without Thunder
synopsis: Dreary talking-heads feature offers a series of repetitious interviews about the case of a woman (Ali Thomas) convicted of fetal murder in the year 2042 after a Constitutional Amendment has made abortion illegal. Instead of a movie, writer-director Gary Bennett has made a cheap propaganda piece substituting cardboard figures for human beings and straw arguments for conflicting moral principles. Unfairly caricatures the moral issue of abortion

title: Raise the Red Lantern
synopsis: Exquisitely mounted period piece about a young Chinese bride (Gong Li) who competes daily with her husband's three other wives to win his favor and establish pre-eminence in the household. Director Zhang Yimou's tragic story of women reduced to treachery to maintain self-esteem is depicted in the context of a closed, tyrannical society. Subtitles. Much sexual innuendo and malicious intrigue

title: Raise the Titantic!
synopsis: Failed action melodrama with Jason Robards and Richard Jordan in a story about attempts by American and Russian soldiers of fortune to recover rare minerals from the sunken luxury liner. Director Jerry Jameson's lackluster underwater adventure is unbelievably lethargic and muddleheaded

title: Raise Your Voice
synopsis: Uplifting 'tween drama about a small-town girl (Hilary Duff) who must overcome self-doubts when she is accepted into an ultracompetitive summer music program at a prestigious conservatory in Los Angeles. Directed by Sean McNamara, the film makes up for a lack of originality with its positive, heartfelt message and appealing performance by Duff. A fatal car crash, an instance of drunkenness and some mildly crude language

title: Raising Arizona
synopsis: Nicolas Cage and Holly Hunter play a simple-minded childless couple who kidnap one of a set of quintuplets to raise as their own in this madcap comedy from the Coen brothers, Joel and Ethan. Stridently effective parody of socially conscious drama has some vulgar and brutal moments played with deadpan intensity by Cage and a host of crude and profane heavies, perfectly restrained at the borderline of good taste

title: Raising Cain
synopsis: An unfaithful wife (Lolita Davidovich) suspects her eccentric husband (John Lithgow) when neighborhood women and their toddlers, including her own, begin disappearing. Writer-director Brian de Palma parodies his own and other horror movies in a clunky mix of comedy and terror that never meshes individual scenes into a cohesive whole. Intermittent violence, a discreet sexual encounter and occasional rough language

title: Raising Helen
synopsis: Pleasant enough story about a spirited single gal (Kate Hudson) who is given custody of her nieces and nephew (Hayden Panettiere, Abigail Breslin and Spencer Breslin) when her sister unexpectedly dies in a car accident, forcing the career-minded young woman to re-evaluate her priorities. Despite some endearing, funny moments and a cast that charms, director Garry Marshall's lightweight film isn't able to strike a balance between comedy and drama, resulting in mediocre fare. Brief, mild sexual innuendo, implied underage drinking and a few instances of crass language

title: Raisin in the Sun, A
synopsis: Fine screen version of the Lorraine Hansberry play about a young black man in a Chicago slum (Sidney Poitier) whose ambitions to get ahead in the world come into conflict with the values of his mother (Claudia McNeil in a remarkable performance). What keeps this story about the evils of racial segregation from being dated is that director Daniel Petrie and a very capable cast have focused their energies on depicting human aspirations common to all and transcending limits of plot and period

title: Rake's Progress, The
synopsis: ( see "Notorious Gentleman" )

title: Rambling Rose
synopsis: A kindly Southern family (headed by Robert Duvall and Diane Ladd) in 1935 takes in an abused 19-year-old (Laura Dern) whose promiscuous habits cause continual problems in the community. Directed by Martha Coolidge, the story begins playfully but sensitive performances and the lead character's eventual maturity make this an uncommon and wistful movie. Discreet scene of foreplay by teen-agers, numerous references to promiscuity and a flash of nudity

title: Rambo: First Blood Part II
synopsis: Rambo (Sylvester Stallone) is released from prison to undertake a secret mission to free Americans still being held in Vietnam and, after much slaughter, does so only to face the traitor who wanted the mission to fail. Playing shamelessly upon the fears and hopes of the relatives of MIA's, this comic-strip movie features excessive violence

title: Rambo III
synopsis: One-man wrecking crew John Rambo (Sylvester Stallone) returns to the battlefield, this time in Afghanistan, to save his mentor, Col. Trautman (Richard Crenna), from certain death at the hands of his Soviet captors. Directed by Peter MacDonald, the movie's plot is as simplistic as its politics and Stallone's performance is notable only for some self-mocking humor. Excessive violence and rough language

title: Rambo
synopsis: ( see: "First Blood" )

title: Rampage
synopsis: Flat adventure tale in which a German zoo hires an American wildlife trapper (Robert Mitchum) to bring back some tiger specimens from Malaya with the help of a veteran big game hunter (Jack Hawkins) and a native overseer (Sabu). Directed by Phil Karlson, the plot gets stuck on the aging hunter slowly going bonkers as his mistress (Elsa Martinelli) falls for the trapper, with entirely unconvincing results. Stylized violence, menace, sexual situations and much innuendo

title: Rampage
synopsis: When a particularly perverse serial murderer (Alex McArthur) pleads insanity at his California trial, the young prosecutor (Michael Biehn) argues that society will only be safe from this mad killer if he is given the death penalty. Writer-director William Friedkin's courtroom drama centers on the slow, tortuous processes of the law rather than the gruesome details of the sadistic crimes, though it becomes increasingly clear that the movie is weighted on the side of capital punishment. Restrained depiction of grisly killings, the desecration of a church and the bizarre ravings of a sick mind

title: Rampage at Apache Wells
synopsis: Hokey German-produced Western from a Karl May story about the heroics of veteran frontiersman Old Surehand (Stewart Granger) in saving a wagon train from attack by Indians stirred up by an evil oil baron. Harald Philipp directs the melodramatics with a heavy hand and the ludicrous results are not helped by inept dubbing. Stylized violence and silly frontier stereotypes

title: Ramparts of Clay
synopsis: French director Jean-Louis Bertucelli uses scenes of everyday life in a small Tunisian village at the edge of the Sahara to tell the story of a young woman (Leila Schenna) who can no longer accept the old patterns in which she has been raised. This is a beautiful work showing the dignity of a simple way of life, while conscious of the irreversible forces that will transform it

title: Ramrod
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Andre de Toth in which a manipulative woman rancher (Veronica Lake) goads a larger rancher (Preston Foster) into a range war costing the lives of a top hand (Don DeFoe), the local sheriff (Donald Crisp) and others before her honest foreman (Joel McCrea) stops it, then quits her for another (Arleen Whelan). Some nasty violence and romantic complications

title: Ran
synopsis: Samurai version of Shakespeare's King Lear by director Akira Kurosawa is, unfortunately, little more than an opulently staged historical pageant, lacking pathos and tragic force. Many battle scenes but the violence is stylized

title: Rancho Deluxe
synopsis: Jeff Bridges and Sam Waterson star as footloose and free-spirited modern rustlers finally apprehended by a bumbling Slim Pickens. Director Frank Perry's unfunny comedy is further undone by nudity and graphic sexuality

title: Random Harvest
synopsis: Romantic melodrama in which a shell-shocked English officer (Ronald Colman) escapes an asylum at the end of World War I, marries a loving music-hall singer (Greer Garson), then forgets his new life when a head injury restores his pre-war memory and he returns to run the family business until his wife sees his picture in a newspaper. Directed by Mervyn LeRoy from James Hilton's novel, the contrived proceedings are kept from becoming too maudlin by a compelling cast and interesting period settings, but the sentimental results seem largely bogus today. Romantic complications

title: Random Hearts
synopsis: After discovering his wife and the husband of a Congresswoman were having an affair when both were killed in a plane crash, a Washington D.C. cop (Harrison Ford) becomes romantically involved with the man's widow (Kristin Scott-Thomas), jeopardizing her re-election. Director Sydney Pollack explores the painful aftermath of adultery in a plodding drama whose melodramatic subplot is similarly uninvolving. A discreet sexual encounter, brief violence, minimal profanity and an instance of rough language

title: Randy Rides Alone
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Harry Fraser in which an express agent (John Wayne) pretends to join an outlaw band in order to get the goods on its leader who's established a respectable front in town as a mute shopowner. Frontier violence

title: Range Beyond the Blue
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Ray Taylor in which an insurance investigator (Eddie Dean) poses as a singing cowboy while getting the goods on the man behind a series of stagecoach robberies. Frontier violence

title: Range Busters, The
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Roy Luby in which the title cowboy trio (Ray "Crash" Corrigan, John "Dusty" King and Max "Alibi" Terhune) find the killer who has been terrorizing a ranch near an abandoned gold mine. Stylized violence

title: Rango
synopsis: Sophisticated, comparatively edgy animated riff on Westerns during which a lonely chameleon (voiced by Johnny Depp) stumbles upon a Mojave Desert town where water and heroism are in short supply. Reteaming with the star of his "Pirates of the Caribbean" series, director Gore Verbinski oversees a visually striking, quite literate movie whose darker, existential ambitions would befuddle and bore kids, when not scaring them, and whose passing, but ill-advised foray into religious humor will jar on the sensibilities of many grownups. Some fairly intense cartoon violence, brief irreverent and frequent toilet humor, occasional innuendo and sexual references, an inaudible crude term and at least one instance of crass language

title: Ransom
synopsis: Talky, flat-footed suspenser in which a wealthy executive (Glenn Ford) and his hysterical wife (Donna Reed) agonize about the morality as well as practicality of paying kidnappers to return his young son. Director Alex Segal's serious but simple-minded picture suggests that there would be no kidnappings if no one paid ransom, but the concept is lost in the melodramatics of the harrowing situation. Much soul-searching and emotional duress

title: Ransom
synopsis: Fearing his kidnapped son will be killed anyway, an enraged father (Mel Gibson) spurns the FBI's advice to pay the ransom money and offers it instead to anyone who can identify the abductors (led by Gary Sinise) as he races against time to locate the boy. Director Ron Howard's taut action thriller twists and turns suspensefully, although its point-blank violence is disturbingly realistic. Several gory killings, deadly menace to a child, frequent profanity and much rough language

title: Rapa Nui
synopsis: Overblown melodrama set on Easter Island shortly before its first contact with Europeans follows two brawny natives (Jason Scott Lee and Esai Morales) as they compete in brutal physical ordeals to become leader of the island's clans and win the hand of the beautiful woman (Sandrine Holt) they both love. Directed by Kevin Reynolds, the story plays on the level of trite romance with uninvolving, undeveloped characters, the result being a visually striking but otherwise barren fiction. Some gruesome violence, much ethnographic nudity and a premarital sexual relationship

title: Rape of Love
synopsis: Difficult French drama about an attractive, self-possessed and quite intelligent young nurse (Nathalie Nell) who is abducted by four men and brutally raped. Directed by Yannick Bellon, it is a serious attempt to deal with a detestable crime of violence and its consequences, not only for the victim, her fiance, family and friends, but also for the rapists and society as a whole. Despite its good intentions, however, the rape scene is unnecessarily graphic and extended

title: Rapid Fire
synopsis: Having witnessed a mob murder, a college student (Brandon Lee) is betrayed in the federal witness protection program and reluctantly relies on two Chicago cops (Powers Boothe and Kate Hodge) and his own martial arts skills to stay alive. Dwight H. Little directs a graphic action yarn that does a slick job of exploiting murderous violence as exciting entertainment. Excessive violence, a brief sexual encounter, occasional nudity and much rough language

title: Rappin'
synopsis: A young ex-convict adept at rapping (the street art of fast talking) comes to the aid of the urban poor victimized by nasty landlords and the like. The actors, under Joel Silberg's direction, are personable but the flimsy story is nothing but a frame for a skill that's not likely to enthrall most viewers

title: Rapture, The
synopsis: Wooden tale of a depressed woman (Mimi Rogers) who tires of trying to fill the emptiness of her life with meaningless sexual encounters, joins a psuedo-Christian cult and becomes a deranged religious fanatic. Writer-director Michael Tolkin's blankly superficial treatment of the subject results in an unpalatable brew of sex, religious rhetoric and irrational psychology. Excessively graphic depictions of sexual encounters, eccentric interpretations of biblical texts and occasional rough language

title: Rare Breed, The
synopsis: Languid Western in which an English widow (Maureen O'Hara) and her grown daughter (Juliet Mills) arrive in 1884 Texas to deliver a prize Hereford bull purchased for a Scottish rancher (Brian Keith), but he's interested only in the widow and it's up to a veteran cowpuncher (James Stewart) to prove the bull's value in improving the longhorn breed of cattle. Directed by Andrew V. McLaglen, the narrative relies mainly on the comic potential of upper-class ladies coping with the rugged ways of the range, enlivened by occasional fistfights, shootouts and a stampede. Frontier violence and mild romance

title: Rascal
synopsis: A boy (Bill Mumy), a dog and a mischievous racoon spend a summer together in Small Town, U.S.A., in the innocent days just before World War I. Director Norman Tokar keeps the action lively (especially that of Rascal, the racoon) and the sentiment wholesome in this Disney production celebrating the virtues of rural America

title: Rashomon
synopsis: Medieval Japanese story in which a bandit (Toshiro Mifune) is charged with murdering a samurai and raping his wife but the three (the samurai speaks through a medium) give contradictory accounts, to which is added a yet different version of events as witnessed by a woodcutter (Takashi Shimura). Director Akira Kurosawa makes brilliant use of the actors and the sunlit forest setting in flashbacks restaging the four versions of the crime, but the result is less about the relativity of truth than about the human capacity for evil and deceit, a theme which ends on a hopeful note as the woodcutter rescues an abandoned baby. Subtitles. Stylized violence and sexual situations

title: Raspad
synopsis: Harrowing political drama, set during and just after the Soviet nuclear reactor explosion at Chernobyl in April 1986, follows a skeptical reporter (Sergei Shakurov) around as the official government continues to deny the enormity of the disaster. Director Mikhail Belikov compellingly converts a tragic incident in history into deeply-felt personal statement resonating with moral outrage. Subtitles. Somber theme and flashes of nudity

title: Rasputin
synopsis: Failed British dramatization of a sinister monk (Christopher Lee) in the Czar's court before the Russian Revolution. Directed by Don Sharp, the evil actions depicted are excessive in their visual detail

title: Ratatouille
synopsis: Delectable animated tale of a cute rat (voiced by Patton Oswalt) who, inspired by the spirit of a famous late chef (Brad Garrett), develops his improbable passion for cooking by becoming the secret adviser to an esteemed Paris restaurant's hapless garbage boy (Lou Romano), turning the latter into a star chef, while the eatery's jealous head chef (Ian Holm) contrives to uncover the secret of the boy's success. Writer-director Brad Bird's gorgeously animated production has a rare sophistication that should entertain adults as much as their children, while the messages of teamwork, honesty and following one's dreams are strongly conveyed. Subtle implication of a character born out of wedlock

title: Ratboy
synopsis: A boy whose facial deformity makes him look like a rodent becomes exploited for monetary gain. Directed by actress Sandra Locke (who also plays a leading role as one of those taking advantage of the boy), this version of the beauty-and-the beast fable lacks any convincing insight and relies upon conventional plot devices, including negative stereotyping of black Los Angelinos and people in the entertainment business. Liberal sprinklings of profanity

title: Rat Race
synopsis: Harebrained comedy about a billionaire Las Vegas casino owner (John Cleese) who sets up a gambling scheme in which betters wage on which of six candidates (including Cuba Gooding, Jr., Whoopi Goldberg and Jon Lovitz) can first reach a locker containing $2 million. Predictably, one obstacle after another is thrown in the candidates' way, but director Jerry Zucker's road comedy garners several laughs despite the familiar concept. Intermittent comically intended violence and menace, fleeting sexual innuendo and partial nudity, brief toilet humor and some crass language with profanity

title: Rat Race, The
synopsis: Predictable comedy-drama from Garson Kanin's play in which a saxophone player from Milwaukee (Tony Curtis) seeks to make good in Manhattan while saving money by sharing a flat with a struggling dancer (Debbie Reynolds), but their strictly platonic relationship unsurprisingly turns romantic. Directed by Robert Mulligan, the picture has some fun with familiar New York types and big-city hussles, but the artificial antics of two leads are too contrived to sustain interest. Sexual situations and innuendo

title: Rat's Tale, A
synopsis: Disappointing family fantasy in which a pair of enterprising rats save their community from a new rodent poison by finding an antidote in the flowers of a long-lost magical garden hidden in the subterranean rock beneath Manhattan. Directed by Michael F. Huse, the German production mixes live-action American actors and settings with beautifully crafted German marionettes and studio backgrounds, but the thin story of talking animals and magical powers is too belabored to hold much interest or charm

title: Ravenous
synopsis: Grisly thriller set in the 1847 Sierra Nevadas where a tiny group of soldiers (including Guy Pearce and Jeffrey Jones) are set upon by a cunning stranger (Robert Carlyle) claiming to have fled a cannibalistic killer in the area but it is he who has devoured numerous pioneers and now turns on the unwary soldiers. Director Antonia Bird's repulsive tale is made all the more stomach-churning by its graphic visuals, giddy music and jokey tone completely at odds with the continual slaughters. Excessive violence and gore, desecration of corpses, fleeting nudity and occasional profanity

title: Raven, The
synopsis: Grisly horror movie in which a surgeon (Bela Lugosi) goes batty after being rejected by a woman (Irene Ware) whose life he saved, then seeks his revenge with the help of an escaped killer (Boris Karloff) who needs the doctor to repair his disfigured face. Directed by Louis Friedlander (aka Lew Landers), the contrived proceedings grow ridiculously overwrought as the sadistic surgeon imprisons the woman and her loved ones in a torture chamber inspired by Edgar Allan Poe stories. Stylized violence, menacing situations and some gruesome visuals

title: Raven, The
synopsis: Edgar Allan Poe's poem is turned into a comic fantasy involving a serious conjuror (Vincent Price) and an inept colleague (Peter Lorre) who combine their magical powers in a duel to the death against a power-mad wizard (Boris Karloff). Directed by Roger Corman, the thin story offers some off-beat humor, mainly from Lorre's manic son (Jack Nichoson), but things turn lively once the duel of magic gets underway. Supernatural hokum

title: Raw Deal
synopsis: Fueled by pride and a promise, a small town sheriff (Arnold Schwarzenegger) massacres an entire crime syndicate in a bloody shootout providing a primitive brand of justice on the behalf of the slain son of his former FBI buddy (Darren McGavin). The excessive violence isn't justified by plot or characterization

title: Raw Edge
synopsis: Muddled Western set in 1842 Oregon where a cowboy (Rory Calhoun) takes on the cattle baron (Herbert Rudley) who murdered his brother, then saves the villain's wife (Yvonne De Carlo) when she's threatened by a lustful gunman (Neville Brand) during an Indian uprising. Directed by John Sherwood, the dire proceedings are often desperate but mostly senseless. Nasty violence including a lynching and attempted sexual assaults

title: Rawhide
synopsis: Low-budget Western in which N.Y. Yankee Lou Gehrig quits baseball to join his sister (Evalyn Knapp) in buying a ranch but once there, he runs into a protection racket which he busts with the help of a singing cowboy-lawyer (Smith Ballew), then returns to the peace and quiet of the Yankee ball park. Directed by Ray Taylor, there's some two-fisted action but Gehrig's genial tenderfoot is the whole show and worth seeing

title: Rawhide
synopsis: Suspenseful Western set in an Arizona stagecoach relay station where the attendant (Tyrone Power), a mother (Susan Hayward) and her toddler are held prisoner by escaped convicts (led by Hugh Marlowe) waiting to rob a gold shipment on an incoming stage. Director Henry Hathaway establishes the station's isolation and the helplessness of the captives, then tightens the tension as the two try to escape in time to warn the stage. Frontier violence and mounting menace

title: Rawhide Years, The
synopsis: Middling Western in which a riverboat gambler (Tony Curtis) is framed for murder, then tracks down those responsible (Peter Van Eyck and William Demarest), with a little help from a down-on-his-luck gunman (Arthur Kennedy). Director Rudolph Mate tries to make Curtis credible as an action hero but succeeds better with the colorful Western backgrounds and hard-bitten frontier types who made it dangerous. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Raw Wind in Eden
synopsis: Hokey romantic adventure in which an American playgirl (Esther Williams) crash-lands on an isolated Mediterranean island inhabited by a mysterious American (Jeff Chandler) who wants to be alone. Directed by Richard Wilson, the bogus situation goes nowhere until a climactic shootout resolves matters predictably. Romantic complications and sexual innuendo

title: Ray
synopsis: Jamie Foxx gives a bravura performance as Ray Charles, in this superior biographical film which traces the legendary singer's life, from childhood and early blindness in rural Florida to his rise from obscure pianist to chart-topping superstar, as he battles heroin addiction and navigates his solid home life with romantic liaisons on the road. Foxx's impersonation is amazingly accurate, but the entire cast is first-rate, and Taylor Hackford's direction seamlessly melds the satisfying, often exciting, musical numbers with the solid dramatic aspects of the story, which ends on an inspirational note in 1966 with Charles conquering his drug dependence. A handful of crude and profane words, sexual innuendo, racial epithets, drug use and discreet sexual situations

title: Razor in the Flesh
synopsis: Brazilian drama about a prostitute tormented by her pimp who in turn is taunted by a homosexual until the roles are reversed and attacker becomes victim and the story becomes a parable about the interchangeable roles of oppressor and oppressed. Directed by Braz Chediak, the movie is about characters living at the last extremities of humanity, vividly reacting with the desperation of those who can only hurt others and themselves because they have nothing left to hope for. As a reminder of our common human fraility, it cuts to the bone

title: Razor's Edge, The
synopsis: Glossy adaptation of W. Somerset Maugham's story of an American (Tyrone Power) who returns from World War I convinced there is more to life than attaining wealth, quits his society friends for Paris to rethink his goals, then winds up in India seeking spiritual wisdom. Directed by Edmund Goulding, the man's growing idealism leads him to give up the love of a socialite (Gene Tierney) and devote himself instead to helping a deeply troubled woman (Anne Baxter), but the result of all this selflessness adds up to little more than a slickly contrived tearjerker. Romantic complications and vague spiritual yearnings

title: Razor's Edge, The
synopsis: The path to salvation is hard in this ill-conceived and shallow remake of the 1946 version of the W. Somerset Maugham novel. Bill Murray plays a World War I veteran who travels in Europe to find the meaning of life and some measure of inner peace. Under the direction of John Byrum, Murray has difficulty displaying the emotion and sensitivity required by the role. Empty parable with some harsh language

title: Reaching for the Moon
synopsis: Slack Depression-era comedy about a financial tycoon (Douglas Fairbanks) who pursues a flighty socialite (Bebe Daniels) on an England-bound liner, then learns she's engaged and he's been wiped out on Wall Street. Directed by Edmund Goulding, Fairbanks flounders in a flat role that invites little sympathy and offers few opportunities for his athletic talents, except some silly pranks after drinking an especially potent cocktail. Sexual situations and innunedoes

title: The Reader
synopsis: Necessarily bleak but well-played and directed (by Stephen Daldry) adaptation of Bernhard Schlink's controversial best-seller set in postwar Germany about the morally complex relationship between a lawyer (Ralph Fiennes) and the older woman (superb Kate Winslet) with whom he had an affair when he was a teenager (18-year-old David Kross), and to whom he would read the great works of literature. Though that early liaison is morally unacceptable, it serves as a metaphor for Germany's collective guilt and its impact on later generations, gingerly suggesting the possibility of emotional reconciliation. Underage sexual relationship including several encounters, nudity, divorce, suicide, disturbing Holocaust material

title: Ready to Rumble
synopsis: Mindless comedy in which a dissolute ex-wrestling champ (Oliver Platt) is persuaded by two adoring, brainless fans (David Arquette and Scott Caan) to try to recapture the title. Director Brian Robbins simply magnifies the body-thrashing sound effects, piles on putrid toilet humor and unleashes a slew of loud, lowlife characters in a vulgar, dumber-than-dumb comedy. Exaggerated wrestling violence, implied sexual encounters, brief nudity, gross toilet humor, occasional profanity and an instance of rough language

title: Ready to Wear
synopsis: In this overlong, overripe jape at the phony pretentions of the fashion industry, the apparent murder of the head (Jean-Pierre Cassel) of Paris' biggest fashion show is mourned by his mistress (Anouk Aimee), applauded by his estranged wife (Sophia Loren) and shrugged off by the chief suspect (Marcello Mastroianni) while the show goes on its silly, inconsequential way. Robert Altman directs an empty film about a hollow profession, squandering an embarrassingly large cast in a slapdash series of unconnected shaggy dog stories about characters with whom one wouldn't want to spend five minutes, let alone 2 1/2 hours. Extended scenes with full nudity, much sexual promiscuity, some rough language and occasional profanity

title: Real Blonde, The
synopsis: Scattershot romantic comedy about a fashion make-up artist (Catherine Keener) and her live-in love, a struggling actor (Matthew Modine), whose relationship is tested by new romantic interests. Writer-director Tom DiCillo is better at mocking the superficial worlds of fashion and entertainment than in developing interesting central characters. Sexual situations with occasional nudity, frequent rough language and intermittent profanity

title: Real Genius
synopsis: When a college science whiz (Val Kilmer) and his fellow students discover they have been tricked by their professor (William Atherton) into helping create a laser weapon for the military establishment, they revolt and destroy their work. Director Martha Coolidge is unable to get any laughs from this failed satire on higher education. Some vulgar language and sexual promiscuity

title: Real Glory, The
synopsis: Training Filipino recruits to defend their land against invading Moros, a handful of American soldiers (notably Gary Cooper, David Niven and Broderick Crawford) help their "little brothers" learn to fight a fanatic enemy while also having to contend with a cholera outbreak. Director Henry Hathaway builds plenty of tension in the plight of the remote island outpost and stages some classy battle scenes but the patriotic melodrama seems dated hokum today, not least because of its patronizing attitude toward the Philippine people. Stylized violence, some of it rather grisly

title: Reality Bites
synopsis: While searching for a job, a novice filmmaker (Winona Ryder) becomes romantically involved with an ambitious TV programmer (Ben Stiller), much to the disgust of her lethargic musician friend (Ethan Hawke) who can't express his own romantic feelings for her. Also directed by Stiller, the movie takes a mildly comic look at the twentysomething generation caught between trying to juggle confusing adult relationships and starting careers in an economy with few opportunities. Implied premarital affairs

title: Real Life
synopsis: Episodic comedy, written and directed by comedian Albert Brooks, in which he plays the role of a moviemaker who wants to capture on film the life of a real American family, a Phoenix veterinarian (Charles Grodin), his wife (Francis Lee McCain) and their two children. While frequently hilarious, with a touch of black humor, many of the jokes are adult in nature but probably not too strong for older teenagers

title: Real McCoy, The
synopsis: When her little boy is kidnapped by criminals who need her expertise, a paroled bank robber (Kim Basinger) is forced to attempt one more treacherous bank job, with the help of her inept assistant (Val Kilmer). Russell Mulcahy directs a dull and plodding comedy of no originality and completely lacking romantic sparks between the couple. Intermittent violence, an uncritical attitude toward ill-gotten gain and an instance of rough language

title: Real Women Have Curves
synopsis: Credible coming-of-age story set in East Los Angeles where a heavyset 18-year-old Latina (America Ferrera) who is constantly criticized by her mother (Lupe Ontiveros) is torn between accepting a distant university scholarship or helping her older sister (Ingrid Oliu) keep her struggling sewing factory afloat. Director Patricia Cardoso captures the hardscrabble lives of a close-knit Mexican-American family and the half-dozen factory women who come to accept and find solidarity in their less-than-svelte figures. Some subtitles. An off-screen sexual encounter and an instance of rough language

title: Re-Animator
synopsis: In this abysmal effort, a zealous young scientist (Jeffrey Combs) develops a serum to raise the dead. Directed by Stuart Gordon, it's an abundantly gory affair made all the more revolting by its attempts at grisly humor

title: Reap the Wild Wind
synopsis: In this 19th-century adventure yarn, a sea captain (John Wayne) and a maritime lawyer (Ray Milland) fall for the same damsel (Paulette Goddard) while fighting a pirate wrecker-salvager (Raymond Massey) operating off the Florida Keys. Director Cecil B. DeMille depicts the era of sailing ships in colorful fashion with some rousing action sequences, including Wayne's battle with a giant squid, but the narrative frequently bogs down in fitful romance and soggy soul-searching. Some menace and stylized violence

title: Rear Window
synopsis: Stylish thriller in which a Manhattan photographer (James Stewart), immobilized by a broken leg, idly passes the time watching his neighbors across the way until witnessing a murder, then uses his girlfriend (Grace Kelly) to catch the killer (Raymond Burr). Director Alfred Hitchcock gradually notches the level of suspense to fever-pitch in the conclusion. Much menace and a stylized act of violence

title: Rebecca
synopsis: Daphne du Maurier's classic tale of mystery and romance tells of the remarriage of a wealthy British widower (Laurence Olivier) whose young bride (Joan Fontaine) is intimidated by the great estate of Manderley and its disapproving housekeeper (Judith Anderson) until she discovers the truth about the death of her husband's former wife. Alfred Hitchcock's first movie to be directed in the U.S. is slow and deliberate in turning Manderley into a sinister setting whose empty halls reverberate with the echoes of her brooding husband's deceased wife. Though more romantic than mysterious, it's effectiveness as an eerie exercise in suspense might rattle the very young

title: Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm
synopsis: Pedestrian Shirley Temple vehicle gives her the role of a "self-reliant" motherless child whose country aunt (Helen Westley) won't hear of her becoming a radio star until talent wins out. Directed by Allan Dwan, the predictable plot complications keep getting in the way of mild romance (Randolph Scott and Gloria Stuart), pale comedy (Slim Summerville, Jack Haley and William Demarest) and Shirley's singing and hoofing with Bill Robinson. Dated but innocent fun

title: Rebellion in Patagonia
synopsis: When armed violence broke out in 1921 between the landowners and striking workers of Patagonia, Argentina's southernmost state, the government intervened by sending in troops to help the landowners crush the workers. Large-scale Argentinian re-creation directed by Hector Olivera has much colorful action with hard-riding gaucho bands pitted against columns of soldiers in vintage autos. There are, however, some strong scenes of violence illustrating the inequities of power and class

title: Rebel with a Cause
synopsis: ( see "The Loneliness of the Long Distance Runner" )

title: Rebel Without a Cause
synopsis: Unconvincing tale of teenage angst portrays troubled Los Angeles youths (James Dean, Natalie Wood and Sal Mieno) whose alienation from affluent parents propels them into dangerous scrapes that eventually end in tragedy. Directed by Nicholas Ray, the picture's intended theme is more substantial than its clumsy execution and self-serving picture of adults as hypocritical and uncaring. Stylized violence

title: Rebound
synopsis: Diverting, if formulaic, comedy about a hotheaded, big-time college basketball coach (Martin Lawrence) who, after being banned from coaching on the collegiate level, finds redemption by turning a hapless junior high school hoop squad into winners and leading them to the state championship. Directed by Steve Carr, the warmed-over "Bad News Bears"-flavored premise has been done before (and much better), but Lawrence scores some points in his first family-friendly role, as does the film's feel-good message about teamwork, sportsmanship and believing in yourself. Some mildly crude language and humor and minor comic violence

title: Recess: School's Out
synopsis: Innocuous animated movie about six elementary school youngsters foil the plans of a bitter former principal (voice of James Woods) to wipe out summer vacation. Based on the cartoon TV show, director Chuck Sheetz's film feels like an extended series episode with flat animation and a flimsy narrative. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Reckless
synopsis: Pretentious, slow-moving account of star-crossed teenaged lovers (Aidan Quinn and Daryl Hannah) in a grimy, impoverished steel town treads numbingly familiar ground. Director James Foley has found no way to recharge the old formula nor has writer Chris Columbus discovered anything of significance. Aimed at a teenage audience, it has an abundance of nudity and graphic sex

title: Reckoning, The
synopsis: Nicol Williamson gives a brilliant performance as a London businessman who drinks too much, drives too fast, uses and abuses women, ruins business rivals, and even commits murder to avenge his father's death back in the Liverpool slum where he grew up. It is a portrait of a ruthless, amoral fellow, and yet director Jack Gold's fast-moving action melodrama takes a reckoning not only of him but of a society that rewards his brand of cut-throat tactics in life as well as the business world. A disturbing movie not intended as escapist fare

title: RED
synopsis: Witty but mayhem-packed spy caper in which a retired CIA agent (Bruce Willis) and his newfound girlfriend (Mary-Louise Parker) take to the road after being targeted for death by a high-level government and business cabal. Their efforts to unravel the conspiracy -- and to evade the hit man (Karl Urban) tasked with eliminating them -- are aided by a trio of the operative's old associates (Morgan Freeman, John Malkovich and Helen Mirren). They are allies who range from the reliable (Freeman) to the entertainingly flaky (Malkovich). Director Robert Schwentke's amusingly executed adaptation of Warren Ellis and Cully Hamner's graphic novel features a refreshingly chaste central romance. But its succession of gunfights and explosions, though mostly stylized, restrict its appropriate audience. Frequent, largely bloodless violence, brief gruesome imagery, a couple of uses of profanity, at least one use of the F-word, some crude language

title: Red
synopsis: Elusive but compelling tale in which a Swiss fashion model (Irene Jacob) with an ebbing long-distance romance strikes up a friendship with a retired judge (Jean-Louis Trintignant) whose life had been blighted as a young man when the woman he loved chose another, precisely the situation confronting a novice jurist (Jean-Pierre Lorit) who happens to be the model's neighbor, though the two don't meet until later drawn together by an act of fate.
