Preceded by "Blue" and "White," the concluding portion of director Krzysztof Kieslowski's "Three Colors" triology involves the viewer in the intertwining lives of three lonely individuals as it probes the connections between people and their place within a rational but uncertain universe. Subtitles. Mature themes with a fleeting but intense bedroom scene

title: Red and the White, The
synopsis: Hungarian dramatization about the confused struggles between Communists and anti-Communists that broke out in Eastern Europe after the Russian Revolution. Director Miklos Jancso's picture of a violent era when a man's shirt was worth more than his life is set against the bleak but hauntingly beautiful Volga countryside

title: Red Badge of Courage, The
synopsis: Powerful though uneven dramatization of Stephen Crane's novel about an Ohio youth (Audie Murphy) coming of age in combat during the Civil War. Brutally truncated by the studio before its release, what remains of director John Huston's effort is a strong, naturalistic re-creation of the period's bloody warfare of attrition and the human cost for those who fought it. The battlefield violence is strong fare for youngsters

title: Red Ball Express
synopsis: Standard World War II story of an Army unit of misfits (led by Jeff Chandler) formed after Normandy to move supplies to the front lines in truck convoys that often have to fight their way through by-passed enemy pockets. Directed by Budd Boetticher, the action is energetic and purposeful, though the characters (including Alex Nicol, Hugh O'Brien and Sidney Poiter) are the usual cross-section of comic, sentimental and heroic types. Wartime violence

title: Red Beard
synopsis: Japanese character study of a 19th-century doctor (Toshiro Mifune) who must be incredibly tough and unbending in running a clinic for the poor and yet tender and loving in his ministry to those who need his care. Director Akira Kurosawa's movie conveys the complexities of compassion in the person of this hard-headed, single-minded doctor made credible by Mifune's great performance. Realist depictions of the period's crude operating facilities

title: Red Beret, The
synopsis: ( see: "Paratrooper" )

title: Red Blood of Courage
synopsis: Adventure programmer directed by Jack English in which an undercover Canadian Mountie (Kermit Maynard) saves a woman (Ann Sheridan) being held hostage by a gang after her uncle's oil-rich land. Stylized violence

title: Red Boots for Christmas
synopsis: Animated tale about a long-ago Christmas in a small German town where Hans, a morose shoemaker with no family and few friends, feels left out of the season's cheer until visited by an angel with the promise of a special gift which causes Hans to labor on a special gift of his own. The half-hour video features colorful animation by Cuckoos Nest and a compelling story whose events lead Hans and viewers to understand the the Christian significance of the Christmas season. Worthwhile family entertainment

title: Red Corner
synopsis: Framed after a one-night stand for rape and murder, an American lawyer (Richard Gere) in China must rely on a government-appointed defense attorney (Bai Ling) to save him from imminent execution, but uncovering the facts puts her own life in jeopardy. Director Jon Avnet's dense political thriller hinges on a barely credible plot twist but manages to maintain suspenseful momentum up to a mushy conclusion. Some gory violence, a fleeting sexual encounter and brief nudity

title: Red Dawn
synopsis: Director John Milius presents a preposterous and heavy-handed war movie with the premise that the United States has been invaded by Russian and Cuban troops. A group of teenage Rambo's (led by Patrick Swayze and C. Thomas Howell) take up guerrilla warfare to preserve the integrity of America. Because of its violence and its glorification of the macho rather than patriotism, it is not for immature viewers

title: Red Desert, The
synopsis: Vague Italian mood piece about a troubled woman (Monica Vitti) living in the industrial city of Ravenna who struggles to find human warmth and hope in a seemingly alienated world. Directed by Michelangelo Antonioni, the unconventional narrative is more concerned with interior feelings than the exposition of events and many may find its images of disorientation irritatingly abstract and meaningless. Subtitles. Needlessly detailed treatment of sexual matters

title: Red Dragon, The
synopsis: Routine Charlie Chan mystery directed by Phil Rosen with the Chinese-American detective (Sidney Toler) in Mexico City helping a local cop (Fortunio Bonanova) solve a series of murders involving atomic secrets and the rare Chinese ink of the title. Comic racial stereotypes with Chan's #3 son (Benson Fong) and chauffeur (Willie Best)

title: Red Dragon: The Pursuit of Hannibal Lecter
synopsis: ( see: "Manhunter" )

title: Red Eye
synopsis: Uneven psychological thriller about a young air passenger (Rachel McAdams) en route to Miami who becomes an unwilling accomplice in a deadly assassination plot against a high-ranking government official orchestrated by the charming stranger (Cillian Murphy) sitting next to her on the plane, who coerces her cooperation by threatening to have her father back home in Florida killed if she refuses. Directed by Wes Craven, the initial takeoff is smart and suspenseful, but the film hits story turbulence midflight before nose-diving in the third act. Several instances of intense violence, including a graphic throat puncturing, as well as some crude language

title: Red Garters
synopsis: Flat-footed musical spoof of the Wild West where a cowboy (Guy Mitchell) rides into town, becomes involved with a saloon singer (Rosemary Clooney) and gets in trouble with the local big shot (Jack Carson). Directed by George Marshall, the thin story is spun out as a series of skits played against theatrical stage sets with forgettable songs by Jay Livingston and Ray Evans. Stylized violence and heavy-handed sexual innunendo

title: Redhead and the Cowboy, The
synopsis: Far-fetched Western adventure directed by Leslie Fenton follows a Confederate courier (Rhonda Fleming) making her way through Union territory with the help of a genial cowpoke (Glenn Ford) and a Yankee undercover agent (Exdmond O'Brien) until she reaches the hideout of a rebel guerrilla leader (Alan Reed). Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Redhead from Wyoming, The
synopsis: Stale Western directed by Lee Sholem in which a sheriff (Alex Nicol) teams with the title casino owner (Maureen O'Hara) to stop an ambitious crook (William Bishop) from starting a range war. Frontier violence and romantic complications

title: Red Heat
synopsis: Buddy-cop action thriller pairing a tight-lipped Soviet cop (Arnold Schwarzenegger) with a loud-mouthed Chicago cop (Jim Belushi) in a manhunt for a Soviet drug smuggler (Ed O'Ross) on the streets of Chicago. Directed by Walter Hill, the movie's international dimension adds nothing to the tired, overly familiar formula plot. Excessive violence and foul language

title: Red, Hot and Blue
synopsis: Tiresome, silly musical directed by John Farrow features Betty Hutton belting out some Frank Loesser tunes ("Where Are You Now That I Need You") as a would-be showgirl from Ohio whose dizzy schemes for publicity get her kidnapped by New York gangsters, then rescued by boyfriend Victor Mature, a struggling Broadway director. Mild showbiz romance with some comic violence

title: Red House, The
synopsis: Tangled psychological thriller about a crippled farmer (Edward G. Robinson) trying to save his adopted daughter (Allene Roberts) from discovering the terrible truth about her parent's death which lies hidden deep in a nearby woods. Writer-director Delmer Daves creates a suitably eerie atmosphere for a plot that never quite delivers the intended impact. Some stylized violence and romantic complications present and past

title: Redline
synopsis: Over-the-top action movie about illegal road racing in which a war hero (Nathan Philips) avenges the racing death of his brother (Jesse Johnson) and rescues a race-car driver (Nadja Bjorlin) from his shady high-rolling uncle (Angus Macfadyen). Director Andy Cheng's style is halfway between a music video and a video game, and the tone is a regrettable celebration of material excess. Some crude and crass language; mild sexual innuendo; an excessive amount of skimpily dressed women, though no nudity; some bloodless fight scenes; shots fired and explosions; and two killings

title: Red Line 7000
synopsis: Episodic story of racing car drivers (James Caan, John Robert Crawford and James Ward) and the women in their lives (Marianna Hill, Gail Hire and Laura Devon respectively). Director Howard Hawks fails to get much emotion out of cardboard characters whose romantic involvements are of less interest than the newsreel footage of auto races such as the Daytona 500 which furnish the movie's only real excitement. Racing accidents and sexual situations

title: Red Mantle, The
synopsis: ( see: "Hagbard and Signe" )

title: Red Mountain
synopsis: Convoluted Western in which a Confederate officer (Alan Ladd) is sent to the Colorado Territory to join a guerrilla band under Gen. Quantrell (John Ireland), discovers he's a renegade out to create his own empire by uniting the Plains Indians and determines to stop him. Directed by William Dieterle, matters are complicated by a subplot involving a gold prospector (Arthur Kennedy) and his fiancee (Lizabeth Scott), but the results are as predictable as they are contrived. Stylized violence, romantic complications and sexual innuendo

title: Red Planet
synopsis: Tepid sci-fi drama set in the year 2050 in which a team of astronauts (including Val Kilmer, Carrie-Anne Moss and Benjamin Bratt) is sent to Mars to set up an alternate place for humans to live since Earth is an environmental mess, but their crash landing leaves them without a viable means of escape. Director Antony Hoffman's predictable plot is mixed with mumbo-jumbo scientific chatter and gimmicky special effects which add up to a dull, tediously paced film. Some sci-fi violence, brief nudity, an instance of rough language and minimal crass language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Red Pony, The
synopsis: Uneven adaptation of John Steinbeck's story about a young boy (Peter Miles) growing up on a California ranch where he wrongly blames the death of a beloved colt on the hired hand (Robert Mitchum) until reconciled to its loss by the promise of another. Director Lewis Milestone does better with the troubled family relationships (aloof mom Myrna Loy, browbeaten dad Shepperd Strudwick and overbearing grandpa Louis Calhern) than the youngster's world and the ranch hand's surrogate role in it. Some harrowing moments, including the boy's hand-to-hand battle with a buzzard

title: Red Psalm
synopsis: Hungarian import uses a 19th-century peasant revolt as a socialist hymn celebrating the collective power of the people in their continuing struggle against oppression. Director Miklos Jancso's lyric flow of images is choreographed to a symphony of folk song and the movie's poetic strength is rooted in its agrarian setting and Eastern European folk traditions. Some may be offended by the work's appropriation of religious symbolism in a revolutionary context

title: Red Riding Hood
synopsis: This uninvolving update of the classic fairy tale, set in an imaginary medieval village, finds the maiden of the title (Amanda Seyfried) pursued by the youth she has loved since childhood (Shiloh Fernandez), by the scion (Max Irons) of the richest family in town -- to whom her parents (Virginia Madsen and Billy Burke) have betrothed her -- and, to a different end, by the local werewolf. A priest (Gary Oldman) renowned for laying lycanthropes low arrives, but turns out to be a cynical, sensual inquisitor. As directed by Catherine Hardwicke, the glum proceedings are low on entertainment value or emotional impact, while the off-kilter portrayal of the church makes this "Twilight" wannabe totally unsuitable for targeted teen audiences. Skewed treatment of Catholicism, brief nongraphic premarital sexual activity, moderate but sometimes gory violence

title: Red River
synopsis: Western classic in which a hardbitten Texas rancher (John Wayne) stakes his future on getting his herd to Abilene, but on the way he pushes his riders so hard they turn against him in a revolt led by his foster son (Montgomery Clift). Director Howard Hawks raises the story of a rugged cattle drive to epic proportion with sweeping action scenes, colorful characters, numerous mishaps along the trail and, at its center, the conflict between the rancher and the grown man he's raised from a boy. Harsh period violence and a sexual situation

title: Red River Renegades
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Thomas Carr in which an undercover government agent (Sunset Carson) investigates bizarre reports of stagecoaches setting out with valuable cargoes, then vanishing without a trace. Stylized violence

title: Red Rock West
synopsis: Mistaken for a hired killer, an honest drifter (Nicolas Cage) gets caught between a husband (J.T. Walsh) and wife (Lara Flynn Boyle), each plotting to murder the other, but things get really complicated when the actual hitman (Dennis Hopper) shows up. John Dahl directs an atmospheric and quirky suspense thriller whose plot coincidences are totally unconvincing but add some wry humor. Brief violence, fleeting bedroom scene and much rough language

title: Reds
synopsis: Epic-scale re-creation of the turbulent life and times of radical American journalist John Reed (Warren Beatty), best known for his sympathetic coverage of the 1917 Russian Revolution. Also written and directed by Beatty, the production intelligently balances the sheer spectacle of events with Reed's involvement in them and his personal relations with others, especially his wife (Diane Keaton). Benign view of adultery and revolutionary politics

title: Red Scorpion
synopsis: Violence-saturated action adventure set in an obscure African country where a deadly Soviet superagent (Dolph Ludgren) is saved from death by kindly bushmen and is transformed into a good guy who sees firsthand how his fellow Russians are cruelly decimating the native rebels. Director Joseph Zito fills his desert landscape with long, tedious chase and battle sequences, grisly violence, gruesome torture scenes and much profanity

title: Red Shoes, The
synopsis: Life imitates art in the romantic tragedy of a dedicated ballerina (Moira Shearer) in a company whose manipulative impresario (Anton Walbrook) forces her to choose between her love for a talented composer (Marius Goring) and her dedication to dancing. Written, produced and directed by Michael Powell and Emeric Pressburger, the convincing portrayal of the ballet world, on-stage and off, proves of more interest than the star-crossed romance and its relation to the title ballet which is the movie's thematic center. Suicide in the plot resolution

title: Red Sky at Morning
synopsis: Mindless World War II coming-of-age story set in New Mexico where a callow youth (Richard Thomas) lusts after a plump schoolmate (Catherine Burns) while his boozy mother (Claire Bloom) needs help fending off amorous "uncles." Directed by James Goldstone, the plot's serious level is hindered by the melodramatic treatment, with moral insights getting lost in the shuffle

title: Red Sonja
synopsis: Plodding, lackluster sword-and-scorcery movie directed by Richard Fleischer and starring muscleman Arnold Schwarzenegger who helps out a woman warrior intent on vengeance. The only bright spots are bits of unintentional humor. Some violence

title: Red Sun
synopsis: The gimmick for this bloody European Western teams a hard-bitten cowboy (Charles Bronson) with an inscrutable samurai warrior (Toshiro Mifune) in order to track down an outlaw (Alain Delon) who double-crossed the cowboy and dishonored the samurai. Along for the ride is a superfluous prostitute (Ursula Andress). Granted the fantasy plot, director Terence Young treats the derring-do with too little whimsical flair and too much prosaic gore

title: Red Sundown
synopsis: Formula Western directed by Jack Arnold in which a reformed badman (Rory Calhoun) helps the local sheriff (Dean Jagger) reform a lawless town. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Red Sun Rising
synopsis: Sluggish martial arts picture directed by Francis Megahy follows a Japanese cop (Don Wilson) who tracks a gangster (Soon-Teck Oh) to Los Angeles, then teams with a woman cop (Terry Farrell) and his former teacher (Mako) to stop the villain from selling military weapons to rival street gangs. Stylized violence, ninja psychic powers, sexual situations and occasional rough language and profanity

title: Red Tent, The
synopsis: Ambitious Italian-Russian re-creation of the crash of an Italian dirigible over the North Pole in the spring of 1928. Under the command of General Umberto Nobile (Peter Finch), the crew pitches a red tent hoping to be spotted by rescuers while three of their members go in search of help. Directed by Mikhail K. Kalatozov, the classic adventure of man vs. nature aspires to epic height but blunders with a frame device of Nobile's tortured memories and feelings of failure. Gruelling picture of struggle for survival that has one of the leading characters (Sean Connery) committing suicide

title: Red Tomahawk
synopsis: Lackluster Western set immediately after the 1876 Custer massacre with an Army captain (Howard Keel) warning the citizens of Deadwood to prepare for an attack while he and two locals (Broderick Crawford and Scott Brady) try to get through the Sioux war parties with a pair of Gatling guns for an approaching troop column. Directed by R.G. Springsteen, the formula exercise is chiefly of interest for its aging cast of familiar faces (Joan Caulfield, Wendell Corey, Richard Arlen, Tom Drake and others). Frontier violence and much menace

title: Red Violin, The
synopsis: Sumptuous drama spans more than 300 years as an exquisitely handmade violin passes from its grief stricken maker in 1681 Italy to a child prodigy in Vienna a century later, a passionate virtuoso in late 1800's England, a disgraced music teacher during Mao's Cultural Revolution and on to an eventful auction in contemporary Montreal. Enhanced by the movie's haunting music track, director Francois Girard orchestrates the numerous stories with dramatic flair and fine visual details although the pace is halting. Some subtitles. Instances of theft, a fleeting sexual encounter, brief nudity, momentary opium use and a few instances of profanity

title: Red, White and Blue
synopsis: Taking as its pretext the 1971 Report of the Commission on Obscenity and Pornography, the exploitation documentary even gives the President's commissioners a minute or two of interview time before getting to explicit illustrations of the report's subject

title: Reed: Insurgent Mexico
synopsis: John Reed, the American newspaper correspondent who gained fame through his reports on the Russian Revolution, had previously covered Mexico in the revolutionary chaos of 1913-1914. Reconstructing this period is a Mexican movie following Reed's sojourn with various rebel units, his struggle to maintain his objectivity about events in the face of his inclinations to side with the oppressed, and his symbolic act of solidarity with the revolution that ends the movie. The result has the feeling of an historical document as well as a convincing character study of an idealist

title: Reefer Madness
synopsis: Reissue of a movie antique about the evils of marijuana has appeal today apparently because it is so easy to laugh at but also perhaps because it all seems so familiar. It underscores the point, however, that preachy exaggeration is the worst kind of propaganda

title: Reflection of Fear, A
synopsis: Failed Gothic horror movie about a disturbed young woman (Sandra Locke) who lives with her mother (Mary Ure) in a sinister mansion where a series of gruesome murders take place when her estranged father (Robert Shaw) pays a call. Directed by William Fraker, it has a good cast, moody atmosphere but muddled script with a ludicrous conclusion. Heavy-handed sexual implications

title: Reflections in a Golden Eye
synopsis: Screen version of the Carson McCullers' novel about the twisted relationships and abnormal inclinations of a homosexual Army officer (Marlon Brando). Directed by John Huston, the movie's treatment of its various characters communicates little insight or compassion. Exploitative nudity

title: Ref, The
synopsis: Escaping from the cops on Christmas Eve, a jewel thief (Denis Leary) takes a battling married couple (Judy Davis and Kevin Spacey) hostage in their home, pretending to be their marriage counselor when relatives arrive for dinner. Ted Demme's comedy of barbs is at times wickedly funny but its one-joke premise gradually runs out of steam before the fuzzy ending. Fleeting violence, a dysfunctional family, some sexual innuendo and much rough language

title: Regarding Henry
synopsis: Inspirational drama about a high-rolling Manhattan attorney (Harison Ford) who loses nearly all his memory and motor functions after a brain injury and must reacquaint himself with his very neglected wife and 11-year-old daughter (Annette Bening and Mikki Allen). The positive message in director Mike Nichols well-acted drama is undercut by the snail-like pace of its leaden, overly manipulative script. A brief scene of violence, some adulterous references and an instance of rough language

title: Regeneration
synopsis: Absorbing World War I story of a psychologist (Jonathan Pryce) in a British psychiatric hospital who in 1917 is assigned to rid poet Siegfried Sassoon (James Wilby) of his anti-war views and return him to combat duty. Directed by Gillies Mackinnon, the movie centers in therapy sessions and casual conversations between the two about the lunacy of war and its cost to the human spirit, but these dialogue scenes are paced and given deeper meaning by flashbacks to the horrors of the battlefield, their traumatic effect on other patients and the treatment they receive to mend their broken psyches. Graphic battlefield scenes, disturbed psychiatric patients, sexual situations, brief nudity and a profane expletive

title: Reg'lar Fellers
synopsis: Weak formula comedy directed by Arthur Dreifuss and based on Gene Byrnes' comic strip about a bunch of small-town kids (Carl "Alfalfa" Switzer, Billy Lee and others) who busy themselves on makeshift inventions which come in handy when they try to save a mean old lady (Sarah Padden) from big-city swindlers. Dated amusement

title: Regret to Inform
synopsis: Evocative documentary visits with American and Vietnamese women whose husbands were killed in the war to explore the lingering effects of war on its survivors on both sides of the conflict. Writer-director Barbara Sonneborn, herself a Vietnam war widow, weaves together a haunting series of recollections from the homefront and from villagers who were under siege which eloquently make a strong anti-war statement. Some disturbing images of war victims

title: Reign of Fire
synopsis: Ridiculous sci-fi flick set in futuristic England in which an American militia leader (Matthew McConaughey) and a British “fire chief” (Christian Bale) team up to destroy centuries old fire-breathing dragons that are scorching the Earth. The convoluted narrative in director Rob Bowman’s visually murky film is punctuated by frenetic action sequences which are remarkably similar and suffocatinglyconstructed. Much strong action violence and brief crass language

title: Reign Over Me
synopsis: Singularly offbeat, albeit poignantly etched, buddy film about a successful dentist (Don Cheadle) who meets up with and tries to rehabilitate his college roommate (Adam Sandler), once a dentist himself and now sadly childlike, suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder as a result of his wife and children perishing Sept. 11, 2001, and in the process comes to terms with some of his own emotional issues. Writer/director Mike Binder's drama is well-intentioned, and Sandler pulls off a difficult part with distinction, but the script is paradoxically original yet formulaic with often implausible character motivation, though the 9/11 theme and Sandler's heart-wrenching character tug at the emotions. Pervasive rough and crude language and occasional profanity, some forthright and crass sexual discussion, and emotional outbursts

title: Reincarnate, The
synopsis: Creepy 8,000-year-old man (Jack Creley) convinces a reluctant young sculptor (Jay Reynolds) to give up his body when he explains that a mind transplant involves the deflowering of a young virgin. Wooden acting and leaden script detailing the intricacies and advantages of reincarnation result in occult balderdash, seasoned with some coy titillation

title: Reincarnation of Peter Pound, The
synopsis: Young man (Michael Sarrazin) dreams of his own murder in a previous life and falls in love with the woman (Jennifer O'Neill) who was his daughter in that life. Director J. Lee Thompson's muddled story has frequent nudity and graphic sex scenes

title: Reindeer Games
synopsis: Multiple double crosses abound when a paroled car thief (Ben Affleck) is pressured by his new girlfriend (Charlize Theron) into joining murderous thugs (led by Gary Sinese) to rob a casino. Director John Frankenheimer's cynical crime thriller has the sole good character committing deliberate murder after a slew of implausible plot twists. Recurring violence and mayhem, a sexual encounter, some nudity, much profanity and constant rough language

title: Reivers, The
synopsis: Screen version of William Faulkner's last novel about a 12-year-old boy (Mitch Vogel) from a small Southern town in 1905 who is introduced to some of the realities of the adult world when taken on a trip to Memphis by a devil-may-care cousin (Steve McQueen). Director Mark Rydell has created a rich bit of Americana that owes as much to Mark Twain as to Faulkner, but its story of growth towards manhood may be perplexing for youngsters, especially a lengthy brothel sequence

title: Relations
synopsis: The stale theme of this Danish exploitation import is the infatuation of a middle-aged businessman (Bjorn Puggard) for a scheming teenager (Gertie Jung) who gets his cash for her procurer-boyfriend (Paul Glargard). Director Hans Abramson prolongs the trio's restless relations to the point of senseless boredom

title: Relentless
synopsis: Routine Western in which a horse breeder (Robert Young) leaves a prize colt in the care of an itinerant peddlar (Marguerite Chapman) while eluding a posse as he tries to track down the claim jumper (Barton MacLane) who framed him for a triple murder. Director George Sherman paces the action with some cute antics from the colt and low-key romance between the preoccupied wanted man and the patient woman who helps him. Frontier violence

title: Relentless
synopsis: Los Angeles serial killer (Judd Nelson) goes on the rampage, slaughtering victims who share his name, while a mismatched detective duo (Leo Rossi and Robert Loggia) bicker their way to a far-fetched capture, though not before viewers witness the psycho's sadism up close. Director William Lustig has too many plotlines to deal with and ends up exploiting the violence and the killer's abusive upbringing. Much grisly sadistic violence and profanity

title: Relic, The
synopsis: Gruesome horror flick in which a genetically altered creature goes on a murderous rampage at a gala museum party while a homicide detective (Tom Sizemore) and a biologist (Penelope Ann Miller) at the gathering work to kill it before they all die. After much murky plotting, director Peter Hyams' dark monster movie delivers a final half-hour of suspenseful jolts. Graphic fantasy violence with shots of decapitated heads, some rough language and intermittent profanity

title: Reluctant Astronaut, The
synopsis: Halting comedy directed by Edward J. Montagne features Don Knotts as a janitor in a space training center where he briefly overcomes his fear of heights to take a solo flight in a space capsule whose automated control system is not quite foolproof. Silly misunderstandings and deceptions

title: Remains of the Day, The
synopsis: Having utterly sacrificed his personal life in the service of an English Lord (James Fox) who ended up as a disgraced Nazi sympathizer, an aging English butler (Anthony Hopkins) journeys to the West of England in 1958, hoping to rehire and possibly risk romance with the spirited housekeeper (Emma Thompson) whose love he dutifully spurned decades earlier. James Ivory meticulously directs a splendid portrait of personal tragedy as a selfless man sadly comes to realize in his unquestioned devotion to his master he has missed out on the all the best things in life. A few emotional confrontations

title: Remarkable Andrew, The
synopsis: Patriotic whimsey with the ghost of Andrew Jackson (Brian Donlevy) coming to the aid of his namesake (William Holden), an honest bookkeeper accused of embezzlement by corrupt officials (Porter Hall, et al.) after he finds a discrepancy in the city accounts. Director Stuart Heisler treats the thin proceedings in light-hearted fashion, but the fantasy elements can't overcome the predictable civics lesson at its core

title: Remarkable Mr. Kipps, The
synopsis: When a lowly drapper's apprentice (Michael Redgrave) in Edwardian England inherits a fortune, his childhood sweetheart (Phyllis Calvert) saves him from being turned into a snob by a socialite (Diana Wynyard). Director Carol Reed scores with this leisurely paced, finely detailed version of H.G. Wells' gentle comedy of manners about a easy-going commoner's sudden rise in society. A bit of a stretch for youngsters

title: Remember My Name
synopsis: Woman (Geraldine Chaplin), sent to prison for trying to kill her husband's mistress, returns to harrass her now ex-husband (Anthony Perkins) and his new wife (Berry Berenson), at first from a distance, but then moves in for closer encounters of various kinds. The melodrama is rather flat and listless, further dragged down by mannered performances and the uninspired direction of Alan Rudolph. Rough language and adult situations

title: Remember the Night
synopsis: Wryly sentimental romance has a New York prosecutor (Fred MacMurray) spend the Christmas recess by taking an accused jewelry-store shoplifter (Barbara Stanwyck) to his mother's home in Indiana where they fall in love, then return to face the music in court. Director Mitchell Leisen keeps the romance bright and amusing, yet gives it substance with a warm depiction of the Hoosier homestead (Beulah Bondi, Elizabeth Patterson and Sterling Holloway) and its homespun values. Innocent romantic situations and legal complications

title: Remember the Titans
synopsis: Uplifting drama set in 1971 about the desegregation of two powerhouse high school football teams that learn to overcome racism and go on to victory under the leadership of their African-American coach (Denzel Washington). Aside from occasionally faltering with emotional manipulation, director Boaz Yakin's heartwarming, fact-based saga shows the triumph of the human spirit over adversity, fear and societal prejudices. Racism theme, fleeting homosexual kiss and minimal crass language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Reminiscences of a Journey to Lithuania
synopsis: Independent filmmaker Jonas Mekas' record of a visit to the land of his birth is as informal as a family album and as filled with warmth and affection. Mekas serves as an always enthusiastic guide to this celebration of his past through the present and his unpretentious pleasure at showing his family bonds will most likely stimulate remembrances of one's own immigrant roots

title: Remo Williams: The Adventure Begins
synopsis: A New York policeman (Fred Ward) who was apparently slain in an encounter with muggers has actually been given a new identity as a member of a secret organization dedicated to seeing that justice is done despite a defective legal system. Though amoral in concept, director Guy Hamilton's movie is so divorced from reality that it is for the most part inoffensive. Aside from a brutal opening scene, the violence is muted

title: Renaissance
synopsis: Interesting animated film set in the Paris of 2054 about a kidnapped scientist (Romola Garai), the former protege of a renowned geneticist (Ian Holm), who works for a sinister megacompany promising eternal youth and beauty, and the cop (voiced by Daniel Craig) assigned to rescue her, assisted by the woman's older sister (Catherine McCormack), who fends off the sinister forces of the company's vice president (Jonathan Pryce) with his own motives for finding her first. Director Christian Volckman's debut feature film -- basically a graphic novel come to life -- has a sometimes overly complex plot that, in its essentials, we've seen before, but the striking black-and-white design and committed acting by the prestigious voice talent hold your interest. Action violence, scenes of peril, murder, a brief nongraphic sexual scene, partial nudity elsewhere, some innuendo, and rough and crude language

title: Renaissance Man
synopsis: Appealing comedy-drama in which a jobless adman (Danny DeVito) hired by the Army to teach basic English skills to semiliterate recruits succeeds in getting them to read Shakespeare, despite interference from their skeptical drill sergeant (Gregory Hines). Director Penny Marshall maintains a consistent level of genuine humor throughout a script peppered with self-help themes sandwiched between the laughs. An instance of rough language

title: Renaldo & Clara
synopsis: Singer Bob Dylan makes his debut as a movie director by taking footage from one of his concert tours and interspersing it with some absurd and awkward episodes acted out in improvisational style by himself, his wife and friends (Sam Shepard, Ronee Blakley, Joni Mitchell, Arlo Guthrie and Joan Baez). The result is a tedious, dismal exercise in self-indulgence. Although there is some rough language, like much of the other dialogue, it is almost unintelligible

title: Rendezvous in Paris
synopsis: Three droll anecdotes of the mating game involve a law student (Clara Bellar) and her unfaithful boyfriend; a woman (Aurore Rauscher) who insists on meeting a suitor in out-of-the-way parks; and a painter (Michael Kraft) infatuated with a woman (Benedicte Loyen) he follows into a museum. Writer-director Eric Rohmer playfully spins each tale around the fragile, uncertain relationships between intelligent people with more on their minds than sex. Subtitles. Mature themes

title: Rendition
synopsis: Quietly intense thriller about a wife's (Reese Witherspoon) efforts to discover the whereabouts of her Egyptian-born husband (Omar Metwally) who has been abducted by the U.S. government upon returning to the States from a business trip, and taken to an unspecified North African country where he is tortured and interrogated as a suspected terrorist, while a novice CIA analyst (Jake Gyllenhaal) is given the task of monitoring the case. Director Gavin Hood raises valid questions about the government's use of this abduction procedure called "extraordinary rendition" in combating terrorism, yet the ambiguity about the Egyptian character is frustrating, and a time twist at the end seems rather pointless, but the film is absorbing throughout, and Meryl Streep has a good role as the CIA honcho who orders the arrest. Torture, shadowy partial and rear nudity, a nonmarital relationship, brief profanity, and a suicide bombing with bloodshed

title: Renegades
synopsis: Routine Western directed by George Sherman follows the travails of an outlaw's honest son (Larry Parks) and the woman (Evelyn Keyes) who sticks up for him. Stylized violence

title: Renegades
synopsis: An undercover cop (Kiefer Sutherland) and a Native American (Lou Diamond Phillips) uneasily join forces to nab some murderous jewel thieves. The two leads are appealing and the stunts are hair-raising, but the storyline is implausible and director Jack Sholder does little with a promising Indian subplot. Some profanity, several cold-blooded murders and intense comic book chases

title: Renfrew on the Great White Trail
synopsis: Routine adventure directed by Al Herman in which the singing Canadian Mountie of the title (James Newill) investigates several murders committed at a trading post, then gets his man after a harrowing dog-sled chase. Stylized violence

title: Reno 911!: Miami
synopsis: Ultraraunchy, big-screen version of the Comedy Central cable-TV series has the bumbling deputy sheriffs from Reno (Robert Ben Garant, Thomas Lennon and Kerri Kenney-Silver) traveling to Miami for a police convention. Due to an act of bioterrorism that confines all the real cops to the meeting hall, the eight hapless officers are forced to patrol Miami's sun-drenched streets and must deal with a beached whale, a drug kingpin and their own perverse sexual tendencies. Amazingly, they save the day; yet watching the warped crudity on parade is too high a price to pay for justice in director and co-writer Garant's putative comedy. Pervasive vulgar language, nudity, sex acts, masturbation, scatological humor, episodes of cartoonish violence and drug use

title: Rent
synopsis: Imaginative expansion of the late Jonathan Larson's long-running Broadway musical -- an updating of "La Boheme" -- about the lives and loves of New York's East Village artists, several of them HIV-positive. Director Chris Columbus has remained largely faithful to the original -- and many of the original cast members reprise their roles here -- while the dissolute lifestyles of some of the characters take second place to the overriding themes of love, connection and fellowship, and the film encapsulates a significant cultural era. Implied drug use, same-sex relationships, suggestive dancing and movement, some rough and crude language and an anti-establishment outlook

title: Rent-a-Cop
synopsis: Sleazy crime picture in which a Chicago ex-cop (Burt Reynolds) joins forces with a reformed prostitute (Liza Minnelli) to nab a mad-dog killer (James Remar) working for a drug lord (John Stanton). Directed by Jerry London, the formula plot is awash in repulsive characters with sour results. Gory violence, sexual situations, profanity and rough language

title: Replacement Killers, The
synopsis: Bullet-riddled action movie in which a hitman (Chow Yun-Fat) finds himself targeted for death after refusing an assignment, then unwittingly ensnares a shady lady (Mira Sorvino) in his desperate attempts at flight. Directed by Antoine Fuqua, the mindless story merely shuffles its flat, unsympathetic characters from one bloody shootout to the next with boring predictability. Excessive violence, some rough language and a few instances of profanity

title: Replay
synopsis: When a young woman (Marie-Jose Nat) loses her memory in an auto crash, her loving husband (Victor Lanoux) seems overly solicitous in his efforts to help her regain her past. Director Michel Drach's psychological melodrama provides little more than some modest diversion, adult in theme, with infidelity figuring as a minor element in the plot

title: Repo Man
synopsis: Absurdist mix of social satire and sci-fi thrills is tied to the story of an aimless youth (Emilio Estevez) learning the tricks of the auto-repossession trade from a hardened pro (Harry Dean Stanton), but their quirky misadventures end in wild pursuit of a stolen car with radioactive aliens in the trunk. Writer-director Alex Cox lumbers along erratically with a scenario aiming pot shots at mindless consumerism and urban subcultures but without substantial results. Gritty violence, sexual situations and rough language

title: Repo Men
synopsis: Extremely violent futuristic thriller about two men (Jude Law and Forest Whitaker) whose job is to repossess artificial human organs when the recipient falls behind on exorbitant interest payments owed to a malevolent corporation. Despite a major twist involving virtual technology, there's scant evidence that director Miguel Sapochink wants to spin a profound science-fiction yarn, let alone offer a serious cautionary tale or insightful social satire; with no redeeming qualities to offset the butchery and degradation, it counts instead among the most distasteful and morally barren movies to appear in recent years. Unrelenting brutal, graphic violence; grisly images of surgical incisions and operations; instances of drug use; fleeting glimpses of bystanders engaged in sex acts; several implied or simulated nonmarital sexual encounters between the leading male and female characters; partial rear nudity; and pervasive rough, crude and profane language

title: Report from China
synopsis: Japanese documentary filmed in 1966-67 during the flux of the Cultural Revolution shows the total faith of the Chinese leadership in the efficacy of ideology to solve their many economic and social ills as well as their willingness to sacrifice everything for the future

title: Report on the Party and the Guests, A
synopsis: A friendly outing in the woods is disrupted when some menacing strangers escort the group of picnickers to a lakeside party where they are commanded to enjoy themselves. When one escapes the party, his friends join in the deadly pursuit. Czechoslovakian director Jan Nemec's parable on freedom and force has a threatening atmosphere of restraint and absurdity that makes for some very unsettling viewing, which is the reason it was originally banned by Communist officials

title: Report to the Commissioner
synopsis: Violent urban drama about a young detective (Michael Moriarity) and his baptism of fire as a member of a New York City undercover narcotics squad. Directed by Milton Katselas, the movie is partially successful in conveying its complex vision of a claustrophobic urban hell. Sordid backgrounds and incidents

title: Reprieve
synopsis: ( see: "Convicts 4" )

title: Reprisal!
synopsis: Buying a small ranch in an area where killing Indians is considered sport, a half-Indian cowboy (Guy Madison) has to choose sides. Directed by George Sherman, the action plot is nothing out of the ordinary but its pro-Indian slant is emotionally engaging, though not fully realized. Stylized violence

title: Reptile, The
synopsis: Minor British horror movie directed by John Gilling unfolds 19th-century tale of an Englishwoman (Jacqueline Pearce) who returns from travels in Borneo cursed with the power of periodically turning into a deadly human cobra. Stylized violence and mild hokey effects

title: Reptilicus
synopsis: Formula monster movie directed by Sidney Pink in which a giant prehistoric reptile is regenerated by Danish scientists, then escapes to run amok in Copenhagen. Hokey animated monster and special effects destruction

title: Requiem
synopsis: Truth-inspired, but fictionalized, drama set in Germany about a sheltered, devoutly Catholic, epileptic college student (Sandra Huller) who suffers increasingly severe episodes and comes to believe that she is possessed by demons, prompting conflicting responses from her religious parents (Burghart Klaussner and Imogen Kogge), parish priests (Walter Schmidinger and Jens Harzer) and secular-minded students (Nicholas Reinke and Anna Blomeier). Loosely based on the same 1976 case as �The Exorcism of Emily Rose,� director Hans-Christian Schmid�s deliberately paced consideration of faith, psychology and suffering avoids sensationalism and horror cliches for sober realism. Schmid maintains respectful impartiality in presenting the various points-of-view � taking the family�s beliefs seriously � and though the film would seem to suggest a scientific, rather than a supernatural, explanation, it ultimately remains inconclusive on the central question. Subtitles. Disturbing scenes of mental affliction or possible demonic possession, an implied sexual encounter, and some crude language

title: Requiem for a Dream
synopsis: Harrowing drama about a mother and her son who face dire consequences when they respectively become addicted to diet pills and cocaine. Despite its visual polish, director Darren Aronofsky's dark film savagely presents the brutal agonies of legal and illegal drug addiction but in an inescapably and gratuitously raw manner. A lewd homosexual act as well as a few sexual encounters, nudity, graphic portrayal of drug addiction, some violence and recurring rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Requiem for a Heavyweight
synopsis: Gritty drama in which a social worker (Julie Harris) tries to help a punched-out prizefighter (Anthony Quinn) find a new line of work until stymied by his manager (Jackie Gleason) who plans to square his debts by turning the boxer into a clownish wrestler. Directed by Ralph Nelson from Rod Serling's TV script, the result is an emotionally strong picture of a broken-down boxer trying to retain some human dignity after 17 years in the ring. Brutal boxing scenes and corrupt aspects of the fight game

title: Requiem for a Secret Agent
synopsis: Dubbed Italian clunker directed by Sergio Sollimo in which a U.S. spy agency hires a free-lance agent (Stewart Granger) to nail an ex-Nazi (Peter Van Eyck) operating in Tangiers. Stylized violence and an implied sexual encounter

title: Requiem for Dominic
synopsis: A Romanian expatriate (Felix Mitterer) returns to his homeland during the December 1989 Revolution to help a wounded friend (August Schmolozer) but discovers the man is dying in police custody after being falsely accused as a terrorist. Using actual footage from the Revolution, director Robert Dornhelm's disjointed dramatization personalizes Romania's political oppression through the fact-based story of a committed Christian who shows remarkable compassion on his deathbed. Subtitles. Graphic views of massacred and naked corpses

title: Rescue Dawn
synopsis: Uplifting film salutes the valor of rank-and-file military personnel by chronicling the real-life ordeal of German-born U.S. Navy pilot Dieter Dengler (Christian Bale), who was shot down over Laos in 1966 and taken prisoner by soldiers allied with the North Vietnamese. Without hyperbole of any kind, German writer-director Werner Herzog presents a vivid, lyrical portrait of a courageous and compassionate man whose dream of becoming an aviator led him to America and then to the forbidding jungles of war-torn Southeast Asia. Powerful but nongraphic scenes of violence and torture, some crude language and profanity, some locker-room-style banter and scatological references appropriate to the context

title: Rescuers Down Under, The
synopsis: Animated tale of a little Australian boy and a beautiful eagle who must be saved from the snares of an evil poacher by Bernard and Miss Bianca, two top mouse agents. Directors Hendel Butoy and Mike Gabriel have created a delightful family fantasy, a captivating eyeful that never flags and is filled with good humor and innocent charm. Several moments of danger and menace

title: Rescuers: Stories of Courage -- Two Women
synopsis: Fact-based dramatization about two Catholic women who risk their lives to save Jews during World War II, one of whom is a Polish governess (Elizabeth Perkins) who protects her late employer's only child from Nazi round-ups, then raises him as a Jew, the other a Frenchwoman (Sela Ward) who hides a Jewish family in the attic of her home until the liberation. Directed by Peter Bogdanovich, the Showtime cable movie convincingly re-creates the terrors of the era in which these desperate activities took place, poignantly evoking the human drama in each story with fine performances from the two leads. Heart-wrenching depiction of the plight of Holocaust victims, considerable menace and an instance of rough language

title: Rescuers, The
synopsis: Disney animated feature in which two tiny members of the International Rescue Aid Society of mice are dispatched to save an orphan girl from the clutches of wicked Madame Medusa ensconced in her lair on a Mississippi sternwheeler beached in the dark Louisiana swamps. Director Wolfgang Reitherman paces the action rather smartly, though some scenes may be a bit scary for the very young. All others, however, will find it entertaining enough, helped along by an imaginative assortment of human and animal characters as well as several pleasant songs

title: Rescue, The
synopsis: Implausible fantasy about five youngsters whose larkish, bloodless rescue of their Navy fathers from a North Korean prison camp might have been pulled off by the Hardy Boys, but not by these ragtag Navy brats. Director Ferdinand Fairfax jumps from one farfetched turn to another, with little sense of menace or suspense until the improbable climax. Some rough language and comic-book violence

title: Reservation Road
synopsis: Riveting drama about the efforts of an increasingly obsessive father (Joaquin Phoenix) to identify the driver (Mark Ruffalo) who killed his son in a hit-and-run accident, while the guilt-racked offender, a father with a boy the same age, struggles to do the right thing. Director and co-writer Terry George's film -- from co-writer John Burnham Schwartz's 1998 novel -- has considerably more moral complexity than your standard revenge melodrama, while Phoenix and Ruffalo are each superb in difficult roles. A violent though nongraphic car accident; some profanity, rough language and crude expressions; and domestic discord. Acceptable for older teens

title: Reservoir Dogs
synopsis: Inept low-budget movie about bungling gangsters (Harvey Keitel among them) featuring incessant rough language and gory brutalities that are pretentiously meant to be outrageous but only dull the sensibilities of unfortunate viewers of the aptly titled woofer written and directed by Quentin Tarantino

title: Resident Evil
synopsis: Savage action horror thriller focuses on a military group (led by Milla Jovovich and Michelle Rodriguez) fighting a powerful computer gone berserk after a deadly virus is released which turns workers in an underground laboratory into flesh-eating zombies. A spin-off of the eponymous video game, director Paul Anderson's frenetic sci-fi flick has an absurd story that uses explicit violence and tuneless, ear-piercing music to fill in cavernous narrative holes. Graphic violence with many vile images, fleeting sex scene with partial nudity and recurring rough language and profanity

title: Resident Evil: Apocalypse
synopsis: Mindless action/horror sequel taking up where the first film left off, as a ragtag handful of survivors (led by Milla Jovovich, genetically enhanced with superhuman powers this time around) fight their way to safety after the deadly virus unleashed in the first film escapes underground containment, turning the infected surface population into flesh-eating zombies. Based on the ultraviolent video game and directed by Alexander Witt, this "Dawn of the Dead" clone is devoid of anything remotely resembling narrative, character or redeeming moral value, opting instead for nonstop, gratuitous carnage. Excessive graphic violence, desecration of religious objects and brief partial nudity, as well as recurring rough language and profanity

title: Resident Evil: Extinction
synopsis: When an international conglomerate unleashes a virus on the world, most people are turned into flesh-eating zombies and the earth into a desert, leaving a band of survivors, led by two men (Oded Fehr and Mike Epps) and two women (Ali Larter and Ashanti), to form a convoy in search of other uninfected people, their travels at length bringing them into contact with a superwoman (Milla Jovovich) who is out to fight the evil doctor (Iain Glen) who experimented on her and who still hopes to turn the virus to the corporation's advantage. Watching director Russell Mulcahy's gorefest may be the cinematic equivalent of combat: moments of jarring fear are interspersed with long periods of abject tedium. Nearly constant blood, gore and mutilation, cannibalism, brief frontal and upper female nudity, drug use, and much crude and some crass language

title: Restless Natives
synopsis: Lighthearted comedy features exquisite scenic backgrounds of the Scottish highlands in an implausible story about two youths (Joe Mullaney and Vincent Friell) who devise an outlandish scam to extort money from tourists in the hope of gaining financial security before they hit the ripe old age of 20. Their only potential problem is a vacationing CIA agent (Ned Beatty). Director Michael Hoffman concentrates on the relationship between the two friends rather than the flimsy plot and its twist ending

title: Restless Years, The
synopsis: Inane teenage sudser directed by Helmut Kautner centers on a withdrawn adolescent (Sandra Dee) whose overly protective mother (Teresa Wright) tries to shield her from making the same mistake she had made at her age, while a new classmate (John Saxon) befriends the girl and defies a bunch of small-town hypocrites. Muted sexual innuendoes and references to illegitimacy

title: Restoration
synopsis: Elaborate but uneven costume drama in which a frivolous physician (Robert Downey Jr.) in the 17th-century court of King Charles II (Sam Neill) reluctantly finds his humanity by treating London's poor after being tossed out of court on a royal whim. Director Michael Hoffman switches gears rather awkwardly in going from bedroom farce to a more substantial drama of personal transformation. Fleeting bedroom scenes with nudity and frequent references to sexual court intrigues

title: Resurrecting the Champ
synopsis: Compelling film, based on true events, about the evolving friendship between a young sportswriter (Josh Hartnett) and a homeless former boxing champ (Samuel L. Jackson) which forces the writer to take a fresh look at himself and to reevaluate his basic relationships, including those with his wife (Kathryn Morris) and son (Dakota Goyo), and the troubling memory of his deceased father. Director Rod Lurie's deeply moving -- as well as moral -- film features morally complex characters who experience redemption, an excellent script, and outstanding performances, though the boxing sequences may prove disturbing to those with a low tolerance for the sport. Occasional vulgarity and profanity, boxing violence including one sequence with blood, skimpy costuming and suggestive movements, public urination and images of a disturbing body scar

title: Resurrection
synopsis: Engrossing but flawed drama about a woman (Ellen Burstyn) who discovers that she has the power to heal people after barely surviving a tragic accident in which she loses her husband. The screenplay by Lewis John Carlino sets up a fascinating situation, but neither Carlino nor director Daniel Petrie is able to work it out in satisfactory fashion. The spiritual side of faith healing is dealt with in very unimaginative fashion showing the afterlife, for example, as being, quite literally, the light at the end of the tunnel. Theme and language require a mature perspective

title: Resurrection
synopsis: Brain-dead gore fest directed by Russell Mulcahy in which a Chicago cop (Christopher Lambert) goes after a serial killer collecting body parts from his victims to be reassembled at Easter as a symbol of the Second Coming. Graphic violence, frontal nudity, degrading use of Christian beliefs, profanity and rough language

title: Return from Witch Mountain
synopsis: The further adventures of the two castaway space children from :2OEscape to Witch Mountain'' with Tony falling into the villainous hands of Christopher Lee and Bette Davis who are intent on using the boy's powers for personal gain. Tia, with the aid of the lovable kind of street gang that exists nowhere outside of Disney films, rescues him in the nick of time. The sequel, directed by John Hough, is a movie that younger children will enjoy

title: Return of a Man Called Horse, The
synopsis: Sequel finds bored English nobleman (Richard Harris) back in South Dakota when his adopted Indian tribe needs a leader. After another gruesome purification ceremony consisting of mind-altering drugs and of having bones inserted into his chest, he leads his tribe to victory over their enemies. Director Irvin Kershner delivers a serious film, entertaining and beautifully photographed but, its emphasis on violence makes this decidedly mature fare

title: Return of Count Yorga, The
synopsis: Though this time the gentlemanly ghoul (Robert Quarry) falls in love (his one weakness), most of his time is spent, however, preying upon a neighboring orphanage. The sequel is properly amusing and frightening, with director Bob Kelljan sprinkling the proceedings with enough blood, however, to warrant caution for young or squeamish viewers

title: Return of Dracula, The
synopsis: Offbeat horror tale in which the legendary vampire (Francis Lederer) flees pursuers in post-World War II Eastern Europe by emigrating to California where he's taken in by the unsuspecting relatives of the man he killed for his identity papers. Directed by Paul Landres, the hokey proceedings generate little suspense though the genial small-town setting provides some eerie moments and Lederer's modern-day Dracula exudes sinister intensity. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Return of Frank James, The
synopsis: Dandy sequel to "Jesse James," largely with the same cast and settings, follows Frank as he sets out to avenge his brother's death by killing the cowardly Ford brothers (John Carradine and Charles Tannen), then gets sidetracked by a Denver reporter (Gene Tierney) from whom he learns his black farm hand (Robert Whitman) is to be hung as his accomplice unless he returns. Director Fitz Lang gets a fine performance from Fonda as the reformed outlaw who wrestles with his conscience over revenging a past wrong or saving an innocent life, then puts his life at risk in the taut trial sequence in the dramatic finale. Brief stylized violence, some muddled motives and several period racial expressions

title: Return of Jack Slade, The
synopsis: Uneven Western directed by Harold Schuster in which the title outlaw's son (John Ericson) tries to atone for his father's crimes by joining the notorious Hole in the Wall gang in 1886 Wyoming, then luring them into an ambush set up by Pinkerton agents. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Return of Jafar, The
synopsis: Peppy animated sequel to "Aladdin" in which the evil wizard of the title (voice of Jonathan Freeman) escapes from the magic lamp and attempts to seize power by forcing reformed parrot Iago (voice of Gilbert Gottfried) to betray Aladdin (voice of Scott Weinger) and the princess (voice of Linda Larkin). Directed by Tad Stones, Toby Shelton and Alan Zaslove, the result lacks the original's superior animation and the inspired humor of Robin Williams but delivers zippy pacing to the story's misadventures along with some mildly enjoyable musical numbers

title: Return of Martin Guerre, The
synopsis: Engrossing, fact-based French production about a 16th-century peasant who abandons his wife and disappears from his native village to reappear some eight years later, much improved in every way. Accepted by his wife and most of the villagers, a squabble over property a few years later provokes the accusation that he's an imposter, and a trial with tragic results ensues. Written by Jean-Claude Carriere and directed by Daniel Vigne, the movie is partly a mystery but most of all a love story that most adults will find intriguing entertainment. Brief nudity and sexual references

title: Return of Maxwell Smart, The
synopsis: TV's secret agent Maxwell Smart (Don Adams) is assigned to thwart a villain (Vittorio Gassman) who has developed a bomb capable of destroying all the clothing in the world. Director Clive Donner's woefully inept and dull comedy relies on sexual innuendo

title: Return of Mr. Moto, The
synopsis: Muddled mystery in which the Japanese detective (miscast Henry Silva) helps Scotland Yard unmask an international conspiracy to control Mideast oil production. Directed by Ernest Morris, the low-budget picture goes nowhere with its dull formula plot and lackluster cast. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Return of Sabata
synopsis: Frank Kramer (alias Gianfranco Parolini) directs this third installment in the spaghetti Western series spoofing spaghetti Westerns. This time the sooty-suited hero with the twitching nostrils (Lee Van Cleef) matches wits and weapons with the Irish boss of a cardboard Texas town whose citizens are being taxed to the tune of a million dollars. Sabata comes to the rescue and sneers at the audience as he rides away from his bordello beauty and a cast full of sloppily-dubbed characters

title: Return of Swamp Thing, The
synopsis: Forgettable sequel in which the crime-busting human plant (Dick Durock), a former scientist who keeps the bayou safe for kids and damsels in distress, falls for the stepdaughter (Heather Locklear) of a gene-tampering scientist (Louis Jourdan). Directed by Jim Wynorski, the cheesy sets and sleepwalking actors negate the good stuff which includes clever make-up and the heroic antics of the asparagus stalk with a heart of gold. Some sexual innuendo, rough language and much comic-book violence

title: Return of the Badmen
synopsis: Pioneering Oklahoma settler (Randolph Scott) takes on the worst of the Old West's outlaws, the nastiest of which is the Sundance Kid (Robert Ryan). There's some comic relief (Gabby Hayes) and the hero gets the girl (Jacqueline White) in the last reel, but otherwise director Ray Enright's shoot-'em-up is strictly routine action fare. Frontier violence

title: Return of the Fly
synopsis: Thin sequel in which the son (Brett Halsey) of the Montreal scientist whose molecular structure got mixed with that of a housefly continues his father's experiments, with similar botched results until his uncle (Vincent Price) intervenes. Directed by Edward L. Bernds, the hokey plot and mediocre special effects hold little interest. Some stylized violence and occasional menace

title: Return of the Gunfighter
synopsis: Retired gunslinger (Robert Taylor) sets out to find the murderers of a Mexican couple who were his friends, taking along their daughter (Ana Martin) to identify them as well as a wounded cowboy (Chad Everett) he meets along the way. Director James Neilson's formula Western has some good action sequences, a respect for the Mexican settlers of the Southwest and a strong performance from Taylor. Frontier violence

title: Return of the Jedi
synopsis: In the third installment of the Star Wars trilogy, Luke Skywalker (Mark Hamill) has a revealing confrontation with Darth Vader, Princess Leia (Carrie Fisher) and Han Solo (Harrison Ford) finally get somewhere with their romance, Billy Dee Williams saves the day with his air support and R2D2 and C3PO steal some major scenes. Directed by Richard Marquand, it's fun for action fans but the violence and tension from some of the nasty characters (Jabba the Hutt is not only scary, but disgusting) may be too intense for the younger crowd

title: Return of the Living Dead
synopsis: Written and directed by Dan O'Bannon, this is yet another tedious variation on the horror movie theme of the dead coming to life and devouring the living. Nudity, violence and bloodly gore

title: Return of the Musketeers, The
synopsis: Flabby seriocomic sequel directed by Richard Lester picks up the story 20 years later with D'Artagnan (Michael York) and his aging comrades (Oliver Reed, Frank Finlay and Richard Chamberlain) trying to stop Cromwell's execution of Charles II, thwart the court intrigues of Cardinal Mazarin (Philippe Noiret) and escape the vengeance of Lady de Winter's daughter (Kim Cattral). Aimless mix of mock heroism and cardboard villainy with stylized violence, sexual situations and religious hypocrites

title: Return of the Pink Panther, The
synopsis: The Pink Panther, the sacred jewel of the Middle East kingdom of Lugash, has been stolen again and only Inspector Clouseau (Peter Sellers) can get retrieve it. Directed by Blake Edwards, the comedy is relatively innocent and, thanks to Sellers, has more then a few funny moments. Some slapstick violence

title: Return of the Secaucus Seven, The
synopsis: Nothing much happens except a weekend of talking during a reunion of seven friends who, as college students on a 1960's protest march, once spent a night together in jail in Secaucus, N.J. Written and directed by John Sayles on a shoestring budget, the movie won't satisfy everyone, but the dialogue is bright and some of the insights are clever. The frankness of the language, especially about sex, would rule out younger viewers

title: Return of the Seven
synopsis: Director Burt Kennedy's shallow, violent sequel to John Sturges' 1960 "The Magnificent Seven," lacks original's flair and high-powered sense of adventure. Yul Brynner, Robert Fuller and Jordan Christopher are three of the deadly septet, leading a small parade back to a little Mexican town where one of their companions is being held prisoner

title: Return of the Soldier, The
synopsis: Wealthy middle-aged man (Alan Bates) returns from World War I with a case of selective amnesia. Forgotten are the years with his spoiled, ill-tempered wife (Julie Christie); remembered instead is his first love, a working-class woman (Glenda Jackson) now grown quite dowdy and, like himself, married. Well-acted English production directed by Alan Bridges from the Rebecca West novel, but the period piece is very slight and its neat resolution is unsatisfying

title: Return of the Streetfighter, The
synopsis: Japanese karate action film the villain being the American heading the Mafia branch in the Far East. Minimal production values and excessive violence

title: Return of the Tall Blond Man with the One Black Shoe, The
synopsis: French production in which Pierre Richard again stars as the concert violinist mistaken for a superspy and unaware that he is the object of assassination attempts. This time the action takes place in Rio de Janiero with the lovely Mireille Darc on hand as decoration but director Yves Robert's comic touch is not nearly as deft as it was in the original. Restrained violence

title: Return of the Vampire, The
synopsis: Minor horror tale about a vampire (Bela Lugosi) who was buried with a spike through his heart in 1918 London, then is unearthed by a bomb in the 1941 Blitz and seeks revenge on the daughter (Nina Foch) of the doctor who did him in. Directed by Lew Landers, there are a few eerie scenes in an otherwise pedestrian story with a muddled subplot about a wolfman under the vampire's spell and weak comic relief from the bemused Scotland Yard chief (Miles Mander). Stylized violence and hokey menace

title: Return to Macon County
synopsis: Two young men (Nick Nolte and Don Johnson) bound for California in a souped-up car pick up a chunky girl who constantly smiles when she is not pointing a large pistol at people and sometimes even when she is. Director Richard Compton's thin, aimless youth movie dips into sexual exploitation for want of anything better to do

title: Return to Me
synopsis: Surprisingly delightful romantic comedy in which a widower (David Duchovny) falls in love with a donor recipient (Minnie Driver) who, unbeknownst to him, has received his late wife's heart. As directed by Bonnie Hunt, the lighthearted film offers an appealing look at romance and second chances with honest, funny dialogue and good performances, although a somewhat predictable, rambling plot diminishes its charm. Fleeting profanity and crass language

title: Return to Never Land
synopsis: Mildly amusing animated sequel to the 1953 classic "Peter Pan" begins in World War II London when Wendy's daughter (voiced by Harriet Owen) is whisked off by Captain Hook (voiced by Corey Burton) to Never Never Land where she rediscovers her sense of imagination and adventure before Peter Pan (voiced by Blayne Weaver) helps her fly home. Directed by Robin Budd, the film has the usual quality animation, but its flat songs and skimpy story render it unmemorable. A few mildly menacing scenes

title: Return to Oz
synopsis: Grim, joyless sequel to the grand Judy Garland original that attempts to make up for its lack of warmth and imagination by substituting an abundance of special effects. The scariness of some of the latter are inappropriate for pre-teenagers

title: Return to Paradise
synopsis: Flawed tale of an American (Joaquin Phoenix) facing execution in Malaysia on a drug conviction unless his lawyer (Anne Heche) can convince his buddies (Vince Vaughn and David Conrad) to return and serve three years in prison for their part in buying the drugs. Director Joseph Ruben allows a premise meant to explore difficult moral choices to gradually descend into overwrought melodrama. Brief violence and recreational drug abuse, an implied affair, recurring profanity and much rough language

title: Return to Peyton Place
synopsis: Imitation sudser with a lifeless script ineptly directed by Jose Ferrer has the illegitimate daughter (Carol Lynley) of an adulteress (Eleanor Parker) write a best-selling novel about the peccadilloes of the folks in her home town. Sexual references

title: Return to Snowy River
synopsis: Enterprising horse rancher (Tom Burlinson) in 19th-century Australia must overcome an aristocratic blackguard (Nicholas Eadie) to wed the daughter (Sigrid Thornton) of an American settler (Brian Dennehy). Director Geoff Burrowes' sequel to "The Man from Snowy River" is filled with picturesque scenery and spirited horses but the human narrative is thin and the action sluggish. Stylized violence, including some fierce hand-to-hand combat, and romantic situations

title: Return to the Blue Lagoon
synopsis: Insipid fantasy in which once again a boy and girl (Brian Krause and Milla Jovovich) come of age while stranded on an uninhabited South Pacific island. Producer-director William A. Graham handles the adolescents' emerging sexuality with a self-performed wedding ceremony and a lamely predictable storyline that languidly repeats the 1980 original. Brief scenes of violence and a few shots of partial nudity

title: Reuben, Reuben
synopsis: Alcoholic, womanizing Scottish poet (Tom Conti) sponges his way through the New England campus circuit in director Robert Ellis Miller's uneven social satire which details the slow disintegration of a creative soul. The script is very literate and Conti's performance is exquiste but his several sexual conquests compound the movie's already muddled moral perspective

title: Revenge
synopsis: Intriguing but ultimately muddled tale of a newly retired Navy pilot (Kevin Costner) who is implausibly lured into an affair with the wife (Madeleine Stowe) of his best friend, a ruthless Mexican powerbroker (Anthony Quinn). Directed by Tony Scott, the exotic Mexican locale takes precedence over character development in this story of male friendship, betrayal and retribution. Some brutally graphic violence, several scenes involving adultery and a rape and incidental rough language

title: Revenge of Frankenstein, The
synopsis: Uneven horror sequel opens in 1860 as Baron Frankenstein (Peter Cushing) escapes the guillotine to reimerge as Dr. Stein in a distant town where he constructs a new creature with the brain of a deformed assistant (Michael Gwynn) but the result turns into a cannibalistic killer. Directed by Terence Fisher, the elaborate variations on the original are ambitious but prove too cumbersome to sustain interest. Stylized violence and some grisly visuals

title: Revenge of the Creature
synopsis: Thin sequel to "The Creature from the Black Lagoon" has the captured Gill Man taken from the Amazon to a Florida theme park where he's angered by a scientist (John Agar), then breaks loose, terrifies crowds of visitors and escapes with a park official (Lori Nelson). Directed by Jack Arnold, the hokey proceedings finally work up some mild tension as the prehistoric creature is hunted down but without evoking the sympathy generated by the original

title: Revenge of the Dead
synopsis: ( see: "Night of the Ghouls" )

title: Revenge of the Musketeers
synopsis: French swashbuckler in which the graying d'Artagnon (Philippe Noiret) is persuaded by his spunky daughter (Sophie Marceau) to come out of retirement and join his three Musketeer comrades in foiling a conspiracy against the young Louis XIV. Directed by Bertrand Tavernier, the 1994 production wrings a lot of tongue-in-cheek action from a breezy plot revolving around the aging heroes, a villainous aristocrat (Claude Rich) and the devious Cardinal Mazarin (Luigi Proietti). Subtitles. Period violence, sexual situations, brief nudity and ribald humor

title: Revenge of the Nerds
synopsis: Misfit college freshmen (Robert Carradine and Anthony Edwards) form a fraternity to protect themselves and fight the persecution of college jocks. The underdog heroes' attitude toward women is as reprehensible as that of their tormentors. Director Jeff Kanew's farce is full of vulgarities, much nudity and the romantic treatment of what is in effect rape

title: Revenge of the Nerds II: Nerds in Paradise
synopsis: Director Joe Roth's silly sequel has the goofy Tri Lambdas seeking to retrieve their integrity at a fraternity conference in Fort Lauderdale. Though its theme is not to judge others on surface values, it reinforces false stereotypes of women, bad habits and vulgarity via peekaboo nudity, slapstick humor and crude sight gags

title: Revenge of the Ninja
synopsis: Japanese warrior (Sho Kosugi) comes to the United States where he makes short order of an illegal drug operation and battles old enemies. Directed by Sam Firstenberg, the action is mostly of the martial arts variety but a number of weapons are used in achieving an extremely bloody victory. Excessive violence and gore

title: Revenge of the Pink Panther
synopsis: Peter Sellers romps again as the bumbling Inspector Clouseau who gains glory, inadvertently as usual, by breaking up an international drug ring headed by Robert Webber, thanks to some timely help from Webber's mistress, Dyan Cannon. Directed by Blake Edwards, the plot is cluttered and noticeably less scintillating than its predecessors. Some sexual innuendo

title: Revengers, The
synopsis: William Holden stars as a rancher who, after his family is slaughtered by renegade Indians, dedicates his life to avenging them and, with the help of a second-string wild bunch (including Ernest Borgnine and Woody Strode), he kills just about everyone who crosses his path until gentled by an Irish spinster (Susan Hayward). Directed by Daniel Mann, this violent and bloody Western has a totally unmotivated ending

title: Reversal of Fortune
synopsis: Fact-based re-creation of the successful appeal by a Harvard law professor (Ron Silver) of the conviction of Claus von Bulow (Jeremy Irons) for the attempted murder of his socialite wife (Glenn Close). Director Barbet Schroeder's wickedly witty film offers several possible scenarios for the victim's two comas and details how the case was won legally without resolving the question of von Bulow's innocence. Adulterous relationships and occasional rough language

title: Revolution
synopsis: Jack O'Connell's documentary presents a one-sided view of the hippie counterculture with an emphasis upon sex and nudity

title: Revolution
synopsis: Director Hugh Hudson's epic treatment of the American Revolution is grand spectacle but lacks a credible human dimension. What it offers, instead, are underdeveloped characters (notably Al Pacino in the central role) and episodic plot contrivances. Violent battle scenes

title: Revolutionary Road
synopsis: Impeccably filmed and acted adaptation of Richard Yates' greatly lauded 1961 novel about an unhappy suburban Connecticut couple (Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet) torn between middle-class inertia and fulfilling their youthful aspirations by uprooting to Paris. Director Sam Mendes takes a strikingly stylized approach to the repressed 1950s milieu, and the story speaks powerfully to the restrictive conformity of that era, but the thematic material -- including adultery and abortion -- and sporadically strong language may not be to every taste. Extreme domestic discord, rough language and profanity, adultery, brief upper female nudity, abortion references, two nongraphic sexual encounters and heavy smoking

title: Revolutionary, The
synopsis: College student (Jon Voight) moves from a radical student movement, to a socialist worker's organization, to a short-lived stint in the army and, finally, to an anarchists' bomb plot. The result is less the story of a young man's political radicalization than it is the meanderings of a social misfit. Paul Williams' low-keyed direction tends to level rather than highlight plot development and leaves too many significant questions unanswered

title: Reward, The
synopsis: On the arid, sun-drenched plains of Mexico, a small band of bounty hunters are destroyed by their greed and moral decay. Director Serge Bourguignon's story of death in the desert makes its point about life by turning the desperate journey of the last survivor (Max Von Sydow) to reach a lake into the quest for a moral oasis

title: Rhapsody in August
synopsis: Three generations of a Japanese family in Nagasaki react quite differently to a surprise visit by an U.S. relative (Richard Gere) who has come to remember the family patriarch who was killed in the American bombing of the city 45 years earlier. Writer-director Akira Kurosawa presents a poignant look at the futility of war through the eyes of the elderly who remember, the middle-aged who prefer to forget, and children who are curious about their past. Subtitles. References to the horror of mass death and destruction caused by the A-bomb

title: Rhapsody in Blue
synopsis: Long but mostly engaging tribute to composer George Gershwin (1898-1937) from his early success with Broadway show tunes to his more serious works, including the title concert piece, with Robert Alda playing the composer as a driven musical genius whose ambition leaves no room for love (Joan Leslie and Alexis Smith). Directed by Irving Rapper, the Hollywood version of Gershwin's life is well-crafted melodrama, and the plentiful musical portions are first-rate. Romantic complications

title: Rhinestone
synopsis: Embarrassingly bad romantic match-up in which Dolly Parton tries to make a country-western singer out of tough New York cabby Sylvester Stallone. Director Bob Clark's unfunny musical comedy exploits Parton's physical attributes and musical abilities but merely makes Stallone look silly. Vulgar dialogue and benign view of casual sex

title: Rhubarb
synopsis: Lightweight comedy in which the scrappy cat of the title inherits a millionaire's estate, including a major-league baseball club, with the will's acerbic executor (Ray Milland) fending off nasty interlopers as the team heads for the pennant and his fiancee (Jan Sterling) develops an allergy to cats. Director Arthur Lubin turns the daffy premise into a slow-moving vehicle for mostly minor amusements. Some mean-spirited skullduggery

title: Rhyme & Reason
synopsis: Documentary celebrating almost 20 years of rap music and the hip-hop subculture as commented on by some 70 performers from Ice-T to Dr. Dre and the late Tupac Shakur.
