Directed by Peter Spirer, the result is basically self-promotional, providing an uncritical view of rap as a form of social protest using verbal violence and sexually explicit lyrics to express the oppression of ghetto life, an explanation which will not satisfy those who reject rap as socially irresponsible. Recurring violent rhetoric and sexual expletives

title: Rhythm on the River
synopsis: Tuneful nostalgia from director Victor Schertzinger in the slight tale of an established songwriter (Basil Rathbone) who buys his compositions from unknowns, two of whom (Bing Crosby and Mary Martin) fall for each other while trying to establish independent songwriting careers. Creaky but cheery musical with a quite charming romance

title: Rich and Famous
synopsis: Screen version of the John Van Druten play about two very different women (Candice Bergen and Jacqueline Bisset), both writers, who preserve a friendship for more than two decades despite the strains caused by emulation and jealousy. Directed by George Cukor, the glossy soap opera pays more attention to its glamorous locations than to the human dimension of its story. The sole redeeming feature is good acting by the principals. General air of vapid amorality and two graphic sexual sequences

title: Rich and Strange
synopsis: Whimsical tale in which a London couple use an inheritance to take a cruise to the Far East where the wife (Joan Barry) is charmed by a genial plantation owner (Percy Marmont) while the husband (Henry Kendall) is fleeced by a phony princess (Betty Amman), then they get shipwrecked on the return voyage and arrive home with a new appreciation of ordinary life. Director Alfred Hitchcock treats the proceedings with tongue firmly in cheek, adding a few bizarre touches and some grisly humor along the way with still enjoyable results. Stylized violence, implied infidelity and some rude language

title: Richard
synopsis: Political spoof with little satirical bite blending newsreel footage with staged segments in order to trace Richard Nixon's journey from whipping cookie batter of an evening in Whittier, Calif. to fireside reminiscenes at the White House. Directed by Lorees Yerby and Harry Hurwitz, the resulting lampoon, more than anything else, provides proof that this is a free country

title: Richard III
synopsis: Wildly imaginative updating of Shakespeare's play to 1930's Britain where civil war brings a new monarch to the throne coveted by his duplicitous brother, the Duke of Glouster (Ian McKellan), who sets out to gain it through murder. Directed by Richard Loncraine, the result places Shakespeare's Elizabethan language and medieval subject in a 20th-century context of fascist movements and absolute dictatorships that give fresh significance to the play's portrait of an autocratic villain. Stylized violence and sexual references

title: Richard Pryor Live on Sunset Strip
synopsis: Stand-up comic performance, with the usual obscenities and scatological references, though Pryor is in a mellower, more humane mood than in his previous performance movie. Under Joe Layton's direction, Pryor's humor and his perception of human nature are usually on target and often extremely funny, but his sexually oriented jokes and vulgar language may offend those unfamiliar with his style

title: Richest Girl in the World, The
synopsis: Eccentric romantic comedy in which an heiress (Miriam Hopkins) changes places with her private secretary (Fay Wray) in order to test the real intentions of a would-be suitor (Joel McCrea). Director William A. Seiter keeps the implausible situations light and mostly fun, with a fine cast making all the duplicity seem almost credible. Sexual situations

title: Richest Man in the World: Andrew Carnegie, The
synopsis: An "American Experience" biography of the Scottish-born 19th century industrialist who went from rags to riches in America by ruthless business practices, but who gave much of his wealth away believing, "A man who dies rich dies disgraced." Filmmaker Austin Hoyt explores the darker side of Carnegie's complex persona without dismissing his tremendous economic achievements and unparalleled philanthropy. A few profanities

title: Richie Rich
synopsis: Uninspired comedy about a lonely but plucky 12-year-old (Macaulay Culkin) who conspires to outwit a nasty businessman (John Larroquette) out to steal his inheritance when the boy's parents (Edward Herrmann and Christine Ebersole) are presumed dead after their private jet blows up. Director Donald Petrie's formula comedy has few surprises and only minor amusements for easily satisfied viewers. Some mock comic violence, occasional double entendres and a crude expression

title: Rich in Love
synopsis: A Southern teenager (Kathryn Erbe) puzzles over life and love after her mother (Jill Clayburgh) deserts her father (Albert Finney) without explanation and her pregnant sister (Suzy Amis) moves back home, unsure whether she wants to stay married to her new husband (Kyle MacLachlan). Director Bruce Beresford unveils richly textured characters caught between the pain of change and the mundane joys of family living. Implied extra-marital relationships

title: Rich Kids
synopsis: Uneven melodrama about the effect of divorce on two adolescents (Trini Alvarado and Jeremy Levy) whose wealthy and adulterous parents (John Lithgow and Kathryn Walker) seem unconcerned about their offspring. The two teenagers spend a weekend together in an exotically appointed bachelor apartment. The situation leads to an angry, recriminatory adult confrontation, involving spouses current and former, lovers, friends, and one or two relatively innocent bystanders Directed by Robert Young, the movie raises but doesn't probe too deeply into questions of parental responsibility and glosses over the sexual implications of the young people's weekend together

title: Rich Man's Wife, The
synopsis: Preposterous thriller in which an unfaithful wife (Halle Berry) fears being implicated in the murder of her philandering husband (Christopher McDonald) by a homicidal maniac (Peter Greene) who wants a share of the widow's inheritance. Writer-director Amy Holden Jones drags out a tawdry tale of the devious deeds of unsympathetic characters in a clumsy, slow-moving plot taxing credibility and viewers' patience. Some strong scenes of violence, threatening situations, marital infidelity and occasional rough language

title: Ricochet
synopsis: Hard-edged revenge drama pits a hero cop-turned-prosecutor (Denzel Washington) against an escaped psychopath (John Lithgow) who frames him for murder and involvement in kiddie porn. Solid action scenes and chilling performances are outweighed by director Russell Mulcahy's emphasis on killings and sexual violence. Excessive violence, the repeated use of a graphic rape scene and much rough language

title: Riddle of the Sands, The
synopsis: British melodrama about two chaps from Oxford who accidentally uncover German preparations for an invasion of England in 1901. Michael York and Simon MacCorkindale are fine as the stuffy pair who prove their mettle once the going gets tough, but they can't save a languid movie that lacks even a good villain. Director Tony Maylam succeeds best with the period atmosphere but its intrigue and derring-do are only mildly diverting

title: Ride a Crooked Trail
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Jesse Hibbs in which an outlaw (Audie Murphy) turns honest after a small-town judge (Walter Matthau) mistakes him for a famed lawman and appoints him marshal, whereupon he tracks down a bank robber (Henry Silva) and weds a former accomplice (Gia Scala). Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Ride a Wild Pony
synopsis: Colorful Disney adventure, set in the Australian Outback before World War I, in which a poor lad attempts to recover his pony after it has come into the possession of a spoiled cripple, the little daughter of the town's wealthiest family. It is up to the horse, in the satisfying conclusion, to decide for one child or the other. Better than average children's movie directed by Don Chaffey with some good touches of reality and a solid theme of human selflessness

title: Ride Beyond Vengeance
synopsis: After a long absence, a buffalo hunter (Chuck Connors) returns home with a sizable sum of money and then revenges on the three who steal it from him. Directed by Bernard McEveety, it is a tough, almost cynical story of human greed and brutality. Much violence

title: Ride Clear of Diablo
synopsis: Standard Western directed by Jesse Hibbs with a straight-shooting cowboy (Audie Murphy) trailing the rustlers who murdered his father and brother but, along the way, he becomes a sheriff's deputy and arrests the area's worst badman (Dan Duryea) whom he wrongly accuses of the crime. Stylized violence and muddled serio-comic plot

title: Ride Him, Cowboy
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Fred Allen in which a cowboy (John Wayne) saves a fine horse from being mistakenly destroyed as a vicious animal, and then the horse saves the cowboy from being killed by outlaws. Stylized violence

title: Ride Lonesome
synopsis: Strong Western in which a bounty hunter (Randolph Scott) tracks down a killer (James Best), then uses him as bait to bring his outlaw brother (Lee Van Cleef) to justice for a grisly crime committed years before. Director Budd Boetticher notches the suspense by having the bounty hunter joined on the trail by an abandoned wife (Karen Steele) and a couple of cowboys (Pernell Roberts and James Coburn) with their own designs on the killer. Stylized violence and considerable menace

title: Rider from Tucson
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Lesley Selander in which Arizona rodeo riders (Tim Holt and Richard Martin) help a Colorado friend save his gold mine from claimjumpers. Frontier violence and a woman held hostage

title: Rider on the Rain
synopsis: Intriguing French mystery thriller about a newlywed (Marlene Jobert) who kills her attacker and then is afraid to tell husband, friends, or the police. After she has disposed of the body, a stranger (Charles Bronson) begins to badger her about it and a neatly matched duel of wits ensues. Director Rene Clement has hit the mark with this suspenseful melodrama, with plenty of moody atmosphere and engaging characterizations. The tribulations of the heroine are not for the youngsters

title: Riders of Destiny
synopsis: Low-budget Western directed by Robert N. Bradbury in which undercover government agent Singing Sandy (John Wayne) foils a gang plotting to drive local ranchers off the range by depriving them of water. Tame action fare

title: Riders of the Northwest Mounted
synopsis: Low-budget adventure picture follows a Canadian Mountie (Russell Hayden) on the trail of a gang of fur robbers. Directed by William Berke, the formula story has some picturesque scenery, the singing of Bob Wills and his Texas Playboys and comic relief by Dub Taylor. Stylized violence

title: Riders of the Rio Grande
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Howard Bretherton with the Three Mesquiteers (Bob Steele, Tom Tyler and Jimmie Dodd) on the run from the law after being mistaken for gunslingers, but this doesn't keep them from saving a town's leading citizen (Edward Van Sloan) from ruin. Frontier violence

title: Ride the High Country
synopsis: Hired by a bank to escort a gold shipment from a mining camp in the Sierra Mountains, a retired lawman (Joel McCrea) takes along an old friend (Randolph Scott) who has his own plans for the ore. Director Sam Peckinpah's off-beat Western mixes in a farmer's daughter (Mariette Hartley), a novice gunfighter (Ronald Starr) and a brawling brood of brothers, but the focus is on the two veteran cowboys and their differing notions of duty and honor. Some stylized violence, sexual references and ribald humor

title: Ride the Pink Horse
synopsis: Atmospheric crime story set in a New Mexico town during a fiesta when a war profiteer (Fred Clark) double-crosses and almost kills a cynical Army vet (Robert Montgomery) who's saved by a Indian girl (Wanda Hendrix), a Mexican merry-go-round operator (Thomas Gomez) and a wry FBI agent (Art Smith). Also directed by Montgomery, the plot is full of holes but the colorful characters make the situation of more than usual interest. Stylized violence

title: Ride the Wild Surf
synopsis: Innocuous tale of college-age beach buddies (Fabian, Tab Hunter and Peter Brown) finding high waves and low-voltage romance (Shelley Fabares, Barbara Hunt and Barbara Eden, respectively) on a New Year's vacation in Hawaii. Directed by Don Taylor, the picturesque locales and surfboard action make up for the generally inept dramatic proceedings. Innocent but shallow escapist fare that children are likely to find simply tedious

title: Ride to Hangman's Tree, The
synopsis: Formula Western directed by Alan Rafkin in which a robber (James Farentino) of Wells Fargo gold shipments is forced to split the loot with an ex-partner (Jack Lord), though the result is far less interesting than "Black Bart," the 1948 movie upon which it is based. Stylized violence and some heavy sexual innuendo

title: Ride, Vaquero
synopsis: A Mexican bandit leader (Anthony Quinn) grows testy when his life-long friend and top gun (Robert Taylor) sides with a Texas rancher (Howard Keel) and his wife (Ava Gardner) against his former comrades. Director John Farrow's quirky little melodrama has its interesting moments, among them the local priest (Kurt Kasznar) taking a hand in the action and Taylor's stinging rejection of Gardner's advances. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Ride With the Devil
synopsis: Somber Civil War drama centers on two Missouri lads (Tobey Maguire and Skeet Ulrich) and a former slave (Jeffrey Wright) fighting unofficially as pro-Southern Bushwackers on the Kansas-Missouri border while they reflect on the bloody conflict and how it has torn their families apart. As directed by Ang Lee, the historical backdrop holds more interest than the plot's flatly dramatized personal stories. Recurring battlefield violence, implied sexual situations and a breast-feeding scene

title: Ridicule
synopsis: Lush costume drama set at the court of Versailles in 1783 as an altruistic country engineer (Charles Berling) discovers he must first bed the king's cunning mistress (Fanny Ardent) and develop the art of witty sarcasm before he can win the king's ear. Directed by Patrice Leconte, the satirical period piece focuses on the rampant decadence and superficiality of court life that culminated a few years later in the French Revolution. Subtitles. Brief violence including a suicide, fleeting bedroom scenes and gratuitous frontal male nudity

title: Riding High
synopsis: Happy-go-lucky racehorse owner (Bing Crosby) stakes his future on a horse he's raised from a colt and, with the help of its trainer (Clarence Muse) and a rooster mascot, wins the big race and the daughter (Colleen Gray) of an ulcer-ridden tycoon (Charles Bickford). Despite period updating and some songs, director Frank Capra's remake of his 1934 "Broadway Bill" oversentimentalizes the slim plot, though a talented veteran cast (Oliver Hardy, Margaret Hamilton, James Gleason, Raymond Walburn, William Demarest, Gene Lockhart and Douglass Dumbrille) provides some amusement. Romantic complications leading to divorce

title: Riding in Cars With Boys
synopsis: Uneven drama in which a pregnant 15-year-old (Drew Barrymore) with dreams of college and career reluctantly marries her substance-abusing boyfriend (Steve Zahn) and later finds the demands of single parenting frustrate her ambition. Told as her 20-year-old son looks back on their rocky relationship, director Penny Marshall's fact-based film succeeds as a cautionary tale and in presenting realistic characters with warts and flaws, but the film's sentimental streak culminates in a cloying conclusion. Fleeting violence, adolescent affairs, recreational drug use and an instance of rough language and profanity

title: Riding Shotgun
synopsis: Western misfire directed by Andre de Toth in which a town suspects a stagecoach guard (Randolph Scott) is in cahoots with a notorious outlaw gang, but he escapes being lynched in time to save them from the outlaws. Stylized violence

title: Riff-Raff
synopsis: Gritty look at what Britain's double-diget unemployment statistics mean in the life of one out-of work laborer (Robert Carlyle) who takes a low-paying job on a non-union construction project, becomes a squatter in a vacant apartment complex and falls for an untalented, unrealistic would-be singer (Emer McCourt). Using a largely non-professional cast whose accents require subtitles, director ken loach gets a good measure of blue-collar reality in a variation on the old story of greedy employers, exploited workers and the struggle for economic justice. Its treatment of justice themes includes a devastating accident, a premarital relationship, drug use, crude humor and much rough language

title: Right On!
synopsis: Documentary of performances by a talented but angry rock group, The Original Last Poets (Gylan Kain, David Nelson, and Felipe Luciano), whose songs echo the pain and frustration of ghetto life and insist on racial pride as the means for redeeming the future. By filming the group in New York slums framed by the Manhattan skyline, director Herbert Danska finds the visual equivalent to their music. Some violent and vulgar lyrics, but motivated by a sense of hope rather than hopelessness

title: Right Stuff, The
synopsis: Screen version of Tom Wolfe's book about the original seven astronauts is an extraordinary tribute to the pioneers of the U.S. space program, notably Chuck Yeager (Sam Shepard), Alan Shepard (Scott Glenn) and John Glenn (Ed Harris). Director Philip Kaufman captures the gallant endeavor in a style that's at once respectful yet exuberant, lavishly entertaining and very inspiring. Unfortunately, a scene involving masturbation, intended as a bit of comic relief during a sequence of laboratory tests, is mature fare

title: Rikky and Pete
synopsis: Australian road picture pairing a brother-sister team (Stephen Kearney and Nina Landis) who leave their wealthy family in Melbourne to start a new life in a mining town in the Australian Outback. Director Nadia Tass gets some offhand humor in scenes featuring Pete's Rube Goldberg inventions but the focus is on Rikky who is the stronger of the two and protective of her spacey brother. Brief nudity and much rough language

title: Rikyu
synopsis: A 16th-century Japanese warlord (Tsutomu Yamazaki) and his tea master (Rentaro Mikuni) perfect the art of the tea ceremony while clashing over the warlord's burgeoning political ambitions. Exquisite delicacy and simplicity mark director Hiroshi Teshigahara's homage to Japanese culture with powerful performances from the two opposed characters. Subtitles. Suicide within a cultural perspective

title: Ringmaster
synopsis: Tawdry tale of two sets of dim characters who bring their tangled sexual problems to the TV talk show hosted by master of insincerities Jerry Springer, with the results predictably featuring scenes of sex and violence on and off the show. Directed by Neil Abramson, this low-budget promo for the TV talk show is a tedious exercise in sexual exploitation and human manipulation. Numerous sexual encounters, some nudity, physical and verbal violence, much rough language and occasional profanity

title: Ring of Bright Water
synopsis: London clerk (Bill Travers) leaves his computerized job to move to a small cottage in the Scottish highlands with an otter. Unpretentious British story directed by Jack Couffer proves intelligent, entertaining family fare

title: Ring of Fire
synopsis: Combination crime and disaster thriller starts with a police officer (David Janssen) being taken hostage by marauding teenagers (Frank Gorshin and Joyce Taylor) who are captured in the Oregon wilderness where one of their cigarettes causes a forest fire which threatens to engulf a nearby town. Writer-director Andrew L. Stone's busy scenario shifts abruptly from the nasty teen menaces to the low-budget conflagration ending with Janssen at the throttle of a trainload of panicked townspeople in the fiery climax. Much menace, some stylized violence and occasional sexual innuendo

title: Rings Around the World
synopsis: Compilation movie showing famous circus acts from various countries produced and directed by Gilbert Cates and narrated by Don Ameche

title: Ring, The
synopsis: Small but effective picture of a Mexican-American youth (Lalo Rios) who sets out to help his family by becoming a prizefighter but, despite the efforts of a veteran trainer (Gerald Mohr), gets beaten to a pulp and quits the ring to look elsewhere for succeess. Directed by Kurt Neumann, the movie presents a positive view of Latinos while showing the seamy side of the fight game. Violent boxing scenes

title: Rio
synopsis: Buoyant animated adventure with music about a Brazilian-born macaw (voice of Jesse Eisenberg) raised as a cosseted pet in Minnesota. Informed by an eccentric Rio-based scientist (voice of Rodrigo Santoro) that her feathery friend is the last male of his species, his devoted owner (voice of Leslie Mann) reluctantly brings him back to his native land so that he can mate with his sole remaining female counterpart (voice of Anne Hathaway). But the potential lovebirds get caught up in the illegal avian trade. Lessons about environmental stewardship and love-inspired loyalty are decked out in kaleidoscopic colors and delivered in an overwhelmingly child-friendly tone in director Carlos Saldanha's 3-D flight of fancy. A few nursery-level bathroom references, a fleeting double entendre

title: Rio Bravo
synopsis: Long-winded but pungent Western in which a seasoned sheriff (John Wayne) tries to keep a killer (Claude Aikens) from being busted out of jail by his brother's army of gunslingers with only a drunken deputy (Dean Martin), an elderly cripple (Walter Brennan), a callow cowboy (Ricky Nelson) and a saloon hostess (Angie Dickinson) to back him up. Director Howard Hawks savors the desperate situation and its collection of odd-ball characters as the tension builds to the long-delayed slambang conclusion. Assorted stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Rio Conchos
synopsis: Ponderous Western in which an Army officer (Stuart Whitman) heads into Mexico with a black sergeant (Jim Brown), a hardened Apache killer (Richard Boone) and a convicted murderer (Tony Franciosa) seeking to recover 2,000 stolen repeating rifles before they wind up in the hands of Apache hostiles. Directed by Gordon Douglas, there's plenty of rugged action but it's all as wildly improbable as the plans of the mad Confederate colonel (Edmond O'Brien) who stole the rifles to arm the Apaches for an invasion of 1867 Texas. Nasty frontier violence, brutality and sexual situations

title: Rio Grande
synopsis: Veteran cavalry officer (John Wayne) commanding a frontier outpost has his hands full when his estranged wife (Maureen O'Hara) arrives with their West Point son (Claude Jarman, Jr.) but the untested youth proves his mettle on a raid across the Mexican border to rescue children captured by the Apaches. Director John Ford plays the commander's domestic problems for laughs but turns grimly serious in the climactic border raid. Stylized violence

title: Rio Grande Patrol
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Lesley Selander in which a border patrol officer (Tim Holt) takes on a gang trying to smuggle a shipment of machine guns to Mexican rebels. Stylized violence

title: Rio Lobo
synopsis: Stylish Western with John Wayne as a Civil War veteran pursuing two traitors for hijacking an army payroll, and not perturbed in the least by a small army of hired gunslingers nor a final thunderous shootout with an entire town taking part. Under Howard Hawks' deft direction, there is plenty of rough horseplay and tongue-in-cheek references to Wayne's overweight condition and old age in general. Violence, both physical and psychological, and some adult sexual references

title: Riot
synopsis: Set within the grime and frustration of prison life is a realistic drama in which an inmate (James Brown), unwittingly caught up in fast-moving events, assumes leadership of a full scale revolt by the entire prison. Director Buzz Kulik's movie is by no means casual entertainment but it is very knowing about prison life and injustices. Several violent, bloody sequences bolster the dramatic action and the dialogue is a bit rough

title: Riot in Juvenile Prison
synopsis: Tough juvenile delinquent Scott Marlowe is no match for crusading penal reformer Jerome Thor in director Edward L. Cahn's dreary low-budget clunker. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Ripper, The
synopsis: Flat-footed melodrama in which a Scotland Yard inspector (Patrick Bergin) romances a poor working girl (Gabrielle Anwar), then uses her as bait to nab a serial killer of prostitutes in the East End slums of 1888 London. Directed by Janet Myers, the TV movie is a tired variation on the familiar story of Jack the Ripper, who is here identified as a member of the royal family, but the unimaginative plot gets lost in detailing the Victorian snobbery which keeps the inspector from solving the lurid case. Some brief graphic violence and occasional profanity

title: Rise and Fall of Legs Diamond, The
synopsis: Formula gangster movie directed by Budd Boetticher follows the ruthless methods by which its title character (Ray Danton) comes to rule the mobs of Prohibition-era New York, then is cut down by a syndicate organizing crime on a national basis in the 1930s. Stylized violence, some of it quite nasty, and sexual situations

title: Rise of Catherine the Great, The
synopsis: ( see: "Catherine the Great" )

title: Rise of Louis XIV, The
synopsis: French historical dramatization meticulously traces the gradual assumption of power by the Sun King, from the time he assumed the crown to his undercutting the noblity by enticing them to spend their lives in the frivolous splendors of the court at Versailles. Directed by Roberto Rossellini, the re-creation of the period is beautifully exquisite and painstakingly detailed but those uninterested in history may find the pace interminably slow

title: Rising Sun
synopsis: Investigating a sex murder in a Japanese-owned building, two Los Angeles police detectives (Sean Connery and Wesley Snipes) run up against a complex cover-up involving a politically sensitive sale of an American company to Japanese businessmen who must avoid scandal at all costs. Director Philip Kaufman's coldly stylish and wholly cynical thriller from Michael Crichton's novel exploits sexual violence against women in a story presenting a disturbing view of Japanese commerce on our shores. Repeated replay of a taped graphic sex killing, some nasty violence, recurring nudity and much rough language

title: Risky Business
synopsis: Enterprising young prostitute (Rebecca De Mornay) persuades a high school senior (Tom Cruise), while his affluent parents are away on vacation, to turn his plush Chicago home into a bordello for his classmates. Written and directed by Paul Brickman, it is much slicker than similar exploitation movies aimed at teenagers but it is appallingly crass in its celebration of promiscuity. Nudity and graphic sexuality as well as a benign view of deceit, manipulation and sexual indulgence

title: Rita, Sue and Bob Too
synopsis: British sex farce posing as ribald social satire about two lower-class teenagers sexually exploited by a married man who in turn ruin his already failing marriage and then exploit him. Director Alan Clarke displays a callous hand in his graphic depiction of sex with minors, including nudity and profanity

title: Ritz, The
synopsis: Screen version of a mediocre Broadway comedy about an Italian-American businessman from Cleveland (Jack Weston) hiding out from a murderous brother-in-law (Jerry Stiller) in a homosexual bathhouse where he is pursued by an off-key Puerto Rican singer (Rita Moreno) who thinks he is a Hollywood producer. Directed by Richard Lester, it's an ugly, disagreeable attempt at farce. Ethnic stereotyping and some foul language

title: Rivals
synopsis: Clunker about an Oedipal 10-year-old brat (Scott Jacoby) who is so fatally jealous of his widowed mother (Joan Hackett) and her childish second husband (Robert Klein) that he makes a humiliating mess of trying to have sex with his dumb but nubile babysitter. Director Krishna Shah is hopelessly adrift in dealing with the esoteric lifestyles of Americans with too much money. Repugnant trash

title: River Lady
synopsis: Muddled romantic adventure directed by George Sherman in which the owner (Yvonne De Carlo) of a gambling riverboat uses a slick agent (Dan Duryea) to create a logging syndicate until stopped by her former logger beau (Rod Cameron) who forms a combine of independent loggers. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: River Niger, The
synopsis: Powerful drama about a black American's struggle to forge his own identity out of a tragic history of blacks as the eternally Displaced Persons of our nation. Though director Krishna Shah fails to overcome the stage origins of the work, this does lessen the value of its hopeful message about the choices facing our society, its moving portrait of closely-knit family life and the strong performances of James Earl Jones, Cicely Tyson and Glynn Turman. Mature themes

title: River of No Return
synopsis: Slack Western in which a backcountry farmer (Robert Mitchum) saves his son (Tommy Rettig) and a saloon singer (Marilyn Monroe) from rampaging Indians by rafting downstream to safety in a town where he confronts the crooked gambler (Rory Calhoun) who had run out on them. Directed by Otto Preminger, the rugged raft scenes work up considerable tension but the rest of the picture is a letdown over the contrived relationships of cardboard characters. Frontier violence, romantic complications and sexual innuendo

title: Riverrun
synopsis: When a sea-going father (John McLiam) visits the sheep farm where his daughter (Louise Ober) and her young man (Mark Jenkins) live, he is at first amused by their attempt to get back to nature and escape the dehumanization of city life, but when he learns that she is pregnant and not formally married, he is determined to take her away. Written and directed by John Korty, the contrivances of romantic melodrama are evident but the generational theme of value systems is handled sensitively and treated with honesty

title: River Runs Through It, A
synopsis: Meditative reflections on the experiences of a youth (Craig Sheffer) growing up in rural Montana in the first part of the century, chiefly comprising his relationship with his rebellious younger brother (Brad Pitt), minister father (Tom Skerritt) and the great outdoors. Directed by Robert Redford, the tone of the episodic narrative is earnest, the pace leisurely and the result largely dependent upon how one relates to the poetry of nature. Some scenes of inebriation and discreet sexual references, several shots of rear nudity, teens in a life-threatening situation and occasional profanity

title: River's Edge
synopsis: The callous sex killing of a young high school girl is viewed by her apathetic peers as an occasion for protective support of her psychopathic boy friend who becomes the equally innocent victim of an adult psychotic (Dennis Hopper). Director Tim Hunter's picture of several troubled youths downplays emotional and spiritual issues in favor of surface sensationalism, including permissive teen sex, nudity and profanity

title: River, The
synopsis: Ernest but dull effort to dramatize the plight of the American farmer tells the story of a farm family (Mel Gibson and Sissy Spacek) who must battle nature, bill collectors and public indifference in their struggle to hold on to their land and livelihood. The characters simply do not come alive in an unfocused script directed by Mark Rydell. Some violent encounters and a restrained bedroom scene

title: River Wild, The
synopsis: Taut outdoors thriller in which a former river guide (Meryl Streep) on a white-water rafting vacation with her unathletic husband (David Strathairn) and young son (Joseph Mazzello) is forced to take two fugitives (Kevin Bacon and John C. Riley) down a deadly stretch of river, knowing the two will kill her and her family even if they survive the trip down the rapids. Director Curtis Hanson underplays the characterizations but maintains edgy suspense as the woman becomes increasingly resourceful in her efforts to save her loved ones. Frequent menace and brief shots of brutal violence

title: Road House
synopsis: Bleak sudser about a singer (Ida Lupino) who comes between best friends when her boss, the road house owner (Richard Widmark), pursues her while she prefers the arms of his manager (Cornel Wilde). Directed by Jean Negulesco, the contrived story is less interesting than the flawed characters, one of whom is driven bonkers by the unbalanced triangle. Stylized violence, some intense menace and sexual innuendo

title: Road House
synopsis: College-educated bouncer (Patrick Swayze) cleans up a nasty nightclub in Missouri only to incur the wrath of the town's sleazy kingpin (Ben Gazzara). In director Rowdy Herrington's modern-day Western, women are the resident playthings and men the resident idiots. Interminable fisticuffs, graphic sexual encounters, nudity and endorsement of vigilantism

title: Roadhouse Murder, The
synopsis: Sappy melodrama directed by J. Walter Ruben in which a cub reporter (Eric Linden) stumbles on a double murder, plants evidence of his own guilt so he can write front-page stories about being hunted by the police, then is captured, tried and convicted after the real murderer (Bruce Cabot) steals the evidence that would clear him. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Roadie
synopsis: Failed spoof of rock music's subculture follows the misadventures of a country bumpkin (rock singer Meatloaf) who is convinced by a whacky groupie to become a "roadie" or general roustabout and handyman for a traveling rock group. Director Alan Rudolph offers few good sight gags and plenty of bad ones, with lots of ear-numbing music. Some jokes about sex and drugs

title: Road Movie
synopsis: Wildly exaggerated melodrama about two truck drivers (Robert Drivas and Barry Bostwick) whose friendship is shattered when they pick up a fuel-stop prostitute (Regina Baff) in a story that ends with the destruction of the truck and the death of one of them. Directed by Joseph Strick, whatever intentions the movie had as social commentary on the dangers of the road is undone by the movie's meanness of characters and their rough language

title: Road Show
synopsis: Comic misfire directed by Hal Roach in which an eccentric millionaire (John Hubbard) escapes a mental asylum with the help of an inmate (Adolphe Menjou), then is hidden by the soft-hearted owner (Carole Landis) of a failing carnival, with predictable results. Romantic complications, slapstick violence and a comic black stereotype (Willie Best)

title: Roadside Prophets
synopsis: Shapeless road movie follows a loner (John Doe) as he motorcycles through the Nevada desert meeting assorted oddballs and outcasts along the way, including a would-be friend (Adam Horovitz) who stubbornly trails him. Writer-director Abbe Wool needles the establishment with minimal wit and drab counterculture twaddle. Implied sexual encounter, fleeting violence and nudity, occasional substance abuse and recurring rough language

title: Road to Bali
synopsis: Fitful comedy in which a hapless pair of entertainers (Bing Crosby and Bob Hope) try diving for sunken treasure in the South Seas, then vie for the affections of an island princess (Dorothy Lamour) while saving her from court intrigues, cannibals and an erupting volcano. Directed by Hal Walker, the 6th "Road" picture sputters along on a haphazard mix of silly situations, daffy one-liners and cameos by Jane Russell, Humphrey Bogart and Martin and Lewis. Menacing situations and mild sexual innuendo

title: Road to Denver, The
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Joe Kane in which a Texas cowboy (John Payne) becomes a partner in a Colorado stage line, then is confronted by his trigger-happy younger brother (Skip Homeier) who's working for the competition (Lee J. Cobb). Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Road to El Dorado, The
synopsis: Disappointing animated adventure about two Spanish con men (voices of Kenneth Branagh and Kevin Kline) who find El Dorado, the legendary city of gold, but run into trouble when the natives mistake them for gods. As directed by Eric Bergeron and Don Paul, the film has a strong cast of voices and vibrant coloring, but the story sometimes limps and the flat, formulaic music is forgettable. Mild animated violence that may scare younger children and fleeting crass language

title: Road to Glory, The
synopsis: Creaky World War I tale about a battle-fatigued French captain (Warner Baxter) who leads his company, among whom is his aged father (Lionel Barrymore), in a 1916 offensive which costs him his eyesight, then learns his Red Cross girlfriend (June Lang) loves a lieutenant (Fredric March) and returns to the front where his father guides him on a suicide mission. Director Howard Hawks struggles with the credibility of the plot's contrived melodramatics but excels in vivid scenes of trench warfare and the gallows humor of combat soldiers. Battlefield violence and muted sexual innuendo

title: Road to Hong Kong, The
synopsis: In the 7th and final "Road"' picture, Bing Crosby and Bob Hope play con artists kidnapped in the Orient by an agent (Joan Collins) of a would-be world dictator (Robert Morley) and they wind up on a one-way rocket trip to the moon. Directed by Norman Panama, the low-budget British production doesn't give the veteran duo much to work with, though occasionally the old boys put some new life in the stale proceedings. Stylized violence and a few mild double entendres

title: Road to Morocco
synopsis: Wacky comic romp in which castaways Bing Crosby and Bob Hope land in a desert kingdom, vie to wed its princess (Dorothy Lamour) and wind up captives of a rebel Arab chieftain (Anthony Quinn). Directed by David Butler, the third Road comedy continues the pair's genial buffoonery as small-time hustlers trying to woo Lamour amidst throwaway gags, one-liners, talking camels and occasional songs. Some mild sexual innuendo

title: Road to Perdition
synopsis: Gripping drama set in Depression-era Chicago in which a hit man (Tom Hanks) working for the leader of the Irish mob (Paul Newman) embarks on a journey to protect his 12-year-old son and avenge the death of the rest of his family. Examining complicated father-son relationships, director Sam Mendes’ evocative moral tale presents a calculated visual tapestry of intrigue and multi-layered characters which smoothly weaves in themes of betrayal, redemption, filial love and family responsibility.� Some brutal scenes of violence with sporadic rough language and profanity

title: Road to Rio
synopsis: After accidentally torching a carnival, a hapless pair of musicians (Bing Crosby and Bob Hope) stow away on a Brazilian-bound ocean liner where they befriend an heiress (Dorothy Lamour) hypnotized by her wicked aunt (Gale Sondergaard). Directed by Norman Z. McLeod, the fifth "Road" comedy continues the series' tradition of zany plots strewn with wisecracks, sight gags and musical interludes, this time including the Andrew Sisters and the three manic Wiere Brothers. Silly but fun

title: Road to Salina
synopsis: Dreadfully pretentious European production set in the middle of a baked salt flat where Lana Turner runs a gas station-cafe and mistakes Robert Walker for her runaway son. Her daughter (Mimsy Farmer) goes along with the situation by engaging in a sexual relationship that had originally sent the son packing. Directed by Georges Lautner, the muddled incest theme is conveyed with many arty scenes of graphic lovemaking

title: Road to Singapore
synopsis: Romantic comedy about a scandal-ridden playboy (Bing Crosby) who hides out with a dim but trusted chum (Bob Hope) in a Far Eastern backwater where both fall for a local maid (Dorothy Lamour). Directed by Victor Schertzinger, the thin plot wasn't very funny but the Crosby-Hope byplay sparked enough laughs to engender their own series in the Road comedies that followed. Some sexual innuendo

title: Road to Utopia
synopsis: Bing Crosby and Bob Hope con their way to the Alaskan gold fields where they foil crooks (Douglass Dumbrille and Jack La Rue) trying to steal a rich mine from its rightful owner (Dorothy Lamour). Directed by Hal Walker, the boys are in fine form masquerading as a pair of wanted killers, with Robert Benchley's addled commentary adding to the zany proceedings. Some sexual innuendo

title: Road to Wellville, The
synopsis: Unappetizing satire about the bizarre digestive and sexual practices at a loosely fact-based turn-of-the-century Battle Creek health spa run by cornflakes inventor Dr. Kellogg (Anthony Hopkins) centers on the antics of a confused married couple (Matthew Broderick and Bridget Fonda), a would-be cereal tycoon (John Cusack) and the fanatical doctor's lunatic son (Dana Carvey). Director Alan Parker's failed comedy plumbs the depths of repellent scatological humor as cardboard characters drone on endlessly about their private bodily functions. Recurring nudity, an adulterous situation, continuous toilet humor, an accidental electrocution and an instance of rough language

title: Road to Zanzibar
synopsis: Zany fun with a pair of con-men (Bing Crosby and Bob Hope) whose witless schemes leave them stranded in Africa until they join a jungle safari with two Brooklyn entertainers (Dorothy Lamour and Una Merkel) in quest of a rich hunter. Directed by Victor Schertzinger, the second "Road" picture relies on the boys' shennanigans to carry the weak plot, and they do so in amusing fashion. Some sexual innuendo

title: Road Trip
synopsis: because several sexual encounters, sporadic nudity, intermittent drug use, comic depiction of suicide and recurring rough language,

title: Road Warrior, The
synopsis: Set in a post-nuclear wasteland, this Australian action thriller pits a surviving outpost of civilization clustered around a still functioning oil refinery against the barbarian horde who need gasoline for their motley assortment of vehicles. Max (Mel Gibson), a wandering loner, is chosen to deliver the gas through hostile lines. Except for director George Miller's stylish use of the setting, there is little in this blood-and-gore epic to occupy the mind. Excessive violence

title: Roaring Twenties, The
synopsis: Classy gangster melodrama in which a jobless World War I vet (James Cagney) makes a fortune as a bootlegger during Prohibition but goes bust in the Stock Market crash, then tangles with his prosperous ex-partner (Humphrey Bogart) to save the husband (Jeffrey Lynn) of his old flame (Priscilla Lane). Directed by Raoul Walsh, a newsreel narration sets the plot developments in the context of the times, with Cagney in top form as the good badguy who comes to a tragic end. Stylized violence, some of it quite nasty

title: Robbery
synopsis: Fact-based British thriller about the hijacking of the Royal Mail train with three millions pounds in cash and the escape of the robbery's mastermind (Stanley Baker) from the police dragnet. Director Peter Yates builds a lot of excitement and suspense, with a refreshingly minimum amount of violence

title: Roberta
synopsis: > Adaptation of composer Jerome Kern's Broadway hit, here starring Irene Dunne and Randolph Scott as a Russian princess and an American football player who inherits a Parisian fashion business. William A. Seiter directs, and look closely and you'll spot a blonde Lucille Ball as a model. Songs include "Smoke Gets in Your Eyes" and "I Won't Dance," and though Astaire and Rogers have only supporting roles they steal the picture A-I (nr) 1935

title: Robert A. Heinlein's The Puppet Masters
synopsis: ( see: "Puppet Masters, The" )

title: Robert et Robert
synopsis: Slight French comedy about two hapless and, apparently, hopeless bachelors (Jacques Villeret and Charles Denner) who meet while enlisting aid from a computerized matrimonial service and find themselves banding together against a hostile world. Directed by Claude Lelouch, the two principals are forced to fall back upon their quirks of character to keep the humor going. Mature theme and treatment

title: Robe, The
synopsis: Reverent but plodding Gospel-era story from the Lloyd C. Douglas novel about a Roman tribune (Richard Burton) whose gambling wins Christ's robe at the Crucifixion, then fears the robe's power to bewitch him until later becoming a Christian martyr in Rome. Directed by Henry Koster, the fictional tale is sincere but dramatically less than convincing in storyline and performances ranging from wooden to scenery-chewing, with the resulting inspiration more in the eye of the beholder than on the screen. Stylized violence and veiled sexual references

title: Robin and Marian
synopsis: Disappointing British addition to the Robin Hood legend set some 20 years after his youthful adventures in Sherwood Forest. Robin (Sean Connery) and his now melancholy men rescue Maid Marian (Audrey Hepburn) from a convent and the clutches of the dastardly Sheriff of Nottingham (Robert Shaw). Under Richard Lester's direction the performances are very good but the mood of the piece is confused, halfway between genuine romance and clumsy demythologizing. Some violence, crude humor and a sympathetically viewed suicide

title: Robin and the Seven Hoods
synopsis: Uneven gangster spoof set in 1928 Chicago where the top mob (headed by Peter Falk) tries to crush a smaller gang (led by Frank Sinatra) which gains public sympathy by donating its loot to charitable organizations. Directed by Gordon Douglas, the silly Robin Hood gimmick adds little to the sprawling comedy's hit-or-miss humor from a cast including Dean Martin, Sammy Davis, Jr., Edward G. Robinson, Bing Crosby and Barbara Rush. Comic violence and underworld activities

title: Robin Hood
synopsis: Disney feature cartoon offers a humorous version of the exploits of the English folk hero who robbed from the undeserving rich to give to the exploited poor. The cast consists of crisply drawn animals who lend themselves to such characterizations as Robin being a crafty fox and King John as an anemic lion. Older viewers will appreciate the classic Disney-style animation under the direction of Wolfgang Reitherman, while younger viewers enjoy the comic derring-do

title: Robin Hood: Men in Tights
synopsis: Mel Brooks' wacky send-up of the Sherwood Forest legend has the band of singing, prancing Merry Men attempting to rescue the captured Robin Hood (Cary Elwes) while Maid Marian (Amy Yasbeck) reluctantly agrees to marry the dastardly Sheriff of Rottingham (Roger Rees) to save him. As co-written, produced and directed by Brooks, the goofy spoof has moments of refreshing lunacy as well as his trademark brand of tasteless jokes that make this a hit-and miss affair. Much comic violence and some crude humor

title: Robin Hood of El Dorado, The
synopsis: Creaky Hollywood saga of California's legendary 19th-century Hispanic outlaw, Joaquin Murrieta (Warner Baxter), who becomes a bandit after gringo gold miners kill his wife and drunken Americanos lynch his brother. Director William Wellman romanticizes the bandits and their exploits in a plot muddled by unresolved notions of justice and revenge that ultimately have tragic consequences. Considerable stylized violence and menace in treating the theme of an oppressed minority

title: Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves
synopsis: Returning from the Crusades, Robin Hood (Kevin Costner) and his Moorish protector (Morgan Freeman) join the outlaws of Sherwood Forest in defiance of the cunning Sheriff of Nottingham (Alan Rickman) and his plans to marry Maid Marian (Mary Elizabeth Mastrantonio). Director Kevin Reynolds gives a frenzied, fresh spin to the oft-told tale which, despite many scattered flaws, boasts glorious cinematography and production design in addition to fine performances, especially Rickman's campy villain. Some gory violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Robinson Crusoe and the Tiger
synopsis: Amateurish Spanish version of the Daniel Defoe classic tale of shipwreck and survival with Crusoe played by Hugo Stiglitz who double-takes his way through various episodes of being chased by everything from sharks and panthers to bats and tigers. Directed by Rene Cardona Jr., its stagey camerawork and droning narration may put the small fry to sleep

title: Robinson Crusoeland
synopsis: ( see: "Utopia" )

title: Robinson Crusoe on Mars
synopsis: Engaging sci-fi variation on the Defoe story with an astronaut (Paul Mantee) marooned on Mars with only a monkey as company, then rescuing a human-like slave (Vic Lundin) from an alien spaceship. Directed by Byron Haskin, the story is told in imaginative fashion holding interest to the end which is a new beginning

title: Robinson Crusoe
synopsis: ( see: "The Adventures of Robinson Crusoe" )

title: RoboCop
synopsis: Futuristic urban crime drama about a good Detroit cop (Peter Weller) shot up by hoods and recycled into a robotized part-man, part-machine programmed to rid the streets of crime. Dutch director Paul Verhoeven doesn't spare any blood and gore in his relentlessly graphic depiction of violent law enforcement tactics used aganist equally violent criminals. Conveys a dangerous ends-justifies-the-means brand of justice

title: RoboCop 2
synopsis: About to be relegated to the junk heap, RoboCop (Peter Weller) struggles to maintain his identity while searching for Detroit's drug lord (Tom Noonan), whose demonic mind is being used by an evil corporation to create a far worse enemy: RoboCop 2. Directed by Irvin Kershner, the story is overwhelmed by an endless avalanche of explosive special effects and machine gun mayhem, with the particularly objectionable use of a pre-teen portrayed as a hardened criminal. Excessive violence, intense menace and rough language

title: RoboCop 3
synopsis: Slack but violent sequel in which the part-human cop (Robert John Burke) joins Detroit's citizen rebels who have gone underground to fight the systematic destruction of their homes by the powerful development corporation that runs the beleaguered city. Directed by Fred Dekker, the long, unrelieved formula tale offers little more than wall-to-wall bullets and bloodshed. Much mindless mayhem and gratuitous violence

title: Robots
synopsis: Technically dazzling but disappointingly formulaic animated feature about would-be inventor robot Rodney's (Ewan McGregor) coming of age, as he leaves his parents to make his mark in far-off Robot City and joins forces with master inventor Bigweld (Mel Brooks) and some misfit robot friends to help defeat the evil Madame Gasket (Jim Broadbent) and her power-hungry son, Ratchet (Greg Kinnear), who are consigning "outmoded" robots to the scrap heap rather than equipping them with new parts. Chris Wedge's overly busy follow-up to "Ice Age" is further undermined by a merely serviceable script that substitutes some needlessly vulgar humor and a pat follow-your-dream sentiment for true wit and originality. Despite the all-star voice cast, including Halle Berry, Drew Carey and Amanda Bynes, the "bots" fail to have really distinct personalities -- their mechanized body parts allowing only limited expression -- and even Robin Williams seems subpar in this setting. Some questionable humor and innuendo and crass expressions

title: Rob Roy
synopsis: Romantic tale of the struggle for justice waged by the title's 18th-century Scottish highlander (Liam Neeson) who becomes a fugitive after the money loaned to him by a venal nobleman (John Hurt) is stolen by a ruthless thief (Tim Roth) who also violated Rob's wife (Jessica Lange). Although overlong and ponderously directed by Michael Caton-Jones, the result succeeds better as the personal story of a loving couple than as a sweeping historical epic. Some sexual innuendo and intermittent violence, including a restrained rape scene and an off-screen suicide

title: Rock-a-Bye Baby
synopsis: Weak Jerry Lewis vehicle directed by Frank Tashlin has the befuddled comic playing nursemaid to the infant triplets of a former girlfriend (Marilyn Maxwell), now a voluptuous Hollywood star trying to keep her marriage and motherhood hidden from the public. Occasional fun for those willing to overlook all the sappy contrivances

title: Rock-a-Doodle
synopsis: In a story combining animation with live-action, a runaway rooster (voice of Glen Campbell) finds fame as an Elvis impersonator but doesn't forget his barnyard pals when they need him. Director Don Bluth turns out a busy musical fairy tale that holds some fun for the kiddies while being tolerable for adults

title: The Rocker
synopsis: Musical adventures of a likable lunkhead (Rainn Wilson) who, 20 years after being dumped by his band mates just before they catapulted to stardom, gets a second chance at fame when he joins a group made up of his socially challenged nephew (Josh Gad), a too-cool-to-smile guitarist (Emma Stone) and an angst-ridden singer-songwriter (Teddy Geiger), his bond with the last being strained by a budding romance with the lad's mother (Christina Applegate). Director Peter Cattaneo's sporadically funny comedy touches on themes of maturity and reconciliation and, though its values are somewhat hedonistic, this is largely a matter of talk, since Mom goes on tour as chaperone. Brief rear nudity, nonmarital cohabitation, sexual and scatological humor, one use of the f-word and some crass language, and drug and venereal disease references

title: Rocketeer, The
synopsis: Dumb story set in 1938 Los Angeles where a gangster (Paul Sorvino) and a movie star-turned-Nazi (Timothy Dalton) conspire to recover a stolen rocket-powered backpack from a daredevil pilot (Bill Campbell) by kidnapping his girlfriend (Jennifer Connelly). Director Joe Johnston's lively but cornball adventure features amusing special effects which help offset the hero's colorless personality. Sporadic comic-book violence

title: Rocket Gilbraltar
synopsis: Limply sentimental story of a family gathering to celebrate the 77th birthday of the clan's patriarch (Burt Lancaster) whose grown children are self-absorbed yuppies with mid-career problems but whose young grandchildren (notably Macaulay Culkin) heed his wish for burial at sea in a Viking's funeral. Director Daniel Petrie's romanticized version of life and death in a wealthy American suburb looks good but is empty of substance, both cerebral and emotional. Soggy human values, maudlin treatment of death and a benign view of promiscuity

title: RocketMan
synopsis: Dull comedy in which an annoyingly infantile computer nerd (Harland Williams) saves the day while aboard a space mission to Mars that goes awry. Directed by Stuart Gillard, the charmless proceedings are reduced to a series of clumsy pratfalls and rude body-function humor. Mild menace and toilet humor

title: Rocket Man, The
synopsis: Low-budget fantasy about an orphan (George Winslow) whose magic rocket gun saves the town orphanage from a crooked politician. Directed by Oscar Rudolph, the juvenile story offers little except veterans Spring Byington and Charles Coburn as small-town types

title: Rocket Science
synopsis: Quirky and sublime first-love dramedy about a stuttering young high-school boy (Reece Daniel Thompson) and the driven debating champ (Anna Kendrick) who to his surprise wants him as her debate-partner protege. Writer-director Jeffrey Blitz, without being preachy or obvious, shows us how family can come through when you least expect it, and how sometimes we can become better by going through what seems like the absolute worst. One instance each of rough language and profanity, several instances of crude and crass language, three scenes of young teens smoking or drinking, rude gestures, brief nudity in classical-art drawings, some pubescent sex talk, much debate-club discussion of abstinence policies and one instance each of implied sexual groping and off-camera sex sounds, both by adult characters

title: Rocking Horse Winner, The
synopsis: Unsettling British adaptation of D.H. Lawrence's story about a young boy (John Howard Davies) trying to help his spendthrift mother (Valerie Hobson) by getting winning tips on horse races from frenzied rides on his rocking horse. Writer-director Anthony Pelissier handles the boy's attempt to shoulder responsibility for his careless mother's financial needs but his strange system for picking winners turns the ending into uneasy fantasy. Parental neglect and its tragic result

title: Rock Island Trail
synopsis: Uneven Western directed by Joseph Kane in which an Illinois railroad owner (Forrest Tucker) bridges the Mississippi, then pushes his line across Iowa, despite acts of sabotage caused by a riverboat company owner (Bruce Cabot). Frontier violence

title: Rock Star
synopsis: The frontman (Mark Wahlberg) for a heavy metal cover band is chosen to replace the lead singer of the actual rock group he adores but learns his fantasy-come-true is not what he expected. Director Stephen Herek takes the viewer full circle in the predictable yet slightly appealing film, but the story is mostly shallow with a corny, feel-good ending. An implied sexual encounter with homosexual undertones, some nudity, brief drug content, fleeting fisticuffs and intermittent rough and crass language

title: Rock, The
synopsis: Violent action thriller involves the down-to-the wire efforts of a FBI chemicals expert (Nicolas Cage) and a former Alcatraz prisoner (Sean Connery) to defeat a disgruntled military hero (Ed Harris) from detonating poison-gas rockets aimed at vaporizing San Francisco. Director Michael Bay's slickly manipulative macho fantasy exaggerates murderous mayhem in a drawn-out exercise glorifying violence as he-man heroics. Excessive violence, brief bedroom scene and constant rough language

title: Rocky
synopsis: Underdog Philadelphia club fighter Rocky Balboa (Sylvester Stallone) has a shot at the heavyweight championship with the help of a tough old trainer (Burgess Meredith). Director John Avildsen concentrates on the gritty, back-street quality of life in the old neighborhood and the relationship that grows between Rocky and the introverted sister (Talia Shire) of his best friend (Burt Young). The bloody brutality of the prizefight game is abundantly evident

title: Rocky Balboa
synopsis: Sixth and ostensibly final round in the "Rocky" saga, in which former heavyweight champ Rocky Balboa (Sylvester Stallone), now a widower, estranged from his son (Milo Ventimiglia) and running a restaurant, comes out of retirement, stepping into the ring against the current champ (Antonio Tarver) to prove he has plenty of heart left in his aging body. Written and directed by Stallone, this new chapter is arguably the best in the series since the 1976 original, emphasizing character and emotional drama over fight action, while imparting an inspirational message about perseverance and giving it your all, win or lose. Some bloody boxing violence and a few mildly crude expressions

title: Rocky Horror Picture Show, The
synopsis: An engaged couple (Susan Sarandon and Barry Bostwick), stranded on a back road late at night, wander into an eerie mansion where they join in the kinky games of a Transylvanian transvestite (Tim Curry) and his weird band of followers. Directed by Tim Sharman, this clumsy adaptation of a campy British musical spoofs old horror movies while trashing traditional values in a tiresome display of bad taste and moral vacuity. Excessive emphasis on sexual license and some scenes of violence

title: Rocky II
synopsis: Writer-director Sylvester Stallone stars as the prizefighter unable to settle down with a new wife (Talia Shire), house and baby. Low on cash and brains, he accepts a rematch with Apollo Creed (Carl Weathers), the undefeated champ whom he almost beat in the first film. Though the sequel is formula entertainment with its theme of the victorious underdog, the movie clearly celebrates the violence of the ring, assigning value as much to the brutal sport as to its likeable hero's will and determination

title: Rocky III
synopsis: Apollo Creed (Carl Weathers) trains his former opponent (Sylvester Stallone) so that he can hold on to his title against a snarling and vicious challenger (Mr. T.). Also written and directed by Stallone, it may not be a knockout but it is good, solid entertainment. The carnage in the ring, though of briefer duration than previously, is still very intense

title: Rocky IV
synopsis: Sylvester Stallone gets back in the ring for the fight of his life against a Russian Olympic boxing machine (Dolph Lundgren). Stallone directs himse1f fighting to avenge the death of Apollo Creed (Carl Weathers) while regaining American honor. The sensitive may find the fight scenes too brutal

title: Rocky Mountain
synopsis: Once again, Errol Flynn dies with his boots on, this time when Shoshone Indians massacre his column of Confederate cavalry (including Guinn Williams and Slim Pickens) in California to stir up trouble just before the end of the Civil War. Under William Keighley's lackluster direction, the grimly stirring finale can't save the talky, slow-paced narrative preceding it. Stylized violence and an unconvincing tribute to a lost cause

title: Rocky V
synopsis: When brain damage forces Rocky (Sylvester Stallone) to retire from the ring, he tries a new career as a manager but in the process neglects his wife (Talia Shire) and son (Sage Stallone) until a startling blow from his protege (Tommy Morrison) brings him to his senses. As scripted by Stallone and directed by John Avildsen, there's still energy and brutality left in the sequel formula which this round concentrates on preserving family values despite the loss of material goods. Graphic boxing violence

title: Rodan
synopsis: Dubbed Japanese monster movie with Inoshiro Honda directing ugly-looking mega-creatures stirred from prehistoric slumber by H-bomb tests and decked out in rubber suits, the most threatening of which are the two pterodactyls of the title whose flapping wings cause typhoon-force winds. Formula menace and stylized violence, mostly in the destruction of scale-model miniatures

title: Roger Corman's Frankenstein Unbound
synopsis: Campy sci-fi horror yarn in which a scientist from the future (John Hurt) zooms back to the 19th century for a perilous confrontation with Dr. Frankenstein (Raul Julia) and his gabby monster (Nick Brimble). Director Roger Corman jumbles genres, using gore for comic effect, in this silly but eye-catching update of the monster myth. Stylized grisly violence and a casual attitude toward promiscuity

title: Roger & Me
synopsis: Arresting documentary on the economically depressed city of Flint, Michigan, once the prosperous bastion of good old-fashioned capitalism and now a town with 30,000 unemployed auto workers due to General Motors' plant closings. Written, produced and directed by Michael Moore, a Flint native, the work's subjective treatment contains much irony and black humor as it documents the city's decline and pitiful attempts to rejuvenate itself while trying to bring GM chairman Roger Smith face-to-face with the results of these layoffs. Some profanity laced with vulgar ethnic and sexist references and the gratuitous inclusion of a rabbit's slaughter and skinning

title: Rogue Cop
synopsis: Hard-boiled story of a veteran police detective (Robert Taylor) who's on the mob's payroll until they kill his younger cop brother and he pays them back in kind. Directed by Roy Rowland, the result is an overly familiar crime-does-not-pay story with few interesting details and no surprises. Nasty stylized violence and some sexual innuendo

title: Rogues' Regiment
synopsis: Convoluted tale of a U.S. agent (Dick Powell) joining the French Foreign Legion in Indo-China in order to nab an escaped Nazi war criminal (Stephen McNally). Directed by Robert Florey, the Nazi-hunter's pursuit of his quarry holds no surprises, but the result has interest in what it shows of the guerrilla tactics of the Viet Minh rebels, especially their use of underground tunnels. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Role Models
synopsis: A carefree salesman (Seann William Scott) and his caustic partner (Paul Rudd), sentenced to community service, ineptly mentor a tough-talking fifth-grader (Bobb'e J. Thompson) and a socially awkward teen (Christopher Mintz-Plasse). Despite a redemptive story line and some solid performances, director and co-writer David Wain's buddy comedy -- which also features Jane Lynch as the mentoring program's manic director -- goes awry mining laughs from casual sex and an expletive-spouting, sexually precocious child. Strong sexual content, including frontal-male, upper-female and rear nudity and nongraphic, nonmarital sexual activity; cohabitation; much sexual humor; pervasive rough and crude language; the occasional use of profanity; and drug use

title: Roll Bounce
synopsis: Cute but contrived coming-of age comedy set in Chicago during the roller-disco craze of the 1970s about a roller-skating obsessed teen (Bow Wow) who, together with his buddies, enters a skating contest against their crosstown rivals, while dealing with unresolved emotions over the recent loss of his mother and strained relationship with his dad (Chi McBride), who is struggling to raise his children alone. Directed by Malcolm D. Lee, the movie has heart, but its sentimental themes of parental loss and family love are saddled with a formulaic, albeit feel-good, narrative and occasional -- and most unnecessary -- crassness. Some sexual humor, as well as scattered crude language and gestures, making it most suitable for older adolescents and up

title: Rollerball
synopsis: Mindless remake set in 2018 in which the popular player (Chris Klein) of a brutal blood sport which combines roller derby, motorcycle racing and hockey, discovers that the team's owner (Jean Reno) is behind the serious on-court accidents aimed at increasing TV viewership. Sci-fi action flick is relentlessly repetitive with an absurd plot that director John McTiernan doesn't even bother to develop, concentrating instead on the violent extreme-sports antics and lavish, bizarre costuming. Intermittent violence, an implied sexual encounter, fleeting drug abuse and recurring profanity and crass language

title: Rollerball
synopsis: The title refers to a brutal game invented by the rulers of a future society in order to keep their subjects docile by watching the violence of others. When one of the star players (James Caan) begins attracting his own followers, he is ordered to retire but instead leads a revolt. Directed by Norman Jewison, the movie has little to offer except the lavish violence of the game and then of the revolt, thereby exploiting what supposedly it intended to condemn

title: Roller Boogie
synopsis: Spoiled little rich girl (Linda Blair) flees parents and promising career as flutist for the joys of the roller skating rink. Director Mark L. Lester forgets the plot to focus on scenes of nubile youngsters in scanty costumes skating and dancing to disco rhythms. The boring exercise in coed velocity has little to offer its intended teenage audience

title: Rollercoaster
synopsis: Slack thriller about an extortionist (Timothy Bottoms) who plants bombs on rollercoasters and the safety inspector (George Segal) who chases him across the country. Directed by James Goldstone, the movie's sole aim is visceral excitement unhindered by any larger concerns, including the risk entailed by putting such an idea into the public consciousness. Graphically depicted rollercoaster crash

title: Rolling Thunder
synopsis: When a returned Vietnam prisoner-of-war (William Devane) finds that his wife and son have been murdered during a robbery, he sets out to exact a bloody vengeance. Written by Paul Schrader and directed by John Flynn, the movie's mayhem and slaughter exploits the serious issue of the problems of returned prisoners-of-war. Its reverence for guns approaches fetishism

title: Rollover
synopsis: Slick romantic melodrama about a bank president's widow (Jane Fonda) who uncovers fraud in the international monetary system after Arab finaciers decide not to redeposit (rollover) their huge sums in her bank and her boy friend (Kris Kristofferson) tries to save the day. Directed by Alan J. Pakula, the plot is so contrived that the proceedings are hard to take. Several restrained sex scenes and some rough language

title: Roma, Citta Aperta
synopsis: ( see: "Open City" )

title: Roman de Gare
synopsis: Impeccably crafted suspense tale from great director Claude Lelouch in which a young woman (Audrey Dana) abandoned at a gas station after a fierce argument with her fiance accepts a lift from an ominous stranger (Dominique Pinon) who agrees to drive her to her parents' farm and pose as her fiance. Stunningly acted by all -- including Fanny Ardant as a best-selling author whose story, along with that of a woman (Michele Bernier) whose husband has suddenly gone missing, eventually intersects with the main one -- and cleverly written to keep you guessing right up to the end, the film is keenly observant about human nature, the creative process and love. Sporadic rough language and crude expressions, brief frank sexual dialogue and suicide. In French. Subtitles

title: Romance and Riches
synopsis: ( see: "The Amazing Adventure" )

title: Romance of a Horsethief
synopsis: Folk tale set in a Polish village near the German border in 1904 where most of the peasants subsist by selling stolen horses to the Imperial German Cavalry. When the local Cossack commander (Yul Brynner) requisitions all horses and conscripts the young men for the Czar's war against Japan, some of the villagers (Eli Wallach, David Opatoshu and Lainie Kazan) turn the tables on the Russian officer. Director Abraham Polonsky tells the tale in lively farcical fashion but some indulgent nudity and rough verbal exchanges between wily Wallach and his mistress Kazan spoil what should have a lighthearted adventure

title: Romance on the Range
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Joseph Kane in which a singing ranch foreman (Roy Rogers) nabs the fur thieves who have been raiding the outfit's trap-lines, with a little help from his cook (George "Gabby" Hayes) and the ranch's Eastern owner (Sally Payne). Stylized violence

title: Romancing the Stone
synopsis: Sedate novelist (Kathleen Turner) finds herself plunged into wild adventure when she goes to Colombia to ransom her kidnapped sister but a handsome American adventurer (Michael Douglas) turns up to save her at fairly regular intervals. Directed by Robert Zemeckis, the exotic romance strives hard for, but never achieves, a tongue-in-cheek style to take the realistic edge off the action and allow for laughs. Some graphic violence, rough language and partial nudity in a bedroom scene

title: Roman Holiday
synopsis: Charming romantic comedy in which a young princess (Audrey Hepburn) on an official visit to Rome slips away from her stuffy entourage to see the sights in the company of two American reporters (Gregory Peck and Eddie Albert), one of whom inevitably falls for her. Directed by William Wyler, the plot begins as light-hearted fluff, proceeds with warm camaraderie along the avenues and byways of the Eternal City, then turns serious as romance blossoms until the bittersweet ending. Romantic situations

title: Roman Scandals
synopsis: After a vivid dream about being a slave in ancient Rome plotting against a corrupt emperor (Edward Arnold), a jobless menial (Eddie Cantor) awakens to save his small town from a corrupt mayor. Directed by Frank Tuttle, the musical comedy has some good gags and funny routines featuring racing chariots, laughing gas and poisoned food, but several outlandish production numbers featuring slave girls fall flat. Sexual innuendo and a period blackface routine

title: Roman Spring of Mrs. Stone, The
synopsis: When her rich husband dies, an aging Broadway actress (Vivien Leigh) retires to Rome, meets the wrong people (notably Lotte Lenya) and takes an Italian gigolo (miscast Warren Beatty) as her lover until he turns to a younger woman (Jill St. John). Directed by Jose Quintero from the Tennessee Williams novel, the shallow proceedings are beautifully photographed but the characters and situations are largely unconvincing, despite Leigh's poignant performance in the title role. Sexual situations

title: Romantic Comedy
synopsis: Mediocre screen version of Bernard Slade's play about a successful Broadway playwriting team (Dudley Moore and Mary Steenburgen), whose professionalism takes a decade or so to ripen into romance. As directed by Arthur Hiller, the movie is not very romantic or comic, but the charm of the principals makes it a shade less unbearable. Though adultery figures in the plot, it is not condoned and the whole enterprise is rather innocuous

title: Romantic Englishwoman, The
synopsis: Starts out in a Central European spa and quickly goes from Baden-Baden to worse in a continental triangle involving Michael Caine, Helmut Berger and Glenda Jackson. Very British production directed by Joseph Losey attempts to be civilized and very arch, but aside from an occasional joke that comes off, it is a pretentious nothing. Sexual situations and some nudity

title: Rome Adventure
synopsis: Romantic clunker about a young American (Suzanne Pleshette) in Rome to see the sights while looking for a job, then finds true love with an art student (Troy Donahue) until his former flame (Angie Dickinson) turns up to reclaim him. Writer-director Delmer Daves pours on the treacle shamelessly, but the only romance going on here is the camera's love affair with the beautiful Italian landscapes and grand cultural monuments. Romantic complications and sexual innuendo

title: Romeo and Juliet
synopsis: Director Franco Zeffirelli's somewhat free interpretation of Shakespeare's tragedy of young love offers much energetic action in a stylish production with teenaged Olivia Hussey and Leonard Whiting in the title roles. Brief nude scene

title: Romeo and Juliet
synopsis: ( see: "William Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet" )

title: Romeo Is Bleeding
synopsis: Crooked New York cop (Gary Oldman) doubling as a mob informer-hitman for big bucks gets in way over his head when he falls for a sexually voracious murderess (Lena Olin) he's been ordered to kill. Director Peter Medak sensationalizes a host of vicious characters in a garish, blood-drenched potboiler about soulless killers-for-hire. Much grisly violence, seamy sexual encounters, recurring nudity and constant rough language

title: Romeo Must Die
synopsis: Entertaining hip-hop action drama about an ex-cop (Jet Li) who escapes from a Hong Kong prison to avenge the death of his beloved brother in California only to get caught in a gang war between Asians and African-Americans, and by chance, fall in love with the rival gang leader's daughter (Aaliyah). Director Andrzej Bartkowiak's feature debut combines skillfully choreographed martial-arts action with cutting-edge music but the surprising twists and double crosses produce a convuluted plot marred by skimpy character development. Recurring violence, brief homosexual innuendo, fleeting nudity, brief recreational drug use, and some rough language

title: Romero
synopsis: Powerful dramatization of the last three years in the life of Archbishop Oscar Romero of San Salvador whose condemnation of human rights abuses led to his assassination in 1980. Director John Duigan gets a brilliant performance from Raul Julia who invests the title role with an intense spiritual dimension that makes credible Romero's courage in condemning the immorality of a ruthless regime. Its graphic scenes of violence are not for the immature, though most adolescents will understand the justice issues involved

title: Romper Stomper
synopsis: Sour Australian production follows a group of skinheads who spout white supremacist slogans while brutalizing Asians and others in and around Melbourne. Writer-director Geoffrey Wright's dreary story of society's rejects and drop-outs turning into Neo-Nazi thugs leads nowhere and proves as aimless as the mayhem and destruction it spends all its energy depicting. Excessive violence, explicit sex scenes, racist rhetoric and occasional rough language

title: Romy and Michele's High School Reunion
synopsis: Thin comedy about two blonde airheads returning for their tenth class reunion and trying to prove they are as bright as everyone else. Directed by David Mirkin, the feather-brained situation is tiresomely padded out with sophomoric jokes and unamusing sexual references. Some restrained sex scenes, crude discussions of sexual subjects and frequent rough language with a blatant instance of profanity

title: Ronin
synopsis: Well-crafted action thriller in which a band of professional gunmen (including Robert De Niro, Jean Reno and Stellan Skarsgard) are hired to hijack a metal case, but the plan goes awry when one of them escapes with it and leads them on a chase across France. Veteran director John Frankehimer turns in a taut, fast-paced crime caper filled with shootouts, car chases, murky international intrigue and picturesque French locales, all of which will be enjoyed by fans of old-fashioned action movies. Much stylized violence, some rough language and occasional profanity

title: Ronja, Robbersdaughter
synopsis: Swedish import directed by Tage Danielsson features two children reacting to the selfish insensitivity of their fueding families in a medieval forest setting. Exemplary for its insight and understanding about the feelings of children in relation to parental weaknesses, the movie has two brief scenes of nudity, treated innocently and humorously, in an otherwise delightfully entertaining feature for children

title: Rooftops
synopsis: Fantasy about New York City street kids who use a form of martial arts called combat dancing to defend their turf from crack dealers. Included are a thwarted love affair between a white boy and an Hispanic girl (Jason Gedrick and Troy Beyer), some comic relief by a graffiti artist (Alexis Cruz) and dastardly deeds by a crack dealer (Eddie Velez). Despite its anti-drug message and some energized music and dance, veteran director Robert Wise's urban fairy tale is no "West Side Story." Much profanity, some intense violence and a fleeting, graphic sexual encounter

title: Rookie of the Year
synopsis: Lightweight but mostly enjoyable comedy with a 12-year-old youth (Thomas Ian Nicholas) becoming the star pitcher for the Chicago Cubs after his broken arm heals in a fashion enabling him to throw 103-mph fastballs. Director Daniel Stern pins most of the laughs on the incongruity of a youngster competing successfully with big leaguers, though adults may find the predictable results of this boyhood fantasy rather mechanical little league entertainment. Mild sexual innuendo involving adults

title: Rookie, The
