synopsis: Peter Frampton and the Bee Gees attempt to turn the Beatles' famous music album into a movie in which they play small-town musicians temporarily corrupted by becoming Los Angeles rock stars. When they learn that baddies have despoiled their home town, they return to right all wrongs. Director Michael Schultz gets more the feel of an animated cartoon than a live-action and George Burns does some narration since the movie has no dialogue. Some suggestive gestures and lyrics as well as pot smoking and the use of cocaine

title: Shadow Conspiracy
synopsis: Slick thriller in which a top presidential aide (Charlie Sheen) becomes the target of an assassin while working with the White House chief of staff (Donald Sutherland) to find the high-level officials plotting to topple the government. Directed by George P. Cosmatos, the chase scenes are skillfully executed but the story's muddled plot becomes increasingly less than credible. Numerous stylized murders, occasional profanity and intermittent rough language

title: Shadow Hours
synopsis: Monotonous drama about a recovering drug addict (Balthazar Getty) hoping to provide for his pregnant wife (Rebecca Gayheart) and live a clean life who is lured into the seedy, exotic underworld of Los Angeles by a suave writer (Peter Weller). Director Isaac Eaton's lackluster film cheats by using revolting images to disturb the viewer but a clumsy, unimaginative narrative and stilted performances fail to make it worthwhile. Several scenes of gratuitous violence and vilely masochistic images, recurring drug use, a sexual encounter with nudity, and intermittent rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Shadowlands
synopsis: Fact-based story of Anglican writer and Oxford don C.S. Lewis (Anthony Hopkins) whose closely guarded scholarly seclusion is unsettled late in life by one of his readers, a divorced American writer (Debra Winger) who stirs the lifelong bachelor to discover the friendship of a woman, then the emotional fulfillment of marriage and finally the pain of loss when she dies of cancer. Director Richard Attenborough's 1950's period piece explores the gradual transformation of a man who has devoted his life to intellectual pursuits until his heart is touched by a woman whose death plunges him in dark despair that challenges the consolation of his Christian faith. The tragic ending to this romantic story raises questions of life's true meaning

title: Shadow Magic
synopsis: Engaging period piece set in 1902 Peking where an Englishman (Jared Harris) opens up the country's first moviehouse, aided by an enthusiastic native (Xia Yu) whose interest in Western innovations jeopardizes his job and his love life. Director Ann Hu's fact-based tale is a valentine to the art of cinema as a universal language transcending race, language and cultural barriers. Partially subtitled. Mild violence. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Shadow of a Doubt
synopsis: Young girl (Teresa Wright) begins to suspect that her favorite uncle (Joseph Cotton) is wanted for a series of murders. Director Alfred Hitchcock unfolds his usual dark doings in the commonplace setting of small-town America's solid citizenry with uncommonly suspenseful results. A classic psychological thriller rich in visual understatement rather than shocking graphics

title: Shadow of the Hawk, The
synopsis: Terribly amateurish movie about an Indian medicine man (Chief Dan George) who wants his grandson (Jan-Michael Vincent), an IBM executive, to take over his practice and ward off the evil that threatens the tribe. Canadian production directed by George McCowan, the story is awfully far-fetched and not particularly scary

title: Shadow of the Thin Man
synopsis: Intriguing mystery sequel in which retired San Francisco sleuth Nick Charles (William Powell) helps a homicide detective (Sam Levene) solve several murders tied to a gambling syndicate, while wife Nora (Myrna Loy) befriends one of the suspects (Barry Nelson) and his girlfriend (Donna Reed). Directed by Major W.S. Van Dyke II, the plot employs numerous criminal types, including Stella Adler as a gold digger, but matters are lightened by some witty domestic scenes with three-year-old Nicky, Jr. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Shadow of the Vampire
synopsis: Creepy drama about the making of F.W. Murnau's 1922 silent horror classic "Nosferatu" which suggests that Murnau (John Malkovich) made a pact with an actual vampire (Willem Dafoe) to play the title role in exchange for the neck of the film's leading lady. Director E. Elias Merhige's warped film is absorbing in part, but not entirely consistent as it sometimes produces unintentional giggles despite the eerie nature of the film. Some violence and drug use, a few sexual references, brief nudity and minimal profanity and rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Shadow of the Wolf
synopsis: When an Eskimo hunter (Lou Diamond Phillips) kills a drunken white trader in the Far North of 1935, he and his wife (Jennifer Tilly) flee their village to live in the vast Arctic wilderness on their own but they cannot escape the curse of his shaman father (Toshiro Mifune) and the inexorable pursuit of white justice. In this beautifully photographed Canadian production based on the novel by Yves Theriault and directed by Jacques Dorfmann, the story of the individual hunter's struggle with the elements gets lost in the larger story of a native people's eroding culture but, dwarfing all, is the awesome splendor of this isolated, inhospitable, frozen world. Some stylized violence, including savage native customs, several sexual situations with fleeting nudity and a few instances of profanity

title: Shadows
synopsis: Low-budget picture of two black musicians (Ben Carruthers and Hugh Hurd) whose light-skinned sister (Lelia Goldoni) comes for a visit after graduating from college, then is seduced by a white writer (Anthony Ray) who scrams after learning her race. Directed by John Cassavetes, the Manhattan settings and cultural mix provide a realistic backdrop for situations improvised with some credibility by a talented cast, though the characters' problems are left unresolved. Some nasty violence, sexual situations and crude language

title: Shadows and Fog
synopsis: Drafted by vigilantes hunting a strangler in a 1920's European town, a timid clerk (Woody Allen) wanders the nighttime streets afraid of his own shadow until befriending a jilted circus performer (Mia Farrow) whose spunk inspires him. Using atmospheric black-and-white photography reminiscent of German silent movies, writer-director Allen creates a spooky story of chance meetings that hits as often as it misses with its forays into wry humor and philosophical musings. Some stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Shadows Over Chinatown
synopsis: Formula mystery with Charlie Chan (Sidney Toler) getting help from the San Francisco Missing Persons Bureau in nabbing a gang murdering people for their insurance. Directed by Terry Morse, a mysterious pickpocket (Jack Norton) adds some interest to the proceedings, with the usual comic relief from Chan's chauffeur (Mantan Moreland) and Number Two Son (Victor Sen Young, aka Yung). Menacing situations

title: Shadow Strikes, The
synopsis: Creaky mystery directed by Lynn Shores and based on the Street and Smith pulp magazine hero, Lamont Cranston, who secretly fights crime in the guise of the mysterious Shadow. Here Cranston (Rod La Rocque) impersonates a big-time lawyer to get the goods on a blackmailer (Cy Kendall) while also solving a murder with some comic-relief help along the way from his bumbling English butler (Norman Ainsley). Menacing situations

title: Shadow, The
synopsis: Empty adaptation of the pulp novel-radio series in which a 1930's playboy and secret crimefighter (Alec Baldwin) joins forces with his mind-reading girlfriend (Penelope Ann Miller) to prevent a power-mad villain (John Lone) from detonating a catastrophic bomb in Manhattan. Director Russell Mulcahy's plodding adventure fantasy is awash in glamorous art deco decor but its throwaway plot fails to come to grips with the title character's dual nature. Some stylized but nasty violence and fleeting sexual innuendo

title: Shadrach
synopsis: Depression-era tale of an impoverished rural Virginia family (headed by Harvey Keitel and Andie MacDowell) that takes in a 99-year-old former slave (John Franklin Sawyer) who wants to be buried on the grounds of their ancestors' plantation where he grew up. Based on a William Styron short story and seen through the eyes of a 10-year-old boy, director Susanna Styron's slowly paced movie is a poignant portrait of hardscrabble folk reaching out to help a stranger die with dignity. Some alcohol abuse, fleeting sexual innuendo, juvenile skinny-dipping and constant profanity

title: Shaft
synopsis: Slick action drama about an NYPD detective (Samuel L. Jackson) who must track down the only witness (Toni Collette) to a racially-motivated murder to bring a slippery rich-boy killer (Christian Bale) to justice. Brutality and sharp street language tarnishes director John Singleton's update to the 1971 original that otherwise provides magnetic performances and an absorbing narrative loaded with twists and surprises. Recurring violence, constant rough language, and fleeting shadowy nudity. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Shaft
synopsis: Director Gordon Parks adroitly uses New York City as the backdrop for what is really only a routine, if fast-paced and savvy, detective story involving a private eye (Richard Roundtree) and the police department in a power struggle between a black mobster (Moses Gunn) and the Mafia to control the drug, prostitution and numbers racket in Harlem. Some sharp and vicious violence, brief nudity and realistic street language

title: Shaft in Africa
synopsis: John Shaft (Richard Roundtree) is taken out of Harlem by an African diplomat who requires his services to break up a contemporary slave ring being run by a depraved Arab (Frank Finlay). Directed by John Guillermin, the plot is merely a pretext for indulging in graphic violence, explicit nudity and extremely crude dialogue

title: Shaft's Big Score
synopsis: When a big-time Harlem numbers operator dies, there is a scramble by black and white mobsters to take over the racket. Director Gordon Parks has turned his sequel into black exploitation, once again using Richard Roundtree as his hip private detective but this time smothering him in both easy (and often nude) women and gimmicky situations. Abundance of explicit violence and nudity

title: Shaggy D.A., The
synopsis: Disney sequel has the now grownup hero (Dean Jones) a crusading district attorney candidate running against a crooked incumbent (Keenan Wynn) and severely inconvenienced by his sudden transformations. Directed by Robert Stevenson, the humor is very broad and the slapstick heavy-handed even by Disney standards. All but very young children will likely be bored much of the time

title: Shaggy Dog, The
synopsis: Disney comedy directed by Charles Barton in which a magic ring causes a teenager (Tommy Kirk) to be transformed into a big bushy dog every now and then. The comic premise will appeal to youngsters, if not their parents

title: Shag: The Movie
synopsis: Nostalgic, feel-good story, set in 1963, tracks the last weekend fling of four recent high school grads (Page Hannah, Bridget Fonda, Annabeth Gish and Phoebe Cates) at Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, where boys, the annual Sun Fun Festival and a Shag dance contest are attractions. When one loses her virginity and breaks her engagement, the stage is set for an agonizing moral dilemma despite the cartoon plot. Director Zelda Barron respects her young subjects who giggle a lot about sex but have mostly harmless things on their minds. Some locker room language laced with mild sexual vulgarities

title: Shakedown
synopsis: Another buddy crime-buster movie in which a flakey legal aid attorney (Peter Weller) and a vigilante plainclothes detective (Sam Elliot) attempt to snare some crooked New York City cops who live high on the hog by stealing from drug dealers. With little chemistry between the leads, director James Glickenhaus relies on intense chase scenes and graphic violence. Gritty scenes within a posh drug club and a grim 42nd Street sex parlor featuring frontal nudity and much street language

title: Shake Hands with the Devil
synopsis: In the 1920s, an American student (Don Murray) in Ireland gets drawn into the struggle against British rule by a tough rebel leader (James Cagney). Director Michael Anderson is less interested in the issues of the conflict than in the human casualties caused by a spiraling cycle of violence. Some stylized violence and considerable tension

title: Shake, Rattle & Rock!
synopsis: Pop music programmer directed by Edward L. Cahn in which a citizen's group (led by Douglass Dumbrille, Margaret Dumont and Raymond Hatton) protests rock music as undermining teen morality until a disk jockey (Touch Connors) stages a TV trial on the issue, with help from Fats Domino and other rock stars. Stylized teen violence

title: Shakespeare in Love
synopsis: Spirited farce in which young Will Shakespeare (Joseph Fiennes) has problems writing "Romeo and Juliet" until he falls for a passionate beauty (Gwyneth Paltrow) who is engaged to a callous nobleman (Colin Firth) but disguises herself as a boy to play the role of Romeo. Director John Madden's rousing play-within-a-film is a zesty concoction of mistaken identities, outsized egos and doomed romance served up with contemporary humor. Brief comic violence, some sexual encounters with nudity and occasional double entendres

title: Shakespeare Wallah
synopsis: Director James Ivory's gentle study of the old and the new in modern India centers around an itinerant group of Shakespearean actors who find it difficult to bridge the gap between the old Anglo-Indian past and the changing values of the new India. One of the highlights is its ironic contrast between the romantic notions of a young English actress (Felicity Kendal) and the materialism of an Indian movie star to whom she is attracted. Utterly disarming picture of a culture in transition, though with some mature situations

title: Shakes the Clown
synopsis: A womanizing alcoholic clown (Bobcat Goldthwait) is framed for the drug-related murder of his boss (Paul Dooley) by a rival clown (Tom Kenny). Also written and directed by Goldthwait, the poorly-made black comedy wallows in the spiritual emptiness of the characters and is unredeemed by a phony righteous ending. Sporadic nasty violence, incessant rough language, numerous sexual references and recreational drug use

title: Shakiest Gun in the West, The
synopsis: Western comedy in which Don Knotts stars as a dentist who bungles his way to becoming a hero. Directed by Alan Rafkin, it's a pint-sized version of Bob Hope's "Paleface," but not nearly as amusing

title: Shakleton
synopsis: Absorbing but overlong drama which captures the amazing story of renowned British explorer Sir Ernest Shackleton�s (Kenneth Branagh) attempt to reach the South Pole. Visually spectacular, the film excels at presenting the camaraderie among the men with Shackleton as a complex man capable of great things. The main thrust of the film is on the survival of the men and Shackleton�s unwavering resolution to keep them all alive but there is fleeting profanity, an instance of rough language and a brief representation of Shackleton�s extramarital affair. 2002

title: Shalako
synopsis: Unconvincing Western about an aristocratic hunting expedition caught poaching on Apache land and rescued by a wily Indian fighter (Sean Connery). Director Edward Dmytryk handles the episodic action quite clumsily and the contrived love interest is ridiculous. Stylized violence

title: Shallow Grave
synopsis: Macabre thriller in which three young professionals (Kerry Fox, Christopher Eccleston and Ewan McGregor) sharing a flat in Edinburgh take in a roommate who soon overdoses leaving a suitcase full of cash which the three decide to keep after disposing of the body, but their sudden wealth has deadly consequences. Director Danny Boyle alternates unsettling humor with menacing visuals as the tension mounts between the bright, self-absorbed trio whose greed drives them to ghoulish deeds in guarding the money from the dead man's colleagues and eventually each other. Some graphic violence, images suggesting dismemberment, much menace, fleeting nudity and occasional rough language

title: Shallow Hall
synopsis: Shallow Hal -- A superficial guy (Jack Black) is temporarily hypnotized to see an obese woman as a slender beauty (Gwyneth Paltrow), with whom he falls in love, but he then must come to terms with her actual appearance. Director-brothers Bobby and Peter Farrelly's turn in a good-hearted moral tale but the one-joke situation is stretched to the limit as it walks the fine line between comedy and poor taste. An implied sexual encounter, a few sexist wisecracks, fleeting rear nudity and some crass phrases and profanity with an instance of rough language

title: Shall We Dance
synopsis: Delightful remake of 1996 Japanese film, now set in Chicago, about a lawyer (Richard Gere) in a rut with his loving but preoccupied wife (Susan Sarandon) and two teenage kids, whose life is transformed when he secretly enrolls in a ballroom dancing school, after he observes a beautiful and sad woman (Jennifer Lopez) looking out of the school's window. Director Peter Chelsom directs Gere in one of his best roles, Sarandon is appealing as the wife wondering at her husband's late nights, and Lopez has an ideal part as the emotionally damaged dance instructor with whom the husband bonds, with the dancing scenes a special treat. Wonderful feeling of uplift in terms of following one's dreams, and strong affirmation of family. A few instances of rough and crass language

title: Shall We Dance
synopsis: Thin musical comedy in which a ballet dancer (Fred Astaire) and a musical revue star (Ginger Rogers) team for a Broadway show, then get married in name only to avoid a scandal, but true love predicatably wins out in the end. Directed by Mark Sandrich, the fluffy story creaks with contrived comic complications and show business eccentrics but the song-and-dance numbers provide some first-rate entertainment

title: Shame
synopsis: Bleak Swedish drama about a couple (Liv Ullmann and Max Von Sydow) who escape a civil war by living on an island where they torment one another until the war drives them to a lifeboat drifting to sea. Director Ingmar Bergman's theme is the responsibility, personal and societal, for the kind of self-destruction imaged by civil war. Subtitles. Very intense, introspective picutre but powerfully told and worth seeing despite some scenes of violence

title: Shame
synopsis: Woman barrister skilled in the martial arts (Deborra-Lee Furness) motorcycles into a rural Australian town whose menfolk think nothing of molesting and raping women as a group sport. Director Steve Jodrell's heroine uses the time-honored methods of macho screen stars to right these wrongs. Rough language with sexual connotations, a continuing sense of menace and an intense grisly climax

title: Shameless Old Lady, The
synopsis: Gently satiric French story of an old lady (Sylvie), widowed in her seventies, who is clearsighted enough not to let her offspring take charge of her affairs but uses her small estate to enjoy the final months of her life. Directed by Rene Allio, it is an objective yet tender look at old age and the passive role assigned to it by social convention

title: Shampoo
synopsis: Warren Beatty stars as a Beverly Hills hairdresser who becomes involved with his clients, especially Julie Christie, Goldie Hawn and Lee Grant. Directed by Hal Ashby, it is mindless fare as much devoid of humor as of humanity. Verbal obscenities and graphic depiction of sexual misbehavior

title: Shamus
synopsis: Tough private eye from Brooklyn (Burt Reynolds) gets embroiled in a nasty little adventure involving diamond-heisting, gun-running, and double-crossing double-crossers. Directed by Buzz Kulik, the shallow plot's fast-paced action is done with some genial humor which helps diffuse numerous savage beatings and several restrained sex scenes

title: Shane
synopsis: Classic Western about a former gunfighter (Alan Ladd) who is befriended by a farm family (Van Heflin, Jean Arthur and young Brandon De Wilde), then saves them from being run off their land by a rancher's hired gun (Jack Palance). Directed by George Stevens, it's an epic tale of the conflict over land rights pitting the cattlemen's six-shooters against the homesteaders' moral fortitude and family roots. Stylized frontier violence

title: Shanghai Chest, The
synopsis: Formula Charlie Chan mystery directed by William Beaudine pits the Chinese-American detective (Roland Winters) against a murderer in an insurance scam, with the usual comic relief supplied by Chan's chauffeur (Mantan Moreland) and No. 2 son (Victor Sen Yung). Mild racial stereotyping

title: Shanghai Express
synopsis: Classic romantic adventure in which a British officer (Clive Brook) and the woman he once loved (Marlene Dietrich) meet on a passenger train which is captured by Chinese rebels whose ruthless leader (Warner Oland) agrees to spare the officer provided she becomes his consort. Directed by Josef von Sternberg, the melodramatic plot gains emotional credibility from Lee Garmes' Academy Award camerawork which alternates stark images of the wartime Chinese setting with poetic visuals of the couple's romantic struggles. Stylized violence, romantic complications and sexual innuendo

title: Shanghai Killers, The
synopsis: Routine martial arts programmer from Hong Kong in which the warrior swords go snicker-snack and the studio crew throw rubber hands and arms and buckets of blood around with wild abandon, all in service of the usual senseless violence

title: Shanghai Knights
synopsis: Madcap action comedy set in 1887 London where a carefree adventurer (Owen Wilson) helps his serious Chinese buddy (Jackie Chan) seeking to avenge the death of his Imperial Guard father and foil a royal family assassination plot. Director David Dobkin tosses current-day music and expressions into an escapist, comic mix of silly shenanigans and martial-arts derring-do. Frequent stylized violence, some sexual innuendo and an instance of profanity

title: Shanghai Noon
synopsis: because of intermittent stylized violence, implied sexual encounters, fleeting drug use and brief crass language,

title: Shanghai Surprise
synopsis: Sean Penn and Madonna give woefully inadequate performances in a supposedly romantic adventure set in 1930's China involving a search for a lost shipment of opium intended for wounded soldiers in a mission hospital. Brutal violence, sex scenes and profanity

title: Shanghai Triad
synopsis: Gangster tale set in 1930's China chronicles the power struggle between a Chinese crime boss, his trusted assistant and the beautiful mistress (Gong Li) they share, as seen through the naive eyes of her 14-year-old servant boy. Director Zhang Yimou captures the emptiness of ill-gotten material wealth in a powerful story of evil characters, their betrayals and reprisals. Subtitles. Some stylized violence, sexual innuendo and rough language

title: Shanks
synopsis: Odd but inept chiller starring French mime Marcel Marceau in the dual role of an ancient scientist and his deaf-mute assistant in a story-within-a-story involving an electronic device which can restore the dead to life. Directed by William Castle, the disjointed segments of the generally aimless and confused plot are introduced by title cards which don't help a bit. Some gruesome and violent visuals

title: Sharks' Treasure
synopsis: Not very exciting movie about diving for sunken treasure and a boat hijacking by murderous escaped convicts. Directed by Cornel Wilde (who also stars), it's routine adventure fare save for a homosexual reference in the plot

title: Shark Tale
synopsis: Visually sparkling, but otherwise underwhelming deep-sea animated comedy about a jive-talking little fish (voiced by Will Smith) who, after taking undeserved credit for slaying a great white shark menacing his coral reef community, finds himself up to his gills in trouble with the shark's dad (voiced by Robert DeNiro), the godfather of the underwater underworld. Directed by Vicky Jenson, Bibo Bergeron and Rob Letterman, the vibrant fish fable is swimming with clever mob movie references, but founders when it comes to story and characters, several of whom may be perceived as reinforcing negative ethnic stereotypes. An instance of violently descriptive dialogue and some mildly crude language and humor

title: Sharky's Machine
synopsis: Burt Reynolds (who also directed) plays a tough and aggressive Atlanta detective demoted for overzealousness to the vice squad where he cracks down on prostitutes and drug dealers. Though the crime movie has some good moments (such as burly policeman Bernie Casey being a Zen devotee) and is consistently entertaining until its lackluster conclusion, the action includes a harrowing and far-fetched torture scene, some other graphic violence and very crude language

title: Shattered
synopsis: Convoluted thriller in which a wealthy land developer (Tom Berenger) suffering from amnesia after a near-fatal car crash enlists a cagey gumshoe (Bob Hoskins) to determine if his adulterous wife (Greta Scacchi) set up the accident. Writer-director Wolfgang Petersen spins an intricate tale of treachery and deceit greatly abetted by Hoskins' colorful characterization. Brief but recurring adulterous shots with nudity, momentary violence and some rough language

title: Shattered Glass
synopsis: Fact-based drama about a hotshot Washington journalist (Hayden Christensen) whose rising star is shot down when his editor (Peter Sarsgaard) discovers that many of the stories he wrote were total fabrications. While director Billy Ray's intelligent biopic takes a strong ethical stance, raising important questions concerning public trust issues, the film offers little insight into why its flawed protagonist indulged in such deception, resulting in a less-than-satisfying defense of journalistic integrity. Some rough and sexually crude language, sporadic profanity, as well as an instance of drug abuse

title: Shattered Image
synopsis: Violently surreal tale in which a wealthy bride (Anne Parillaud) on her honeymoon can't decide whether her husband (William Baldwin) is plotting to kill her or whether she's actually a professional hit woman and he's her next target. Though director Raul Ruiz wraps the dreamlike proceedings in an atmosphere of sinister mystery, the result is simply a tawdry potboiler littered with lurid scenes of real or imagined murders. Recurring violence, sexual encounters with nudity and some rough language

title: Shawshank Redemption, The
synopsis: Gritty prison drama begins in 1946 when a quiet banker (Tim Robbins) is wrongly convicted of murder, then spends the next two decades inside a brutal and corruptly run penitentiary where he has positive effects on the hapless inmates, especially another lifer (Morgan Freeman), before his unexpected departure. Director Frank Darabont does not spare viewers the dehumanizing ugliness of life behind bars in a story notable for its portrayal of a man who inspired hope in others while coping with the injustice done to him. Some graphic prison violence and suicides, crude sexual innuendo, brief nudity and much rough language

title: She
synopsis: Slim escapist entertainment from H. Rider Haggard's novel of adventurers (Peter Cushing, Christopher Lee and John Richardson) exploring the African desert in search of a hidden city, a lost civilization and an eternal female (Ursula Andress). Director Robert Day adds nothing new to the old story of derring-do in quest of the fantastic. Stylized violence and romantic situations

title: Sheba Baby
synopsis: Avenging black woman (Pam Grier) annihilates an army of hoods of various hues. Directed by William Girdler, it is a tasteless fantasy of sex and violence, though handled with some restraint

title: She Couldn't Say No
synopsis: Lackluster romantic comedy in which an oilman's daughter (Jean Simmons) causes havoc in a small Arkansas town by lavishing anonymous gifts of money on its genial rustics until the local doctor (Robert Mitchum) rechannels her generosity. Directed by Lloyd Bacon, the strained plot premise and charmless characters get in the way of the story's whimsical situations and country humor, with mostly unamusing results

title: She-Creature, The
synopsis: Feeble thriller directed by Edward L. Cahn in which a financier (Tom Conway) becomes partners with a strange mesmerist (Chester Morris) whose hypnotized assistant (Marla English) recalls various reincarnations until turning into a prehistoric sea monster. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: She-Devil
synopsis: Plodding comic fantasy about the revenge of a wife (Roseanne Barr) on her philandering husband (Ed Begley Jr.) and his rich mistress (Meryl Streep). Produced and directed by Susan Seidelman, the comic premise is handled so methodically that it quickly loses interest, except for Streep's broadly funny performance as an empty-headed, outrageously pretentious author of romance novels. Some profanity and several sex scenes intended as satire

title: Sheena
synopsis: Comic book jungle drama about a female Tarzan named Sheena (Tanya Roberts) who runs through Africa scantily clad in animal skins, pursued by a romantic TV reporter (Ted Wass). Directed by John Guillermin, it is so bad that it provokes laughter in all the wrong places. Extensive nudity

title: Sheepman, The
synopsis: Genial Western comedy in which an ornery cowboy (Glenn Ford) establishes a sheep ranch in the middle of cattle country, then unmasks the region's biggest rancher (Leslie Nielsen) as a crook, thereby winning over the local cattlemen and the man's fiancee (Shirley MacLaine). Director George Marshall paces the good-natured narrative with Ford's quirky characterization as an experienced gunman who would rather talk things out than engage in a shootout

title: She Hate Me
synopsis: Disjointed and didactic drama about a Harvard-educated vice president (Anthony Mackie) of a large pharmaceutical company on the verge of unveiling an AIDS vaccine who, after being fired and having his bank accounts frozen for blowing the whistle on his corporate higher-ups for Enron-like financial malfeasance, is persuaded by his entrepreneurial, lesbian ex-fiancee (Kerry Washington) to impregnate her and other maternally desperate lesbians at $10,000 a head. Working off a discursive script, director Spike Lee never really decides which story he wants to tell, cramming his potluck plot with a logjam of hot-button topics -- including white-collar crime, corporate greed, sexual politics, Watergate and racism -- while suggesting a radically unconventional redefining of family and sexual identity. Several explicit sexual encounters with nudity, same-sex kissing, a graphic suicide, strong sexual language and humor, as well as racial and ethnic stereotypes

title: Shelia Levine Is Dead and Living in New York
synopsis: Failed screen version of Gail Parent's acerbically witty novel about a small-town girl (Jeannie Berlin) who escapes to New York in search of meaning and marriage, finds a doctor (Roy Scheider) and convinces him that country virtues are better than urban sophistication. Not only are the principals miscast, but director Sidney Furie is out of his element in working with a script that has the deadly mediocre level of TV situation comedy

title: Sheltering Sky, The
synopsis: Visiting North Africa in the late 1940s, a troubled married couple (Debra Winger and John Malkovich) and their traveling companion (Campbell Scott) take a trip into the Sahara where they encounter typhoid fever, infidelity and madness. Director Bernardo Bertolucci's bleak journey into the void is a roadmap to despair given some poignancy by the beautifully photographed desert environment that devours the characters in this intense and harrowing film. A number of graphic adulterous liaisons with brief shots of full nudity

title: Shenandoah
synopsis: Civil War story of a Virginia family patriarch (James Stewart) whose opposition to slavery keeps him out of the war until one of his sons is captured and he fights his way through Union lines trying to find him. Director Andrew McLaglen does best with the action scenes showing the futile havoc of war but is less effective in portraying its consequences on the family and its members. Wartime violence

title: Shepherd of the Hills
synopsis: Creaky rural saga set in the Ozarks where revenue agents pursue moonshiners while a mysterious stranger (Harry Carey) wins over the suspicious mountain folk, except for a troubled young woodsman (John Wayne) who vows to kill him despite the protests of the girl (Betty Field) who loves the boy. Director Henry Hathaway establishes the isolated backwoods setting convincingly but the melodramatic story of tangled family relationships does not date well and the result is chiefly of interest for its good cast. Stylized violence and domestic strife

title: Sheriff of Cimarron
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Yakima Canutt in which a cowboy (Sunset Carson) accepts the vacant job of sheriff, then cleans up a gang of gold robbers, one of whom is his crooked brother. Frontier violence

title: Sheriff of Fractured Jaw, The
synopsis: Leaden Western spoof directed by Raoul Walsh delivers a mirthless misfire with Kenneth Moore as an English gun salesman pressed into service to protect a frontier town from warring ranchers (Bruce Cabot and William Campbell), with only Jayne Mansfield and a motley band of Indians for support. Stylized violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Sheriff of Wichita
synopsis: Western programmer directed by R.G. Springsteen in which the title lawman (Allan "Rocky" Lane) tracks some suspicious characters to an abandoned Army fort where a payroll mysteriously disappeared years before. Stylized violence

title: Sherlock Holmes and the Secret Code
synopsis: ( see: "Dressed to Kill" )

title: Sherlock Holmes and the Secret Weapon
synopsis: Dated mystery directed by Roy William Neill in which Holmes (Basil Rathbone) takes a hand in World War II by smuggling a bombsight inventor (William Post, Jr.) out of Switzerland, only to lose him in England to kidnappers led by Professor Moriarty (Lionel Atwill). Stylized violence, including a scene of torture

title: Sherlock Holmes and the Spider Woman
synopsis: ( see: "The Spider Woman" )

title: Sherlock Holmes and the Voice of Terror
synopsis: Called in by British intelligence to silence short wave broadcasts of Nazi sabotage, Holmes (Basil Rathbone) and Watson (Nigel Bruce) succeed with some help from the London underworld and a patriotic widow (Evelyn Ankers). Directed by John Rawlins, it's an interesting period piece, with colorful atmosphere and a good supporting cast (Thomas Gomez, Reginald Denny and Henry Daniell). Wartime menace

title: Sherlock Holmes Faces Death
synopsis: Intriguing entry in the updated Conan Doyle detective series with Holmes (Basil Rathbone) and Watson (Nigel Bruce) after a killer (Arthur Margetson) in a creeky English manor being used by convalescent Allied officers. With a script based on "The Musgrave Ritual," director Roy William Neill works up a lot of sinister atmosphere in the story of murdered brothers and a chess riddle involving a secret family inheritance. Menacing situations

title: Sherlock Holmes in Washington
synopsis: Fair World War II mystery in which Holmes (Basil Rathbone) and Watson (Nigel Bruce) search the U.S. capital for a missing British secret document which must be found before it falls into the hands of a Nazi spy ring (led by George Zucco). Directed by Roy William Neill, the plot involves the use of microfilm and a book of matches, with Watson providing the usual comic relief amidst the patriotic fervor of the period

title: She's All That
synopsis: Predictable teen romance in which a handsome senior (Freddie Prinze, Jr.), after being dumped by his glamorous girlfriend (Jodi Lyn O'Keefe), bets he can transform the class loner (Rachael Leigh Cook) into a popular beauty by prom night. Director Robert Iscove's derivative comedy is all too familiar and the self-absorbed adolescents prove uninteresting. An implied affair, some sexual references, brief alcohol abuse and a few instances of profanity and of rough language

title: She's Gotta Have It
synopsis: A serio-comic movie about a strong-willed, independent black woman (Tracy Camila Johns) who confounds three egocentric males. Director Spike Lee brings imagination and vitality to this low budget, black-and-white feature that offers some interesting characterizations with an accomplished all-black cast. Explicitly depicted sexual encounters, nudity and one scene of sexual brutality

title: She's Having a Baby
synopsis: Writer-producer-director John Hughes' coming-of-age comedy about a young man (Kevin Bacon) who must learn to face the responsibilities of married life before he and his wife (Elizabeth McGovern) have a baby. Fantasy sequences comically reflect Jake's inner turmoil, but the technique is overused to the detriment of the narrative. Sexual situations within marriage, fleeting nudity and some profanity

title: She's Out of Control
synopsis: Mindless, one-joke film about an overly protective single father (Tony Danza) who lies and spies on his 15-year-old daughter (Ami Dolenz) when she begins dating. Directed by Stan Dragoti, there are no subtleties in this picture of a distrustful parent-child relationship. Some sexually vulgar innuendoes

title: She's So Lovely
synopsis: Gritty, unappealing story of a woman (Robin Wright Penn) who's torn between her first husband (Sean Penn) who's just been released from a 10-year stay in a psychiatric asylum and her present husband (John Travolta) who has provided a good home for her and their three children. Directed by Nick Cassavetes from a script by his late father, John Cassavetes, the arbitrary love story involves three unlikeable people in sordid situations that evoke little sympathy, though there are occasional flashes of wit and originality sprinkled throughout. Some violence including an off-screen rape, sexual references, occasional profanity and much rough language

title: She's the Man
synopsis: Breezy if uneven modernizing of Shakespeare's comedy of mistaken identities, "Twelfth Night," about a teenage tomboy (Amanda Bynes) who poses as her twin brother (James Kirk), enrolls in his coed boarding prep school to play soccer, and winds up falling in love with his/her jock roommate (Channing Tatum), who has a crush on a pretty student (Laura Ramsey), who, in turn, is smitten with the new "guy," leading to predictable romantic complications. Director Andy Fickman cleverly updates Shakespeare's plot devices -- mixed-up lovers, triangular attractions, and gender-bending deception -- to mostly good effect, and the film overcomes forced humor in large measure due to Bynes' effervescence, though its occasionally crude comedy makes it best suited for older teens and up. Some sexual humor and innuendo, a bathroom brawl between three girls, brief implied nudity, sports roughness, a few crass expressions, as well as an instance of profanity

title: She's the One
synopsis: Talky domestic comedy in which two Irish Catholic brothers face marital breakups when the younger, fiercely competitive brother (Mike McGlone) begins cheating on his wife with the former fiancee of his newly married brother (Ed Burns). Also written and directed by Burns, the lightweight story explores issues of commitment vs. selfishness with airy charm, but scant substance. Theme of infidelity, numerous sexual references and frequent rough language as well as profanity

title: She's Working Her Way Through College
synopsis: Lackluster musical about a dancer (Virginia Mayo) who quits burlesque to go to college, then faces expulsion over her past until a downtrodden professor (Ronald Reagan) rallies the students in her support. Directed by Bruce Humberstone, the predictable proceedings include a hypocritical college trustee (Roland Winters), the former beau (Don DeFore) of the prof's wife (Phyllis Thaxter) and a musical football star (Gene Nelson), though the highlight is Reagan's game but inept performance in a comic drunk scene. Sexual situations and marital misunderstandings

title: She Wore a Yellow Ribbon
synopsis: Superior Western about a frontier outpost where a veteran cavalry officer (John Wayne) averts an Indian war on the eve of his mandatory retirement. Director John Ford's tribute to the horse soldiers who pacified the Western wilderness makes glorious use of Monument Valley in framing the action and warmly depicts the details of garrison life. Frontier violence

title: Shiloh
synopsis: After lying to his stern but loving father (Michael Moriarty) in order to save an abused puppy from its cruel master (Scott Wilson), an 11-year-old lad (Blake Heron) learns the painful consequences of dishonesty. Writer-director Dale Rosenbloom uses the appealing bond of boy and dog to probe the father-son relationship in a meaningful way but the narrative is too slow-paced and repetitive to be entirely successful as drama. Strong threat of animal abuse and domestic tensions

title: Shiloh 2: Shiloh Season
synopsis: The further adventures of a young boy (Zachary Browne) and his beagle center on growing problems with the dog's former owner (Scott Wilson) until a car accident seriously injures that mean-spirited, hard-drinking miscreant whose nasty disposition is slowly undone by the lad's conspicuous attempts to help out during his recovery. Directed by Sandy Tung, the story is dramatically uneven and occasionally dull, but its picture of a caring family is quite rewarding and the mixture eventually pays off in an emotionally satisfying conclusion, especially for young viewers. Menacing situations, an alcoholic central character and some vulgarity

title: Shinbone Alley
synopsis: Disappointing cartoon version of the Broadway musical based on Don Marquis' classic "archy and mehitabel" about the cockroach chronicler of the irrepressible alley cat whose spirit has transmigrated from Cleopatra. Directed by John D. Wilson, with the central characters voiced by Eddie Bracken and Carol Channing, the result simply lacks the elemental zest and witty irony of the Marquis original

title: Shine
synopsis: Remarkable fact-based story of an Australian musical prodigy who suffers a mental collapse as a youth (Noah Taylor) because of his iron-willed father (Armin Mueller-Stahl), then resumes a brilliant career as classical pianist in middle age after he (Geoffrey Rush) weds an understanding woman (Lynn Redgrave). Director Scott Hicks gives a universal dimension to this story of the damage done by a father's possessive, destructive love being undone by a woman's patient, redemptive love. Domestic violence, a fleeting bedroom scene and brief nudity

title: Shine A Light
synopsis: High-energy documentary capturing parts of two hard-driving performances by veteran rockers the Rolling Stones (Mick Jagger, Keith Richards, Charlie Watts and Ronnie Wood) at New York City's Beacon Theatre in fall 2006 during which they perform some of their most familiar songs as well as lesser-known original numbers and cover material. Director Martin Scorsese deploys 19 camera operators to create a fluid, consistently on-target visual record of the age-defying quartet as they strut, grimace and groove. Occasional rough and crude language, drug references, irreverent and suggestive lyrics

title: Shining, The
synopsis: Disappointing screen version of the Stephen King novel is a haunted house movie on a grand scale with Jack Nicholson as a writer who takes the job of winter caretaker of a hotel resort in the Colorado Rockies, accompanied by wife (Shelley Duvall) and young son (Danny Lloyd). Tormented and manipulated by the evil lurking in the massive hotel (the scene of a brutal axe murder), he is taken to the brink of madness and tries to kill his family. Director Stanley Kubrick's ponderous horror movie is predictable and slow-paced in building to its violent climax. Graphic violence, a needlessly extended erotic sequence and some rough language

title: Shining Through
synopsis: Blandly romantic World War II espionage tale follows an OSS Colonel (Michael Douglas) into Nazi Germany to rescue his spy-girlfriend (Melanie Griffith) who's trying to get crucial war plans from a high-ranking German officer (Liam Neeson). Though the actors try their best, they cannot overcome the plot implausibilities underlying writer-director David Seltzer's slack wartime love story. Brief violence and fleeting bedroom scene

title: Ship of Fools
synopsis: Abby Mann's flawed yet powerful adaptation of Katherine Anne Porter's allegorical novel centers on the foibles and self-delusions of some two dozen passengers (including Vivien Leigh, Oskar Werner, Simone Signoret, Jose Ferrer and Lee Marvin) on a German liner sailing from Mexico to its home port in 1933, the year Hitler came to power. Though producer-director Stanley Kramer is not always successful in giving dramatic credibility to the truncated stories of the numerous characters, he does manage to convey the inability of most to comprehend the Nazi menace as well as to suggest through the narrator (Michael Dunn) that viewers may discover something of themselves in this portrayal of human frailty. Some anti-Semitic references and sexual situations

title: Ship of Lost Men, The
synopsis: Silent German melodrama aboard a creaky old windjammer bound for Brazil with contraband cargo and a cruel captain (Fritz Kortner) whose mistreated crew mutiny, then turn against an unwilling American passenger and a downed woman pilot (Marlene Dietrich) he rescued from the sea. Written and directed by Maurice Tourneur, the murky story shows the self-destructive nature of violence with appropriate visual force, mixing realistic shots of the sailing ship with darkly menacing interiors and occasionally surrealistic images. Periodic violence, threatening situations and sexual innuendo

title: Shipwrecked
synopsis: Young Norwegian lad (Stian Smestad) goes to sea as a cabin boy but his ship is shanghaied by pirates, then wrecked by a tropical storm and the boy washed overboard to wind up on a deserted island where he finds the pirates' treasure and frees his shipmates from their fearsome captor (Gabriel Byrne). Directed by Nils Gaup, the 19th-century adventure of a youth coping in a man's world has the excitement of an ocean voyage under full sail and the inventiveness of a 14-year-old Robinson Crusoe but the personal level tends to get lost in the narrative's constant action. Much menace and some frightening moments for young children

title: Shirley Valentine
synopsis: In a British comedy of some wit and intelligence, a 42-year-old Liverpool housewife (Pauline Collins) leaves hubby and grown children for a two-week holiday in Greece where she meets a clay-footed womanizer (Tom Conti) but rediscovers on her own a long-submerged zest for life. Adapted from his own stage play by Willy Russell and directed a bit too literally by Lewis Gilbert, the adult comedy about a spunky middle-aged woman has a lot of heart and a memorable title performance. Some mature themes, fleeting nudity and comic use of a sexual expletive

title: Shoah
synopsis: Death camp survivors, former Nazi officials and Poles living in the vicinity of the extermination sites are interviewed by producer-director Claude Lanzmann in this French documentary on the Holocaust. Although it does not show any photographs of Hitler's mass murder of European Jewry, the survivors' oral history of events is powerful and often shocking, all the more so because it personalizes the horror of the camps. Subtitled and more than nine hours in length, the work is a valuable educational resource on the Holocaust

title: Shocker
synopsis: When a TV repairman (Mitch Pileggi) is electrocuted for murdering entire families, he is sucked into the TV airwaves from which he returns to slash more families until freeze-framed by a telepathic college football hero (Peter Berg). Writer-director Wes Craven mixes black humor and simple-minded satire with much profanity and grisly mass murders

title: Shocking Miss Pilgrim, The
synopsis: Mild musical comedy set in 1874 when Boston's first woman typist (Betty Grable) has a hard time keeping her job with a sexist boss (Dick Haynes) who ultimately proposes marriage. Writer-director George Seaton tries to have some fun playing both sides of the street but neither feminists nor chauvanists are likely to be amused, though some may enjoy the Gershwin music. Bland romantic complications and dated treatment of gender roles

title: Shock to the System, A
synopsis: Mild-mannered Manhattan ad executive (Michael Caine) finds that he can easily murder his demanding wife (Swoosie Kurtz) and yuppie colleague (Peter Riegert), among others who stand in his way. With flat direction by Jan Egleson, the movie balances uncomfortably between a satiric black comedy and a serial murder drama, providing a view of moral corruption that would be utterly distasteful if not for Caine's fine performance. Condones murder as an acceptable means to an end, a jokey on-screen suicide, some rough language and sexual innuendoes

title: Shock Troops
synopsis: French-Italian production about a group of French resistance fighters in World War II who raid a German prison to rescue 12 men sentenced to death but find that they have saved one man too many (Michel Piccoli) and suspect he may be a spy. Directed by Costa-Gavros, the story is much like other movies about the French Resistance, though its action scenes are almost documentary-like in effect. Wartime violence and brutality

title: Shoes of the Fisherman, The
synopsis: Uneven screen version of the Morris L. West novel about a Russian bishop (Anthony Quinn) who becomes Pope and decides that the Vatican's wealth be given to the world's poor. Directed by Michael Anderson, the point of the story gets lost in a series of murky subplots involving international intrigue. The religious pageantry is eye-catching but conveyed largely on a superficial level

title: Shogun Assassin
synopsis: Samurai swordsman wields his blade tirelessly in dispatching legions of assassins in this campy Americanized version of a Japanese martial arts movie directed by Kenji Jisumi. Narrated by a child, the action is a visual ballet of incessant violence and bloodshed

title: Shoot
synopsis: Painfully well-intentioned diatribe directed by Harvey Hart against the cult of guns has a preposterous story of two groups of hunters who, because of an accidental shooting death, begin an armed war against each other. Much violence

title: Shoot 'Em Up
synopsis: Ultraviolent action film about a mysterious sharpshooter (Clive Owen) and a prostitute (Monica Bellucci) with a baby in tow, on the run from a deadly assassin (Paul Giamatti). Writer-director Michael Davis' film is played tongue-in-cheek and with flashes of genuine wit, the two leads make charismatic adversaries with Giamatti relishing his villain's role, and there's even an anti-gun subtext, but the film is fast-paced to the point of exhaustion, and the intensity of the violence and myriad sordid elements preclude endorsement. Intense visceral violence with numberless killings, torture, a graphic sexual encounter and others less explicit, partial nudity, pervasive rough language and profanity, crude expressions, innuendo and an irreverent sight gag

title: Shooter
synopsis: Satisfying conspiracy thriller that plays like a Tom Clancy "Rambo," with Mark Wahlberg as an ex-U.S. Army sniper framed by government bigwig Danny Glover for an attempted presidential assassination that killed a foreign bishop instead. Director Antoine Fuqua, who knows his way around guns 'n' ammo from "Training Day" and "Tears of the Sun," keeps the grimly photographed action brisk and believable, and the plot twists mostly convincing. Some rough and crude language, much military violence with bloodshed, a scene of anonymous soldiers immolated by napalm, two scenes of torture aftermath, and a woman in partial states of undress, though no nudity

title: Shooting Party, The
synopsis: In the fall of 1913, some aristocrats gather at the estate of a nobleman (James Mason) to do a bit of shooting and carry on some romantic intrigues on the eve of the war that would end their world forever. Alan Bridges directs a thoughtful and entertaining film, if a bit slow-moving and predictable at times. Superbly acted but contains a rather explicit bedroom scene

title: Shooting, The
synopsis: Muddled Western in which a woman (Millie Perkins) hires two cowboys (Will Hutchins and Warren Oates) to help her track a man in the wilderness, then they tangle with a sinister gunslinger (Jack Nicholson) who's been trailing them, with surprising results. Directed by Monte Hellman, the obscure plot is secondary to the colorful characters and strange incidents encountered along the way. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Shooting the Past
synopsis: Character-driven drama in which the devoted staff of an obscure London photo archive, which is about to be discarded by its new American owner (Liam Cunningham), connives to find a new home for their treasured stills. Writer-director Stephen Poliakoff's quirky tale is somewhat flawed but captures the still camera's ability to freeze a moment in time forever. Ethical issues, drug references and a few Victorian-era nude photos

title: Shootist, The
synopsis: Uneven Western directed by Don Siegel in which a legendary gunfighter (John Wayne), told by a doctor (James Stewart) that he is dying of cancer, engages in a final shoot-out. The movie's glossing over of the hero's various moral failings makes it mature fare

title: Shootout
synopsis: Familiar revenge plot about a stoic ex-con (Gregory Peck) on his way to settle accounts with a double-crossing partner starts going astray when he is detained by a dependent widow (Pat Quinn) and a homeless waif (Dawn Lyn) who may be his daughter by a prostitute. Director Henry Hathaway leaves family audiences far behind with some sadistic violence, including a gang rape in a brothel and coarse language out of the mouth of a nine-year-old. Grim stuff

title: Shoot-Out at Medicine Bend
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Richard L. Bare in which an ex-Army officer (Randolph Scott) masquerades as a Quaker in order to get the goods on a man (James Craig) selling defective guns to settlers beset by Indian raids. Frontier violence

title: Shoot the Moon
synopsis: Successful Hollywood writer (Albert Finney) walks out on his wife (Diane Keaton) and four young daughters in director Alan Parker's account of sometimes savage martial strife. Though there are some effective touches, the movie withholds so much vital information about the principals that it becomes irritating and pretentious. Some intense violence and very rough language

title: Shoot to Kill
synopsis: Taut, at times harrowing, thriller about a street-smart FBI agent (Sidney Poitier) and a woods-wise guide (Tom Berenger) who learn to trust one another in the course of tracking down a psychotic killer. Director Roger Spottiswoode handles the action scenes effectively but the relationship between the two principals is too contrived to be entirely convincing. Some brief but intense violence and considerable menace

title: Shop Around the Corner, The
synopsis: Delightful romantic comedy set in a Budapest department store where two clerks (James Stewart and Margaret Sullavan) nurture a mutual dislike of the other while each exchanges love letters with a lonelyheart's penpal until ultimately discovering they have been corresponding with each other. Director Ernst Lubitsch treats the workaday friction between the clerks with some wry humor while building sympathy for both, then brings them together in an emotionally satisfying conclusion that has charmed viewers ever since. Romantic complications

title: Shopgirl
synopsis: Languidly paced story of lonely and lovelorn Saks salesclerk (an appealing Claire Danes) who, after a tentative fling with a nerdy, awkward font artist (Jason Schwartzman), meets a wealthy older man (Steve Martin) and commences a no-strings-attached affair that proves only fitfully satisfying for her. Director Anand Tucker's adaptation of Martin's novella -- though striving for old-fashioned Hollywood gloss and a bittersweet tone about people's search for connection -- feels patently unreal, and the characters (although human in their imperfections) display less-than-commendable behavior, though the ending would seem to be morally sound. Smattering of crude language, brief profanity, partial and rear nudity, sexual situations and banter, a permissive view of premarital sex and condom use

title: Shop on Main Street, The
synopsis: Czechoslovakian tragicomedy of life under a puppet Nazi regime sensitively details the unusual friendship that develops between a simple man (Josef Kroner) and an elderly Jewish widow (Ida Kaminska) over whose botton shop he has been appointed "Aryan Controller." Director Jan Kadar draws the situation with a loving sense of human character that helps underscore the movie's condemnation of moral passivity in the face of inhumanity. Subtitles

title: Short Circuit
synopsis: Number Five is a lovable robot who acquires human attributes after being struck by lightning and befriended by Ally Sheedy, an ill-tempered snack-wagon operator. Steve Guttenberg plays Number Five's inventor in this routine romance from director John Badham. Some suggestive comments and mild profanity are lost in the context of chase scenes

title: Short Circuit 2
synopsis: Robot Number Five returns as Johnny Five to help a friend (Fisher Stevens) launch a toy robot company, but gets caught up in all sorts of mayhem, including a jewel heist. Directed by Kenneth Johnson, the loveable erector set steals the show, but some harrowing attacks on the robot may upset very young children. Rough language

title: Short Cuts
synopsis: Long, sprawling narrative intertwines the troubled lives and eccentric experiences of 9 families numbering 21 major characters (among them, Andie MacDowell, Bruce Davison, Jack Lemmon, Matthew Modine, Anne Archer, Tim Robbins and Lily Tomlin) over the course of several days in a Los Angeles suburb. Loosely based on short stories by Raymond Carver and directed by Robert Altman, the result is a messy collage of egocentric lives, arbitrarily thrown together through overlapping storylines whose flawed characters and dysfunctional behavior turn into a dreary sideshow of human frailities. Extramarital affairs, explicit discussions of sex, nudity, violence, substance abuse and rough language

title: Short Eyes
synopsis: Screen version of Miguel Pinero's play about prison life tells the story of a man (Bruce Davison), accused of molesting a little girl, who is thrust into a volatile environment where the other prisoners subject him to systematic and brutal harassment as someone who is lower than them. Directed by Robert M. Young, the movie's strength is in the almost overpowering realism of its mood and setting and the compelling personalities of its characters. Although the rough language, the violence and the threatening atmosphere are thoroughly justified in content, the movie is not for everyone

title: Shorts
synopsis: Clever children's fantasy about a rainbow-colored rock that grants the wishes of anyone holding it, and the chaos its misuse wreaks on the lives of a bullied schoolboy (Jimmy Bennett), his parents (Jon Cryer and Leslie Mann), his chief persecutor (terrific newcomer Jolie Vanier), her tycoon father (James Spader) and their suburban community in general. Told in a series of nonsequential episodes, writer-director Robert Rodriguez's lively yarn, which carries messages about the dangers of power and the isolating effects of contemporary technology, generally makes for appealing family entertainment, though perilous special effects may overwhelm the most sensitive viewers, while some parents may find a story line about a mucus monster unpleasant. Occasional menace and mildly gross humor

title: Short Time
synopsis: Mildly amusing comedy about a Seattle police officer who, after being mistakenly told he has only a few weeks to live, sets out to be killed in the line of duty so his ex-wife can collect his insurance and send his son to Harvard. Directed by Gregg Champion, the one-joke comedy is an uneasy melange of slapstick humor, melodramatic sentimentality and action stunts but its chief asset is Coleman who knows how to wring a good laugh from slim material. Mature theme, some hard-edged violence, a bedroom scene and needless profanity

title: Shot in the Dark, A
synopsis: French police inspector Clouseau (Peter Sellers) drives his superior (Herbert Lom) round the bend during a murder case involving a pretty maid (Elke Sommer) whom his bungling, accident-prone subordinate keeps trying to prove is innocent. Director Blake Edwards has fun with a farcical plot and characters to match, but its parade of sight gags (including a nudist colony) is overlong and mostly self-indulgent. Slapstick violence and much sexual innuendo

title: Shout
synopsis: Lame 1950s youth drama set in a delinquent boys' home where a rebellious teen (James Walters) defies the man in charge (Richard Jordan), pursues his daughter (Heather Graham) and conspires with a music teacher (John Travolta) to form a forbidden rock 'n' roll band. Director Jeffrey Hornaday milks familiar anti-authority and coming-of-age themes for a plastic story lacking dramatic or even musical energy. A brief bedroom scene with adolescents and momentary violence

title: Shout at the Devil
synopsis: Comedy about a boozy buccaneer (Lee Marvin) in World War I Southeast Africa who cons upright Britisher (Roger Moore)into a little elephant-tusk poaching on German territory suddenly turns nasty when Moore's wife is brutalized and his infant daughter burned to death by German forces. Directed by Michael Klinger, the movie has a blood-and-gore conclusion

title: Shout, The
synopsis: Intriguing psychological thriller about a mysterious stranger (Alan Bates) who threatens the husband (John Hurt) of a woman he wants to take (Susannah York) with the lethal power of a shout capable of killing everything within hearing distance, a mystical technique learned during a long stay among Australian aborigines. British production directed by Jerzy Skolimowski, it is beautifully photographed and performed but it cannot sustain its fragile premise. Mature treatment

title: Show Boat
synopsis: Fine version of the Jerome Kern-Oscar Hammerstein musical about the daughter (Irene Dunne) of a Mississippi riverboat captain (Charles Winninger) and her stormy marriage to an inveterate gambler (Allan Jones) which is counterpointed by a tragic subplot involving a mulatto singer (Helen Morgan). Director James Whale gets some real feeling out of the sentimental melodrama with a talented cast and a convincing turn-of-the-century setting that helps make the nostalgic musical as much a part of Americana as Paul Robeson's deckhand singing "Old Man River." Period depiction of race relations and domestic difficulties

title: Show Boat
synopsis: Glossy remake of the Kern-Hammerstein musical from Edna Ferber's novel about a turn-of-the-century Mississippi riverboat troupe whose ingenue (Kathryn Grayson) weds a dashing, unreliable gambler (Howard Keel), with their troubled marriage finding counterpoint in the tragic victimization of the troupe's mulatto star (Ava Gardner). Director George Sidney's rousing period entertainment has lovely songs, zestful dance numbers and comic relief from riverboat captain Joe E. Brown but short-changes the romance and soft-pedals the era's racial bigotry. Romantic complications and justice issues

title: Showdown
synopsis: Saddle-worn tale of two boyhood chums whose trails diverge but intertwine years later when one of them, an outlaw on the run (Dean Martin) seeks refuge from a one-time girl friend (Susan Clark), now the wife of the other, an upright sheriff (Rock Hudson). George Seaton directs the B-grade Western with deadly earnestness, relieved only by some foggy flashbacks of the pair's boyhood escapades and a few good action scenes

title: Showdown at Abilene
synopsis: Convoluted Western in which Abilene's sheriff (Jock Mahoney) returns from the Civil War guilt-ridden and unable to fire a gun, then finds his girl (Martha Hyer) about to marry a friend (Lyle Bettger) who's become a cattle baron driving local farmers off their land. Directed by Charles Haas, the situation's potential is wasted in muddy motivations as the plot grows increasingly contrived. Stylized violence and some nasty brutality

title: Showdown at Boot Hill
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Gene Fowler, Jr., in which a bounty hunter (Charles Bronson) kills his quarry in self-defence, then has to face the dead man's friends in a frontier town with no one willing to take his side except a lonely waitress who wants to reform him. Several shootouts and an attempt at vigilante justice

title: Showdown, The
synopsis: Revenge Western in which an ex-lawman (William Elliott) seeks his brother's murderer among the cowpunchers (Harry Morgan, Peter Graves and others) working for a Texas rancher (Walter Brennan) and a saloon owner (Marie Windsor). Directed by Dorrell and Stuart McGowan, the hard-bitten proceedings center on the hero's determination to avenge his brother's death until the last reel softens his resolve. Frontier violence, theme of personal retribution and some sexual innuendo

title: Shower
synopsis: Gentle Chinese comedy-drama in which a self-involved businessman (Pu Cunxin) gradually changes his superior attitudes while visiting his ailing father (Zhu Xu) and mentally retarded brother (Jiang Wu) and helping to run their public bathhouse where all are treated as family. Director Zhang Yang insightfully incorporates themes of community, tradition, sacrifice and forgiveness within a leisurely paced and charming character-driven story. Subtitles. A few sexual references, fleeting bathhouse nudity and an instance of rough language and profanity. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Showgirls
synopsis: Relentlessly sleazy potboiler about a hardened Vegas stripper (Elizabeth Berkley) who graduates to performing in a casino's topless show, then steals the star spot by incapacitating its lead dancer. Director Paul Verhoeven's sexist depiction of women is a mindless exercise in sneering, leering voyeurism. A brutal gang rape, simulated sex acts, much exploitative nudity, drug abuse and rough language

title: Show of Force, A
synopsis: Plodding political thriller centers on a San Juan television reporter (Amy Irving) who puts her life in danger tracking evidence of apparent collusion between U.S. and Puerto Rican officials in the deaths of two men at a communications facility. Brazilian director Bruno Barreto depicts the controversial 1978 slayings as being staged by a repressive government in an effort to discredit the local independence movement but its murky, disjointed treatment strains credibility, despite good performances by Andy Garcia as the prosecutor and Lou Diamond Phillips as a double agent. Several strong scenes of graphic violence, much menace and minimal rough language

title: Showtime
synopsis: Cookie-cutter comedy in which a grouchy veteran detective (Robert De Niro) and a hammy rookie cop (Eddie Murphy) are forced to team up as the stars of a new reality-based TV show designed to improve the image of Los Angeles police department. With one-dimensional characters and auto-pilot performances, director Tom Dey's contrived comedy never gathers enough momentum to produce anything more than a few chuckles. A few scenes of explosions and deadly gunplay, brief drug content and much crass language and profanity

title: Shrek
synopsis: Captivating animated film in which a cynical ogre (voiced by Mike Myers) and his smart-alecky donkey (voiced by Eddie Murphy) agree to save the princess bride (voiced by Cameron Diaz) of a nasty lord (voiced by John Lithgow) in exchange for the return of the ogre's swamp home. As directed by Andrew Adamson and Vicky Jenson, the sweet but conventional story of self-acceptance reaches new levels of excellence in its animation and a fine cast of voices further bolsters the film's appeal. Mild crass language and some crude humor. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Shrek 2
synopsis: Whimsical and welcome sequel to the 2001 smash storybook send-up about a green ogre (voiced by Mike Myers) who, this time around, must face something far more imposing than a fire-breathing dragon -- his in-laws -- when he travels with his new bride (voiced by Cameron Diaz) to her parents' kingdom, where they find out that their chances of living happily ever after are threatened by a scheming fairy godmother. With its blend of captivating animation and clever parody, the fairy tale farce, directed by Andrew Adamson, Kelly Asbury and Conrad Vernon, is a worthy follow-up act, whose message of self-acceptance, though somewhat recycled, is one well worth repeating. Some mildly crude and suggestive humor

title: Shrek the Third
synopsis: The saga of the lovable ogre continues in the same high quality vein of the first two films, as Shrek (voiced by Mike Myers) -- aided by a potential heir to Far Far Away's throne (Justin Timberlake) -- must rescue his wife, Fiona (Cameron Diaz), and the kingdom's other residents who have been captured by the evil Prince Charming (Rupert Everett) and an assortment of fairy-tale villains. Writer and co-director (with Raman Hui) Chris Miller's latest installment has a somewhat darker edge, though still plenty of laughs with Shrek's sidekicks, Donkey (Eddie Murphy) and Puss in Boots (Antonio Banderas) in fine form, while the script's careful emphasis on good values such as believing in yourself, sacrificing for others, eschewing violence, and trusting in mankind's innate goodness override the occasional crude and mildly suggestive gags. Implied ogre nudity, some mildly off-color humor and innuendo, and the death of the king

title: Shriek in the Night, A
synopsis: Creaky murder mystery directed by Albert Ray in which rival newspaper reporters (Ginger Rogers and Lyle Talbot) covering a murder case finally join forces when one of them (Rogers) is targeted by the mad killer. Stylized violence, menace and sexual situations

title: Shrike, The
synopsis: Twisted psychological drama in which a successful stage director (Jose Ferrer) goes into a professional tailspin after marrying a would-be actress (June Allyson), leaves her for another women (Joy Page), then tries to commit suicide and winds up in a mental ward. Also directed by Ferrer, the situation tentatively suggests that the man is the victim of a manipulative wife, then reverses course in assessing blame and potential cure. Discreet treatment of domestic problems and troubled individuals

title: Shut My Big Mouth
synopsis: Wacky Western directed by Charles Barton features comedian Joe E. Lewis as a meek horticulturalist mistakenly made sheriff of a town beset by outlaws (Victor Jory, Forrest Tucker and Lloyd Bridges) whom he befuddles by, among other things, dressing as a woman and making allies of a local Indian tribe. Slapstick violence, comic menace and mild sexual innuendo

title: Shutter
synopsis: Glum, morbid horror tale about a Brooklyn photographer (Joshua Jackson) and his bride (Rachael Taylor) whose Tokyo honeymoon is haunted by the wraith of a Japanese girl (Megumi Okina) they accidentally struck down with their car. Director Masayuki Ochiai's remake of the 2004 Thai film of the same name, while not gratuitously bloody, lacks coherence and originality. Implied nonmarital sex, occasional vulgarity, including one use each of the f- and s-words, five uses of profanity, a suicide and a rape theme

title: Shuttered Room, The
synopsis: British supsense thriller directed by David Greene about a couple (Carol Lynley and Gig Young) who journey to a New England island to take possession of the house where the wife grew up but find themselves harassed by the islanders and warned of a dire evil in the house. Excessive violence, a near rape and scenes with semi-nudity

title: Shy People
synopsis: Brash New York writer (Jill Clayburgh) and nymphet daughter (Martha Plimpton) come upon some sinister goings-on in a Louisiana bayou while visiting a distant relative (Barbara Hershey) and her four wild sons. Director Andrei Konchalovsky fills the hothouse drama with American stereotypes. Some intense violence, drug abuse, an explicit striptease sequence and teen sexual promiscuity

title: Sibling Rivalry
synopsis: When a frustrated housewife's (Kirstie Alley) one instance of infidelity kills the guy (Sam Elliott), she makes a hapless salesman (Bill Pullman) think he's responsible and together they concoct a suicide scene which leads to further complications. Director Carl Reiner's minor screwball comedy wedges a tasteless scene among several madcap moments animated by the leads' flair for physical comedy. Comic treatment of extramarital sex and minimal profanity

title: Sicilian Clan, The
synopsis: Epic French heist tale is a duel of wits and guts between white-maned crime patriarch (Jean Gabin) and ambitious Paris hood (Alain Delon) over an impossibly complicated plane hi-jack of a fortune in jewels, with frustrated but persistent police inspector (Lino Ventura) keeping one step behind all the way. Directed by Henri Verneuil, the briskly-paced story of honor among thieves has a number of superior action sequences from an ingenious jail escape at the start to a grandly anti-climactic shoot-out

title: Sicilian, The
synopsis: Failed screen version of the Mario Puzo novel focuses on Salvatore Giuliano (Christopher Lambert), a historical figure whose rebellion against Sicily's Mafia, landowners and churchmen ended in 1950 with his murder. Directed by Michael Cimino, the movie is muddled and disjointed, with a narrative that is often ludicrous and lacking in a sense of the area's culture and history. Graphic violence, brief nudity and some rough language

title: Sicko
synopsis: Michael Moore's excoriating documentary expose of the American health care system, in which he sets out to demonstrate the superior medical treatment people receive in countries such as Canada, England, France and even Cuba, each with tax-based socialized medicine resulting in patients having seemingly few if any out-of-pocket expenses. Moore's approach is audacious and unabashedly one-sided, but with his breezy, sardonic commentary, the film is highly entertaining and makes a strong case for our present system being strangely at odds with the otherwise humane aspects of the American character. However, he's on shakier ground when he suggests the system is a nefarious plot to keep us in fearful submission. Brief shot of a man stitching his own wound

title: Sid and Nancy
synopsis: All the sordid details of physical and spiritual disintegration are celebrated in this harsh and excessively explicit portrait of the sadistic, self-destructive lives of British punk rock music star Sid Vicious and his American girlfriend, Nancy. Without care for the reasons behind Sid's tragic self-destruction, the film is masochistically exploitative

title: Siddhartha
synopsis: Screen version of Hermann Hesse's novel about a Brahmin's son, Siddhartha (Shashi Kapoor), who rebels at his father's asceticism, rejects the message of various holymen, is disappointed with the pleasures of sex and the rewards of business, but finally discovers enlightenment in nature and the unity of life. Written, produced and directed by Conrad Rooks, the movie attempts to create a mystic experience, rendering the abstract and sometimes ponderous philosophizing of the text into the sheer beauty of poetic imagery, ably supplied by Sven Nykvist's camera. Some will find it an uplifting experience, while others will see only an album of pretty pictures. Restrained but erotic sex scene

title: Sidecar Racers
synopsis: Young American (Ben Murphy), at loose ends in Australia, becomes involved in the hazardous sport of sidecar motorcycle racing. Directed by Earl Bellamy, it's an innocuous, mildly diverting action movie but some romantic complications are not for the youngsters

title: Sidekicks
synopsis: Corny tale of asthmatic teen student of karate (Jonathan Brandis) who daydreams of rescuing damsels in distress alongside karate hero Chuck Norris (playing himself), then finds himself partnered with his idol at a competition. Director Aaron Norris depicts his brother Chuck as an awesome good guy in this dull and predictable vanity production that caters to teen macho fantasies. Stylized martial arts violence and periodic menace

title: Sidewalks of London
synopsis: Bittersweet tale in which a London street performer (Charles Laughton) keeps a waif (Vivien Leigh) out of trouble by teaching her his trade, then she becomes a music hall star with the help of an admirer (Rex Harrison) and, years later, tries to repay her old teacher when she discovers he's fallen on hard times. Directed by Tim Whelan, the sentimental story is secondary to the bright performances of Laughton and Leigh. Veiled sexual innuendo

title: Sidewalk Stories
synopsis: The story of a homeless New York City street artist (Charles Lane) and the two-year-old waif (Nicole Alysia) he shelters is told in a virtually silent, black-and-white movie that depends upon the eloquent body language of the actors and an energetic musical score by Marc Marder. Lane also wrote, produced and directed this Chaplinesque tale of two black outcasts which presents a poignant if sentimentalized view of the plight of the homeless. Brief frontal nudity in an erotic dream sequence and some comic book violence

title: Sideways
synopsis: Bittersweet comedy about a depressed novelist and wine aficionado (Paul Giamatti), who, in lieu of a bachelor party, treats his womanizing, though soon-to-be-married best friend (Thomas Haden Church) to a last-hurrah tour of Northern California wineries that becomes a midlife journey of self-discovery. Based on a novel by Rex Pickett, director Alexander Payne's odd-couple road movie serves as a poignant meditation on love, loneliness, fellowship and failed ambition, but is unfortunately stained by some graphic scenes. Several explicit sexual encounters, including one scene with full frontal nudity, a few implied sexual encounters, brief drug content, and much rough and crude language and humor

title: Sidewinder 1
synopsis: Mediocre motorcycle racing movie directed by Earl Bellamy in which engineer Alex Cord develops a new cycle and goes into partnership with driver Michael Parks to refine it. An extramarital relationship makes it adult fare

title: Sidney Poitier: One Bright Light
