synopsis: Engrossing documentary in which the African-American actor-director reflects on his humble beginnings in the Bahamas and teen-age poverty while studying acting in New York before decades of groundbreaking roles that opened doors for new generations of African-Americans aspiring to work in the entertainment industry. Directed by his former co-star, Lee Grant, the program avoids a gushy star treatment and ties in Poitier's choice of roles with the burgeoning civil rights movement

title: Siege of the Saxons
synopsis: When King Arthur (Mark Dignam) is slain by a Cornish usurper (Ronald Howard) in league with Saxony, his daughter (Janette Scott) is rescued by a forest outlaw (Ronald Lewis), proclaimed Camelot's queen by Merlin (John Laurie) and routs England's foes. Director Nathan Juran's cut-rate British production muddles through the outlandish proceedings with the help of action scenes lifted straight out of "The Black Knight" (1954). Clunky Arthurian tale with stylized violence

title: Siege, The
synopsis: Shrill action movie in which an FBI agent (Denzel Washington) and a slippery CIA operative (Annette Bening) join forces to locate Brooklyn-based Arab terrorists responsible for a series of deadly bombings that have left New York City under marital law enforced by a fanatical general (Bruce Willis). Director Edward Zwick's densely plotted thriller raises provocative questions about democracy and racism which prove more interesting than the explosive story at hand. Some intense violence and mayhem, brief sexual innuendo and intermittent rough language

title: Sierra
synopsis: Tangled Western in which a man (Dean Jagger) wrongly accused of murder escapes into the mountains with his son (Audie Murphy) where they complicate their lives by rescuing a woman lawyer (Wanda Hendrix) lost in the wilds. Directed by Alfred E. Green, the unconvincing story meanders along listlessly, though the tedium is relieved occasionally by songs from Burl Ives. Frontier violence

title: Sierra Baron
synopsis: Disappointing Western set in California after its 1848 acquisition by the U.S. enables a crooked American (Steve Brodie) to sell land belonging to a Mexican don (Rick Jason) who holds out with the help of a Texas gunslinger (Brian Keith) until his Spanish title is recognized by the new government. Directed by James B. Clark, the formula proceedings rarely measure up to the subject's rich potential. Frontier violence

title: Sierra Passage
synopsis: Low-budget Western directed by Frank MacDonald tells the tale of an orphan raised by a minstrel troupe (headed by Roland Winters) to be a sharpshooter (Chester Morris), but his sole interest is tracking down the laughing gunman (Alan Hale, Jr.) who murdered his father. Stylized violence and vigilante theme

title: Sierra Stranger
synopsis: Formula Western about a cowboy (Howard Duff) who rides into the middle of a dispute over a mining claim and winds up on the wrong side. Directed by Lee Sholem, the plot is tired and the action tiresome. Stylized violence and mild romance

title: Sign of the Cross, The
synopsis: After Nero (Charles Laughton) condemns the Christians for his burning of Rome in 64 A.D., the city's prefect (Fredric March) promptly falls in love with one (Elissa Landi), but when his efforts to save her are blocked by jealous empress Poppaea (Claudette Colbert), the tribune joins his beloved for a martyr's death in the arena. Producer-director Cecil B. DeMille lavishes more creative imagination on scenes of Roman debauchery and brutality than on the inspirational story of early Christian martyrs, though the result is impressive as historical spectacle, especially the arena sequences. The 1944 reissue opens with a prologue in liberated Rome as World War II millitary chaplains set the scene. Much period violence, menace and sexual innuendo

title: Sign of the Pagan
synopsis: Talky historical melodrama in which Attila the Hun (Jack Palance) leads the barbarians in a march on Rome, but turns away after a meeting with Pope Leo I (Maroni Olsen), then tangles with a Roman legion (led by Jeff Chandler) and is killed by a Christian captive. Directed by Douglas Sirk, this Hollywood version of history oversimplifies the triumph of Christian idealism over barbarian superstitions and wastes time on a romantic subplot involving Chandler's centurion with a Byzantine princess. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Sign of the Virgin
synopsis: Failed Czechoslovakian comedy about a lonely soldier whose girl friend is smuggled onto the base by his comrades so they can spend the evening together in sick bay. Director Zbynek Brynych's attempts at humor are disappointingly clumsy as are several unnecessarily graphic scenes of the young couple

title: Signs
synopsis: Struggling with loss of faith after the sudden death of his wife, an Episcopalian minister (Mel Gibson) fears for the life of his children (Rory Culkinand Abigail Breslin) after he and his brother (Joaquin Phoenix) discover huge circular patterns in his cornfield that suggest an invasion by hostile aliens. Writer-director M. Night Shyamalanmasterfully builds dread and tension while touching upon issues of faith, but the lightweight narrative doesn’t provide a powerful punch to match the unnerving apprehension that shapes the film. Some intensely frightening moments and occasional crass expressions

title: Signs of Life
synopsis: Sketchy drama about the impending closure of a venerable New England family's boat building business and the effects on its elderly owner (Arthur Kennedy), assorted employees and hangers-on. Directed by John David Coles, its inconsequential narrative hints at the occult, includes a botched suicide, a near-drowning and a pointless robbery. Some rough language and a brief sexual encounter

title: Silence of the Lambs, The
synopsis: An FBI trainee (Jodie Foster) seeks the identity of a psychotic serial killer (Ted Levine) from a brilliantly manipulative psychiatrist (Anthony Hopkins), himself an imprisoned multiple murderer. Jonathan Demme directs a riveting thriller eliciting superb performances from Foster and Hopkins while attempting a straightforward treatment of repugnant subject matter by focusing on the novice agent's dedication to her assignment. Some intense violence and graphic shots of mutilated bodies, a flash of nudity and occasional rough language

title: Silence of the North
synopsis: Fact-based Canadian story of a spunky 1920's farm woman (Ellen Burstyn) who, after her husband (Tom Skerritt) perishes trapping in the Northwest Territories, moves to Calgary to raise her three children during the Depression. Director Allan Winton King succeeds in showing the fearsome beauty of Canada's northern wilderness, but the human drama of pioneer folk is smothered in low-key, dull performances. The deadly menace of a hostile environment and a few instances of profanity

title: Silencers, The
synopsis: Shabby imitation spy spoof of James Bond spy adventure movies with Dean Martin playing Matt Helm, free-lance superspy who spends much of his time cracking heads and getting his own bent occasionally. When not thus engaged, he chases an assortment of comely female spies around the set. The comic level is uniformly low and so is the moral tone of the action

title: Silent Death
synopsis: ( see: "Voodoo Island" )

title: Silent Fall
synopsis: Psychological thriller in which a troubled child psychiatrist (Richard Dreyfuss) attempts to learn the identity of a murderer from an autistic 9-year-old boy (Ben Faulkner) who was the sole eyewitness to the stabbing deaths of his parents and is now being cared for by his distraught 18-year-old sister (Liv Tyler). Director Bruce Beresford's poorly developed whodunit suffers from its halting pace until it slams into a lurid, overwrought solution which is in turn capped off by a pat and patently unconvincing finale. A gory murder site, references to incest and adultery and some rough language

title: Silent Hill
synopsis: Bleak and surreal supernatural thriller about a mother (Radha Mitchell) whose desperate search for her missing daughter (Jodelle Ferland) leads her to a haunted ghost town -- ravaged by fire 30 years earlier -- where she faces demonic forces and the town's evil past to get her child back. Suffused with religious motifs, director Christophe Gans' journey through hell abounds with nightmarish visions worthy of Dante, but in exploring themes of faith, fanaticism and motherhood the film, which starts out eerily intriguing, eventually descends into confusion and the gore of its videogame roots, ending on a perplexing note that will leave you, like the haunted hamlet, in a fog. Intensely disturbing and bloody horror images, including a graphic scene of a woman burnt alive, some violence, including a savage off-screen beating, fleeting partial nudity, and recurring rough and crude language and profanity

title: Silent Movie
synopsis: Writer-director Mel Brooks stars as a washed-up director who gets the head of his studio (Sid Caesar) to let him make a silent comedy provided he can get Hollywood's biggest stars to participate. The result is sometimes funny, sometimes not, but it is harmless fun and less vulgar than other Brooks' comedies. Adult humor

title: Silent Night, Deadly Night
synopsis: Maniac dressed in a Santa Claus costume uses an axe to kill people. Dreadfully produced exploitative horror suggests that director Charles Sellier Jr. should think about another line of work. Excessive gory violence

title: Silent Night, Evil Night
synopsis: ( see: "Black Christmas" )

title: Silent Partner, The
synopsis: Dull bank teller (Elliott Gould) keeps out a large cache of money for himself during a bank hold-up but the robber (Christopher Plummer) is a cunning sadist who doesn't like being made a fool of. What follows includes a brutal murder and a savage beating. Directed by Daryl Duke, the film is cleverly done and well acted, but the cheap, corrosive cynicism that permeates it, together with the sex and violence inserted to jolt the audience, is seriously offensive

title: Silent Rage
synopsis: Small-town sheriff (martial-arts whiz Chuck Norris) confronts a seemingly indestructible superman fashioned by an irresponsible scientist. Directed by Michael Miller, it is an utterly inconsequential effort of deadening predictability. Considerable violence, though stylized, and some fleeting nudity

title: Silent Running
synopsis: Above average tale of ecological disaster in the not-too-distant future where the commander (Bruce Dern) of a space ark refuses the order to destroy its precious cargo of plant life that can no longer grow on earth. Directed by Douglas Trumbull, the sci fi effects are good and the story's theme of humanity's relationship to the environment is thoughtful. Unfortunately, the weak story line ends in the confusion of madness and restrained mayhem

title: Silent Stranger, The
synopsis: ( see: "Step Down to Terror" )

title: Silken Skin
synopsis: ( see: "The Soft Skin" )

title: Silk Stockings
synopsis: Belabored musical updating the 1939 romantic comedy, "Ninotchka," has a Soviet commissar (Cyd Charisse) arriving in Paris to replace three faltering comrades (Peter Lorre, Jules Munshin and Sam Wanamaker), then falling for a capitalist movie producer (Fred Astaire.). Despite spirited Cole Porter songs, director Rouben Mamoulien fails to convey any romantic sparks between the Astaire-Charisse duo and the flashy production numbers fail to pep up the lethargic proceedings. Sexual innuendo

title: Silkwood
synopsis: Fact-based story of Karen Silkwood (Meryl Streep), a worker in a plutonium processing factory who died in a 1974 auto accident, on her way to tell a reporter what she knew about unsafe conditions in the plant. The movie does not confront the question of whether this was indeed an accident or a murder committed to prevent her evidence from being revealed. Instead, director Mike Nichols has invested a great deal of labor and care in depicting something of Silkwood's independent lifestyle on the job and in relations to her roommate (Cher) and boyfriend (Kurt Russell). The result is a nicely-crafted disappointment

title: Silverado
synopsis: Big, gaudy Western, as artificial as its title, in which four strangers meet on the road to Silverado and unite to fight evil and injustice. Director Lawrence Kasdan fails to make the bad guys seem very formidable competition for the four lackluster heroes weighed down by a convoluted and contrived story line whose tone wavers between spoof and dead seriousness. Some moderate violence

title: Silver Bears
synopsis: Michael Caine stars in this leaden-paced, largely unfunny comedy of international intrigue involving a hoax about a silver mine. Directed by Ivan Passer, it affects a sympathetic attitude towards adultery

title: Silver Bullet
synopsis: A small town is terrorized by a maniacal killer, coincidentally enough, only when the moon is full. When most of the members of a posse formed to track down the killer are annihilated, it is left to a 12-year-old handicapped boy to convince the town that the killer is a werewolf. Based on a Stephen King novella, director Daniel Attias takes liberties with Hollywood werewo1f conventions that may offend hard-core Lon Chaney fans. Graphic violence with gory murder sequences as well as some vulgar language

title: Silver Chalice, The
synopsis: Biblical clunker from Thomas B. Costain's novel in which an artist (Paul Newman) from Corinth comes to Rome to consult Peter the Apostle (Lorne Greene) about the chalice he's making to hold the cup Christ used at the Last Supper, but a fanatic revolutionary (Joseph Wiseman) and a mad magician (Jack Palance) are intent on its destruction. Directed by Victor Saville, the pot boils over as the callow artist is torn between a pious Christian (Pier Angeli) and an impious hussy (Virginia Mayo), while trying to claim his stolen inheritance and protect the chalice from being stolen. Violence, intrigue and romantic complications

title: Silver City
synopsis: Muddled Western directed by Byron Haskin in which a mining engineer (Edmond O'Brien) helps a miner (Edgar Buchanan) make a silver strike, then wins his daughter (Yvonne De Carlo) while battling a rival miner (Barry Fitzgerald) and an old enemy (Richard Arlen). Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Silver City Bonanza
synopsis: Western programmer directed by George Blair in which an Arizona cowboy (Rex Allen) helps a rancher (Buddy Ebsen) track down his blind brother's killer while locating a lost Spanish silver mine along the way. Stylized violence

title: Silver Lode
synopsis: Bogus marshall (Dan Duryea) turns the title town against its leading citizen (John Payne) in a dreary Western directed by Allan Dwan who compounds the artificality of the revenge plot with lots of unconvincing action. Stylized violence and intermittent menace

title: Silver Streak
synopsis: Gene Wilder and Jill Clayburgh battle a ruthless gang of killers aboard a transcontinental train, aided by Richard Pryor, whose comic talents give the movie a much needed lift when he appears halfway through. Directed by Arthur Hiller, it is moderately entertaining but has some unnecessary profanity and a rather crude love scene

title: Simon
synopsis: Anemic satire about a mischievous group of scientists (headed by Austin Pendleton) who brainwash an eccentric philosophy teacher (Alan Arkin) into believing he is from outer space. Written and directed by Marshall Brickman, the acting is good but the laughs are few and far between. Some sexual innuendo and a feeble thrust at organized religion

title: Simon Birch
synopsis: Old-fashioned tale of friendship between two 12-year-old boys in 1964 Smalltown, U.S.A., one (Joseph Mazzello) seeking the identity of his father while the other (Ian Michael Smith), afflicted with dwarfism, is convinced God has put him on earth to do something heroic. Suggested by John Irving's 1989 novel, "Prayer for Owen Meany," writer-director Mark Steven Johnson's well-meaning attempt to explore faith through the eyes of a doomed child has tender moments but its uplifting message is delivered with a heavy hand. Scene of extreme menace to children, sexual references, a few rude expressions and minimal profanity

title: Simone
synopsis: Likable drama in which a down-on-his-luck director (Al Pacino) secretly creates a computer-generated actress to star in his film and she becomes an instant success, but when the creation becomes more famous than the creator, it threatens to ruin his life. Spiked with some witty dialogue, director Andrew Niccol's film amusingly mocks bratty, egotistical Hollywood actors, but the satire is spoiled by outlandish circumstances and too tidy an ending. Brief sexual suggestiveness and fleeting crass language

title: Simon Magus
synopsis: Strange fable set in a dwindling 19th century European Jewish village where a demented outcast (Noah Taylor) becomes key in the struggle to build a railway station that will bring the village into the modern era. The mixture of romance, fantasy and horror in director Ben Hopkins' dark drama achieves more confusion than success due to the film's laggardly pace, stereotypical characters and awkwardly phrased dialogue. Brief violence, representation of the devil and an instance of crass language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Simon of the Desert
synopsis: Surrealistic Mexican fantasy about a hermit (Claudio Brook), who like his 5th-century namesake, Simeon Stylites, exiles himself to the top of a pillar in the wilderness living in prayer, doing penance, and working miracles, but constantly at war with himself, his followers and the devil (Silvia Pinal). Director Luis Bunuel's satiric foray into the sacred and the profane deals in paradox and the contradictions inherent in human nature. His ironic wit and uncomfortable insights will be appreciated most by those willing to reconcile the movie's ambiguities with their own beliefs

title: Simon the Swiss
synopsis: French crime thriller about a petty crook (Jean-Louis Trintignant) who thinks he's pulled off the perfect crime when he kidnaps a bank clerk's small child and gets the bank to pay a fortune in ransom. Director Claude Lelouch's plot has all kinds of intricate turns and twists and the likable hero is anything but a Robin Hood. Intelligent entertainment with much psychological tension and some physical violence

title: Simpatico
synopsis: Flawed melodrama in which a 30-year-old horse racing crime committed by three former friends (Nick Nolte, Jeff Bridges and Sharon Stone) continues to haunt them as one is determined to shake up the privileged lives of the other two. Adapted from Sam Shepard's play with constant flashbacks to the trio's crucial younger days, director Matthew Warchus' densely plotted movie is involving but turns unconvincing in the homestretch. A harsh sexual encounter, fleeting violence, occasional profanity and intermittent rough language

title: Simple Men
synopsis: Disjointed story of an unsuccessful criminal (Robert Burke) and his college-student younger brother (William Sage) who are given a place to stay by a Long Island inn-keeper (Karen Sillas) while searching for their outlaw father. Written and directed by Hal Hartley, the situation provides a stage for eccentric characters with throwaway dialogue that is by turns comical and mock philosophic, suggesting insights which never materialize. Some stylized violence, sexual references and occasional rough language

title: Simple Plan, A
synopsis: Menacing drama in which two brothers (Bill Paxton and Billy Bob Thornton) and a buddy (Brent Briscoe) stumble upon a snow-covered plane wreck with a cache of four million dollars and decide to keep it, then grow suspicious of one another as they try to hide their guilty secret from the police. Director Sam Raimi's cautionary tale turns into an edgy thriller as ordinary Joes become increasingly corrupted by the desire for immense wealth. Intermittent violence, fleeting nudity, some profanity and recurring rough language

title: Simple Story, A
synopsis: Moody French portrait of a divorced woman (Romy Schneider) in middle age crisis and agonizing over whether to have an abortion or raise her child. Directed by Claude Sautet, the movie avoids sentimental melodramatics in favor of thoughtful, sensitive probing of life's moral priorities

title: Simple Twist of Fate, A
synopsis: Poignant updating of George Eliot's 1861 novel, "Silas Marner," in which a miserly divorced carpenter (Steve Martin) is transformed into a loving foster father after adopting an abandoned baby, only to face losing her at age 11 when her wealthy biological father (Gabriel Byrne) sues to regain custody of the child. Also written by Martin and directed by Gillies MacKinnon, the handsomely shot drama presents well-developed characters who gradually come to terms with past mistakes in an uplifting story of love and acceptance. Negative depiction of drug abuse, mild sexual references and an instance of profanity

title: Simple Wish, A
synopsis: Weak comic fantasy in which an inept male fairy godmother (Martin Short) has trouble granting the wish of a little girl (Mara Wilson) that her dad (Robert Pastorelli) win the lead in a Broadway musical. Directed by Michael Ritchie, the innocuous fun comes from the amusing special effects rather than the frantic antics of Short's klutzy character. Mild menace and a few crude words

title: Simply Irresistible
synopsis: Leaden romantic fantasy in which a small-time New York restaurant owner (Sarah Michelle Gellar) and a swank department store executive (Sean Patrick Flanery) are brought together by a magical force endowing her with extraordinary culinary skills that literally sweep him off his feet. Directed by Mark Tarlov, the unimaginative premise fails to spark any magic in the appeal of the two leads and the resulting romantic complications are too labored to be much more than occasionally amusing. Sexual innuendo, crude language and some profanity

title: Sinbad and the Eye of the Tiger
synopsis: Slow-paced bit of leaden whimsy follows a voyage of Sinbad (Patrick Wayne) to the polar regions to free a prince from a witch's spell. The acting is undistinguished, Sam Wanamaker's direction is haphazard and only a few special effects merit anything more than passing interest

title: Sinbad: Legend of the Seven Seas
synopsis: Animated adventure about the legendary Arabian swashbuckler (voiced by Brad Pitt) who, along with a spunky princess (Catherine Zeta-Jones), must battle fantastical creatures and steal a magic book from a treacherous goddess (Michelle Pfeiffer) in order to save his friend, Proteus (Joseph Fiennes). Despite polished animation which draws from various mythologies, directors Tim Johnson and Patrick Gilmore's lukewarm tale lacks both narrative zip and engaging characters, yet does impart a strong message about the moral value of friendship and selfless courage

title: Since You Went Away
synopsis: When her husband is called up in World War II, a woman (Claudette Colbert) makes ends meet by taking in a boarder (Monty Woolley), is cheered by occasional visits from a family friend (Joseph Cotten) and finally becomes a shipyard welder, while her 17-year-old daughter (Jennifer Jones) gets engaged to a soldier and a younger daughter (Shirley Temple) tends a victory garden. Directed by John Cromwell, the patriotic tribute to the homefront is done in epic fashion, though the sentimentalized situations and idealized characters may seem rather dated today. title: Since You Went Away
synopsis: When her husband is called up in World War II, a woman (Claudette Colbert) makes ends meet by taking in a boarder (Monty Woolley), is cheered by occasional visits from a family friend (Joseph Cotten) and finally becomes a shipyard welder, while her 17-year-old daughter (Jennifer Jones) gets engaged to a soldier and a younger daughter (Shirley Temple) tends a victory garden. Directed by John Cromwell, the patriotic tribute to the homefront is done in epic fashion, though the sentimentalized situations and idealized characters may seem rather hollow today

title: Sin City
synopsis: Visually bold but ultraviolent movie based on Frank Miller's hard-edged graphic novels which weaves together pulp-crime stories from the popular comic book series, including the tale of an honest cop (Bruce Willis) trying to protect a girl from a politically connected sadistic pedophile, and a street brawler (Mickey Rourke) who goes on a killing spree to avenge the murder of a prostitute. Directed by Robert Rodriguez, the movie is a hard-boiled fever dream of excessive brutality, morbid humor and sexual imagery which -- though highly stylized and intentionally over-the-top -- pushes the envelope of even its restrictive R rating. Gratuitous graphic violence, including dismemberment and decapitation, sexual situations with nudity, a suicide, an execution, as well as rough and crude language

title: Sinful Davey
synopsis: Tongue-in-cheek adventure movie about an 18th-century Scottish laddie (John Hurt) who deserts the English army and embarks upon a career as a highwayman. Director John Huston relies upon an abundance of misadventures, escapes and turnabouts in a stylish action story done in fun. Some explicit romantic interludes

title: Sing
synopsis: Poorly focused, reality-based fantasy about Brooklyn's annual high school performance competitions uses a cliched story of romance between a good girl (Jessica Steen) and a petty hood (Peter Dobson) who is turned around by a tough-minded new teacher (Lorraine Bracco). Director Richard Baskin depends on music video flourishes to divert attention from his derivative scenario but gets help from a cast of energized teens, a subplot about community pride and an anti-drug message. Some rough language and sexually suggestive dancing

title: Singapore
synopsis: Soggy melodrama directed by John Brahm follows the return of an American smuggler (Fred MacMurray) to the title colonial outpost after World War II to recover a hidden cache of pearls, but the quest is complicated by a shrewd British policeman (Richard Haydn), a greedy crook (Thomas Gomez) and the American's love for a woman (Ava Gardner) he thought killed in an air raid but who survived, afflicted with amnesia and married to another. Some stylized violence and hokey romantic complications on the rocky road to divorce

title: Singing Guns
synopsis: Western programmer directed by R.G. Springsteen in which a singing gold robber (Vaughn Monroe) shoots a sheriff (Ward Bond), then takes his place while he recovers from his wounds, though the local parson (Walter Brennan) wants to reform the outlaw and a lady gambler (Ella Raines) is after his loot. Frontier violence and a good badman

title: Singing Nun, The
synopsis: Hollywood's tribute to the joyful spirit of a young Dominican nun is colorful, sentimental and lively, though Henry Koster's glossy direction is out of tune with the reality of a basically interior story about the difficulty of secular fame for a member of a religious community. Greer Garson as the mother superior turns in a well-balanced performance while Debbie Reynolds sings prettily and Agnes Moorehead provides comic relief. There is some pleasant amusement, a little uplift and the music of "Soeur Sourire" is well worth hearing

title: Singin' in the Rain
synopsis: Engaging musical spoof of early Hollywood as a silent movie star (Gene Kelly) makes the transition into talking pictures with some help from a loyal pal (Donald O'Connor) and a talented young singer (Debbie Reynolds) who dubs the voice of the star's shrill leading lady (Jean Hagen). Directed by Kelly and Stanley Donen, the period nostalgia is served up as light-hearted fun with the Kelly-Reynolds romance sweetly in the background while the plot rolls along with fine songs, zestful comedy routines and lovely production numbers, from O'Connor's solo "Make 'Em Laugh" to Kelly's memorable title number. Minor sexual innuendo

title: Singles
synopsis: Romantic comedy centers on several romances among the twentysomething tenants (including Bridget Fonda, Scott Campbell, Kyra Sedgwick and Matt Dillon) of a small and homey Seattle apartment building. Writer-director Cameron Crowe takes a genial but superficial look at the emotional rollercoaster of the dating wars with sympathetic, marriage-minded characters. Restrained scene of a sexual encounter, a benign attitude toward premarital affairs and an instance of rough language

title: Single White Female
synopsis: After tossing out her unfaithful fiance (Steven Weber), a young Manhattanite (Bridget Fonda) takes in a shy roommate (Jennifer Jason Leigh) who quickly turns out to be a cunning murderess. Producer-director Barbet Schroeder's tired slasher movie turns a plausible concept into a mindless excerise in sensational violence. Excessive violence, brief sexual encounters, some nudity and occasional rough language

title: Sink the Bismarck!
synopsis: Stirring dramatization of the 1941 British naval victory over the title German battleship after it slips into the North Atlantic, easily defeats the first British warships encountered, then becomes a sitting duck when its rudder is disabled by a carrier plane's torpedo. Directed by Lewis Gilbert, the sea action is intercut with the personal drama involving the Admiralty's director of operations (Kenneth More) his assistant (Dana Wynter), the officers of the ships following his orders and the Nazi admiral (Karel Stepanek) commanding the "Bismarck." Wartime violence

title: Sinners' Holiday
synopsis: ( see: "Christmas Eve" )

title: Sin of Adam and Eve, The
synopsis: Writer-producer-director Michael Zachary's literal visualization of Genesis uses an off-screen narrator to add some sensual embellishments to the Biblical text while on-screen bare, healthy primates George Rivers and Candy Wilson explore an Eden which seems to have been culled from the Burpee Seed Catalogue

title: Sin of Harold Diddlebock, The
synopsis: Interesting comedy opens with footage from "The Freshman" (1925) showing how college go-getter Harold Lloyd's football prowess wins him a job as an accountant at an ad agency, but still at the same job 20 years later Harold finds himself fired, takes his first drink, wins a fortune gambling and buys a circus, none of which he can remember when he awakens a day later, though the aftermath turns him back into a go-getter. Writer-director Preston Sturges comes up with an intriguing storyline and lots of visual funny business for Lloyd who is equally good in exchanges of droll dialogue but the comedy is poorly paced and the result is disappointingly uneven. Some menacing moments and comic inebriation

title: Sins of Rachel Cade, The
synopsis: Sudsy melodrama in which an American nurse (Angie Dickinson) takes charge of a Protestant mission in the Belgian Congo in 1939, wins over the natives and the local Belgian administrator (Peter Finch), but falls in love with a wounded World War II pilot (Roger Moore) who leaves her pregnant. Director Gordan Douglas plods through the narrative with little concern for either the African setting or the title character's moral struggles which are depicted as little more than hypocrisy. Muddled theme of an unwed pregnancy and religious as well as African stereotypes

title: Sin Takes a Holiday
synopsis: Stiff romantic comedy in which a New York divorce lawyer (Kenneth MacKenna) avoids being forced into marriage by wedding his secretary (Constance Bennett) in name only, then sending her to travel in Europe where a friendly bachelor (Basil Rathbone) turns her into the toast of French society, with predictable results. Directed by Paul L. Stein, the dated proceedings are flatly contrived and too obvious to be amusing. Implied adultery and shallow treatment of love and marriage

title: Sirens
synopsis: Coyly pretentious Australian tale of a clergyman (Hugh Grant) and his prim wife (Tara Fitzgerald) who loses some of her sexual inhibitions when they spend a few days with an artist (Sam Neill) and his entourage of models. Writer-director John Duigan's listless, highly romanticized proceedings center on models cavorting in various stages of undress while the wife gradually awakens to lust in what ultimately proves only a glossy exercise in voyeurism. Sexual promiscuity and much nudity

title: Sirocco
synopsis: Murky tale of a cynical American gunrunner (Humphrey Bogart) supplying arms to Syrian rebels in 1925 Damascus where he uses the girlfriend (Marta Toren) of a French intelligence officer (Lee J. Cobb) to avoid arrest, then tries to save the officer from capture by the rebels. Directed by Curtis Bernhardt, the meandering plot is thick with ominous intrigues but the unsavory characters fail to gain interest, let alone sympathy. Stylized violence, menacing situations and sexual innuendo

title: The Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants 2
synopsis: Overcrowded but mostly enjoyable romance sequel updating the lives of four friends (Amber Tamblyn, America Ferrera, Blake Lively and Alexis Bledel) as they pursue disparate adventures during the summer after their first year in college. While director Sanaa Hamri's lightweight adaptation of Ann Brashares' novels promotes youthful self-confidence, it also takes a somewhat permissive view of teen sexuality. Implied nonmarital sexual activity, condom use, suicide theme, a couple of profanities, and one crude and a few crass words; acceptable for older adolescents

title: Sister Act
synopsis: Having witnessed a mob rubout, a Reno lounge singer (Whoopi Goldberg) hides out in a cloistered San Francisco convent disguised as a nun and horrifies Mother Superior (Maggie Smith) by turning their choir into a local sensation and getting the nuns involved in their neighborhood. Director Emile Ardolino parlays Goldberg's sassiness into a lively comedy that treats nuns both as comic figures and spirited, caring individuals with a positive lifestyle. References to an extramarital affair and brief comic violence

title: Sister Act 2: Back in the Habit
synopsis: Fair comedy sequel in which the Las Vegas singer (Whoopi Goldberg) is back in a nun's habit, hoping to save a Catholic high school from closing by transforming a bunch of unruly students into a vibrant choir in time to win the all-state competition. Though lacking the novel premise of the original and off-kilter in its goofy depiction of several priests, director Bill Duke's moderately amusing comedy stresses positive values for youngsters. Mild sexual innuendo, comic treatment of religious characters and an instance of profanity

title: Sister Helen
synopsis: Poignant documentary about Sister Helen Travis, a tough 69-year old Benedictine nun, who runs a halfway house for recovering addicts in a poor section of the Bronx. Filmmakers Ron Fruchtman and Rebecca Cammisa show the harsh reality of the sister's life and the courage she has in following Jesus' example, but repeated scenes of Sr. Helen's hard-nosed interactions with the addicts are wearing. Drug content and sporadic rough language

title: Sister Kenny
synopsis: Stodgy fact-based dramatization about the title Australian nurse (Rosalind Russell) who discovers an effective method for treating polio victims on the eve of World War I but the country's medical organizations refuse to adopt it until she is invited to the United States and proves its worth during World War II. Directed by Dudley Nichols, the production is first-rate but the script suffers from too much windy sincerity and not enough effective dramatization of character and situation

title: Sisters
synopsis: Failed horror thriller about a Staten Island reporter (Jennifer Salt) who happens to observe a bloody murder in a neighboring apartment house occupied by a schizophrenic Siamese twin (Margot Kidder) and her mad doctor-husband (Bill Finley). Assisting her investigation is a bumbling, comic-relief detective (Charles Durning) Directed by Brian De Palma, the movie's mixture of mindless comedy and visceral gore presumes an audience willing to participate in such voyeuristic displays of violence

title: Sitting Bull
synopsis: Failed Western tale of a cavalry officer (Dale Robertson) whose friendship with the Sioux chief (J. Carrol Naish) leads to a court martial after Custer's Last Stand. Directed by Sidney Salkow, the mawkish story mauls American history and frontier stereotypes to no discernable advantage. Frontier violence

title: Sitting Ducks
synopsis: Two bumbling con men (Michael Emil and Zach Norman) steal some mob gambling receipts and flee to Miami with two women who have been hired to bump them off. Amateurish sex farce directed by Henry Jaglom gets off to a good start but becomes progressively less amusing as it wears on. Demeaning treatment of sex and some rough language

title: Sitting Pretty
synopsis: Period comedy in which busy suburban parents (Robert Young and Maureen O'Hara) engage the services of a live-in babysitter (Clifton Webb), a self-proclaimed genius who proves more than capable of handling not only the children but any crisis along the way. Directed by Walter Lang, the whole show is Webb's imperious peformance as the unflappable Mr. Belvedere who is more than superior to any situation, including nosy neighbors. Some muted sexual inferences

title: Sitting Target
synopsis: Atrocious British crime story about an escaped convict (Oliver Reed), his stashed loot and adulterous wife (Jill St. John). Directed by Douglas Hickox, the movie wallows in cruelty, sadism, gore, betrayal and self-destruction

title: Situation Hopeless--But Not Serious
synopsis: Failed black comedy of two downed American fliers (Robert Redford and Michael Connors) taken prisoner in 1944 by a lonely German clerk (Alec Guinness) and held captive in his cellar until six years after World War II's end. Director Gottfried Reinhardt concentrates on the ludicrous humor of the situation rather than the characters and their relationships, with little to show for it except adding to the Guinness gallery of odd characterizations. Uneasy humor in a desperate situation

title: Six Bridges to Cross
synopsis: Crime picture of the uneasy friendship that develops between a dedicated Boston cop (George Nader) and a shrewd but engaging juvenile delinquent (Tony Curtis) whose crimes escalate into a 1950's multi-million dollar heist. Directed by Joseph Pevney, the torturous relationship between law-enforcer and law-breaker plays out unconvincingly, though the Boston locations and gritty criminal action add a realistic veneer to the proceedings. Stylized violence and ambiguous treatment of a criminal

title: Six Days, Seven Nights
synopsis: Mildly comic adventure in which a tropical island pilot (Harrison Ford) and his high-strung passenger (Anne Heche) crash land on an abandoned isle where they must fend off pirates from the sea and their unwanted mutual attraction. Director Ivan Reitman's tired formula is made palatable by the airy banter between appealing performers in an otherwise predictable popcorn movie. Brief violence, some sexual innuendo, recurring profanity and an instance of rough language

title: Six Degrees of Separation
synopsis: New York art dealer (Donald Sutherland) and wife (Stockard Channing) recount to their amused uppercrust friends how a troubled homosexual youth (Will Smith), by pretending to be Sidney Poitier's son, insinuated himself into their lives hoping to become part of their privileged world. Based on John Guare's play and directed by Fred Schepisi, the deftly acted movie uncomfortably mixes scathing satire about patronizing rich folk with the murky plight of a lost, delusional young man. Fleeting homosexual encounter with a flash of frontal nudity, brief violence including suicide and occasional rough language

title: Six-Gun Gold
synopsis: Western programmer directed by David Howard in which a cowboy (Tim Holt) rescues his marshal brother from a gang who have taken over his job to facilitate their hijacking gold shipments from local miners. Frontier violence

title: Six in Paris
synopsis: Light, colorful and entertaining compilation of short vignettes by six French directors (Jean-Luc Godard, Jean-Daniel Pollet, Jean Rouch, Jean Douchet, Claude Chabrol and Eric Rohmer). Despite the assortment of stories and styles, they cohere nicely and leave viewers with a memorable experience of several interesting Parisian characters. Mature themes and treatment

title: Six O'Clock News
synopsis: Impelled by TV's nightly news reports of random violence from crime and natural disasters, documentary filmmaker Ross McElwee began visiting victims of the violence to record what had happened and how they were coping with the aftermath. The result is a series of human interest stories strung together in the form of a video diary with McElwee's wry comments and philosophical musings on human mortality but without achieving its stated aim of trying to make some sense of life's painful, inexplicable tragedies. News footage of crime scenes and disaster areas as well as discussions of violent events

title: Six Pack
synopsis: Kenny Rodgers plays a fading racecar driver who becomes the surrogate father of six needy orphans. Pretty soon he's back on top with the kids as his pit crew and he even decides to marry Erin Gray whom he favors with his presence every few months. Directed by Daniel Petrie, it's sheer, contrived mediocrity from start to finish. Foul language out of the mouths of babes and a benign attitude toward casual sex

title: Six-Pack Annie
synopsis: Young girl (Lindsay Bloom) becomes a prostitute in order to save her aunt's restaurant from foreclosure. Directed by Graydon F. David, the tedious, flat movie is as consistently vulgar as it is unfunny

title: Sixteen Candles
synopsis: A girl (Molly Ringwald) is devastated when her family, in the throes of preparing for her older sister's marriage, forgets about her 16th birthday. Were that not enough, she is pursued by a skinny freshman (Anthony Michael Hall) while longing for a handsome, unattainable senior (Michael Schoeffling). Director John Hughes' old-fashioned comedy about the anguish of adolescence is updated, alas, by a dose of foul language, pervasive vulgarity, some shower room nudity and a benign view of casual sex. Some other not-so-bright spots include nasty stereotyping of Orientals and Italians and some National Lampoon-style laughs at the expense of a girl in a body brace

title: Sixth Man, The
synopsis: Lame comic fantasy in which a college basketball star (Kadeem Hardison) dies in mid-season but his spirit returns to help his brother (Marlon Wayans) lead their underrated team to the championship. Directed by Randall Miller, the cliched sports story offers no surprises and the one-joke premise of a ghostly sixth player seen only by his brother delivers few giggles before growing tiresome. Player's death during a game, strong sexual innuendo and coarse language

title: Sixth Sense, The
synopsis: Failed psychological thriller in which a child psychologist (Bruce Willis) tries to help an 8-year-old child (Haley Joel Osment) who's frightened by seeing dead people walking around, though matters are ultimately not what they seem. Writer-director M. Night Shyamalan provides a story of vague assumptions and boring situations that are suddenly thrown into an entirely new light by a twist ending, though few will find the "surprise" worth waiting for. Gory violence, a menaced child and coarse language

title: Six Ways to Sunday
synopsis: Unfunny crime comedy follows the rise of a violent mama's boy (Norman Reedus) within a mob of Jewish gangsters as he deals with his sexual inadequacies, a smother-mother (Deborah Harry) and a talent for killing friends and foes alike. Writer-director Adam Bernstein substitutes a lamely jokey tone for any insights into the disturbed individual at the story's center. Numerous gory killings, a suicide, implied incest, sexual situations with nudity, intermittent profanity and constant rough language

title: Six Weeks
synopsis: Congressional candidate (Dudley Moore) befriends a youngster dying of luekemia (Katherine Healy) who persuades her wealthy mother (Mary Tyler Moore) to back his campaign but when she succumbs to his charm, he reciprocates and his marriage is in jeopardy. Director Tony Bill's romance is outrageously sentimental, totally detached from both political and human realities and cloyingly smug in its hedonistic values

title: Skateboard
synopsis: Down-on-his-luck agent (Allen Garfield) extricates himself from the clutches of a loan shark by becoming a skateboard entrepreneur. Directed by George Gage, it is a very bad little movie hastily and cheaply slapped together to cash in on a fad, it is also offensive in its benign attitude towards teenage promiscuity and drinking

title: Skatetown, U.S.A.
synopsis: Ho-hum homage to the fad of disco roller skating pits nice young man against tough dude in competing for the big skating crown. Written, produced and directed by William Levey, the undernourished story line constantly halts for unfunny comic sketches (Ruth Buzzey and Flip Wilson), undistinguished songs and skating numbers. Frequently sleazy mood and abundance of marijuana consumption in the background, and sometimes the foreground, make it highly dubious fare for any but mature viewers

title: Skezag
synopsis: Well-intended but amateurish documentary about drug abuse goes on endlessly with New York addicts using street language describing the scene. In the last sequence, however, filmmakers Joel Freedman and Phil Messina revisit an addict who is now a walking dead man, hollow of soul and poisoned of body, conveying most effectively what had been missing so incessantly in the preceding footage. Those last few minutes say more than anyone needs to know about the white powder that destroys so many young Americans

title: Ski Bum, The
synopsis: Failed screen version of a Romain Gary novel about a young drifter (Zalman King) hanging around a Colorado winter resort who becomes embroiled in a crooked business scheme, is roundly double-crossed and left emotionally shattered by the experience. Directed by Bruce Clark, the plot is episodic and underdeveloped, the characters are superficial and their motivations often enigmatic. A confused morality underpins the story

title: Skidoo
synopsis: Retired thug (Jackie Gleason) is ordered by his old boss (Groucho Marx) to rub out a loquacious friend (Mickey Rooney) safely ensconced in prison. Directed by Otto Preminger, it is a mixture of inert comedy and ponderous satire, done in consistently bad taste with some lecherous dialogue and sexual shenanigans

title: Ski Fever
synopsis: Ski instructor (Martin Milner) at an Austrian ski lodge finds his contract requires him to socialize with the guests and, by the time of the movie's romantic fade-out, he has teamed up with one of them (Claudia Martin). Directed by Curt Siodmak, it's an inept story built around some footage of the Austrian Giant Slalom but not even ski enthusiasts will find it worth seeing

title: Skin Deep
synopsis: Menopausal male saga about a famous writer (John Ritter) suffering simultaneously from alcoholism, writer's block and an obsession to bed every nubile female who crosses his path. Written and directed by Blake Edwards, the movie lacks any moral insight in following the lothario from one pointless liaison to another while romanticizing his lust for sex and alcohol. Some nudity and much profanity

title: Skin Game
synopsis: In the pre-Civil War border states, a cunning con artist (James Garner) makes the rounds selling his slave (Lou Gossett) and then waiting with the cash for him to escape and proceed to the next con, until another crook (Susan Clark) adds a new dimension of confusion. Director Paul Bogart blends large doses of improbability with pinches of reality to keep the interracial swindle skimming along its superficial surface, only touching on the serious for comic effect

title: Skin Game, The
synopsis: Dated melodrama from John Galsworthy's play about the bitter antagonism between a family of English aristocrats and their new neighbor, a wealthy businessman (Edmund Gwenn) buying up the surrounding countryside to turn into an industrial park. Directed by Alfred Hitchcock, the conflict is dramatically static and largely uninteresting, except for some sharp montages depicting the era's social changes and a romantic subplot involving class divisions. Suicide in plot resolution

title: Skinwalkers
synopsis: Werewolves-on-motorcycles action movie pits four biker-werewolves (including Jason Behr) against good werewolves (Elias Koteas among them) protecting a 12-year-old boy (Matthew Knight) who was prophesied as being the one to end the curse afflicting them. Director Jim Isaac's low-budget horror film is hardly a classic, but he provides intentional comic-book stylings and pointedly "cool" flourishes, and, admirably, there are no graphically gory effects. One example of rough language and a few instances of crass language, two lengthy gun battles, some supernatural violence that includes a broken neck, the aftermath of torture with the victim tied onto a cross, and one brief nongraphic sex scene

title: Ski Party
synopsis: Formula "Beach Party" fare set in a ski resort where two dim college youths (Frankie Avalon and Dwayne Hickman) hope to learn how to get dates by masquerading as British co-eds. Directed by Alan Rafkin, the unamusingly contrived proceedings are best forgotten. Some menacing situations and sexual innuendo

title: Ski Patrol
synopsis: The schemes of a sleazy land developer (Martin Mull) to take over a trendy ski resort run owned by a popular old-timer (Ray Walston) are thwarted by its dauntless young staff of ski patrolers whose talents also include dancing, singing and partying. Director Richard Correll combines his paint-by-numbers cast with dumb, vulgar hijinks to concoct a basically innocuous sophomoric comedy highlighted by snazzy ski togs and funky daredevil skiing. Minor sexual innuendoes, bathroom humor and incidental rough language

title: Skullduggery
synopsis: Witless, at times tasteless comedy about an anthropologist (Susan Clark) whose New Guinea expedition is led by their guide (Burt Reynolds) into uncharted territory where they discover a species of apes that manifest distinctly human qualities. Directed by Gordon Douglas, the question of whether the creatures are indeed human is kicked around in aimless fashion, matched by banal dialogue and half-dimensional characterizations. Reference to bestiality

title: Skulls, The
synopsis: Convoluted thriller about an ambitious ivy league student (Joshua Jackson) who joins a secret society to gain status and connections but after his best friend's mysterious death he discovers that privileges come with a price. Although visually impressive, director Rob Cohen's confusing plot drags on interminably while the supposed suspense produces unintentional giggles instead of gasps. Brief violence, implied sexual situations and some crass language

title: Skull, The
synopsis: Weak British horror story about a student of the occult (Peter Cushing) who becomes obsessed by the evil powers of the Marquis de Sade's skull. Directed by Freddie Francis, the trappings of black magic and witchcraft are as hokey as the action is clunky. Stylized violence and creaky menace

title: Sky Bandits
synopsis: A British production set in World War I France tells the comic adventures of two bank robbers (Scotty McGinnis and Jeff Osterhage) who join the army to avoid prison and blunder their way through the war in a series of stolen airplanes. Directed by Zoran Perisic, the charm of this elegantly photographed movie derives from high-spirited performances and fanciful sets, props and special effects. A post-bedroom scene and some very stylized wartime violence

title: Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow
synopsis: Visually striking but essentially empty-headed and unrelievedly loud action-adventure film that attempts to pay homage to film noir and the serials of the '30s such as "Flash Gordon" in a tale of an intrepid reporter (Gwyneth Paltrow) and pilot (Jude Law) setting out to find a dastardly villain (a posthumous appearance by Laurence Olivier) who plans to take over the world. Kerry Conran's feature-film debut demonstrates great visual flair, though the digital effects are ultimately wearying, and performances by stars Law and Paltrow are, even within the comic-book constraints of the story, not among the best of their careers, though Angelina Jolie provides some spark as a no-nonsense captain who comes to their rescue. Action violence

title: Sky Dragon, The
synopsis: Formula mystery directed by Lesley Selander in which Honolulu detective Charlie Chan (Roland Winters) gets some help from his Number One son (Keye Luke) in solving the case of a money shipment stolen from an airliner while its passengers and crew were knocked out by drugged coffee. Notable only as the last in the Monogram Chan series. Stylized violence

title: Sky High
synopsis: Fun-filled and smartly crafted coming-of-age comedy about an adolescent superhero (Michael Angarano) attending an elite academy for the children of costumed crimefighters, who must live up to his parents' (Kurt Russell and Kelly Preston) world-saving reputation while navigating the equally trying teen trials of high school. Director Mike Mitchell strikes the perfect blend of campy humor, visual finesse and honest emotion while exploring themes of self-esteem, peer pressure and parental expectations. Comic-book violence and some mild rude language

title: Skyjacked
synopsis: Effective thriller about an American airliner hijacked to Russia. Captain Charlton Heston keeps his planeload of problem characters under control on a flight chock full of dangerous situations, ending in a shootout at Moscow airport. John Guillermin directs with emphasis upon suspense rather than trying to develop characterization or the numerous subplots. Unpretentious escapist entertainment

title: Skyline
synopsis: Apocalyptic yarn (with sequels ahead) about invading aliens in Los Angeles with an insatiable appetite for human brains. Four people (Eric Balfour, Scottie Thompson, Brittany Daniel and Donald Faison) attempt to fight the invasion from a high-rise apartment building. But directing brothers Colin and Greg Strause and screenwriters Joshua Cordes and Liam O'Donnell don't bother to explain anything. Fleeting crass language, a single profanity, a single instance of implied premarital sex, and darkly lit aliens eating glowing human brains

title: Sky Riders
synopsis: Routine melodrama about the rescue of a family kidnapped by terrorists through the intervention of some daring hang-gliding enthusiasts is distinguished only by some spectacular aerial photography. Directed by Douglas Hickox, the movie's violent elements include the terrorists' threatening of a small child

title: Skyscraper Souls
synopsis: Episodic melodrama centering on the ruthless banker (Warren William) behind the construction of a New York skyscraper, the partner (George Barbier) he double-crosses to gain sole ownership, the innocent secretary (Maureen O'Sullivan) he seduces and a myriad of others who work in the building. Directed by Edgar Selwyn, the interlocking personal stories reflect the hard times of the Depression and the hedonistic excesses of the rich, with tragic consequences for some and new-found happiness for others. Stylized violence including murder and suicide as well as sexual situations and innuendo

title: Sky's the Limit, The
synopsis: Lightweight musical romance in which a World War II ace with the Flying Tigers (Fred Astaire) spends a 10-day leave back in the States pretending to be a civilian while trying to romance a magazine photographer (Joan Leslie) who's only interested in getting a war assignment overseas. Directed by Edward H. Griffith, there are several pleasant song-and-dance numbers but Leslie is no Rogers and Astaire can't carry the weak story by himself, despite some help from Robert Benchley

title: Slackers
synopsis: Dreadful college campus comedy about a geeky undergraduate (Jason Schwartzman) who blackmails three cheating students (Devon Sawa, Jason Segel, Michael C. Maronna) into setting him up with the popular girl (James King) he's obsessed with. Waffling between creepy and comedic, first-time director Dewey Nicks' sorry film is a churlish bore that regurgitates familiar gross-out humor and sexual jokes as it panders to the lowest common denominator. Several vulgar sexual situations, some nudity, brief drug use, intermittent toilet humor and recurring rough language and profanity

title: Slams, The
synopsis: Super-bad, super-cool Jim Brown is in the penitentiary but has stashed away $1.5 million in Mafia drug money for his planned break-out to escape to the Caribbean with girl friend Judy Pace. Directed by Jonathan Kaplan, the brutal and sadistic action is as relentless and explicit as the prison language which consists largely of racial, sexual and just plain mean insults

title: Slappy and the Stinkers
synopsis: Feeble family comedy about five 7-year-olds known at school as the Stinkers who sneak Slappy the sea lion out of an aquarium, but before they can free it into the ocean, Slappy is stolen by a villain who intends selling it to a Bulgarian circus. Directed by Barnet Kellman, the result is a mirthless slapstick comedy of "cute" kids outsmarting dopey adults but the property damage and bodily harm caused by the Stinkers' antics is rarely amusing and anything but cute. Slapstick violence, bathroom humor and crude language

title: Slap Shot
synopsis: Paul Newman stars as an aging player-coach who rejuvenates an inept bush-league hockey team by introducing the wonders of dirty playing to his charges. Directed by George Roy Hill. the playing is but one of the dirty elements in a crude, foul-mouthed comedy. Some nudity

title: Slap, The
synopsis: Lightweight comedy drama, a sort of updated "Father of the Bride," in which such talented actors as Lino Ventura, Annie Giradot and Isabelle Adjani struggle gallantly with an aimless script more suited to American televison than a French feature. Sexual innuendo

title: Slaughter
synopsis: Black exploitation story of an ex-Green Beret (Jim Brown) who pummels his way into an international conspiracy and becomes the unwilling employee of the U.S. Government. Directed by Jack Starrett, the production values are minimal, with the emphasis on the hero's biceps and his winning ways with knuckles and bullets. Excessively graphic violence and sex

title: Slaughter Hotel
synopsis: The hotel in question is a country rest home where medieval weapons decorate the parlors and become the means by which a prowling psychopath viciously disposes of sexually frustrated women and their nurses. Dreadfully inept Italian production directed by Fernanado Di Leo with gross violence

title: Slaughterhouse Five
synopsis: Uneven screen version of Kurt Vonnegut Jr.'s time-tripping novel about the progress of a soldier (Michael Sacks) from POW chaplin's assistant, to witness at the 1945 firebombing of Dresden, to post-war participant in the American Way of Life and, at last, the captive of a Hollywood starlet (Valerie Perrine), the girl of his erotic dreams. Directed by George Roy Hill, the wildly seriocomic satire on American manners and mores is mostly on target and the acting is first-rate, though its hero's helplessness in dropping in and out of time tends to be confusing and, at times, incoherent. Marred by unneccesary nudity

title: Slaughterhouse Rock
synopsis: Even some funny moments can't save this teen horror movie set on Alcatraz Island which a local student (Nicholas Celozzi) and friends visit one night to confront the source of his bad dreams - the marauding ghost of a cannibal who once inhabited the island. Directed by Dimitri Logothetis, it's an amateurish production with a nonsensical plot. Much gore and violence, several nude scenes, an attempted rape and some profanity

title: Slaughter of the Innocents
synopsis: Exploitative thriller in which an FBI agent (Scott Glenn) gets some help from his grade-school son in tracking down a serial killer in the badlands of Utah. Writer-director James Glickenhaus concocts synthetic thrills from the demented acts of pseudo-religious cultists and a white supremacist, but the supercop's encouragement of his computer whiz kid's precocious interest in crime is as appalling as it is unconvincing. Some grisly graphics, children in peril and occasional profanity and rough language

title: Slaughter on Tenth Avenue
synopsis: Earnest crimebuster drama in which the murder of a New York longshoreman (Mickey Shaughnessy) causes a dedicated lawyer (Richard Egan) to risk life and career in linking the crime to a mobster (Walter Matthau) controlling a corrupt waterfront union. Directed by Arnold Laven, the predictable storyline is helped along by interesting character bits (Jan Sterling, Sam Levene, Charles McGraw and Dan Duryea) and realistic dock scenes with longshoremen and union goons. Stylized violence and menacing atmosphere

title: Slaughter's Big Rip-Off
synopsis: Big, bad Jim Brown mows his way through the Los Angeles branch of the Syndicate (headed by Ed McMahon) and plows through a number of willing female sex objects. Directed by Gordon Douglas, rip-off is the operative word in this cheap sex-and-violence exploitation job

title: Slaughter Trail
synopsis: Formula Western pits the officer (Brian Donlevy) commanding a military post on the New Mexico border against a murderous bandit (Gig Young) who has stirred a war with the Navaho. Directed by Irving Allen, the slack proceedings are accompanied by an even slacker narrative ballad sung by Terry Gilkyson, with truly irritating results. Frontier violence

title: Slave Girls
synopsis: ( see: "Prehistoric Women" )

title: Slave of Love, A
synopsis: Movie company in the Crimea grinds out melodramatic romances seemingly oblivious to the Bolshevik revolution sweeping across 1917 Russia. In the end, the company's empty-headed but beautiful star (Elena Solovei) joins her cameraman in smuggling out film of czarist atrocities in the area. Gorgeously photographed and engagingly acted, director Nikita Mikhalkov's nostalgic tribute to the silent movies and their age of innocence is an enjoyable experience in spite of perfunctory Soviet propaganda

title: Slavery and the Making of America
synopsis: By its very title, you'd have every reason to expect this four-hour series about that most shameful institution, to be comprised of black-and-white etchings, doleful narration, and the occasional talking head. You'd be right about the talking heads, but the visuals -- at least on the basis of the second hour screened for review -- are actually color dramatizations, and the narration (by Morgan Freeman) compelling. Dante J. James' film looks to be a splendid overview of the subject, made all the more accessible by concentrating on the human stories of the people involved, and the lively visuals. We learn how blacks wrote petitions questioning how whites could talk of not being "slaves" to the British, while keeping slaves themselves, but all these petitions were dismissed. Later, there was the case of Mum Bett, whose successful suit for her freedom against her owner, Col. Ashley, helped lead to slavery's abolition in Massachusetts. Other pivotal figures whose fascinating stories are well-told in the series include Titus, the New Jersey slave who joined the British during the Revolutionary War to win his freedom, and liberated many of his family and friends; Denmark Vesey, a founder of one of the first black churches who tried to mount a Bible-based rebellion against slavery, but was found out and executed; David Walker, who wrote the most important abolitionist document of the era; and Maria Stewart, who took up Walker's cause, addressing audiences of both blacks and whites. The on-air scholars are terrific, with historian James Oliver Horton particularly articulate and interesting, along with fellow historians Thomas J. Davis, Ira Berlin, Norrece T. Jones Jr., Peter H. Wood, and Peter P. Hinks, among others. DVD includes English and Spanish subtitles. (Ambrose Video, (800) 526-4663) 2005

title: Slaves
synopsis: Inept melodrama about a hard-working slave (Ossie Davis) unjustly sold to a bad master (Stephen Boyd) whose mistreatment drives him to foment a slave uprising. Director Herbert Biberman depends largely upon dialogue rather than visuals to convey the historical reality of the terrible injustices of slavery. It is an important subject and it is unfortunate that it has been done poorly. Several scenes with nudity

title: Slaves of New York
synopsis: Director James Ivory's unsuccessful satire of the contemporary downtown Manhattan art scene works overtime to reproduce its chaotic glitz but fails to provide more than superficial commentary on the hedonistic, narcissistic denizens of this throwaway subculture. Satiric glamorization of sexual promiscuity and drug abuse, brief nudity and some profanity

title: Slayground
synopsis: The getaway car in a robbery crashes into a limousine, killing the young daughter of a millionaire who retaliates by hiring a professional hitman to track down the gang's leader (Peter Coyote), a sensitive fellow already badly upset by the tragic turn of events. British production directed by Terry Bedford is a run-of-the-mill chase movie with some pretentious literary overtones. Stylized violence

title: Sleeper
synopsis: Typically wacky Woody Allen spoof on contemporary society's pop foibles in a plot casting Woody as a chap who goes into the hospital for routine surgery and wakes up 200 years from now in a world gone mad with people dependent upon electronic gadgets (most of which don't work). Without an identity, he becomes tapped to lead a revolution and soon finds that his new friends are often more dangerous than his intended enemies. The humor is rapid-fire, mainly of the one-liner and sight gag variety and his satirical targets include just about every institution or group on the scene

title: Sleepers
synopsis: Overblown drama of four inner-city boys who grow up to take revenge on the sadistic guards (led by Kevin Bacon) who abused them in reform school, with two of the four getting away with murder on the perjured testimony of their parish priest (Robert De Niro). Writer-director Barry Levinson's manipulative crime picture romanticizes the bond of friendship between Catholic youths from a working-class neighborhood, then depicts their brutalizing imprisonment in disturbingly realistic detail, with the payoff years later in a dramatically unconvincing murder trial which nonetheless raises morally ambigous justice issues. Harrowing scenes of teen inmates subjected to sadistic violence and sexual abuse, cold-blooded murders, vigilante justice and habitual rough language

title: Sleeping Beauty
synopsis: Animated children's tale in which a bad fairy casts a spell on the Princess Aurora (voice of Mary Costa) causing eternal sleep until her true love, Prince Philip (voice of Bill Shirley), gets some help from a trio of good fairies in overcoming a ferocious dragon and awakening the princess. Directed by Clyde Geronomi with music from the Tchaikovsky ballet, this classic story of love conquering evil remains Walt Disney's last great achievement of storytelling in fully-detailed animation. Fine family entertainment

title: Sleeping Car Murders, The
synopsis: French suspense thriller about a homicidal maniac. Directed by Costa-Gavras, it affects a benign attitude toward premarital sex and unnecessarily graphic treatment of several erotic sequences

title: Sleeping City, The
synopsis: Standard crime melodrama set in New York City's Bellevue Hospital where a detective (Richard Conte) assumes the identity of an interne in order to solve some murders linked to the peddling of drugs among the hospital staff. Directed by George Sherman, the story gets some realistic dramatic tension from being filmed in and around the large metropolitan hospital, but the plot bogs down in the cop's romance with a nurse (Coleen Gray), conventional police work and criminal stereotypes. Stylized violence, romantic complications and drug dealing

title: Sleeping Tiger, The
synopsis: Turgid melodrama in which a London psychiatrist (Alexander Knox) attempts to treat a young thug (Dirk Bogarde) by taking him into his home, but the cunning, resentful youth proceeds to seduce his benefactor's troubled American wife (Alexis Smith), among other nasty deeds. Directed by Victor Hanbury (aka Joseph Losey), the unconvincing proceedings are unredeemed by a tragic ending. Much menace and sexual situations

title: Sleeping with the Enemy
synopsis: When a psychotically jealous husband (Patrick Bergin) discovers his abused wife (Julia Roberts) has faked her own death to escape him, he tracks her down and finds her in the arms of her new love (Kevin Anderson). Director Joe Ruben's sleek thriller efficiently creates suspense by making full use of Robert's beautifully played vulnerability, but falters with a needless cliche at the end. Some violence, restrained marital encounter and minimal rough language

title: Sleepless in Seattle
synopsis: After hearing a Seattle widower (Tom Hanks and his boy (Ross Malinger) on a syndicated radio talk show on Christmas Eve, a young reporter (Meg Ryan) feels irresistibly drawn to the man even though she is engaged and lives in Baltimore. Director Nora Ephron turns in a highly appealing if unabashedly romantic love story about singles and families, liberally sprinkled with comic moments. Some mild sexual references and a live-in relationship

title: Sleep My Love
synopsis: Formula thriller in which a New Yorker (Don Ameche) plans to marry his mistress (Hazel Brooks) after killing his wealthy wife (Claudette Colbert) by staging a fatal "accident," but the scheme begins unraveling when a Boston visitor (Robert Cummings) sticks his nose in. Directed by Douglas Sirk, the predictable plot belabors the obvious as the capable cast go through the motions portraying stereotyped characters. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Sleepover
synopsis: Bubblegum comedy about four 13-year-old girls (including Alexa Vega) whose summer slumber party becomes a high-stakes adventure when they agree to sneak out of the house and enter an all-night scavenger hunt against their �popular� schoolyard rivals. Director Joe Nussbaum does some scavenging of his own, swiping freely from past teen flicks, resulting in a coming-of-age comedy which, despite an appealing young cast, is more formulaic than fun, and includes tasks on the scavenger list that may raise the eyebrows of some parents. Some mildly crude language and humor and thematic elements involving teen dating

title: Sleepwalking
synopsis: Somber working-class story of a good-hearted construction worker (an empathetic Nick Stahl) who bonds with his sister's 11-year-old daughter (AnnaSophia Robb) when her promiscuous mother (Charlize Theron) suddenly deserts them, eventually taking the girl to stay with his abusive farmer father (Dennis Hopper) after he loses his job and they run out of money. The central relationship between uncle and niece is touching, and performances, including Woody Harrelson and Deborra-Lee Furness as the man's concerned workmates, are fine, but first-time director William Maher's film is more sordid than uplifting, and the ending, redemptive in one sense, is morally problematic in another. Pervasive rough language and some profanity, a sexual encounter without nudity, some frank sexual remarks, domestic violence and murder, underage smoking

title: Sleep with Me
synopsis: An impulsive one-night stand between a new bride (Meg Tilly) and the best friend (Craig Sheffer) of her husband (Eric Stoltz) deals a possibly fatal blow to their marriage as the three continually air their pent-up feelings at a series of social gatherings. Written as six vignettes by separate authors, and sluggishly directed by Rory Kelly, the cynical thirtysomething comedy assumes a hip and knowing air about sex, drugs and relationships, but fails to address the problems that are shown to be created by casual sex. Positive depiction of drug and alcohol abuse, brief bedroom scenes with nudity, crude sexual references and constant rough language

title: Sleepy Hollow
synopsis: In this violent adaptation of Washington's Irving's spooky tale of the headless horseman, Ichabod Crane (Johnny Depp) is a pompous, fearful New York constable sent to Sleepy Hollow to find the a triple murderer who has made off with the victim's heads. Although director Tim Burton conjures up a visually gorgeous period piece, the contrived humor doesn't work and the narrative overdoses on scenes of the horseman and another villain gleefully butchering their prey. Recurring grisly decapitations and a discreet sexual encounter

title: Slender Thread, The
synopsis: A telephone is the only means by which a psychology student (Sidney Poitier) can hope to save a woman (Anne Bancroft) who has taken an overdose of barbituates. Director Sydney Pollack's story has an overabundance of contrivances, but the acting of the principals makes it all seem urgent and worth the emotional involvement

title: Sleuth
synopsis: Stylish screen version of Anthony Shaffer's play about an urbane detective-story writer (Laurence Olivier) who invites his wife's lover (Michael Caine) to his mansion and the two engage in a game of wits which becomes progressively more deadly. Directed by Joseph Mankiewicz, the intricately plotted thriller is carried off by the tautly-balanced performances of the two principals but attentive viewers will see through the mystery early on. Some sharp tension and suspense make it mature fare

title: Sliding Doors
synopsis: Halting romantic fantasy set in London develops two scenarios showing alternate versions of what might happen in the life of a woman (Gwyneth Paltrow in a dual role) if she boards a departing subway train or misses it and has to take the next one. Writer-director Peter Howitt sets up a playfully imaginative premise that becomes increasingly predictable as the one prospers after getting rid of a parasitic lover while the other doesn't. Sexual situations including a live-in relationship and a bedroom scene, some crude language and occasional profanity

title: Slightly Honorable
synopsis: Screwball caper in which a hotshot lawyer (Pat O'Brien), aided by a dim assistant (Broderick Crawford), tries to solve a murder case in which he and a crooked politician (Edward Arnold) are prime suspects. Directed by Tay Garnett, the action is treated with comic gusto, especially the lawyer's problems with an underaged female (Ruth Terry), but the mystery gets lost in red herrings and an unsatisfying twist ending. Stylized violence and much sexual innuendo

title: Slightly Scarlet
synopsis: Muddled crime story directed by Allan Dwan with a zealous cop (John Payne) battling city officials in league with a gang boss (Ted de Corsia) who's a friend of the mayor's secretary (Rhonda Fleming) and her troubled sister (Arlene Dahl). Stylized violence and sexual situations

title: Slim
synopsis: After a veteran lineman (Pat O'Brien) befriends an inexperienced novice (Henry Fonda) working on high-voltage wiring jobs, a woman (Margaret Lindsay) comes between the two pals who are a team on and off construction sites. Director Ray Enright convincingly pictures the dangers of a lineman's job and the camaraderie among those who do it for a living, but the story dates badly with its view of a man's world in which women are only a distraction. Occasional stylized violence, menace and romantic yearning

title: Slim Carter
synopsis: Sentimental tale directed by Richard H. Bartlett in which a Hollywood publicist (Julie Adams) helps create the Western cowboy star of the title (Jock Mahoney), but it takes a precocious orphan (Tim Hovey) to bring them together. Some stylized violence

title: Sling Blade
synopsis: Challenging picture of a mentally retarded man (Billy Bob Thornton) after his release from the asylum to which he had been committed as a boy for murdering his mother and her lover. Upon his return to his Southern hometown, he's befriended by a boy (Lucas Black) and his widowed mom (Natalie Canerday) until her abusive boyfriend (Dwight Yoakam) threatens them all. Also written and directed by Thornton, the portrayal of the retarded man earns sympathy through its gentle, sometimes humorous, depiction of his simple, common-sense approach to difficulties, though its dark ending is appropriately disturbing. Some chilling off-screen violence, alcohol abuse and occasional rough language

title: Slingshot, The
synopsis: Showing the resilience of youth is this Swedish tale of a 10-year-old boy growing up in 1920's Stockholm where he suffers the scorn of classmates and teachers because of his Jewish mother and socialist father, tries to earn money to buy a bike by selling slingshots fashioned out of condoms and winds up in reform school for something he didn't do, yet survives it all without his spirit being crushed. Director Ake Sandgren evokes the period tensions of the adult world as seen through the innocent, wondering eyes of a boy too young to comprehend them but precocious and enterprising enough to get into troubles beyond his age. Subtitles. Religious prejudice, stylized violence, sexual references, comic treatment of condoms and occasional profanity

title: Slipper and the Rose, The
synopsis: Richard Chamberlain and Gemma Craven star in a pleasant and very entertaining British version of the Cinderella story as directed by Bryan Forbes

title: Slipstream
synopsis: Visually daring but disorienting drama in which a writer (Anthony Hopkins) has a series of what may or may not be hallucinations peopled by the characters in the screenplay he's revising and by the actors and crew of the movie-within-a-movie (Stella Arroyave, Christian Slater, John Turturro, Michael Clarke Duncan, Camryn Manheim, Jeffrey Tambor, Gavin Grazer, Fionnula Flanagan and Christopher Lawford). The film, Hopkins' writing and directing debut, is technically and philosophically intriguing, but fails to establish any emotional connection with the characters. Shooting and a car accident with blood; much rough, crude and crass language; an obscene gesture; and some innuendo

title: Slither
synopsis: Campy but repulsive horror film about a small town besieged by world-conquering space slugs that turn its residents -- starting with Michael Rooker -- into flesh-eating zombies, leaving it up to the local police chief (Nathan Fillion) and a handful of survivors (including Elizabeth Banks and Tania Saulnier) to save the day. Directed by James Gunn, tongue firmly planted in cheek, the film's affectionate nods to B-horror movies like "Dawn of the Dead," wry flashes of twisted humor and clever social commentary are eclipsed by its pervasive vulgar, nauseating and grisly elements. Strong and exploitative horror violence and gore, many gross-out images, some sexual situations, blurred shower nudity and unrelated brief rear nudity, adultery, pervasive rough and sexually crude language, as well as profanity and some irreverence

title: Slither
synopsis: Offbeat comedy adventure about a dense ex-con (James Caan) and his equally bumbling partner (Peter Boyle) who wend their way across rural California in search of a hidden stash of embezzled cash.
