synopsis: Retrograde thriller about a police sergeant (Charles Bronson) who, discharged for falsifying evidence against the man terrorizing his daughter (Lisa Eilbacher), sets out on his own to stop the handsome psycho (Andrew Stevens) who kills his victims while in the nude. Directed by J. Lee Thompson, the movie's treatment of violence, nudity and graphic sex is thoroughly objectionable

title: 12 Angry Men
synopsis: When a jury begin its deliberations on the guilt or innocence of a youth accused of murdering his father, one man (Henry Fonda) insists they reexamine the evidence before rendering their verdict. Directed by Sidney Lumet, the result is an absorbing character study of the jurors (a brilliant ensemble of character actors, including E.G. Marshall, Lee J. Cobb, Jack Klugman, Martin Balsam and Jack Warden), the preconceptions they bring to the case and the human dynamics of the jury system. Some intense moments

title: 12 Monkeys
synopsis: Convoluted sci-fi tale set in 2035 when the few survivors of a 1997 killer virus seek to learn the cause of the epidemic by sending an expendable criminal (Bruce Willis) back in time to 1996 where a psychiatrist (Madeleine Stowe) helps in tracking the mysterious gang of the title (led by Brad Pitt). Directed by Terry Gilliam, the elaborate narrative gets lost in quirky byways and nasty turns which only obscure what is essentially the story of a youth witnessing his own death as a time-traveller. Some nasty violence, sexual situations and rough language

title: 12 Rounds
synopsis: Routine action adventure in which a vicious thief (Aidan Gillen), sprung from prison and out for revenge on the New Orleans police officer (John Cena) who arrested him and accidentally caused the death of his moll, kidnaps the cop's live-in girlfriend (Ashley Scott) and sets him a dozen hair-raising tasks as ransom. Director Renny Harlin's film offers little more than rapid-fire mayhem and a few suspenseful situations. Considerable action violence, premarital cohabitation, much crude and crass language, and a few sexual references and profanities

title: 13 Conversations About One Thing
synopsis: Downbeat tale follows several Manhattanites (including Alan Arkin, Matthew McConaughey, Clea DuVall and John Turturro) as they navigate through upsetting experiences that lead them to question the meaning of life and the elusiveness of happiness. Director Jill Sprecherkeenly observes alienated characters, most of whom make slight progress in the direction of hope and renewal. Fleeting violence, an implied affair, references to suicide, some rough language and occasional profanity

title: 13 Fighting Men
synopsis: Low-budget Western directed by Harry Gerstad in which a Union patrol (led by Grant Williams) escorting a gold shipment in Georgia at the end of the Civil War is attacked by Confederate irregulars (led by Brad Dexter), with hokey results. Stylized violence

title: 13 Ghosts
synopsis: Silly horror movie about the frights and scares encountered by a meek paleontologist (Charles Herbert), his wife (Rosemary DeCamp) and two offspring when they inherit a haunted house with a spooky housekeeper (Margaret Hamilton) and a hidden treasure. Director William Castle provides an eerie soundtrack but neither the superimposed spooks nor the threadbare plot are likely to frighten anyone. Some occult trappings and supernatural menaces

title: 13 Going on 30
synopsis: Breezy romantic comedy-fantasy about a gawky 13-year-old who, after wishing she was an adult, wakes up in the body of a sexy and successful woman (Jennifer Garner), only to discover popularity and success isn't all it is cracked up to be, and may in fact, ruin her one chance at true love. With enough laughs and heartfelt sweetness to compensate for its warmed-over plot, the film, directed by Gary Winick, gives the old be-careful-what-you-wish-for chestnut a fresh spin and wraps it in the infectious smile of Garner, crafting a effervescent urban fairy tale about regrets and second chances. Some mild sexual humor, a few crass expressions and brief drug references

title: 13 Rue Madeleine
synopsis: Taut World War II story starts in a U.S. espionage school with a tough veteran (James Cagney) training a new group of agents (including Annabella, Richard Conte and Frank Latimore), one of whom proves to be a Nazi spy who jeopardizes an important mission. Director Henry Hathaway treats the material in sober, semi-documentary fashion, though Cagney's exploits to protect his agents in France tax credibility. Wartime violence and moral question of suicide by captured agents

title: 13th Letter, The
synopsis: Dark mystery thriller set in a small Quebec town where a series of poison pen letters accusing a new doctor (Michael Rennie) of having an affair with the young wife (Constance Smith) of an elderly local physician (Charles Boyer) cause consternation and then murder. Director Otto Preminger's remake of the French movie, "Le Corbeau," has plenty of eerie atmosphere and small-town paranoia but the conclusion lacks the intended impact. Stylized violence, menace, an implied sexual encounter and innuendo

title: 13th Warrior, The
synopsis: Chaotic tale of tenth-century Vikings who force a traveling Arab diplomat (Antonio Banderas) to fight with them against savage cannibals decimating one of their kingdoms. As directed by John McTiernan, the constantly panning camera, murky visuals and often incomprehensible dialogue amount to a dark and dreary horror film. Some gory battlefield violence with decapitations

title: 13 West Street
synopsis: Nasty little thriller in which a rocket engineer (Alan Ladd), after recovering from a senselessly brutal beating by five teens, gives up on the L.A. police detective (Rod Steiger) investigating the case and goes after the delinquents himself. Directed by Philip Leacock, the story of a citizen determined to take the law into his own hands gets increasingly muddled until its contrived ending. Much menace and some stylized violence

title: 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea
synopsis: Marvelous Disney version of the classic Jules Verne sea yarn about a maurading red-eyed monster sinking 19th-century ships some of whose survivors (Kirk Douglas, Paul Lukas and Peter Lorre) are taken aboard the submarine "Nautilus" by the embittered Captain Nemo (James Mason) who wants to rule the seas. Directed by Richard Fleischer, the story is great fun for all ages and the special effects are really special

title: 2000 Years Later
synopsis: Weak satire in which an ancient Roman (John Abbott), sent by the god Mercury, fails to warn society of the consequences of its moral corruption. Bert Tenser's Low-budget, amateurish production, lacking any moral focus of its own, merely exaggerates and exploits the more obviously decadent elements of the day

title: 2001: A Space Odyssey
synopsis: Director Stanley Kubrick's epic work, co-written with Arthur C. Clarke, is both science fiction and metaphysical poetry using an unconventional mixture of visuals and music to bridge humanity's reconstructed past, identifiable present and projected future, all tied together by the recurring image of a monolith as symbol of a superhuman existence. The central narrative follows the struggle of two astronauts (Keir Dullea and Gary Lockwood) to wrest control of their spacecraft from HAL, a talking computer (voice of Douglas Rain), on a half-billion-mile trip to Jupiter and the unknown. For young people and imaginative adults but too long, deep and intense for children

title: 200 Cigarettes
synopsis: Strained comedy set in Greenwich Village on New Year's Eve, 1981, as a dozen young adults and two teenage girls desperately try to sexually connect with members of the opposite sex. Writer-director Risa Bramon Garcia's narcissistic characters and the threadbare storyline translate into a tiresomely drawn-out take on the battle of the sexes. Benign view of promiscuity and substance abuse, recurring profanity and constant rough language

title: 200 Motels
synopsis: Written, produced and directed by Frank Zappa, the title refers to the bleak digs occupied by touring groups such as Zappa's The Mothers of Invention during the course of an average year. It features, however, rough language and a smutty lyric, explained with glee by a pair of semi-nude groupies, as well as a raunchy cartoon sequence depicting the sleazy side of life

Sequel to "2001: A Space Odyssey" in which Roy Scheider leads a joint American Soviet probe of Jupiter to discover the fate of the spacecraft sent there in the original. Writer-director Peter Hyams overwhelms the story with spectacular special effects but young people especially should find it an engaging voyage into space

In the disaster movie to end all fiasco flicks, a doomsday cataclysm results in billions losing their lives as the earth's crust breaks apart, dismantling civilization and rearranging the continents. Director Roland Emmerich gives his special-effects wizards license to test the limits of the technically plausible and morally palatable, while asking moviegoers to take heart as the scenario affords a White House geologist (Chiwetel Ejiofor) and a divorced science-fiction writer (John Cusack) the chance to exhibit altruism, even as their exploits are interspersed with disturbing apocalyptic imagery, including the destruction of St. Peter's Basilica and the Sistine Chapel. Considerable crude and crass language, much profanity, a rough gesture and a few instances of sexual innuendo

Hypnotically filmed, well acted story of Hong Kong-based man (Tony Leung) and his liaisons with several women (Ziyi Zhang, Gong Li, Faye Wong, Carina Lau, Dong Jie and Maggie Cheung), though he can connect with none of them. Director Wong Kar Wai has fashioned a poetic sequel to his acclaimed "In the Mood for Love" and explores how the past can hold us back from a fulfilling future, but this one is more oblique, moving through time in nonlinear style, including several futuristic sequences, but the protagonist's repeated failure to connect with any of these women becomes ultimately tiresome. Cantonese, with English subtitles. Strong sexual content including prostitution, partial nudity, crude language, some violent images. The DVD features a behind-the-scenes featurette, interviews with Wai, Leung and Zhang (which help elucidate some plot elements), deleted scenes and an alternate ending

title: 20 Dates
synopsis: Documentary-like chronicle in which a two-person camera crew follow filmmaker Myles Berkowitz (playing himself) around on 20 dates as he searches for, and surprisingly finds, Ms. Right. The contrived results are occasionally amusing despite Berkowitz' whiny personality and the shameless hidden camera tactics he sometimes employs. An implied sexual encounter, some crass sexual references, much rough language and an instance of profanity

title: 20 Million Miles to Earth
synopsis: Weak sci-fi effort from director Nathan Juran in which a specimen of life brought from Venus by U.S. astronauts escapes when their spaceship crashes, then grows to monstrous size (thanks to Ray Harryhausen's animated models) and runs amok in Rome until cornered in the Coliseum. Some special-effects violence and menacing situations

title: 21 Grams
synopsis: Gripping drama about three strangers -- a math professor awaiting a heart transplant (Sean Penn), a recovering drug addict (Naomi Watts) whose husband and two young daughters die in a hit-and-run accident, and the struggling ex-con-turned-born-again-Christian (Benicio Del Toro) responsible for the tragedy -- whose lives converge in a nexus of rage, revenge and repentance. Buttressed by tour-de-force performances, director Alejandro Gonzalez Inarritu interweaves disparate narrative strands, crafting a grim and gritty morality tale which ruminates on the interconnectivity of people's lives while exploring with unflinching emotional honesty themes of fate and faith, life and death, despair and hope, sin and redemption. Several sexual encounters with partial nudity, recurring rough and crude language as well as profanity, some violence and drug abuse, a suicide attempt and a fleeting erotic image

title: 24-Hour Lover
synopsis: Heavy-handed German sex farce about a young wine salesman who dallies on his daily round of kitchens and parlors, until ultimately collapsing from sheer exhaustion. The movie just repeats one long tired joke without wit or style

title: 24 Hour Party People
synopsis: Frenetic musical comedy about Tony Wilson (Steve Coogan), a British TV journalist who founded a recording label in the late-1970s which ushered in a new era of pop culture music including punk and new wave.Set to a blaring soundtrack and defiantly in-your-face, director Michael Winterbottom's biographical cautionary tale follows the development of the local Manchester, England, music scene while blending historical footage with outspoken narration about the sex, drugs and rock 'n' roll excesses of the times. Yet despite the acerbic comedy and attention-grabbing characters, the irreverent and often depraved lifestyles portrayed are discomfiting to watch. Several sexual encounters with frontal nudity, a suicide, sporadic drug use, brief violence and much rough language

title: 24 Hour Party People
synopsis: Director Michael Winterbottom's frenetic musical comedy "24 Hour Party People" (United Artists) is not for everyone. The biographical film tells the story of local British TV journalist Tony Wilson, who founded Factory Records, a Manchester, England, recording label which ushered in a new era of pop culture music including punk and new wave. Those who will most appreciate the film are fans of 1980s bands New Order, Happy Mondays and Stone Roses. But many likely will not enjoy the acerbic comedy or attention-grabbing characters because of the irreverent and often depraved lifestyle portrayed in the film which spells out the sex, drugs and rock 'n' roll excesses of the times in a defiant, in-your-face manner. Charismatic and flirty, British actor Steve Coogan, who portrays Wilson, carries the film with his outspoken narration as he guides the audience through the tumultuous times that left a lasting impact on the music culture. After attending a Sex Pistols gig (a band known for their rebellious nature who went on to punk music infamy) at which only 42 people were present, Wilson is energized by the anarchy of their music and is inspired to form Factory Records for up-and-coming bands. He doesn't believe in contracts. His goals are to give the musicians artistic freedom and to convert an old warehouse into a dance club called The Hacienda, which he goes broke doing. Together with his friend Alan Erasmus (Lennie James), Wilson puts the city of Manchester firmly on the pop-culture map. The film doesn't candy-coat the craziness of the times by making everything seem hunky-dory. This is something that might be missed since the film, at first glance, could be interpreted as a rambunctious, energized party where everyone has a good time. Yet Wilson makes clear that there are casualties. "24 Hour Party People" is a musical cautionary tale about the overindulgence associated with the music industry. Artists become addicted to drugs and ruin their careers -- or worse, die of an overdose. Marriages (Wilson's in particular) break up over mindless infidelities. Some artists like Ian Curtis (Sean Harris), the leader of the precursor band to New Order, commit suicide out of desperation and depression. And ultimately, Wilson's vision of artistic freedom is his own downfall. Set to a blaring soundtrack, visually inventive and blending historical footage with the fictional narrative, the film spans the late 1970s to the early 1990s. The chaotic structure of the film, which was shot in digital video and features many cameos, matches the story of how punk and new wave music was born, how it flourished and how it paved the way for the next generation of musicians before becoming a victim of its own excess. But the centerpiece of the film is Coogan's performance. He is helped by good material from the script, which allows for droll asides to the camera and witty banter for the voice-over narration. However, "24 Hour Party People" is an acquired taste unlikely to match the palate of most Catholic moviegoers. Due to several sexual encounters with frontal nudity, a suicide, sporadic drug use, brief violence and much rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops

title: 24 Hours of the Rebel
synopsis: Mediocre story about the effect the news of actor James Dean's death has upon a group of college students in a small Arkansas town who seem to find movies more real than their own lives. Written and directed by James Bridges, the movie fails to build much sympathy for its two principal characters (Richard Thomas and Deborah Benson) or explain why they are drawn so compulsively to Dean's screen persona. Several scenes of youthful sexual explorations and vulgar language

title: 25th Hour
synopsis: Gritty urban parable charting the final 24 hours of freedom of a convicted New York drug dealer (Edward Norton) struggling to redeem his life and mend tattered personal relations. Directed by Spike Lee and based on David Benioff's novel, the engaging drama offers solid ensemble performances and a strong message about taking responsibility for one's own actions. Sporadic violence, a character's angry anti-Catholic remarks, crude sexual references and situations, and recurring rough language and profanities

title: 25th Hour, The
synopsis: Well-intentioned European co-production showing how senseless coincidences and petty officials separate a Romanian peasant (Anthony Quinn) from his wife (Virna Lisi) during World War II. Their ultimate reunion as a beaten family of displaced persons demonstrates the devastating effects of war on the innocent. Director Henri Verneuil has a worthy theme but the plot contrivances are thin and the production is flat and plodding

title: 27 Dresses
synopsis: Glossy but formulaic romantic comedy about a perennial bridesmaid (the engaging Katherine Heigl) and the wedding reporter (James Marsden) who pursues her incognito, while she silently pines for her boss (Edward Burns) who, in turn, has fallen for her glamorous but superficial kid sister (Malin Akerman). Anne Fletcher's smooth direction, Heigl's self-deprecating charm and the rest of the personable cast compensate somewhat for the predictable script with results never less than pleasant, and there's a satisfying and morally sound plot resolution. Some crude language, crass expressions, a superfluous bathroom scene, an implied nonmarital sexual encounter, and mild sexual banter and innuendo

title: 28 Days
synopsis: Pedestrian seriocomedy in which a successful writer and notorious party girl (Sandra Bullock) is sentenced to rehab for driving under the influence and so must come to terms with her addiction to alcohol and her cynical outlook on life. As directed by Betty Thomas, the cinematography is creative, but the shallow film fails to capture both the real pain and humor of recovery while the few honest moments are lost in melodramatics. Substance abuse theme, implied sexual encounters, some crass language and an instance of rough language

title: 28 Days Later
synopsis: Intensely violent science fiction thriller about a handful of survivors (including Cillian Murphy and Naomie Harris) struggling to stay alive in a post-apocalyptic England decimated by a powerful virus that turns infected humans into rabid, bloodthirsty maniacs. Despite an on-screen blood-and-gore level teetering on the excessive, director Danny Boyle's hard-core horror film raises interesting questions about man's capacity for inhumanity, while offering some genuinely scary moments. Much graphic violence, recurring rough language and profanity, as well as fleeting full frontal nudity within the context of medical treatment

title: 28 Weeks Later
synopsis: Hyperviolent sequel to the 2002 horror film "28 Days Later" with virus-infected zombies on a rampage across Britain, and the efforts of the authorities to repopulate the country decimated by what is called a "rage virus." Despite decent special effects and photography, director and co-writer Juan Carlos Fresnadillo mostly just serves up 101 minutes of mind-numbing, nearly plotless butchery as the cast, including Robert Carlyle, is chased nonstop by virus-infected zombies. Crude and profane language, several instances of the f-word, a fleeting sexual encounter, grotesque mass slaughter and numerous individual violent acts

title: 29th Street
synopsis: The fractious relationship between a shiftless but uncommmonly lucky young man (Anthony LaPaglia) and his debt-ridden father (Danny Aiello) reaches crisis level when the son becomes a six-million-dollar lottery finalist. Writer-director George Gallo turns in a shrill comedy that affirms family ties with stereotypical characters and sledgehammer humor. Benign depiction of car insurance fraud and much rough language

title: 2 Days in the Valley
synopsis: Slickly cynical tale of a brutal slaying by two hitmen (Danny Aiello and James Spader) who proceed to involve a number of others (including Teri Hatcher, Glenne Headly, Eric Stoltz and Paul Mazursky) in the crime's bloody aftermath. Writer-director John Herzfeld's contrived, pulpy story is an upalatable concoction of sadistic violence and sick humor. Much gory violence, sex encounter with nudity, occasional profanity and much rough language

title: 2 Fast 2 Furious
synopsis: Lackluster sequel in which a disgraced cop (Paul Walker) and his childhood friend (Tyrese) are recruited by the feds to put their street car racing smarts to work to corner a money.laundering businessman (Cole Hauser). With plot holes wide enough to drive a Mack truck through, director John Singleton's inane action film stalls and sputters as the amateur effort with a large budget uses fancy car races to dress up a shell of a script. Brief violence and fisticuffs, dangerous illegal street car racing, a few passing sexual references, a flash of rear nudity and some crass language

Noisy, testosterone-charged telling of the legendary battle between ancient Sparta's meager 300 soldiers led by King Leonidas (Gerard Butler) against the vast Persian army headed by the fearsome Xerxes (Rodrigo Santoro), while Sparta's queen (Lena Headey) futilely attempts to sway a corrupt politician (Dominic West) to bolster her husband's troops. With Frank Miller's graphic novel as a springboard, director and co-writer Zack Snyder takes a highly stylized approach -- most of the film is shot in sepia tones, with the impossibly buffed soldiers facing off against digitalized weapons, creatures, and seemingly thousands of Persians -- soon grows tiresome, though the pervasive battlefield violence is somewhat tempered by the often artful cinematography. Much slow-motion fighting with bloodshed, impalings, and decapitations, an adulterous episode with an implied rough sexual encounter, brief upper female and rear nudity, innuendo, some exotic dancing with a lesbian kiss during a brief orgy sequence, skimpy male attire throughout

title: 300 Spartans, The
synopsis: Pedestrian account of Persia's invasion of Greece in 480 B.C. focuses on the confrontation between the mighty forces of King Xerxes (David Farrar) and a small band of Spartans (led by Richard Egan) guarding the pass at Thermopylae, just before the decisive defeat of the Persian fleet by the Athenians (led by Ralph Richardson). Rudolph Mate directs a lifeless script full of cardboard characters and high-school rhetoric about the virtues of democracy and the need for unity, though interest picks up once the battle at the pass is joined with convincing action scenes. Battlefield violence

title: 30-Foot Bride of Candy Rock, The
synopsis: Woefully inept comedy about a garbage man (Lou Costello) whose girlfriend (Dorothy Provine) suddenly grows giant-sized, panicking town and Pentagon. Director Sidney Miller's loud, unfunny script and cheezy effects make Costello's last movie a sorry exercise. Minimal entertainment

title: 3:10 to Yuma
synopsis: Intelligent, well-crafted Western in which a small Arizona rancher (Van Heflin) in need of ready cash takes the job of delivering a captured badman (Glenn Ford) to the federal marshal on the next train but, as they await its arrival, the outlaw's band of a ruthless gunmen show up to free him. Director Delmer Daves concentrates on the shifting relationship between the decent family man and his cynical prisoner in a psychological war of wit and nerve until the suspenseful situation erupts in the final showdown. Stylized violence, much menace and an implied sexual encounter

title: 3:10 to Yuma
synopsis: Generally absorbing remake of the 1957 film, based on an Elmore Leonard story, about an impoverished 1880s rancher (Christian Bale) who, for $200, agrees to escort a notorious Bible-quoting bandit (Russell Crowe) to the train that will transport him to prison and justice before the outlaw's gang can rescue him. The narrative -- diffuse at first -- becomes more cohesive and gripping as director James Mangold's Western throwback builds to its climax, and the performances, including Ben Foster as the outlaw's wild-eyed henchman and Peter Fonda as a corrupt bounty hunter, are fine. There are also interesting moral issues at play, as the charming villain offers to bribe the rancher who's hoping for personal redemption, particularly in the eyes of his 14-year-old son (Logan Lerman) impressed by the criminal. Pervasive but not graphic violence and torture, killings, profanity, rough language, a grisly bullet removal, brief rear nudity and some light sexual talk

title: 36 Fillette
synopsis: Sullen 14-year-old (Delphine Zentout) on summer holiday with her family plays cat-and-mouse sexual games with a much older man and finally loses her virginity to a peer. French director Catherine Breillat's irresponsible portrait of teenage angst features a depressing protagonist, her explicit sexual encounters with a middle-aged lothario and sexually vulgar language. Much nudity

title: 36 Hours
synopsis: Neat suspense thriller about a fantastic plot by German intelligence to get information about the Allied invasion. Directed by George Seaton with Rod Taylor, Eva Marie Saint and James Garner, the gimmicks are entertaining and most viewers will excuse its melodramatic conclusion

title: 39 Steps, The
synopsis: Classic spy thriller about an innocent but resourceful Canadian (Robert Donat) pursued across Scotland by the police and a sinister gang of foreign agents while handcuffed for a time to a woman (Madeleine Carroll) who believes him to be a murderer. Director Alfred Hitchcock has a lot of fun concocting surprising visual twists to the fast-paced suspense story, relieved by occasional comic turns of plot and a charming romance that begins in mutual antagonism. Some stylized violence, much menace and mild romantic references

title: 3 Bad Men
synopsis: Silent Western classic set during the 1877 land rush in the Black Hills of Dakota where a gritty outlaw trio (Tom Santschi, J. Farrell MacDonald and Frank Campeau) help a young woman (Olive Borden) after her father is killed on the trail, then protect her and her cowboy beau (George O'Brien) from a corrupt, womanizing sheriff (Lou Tellegen) and his gang of cutthroats. Director John Ford paces the action with frontier humor, sentimental camaraderie and the sheriff's vile villainy, but what stands out is Ford's masterful visualization of the land rush sequence. Frontier violence and sexual innuendo

title: 3 Needles
synopsis: > Epic three-part drama about the worldwide spread of AIDS through poverty, indifference, ignorance and greed told through three stories: in China, a contraband blood seller (Lucy Liu) sells tainted blood, and a poor farmer (Tanabadee Chokpikultong) tries to get to the bottom of the sickness mysteriously affecting his family and villagers; in Montreal, a porn actor (Shawn Ashmore) passes off his father's blood as his own to avoid HIV detection, while his wily mother (Stockard Channing) indulges in a fraudulent scheme; and in South Africa, a novice (Chloe Sevigny) in a South African community of nuns (including Olympia Dukakis and Sandra Oh) tries to educate and convert the locals dying of the disease. Director Thom Fitzgerald's cautionary tale is majestically photographed and, on the whole, absorbing, though marred by several lurid plot elements, and could have used sharper focus. Full indigenous male and partial female nudity, a circumcision, sexual encounters and multiple rapes, brief pornographic tableaux without nudity, condom use, drug references, some profanity and rough language, and a graphic childbirth scene. Multiple languages and partly subtitled

title: 3 Ninjas
synopsis: Thoroughly contrived comedy follows the three young sons of a neglectful FBI dad (Alan McRae) as they outsmart an arms dealer (Rand Kingsley), thanks to martial arts training by their grandpa (Victor Wong). Directed by Jon Turtletaub, the manipulative formula movie tries to make the youngsters' brutalizing of adults seem hysterically funny, despite inept plot and poor acting. Frequent comic violence and some toilet humor

title: 3 Ninjas: High Noon at Mega Mountain
synopsis: Boring sequel in which four youngsters use their martial arts skills and computer savvy to outwit a band of terrorists (led by Loni Anderson) holding them and many others hostage in a theme park. Director Sean McNamara showcases constant physical aggression in this predictable and juvenile macho fantasy. Much slapstick violence

title: 3 Ninjas Kick Back
synopsis: Uninspired sequel in which the three ninja-loving youngsters (Max Elliott Slade, Sean Fox and Evan Bonifant) land in Japan to rescue their grandfather (Victor Wong) from an evil rival bent on stealing the old man's ceremonial dagger. Director Charles T. Kanganis adds a perky girl ninja to the formula but limits the entertainment to unconvincing bouts between the four children and dozens of adult opponents, with always predictable results. Martial arts violence and some menace

title: 3 Ring Circus
synopsis: Two Army buddies get menial jobs in a circus and, after much blundering, one (Dean Martin) becomes the manager and the other (Jerry Lewis) its top clown. Directed by Joseph Pevney, the colorful circus acts and a good supporting cast (Joanne Dru, Zsa Zsa Gabor, Wallace Ford and Elsa Lanchester) help make up for Dean's singing and Lewis' mugging. Small children may enjoy it

title: 3 Women
synopsis: Director Robert Altman explores the friendship between two single women (Shelley Duvall and Sissy Spacek), unskilled workers in a geriatric facility, and an unhappily married artist (Janice Rule) whose work on a grotesque mural keeps her on the periphery until the movie's bleak, simplistic resolution which brings the three together in a strong, sexless relationship. Though thoughtful in its character study of the women, promiscuity figures in the plot and camera's obsession with the exaggerated sexual characteristics of the mural's semi-human figures make it questionable fare

title: Table for Five
synopsis: Failed tearjerker in which a divorced husband (Jon Voight) takes his three children on a Mediterranean cruise, during which his ex-wife (Millie Perkins) dies in an accident and the children's stepfather (Richard Crenna) starts showing up at ports of call demanding custody of the still unknowing children. Directed by David Seltzer, the sentimental hokem seems interminable. Shipboard romance with a lovely Frenchwoman (Marie-Christine Barrault) is adult fare

title: Tadpole
synopsis: Questionable comedy-drama about a precocious 15-year-old boy (Aaron Stanford) who falls in love with his stepmother (Sigourney Weaver) but has an unexpected one-night stand with his stepmother’s 40-something best friend (BebeNeuwirth), complicating matters all around. In relating teen-age angst and unrequited first love, director Gary Winick’s film has some touching as well as humorous moments, but the teen-age seduction is nonetheless quite off-putting and the digital camerawork weighs down the film’s otherwise bubbly tone. An implied sexual encounter with a minor, a scene of underage drinking and fleeting rough language

title: Tail Spin
synopsis: Routine aviation picture about women pilots competing in the Cleveland Air Show's Powder Puff Race among whom are a socialite (Constance Bennett) and a waitress (Alice Faye) vying for the same man (Kane Richmond). Directed by Roy Del Ruth, there's some comic relief (Joan Davis) but a lot of bad melodrama, including a crash (Edward Norris) and the suicide of the dead pilot's wife (Nancy Kelly). Romantic triangle and muddled treatment of suicide

title: Taipan
synopsis: Rambling epic soap opera leaves out the history, drama and details of the economic exploitation of China during the 1840s when British traders dominated the opium and tea trades, centering instead on the sexual exploitation of bare-breasted Chinese women. Based on James Clavell's best-seller about a Scotchman (Bryan Brown) who loses, then regains control of a lucrative Hong Kong trading post, the photography of actua1 Chinese locales is picturesque but Daryl Duke's direction is ponderous. Much nudity, sexual activity and bruta1ity

title: Take a Girl Like You
synopsis: British production about an innocent young teacher (Hayley Mills) being pursued by her landlord (John Bird) and fellow teacher (Oliver Reed), both nasty rather than romantic types. Directed by Jonathan Miller, the heavy-handed melodrama deals in the corrupting influence of swingers and their world of casual sex

title: Take a Hard Ride
synopsis: Routine Western about a wrangler (Jim Brown), entrusted by his dying boss (Dana Andrews) to bring his widow the money from the sale of a herd, who forms an uncertain alliance with a devil-may-care gambler (Fred Williamson) as various villains pop out of the sagebrush on the way home. Directed by Anthony Dawson, it's bland and harmless save for a lot of unimaginative chases and gunfights

title: Take a Letter, Darling
synopsis: Stylish romantic comedy in which a no-nonsense career woman (Rosalind Russell) hires a starving artist (Fred MacMurray) as a male secretary but their strictly business relationship takes a romantic turn with some amusing help from her woolly business partner (Robert Benchley) and a tobacco millionaire (Macdonald Carey). Director Mitchell Leisen finds heart as well as smiles in the shifting relationship while having some fun along the way with period conventions, gender roles and the advertising game. Romantic complications

title: Take Down
synopsis: Small-town teacher (Edward Herrmann) becomes the reluctant coach of the high school's game but inept wrestling team and has to motivate the one youngster (Lorenzo Lamas) who could boost it to the championship. Though the plot is entirely predictable, director Keith Merrill gives it some heart and his handling of the young cast makes it fun. Wholesome teen entertainment

title: Take Her, She's Mine
synopsis: Failed comedy about the silly troubles an inept dad (James Stewart) gets into while trying to protect his college daughter (Sandra Dee) from amorous lads here and in France. Directed by Henry Koster, the generation-gap proceedings are dully contrived and tiresomely executed, with Stewart particularly ill-used as the lame-brained parent whose blundering antics arouse few smiles and less sympathy. Comic violence and tasteless sexual innuendo

title: Take It All
synopsis: French-Canadian production directed by Claude Jutra about an immoral young man's sexual experiences is offensive in its suggestive treatment in spite of its superficial condemnation of the hero

title: Take Me Home Tonight
synopsis: This slack, morally heedless coming-of-age comedy, set in 1988 Los Angeles, chronicles a transformative night in the life of a recent MIT grad (Topher Grace). He somehow learns a lesson in maturity by stealing a car, attending a wild party and posing as a high-powered investment banker -- in reality, he's an underachieving video store clerk -- in order to impress, and hopefully bed, his elusive high school crush (Teresa Palmer). He's accompanied on these adventures by his mischievous best friend (Dan Fogler) and sexually unabashed twin sister (Anna Faris). Seemingly nostalgic for consequence-free hedonism, rather than any form of innocence, co-writer and director Michael Dowse celebrates his youthful ensemble's sowing of some thoroughly distasteful wild oats. Strong sexual content -- including graphic nonmarital sexual activity, voyeurism and upper female nudity; drug use; about 10 instances of profanity; and pervasive rough and crude language

title: Take Me Out to the Ball Game
synopsis: Genial musical comedy about a turn-of-the-century baseball club whose new owner is a woman (Esther Williams), despite which the team heads for the World Series until its star shortstop (Gene Kelly) gets sidetracked by a crafty gambler (Edward Arnold). Director Busby Berkeley combines the colorful period setting with some zestful song-and-dance numbers in dressing up a romantic plot pairing Kelly with Williams and infielder Frank Sinatra with assertive showgirl Betty Garnett. Smoothly contrived, easy-to-take family fare

title: Taken
synopsis: Formulaic and contrived but effectively tense thriller about an ex-government operative (Liam Neeson) hunting for his missing teenage daughter (Maggie Grace) who's been kidnapped by Albanian sex traffickers in Paris. Director Pierre Morel keeps things moving with a flashy visual style, and Neeson plays with a genuine intensity that almost, but not quite, makes you overlook the improbable setup and ludicrous plot developments. Intense but nongraphic action violence including torture, multiple killings, vigilante justice, some crude language and expressions, and a single profanity

title: Take One False Step
synopsis: Minor chase thriller with a New York educator (William Powell) on the run from L.A. policemen (James Gleason and Sheldon Leonard) certain he's the mystery man in the case of a missing blonde (Shelley Winters). Directed by Chester Erskine, the flabby plot is helped by some bemused humor and interesting turns, including the educator being bitten by a dog he fears has rabies. Some stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Takers
synopsis: Crime drama that devolves into a cliched exercise in gunfire, explosions and insipid dialogue. Director and co-writer John Luessenhop tells the story of a gang of five skilled thieves (Idris Elba, Paul Walker, Chris Brown, Michael Ealy and Hayden Christensen) joined, on his release from prison, by a former cohort (Tip "T.I." Harris) with a plan for the highly engineered robbery of an armored truck. Giving chase is a grumpy Los Angeles police detective (Matt Dillon). Constant stylized gun violence, an instance of male rear nudity, and pervasive crude and fleeting profane and crass language

title: Take, The
synopsis: Billie Dee Williams stars as a cop who's tough on the mob but takes money from them on the side in a muddled detective thriller which tries to create a complex environment where cops and crooks are interchangeable and money makes the world go round. Unfortunately, director Robert Hartford-Davis never bothers to explain the two sides of Williams' character or what the action is really all about, especially why the mob is attacking Paloma, New Mexico

title: Take the High Ground
synopsis: Korean War vet (Richard Widmark) proves tough drill sergeant pushing draftees through 16 grueling weeks of basic training at Fort Bliss, Texas. Director Richard Brooks covers the routine chores of boot camp in pedestrian fashion as the sour sergeant mellows, thanks to a good buddy (Karl Malden) and a girlfriend (Elaine Stewart). Manly posturing and romantic complications

title: Take the Lead
synopsis: Uplifting movie inspired by real-life dance instructor Pierre Dulaine (a very believable Antonio Banderas), who gets permission from the principal of an inner-city high school (Alfre Woodard) to teach ballroom dancing to troubled kids, eventually leading them to participate in a major ballroom competition. Music video director Liz Friedlander makes an assured feature film debut despite the formulaic plot, and has elicited good performances, while imparting admirable messages about trust, dignity and respect. Some crude language and expressions, implied prostitution, an amorous advance to a minor, a vulgar gesture, violent car vandalism and gunplay preclude viewing by younger adolescents

title: Take the Money and Run
synopsis: Woody Allen stars as the world's least dangerous criminal, botching bank jobs and terrorizing no one but himself. Also directed by Allen, it's an entertaining romp through many fields and styles of humor, one-line witticisms, subtle jokes and sight gags galore. Some sexual references and a few profanities

title: Taking Care of Business
synopsis: Tame comedy about an escaped con (James Belushi) who blithely assumes the identity of a stuffy corporate executive (Charles Grodin) after finding his appointment book, credit cards and keys to an oceanside mansion. Under Arthur Hiller's direction, the two leads work hard at creating characters likeable enough to overcome the predictable mistaken-identity plot. A brief sexual encounter, a flash of nudity, some slapstick violence and minimal rough language

title: Taking Lives
synopsis: Smart and stylish thriller about an FBI profiler (Angelina Jolie) called in by Canadian authorities to help solve a string of grisly unsolved murders stretching back 20 years and who becomes emotionally involved with a witness (Ethan Hawke) in danger of becoming the serial killer's next victim. Despite a formulaic cat-and-mouse premise and cookie-cutter creepiness, director D.J. Caruso keeps the action briskly paced and viewers on the edge of their seats, crafting a suspenseful screamer which, though not without some graphically disturbing images, shows restraint in depicting the lurid crimes. Recurring gory violence and associated autopsy images, a sexual encounter with partial nudity, frequent rough and crude language

title: Taking Off
synopsis: Uneven satire on the generation gap in suburbia follows the frantic search of parents (Buck Henry and Lynn Carlin) for their teenaged daughter who they think has run away when, in fact, she has only gone to the big city for a rock musical audition. Directed by Milos Forman, the parents come off worse than the kids, partly because they're older and should know better. It is mostly a series of outrageous burlesques, some riotously funny, others merely outrageous or excessive, such as a strip poker scene and one with youngsters singing an Elizabethan-style ballad with obscene lyrics

title: The Taking of Pelham 1 2 3
synopsis: Brisk but gritty thriller that pits a New York subway dispatcher (Denzel Washington) against a psychopath (John Travolta) whose small gang (including Luis Guzman) has hijacked the titular train, taking its passengers hostage. Performances by the leads and supporting cast -- James Gandolfini as the mayor and John Turturro as a police negotiator among them -- are assured, but director Tony Scott's adaptation of John Godey's bestseller, previously filmed in 1974, treats its villain's Catholic upbringing ambiguously and has interludes of gory violence and relentlessly coarse language throughout. Brief but intense violence, pervasive rough and crude language, occasional use of profanity

title: Taking of Pelham One Two Three, The
synopsis: New York City transit policeman (Walter Matthau) has to outwit a heavily armed band of desperate men (led by Robert Shaw) who have seized control of a subway train and are holding its passengers hostage for ransom. Director Joseph Sergent's rattling-good action movie keeps the mood claustrophobic, the suspense tightly wound and paced with just the right amount of comic relief. The cast is top-notch, all of whom hit the mark as New York types. The only distraction is its relentlessly crude language which, unlike the subway, never stops

title: Taking Sides
synopsis: Failed drama set in post-World War II Berlin about the prosecution of famed German symphony conductor Wilhelm Furtwangler (Stellan Skarsgard) by an American officer (Harvey Keitel). Despite lush, atmospheric settings, director Istvan Szabo's film, which is based on a true story, lacks dramatic tension as it poorly attempts to convey the difficult choice between artistic freedom and political responsibility. Horrific depictions of mass graves and some rough language, profanity and crass expressions

title: Taking Woodstock
synopsis: This fact-based slice of psychedelic history sees the young manager (Demetri Martin) of a failing Catskills motel owned by his downtrodden immigrant parents (Henry Goodman and Imelda Staunton) inadvertently becoming a crucial player in the staging of the iconic 1969 music festival when he uses a legal permit to ease the way for the event's organizer (Jonathan Groff) and introduces him to the owner (Eugene Levy) of the dairy farm that would serve as the concert's setting. Along with the flower people's fondness for disrobing and drug-taking, director Ang Lee's gently rambling adaptation of Elliot Tiber's 2007 memoir portrays its protagonist's public avowal of his homosexuality as a positive step toward emotional maturity. Benign view of homosexual acts, group sex and transvestism, nonsexual full frontal nudity, drug use, a half-dozen uses of profanity, and frequent rough and some crude language

title: Talented Mr. Ripley, The
synopsis: Disquieting melodrama set in 1958 Italy where, after befriending a rich expatriate couple (Jude Law and Gwyneth Paltrow), an impoverished young American (Matt Damon) impulsively takes the man's life, assumes his identity and stops at nothing to keep the risky charade going. Adapted by director Anthony Minghella from Patricia Highsmith's 1955 novel, a chilling cautionary tale of materialism expanding to grotesque evil unfolds replete with seductive visuals and sleek performances but an ambiguous ending. Occasional gory violence, an implied affair, discreet homosexual innuendo, fleeting full nudity and a few instances of rough language

title: Talent for the Game
synopsis: Well-worn baseball story of a big-league scout (Edward James Olmos) discovering a natural fastball pitcher in the Idaho hinterlands, then fighting to save the untried novice's career when he's put on the mound as a publicity stunt. Directed by Robert M. Young, the story's theme contrasts those who love the sport with the new breed who regard baseball as just another business. Mild treatment of a romantic affair and minimal coarse language

title: The Tale of Despereaux
synopsis: Charming animated adventure story about a chivalrous mouse (voice of Matthew Broderick) who is banished to a rat-filled tunnel for fearlessly befriending a distressed human princess (voice of Emma Watson), contrary to the timid customs of his society, and gains the protection of a globe-trotting rat (voice of Dustin Hoffman) with gourmet tastes, who also dreams of derring-do. Though somewhat overloaded with multiple plot lines, co-directors Sam Fell and Rob Stevenhagen's painterly adaptation of Kate DiCamillo's 2003 best-selling, Newbery Medal-winning children's novel is delightfully innocent and idealistic as it celebrates its hero's sense of honor and love of reading and charts his companion's discovery of the power of forgiveness

title: Tales from the Crypt
synopsis: Touring a subterranean burial ground, five sightseers find themselves locked in with the crypt-keeper (Sir Ralph Richardson) who reveals to them the horrible fate that awaits each. Solid British horror movie has a good cast (Peter Cushing, Ian Hendry, Patrick Magee, Nigel Patrick and Joan Collins) and five fairly intriguing tales which Freddie Francis directs with some verve, a lot of polish and even restraint in the visuals

title: Tales from the Crypt, Part II
synopsis: ( see: "The Vault of Horror" )

title: Tales from the Crypt Presents Bordello of Blood
synopsis: Schlocky horror flick in which a cynical private eye (Dennis Miller) stumbles on a funeral home that by night is a brothel whose prostitutes are actually vampires. Producer-director Gilbert Adler's neverending parade of silicon sirens, crass humor and bloodied body parts belongs in the video trash bin. Countless gory killings, much nudity, some profanity and frequent rough language

title: Tales from the Crypt Presents Demon Knight
synopsis: Trashy horror flick in which a satanic creature (Billy Zane) leads assorted goo-drenched demons on a nightlong murderous assault upon the inhabitants of a boarding house in which a newcomer (William Sadler) guards a sacred relic to keep it from falling into demonic hands which would bring humanity's destruction. Mindless mayhem rules the night in this poorly crafted splatter movie whose dumb dialogue and phony spiritual mumbo jumbo are patently pathetic. Intermittent nudity, a bedroom scene, much carnage and recurring rough language

title: Tales from the Darkside: The Movie
synopsis: Clunky horror movie in which a boy delays being served up as dinner by diverting the murderous cook (Deborah Harry) with hackneyed stories of death and doom meted out by an avenging mummy, a diabolical black cat and a lonely monster. Director John Harrison's classy production values and camerawork serve only to dress up an abundance of gory dismemberments and eviscerations. Excessive violence, a sexually promiscuous scene and some rough language

title: Tales from the Hood
synopsis: When a trio of inner-city youths go to a funeral home to buy a cache of drugs found by a mortician (Clarence Williams III), he regales them with supernatural tales of vengeance on racist cops, a white supremacist politician, an African American guilty of domestic abuse and a ghetto drug dealer. Director Rusty Cundieff's feeble exercise in horror spends more time evoking outrage at injustices visited on African Americans by whites as well as blacks than in trying to create an atmosphere of terror and dread. Excessive violence, occasional profanity and intermittent rough language

title: Tales of Manhattan
synopsis: Neatly paced collection of stories tied to a tuxedo tailcoat worn in turn by an actor (Charles Boyer), a playboy (Cesar Romero), a composer (Charles Laughton), a destitute lawyer (Edward G. Robinson) and a criminal (J. Caroll Naish) who tosses it from a plane loaded with money which a black farmer (Paul Robeson) uses to enrich his community on Christmas Eve. Directed by Julien Duvivier, each of the stories is a small dramatic gem, though the centerpiece is the Robinson episode and the ending packs an emotional wallop. Stylized violence, implicit marital infidelity and some sexual innuendo

title: Tales of Terror
synopsis: Uneven trilogy of Edgar Allan Poe stories presents "Morella" in which a dying woman (Maggie Pierce) discovers her dead mother (Lenona Gage) still lives; "The Black Cat" in which a drunken husband (Peter Lorre) walls up his wife (Joyce Jameson) and her lover (Vincent Price); and "The Facts in the Case of M. Valdemer" about a hypnotist (Basil Rathbone) keeping a dying man's brain alive after death. Directed by Roger Corman, the best of the trio is "The Black Cat," though each has the eerie mood of Poe's dark fantasies. Frightening scenes

title: Tales That Witness Madness
synopsis: Failed British terror movie with Donald Pleasance as a psychiatrist explaining four case histories (involving Kim Novak, Peter McEnery, Suzy Kendall, Georgia Brown and Joan Collins) which in the end boil down to a padded cell for the good doctor. Directed by Freddie Francis, neither the frights nor the occasional nudity are worthy of comment or the viewer's time

title: Talk of the Town, The
synopsis: Egalitarian romantic comedy in which a schoolteacher (Jean Arthur) rents her house to a stuffy legal scholar (Ronald Colman) who discovers a suspected arsonist (Cary Grant) hiding in the attic, then decides to help the fugitive prove his innocence in court. Directed by George Stevens, the comedy has some delicious madcap moments as the teacher finds herself emotionally caught between the two men, but the picture's patriotic themes for World War II audiences have worn less well. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Talk Radio
synopsis: Fictional story of a radio talk show host (Eric Bogosian) who makes his living verbally abusing the lonely, livid or just plain loony souls who call in nightly to bait him. Directed by Oliver Stone, it is an intense indictment of the irresponsible individuals who often host this type of shock radio and raises questions about providing a forum for off-the-wall listeners. The language of the radio host is explicitly vulgar, involving sexual, racial and ethnic slurs and is laced with much profanity. There's also a brief but extremely graphic murder scene

title: Talk to Her
synopsis: Troubling Spanish melodrama in which a writer (Dario Grandinetti) whose bullfighter girlfriend (Rosario Flores) is comatose after being gored is befriended by a male nurse (Javier Camara) who loves his own comatose patient (Leonor Watling) and takes extreme action in hopes of bringing her back to consciousness. While writer-director Pedro Almodovar skillfully creates characters who exhibit much caring and tenderness, longing and loneliness, he seems to look benignly on the nurse's wrongheaded choices. Subtitles. Some bizarre sexual situations with nudity, brief violence, an off-screen rape, suicide and a few instances of rough language

title: Talk to Me
synopsis: Formulaic but still touching and inspiring biographical drama of a prominent Washington radio personality and activist (a fine Don Cheadle) from the Vietnam-Watergate era to his death in 1984. Director Kasi Lemmons uses the redemptive power of friendship and strong performances by a cast including Chiwetel Ejiofor as a radio-station executive, Martin Sheen, Vondie Curtis-Hall and Cedric the Entertainer) to create an evocative period piece about second chances. Pervasive rough, crude and crass language and several instances of profanity, sexual encounters with partial nudity, innuendo, alcohol abuse, rioting, infidelity, domestic discord and assorted fighting

title: Talladega Nights: The Ballad of Ricky Bobby
synopsis: Fitfully amusing comedy about a former pit-crew mechanic (Will Ferrell) who rises to the pinnacle of the NASCAR racing circuit, falls from the spotlight and then tries to get back to the top with the help of his beer-guzzling dad (Gary Cole). Despite a goofily entertaining performance by Ferrell, there's not much under the hood when it comes to story and the script by Ferrell and longtime collaborator Adam McKay (who also directs) hits plenty of speed bumps in the form of juvenile jokes by turns vulgar, irreverent, or just unfunny. Recurring crude sexual language and humor, a running gag involving a gay character, some irreverent humor and profanity, drug references, comic violence

title: Tall Blond Man with One Black Shoe, The
synopsis: Entertaining French farce about a violinist (Pierre Richard) who becomes the pawn in a struggle between two counter-espionage factions for no other reason than that he absentmindedly happens to be wearing an unmatched pair of shoes. Richard's droll performance as a man oblivious to all the assassination attempts surrounding his daily routine is neatly abetted by the comic efforts of Bernard Blier, Jean Rochefort and Mireille Darc. Director Yves Robert turns in an amusing, at time hilarious, comedy of errors carried off in high style. Some sexual innuendoes

title: Tall Guy, The
synopsis: Just when a hapless American actor (Jeff Goldblum) becomes the hit of the London stage in a tasteless musical, his budding romance with a starchy English nurse (Emma Thompson) hits the rocks. Director Mel Smith's comedy is an uneven mix of satire and sex farce, sprinkled with amusing moments, thanks in large part to Goldblum's bumbling but sympathetic performance. Comical treatment of promiscuity, occasional brief nudity and minimal rough language

title: Tall in the Saddle
synopsis: After the rancher who hired him is bushwacked, a cowboy (John Wayne) hangs around town dodging bullets and the romantic designs of a local cowgirl (Ella Raines) until he unmasks the killer. Directed by Edwin L. Marin, it's a congenial low-budget Western with an unpretentious mystery plot, the usual stock characters (Ward Bond and Gabby Hayes among them) and occasional rough humor. Stylized violence

title: Tall Man Riding
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Lesley Selander in which a cowboy (Randolph Scott) returns to square accounts with a rancher who had wronged him, then steps in to save him and his daughter (Dorothy Malone) from a vicious gang of landgrabbers. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Tall Men, The
synopsis: Overblown Western in which an ex-Reb (Clark Gable) and his nasty brother (Cameron Mitchell) join a rancher (Robert Ryan) on a cattle drive from Texas to Montana during which they battle blizzards, Sioux attacks and misunderstandings over a woman (Jane Russell) rescued along the way. Directed by Raoul Walsh, the formula story bogs down in cliched action and stereotyped characters, with unsurprising results. Frontier violence and sexual situations

title: Tall Story
synopsis: Romantic fluff from the Howard Lindsay-Russel Crouse play in which a serious-minded college basketball star (Anthony Perkins) proves no match for a conniving, marriage-minded co-ed (Jane Fonda). Produced and directed by Joshua Logan, the thin proceedings generate few laughs in poking fun at college athletics, hypocritical academics and students' raging hormones. Sexual situations and innuendo

title: Tall Stranger, The
synopsis: Murky Western directed by Thomas Carr in which a Union officer (Joel McCrea) returning home after the Civil War is saved from a bushwacker (Michael Ansara) by a wagon train of settlers whom he in turn saves from being massacred in a war between a Colorado cattle baron and a ruthless band of rustlers. Shootouts, fist-fights, a woman fighting off an attacker and an endangered child

title: Tall Tale: The Unbelievable Adventures of Pecos Bill
synopsis: Largely unimaginative fantasy-adventure set the West of 1905 where a 12 year-old boy (Nick Stahl) conjures up a trio of legendary folk heroes (Patrick Swayze, Oliver Platt and Roger Aaron Brown) to save the family farm from villainous land grabbers. Director Jeremiah Chechik's scenic yarn features trite preachments about family values although the narrative often resorts to brawn and bullets to solve problems. Frequent stylized violence and fleeting sexual innuendo

title: Tall Target, The
synopsis: Engrossing thriller set in 1861 aboard a Washington-bound train as New York City detective John Kennedy (Dick Powell) tries to thwart an assassination plot to kill President-elect Lincoln. Director Anthony Mann keeps the suspense tight and the period details add interest, but the ending is a bit of a let-down. Stylized violence

title: Tall T, The
synopsis: Credible Western in which a cowboy (Randolph Scott) foils the plans of ruthless stagecoach bandits (Richard Boone, Henry Silva and Skip Homeier) to ransom a mine owner's daughter (Maureen O'Sullivan). Director Budd Boetticher establishes the murderous nature of the bandits early on, then builds the tension while waiting for the ransom until the cowboy takes on the trio in the final shootout. Stylized violence and menace

title: Tall Women, The
synopsis: Spanish Western directed by Sidney Pink about a wagon train of women facing hostile Indians on the wild frontier has excessive violence and sexual innuendo

title: Tamarind Seed, The
synopsis: Russian spy (Omar Sharif) falls in love with a secretary in the British Foreign Office (Julie Andrews) and their romance becomes hopelessly entangled in international intrigue. Directed by Blake Edwards, its fine cast and gorgeous location photography are wasted by a script that misses both as love story and as spy thriller

title: Taming of the Shrew, The
synopsis: Sparkling but noisy adaptation of the Shakespeare play with bravura performances by Elizabeth Taylor as the comely shrew and Richard Burton as the rowdy tamer. Director Franco Zeffirelli's inventive staging preserves the flavor of the orginal but never seems firmly in control of the action or the actors. Mature treatment

title: Tam Lin
synopsis: Domineering, aging millionairess (Ava Gardner), living on a sinister Scottish estate with a coven of coed decadents, keeps her current paramour (Ian McShane) in line by showing him a few grisly snapshots of what happened to past lovers whose attentions wandered. Hothouse melodrama is best summed up as a soggy misfire by novice director Roddy McDowall

title: Tammy and the Bachelor
synopsis: Sappy romantic comedy in which the innocent teenager of the title (Debbie Reynolds), raised by her grandfather (Walter Brennan) in a bayou backwater, knocks the socks off the scion (Leslie Nielsen) of a once-wealthy family. Directed by Joseph Pevney, the silly situation and insufferable homespun wisdom of the heroine were stale then and haven't gotten any fresher since. Sugary confection not for all tastes

title: Tammy and the Doctor
synopsis: The third outing of the homespun lass from the Mississippi bayous sees Tammy (Sandra Dee) as a nurse's aide spreading her country wisdom among the staff (Peter Fonda, Macdonald Carey and Margaret Lindsay) and patients (Beulah Bondi and Reginald Owen) of a Los Angeles hospital. Directed by Harry Keller, the hokey script offers bland situations and plenty of bogus sentimentality, though youngsters may be amused by the silly goings-on

title: Tammy Tell Me True
synopsis: This time around Tammy (Sandra Dee) hikes across the swamp to enroll in a nearby college where she helps a rich old lady (Beulah Bondi), saves the marriage of a dean (Virginia Grey) and snags a bemused professor (John Gavin). Director Harry Keller's sugary concoction of contrived situations mistakes the virtue of simplicity for the bane of banality. Bland family fare

title: Tampico
synopsis: Minor World War II espionage thriller in which the captain (Edward G. Robinson) of an oil tanker marries a survivor (Lynn Bari) of a torpedoed ship, then suspects she's a Nazi agent. Directed by Lothar Mendes, there's little action and the identity of the traitor is wildly implausible. Wartime violence

title: Tampopo
synopsis: Wry Japanese satire in which a young widow's unsuccessful noodle business is transformed by a burly truck driver is laced with comic asides relating food to passion, commerce and art. Director Juzo Itami's droll, earthy farce has several sexually suggestive scenes, one with partial nudity, which mars the basically innocent appeal of the story

title: Tanganyika
synopsis: Far-fetched adventure directed by Andre de Toth is set in 1903 British East Africa where an American timber contractor (Van Heflin) goes after an escaped killer (Jeff Morrow) who's behind a native revolt, but the manhunt is slowed in rescuing a wounded traveler (Howard Duff) and the survivors of a massacre (Ruth Roman and two children). Stylized violence

title: Tango Bar
synopsis: Beautifully filmed and choreographed anthology of tango dancing set in Argentina and framed by the personal and political musings of a fictional trio of cabaret performers (Raul Julia, Ruben Juarez and Valeria Lynch). Keeping the love triangle and repressive politics in the background, Puerto Rican director Marcos Zurinaga concentrates on the trio's songs and monologues about the history and evolution of the tango as well as staging some breathtaking tango numbers plus clips of tango dancing from Hollywood and foreign movies. Subtitles. Implied sexual relationships

title: Tango & Cash
synopsis: Ultraviolent supercop saga featuring an unlikely pair of Los Angeles detectives (Sylvester Stallone and Kurt Russell) who dislike each other's style but wind up working together to nail the criminal mastermind (Jack Palance) behind their being framed for murder. Directed by Andrei Konchalovsky, the result is a sophomoric exercise in rock'em-sock'em macho violence and bloodletting. Excessive violence, insulting sexual references and rough language

title: Tank
synopsis: Career Army sergeant uses a Sherman tank to rescue his unjustly arrested son from a vicious southern sheriff (G.D. Spradlin) and then heads for the state line stirring the sympathy of the nation. Audience reaction to director Marvin Chomsky's movie is likely to be much less spectacular because after the breakout, the story becomes increasingly silly and unentertaining. Some violence and rough language

title: Tank Force
synopsis: World War II clunker directed by Terence Young is set in the Libyan Desert where some captured Australian soldiers (notably Victor Mature, Leo Genn and Anthony Newley) make their escape, then are recaptured by pro-German Arab nomads, only to escape again. The wartime violence makes it unlikely children's fare

title: Tanks Are Coming, The
synopsis: Formula World War II tale directed by Lewis Seiler in which a hot-shot platoon leader (Steve Cochran) in an American tank unit battling its way through France is roundly hated by his men but, by the time they cross the Siegfried Line into Germany, they realize his harsh methods have saved their lives by making them better soldiers. Wartime violence

title: Tap
synopsis: An entertaining look at the redemption of a talented tap dancer (Gregory Hines) who took a wrong turn and must choose between a potentially low-paying, rewarding career as a dancer and a lucrative life of crime. Writer-director Nick Castle creates a respectful tribute to this American artform and is especially mindful of tap's black roots. A lusty kissing scene, brief heavily shadowed nudity within a fleeting sexual encounter and some locker room language

title: Tape
synopsis: Absorbing drama set in a seedy motel room in which a bitter slacker (Ethan Hawke) confronts an old friend (Robert Sean Leonard) about stealing and possibly having raped his high school girlfriend (Uma Thurman). Set in real time, director Richard Linklater's caustic film contemplates the nature of truth, particularly on sexual matters, but the conclusion's drawn out proceedings become a bit draining. Sporadic drug use, a brief scuffle and much rough language and profanity

title: Taps
synopsis: Highminded teenage cadets take control of a military boarding school when they learn the authorities are going to close it. George C. Scott does his usual fine job as the officer who inspires the boys to make their stand and Timothy Hutton is good as the insurgent leader. Directed by Harold Becker, the rather implausible youth-in-revolt drama fails to make its story of courage and leadership very credible. Some violence and coarse language

title: Tarantula
synopsis: Effective monster fantasy in which a scientist (Leo G. Carroll) experimenting on a growth nutrient becomes grotesquely disfigured, then dies while a spider injected with the nutrient escapes into the Arizona desert, grows bigger than a house and heads for town until stopped by the local doctor (John Agar) and some jet fighters. Director Jack Arnold gets plenty of menace from the low-budget production, though the scientific experiments at the beginning are more frightening than the rampages of the special-effects monster. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Target
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Stuart Gilmore in which a couple of cowboy straight-shooters (Tim Holt and Richard Martin) bust up a gang of railroad landgrabbers in 1893 Texas. Stylized violence

title: Target
synopsis: A middle-aged father (Gene Hackman) gains the admiration of his son (Matt Dillon) when his wife (Gayle Hunnicutt) is kidnapped on a European trip, and dull o1d Dad, who has a secret CIA past, becomes transformed into a superagent as the two attempt to find Mom. Directed by Arthur Penn but so preposterous that it skirts parody in spots, it is, nonetheless, entertaining fantasy fare, especially for fathers weary of feeling 1ike Rodney Dangerfield. A bit of rough language and some violence

title: Targets
synopsis: Modest crime thriller concerning a psychopathic killer (Tim O'Kelly) on the loose with an arsenal of weapons and a retired movie actor (Boris Karloff) who confront each other in a drive-in movie theater. Written and directed by Peter Bogdanovich, the contrast between the horror of reality and that of fantasy don't quite come off, partly because Karloff in his few scenes steals the film. Some stylized violence but no insights

title: Target Unknown
synopsis: Standard World War II tale of a 1944 B-26 bomber crew (led by Mark Stevens) whose German captors (led by Robert Douglas) use devious means to learn of an upcoming raid. Directed by George Sherman, the cat-and-mouse game between German interrogators and U.S. airmen holds interest until the Americans escape in a melodramatic attempt to use the French underground to contact their airbase and stop the raid. Wartime violence

title: Target Zero
synopsis: Contrived Korean War story in which a U.S. infantry patrol (led by Richard Conte) comes across a nurse (Peggy Castle) as well as a British tank while fighting their way back through enemy lines. Director Harmon Jones plods through an unconvincing plot whose wartime heroics aren't helped much by pretentious dialogue and an improbable romance. Battlefield violence

title: Tartu
synopsis: ( see: "The Adventures of Tartu" )

title: Tarzan
synopsis: Ferocious animated tale about an orphaned human baby raised by a jungle gorilla (voice of Glenn Close) who as an adult (voice of Tony Goldywn) encounters his first humans, including a duplicitous hunter (voice of Brian Blessed) intent on capturing his beloved ape family and spunky Jane (voice of Minnie Driver), who tempts Tarzan to return to civilization. Based on Edgar Rice Burrough's characters dating back to 1912, the animation by directors Kevin Lima and Chris Buck is accomplished and the characters appealing, but several fast-paced action scenes of predatory violence are too intense for younger children. Intensely menacing hunting scenes

title: Tarzan and His Mate
synopsis: Dandy sequel to 1932's "Tarzan, the Ape Man" concerns the return of the safari guide (Neil Hamilton) to the African escarpment hoping to bring Jane (Maureen O'Sullivan) back to civilization, though his partner (Paul Kavanagh) wants only the ivory in the elephant's graveyard and shoots Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller) to get it. Directed by Cedric Gibbons, the jungle adventure features battles with fierce native tribes, animals ranging from friendly to murderous and the contentment of the loving couple in their primitive paradise. Stylized violence, incidental nudity, sexual innuendo and African stereotyping

title: Tarzan and the Amazons
synopsis: Thin jungle adventure directed by Kurt Neumann in which Boy (Johnny Sheffield) guides an archaeologist (Henry Stephenson) to a lost city of women warriors whose priestess (Maria Ouspenskaya) spares their lives, then greedy expedition members (Barton MacLane and J.M. Kerrigan) loot the city until Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller) comes to the rescue. Stylized violence

title: Tarzan and the Great River
synopsis: Tarzan (Mike Henry) journeys to the upper reaches of the Amazon to put a halt to some occult goings-on by a tribe of headhunting terrorists. Directed by Robert Day, it's an exciting enough adventure, if all-too-familiar for older members of the family

title: Tarzan and the Green Goddess
synopsis: Slap-dash feature version of a serial directed by Edward Kull with Tarzan (Herman Brix aka Bruce Bennett) in the jungles of Guatemala trying to recover a sacred Mayan idol in which is hidden the formula for a super-explosive. Hokey stylized violence

title: Tarzan and the Huntress
synopsis: Formula jungle adventure directed by Kurt Neumann in which Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller) saves Jane (Brenda Joyce) and Boy (Johnny Sheffield) from the murderous guide (Barton MacLane) of a zoological expedition that has far exceeded its agreed quota of animal specimens. Stylized violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Tarzan and the Jungle Boy
synopsis: Newspaperwoman comes looking for a youngster lost years before in the jungle and runs into a slew of obstacles, including some unfriendly natives (led by Rafter Johnson). Tarzan (Mike Henry) flexes his muscles and puts everything right in director Robert Day's routine adventure

title: Tarzan and the Leopard Woman
synopsis: Formula jungle adventure directed by Kurt Neumann in which Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller), Jane (Brenda Joyce) and Boy (Johnny Sheffield) are taken captive by a murderous leopard cult led by a woman (Acquanetta) fighting colonial rule, with Cheetah coming to the rescue for a Samson-like finale. Stylized violence and threatening situations

title: Tarzan and the Lost City
synopsis: Lackluster tale teams the Ape Man (Casper Van Dien) with his fiancee (Jane March) as they help a jungle tribe prevent a band of mercenaries from plundering their sacred treasures. Directed by Carl Schenkel, the tame, humorless movie has little sense of adventure but plenty of beefcake shots of the title actor. Sporadic stylized violence

title: Tarzan and the Lost Safari
synopsis: Standard jungle adventure directed by Bruce Humberstone has Tarzan (Gordon Scott) save the five occupants of a downed airplane from being turned over to a hostile tribe by a greedy hunter (Robert Beatty). Stylized violence

title: Tarzan and the Mermaids
synopsis: Exotic adventure directed by Robert Florey in which Johnny Weissmuller makes his 12th and final appearance as Tarzan, this time rescuing a woman (Linda Christian) from the high priest (George Zucco) of a bogus god worshipped by her island people until the Ape Man reveals their "god" is only a greedy mortal after their pearls. Stylized violence

title: Tarzan and the She-Devil
synopsis: Formula jungle adventure directed by Kurt Neumann with Tarzan (Lex Barker) saving Jane (Joyce MacKenzie) and a herd of elephants from nasty ivory poachers (Raymond Burr, Tom Conway and Monique Van Vooren). Stylized violence

title: Tarzan and the Slave Girl
synopsis: Hokey jungle adventure directed by Lee Sholem in which Tarzan (Lex Barker) tracks some kidnapped women to a hidden city where he frees the captives while saving Jane (Vanessa Brown) and a jungle nurse (Denise Darcel) from being entombed alive, then helps a doctor (Arthur Shields) cure the city of a deadly disease. Stylized violence and brutality

title: Tarzan and the Trappers
synopsis: Pulp adventure directed by Charles Haas and Sandy Howard in which Tarzan (Gordon Scott) captures a poacher, then thwarts a greedy group of treasure hunters seeking a lost city. Comic-book heroics with hokey violence

title: Tarzan and the Valley of Gold
synopsis: Standard jungle adventure directed by Robert Day with Tarzan (Mike Henry) getting involved with some spies

title: Tarzan Escapes
synopsis: Familiar African adventure in which Jane (Maureen O'Sullivan) is visited by London cousins who want her to return with them just long enough to collect her inheritance, but their guide (John Buckler) is more interested in capturing Tarzan and selling him as a side-show attraction. Directed by Richard Thorpe, a number of previous encounters with animals and native tribes are reused here with the new storyline woven around them with agreeable results. Stylized violence

title: Tarzan Finds a Son!
synopsis: Enjoyable adventure in which Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller) and Jane (Maureen O'Sullivan) rescue a baby boy from a crashed airplane, then five years later have to save him (Johnnie Sheffield) from greedy relatives (Ian Hunter and Frieda Inescort) after his inheritance. Director Richard Thorpe paces the sunny scenes of happy jungle life with the harsh realities of the wild and the deceit of civilized outsiders. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Tarzan Goes to India
synopsis: Formula adventure featuring picturesque Indian locales where Tarzan (Jock Mahoney) befriends an orphaned boy, then uses the lad's elephant to lead a herd of rogue elephants through a mountain pass before they are drowned by the opening of a new dam. Directed by John Guillermin, the pedestrian plot has scant interest save for the scenery and the thundering herd of elephants. Some stylized violence

title: Tarzan's Deadly Silence
synopsis: The Ape Man (Ron Ely), despite being temporarily deafened by an explosion, saves a native tribe from the exploitation of a megalomaniac trying to set up a jungle empire. Directed by Robert L. Friend, it's the usual wilderness adventure, though fans may be disappointed that there is no Jane and no blood-curdling jungle call. Directed by Robert L. Friend

title: Tarzan's Desert Mystery
synopsis: Routine adventure in which Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller) and Boy (Johnny Sheffield) save a woman magician (Nancy Kelly) from Nazi agents (Otto Kruger and Joe Sawyer), avert a war between desert tribes and fight off a giant spider while gathering medicinal plants requested by Jane, now an Army nurse. Directed by William Thiele, the contrived proceedings plod along rather aimlessy until the predictable ending

title: Tarzan's Fight for Life
synopsis: Formula jungle adventure directed by Bruce Humberstone with Tarzan (Gordon Scott) helping a dedicated white doctor save his bush hospital from a tribal witch doctor (James Edwards) and a renegade band of warriors (led by Woody Strode). Stylized violence

title: Tarzan's Greatest Adventure
synopsis: Routine action adventure filmed in Africa with an articulate Tarzan (Gordon Scott) tracking a band of killers (Anthony Quayle, Niall MacGinnis and Sean Connery) on their way to a hidden diamond mine. Directed by John Guillermin, the proceedings are rather sluggish until the action heats up in a fairly nasty showdown. Stylized violence and psychopathic criminals

title: Tarzan's Hidden Jungle
synopsis: Standard adventure directed by Harold Schuster with Tarzan (Gordon Scott) saving a U.N. doctor (Peter Van Eyck) and his nurse (Vera Miles) from an unfriendly tribe (headed by Rex Ingram) stirred up by murderous poachers (led by Jack Elam). Stylized violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Tarzan's Jungle Rebellion
synopsis: Archaeologist (Sam Jaffe) searching for a lost civilization, a native looking for a sacred statue to establish his rule over the jungle and a group simply after gold come up against the lord of the jungle (Ron Ely). Director William Whitney follows the formula without much conviction

title: Tarzan's Magic Fountain
synopsis: Fanciful jungle adventure directed by Lee Sholem in which Tarzan (Lex Barker) tries to keep greedy outsiders (Albert Dekker and Charles Drake) from finding a hidden mountain city whose waters restore youth and heal the sick, though Jane (Brenda Joyce) complicates matters by trying to guide an aviatrix (Evelyn Ankers) and her husband (Alan Napier) there. Stylized violence

title: Tarzan's New York Adventure
synopsis: Enterprising series entry with Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller), Jane (Maureen O'Sullivan) and Chita off to New York to find Boy (Johnny Sheffield) after he's abducted from the escarpment to perform in a circus.
