Directed by Richard Thorpe, Tarzan takes civilization in stride as he climbs down a skyscraper's exterior, dives off the Brooklyn Bridge and leads a troop of circus elephants to the rescue. Menacing situations

title: Tarzan's Peril
synopsis: Routine jungle adventure in which Tarzan (Lex Barker) rescues an African queen (Dorothy Dandridge) and her people from a warring tribe, then hunts down the villain (George Macready) who sold them rifles and has taken Jane (Virginia Huston) hostage. Directed by Byron Haskin, the movie drags between action sequences, though Barker's Tarzan is a rather personable fellow. Stylized violence

title: Tarzan's Revenge
synopsis: Routine jungle adventure with Tarzan (Glenn Morris) rescuing a woman (Eleanor Holm) on safari with her parents (George Barbier and Hedda Hopper) from an Arab prince (C. Henry Gordon) who has paid the safari guide (Joe Sawyer) to kidnap her. Directed by D. Ross Lederman, the situations are more humorous than dangerous, though there's a tense battle on a rope bridge across a chasm and by movie's end Tarzan has found a mate. Some stylized violence

title: Tarzan's Savage Fury
synopsis: Formula jungle adventure directed by Cyril Endfield in which Jane (Dorothy Hart) persuades Tarzan (Lex Barker) to guide a thief (Patric Knowles) posing as his cousin, Lord Greystoke, across the desert to the land of a fierce tribe rich in diamonds. Stylized violence

title: Tarzan's Secret Treasure
synopsis: Routine jungle adventure directed by Richard Thorpe in which Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller) has to save Jane (Maureen O'Sullivan) and Boy (Johnny Sheffield) after they're kidnapped by a ruthless gold hunter (Tom Conway), then captured by a savage tribe. Stylized violence

title: Tarzan's Three Challenges
synopsis: Exotic adventure with Tarzan (Jock Mahoney) leaving Africa for Thailand where he saves the young boy chosen by Buddhist monks to be the country's spiritual leader from being killed by the king's wicked brother (Woody Strode). Directed by Robert Day, the Thai locales are a welcome change to the usual jungle setting, though the action remains much the same. Stylized violence

title: Tarzan the Ape Man
synopsis: Director Joseph M. Newman's flat and unengaging remake of the 1932 original features a lethargic performance by Dennis Miller in the title role and an anemic portrayal of Jane by Johanna Barnes. Stale wildlife adventure

title: Tarzan, the Ape Man
synopsis: Embarrassingly inept version of the jungle hero's adventures with Miles O'Keeffe in the title role, Bo Derek in various stages of undress and the ape in the cast the only character to emerge with any dignity from a debacle directed by John Derek

title: Tarzan the Fearless
synopsis: Feature version of a serial directed by Robert F. Hill in which a woman (Jacqueline Wells) on a safari to find her missing father is saved from Arab slavers by Tarzan (Buster Crabbe) who then rescues her father from a vengeful priest (Mischa Auer) guarding the statue of an Egyptian god whose fingers are embedded with priceless emeralds. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Tarzan the Magnificent
synopsis: Standard action adventure directed by Robert Day in which Tarzan (Gordon Scott) captures a killer (Jock Mahoney) in the jungles of Kenya and, despite ambushes by his murderous father (John Carradine) and three brothers, takes him and some stranded travellers (notably Lionel Jeffries, Betta St. John and Alexandra Stewart) to the nearest police post. Stylized violence, some of it quite nasty

title: Tarzan Triumphs
synopsis: World War II adventure in which Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller) and Boy (Johnny Sheffield) help a woman (Frances Gifford) free her jungle village from Nazi paratroopers after oil and jewels. Directed by William Thiele, Tarzan kills a number of paratroopers without resorting to firearms, though Boy shoots one with a pistol and Cheetah uses a machine gun to get another. Stylized violence, including Nazi brutality

title: Task Force
synopsis: On the eve of his retirement, an admiral (Gary Cooper) recalls his part in the struggle after World War I to prove to the Navy the importance of aircraft carriers, his marriage to a fellow pilot's widow (Jane Wyatt) and his role in the battles of Midway and Okinawa. Written and directed by Delmer Daves, the personal story is most interesting in the early years of carrier development, then gets lost in the World War II battle scenes. Wartime violence and patriotic sloganeering

title: Taste the Black Earth
synopsis: Polish dramatization of the 1920 uprising against the Germans occupying the coal mining region of Silesia is shown through the eyes of a young lad who refuses to let his six older brothers go to battle without him. Written and directed by Kazimierz Kutz, the movie is less an historical narrative than a patriotic ballad told with great feeling, much visual poetry and emphasis on the absurdities of civilians pitted against soldiers

title: Taste the Blood of Dracula
synopsis: Disappointing British horror movie wastes its first half on a ridiculous club dabbling in sex and satanism while the remainder is routine-to-inferior vampire lore in which Dracula (Christopher Lee) has only one big scene. Directed by Peter Sasdy, it offers only some slack suspense and almost no psychological terror

title: Tatie Danielle
synopsis: Wickedly dark comedy about a sly 82-year-old widow (Tsilla Chelton) who moves in with her nephew's family and proceeds to make their lives miserable while appearing to be frail and helpless. French production directed by Etienne Chatiliez deftly blends wit and satire while questioning preconceptions about the elderly and skewering adults who patronize them. Subtitles. Occasional sexual innuendo, brief bedroom shot of a married couple and a few vulgar expressions

title: Tattered Dress, The
synopsis: Melodramatic clunker directed by Jack Arnold in which a top New York lawyer (Jeff Chandler) is charged by a vengeful Nevada cop (Jack Carson) with bribing a juror (Gail Russell) in a local murder case, with the outcome reuniting lawyer and estranged wife (Jeanne Crain). Some stylized violence and heavy sexual innuendo

title: Tattoo
synopsis: Bruce Dern plays a man obsessed with the mystique of tattooing who kidnaps model Maud Adams and proceeds to decorate her body with the fervor of a graffiti artist embroidering his own subway car, until the contrived plot suddenly turns perverted hero into expert lover. Directed by Bob Brooks, the dreary, pretentious story lacks any credible sense of logic. Some nudity and graphic sexuality

title: Tattooed Swordswoman, The
synopsis: Japanese Yakuza (gangster) movie about an imprisoned woman's dream which after her release comes back to haunt her. Director Teyuo Ishii's effort has more of interest than the usual spectacular swordplay because it vividly incorporates elements of supernatural horror within its traditional revenge plot

title: Taxi!
synopsis: Blue-collar tale of a hot-tempered New York cabbie (James Cagney) who marries the daughter (Loretta Young) of a cabdriver killed by a rival taxi company, then goes after the goon who did it, with unconvincing results. Director Roy Del Ruth projects the taxicab war with suitable gusto, but overdoes the cabbie's cocky violence, including knocking out the winner (George Raft) of a dance competition and belting his wife on occasion. Nasty stylized violence, muted sexual innuendo and tacked on moral ending

title: Taxi
synopsis: High-octane, low-wattage buddy comedy about a bumbling New York City cop (Jimmy Fallon) who enlists the aid of a speed-demon cab driver (Queen Latifah) to help him catch a gang of beautiful but deadly female bank robbers (led by Gisele Bundchen). Directed by Tim Story, this revved-up remake of a 1998 French film has a full tank of high-speed car chases, but is running on fumes when it comes to laughs. Recurring vehicular violence, two robberies, a sexually suggestive frisk sequence, crude language and an instance of profanity

title: Taxi Blues
synopsis: Set in present-day Moscow, an embittered cabdriver (Pyotr Zaichenko) reluctantly befriends a self-destructive Jewish saxophone player (Pyotr Mamonov) whose alcoholism causes continual crises. Writer-director Pavel Longuine's character study of two vastly divergent personalities touches on class conflicts, alienation and anti-Semitism in Russia's troubled society with compassion, rude humor and unaccustomed frankness. Subtitles. Brief scene of fairly graphic sexual relations, partial nudity, minimal violence and vulgar expressions

title: Taxi Driver
synopsis: Disturbing portrait of a troubled New York cabby (Robert De Niro), apparently traumatized by service in Vietnam, lost in his macho fantasies and infatuated with a political worker (Cybill Shepherd) whose rejection triggers his suppressed rage into an orgy of killings. Director Martin Scorsese's excursion into urban alienation and irrational violence lacks a distancing objectivity and its attempts to shock are excessively graphic in scenes of bloodshed

title: Taxing Woman, A
synopsis: A woman tax collector (Nobuko Miyamoto) faces her biggest case in trying to crack the sleazy operation of an adult hotel scion (Tsutomu Yamazaki) which leads to various comical interactions. Director Juzo Itami delivers a sometimes amusing but overlong satire on tax evasion which in Japan apparently is fast becoming a national pastime. Subtitles. Several graphic sexual encounters with nudity, a brief sequence involving the physical battering of a woman and some rough language

title: Taxing Woman's Return, A
synopsis: Sequel picks up the career of the feisty Japanese tax inspector (Nobuko Miyamoto) as she investigates a bogus fundamentalist religious sect helmed by a charismatic influence peddler (Rentaro Mikuni). Written and directed by Juzo Itami, the sharp satire of Japanese tax crimes shows the conflicting roles of women in modern Japan and underscores how exploitative bogus "religions" can be. Some rough language, grisly violence and adultery

title: Taza, Son of Cochise
synopsis: Formula Western directed by Douglas Sirk has the title character (Rock Hudson) struggling to fulfill the peace treaty signed by his dead Apache father (uncredited Jeff Chandler) while his younger brother (Bart Roberts) conspires to join a warring band of Apaches led by Geronimo. Frontier violence and Indian stereotypes

title: Tea and Sympathy
synopsis: Dated coming-of-age melodrama in which an effeminate college freshman (John Kerr) suffers all kinds of humiliations from manly fellow students until his housemaster's wife (Deborah Kerr) decides to act as a surrogate love partner. Directed by Vincente Minnelli from Robert Anderson's adaptation of his own play, the stagy proceedings are overlong and dramatically unconvincing. Sexual situations

title: Teachers
synopsis: Nick Nolte stars as a harassed but effective and idealistic teacher in a zoo-like high school. Directed by Arthur Hiller, the crude, disjointed effort seems just another teenage exploitation movie. Rough language, nudity and a sympathetic view of abortion

title: Teacher's Pet
synopsis: Wacky and witty animated musical about a dog (voiced by Nathan Lane) whose quest to become a real boy leads him and his master (voiced by Shaun Fleming) to the lab of a mad scientist (voiced by Kelsey Grammer) who claims he can transform animals into humans, yielding unintended and comic results. It is based on the popular TV series; director Timothy Bjorklund's canine take on the Pinocchio story offers something for everyone, peppering it throughout with zany sight gags, whip-smart zingers, classic film references and even an educational musical number, all while smuggling under the cover of laughter a message about friendship and the dangers of science overstepping its boundaries. Brief, mildly crude humor

title: Teacher's Pet
synopsis: Agreeable comedy in which a tough New York newspaper editor (Clark Gable) enrolls in a night school journalism class after falling for its instructor (Doris Day), then faces her contempt when she discovers his deception. Directed by George Seaton, the two leads brighten the plot's mulling over the relative merits of experience and education in the newspaper profession, with Gig Young adding some amusing support as a genial psychology professor. Romantic complications, mild sexual innuendo and a lengthy segment involving inebriation and its painful aftermath

title: Teaching Mrs. Tingle
synopsis: Corrosive black comedy in which three high school seniors tie their nasty history teacher (Helen Mirren) to her bedposts, taking scandalous bedroom photos of her with the school's drunken married coach in order to prevent their being expelled for cheating. As written and directed by Kevin Williamson, the smug, emotionally manipulative tale of self-absorbed adolescents conniving to control a cruel adult is morally bankrupt in lionizing the teens' outrageously anti-social behavior. Implied justification of criminal acts, an off-screen sexual encounter, some violence, underage drinking and an instance of rough language

title: Tea for Two
synopsis: Slack, unimaginative backstage musical loosely based on "No, No, Nanette" and directed by David Butler is set in the 1920s with a frantic producer (Billy De Wolfe) after a socialite (Doris Day) to back his new show of which she becomes the star singing duets with its songwriter (Gordon MacRae). Mild sexual innuendo

title: Team America: World Police
synopsis: Intentionally outrageous adventure-comedy, with songs, by the "South Park" creators, featuring surprisingly lifelike marionettes (strings and all), about a governmental police team out to thwart global terrorists in Paris, the Mideast and Korea. A Broadway actor is drafted to help the squad take on the nefarious Korean dictator, Kim Jong II, who with the help of Chechen and Middle Eastern terrorists is planning to unleash weapons of mass destruction upon the world. Dexterous puppetry and eye-catching production design -- and yes, some humorous moments -- in Trey Parker's follow-up to "South Park: Bigger, Longer & Uncut," but puppets and humorous intent or not, the sexual content, overall vulgarity and frequent violence go way over the top. Sexual activity both straight and gay, extreme violence, including dismemberment and blood, ethnic stereotypes, crude and profane language, albeit all done by puppets

title: Team America: World Police
synopsis: Intentionally outrageous adventure-comedy, with songs, by the "South Park" creators, featuring surprisingly lifelike marionettes (strings and all), about a governmental police team out to thwart global terrorists in Paris, the Mideast and Korea. A Broadway actor is drafted to help the squad take on the nefarious Korean dictator, Kim Jong II, who with the help of Chechen and Middle Eastern terrorists is planning to unleash weapons of mass destruction upon the world. Dexterous puppetry and eye-catching production design -- and yes, some humorous moments -- in Trey Parker's follow-up to "South Park: Bigger, Longer & Uncut," but puppets and humorous intent or not, the sexual content, overall vulgarity and frequent violence go way over the top. Sexual activity both straight and gay, extreme violence, including dismemberment and blood, ethnic stereotypes, crude and profane language, albeit all done by puppets

title: Tear in the Ocean, A
synopsis: The remnant of the Nazi onslaught of a peaceful Hassidic community in Poland joins the local resistance group operating from the country estate of an idealistic nobleman (Armand Abplanalp) but the ultimate result is tragedy, as the Poles themselves turn on their Jewish allies during the count's absence. Written, produced and directed by Henri Glaeser, the complex movie views the Holocaust from a variety of perspectives, challenging viewers with its questions rather than comforting them with facile answers

title: Tears of the Sun
synopsis: Simplistic war movie-morality play lionizes superheroic Navy SEALs led by Bruce Willis as they rescue refugees and battle evil ethnic-cleansing rebel forces amid a Nigerian civil war. Director Antoine Fuqua's tribute to U.S. military men celebrates fortitude and compassion, but its generic, unconvincing moral dilemmas and dimensionless characters fail as drama. Recurring battlefield violence and restrained depictions of ethnic cleansing, a brief depiction of rape with fleeting nudity, much rough language and intermittent profanity

title: Tea with Mussolini
synopsis: Warmly nostalgic tale in which some matronly English art-lovers (notably Maggie Smith, Joan Plowright and Judi Dench) residing in 1930's Florence come to care for an abandoned boy who returns as a teen-ager to help when they are interned as enemy aliens during World War II. Directed by Franco Zeffirelli, the semi-autobiographical picture shows how the Italian youth comes to appreciate English culture but what succeeds best is its gently humorous depiction of the women's eccentric circle which includes two brassy Americans (Cher and Lily Tomlin) and how they manage to survive the tragic circumstances of wartime Italy. Some threatening situations, sexual references and a few instances of coarse language

title: Ted & Venus
synopsis: Sour comedy about a would-be poet (Bud Cort) whose obsessive pursual of a wary social worker (Kim Adams) ends in death when his infatuation proves unstoppable. Fledgling director Cort stars in a pathetic vehicle whose sick humor seems pointless except to put casual sex in an appealing light. Positive portrayal of promiscuity with some gratuitous nudity, violence and rough language

title: Teenage Caveman
synopsis: Low-budget adventure directed by Roger Corman in which the title Neanderthal character (Robert Vaughn) rebels against the law of his clan and ventures into the land beyond the river, with a sci-fi ending. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Teenage Devil Dolls
synopsis: Low-budget clunker directed by B. Lawrence Price, Jr., follows the growing drug addiction of an unhappy teen (Barbara Marks) who graduates from smoking reefers with a motorcycle gang to getting hooked on heroin until nabbed by a narcotics officer (Robert A. Sherry) whose voice-over narration covers the picture's lack of spoken dialogue, with ludicrous results. Stylized violence and unconvincing portrayals of drug abuse

title: Teenage Frankenstein
synopsis: ( see: "I Was a Teenage Frankenstein" )

title: Teenage Mother
synopsis: Sleazy movie about the social and sexual rivalries of a class of inane high school students and how they are corrupted by a health instructor. Directed by Jerry Gross, the movie's scenes of rape and seduction are restrained but not some documentary footage showing the ghastly details of a forceps delivery of a baby

title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles
synopsis: Live-action feature movie debut of the half-human, half-turtle cartoon heroes who do battle with a rogue Japanese ninja society to win back their kidnapped rat mentor, Splinter. Though music videomaker Steve Barron's direction is amateurish, Jim Henson's turtle costumes expand the frolicking foursome to entertaining life-sized creatures. Much comic-book violence involving bashing and smashing human and turtle bodies and some mild rough language

title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles III
synopsis: Lifeless sequel has the four teen turtles hurtled back in time to feudal Japan to rescue a friend (Paige Turco) and save a wartorn village. Writer-director Stuart Gillard relies on the turtle's established popularity instead of developing something more than a sophomoric story without liveliness, wit and whimsy. Some ethnic stereotyping and several cartoon-like fight scenes

title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles II: The Secret of the Ooze
synopsis: This time rat mentor Splinter and the fiesty foursome are out to recapture the last vial of a dangerously toxic ooze from the clutches of the evil Shredder (Francois Chau) and his ninja thugs. Director Michael Pressman uses non-stop kung fu battles to disguise the amateur hour plot, and Jim Henson's workshop furnishes two new monsters to keep the eyes entertained up to a point. Considerable slapstick martial arts violence

title: Teenage Sex Report
synopsis: German exploitation movie about the sexual fears of teenage girls narrated by a "doctor" and directed by Ernst Hofbauer. Ugh

title: Teen Witch
synopsis: Sappy little story about a teen (Robyn Lively) who learns that she is a witch, uses her magic powers to become the most popular girl in school but discovers that what she really wants is to be liked for herself. Directed by Dorian Walker, there is nothing magical about the inane plot or its trite treatment. A sexually suggestive scene and a number of sexual references

title: Teen Wolf
synopsis: High school lad (Michael J. Fox) becomes a big man on campus when he discovers that he is a werewolf in this moderately funny teenage comedy. Directed by Rod Daniel, the movie is marred by jokes about alcohol and drugs as well as some vulgarity and sexually oriented humor

title: Teen Wolf Too
synopsis: Mild sequel in which the younger brother (Jason Bateman) of the high school student who in the original "Teen Wolf" became a basketball star when he turned into a werewolf goes to college and becomes a boxing champ when he discovers his brother's condition runs in the family. Directed by Christopher Leitch, it is more tiresome than silly, except for the violence of its boxing scenes and a benign attitude towards casual sex

title: Telefon
synopsis: Russian agent (Charles Bronson) is sent to the U.S. to eliminate a fanatical maverick comrade (Donald Pleasence) who is bent upon activating a long-discarded sabotage scheme. Mediocre thriller made more bearable by a lavish production, Don Siegel's smooth direction and Lee Remick's personable performance as an American double agent. Some graphic violence

title: Telegraph Trail, The
synopsis: Low-budget Western directed by Tenny Wright in which an Army scout (John Wayne), a jovial private (Frank McHugh) and an enterprising young woman (Marceline Day) save a telegraph construction crew from Indian raids instigated by a white renegade (Albert J. Smith). Frontier violence with Indian stereotyping

title: Telephone Book, The
synopsis: Squeaky-voiced Alice (Sarah Kennedy) falls in love with surly-voiced John Smith (Norman Rose) during his first obscene phone call to her. The parade of perverts and exhibitionists that follows in writer-director Nelson Lyon's sour enterprise is sheer sexual exploitation

title: Tell Me a Riddle
synopsis: Melvyn Douglas and Lila Kedrova play an elderly Jewish immigrant couple, at odds for decades, who are reconciled while visiting their granddaughter (Brooke Adams). Although the fine acting is at times quite moving, Lee Grant's direction of a script awkwardly updating the 1961 story by Tillie Olsen is often clumsy. Somber theme and an implied acceptance of abortion

title: Tell Me Something
synopsis: ���� Gruesomely violent thriller set in Seoul about a police detective (Han Suk-gyu) investigating the mysterious appearance of black garbage bags filled with the various chopped remains of three men, all of whom were former boyfriends of a beautiful and enigmatic young woman (Shim Eun-Ha). Director Chang Youn-Hyun's well-crafted yet disturbing tale of obsession is overwhelmed by brutal, blood-drenched images and a sordid subplot. Subtitles. Excessive gory violence including dismembered body parts, implied incest, full frontal nudity and brief rough language

title: Tell Me That You Love Me, Junie Moon
synopsis: Screen version of Marjorie Kellogg's novel about a disfigured woman (Liza Minnelli), an epileptic (Ken Howard) and a paralyzed homosexual (Robert Moore) who band together to live on their own. Director Otto Preminger's treatment dredges up a dozen sicknesses and perversions with consistent shallowness and lack of understanding, winding up with a limp moral of love conquers all

title: Tell No One ("Ne Le Dis a Personne")
synopsis: Absorbing mystery thriller about a pediatrician (Francois Cluzet) under renewed suspicion for the death of his wife (Marie-Josee Croze) eight years earlier, now on the run both from the police and some brutish thugs, while he tries to clear his name. Director Guillaume Canet has skillfully adapted American Harlan Coben's novel, with superlative performances from a cast that includes Andre Dussollier, Kristin Scott Thomas, Nathalie Baye and Jean Rochefort, though some episodes of violence and thematic material may not be to all tastes. In French, with subtitles. Brief but brutal violence, some grisly images, murder, suicide, torture, fleeting distant and shadowy nudity, a brief nongraphic sexual encounter, a lesbian relationship, drug use and rough language

title: Tell Them Willie Boy Is Here
synopsis: Reservation Indian (Robert Blake) at the turn of the century is caught between tribal tradition and the white man's law when he kills the father of his sweetheart (Katharine Ross). The clash of two cultures, the injustice of the dominant one and the human fallibility on both sides are themes left largely unexplored in director Abraham Polonsky's drama which spends more time on the abrasive relationship between the fair-minded sheriff (Robert Redford) and the frustrated reservation doctor (Susan Clark). The result is no more than an average Western chase movie with an unhappy ending

title: Tell Your Children
synopsis: ( see: "Reefer Madness" )

title: Tempest
synopsis: Famous architect (John Cassevetes), beset with faddish mid-life crisis, flees wife (Gena Rowlands) and job to an idyllic Greek isle with his daughter (Molly Ringwald) and mistress (Susan Sarandon). Director Paul Mazursky's updating of Shakespeare's autumnal comedy is sometimes charming, certainly never dull, but fails to overcome the handicap of its boorish, unappealing hero. Some frank references to sexual matters, including adultery, and rough language

title: Temptation
synopsis: Sluggish melodrama about an unfaithful wife (Merle Oberon) whose lover (Charles Korvin) persuades her to poison her rich husband (George Brent), but she has a change of heart and poisons the lover instead. Directed by Irving Pichel, the dour story gains some interest from its setting in 1900 Egypt where archeologist Brent is excavating a pharaoh's tomb but it's not enough to save the picture. Stylized violence, menace and implied sexual relationships

title: Tempter, The
synopsis: Italian version of "The Exorcist" whose theme of demonic possession is crudely handled by director Alberto de Martino with improbable appearances by Mel Ferrer and Arthur Kennedy, nauseating special effects and heavy doses of brutal violence and dumb sex

title: Temp, The
synopsis: All-too-obvious thriller concerns a devious secretarial fill-in (Lara Flynn Boyle) whose ambitions to advance her cookie company boss (Timothy Hutton) and then herself include killing her way to the top. Director Tom Holland lets Hutton stumble around while the murderous leading lady and co-star Faye Dunaway chew the scenery in this unappetizing, cookie-cutter formula entertainment. Some stylized violence, sexual innuendo and rough language

title: The Temptress
synopsis: Cast includes Greta Garbo, Antonio Moreno and Marc McDermott. Directed by Fred Niblo. A-III (nr) 1926

title: Temptress Moon
synopsis: Opulent melodrama set in 1920's Shanghai where a thieving gigolo (Leslie Cheung) returns to the decaying estate of his childhood and becomes romantically involved with his opium addicted cousin (Gong Li) despite the protestations of her lovestruck servant (Kevin Lin). While director Chen Kaige's dreamy tale of deceit and intrigue is lovely to look at, its narrative is confusing and emotionally chilly. Subtitles. Fleeting violence, restrained bedroom scenes, drug abuse and an instance of rough language

title: Tenacious D in the Pick of Destiny
synopsis: Big screen expansion of the HBO sketch comedy shorts starring Jack Black and Kyle Gass (playing themselves) fictitiously chronicling the founding of their real-life band "Tenacious D" in which the misfit musicians embark on a quest to become the greatest rock band on earth by swiping a mythical guitar pick -- of satanic origin -- from a heavily guarded museum and ultimately challenging the devil to a "rock off." Directed by Liam Lynch, this sophomoric semi-rock opera's "message" about friendship and following one's dreams is overpowered by a cacophony of vulgarity, irreverence and raunchy lyrics. Pervasive rough and sexually crude language and humor, including an opening scene in which a 10-year-old boy taunts his Christian parents by interrupting dinnertime grace with an obscene ballad, lewd sight gags, recurring drug usage and brief rear nudity

title: Tenant, The
synopsis: Mediocre French thriller in which a meek clerk (Roman Polanski who also directed) rents a room in a rather sinister Paris apartment house, learns that the former occupant threw herself out of the window and, with increasing paranoia, comes to believe his own life is in danger. Some chilling and effective moments lead only to a disappointing anti-climax. Its theme of madness, depicted with some slashing knives and bouncing heads, are adult fare

title: Tenchu!
synopsis: During the civil wars of the 186O's assassin bands of samurai roamed Japan eliminating political opponents and their followers. This film by Hideo Gosha traces the exploits of one such group and the trouble its leader (Tatsuya Nikadai) has in manipulating his most devoted cutthroat (Shintaro Katsu). The result is a lush production that is little more than a routine exercise in the futility of violence

title: Ten Commandments, The
synopsis: Less an inspirational story based on biblical sources than a dramatic vehicle with a sense of history, director Cecil B. DeMille's epic production offers some spectacular re-creations, excellent technical effects and good acting from a fine cast, including Charlton Heston as Moses, Yul Brynner, Anne Baxter, Edward G. Robinson and many other stars of the era

title: Ten Days' Wonder
synopsis: Complex French suspense drama based on an Ellery Queen mystery about a man (Anthony Perkins) who suspects that he has committed murder during a recent mental blackout. Director Claude Chabrol is less interested in the fairly simple mystery than in exploring the relationship between the strange characters (including Orson Welles and Marlene Jobert) living on the man's country estate, the decadent atmosphere that pervades his household and the sense of impending disaster that mounts throughout the film (and it is a shocker). Mature theme

title: Tender Comrade
synopsis: Dated World War II sudser about four warplant workers (Ginger Rogers, Ruth Hussey, Kim Hunter and Patricia Collinge) who share expenses in renting a house while their men are in service. Director Edward Dmytryk's attempt to dramatize the homefront centers on Rogers and her thoughts of soldier hubby Robert Ryan, but the result is clogged with patriotic rhetoric that rings hollow to post-war ears. Chiefly of interest for its idealized version of the domestic problems of the period

title: Tender Mercies
synopsis: Down-on-his-luck country-western singer (Robert Duvall), whose drinking broke up his first marriage, meets and weds a young widow (Tess Harper) who runs a ramshackle motel with her young son (Allan Hubbard). Director Bruce Beresford gets feeling performances from his cast, most especially Duvall in one of his best roles, and treats in a refreshingly uncynical, matter-of-fact manner the widow's strong religious convictions and her quiet pride when she sees her son and husband baptized. A rare movie, tough and gentle, inspiring and immensely entertaining, but the serious nature of the story is more appropriate for adults and older adolescents

title: Tender Moment, The
synopsis: Failed French romantic melodrama about a teenager (Renaud Verley) and an older woman (Nathalie Delon) who fall in love, have an affair and separate when the man the woman had been living with returns. Director Michel Boisrond's story is not one of lost innocence (the boy has been sleeping with a housemaid, even "lending" her to classmates) and his older paramour is presented as something of a nymphomaniac so that the result celebrates nothing but the sexual imperative

title: Tender Trap, The
synopsis: Soppy romantic comedy about a New York theatrical agent (Frank Sinatra) who enjoys being a bachelor playing the field until he falls for a singer (Debbie Reynolds) who won't settle for anything but marriage. Director Charles Walters tries to keep it bright and breezy but what works best is the bittersweet romance between one of the agent's girlfriends (Celeste Holm) and a married pal (David Wayne). The playboy philosophy flunks out

title: Tender Warrior, The
synopsis: Filmed in Georgia, this portrait of a modern Huck Finn provides fine matinee fare for the small fry. The boy (Charles Lee) keeps tabs on all the wild animals of his domain, who respond when he calls them by name. Directed by Stewart Raffill, the photography beautifully captures the swamplands teeming with wildlife as background for this simple story

title: Ten from Your Show of Shows
synopsis: Top comedy in some choice cuts from the classic Sid Caesar television show of the early 1950s, when Sid, Imogene Coca, Carl Reiner and Howie Morris had as much fun doing their wacky bits as viewers have ever since. For those looking for lots of laughs dished up with a heaping spoonful of plain old nostalgia, this is unsurpassed entertainment

title: Ten Little Indians
synopsis: Director George Pollack's routine remake of the classic Agatha Christie movie mystery, :2OAnd Then There Were None'' (1945), has a good cast (Hugh O'Brian, Wilfrid Hyde-White, Stanley Holloway, Leo Genn and Dennis Price) and a still intriguing plot. Stylized violence

title: Ten Little Indians
synopsis: Stylish version of the Agatha Christie mystery in which ten strangers (including Oliver Reed, Stephane Audran, Elke Sommer and Richard Attenborough) confess to past crimes before falling victim to swift punishment. Director Peter Collinson moves the action from a remote island to a byzantine hotel in the middle of a desert and introduces a variant ending written by Dudley Nichols. Restrained violence

title: Tennessee's Partner
synopsis: Formula Western directed by Allan Dwan uneasily links a cowpoke (Ronald Reagan), a gambler (John Payne) and the proprietor of a fancy house (Rhonda Fleming) in a dusty gold-mining town. Stylized violence, romantic complications and sexual innuendo

title: Ten North Frederick
synopsis: Heavy-handed sudser from the John O'Hara novel in which a wealthy lawyer (Gary Cooper) is prodded into politics by an ambitious wife (Geraldine Fitzgerald) who confesses her unfaithfulness after he fails to gain the party's nomination, then romances his daughter's roommate (Suzy Parker) until realizing he's too old to marry her and turns to the bottle for solace. Scripted and directed by Philip Dunne, the soapy proceedings are paced by banal developments and the one-dimensional characters elicit little sympathy. Brief violence, an unwed pregnancy and marital infidelity

title: Tension
synopsis: Clumsy crime thriller directed by John Berry in which a meek pharmacist (Richard Basehart) plots to kill the lover of his two-timing wife (Audrey Totter), then is accused of the murder when someone else beats him to it. Sexual situations and considerable menace

title: Tension at Table Rock
synopsis: Forgettable Western about a good badman (Richard Egan) who helps a gun-shy sheriff (Cameron Mitchell) clean up a crooked town. Directed by Charles Marquis Warren, the cliched plot is not worth the effort the actors put into it. Stylized violence

title: Tentacles
synopsis: Poor Italian imitation of the marine menace formula substitutes a giant octopus for rogue shark. John Huston, Shelley Winters and Henry Fonda are out-acted by several killer whales in a story that is more tedious than threatening. Director Oliver Hellman's special effects are unconvincing, except for the grisly visuals of a bloody victim. Some needless profanity

title: Ten Tall Men
synopsis: Burt Lancaster leads a motley group of French Foreign Legionnaires against the Riffs before they can unite to attack an undermanned garrison town. Directed by Willis Goldbeck, the only thing tall here is the tale which shifts back and forth between straight adventure and spoof. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Ten Wanted Men
synopsis: Western potboiler in which a prosperous Arizona rancher (Randolph Scott) tries to avoid bloodshed when confronted by a rival rancher (Richard Boone) and his gang of hired gunslingers, but in the end has to rely on his six-shooter and some dynamite. Directed by Bruce Humberstone, the final shootouts are even less credible than the rest of the contrived proceedings. Nasty stylized violence, including cold-blooded murders, and some heavy-handed sexual innuendo

title: Teorema
synopsis: Paradoxical Italian drama about the isolated world of a comfortable middle-class family which is transformed by sexual intimacy with a mysterious visitor (Terence Stamp). Director Pier Paolo Pasolini's theme is the corruption of material values but he approaches it in such coldly intellectual style that one is uninvolved in the events. Though the use of sex is symbolic and not graphically depicted, some viewers will reject its appropriateness as a plot premise

title: Tequila Sunrise
synopsis: Slickly produced detective yarn about a Los Angeles cop (Kurt Russell) who uses a restaurant owner (Michelle Pfeiffer) as a pawn to trap an old friend (Mel Gibson) who's attempting to quit the drug smuggling racket and his notorious Latin American dealer (Raul Julia). Writer-director Robert Towne entangles his attractive cast in a confusing plot that reaches incoherence by the time of the movie's improbable ending. Some rough language, a discreetly filmed sex scene and an intense climax

title: Teresa the Thief
synopsis: Italian drama about a woman's tragic life (Monica Vitti) after being abandoned to the streets by an abusive father at age 11, made pregnant by a man who marries her just to escape military service and finally left to a life of prisons and mental institutions. Director Carlo Di Palma only partially achieves the intended blend of pathos and comedy, and the movie's graphic, slice-of-life naturalism is mature fare

title: Terminal Man, The
synopsis: George Segal plays a scientist given to violent seizures who has his brain hooked to a computer to control them but short circuits turn him into a menace for what appears to be most of Southern California. Director Mike Hodges' version of Michael Crichton's novel takes a ridiculous concept to extremes. Much hokey violence

title: Terminal Velocity
synopsis: Routine action movie in which a skydiving instructor (Charlie Sheen) gets entangled with a beautiful, manipulative former KGB agent (Nastassja Kinski) in Arizona tracking a shipment of gold bullion while Russian criminals pursue her with lethal intent. Director Deran Sarafian's empty escapist fare features a nonsensical narrative embroidered with a gimmicky series of death-defying skydiving rescues. Intermittent nasty violence and an instance of rough language

title: Terminator 2: Judgment Day
synopsis: With the fate of the planet depending on the survival of a plucky lad (Edward Furlong), his ferociously strong mother (Linda Hamilton) escapes a psycho ward to protect him while two rival cyborg terminators (Arnold Schwarzenegger and Robert Patrick) arrive from the future to tip the scales. Producer-director James Cameron's flashy sequel to his 1984 sci-fi fantasy has some stunning special effects but the threadbare storyline merely showcases overblown scenes of callous butchery. Excessive violence and some rough language

title: Terminator 3: Rise of the Machines
synopsis: Lavishly violent sci-fi actioner has Arnold Schwarzenegger returning as the cyborg stud from the future sent to protect soon-to-be-savior-of-mankind John Connor (Nick Stahl) from yet another terminator upgrade (Kristanna Loken). Despite a steroid-sized special effects budget, director Jonathan Mostov's film flexes little muscle beyond its smash-and-crash sequences, resulting in an adrenalin-heavy, plot-light reboot of the two earlier films. Excessive, graphic sci-fi violence, some rough language and profanity, as well as fleeting rear nudity

title: Terminator Salvation
synopsis: Explosively violent sci-fi action sequel in which the prophesied victor (Christian Bale) in humanity's post-apocalyptic struggle against a race of murderous supermachines must locate the teen (Anton Yelchin) who will someday travel back in time to become his father while determining whether a bewildered visitor from the past (Sam Worthington) is friend or foe. A few undeveloped philosophical observations are drowned out, in director McG's time-twisting, special-effects extravaganza, by the roar of unremitting battle. Intense and pervasive combat, some gore, and half a dozen crude or crass terms

title: Terminator, The
synopsis: Violent sci-fi movie in which a killing machine in the shape of a man (Arnold Schwarzenegger) comes back from the future to assassinate a young waitress destined otherwise to bear a son who will lead the humans to victory over android rule of a post-nuclear world. James Cameron directs the action in taut, suspenseful fashion but its violence is overdone and a bedroom scene goes much further than necessary

title: Term of Trial
synopsis: Middle-aged schoolmaster (Laurence Olivier), happily married (to Simone Signoret), finds himself pursued by a schoolgirl (Sarah Miles) who works out a nasty trap for him, oblivious to its tragic consequences. Solid adult drama directed by Peter Glenville, with fine performances from all three principals

title: Terms of Endearment
synopsis: Uneven comedy about a mother-daughter relationship, that of a wealthy, imperious Houston widow (Shirley MacLaine) and her only child (Debra Winger) who marries a man her mother detests. The mother herself becomes involved with the wrong sort of man, in the person of a lecherous, dissipated former astronaut (Jack Nicholson), a confrontation of opposites that is sometimes very funny. Though consistently amusing, there is something uncomfortable about the way in which director James L. Brooks invites laughter at his characters for three-quarters of the way and then demands empathy for them in the tearjerker conclusion. Some fairly graphic references to sexual activity and a benign attitude toward sex outside of marriage

title: Terror by Night
synopsis: Intriguing mystery aboard an express train to Scotland with Sherlock Holmes (Basil Rathbone) and Dr. Watson (Nigel Bruce) solving a locked-compartment murder and the theft of a precious jewel, the Star of Rhodesia. Directed by Roy William O'Neill, the combination of mild humor, elementary deductions, eccentric red herrings and modest thrills make it one of the better examples of this 1942-46 series. Some menace and stylized violence

title: Terror from the Year 5000
synopsis: Sci-fi dud directed by Robert J. Gurney, Jr., in which a scientific experiment succeeds in breaking the time barrier by bringing back a deformed mutant (Salome Jens) from the radioactive world of Earth 3,000 years in the future. Stylized violence and some sexual innuendo

title: Terror House
synopsis: ( see: "The Night Has Eyes" )

title: Terror in the Aisles
synopsis: Director Andrew J. Kuehn's haphazard compilation of excerpts from horror movies concentrates on the period from "Psycho" (1960) to approximately fifty years of films, from "The Bridge of Frankenstein" black and whites to modern day terrors but the result is little more than a frivolous jumble of fright scenes joined by writer Margery Doppelt's inane commentary. Gory violence, sexual situations, fleeting nudity and occasional rough language

title: Terror in the Wax Museum
synopsis: Dotty John Carradine's wax dummies appear to come to life and re-enact their grisly crimes in turn-of-the-century London. Director Georg Fenady's plot is as creaky as the museum's backstairs, and the suspense is as phony as the dummies, but for undemanding horror fans it provides some lightweight diversion

title: Terrorists, The
synopsis: A group of political terrorists seize a British ambassador in Scandinavia and demand the release of their comrades from a British prison, something which the country's head of security (Sean Connery) sets out to thwart. Directed by Caspar Wrede, the suspense and excitement are well maintained, though in a chilly, abstract manner, that makes the ironic ending arbitrary and disappointing. Some violence and much threatened violence

title: Terror of Mechagodzilla
synopsis: Muddled Japanese monster movie directed by Inoshiro Honda with a revengeful scientist aiding aliens in their plan to conquer Earth through his control of the sea monster Titanosaurus and a mechanical Godzilla, until the real Godzilla gums up the works. Dubbed American version. Stylized violence and a human turned into a troubled cyborg

title: Terror of the Tongs, The
synopsis: Empty thriller set in 1910 Hong Kong where a secret Chinese crime organization (led by Christopher Lee) mistakenly murders the daughter of a British sea captain (Geoffrey Toone) who sets out to destroy the entire gang on his own. Directed by Anthony Bushell, the thinly plotted story relies on hokey mayhem and halting menace to sustain interest but the results are emotionally unsatisfying and dramatically flat. Much stylized violence, menacing situations and sexual innuendo

title: Terror on a Train
synopsis: Canadian demolitions expert (Glenn Ford) works through the night trying to find and defuse a bomb on a British munitions train, while the police evacuate the area and seek the saboteur. Director Ted Tetzlaff's tight little exercise in suspense is balanced by the stiff-upper-lip demeanor of British officials and civilians. Much tension

title: Terror Strikes, The
synopsis: ( see: "War of the Colossal Beast" )

title: Terror, The
synopsis: Thin chiller directed by Roger Corman mixes a lot of moody photography with a halting narrative about a French officer (Jack Nickolson) separated from his unit during the Napoleonic Wars who is lured into a spooky castle on the Baltic Sea by the apparently dead wife of its resident count (Boris Karloff). Supernatural hokum

title: Terry Whitmore, for Example
synopsis: Vietnam deserter Whitmore, a 21-year-old black Marine corporal from Memphis who was wounded and awarded the Bronze Star, explains his reasons for deserting the Corps in an oral history documentary filmed in Sweden by Bill Brodie. Viewers will have to determine how typical were his experiences and motivation but his account does not seem to have any political axe to grind. Explicit description of a sexual encounter

title: Tess
synopsis: British screen version of the Thomas Hardy novel about the young Wessex woman (Nastassia Kinski) whose life is irrevocably changed when her father discovers that the family are the impoverished descendants of a noble line. Directed by Roman Polanski, it is an always beautiful, at times powerful, drama whose somber theme of a woman doomed by class and circumstance is not for younger viewers

title: Tess of the Storm Country
synopsis: Artificial melodrama clumsily unfolds as a Scottish lass (Diane Baker) moves to an American farm, sides with those protesting a local chemical plant, then falls for an upright Mennonite neighbor. Director Paul Guilfoyle squanders the beautiful rural setting in stilted scenes with cardboard characters of little emotional interest. Superficial depiction of a religious sect and discreet treatment of an unwed pregnancy

title: Testament
synopsis: A family in a small American community attempts to cope with the aftermath of a nuclear war in this grim but extraordinary movie about a mother (Jane Alexander) who tries to make life go on for her three children after her husband (William Devane) perishes in the nuclear strike. The warmth and compassion she embodies vivifies and makes moving a story that otherwise might be unbearable. Director Lynne Littman spares the audience most of the more horrific results of nuclear disaster, but what it shows and what it implies are unsettling enough. The subject matter and a restrained bedroom scene are more suited for adults and older adolescents

title: Test of Love, A
synopsis: A courageous teacher (Angela Punch McGregor) takes an institution to court to effect the release of a bright child suffering from cerebra1 palsy who has been diagnosed as severely retarded. Fine Australian production directed by Gi1 Brealey offers so1id entertainment and is immensely inspiring

title: Tex
synopsis: Good Disney version of S.E. Hinton's story about two teenage brothers, one earnest and responsible (Jim Metzler), one amiable but somewhat feckless (Matt Dillon), who attempt to cope with life while living by themselves on a rundown ranch outside Tulsa. Though director Tim Hunter's plot is overloaded with incident and occasionally veers into extravagant melodrama, its virtues outweigh its flaws, making it entertaining and sometimes moving. Restrained scene of teenage sexual discovery and some jocular references to sex and drugs

title: Texas
synopsis: Dandy Western about a genial pair of ex-Rebs (William Holden and Glenn Ford) who wind up on opposite sides in a war between ranchers and rustlers, as well as rivals courting the same gal (Claire Trevor). Director George Marshall turns the formula plot into robust entertainment with plenty of frontier action, paced by zesty humor, intriguing plot twists and off-beat characters (local booster George Bancroft and laconic dentist Edgar Buchanan). Vigorous stylized violence and underhanded dealings

title: Texas Across the River
synopsis: Spanish nobleman (Alain Delon) has trouble adjusting to the ways of the Old West, especially those of an outlandish cowboy (Dean Martin) and his peculiar Indian companion (Joey Bishop). Director Michael Gordon makes no pretense of a plot but strings together a series of humorous mishaps spoofing Western conventions. Threadbare but mostly innocuous comedy

title: Texas Carnival
synopsis: Flat romantic comedy about a small-time carnival concessionaire (Red Skelton) being mistaken for an oil millionaire (Keenan Wynn), with predictable results. Directed by Charles Walters, the comic possibilities of the situation wear out quickly and, except for some tacked-on musical numbers, the rest of the cast (Esther Williams, Ann Miller and Howard Keel) has little to do. Mild romantic complications

title: The Texas Chainsaw Massacre
synopsis: Revolting splatterfest about a vanload of teen slackers (including Jessica Biel and Eric Balfour) who find themselves marooned in rural Texas and hunted by a chainsaw-wielding maniac. Director Marcus Nispel's formulaic slasher flick treats mutilation and mayhem as entertainment, assaulting viewers with unabated gratuitous gore fueled by a dehumanizing sadism and objectification of women. Excessive violence including a graphic suicide, an instance of drug abuse, pervasive rough and crude language, as well as profanity

title: Texas Chainsaw Massacre, Part II, The
synopsis: Grotesque parody of the blood-and-gore genre of horror films features a leather-faced maniac twitching riotously in the air each time he approaches a new victim with his chainsaw. Making it even worse is director Tobe Hooper's vain attempt to distance the viewer from the movie's sadistic action through misconceived comic exaggeration. Gory violence, often in a sexua1 context

title: Texas Chainsaw Massacre, The
synopsis: Fiendish butcher out in the Texas bush country carves up four or five (it is difficult to determine the sum from the scattered parts) outdoors adventurers and then goes on a wild rampage of slaughter with chainsaw and other instruments of destruction, including a meat hook. Directed by Tobe Hooper, what is more dehumanizing than all the violence is that the treatment seems to regard it as amusing

title: Texas Chainsaw Massacre: The Next Generation
synopsis: Repulsive horror yarn in which a sadistic quartet of rural psychopaths (led by Matthew McConaughey) torture and murder teens on prom night with only one survivor (Renee Zellweger). Writer-director Kim Henkel's sick sequel to its 1974 and �86 predecessors borders on the depraved with its continual display of jokey graphic mayhem. Excessive violence, a flash of nudity, much profanity and recurring rough language

title: Texas Lady
synopsis: Thin Western directed by Tim Whelan is set in an 1885 Texas town whose newspaper's new owner (Claudette Colbert) gets into serious trouble with the nasty cattle baron (Ray Collins) who owns everything in the vicinity, then gets some help from a Mississippi riverboat gambler (Barry Sullivan). Frontier violence

title: Texas Rangers
synopsis: Terrible western about a bunch of rag-tag soldiers (including James Ven Der Beek and Ashton Kutcher) led by a former preacher (Dylan McDermott) who vow to protect the innocent by rounding up a renegade faction of ruthless outlaws. In between the many hangings, foolish dialogue and muddled machinations of the rambling plot, director Steve Miner feebly squeezes in the message that might does not make right. Much western violence including gunplay and explosions and brief profanity

title: Texas Rangers, The
synopsis: Low-budget oater directed by Phil Karlson with George Montgomery and Noah Berry, Jr., tricking an unlikely collection of legendary badmen -- Sam Bass, John Wesley Hardin, Butch Cassidy, the Sundance Kid and many others --into robbing a gold train with the Rangers waiting in ambush. Hokey plot with formula frontier action

title: Texas Terror
synopsis: Formula Western directed by R.N. Bradbury features John Wayne as a former lawman who helps a murdered rancher's daughter (Lucille Brown) fend off rustlers while his Indian friends aid in capturing her dad's killer. Frontier violence

title: Texas Trail
synopsis: Western programmer in which Hopalong Cassidy (William Boyd) forms a troop of cowboys to join Teddy Roosevelt's Rough Riders in the Spanish-American War, then is ordered to round up a herd of wild horses needed by the Army, though a gang of rustlers (led by Alexander Cross) gets in the way. Frontier violence

title: Texasville
synopsis: When the former high school sweetheart (Cybill Shepherd) of a nearly broke Texas oilman (Jeff Bridges) arrives back in town, she flirts with her old beau but is more successful in winning over the man's unhappy wife (Annie Potts) and unruly children. Director Peter Bogdanovich's sequel to "The Last Picture Show" is less a touching reunion story than a lame putdown of family life and values wrapped up in a rambling soap opera with little structure, less wit and no dramatic tension

title: Texican, The
synopsis: Plodding formula Western in which an outlaw (Audie Murphy) leaves his Mexican refuge to avenge his brother's murder by the vicious boss (Broderick Crawford) of a corrupt border town. Directed by Lesley Selander and filmed in Spain, the dubbed dialogue is as clunky as the phony action. Stylized violence

title: Tex Rides with the Boy Scouts
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Ray Taylor in which a singing cowboy (Tex Ritter) and his pals (Horace Murphy and Snub Pollard) nab a gang of gold robbers with the help of a local Boy Scout troop. Stylized violence

title: Thank God, It's Friday
synopsis: Youth exploitation movie about the problems that develop one Friday night at a disco, set against a blaring background of frenetic music. Directed by Robert Klane, it juggles a dozen or so stereotyped characters and, though the pace is lively, the comedy is tiresome and repetitious. Some failed jokes about sex and drugs

title: Thank You All Very Much
synopsis: British melodrama in which a young woman (Sandy Dennis) living alone in London becomes pregnant as the result of her first and only sexual experience, decides against abortion and becomes an unwed mother. Director Waris Hussein does well in depicting the life of Londoners and is sensitive to the young woman's situation but the treatment is superficial and makes no attempt to understand the woman and her future

title: Thank You and Goodnight!
synopsis: Fact-based account of a young woman (Jan Oxenberg) coming to terms with the terminal illness of her grandmother (Mae Joffe) who looks back on her life as family and friends comfort her. Writer-producer-star-director Oxenberg es actual family members and precariously balances a humorously philosophical attitude toward life and death with emotionally honest scenes of pain and loss. A skeptical attitude toward the afterlife

title: Thank You, Aunt
synopsis: ( see: "Grazie Zia" )

title: Thank You for Smoking
synopsis: Trenchant black comedy about tobacco industry lobbyist (a perfectly cast Aaron Eckhart) who, under the approving eye of his boss (Robert Duvall), will stop at nothing to promote cigarette smoking, as he manipulates talk show hosts (Joan Lunden and Dennis Miller), an anti-smoking Vermont senator (William H. Macy), a Hollywood agent (Rob Lowe), and an investigative reporter (Katie Holmes), while wondering about the effect of his questionable tactics on his young son. Writer-director Jason Reitman's highly amusing and well-acted adaptation of Christopher Buckley's novel sustains its satiric stance without losing sight of the grave issues at hand. Much rough and crude language and expressions, a couple of sexual encounters with no nudity and sexual banter, an irreligious remark

title: Thank You, Jeeves
synopsis: Diverting fun with P.G. Wodehouse's sterling butler, Jeeves (Arthur Treacher), who here saves his asinine employer (David Niven) from a gang of spies. Directed by Arthur Greville Collins, the comedy is light and breezy escapist fare. Mild comic violence

title: Thank You, Mr. Moto
synopsis: Intriguing entry in the mystery series with Japanese detective Moto (Peter Lorre) in China to search for an ancient scroll showing the burial site of Genghis Khan and his treasures. Director Norman Foster uses the Oriental setting to provide a sinister atmosphere for a plot involving an American tourist (Jayne Regan), a White Russian count (Sig Ruman), the mother (Pauline Frederick) of a Chinese prince (Philip Ahn) and a ruthless gang leader (Sidney Blackmer). More menace than violence

title: That Championship Season
synopsis: Jason Miller directs his own adaptation of his prize-winning play about four middle-aged men (Bruce Dern, Paul Sorvino, Stacy Keach, and Martin Sheen) who gather with their former coach (Robert Mitchum) to celebrate the 24th anniversary of winning the state high school basketball championship. As the evening of drinking wears on, the guilty secrets of each come out, but before they do, most viewers will have lost interest. Some strong language

title: That Cold Day in the Park
synopsis: Failed psychological melodrama in which a lonely spinster (Sandy Dennis) invites a drifter (Michael Burns) in out of the rain for a hot meal and goes to bizarre lengths trying to get him to share her bed. Director Robert Altman juxtaposes two unbelievable characters in a series of impossibly phony situations that lead to no insights about social alienation but only to morbid, sexually explicit sensationalism

title: That Darn Cat
synopsis: Disney live-action adventure comedy in which Hayley Mills gets FBI agent Dean Jones to follow the trail of a mischievous cat who is the only clue to the whereabouts of a kidnapped bank-teller. Robert Stevenson directs the antics but it is the cat who steals the show. Amusing for youngsters and not too hard on parents either

title: That Darn Cat
synopsis: Convinced her cat has found a clue to the whereabouts of a kidnapping victim, an alienated teen (Christina Ricci) enlists the help of a hapless FBI agent (Doug E. Doug) in solving the crime by following the frisky feline around town. Director Bob Spiers' shoddy remake of the 1965 comedy overdoes the resulting mayhem and chaos in a mistaken attempt at humor. Frequent slapstick violence

title: That Hamilton Woman
synopsis: Fact-based historical romance recounts the ill-fated extramarital affair between Lady Hamilton (Vivian Leigh), the low-born wife of the British ambassador to Naples (Alan Mowbray), and Lord Nelson (Laurence Olivier), the admiral who crushed Napoleon's fleet at Trafalgar. While director Alexander Korda treats the characters sympathetically, their romance is placed within the context of the times which hopelessly doomed their affair to unhappiness. Wartime violence and discreet treatment of marital infidelity

title: That Kind of Woman
synopsis: Contrived sudser begins in June 1944 aboard a Miami-to-New York train where a small-town Army private (Tab Hunter) falls for the glamorous mistress (Sophia Loren) of a rich war contractor (George Sanders), then spends his leave trying to convince her to marry him. Director Sidney Lumet gets an appealing performance from Loren as well as from Barbara Nichols and Jack Warden in a parallel subplot, but Hunter fails to make the grade and the situation never fulfills its promise. Probes the relationship between love and sex

title: That Lady in Ermine
synopsis: Failed romantic comedy in which a tiny 1861 principality is occupied by Hungarian hussars whose dour colonel (Douglas Fairbanks, Jr.) Mellows after falling for its ruling countess (Betty Grable) while her husband (Cesar Romero) flits around disguised as a Gypsy. Directed by Ernst Lubitsch (who died during its production), the situation yields little comedy and even less whimsey, especially some heavy-handed musical fantasy sequences involving the countess' ancestors. Sexual situations and innuendo

title: That'll Be the Day
synopsis: British drama, based loosely on the formation of the Beatles rock group, tells the story of an young man (David Essex) who is helped to find some direction in his life by a casual friend (Ringo Starr in a non-musical role). Director Claude Whatham's movie is raw, often ragged, but full of feeling and compassion, and it will interest both rock fans and those who like unvarnished pictures of unwashed types

title: That Man Bolt
synopsis: Fred Williamson stars as the super-smooth courier of valuables for well-heeled international clients but this trip he's double-crossed by his employers and he works out a nifty cross of his own. Directed by Henry Levin, it has plenty of action, often quite violent but relieved by whimsical staging, and there's some sexual innuendo

title: That Man from Rio
synopsis: French production with Jean-Paul Belmondo and Francois Dorleac in an hilarious spoof of stereotype characters and stock situations that typify mystery adventure movies. Directed by Philippe de Broca with real Gallic flair, the comedy is first-class entertainment

title: That Night
synopsis: Coming-of-age melodrama seen from the perspective of a starry-eyed 10-year old (Eliza Dushku) who idolizes her 17-year-old neighbor (Juliette Lewis) and tries to reunite her with her boyfriend (C. Thomas Howell) after the teen is quietly shipped off to a Catholic home for unwed mothers in the early '60s. Writer-director Craig Bolotin tries to present a sympathetic portrait of teen passion colliding with painful realities, but his formulaic treatment of cardboard characters is heavy-handed and muddled by the child's simplistic point-of-view towards the lovers. A pre-marital relationship, many sexual references, fleeting violence and an instance of profanity

title: That Night in Rio
synopsis: Glossy musical comedy set in Rio de Janeiro where an American nightclub entertainer (Don Ameche) gets in trouble with his girlfriend (Carmen Miranda) when he's hired to impersonate a count (also Ameche) whom he resembles so closely even the countess (Alice Faye) can't tell them apart. Directed by Irving Cummings, the comedy of mistaken identities wears increasingly thin, though the cast is generally entertaining and the Brazilian novelty numbers are diverting. Sexual situations and innuendo. A-II (br) 1941

title: That Obscure Object of Desire
synopsis: Disappointing French production in which a wealthy middle-aged Parisian (Fernando Rey) falls hopelessly in love with a young Spanish woman (alternately played by Carole Bouquet and Angela Molina) who leads him a merry chase. Director Luis Bunuel's surrealistic treatment of the romantic situation makes shallow attempts at social commentary. Excessive use of nudity

title: That Old Feeling
synopsis: Reunited at their daughter's wedding, a bitterly divorced couple (Bette Midler and Dennis Farina) in stable second marriages impulsively surrender to passion then spend the next two days trying to evade facing their horrified spouses and shocked daughter as they ponder what to do next. Director Carl Reiner lampoons matrimony in a farcical story tailor made for Midler's brassy acting style. Comic treatment of adultery and instances of profanity and rough language

title: That's Dancing!
synopsis: A film compilation of great moments in dancing from the film musicals of the 1930s to the recent past. Produced by Jack Haley Jr., the movie is very entertaining but real fans will note some significant omissions and yearn for more extended selections

title: That's Entertainment!
synopsis: Singing, dancing historical survey of the best of the MGM musicals charms the eye and ear with romantic fantasy. Written, produced and directed by Jack Haley Jr., the selection of excerpts from these musicals demonstrates effortlessly why their appeal endures from generation to generation

title: That's Entertainment! III
synopsis: Yet more excerpts from MGM musicals, this time featuring the studio's gallery of stars in offbeat and unusual production numbers as well as some musical routines that landed on the cutting room floor. Producer-directors Bud Friedgen and Michael J. Sheridan's compilation of less familiar footage from the golden age of Hollywood musicals is lively and engaging family fare with special appeal for nostalgic adults

title: That's Entertainment, Part 2
synopsis: Fred Astaire and Gene Kelly (who also directs) serve as hosts for this anthology from Hollywood's musical past, though there are brief glimpses of such comedians as the Marx Brothers, Jimmy Durante, Laurel and Hardy, and Abbott and Costello as well as a sequence devoted to the films of Spencer Tracy and Katherine Hepburn. Highly enjoyable but not up to the original's consistent quality

title: That's Life
synopsis: Fumbling, self-centered husband (Jack Lemmon), preoccupied with thoughts of old age and death, is insensitive to the needs of his wife (Julie Andrews) as she awaits the results of a cancer test. Director Blake Edwards uses sexual encounters as a source of comic relief in an exploration of family ties that has few genuine moments. His infidelity is treated as a symptom of an inner insecurity left unresolved and overshadowed by the image of a strong woman and mother who absorbs all family ills. Brief nudity

title: That's My Boy
synopsis: Lame comedy in which a dim father (Eddie Mayehoff) who was a college football hero wants his hypochondriac son (Jerry Lewis) to do the same and gets the team's star (Dean Martin) to show him how, but they have a falling out over a co-ed (Marion Marshall). Directed by Hal Walker, the proceedings are more sentimental than comic, though Lewis' antics raise an occasional giggle. Scenes of inebriation

title: That Splendid November
synopsis: Failed Italian melodrama about the nymphomaniacal aunt (Gina Lollobridgida) and her determinedly incestuous nephew (Paolo Turco), both of whom are but one small part of a large Sicilian clan specializing in sexual pastimes. Directed by Mauro Bolognini, the result is an inept exercise in studied decadence and heavily erotic atmosphere

title: That's Right -- You're Wrong
synopsis: Dated musical comedy in which band leader Kay Kyser comes to Hollywood to make a movie, but when the studio producer (Adolphe Menjou) can't come up with a suitable script, he and the gang return to their radio show

title: That Thing You Do!
synopsis: Warm-hearted comedy in which four clean-cut teens from Erie, Pa., form a rock`n'roll band in 1964, then briefly rocket towards the top of the pop charts under the savvy guidance of their record-label manager (Tom Hanks). Also written and directed by Hanks, the thin story brims with youthful exhuberance in a vivid picture of a more innocent era. A few rude expressions

title: That Touch of Mink
synopsis: Flat romantic comedy in which a nice young woman (Doris Day) succumbs to the charms of a wealthy philanderer (Cary Grant), then backs off until he's willing to marry her. Directed by Delbert Mann, the glossy proceedings are slickly contrived, relatively witless and, despite the tacked-on ending, lack any deeper sense of romance than sex and dollar signs. Sexual situations and innuendo

title: That Uncertain Feeling
synopsis: Droll comedy in which a dull insurance executive (Melvyn Douglas) agrees to give his dippy wife (Merle Oberon) a divorce after she gets involved with an eccentric pianist (Burgess Meredith), then proceeds to win her back on his own terms. Producer-director Ernst Lubitsch has some witty fun with the idle rich who can afford to turn minor problems into major ones, but Meredith steals the show as a wacky egoist. Comic treatment of marriage and sexual innuendo

title: That Was Then, This Is Now
synopsis: From the work of novelist S.E. Hinton, the bard of misunderstood youth, comes a story of two boys (Craig Sheffer and Emilio Estevez) who hang out together wondering about the meaning of it all until one falls in love and gets a job while the other wallows yet deeper in self-pity. Directed by Christopher Cain, the movie is so dull and pretentious that it is painful to watch. Benign view of premarital sex

title: Theatre of Blood
synopsis: Gruesome British chiller has its genuinely amusing moments as a B-grade Shakespearean actor (Vincent Price) takes his revenge on the stuffy circle of London critics who thwarted his career. Each execution is conducted through a re-enactment of the murder scene from one of the Bard's tragedies in which the critic had lambasted Price's performalce. Directlr Dougl`s Hickox stages the acthon with a distinct flaip and the capt of Brhtish ch`racter `ctors ip marvellus. Thd gore ready dead body because his girlfriend (Susan Hayward) had just been identified as his wife after dying in a fiery auto accident. Director Irving Pichel gets a convincing performance from Young as a coldly calculating cad, but the contrived proceedings don't make much sense even after the twist ending. Off-screen violence and marital infidelity

title: Thelma & Louise
synopsis: Two girlfriends from Arkansas (Susan Sarandon and Geena Davis), intent on a carefree getaway weekend in a '66 Thunderbird, find themselves dodging police all the way to Arizona after one murders an attempted rapist. Director Ridley Scott's flashy road movie makes the two women highly appealing but glamorizes their willing, sometimes gleefully made choices to break the law and escape the consequences. Rationalization of murder and suicide, casual marital infidelity, brief but graphic attempted rape scene and intermittent rough language

title: Then She Found Me
synopsis: Fitfully engaging but mostly humdrum tale of a glum Jewish schoolteacher (Helen Hunt) who reconnects with the gregarious birth mother (Bette Midler) she never knew, and falls in love with a single father (Colin Firth) after her adopted mother dies and her husband (Matthew Broderick) walks out on her. Co-writer Hunt competently directs this adaptation of Elinor Lipman's novel, and performances are solid, but her character is frequently irksome and several plot points are problematic from a Catholic perspective. Nongraphic sexual encounters; some nonmarital, frank sexual talk; partial female nudity; profanity and some rough language; and artificial insemination

title: Theodora Goes Wild
synopsis: > Wacky romantic comedy in which a young woman (Irene Dunne) shocks her prim Connecticut hometown by revealing she's the author of a risque best seller, then goes after the married heel (Melvyn Douglas) who wooed her only to return to his wealthy wife. Director Richard Boleslawski makes an easy target of small-town hypocrisy and gets some funny results from the slapstick situations of a plot whose theme of self-liberation from social convention proves more sentimental than subversive. Shallow treatment of marriage

title: There Will Be Blood
synopsis: Extraordinarily fine drama loosely based on Upton Sinclair 1927 novel, "Oil!" set during the early 20th century, about the rise and fall of a ruthless oil tycoon (Daniel Day-Lewis) who, accompanied by his young son (Dillon Freasier), fleeces a poor central California family of their land, and eventually finds himself pitted against one of the family's sons, a charismatic preacher (Paul Dano). Director Paul Thomas Anderson has used the novel as a springboard to fashion a classic piece of American cinema, with Day-Lewis' galvanizing performance among the great ones, though the confrontation between the tycoon and the preacher that forms the film's climax is truly disturbing. Some brief but brutal violence, murder, three uses of profanity and several crude expressions

title: There Be Dragons
synopsis: Generally powerful, partly fictionalized dramatization of passages in the life of St. Josemaria Escriva de Balaguer (1902-75), founder of Opus Dei, here intensely yet appealingly portrayed by Charlie Cox. As a fictitious Spanish-born reporter (Dougray Scott) investigates Escriva's life, he discovers that his own father (Wes Bentley) -- from whom he has long been estranged -- was the future spiritual leader's childhood friend and seminary classmate. But, with the violent tumult of the Spanish Civil War looming, the two men took diametrically different paths -- one toward the establishment of a movement dedicated to achieving personal sanctity through everyday work, the other toward a duplicitous role in the conflict engulfing their society. While the striking portrait of an anything-but-plaster saint that forms the heart of writer-director Roland Joffe's hybrid tale grippingly conveys its subject's struggle to discern his vocation and to live out the Christian message of peace, the impact of these biographical elements is blunted by the fictive framework, much of which never seems quite convincing. Probably acceptable for older teens. Occasionally bloody action violence, a few sexual references, a couple of crude and a half-dozen crass terms

title: Therese
synopsis: Earnest if modest period piece which reverently dramatizes the life of St. Therese of Lisieux (Lindsay Younce), known more affectionately as the "Little Flower." Based on her posthumously published autobiography, "The Story of a Soul," and directed by Leonardo Defilippis, the film is not so much a textured spiritual portrait of the young French nun considered by Pope Pius X "the greatest saint of modern times" but a series of hagiographic tableaus which many Catholic viewers may find edifying. The beauty of Therese's inspirational life and words still shine through the film's production limitations. Thematic elements involving parental death, and a criminal execution

title: The Tailor of Panama
synopsis: Intriguing thriller in which a British spy (Pierce Brosnan) demoted to duty in Panama relies on a tailor (Geoffrey Rush) to glean information from his politician clients, but is mislead by the tailor's lies which have unforseen consequences. As directed by John Boorman, the smart film is filled with irony and wry humor, although the meandering story line and an atmosphere of promiscuity diminish the overall effect. Numerous sexual situations, some nudity, brief violence and much rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: The Taste of Others
synopsis: Witty French comedy-drama in which a successful but bored businessman (Jean-Pierre Bacri) attends a play with his wife and becomes enamored with the lead actress (Anne Alvaro) whom he later discover is his English tutor. As directed by Agnes Jaoui, the character-driven plot fumbles a bit, but is nonetheless an often engaging story told with poignancy and humor about the attraction of opposites. Subtitles. A few implied sexual encounters, some drug content and intermittent rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: The Ten Commandments
synopsis: Epic and effective retelling of the Exodus story using 3-D computer-generated imagery animation and narration by Sir Ben Kingsley to show how Moses (voice of Christian Slater), in obedience to the call of God (Elliott Gould) and with the support of his brother, Aaron (Christopher Gaze), and sister, Miriam (Kathleen Barr), put an end to Israel's enslavement under the Egyptian Pharaoh (Alfred Molina) and, despite the opposition of a clique of complainers, headed by Dathan (Lee Tockar), led God's people into the desert -- where they received his law -- and on to the threshold of the Promised Land. Directors Bill Boyce and John Stronach's film, though occasionally stiff in both action and tone, nonetheless provides a reasonably good introduction to a vital piece of biblical history for children, also serving as a pleasant refresher course for the adults who accompany them. Some images may be mildly frightening for very young children

title: The Terminal
synopsis: Disappointing romantic comedy about an Eastern European traveler (Tom Hanks) who, after his homeland's government is overthrown by a coup while he is en route to the United States, is denied access to American soil and forced to live in an airport terminal where he befriends several members of the maintenance staff and finds love with a lonely flight attendant (Catherine Zeta-Jones). Loosely based on real-life events, the lackluster movie, directed by Steven Spielberg, though full of political pretensions, never really offers any insights into the immigrant experience but instead keeps viewers' attention in a holding pattern of manufactured emotion. Brief crude language and some drug references

title: The Texas Chainsaw Massacre: The Beginning
synopsis: Prequel to the 2003 horror film that revisits the homicidal Hewitt clan (headed by R. Lee Ermey), revealing the early years of the franchise's chainsaw-wielding killer, "Leatherface" (Andrew Bryniarski), with a quartet of young road-trippers (Jordana Brewster, Taylor Handley, Diora Baird and Matt Bomer) served up for slaughter. Director Jonathan Liebesman forgoes plot to pile on the bloody sadism. Such gratuitous brutality isn't entertainment, but something closer to pornography. Excessive gory violence, including graphic scenes of mutilation and dismemberment, a sexual situation, much rough and crude language

title: The Thief Lord
synopsis: > Family-friendly adventure about two orphaned brothers (Aaron Johnson and Jasper Harris) who, fleeing their mean aunt, escape to Venice, Italy where they fall in with thieving street urchins led by a mysterious masked teen, �the Thief Lord� (Rollo Weeks), helping him in a caper involving an enchanted merry-go-round.
