synopsis: Stilted murder mystery set in an English convent hospital where a convicted murderess (Ann Blyth) and her police guards are marooned by a flood while one of the nuns (Claudette Colbert) tries to prove the prisoner's innocence. Director Douglas Sirk fails to work up much suspense despite the plot's many contrivances and uses the convent setting for little more than pious atmosphere and nun stereotypes (Gladys Cooper and Connie Gilchrist). Implied marital infidelity and brief menace

title: Thunder Over the Plains
synopsis: Standard Randolph Scott vehicle directed by Andre de Toth is set in postbellum Texas where a loyal Union officer (Scott) overcomes a callow fellow officer (Lex Barker) to save a rebel leader (Charles McGraw) from hanging for a murder committed by a greedy carpetbagger. Stylized violence and a scene of unwanted romantic advances

title: Thunder Road
synopsis: Earnest melodrama set in the Tennessee hills where a driver (Robert Mitchum) makes moonshine deliveries despite roadside ambushes by federal agents (led by Gene Barry) and gangsters (led by Jacques Aubuchon) trying to muscle in on the bootleg traffic. Directed by Arthur Ripley, the backcountry location photography and flinty rustic characters are more convincing than the predictable plot about outsiders interfering with traditional country ways. Stylized violence, harrowing car chases and romantic complications

title: Thursday's Child
synopsis: Thoughtful British melodrama about a 12-year-old girl (Sally Ann Howes) who becomes a child movie star and how this affects her family and her own plans for the future. Writer-director Rodney Ackland deglamorizes the movie business effectively, gets solid performances from a good cast (including Wilfrid Lawson, Stewart Granger and Felix Aylmer) and ends on a positive, though realistic note. Romantic situations

title: THX 1138
synopsis: In a futuristic underground world, a minor technician named THX 1138 (Robert Duvall) rebels against its sterile, dehumanizing conditions and tries to escape through a maze of electronic devices and guard robots to the unknown outside world. Director George Lucas creates a terrifying technological future out of the materials of today but it is difficult to empathize with the story's dehumanized characters who have been stripped of all sensitivity and emotion. Though the movie is visually extraordinary and its story has substance, a rather explicit love scene and an extended sequence with a nude dancer limit its audience

title: Ticket to Heaven
synopsis: Well-made Canadian movie about the efforts to rescue a young man (Nick Mancuso) who left his Toronto home and turned up in San Francisco, gaunt-cheeked and hollow-eyed, selling flowers on a street corner as a member of a religious cult. Directed by Ralph L. Thomas, the dramatization has unusual credibility and will be of special interest to teenagers and concerned parents

title: Ticket to Tomahawk
synopsis: Uneven Western comedy in which a traveling salesman (Dan Dailey) and a sheriff's granddaughter (Anne Baxter) help establish a railroad line in 1876 Colorado, despite rampaging Arapaho braves and a gunslinger (Rory Calhoun) working for a stagecoach competitor. Director Richard Sales makes the most of the colorful characters and picturesque Rocky Mountain locales, but the thin plot meanders fitfully along until its predictable ending. Frontier violence and mild romance

title: Tickle Me
synopsis: Thin star vehicle with Elvis Presley as an out-of-work singing cowboy who gets a job at a women's health ranch, falls for a staff member (Jocelyn Lane) and helps her search for the fortune left by her grandfather. Directed by Norman Taurog, Elvis charms the ladies with some crooning, brawling and rodeo riding, but the real fun is saved for the mildly spooky finale in a ghost town. Sexual innuendo

title: Tick...Tick...Tick...
synopsis: Using their newly acquired voting privileges, the blacks of a small Southern county elect one of their own (Jim Brown) as sheriff and, after some stereotyped black and white hostilities, a crisis unites both races behind their sheriff and the ending indicates a rosy future of racial harmony. Shallow treatment by director Ralph Nelson of a serious subject

title: Tidal Wave
synopsis: Clumsy Americanized version of a Japanese disaster movie directed by Shiro Mariano is not only episodic and lacking any sense of pace but it is badly dubbed and cluttered with unconvincing inserts of Lorne Greene as a U.N. delegate. Though one gets bored of the same old shot of lava flowing into the sea, several scenes are too graphic for very young viewers

title: Tie Me Up! Tie Me Down!
synopsis: Released mental patient (Antonio Banderas) binds and gags an actress (Victoria Abril), holding her prisoner in her apartment until she falls in love with him. Writer-director Pedro Almodovar's Spanish production tries to parlay a sick male sexual fantasy into a kinky sex comedy but there is nothing amusing in seeing a woman's brutal victimization. Perverse theme and extended depictions of sex acts

title: Tie That Binds, The
synopsis: Trashy thriller in which crazed fugitives from the police (Keith Carradine and Daryl Hannah) attempt to recover their six-year-old daughter by killing the couple (Vincent Spano and Moira Kelly) planning to adopt her. Director Wesley Strick turns in a trite, formula tale of one-note characters in a plot thick with grotesque tortures and murders. Recurring gory violence and brutal beatings, intense menace to a child and several instances of rough language

title: Tiger Makes Out, The
synopsis: Postman Eli Wallach decides one day to revolt against bureaucratic routine, kidnaps suburban housewife Anne Jackson and she undertakes to educate her captor. Directed by Arthur Hiller, the subsequent action tends to be overdone, but what is enjoyable are the excellent performances of the two principals

title: Tiger Shark
synopsis: When one of his crew is killed by sharks, a San Diego fishing captain (Edward G. Robinson) looks after the dead man's troubled daughter (Zita Johann) who eventually agrees to marry him out of gratitude, then falls for his closest friend (Richard Arlen), but a shark resolves the situation. Directed by Howard Hawks, the fishing sequences and the ever-present sharks establish a realistic context for Robinson's compelling performance as the gruff, good-hearted Portuguese fisherman but the triangle plot is heavily melodramatic and its outcome predictable. Fierce shark attacks and romantic complications

title: Tigger Movie, The
synopsis: Buoyant animated feature in which Tigger, Winnie the Pooh's cheerful bouncing friend, tries to Learn Whether he's the only one as he seeks out his own ``tigger'' family. The artfully crafted animation leaps out with vivid colors and three-dimensionality in director Jun Falkenstein's happy exploration as Tigger is joined by Pooh, Piglet, Roo, Owl, Rabbit and all the others in the clever musical adventure

title: Tightrope
synopsis: Clint Eastwood plays a New Orleans police detective searching for a sadistic killer whose aberrant sexual proclivities he fears he might share. Written and directed by Richard Tuggle, the movie embodies an interesting theme, but the execution of it falls short, even though Eastwood's performance is one of his best. The sex and violence loom much too large

title: Tight Spot
synopsis: Potential government witness (Ginger Rogers) against a crime boss (Lorne Greene) holes up in a New York hotel room while the federal prosecutor (Edward G. Robinson) tries to persuade her to testify and a swarm of policemen (led by Brian Keith) try to keep her from being killed by the mob. Director Phil Karlson's classy crime melodrama paces the suspense with some nifty curves and a sassy performance by Rogers as a one-time shady lady with a chance to be a gangbuster. Stylized violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Tiko and the Shark
synopsis: Harmless, sometimes charming story of the romance between a Polynesian boy and girl, the lad's friendship with a shark and their role in the activities of an island fishing village. Directed by Falco Quilici, the movie's simple story and gorgeous photography should appeal to youngsters

title: Till Marriage Do Us Part
synopsis: Italian sex comedy directed by Luigi Comencini deals with the many tribulations endured by a noble Sicilian lady (Laura Antonelli) who discovers on her wedding night that her husband is in fact her brother. Excessive nudity and graphic sexuality

title: Till the End of Time
synopsis: Sudsy tearjerker about returning World War II vets centers on an ex-Marine (Guy Madison) and a troubled war widow (Dorothy Malone) who tries to help him adjust to civilian life. Director Edward Dmytryk delivers a soppy melodrama that winds up in a patriotic barroom brawl between some vets and group of hometown bigots. Dated period romance

title: 'Til There Was You
synopsis: Drawn-out romantic comedy which tracks the failed romances of a ghostwriter (Jeanne Tripplehorn) and an architect (Dylan McDermott) who almost meet each other countless times before finally connecting at movie's end. Directed by Scott Winnant, the romantic comedy is clumsily contrived to keep the would-be sweethearts apart yet in close proximity for years on end. Pre-marital affairs, some crude expressions and an instance of rough language

title: Timberjack
synopsis: Routine adventure directed by Joe Kane in which a Montana lumber company is being driven into bankruptcy by a ruthless rival (Brian Keith) until the owner's son (Sterling Hayden) arrives to stop the villain, with some help from the local saloon owner (Vera Ralston) and her tipsy father (Adolphe Menjou). Much stylized violence

title: Tim Burton's Corpse Bride
synopsis: Darkly enchanting animated love story based on a Russian folk tale about a timid groom (voiced by Johnny Depp) whose arranged marriage to the shy daughter (voiced by Emily Watson) of stuffy aristocrats, is derailed the night before they are to wed when, practicing his vows alone in the woods, he finds himself betrothed to a dead girl (voiced by Helena Bonham Carter) he inadvertently reanimates. Though a bit morose for young children, co-directors Tim Burton and Mike Johnson have crafted a delightfully macabre fable that imparts a gentle message of selfless love which should warm most hearts -- beating or not. Mature thematic elements, a villainous clerical character and folkloric fantasy content

title: Time After Time
synopsis: H.G. Wells (Malcolm McDowell) uses a time machine to pursue Jack the Ripper (David Warner) to modern-day San Francisco where the author and a liberated woman executive (Mary Steenburgen) get involved in a duel of wits with the mad killer. Director Nicholas Meyer's romantic thriller is moderately entertaining, especially the satiric asides about modern technology, but it has some rather violent touches involving the Ripper's crimes, some profanity and implied premarital sex

title: Time and Tide
synopsis: Ferocious martial-arts action film set in present-day Hong Kong in which a streetwise young man (Nicholas Tse) becomes a bodyguard to make quick money and befriends a mercenary (Wu Bai) to foil an assassination attempt. As directed by Tsui Hark, the confusing and far-fetched plot is engulfed by the film's non-stop brutality. Much gratuitous violence, brief drug use, an implied sexual encounter, homosexual innuendo, and some crass language. Subtitles. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Time Bandits
synopsis: Witty British comedy about a gang of greedy but good-hearted dwarfs who steal a map of creation from the Supreme Being (Ralph Richardson) and use it to bring an adventurous lad into a variety of historical epochs, meeting Napoleon (Ian Holm), Greek warrior Agamemnon (Sean Connery) and Robin Hood (John Cleese). Directed by Terry Gilliam, it is sometimes amusing and always intelligent, but its appeal for youngsters is spoiled by typical Monty Python vlulgarities and black humor, some of it violent

title: Time Bomb
synopsis: ( see "Terror on a Train" )

title: Timecop
synopsis: Ultraviolent action movie set in the year 2004 when a widowed cop (Jean-Claude Van Damme) time-travels back to the 1990s to prevent a murderous politician (Ron Silver) from manipulating the future while also saving his own wife (Mia Sara) from being murdered. Director Peter Hyams goes through the motions in a tired, boring story overstuffed with earsplitting martial arts battles, constant deadly shootouts and jazzy special effects amounting only to a stream of mindless mayhem. Excessive violence, some nudity and frequent rough language

title: Time for Burning, A
synopsis: Extraordinary documentary of what happened when a pastor tried to get his all-white congregation to meet with nearby blacks. Produced by the Lutheran Film Associates and directed by William Jersey, it is a moving document of troubled times and the need for human understanding

title: Time for Killing, A
synopsis: ( see: "The Long Ride Home" )

title: Time in the Sun, A
synopsis: Sensitive Swedish drama about a young journalist (Lars Passgard) who pursues and wins the woman (Grynet Molvig) of his dreams, despite the fact that she is fatally afflicted with Hodgkin's Disease. Director Ake Falck invests a good deal of human warmth in an unusual story of married life, human suffering and the healing power of love. Restrained lovemaking scene

title: Timeline
synopsis: Stale sci-fi actioner based on Michael Crichton's novel about a team of student archeologists (including Paul Walker and Gerard Butler) who must travel back in time to rescue their professor trapped in the 14th century. Despite an intriguing premise, director Richard Donner's medieval adventure is hampered by a hackneyed script, lame dialogue and wooden performances, resulting in a film that proves about as entertaining as a turn on the rack. Intense battle violence and some crude language

title: Time Lost and Time Remembered
synopsis: Unhappily married woman (Sarah Miles) returns to her home town in the West of Ireland to find the boy she loved now engaged to another. Director Desmond Davis evokes beautifully the Irish atmosphere and locale but the story is somewhat sentimentalized. Mature themes

title: Time Machine, The
synopsis: Imaginative adaptation of H.G. Wells' fanciful tale of an English inventor (Rod Taylor) who travels from 1900 into the far distant future where he tries to rally an oppressed people against their loathsome overlords, the radiation-damaged Morlocks. Directed by George Pal, the special effects may not be very elaborate but they're effective enough to convey the fantastic nature of the sci-fi scenario and its underlying anti-war theme. Some stylized violence

title: Time of Destiny, A
synopsis: Old-fashioned romantic melodrama set during World War II in San Diego and Italy traces the catastrophic effects on the family of a wealthy Basque-American rancher when he interferes in the elopement of his favorite daughter (Melissa Leo) with a young penniless soldier (Timothy Hutton). The filmmakers, Gregory Nava and Anna Thomas ("El Norte"), handle the themes of young love, revenge and Old World values with operatic relish. A few scenes of intense violence and some profanity

title: Time of Favor
synopsis: Using the political tensions in Israel as a backdrop, the flawed yet thought-provoking drama intertwines a love triangle with religious fervor in which a young military officer (Aki Avni) falls for the daughter (Tinkerbell) of an orthodox rabbi (Asi Dayan) who wants her to marry his prize pupil (Edan Alterman). In the self-contained world presented by director Joseph Cedar, clear judgment is clouded by religious devotion, personal will and political commitment, however, the thriller's build-up is more engrossing than its melodramatic finale. Subtitles. Brief violence, menacing situations and an instance of crass language

title: Time of Roses
synopsis: Tangled tale from Finland about a supposedly perfect society in 2012 whose government manipulates the news, unaware of a plot to expose its deceptive methods through a television documentary about a woman who died in 1976. Directed by Rista Jarva, the movie's intriguing and challenging themes are treated with a cerebral aloofness that leaves the viewer uninvolved and unmoved

title: Time of the Gypsies
synopsis: Yugoslavian import tells of a Gypsy adolescent (Davor Dujmovic) who is lured to his destruction after poverty and his sister's illness force the boy to seek help from the richest, most corrupt Gypsy in town. Relying on a largely non-professional cast, director Emir Kusturica provides some insight into Gypsy myth, morality and family life. Subtitles. Some violence, sexually suggestive scenes with nudity and the rape of a minor

title: Time of Their Lives, The
synopsis: Killed mistakenly as traitors in the Revolutionary War, two ghosts (Lou Costello and Marjorie Reynolds) cause comic havoc for the residents (Bud Abbott, Binnie Barnes and Gale Sondergaard) of a country estate until proof of their loyalty is found. Directed by Charles Barton, this classy Abbott and Costello effort replaces the usual string of gags with a real story that has plenty of charm and engaging humor with simple yet amusing special effects, The spirits and their predicament as well as a spooky seance scene may scare very young children

title: Time of Your Life, The
synopsis: Static version of William Saroyan's play set in a San Francisco bar whose easy-going owner (William Bendix) enjoys his eccentric clientele, including a philosophical lounger (James Cagney), his dim go-fer (Wayne Morris), a lonely woman (Jeanne Cagney), a dancer (Paul Draper) and a woolly teller of tall tales (James Barton). Under H.C. Potter's direction, the scenes sputter unevenly without ever jelling into a whole, though Saroyan's exotic characters certainly hold attention. A scene of stylized violence and some sexual inferences

title: Timerider
synopsis: Motorcycle racer (Fred Ward) finds himself whisked back in time to the late 19th century where he gets mixed up with some lowlifes of various sorts. Directed by William Dear, it is a simple-minded attempt to combine science fiction and the Western with little result. Considerable, though restrained, sex and violence

title: Time to Kill, A
synopsis: A novice Southern white lawyer (Matthew McConaughey) and an enterprising law student (Sandra Bullock) collaborate to defend an African-American father (Samuel L. Jackson) who has killed the two thugs who raped and nearly murdered his 10-year-old daughter. Adapted from John Grisham's bestseller, director Joel Schumacher's solid but slick courtroom melodrama provides engrossing entertainment while oversimplifying race relations and the revenge-based murders. Ambiguous treatment of justice issues, disturbing violence including an off-screen rape and crude language with racial epithets

title: Time to Love and a Time to Die, A
synopsis: Flat romance from Erich Maria Remarque's novel in which a German soldier (miscast John Gavin) on leave from the Russian front in the spring of 1944, finds his city in ruins, searches for his missing parents, witnesses Nazi oppression and marries one of its victims (Lilo Pulver) before returning to the front. Director Douglas Sirk's picture of the moral dilemma facing decent Germans under an evil regime gets lost in unconvincing drama, though the result has some interest as social history. Wartime violence and Nazi excesses

title: Time to Remember, A
synopsis: A young boy (Ruben Gomez) regains his voice when he has a vision of the Madonna during Christmas Midnight Mass. Directed by Tom Travers, the well-intended but inept and saccharine melodrama offers some wholesome, if shallow, entertainment for undemanding viewers

title: Time to Sing, A
synopsis: Country musical comedy about a farm boy (Hank Williams Jr.) who becomes a singing star despite many obstacles in a cliched, sentimental but tuneful picture directed by Arthur Dreifuss. For those who enjoy the country music sound

title: The Time Traveler's Wife
synopsis: A librarian (Eric Bana) afflicted with a genetic disorder that causes him to disappear from the present and travel -- involuntarily and randomly -- through time pursues romance with an artist (Rachel McAdams) who has known him since childhood, when he befriended her during visits from his future. At its core the enjoyable tale of a lifelong committed relationship, director Robert Schwentke's adaptation of novelist Audrey Niffenegger's 2003 best-seller features persuasive central performances that divert attention from the logical loose ends, though not from some behavior that would be objectionable in less far-fetched circumstances. Brief nongraphic premarital sexual activity, rear nudity, a sterilization theme, a few uses of profanity, and some crude and crass language

title: Time without Pity
synopsis: Heavy British thriller in which a recovering alcoholic (Michael Redgrave) arrives in London the day before his son (Alex McCowen) is to be executed for murder, then races the clock seeking new evidence for a stay of execution. Directed by Joseph Losey from the Emlyn Williams play against capital punishment, the intriguing premise bogs down in frantic interrogations, overwrought encounters and ominous visuals, but the game cast manages to hold interest until the desperate conclusion. Stylized violence, implied sexual affairs and justice questions

title: Tin Cup
synopsis: An underachieving golf pro (Kevin Costner) enters the U.S. Open in order to win the love of a psychologist (Renee Russo) who is the girlfriend of his longtime golf rival (Don Johnson). Director Ron Shelton's low-key romantic comedy offers a genial cast of characters in a drawn-out story which fails to generate sufficent romantic or comedic momentum. A discreet sexual encounter, fleeting nudity and frequent rough language as well as profanity

title: Tin Drum, The
synopsis: German adaptation of Gunter Grass' satiric novel about a boy (David Bennent) who, in protest against the absurd world of adults, decides to stop growing on his third birthday and shows his anguish at events by beating on a tin drum. Directed by Volker Schlondorff, the work is a serious attempt to show the moral and political corruption of the 1930s that led to Germany's defeat in the cataclysm of World War II. Though it has moments of brilliance, it founders on trying to accomodate its vivid, often gross slice-of-life realism to some abrupt and arbitrary excursions into absurdity. Crudely graphic treatment of sex, especially in scenes with the 13-year-old Bennent

title: Tingler, The
synopsis: Creaky horror hokum from producer-director William Castle with Vincent Price as a doctor who discovers that fear triggers a physical substance in the body powerful enough to fracture the spine unless neutralized by screaming. Ridiculous concept in a dull plot with some tongue-in-cheek menace and a few cut-rate frights

title: Tin Men
synopsis: Danny DeVito and Richard Dreyfuss are 1960s aluminum siding salesman obsessed with getting even with each other over a car accident. Barbara Hershey plays DeVito's estranged wife who becomes fair game for vindictive seduction by Dreyfuss in director Barry Levinson's wry and ribald comedy whose main sources of humor, unfortunately, are adultery and profanity

title: Tin Pan Alley
synopsis: Standard musical in which struggling song publishers (John Payne and Jack Oakie) in 1915 New York get singing sisters (Alice Faye and Betty Grable) to plug their songs, but Grable soon leaves to become a star, and Faye follows after the overly ambitious Payne breaks her heart, then all four are reunited as the boys go off to fight in World War I. Directed by Walter Lang, the soggy romance is bolstered by the colorful period backgrounds, enjoyable songs and a running gag with Oakie struggling to find words for a tune which finally becomes "K-K-K-Katy." Romantic complications

title: Tin Star, The
synopsis: Solid Western in which a veteran bounty hunter (Henry Fonda) helps a young sheriff (Anthony Perkins) capture a pair of outlaws and stop a lynching. Scripted by Dudley Nichols and directed by Anthony Mann, the laconic hero and his grudging protege are fully developed as likeable individuals in an involving, well-paced and low-keyed story of frontier justice. Some stylized violence

title: Tioga Kid, The
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Ray Taylor in which a Texas Ranger (Eddie Dean) is mistaken for the lookalike outlaw of the title while trailing a gang of rustlers. Stylized violence

title: Tip-Off, The
synopsis: Breezy adventure directed by Albert Rogell in which a radio repairman (Eddie Quillan) falls for a gangster's unhappy girlfriend (Joan Peers), then steals her away from the mob with the help of a middleweight boxer (Robert Armstrong) and his sassy fiancee (Ginger Rogers). Stylized violence and some heavy sexual innuendo

title: Titan A.E.
synopsis: Convoluted animated sci-fi thriller set in 3028 A.D. in which earth is destroyed by an evil alien race and only a teenager (voice of Matt Damon) with a genetically encoded map can find a mysterious "earthship'' that holds the key to rebuilding the planet. As directed Don Bluth and Gary Goldman, the film forgoes a clear narrative for nifty, colorful animation and kicking rock music, but the ludicrous premise that humans will have the power to create another earth is somewhat problematic. Some animated action violence and fleeting rear nudity. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Titanic
synopsis: Uneven dramatization of the 1912 sinking of the "unsinkable" title liner bogs down in the shipboard strife between a rich dandy (Clifton Webb) and his estranged wife (Barbara Stanwyck), though it achieves tragic proportions after the liner's hull is ripped open by an iceberg. Director Jean Negulesco spends most of the movie developing characters who only become compelling in their varied reactions to the ship's disaster and lack of lifeboats for all the passengers. Marital discord and life-threatening situations

title: Titanic
synopsis: The epic 1912 disaster which took over 1500 lives in the sinking of the title luxury liner is recounted mainly in the story of a torrid shipboard romance between two first-class passengers (Catherine Zeta Jones and Peter Gallagher) and the wooing of a Danish immigrant (Marilu Henner) by a young thief (Mike Doyle) in the steerage section. Directed by Robert Lieberman, the 165-minute TV production largely wastes the human drama inherent in the historic tragedy by focusing on banal fictional characters provided by an inept script, though the re-creation of the majestic vessel and the terrible fate of so many of its passengers is still awesome. Fearsome body count, much menace and some sexual encounters

title: Titanic
synopsis: Lavish re-creation of the 1912 sea disaster begins with an exploration of the sunken luxury liner today, then follows its fateful voyage keyed to the improbable shipboard romance between a first-class passenger (Kate Winslet) and one in steerage (Leonardo DiCaprio) until an iceberg sends the ship and over 1500 people to the bottom. Writer-producer James Cameron reduces the human dimension of the tragedy to a paltry soap opera about two lovestruck youths, though the special effects re-creating the human drama aboard the sinking vessel are truly spectacular. Agonizing death scenes on a massive scale, sexual situations, brief nudity and sporadic rough language and profanity

title: Titans
synopsis: ( see: "My Son, the Hero" )

title: Titicut Follies
synopsis: Emotionally wrenching documentary looks unblinkingly and without commentary at the appalling conditions of life for inmates at Massachusetts' Bridgewater State Hospital for the Criminally Insane. Produced, directed and edited by Frederick Wiseman, its impressionistic picture of this state institution ranges from a musical entertainment put on by staff and inmates to scenes from the ward for the profoundly disturbed where inmates are housed without clothing as well as a staff meeting with an inmate who claims to have been wrongly committed. Though some adults may find certain scenes quite distressing, it is important that the public be aware of such conditions and, indeed, an afterward states that Bridgewater has since changed. Scenes of brutalizing conditions, some frontal male nudity and occasional rough language

title: Titus
synopsis: Epic drama in which a wronged mother (Jessica Lange) avenges the death of her first-born son at the hands of a Roman war hero (Anthony Hopkins) by bringing death and despair on the hero and his family. In this adaptation of Shakespeare's first success, director Julie Taymor matches the characters' consuming feelings of revenge by showing the unrestrained brutality and decadence that Shakespeare usually left to the imagination. Recurring graphic violence, several explicit sexual situations, and nudity

title: T-Men
synopsis: Gritty tale of Treasury Department agents (Dennis O'Keefe and Alfred Ryder) infiltrating a Los Angeles counterfeiting ring by masquerading as gangsters from Detroit. Directed by Anthony Mann, the story is narrated in semi-documentary style as the undercover agents try to get the goods on hardened criminals (notably Charles McGraw who kills informer Wallace Ford in a steam bath), with tension mounting from moody visuals and credible plot twists. Stylized violence in realistic underworld situations not for young children

title: TMNT
synopsis: Computer-animated feature revives the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle franchise, as four brothers set out to defeat a villain poised to unleash 13 monsters on New York. Writer-director Kevin Munroe navigates a rather overly complicated plot with aplomb, successfully balancing action and humor while enforcing the values of solidarity and atonement. Cartoon-level combat and swordplay, a subtle acceptance of a premarital living situation, two instances of belching and some disrespectful banter, and a mild instance of profanity

title: TNT Jackson
synopsis: Standard black exploitation movie directed by Cirio Santiago with Jeanne Bell as a martial arts addict. Excessive violence and nudity

title: Toast of New York, The
synopsis: Fictionalized biography of Jim Fisk (Edward Arnold), a Yankee peddler who smuggles cotton during the Civil War, then becomes a Wall Street financier, falls for a would-be actress (Frances Farmer) and causes a panic trying to corner the gold market. Director Rowland V. Lee tricks up the period settings effectively, but the story is pure Hollywood hokum, especially the romantic angle involving Fisk's girlfriend with his partner (Cary Grant). Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: To Be Free
synopsis: Psychiatrist tries hypnotism as short-cut therapy for a sexually confused young woman, with obviously dire consequences for them both. Director Ned Bosnick's banal plot is treated with gimmicky camera techniques and a soft-core approach to sexual anomalies

title: To Be or Not To Be
synopsis: Classic World War II comedy about a Polish actor (Jack Benny) whose impersonation of a murdered Nazi spy hoodwinks Warsaw's bumbling Gestapo chief (Sig Ruman) and saves his wife (Carole Lombard), his theater company and the Polish underground. Director Ernst Lubitsch, a master of sophisticated comedy, finds much humor and some wit in what is essentially a darkly menacing wartime subject and Benny, teamed with Lombard, was never better or funnier. Restrained violence and a sexual innuendo or two

title: To Be or Not to Be
synopsis: Director Mel Brooks fails in his attempt to remake the 1942 Ernst Lubitsch black comedy about a Warsaw drama troupe who outwit the Nazis and save the Polish underground, with himself and Anne Bancroft in the roles created by Jack Benny and Carole Lombard. Unfortunately, Brooks has neither the sophisticated wit of Lubitsch nor Benny's subtlety and sense of timing. Instead his humor runs from crude slapstick to bad taste, trivializing the Nazis and there is nothing intrinsically amusing about the Gestapo, however klutzy, however roly-poly

title: Tobor the Great
synopsis: Hokey sci-fi tale directed by Lee Sholem in which a scientist (Taylor Holmes) invents the title robot which has extrasensory perception enabling it to pilot the first space rocket, then he and his 11-year-old grandson (Billy Chapin) are abducted by Red agents (led by Steven Geray) until the trusty Tabor comes to their rescue

title: Tobruk
synopsis: World War II story about a British commando column (Rock Hudson, George Peppard, Nigel Green) disguised as a German convoy bringing Allied prisoners through the desert into the German base of Tobruk to destroy its oil stockpiles. Directed by Arthur Hiller, the straightforward action narrative alludes to the absurdity of war and has an interesting sub-plot dealing with anti-Semitism. It brings a measure of intelligence to the usual mindless war formula. Stylized violence

title: Toby Tyler, Or Ten Weeks with a Circus
synopsis: Sturdy little Disney production about the turn-of-the-century adventures of an orphan (Kevin Corcoran) when he runs away from aunt and uncle to join a traveling one-ring circus. Directed by Charles Barton, the earnest little fellow makes a lot of friends, the most notable being a mischievous monkey. Pleasant, uncomplicated story, though its main appeal is to youngsters

title: To Catch a Thief
synopsis: Fluffy romantic thriller set on the French Riviera where a string of jewel robberies have the local gendarmes chasing a one-time cat burglar (Cary Grant) who uses an heiress (Grace Kelly) to catch the real crook. Alfred Hitchcock directs the chic proceedings with his usual flair for the eccentric and off-beat, but there's more romance than suspense. Some stylized violence and veiled sexual references

title: To Commit a Murder
synopsis: French spy thriller in which an agent (Louis Jordan) either has to prevent a noted scientist from defecting to Red China or kill him and his accomplice (Edmond O'Brien). Directed by Edouard Molinaro, the formula plot is neatly packaged and moderately entertaining. Some violence

title: Today We Kill ...Tomorrow We Die!
synopsis: Poor Italian Western about a rancher (Montgomery Ford) who recruits four gunslingers to wipe out the gang responsible for the rape-murder of his wife. Director Tonino Cervi's production values are laughable but the violence is not

title: Todd Killings, The
synopsis: Lurid fact-based melodrama about a perverse killer (Robert F. Lyons) who sexually assaulted and mutilated a number of teenage girls in Tucson, Ariz. Directed by Barry Shear, the movie dwells on the sensational aspects of the case and as a result is quite sordid in its details

title: To Die For
synopsis: Black comedy in which an ambitious small-town TV weather forecaster (Nicole Kidman) begins filming a documentary about three teen-agers, then persuades them to murder her husband in order to make the film sensational enough to attract TV and movie sales. Director Gus Van Sant's biting satire lampoons the pursuit of fame and the media's avid coverage of killers while tending to trivialize a murderous act of vengeance that climaxes the story. Ambiguous treatment of revenge murder, brief violence, a few bedroom encounters and intemittent rough language

title: To Die in Madrid
synopsis: Excellent French documentary by Niclole Stephane and Frederic Rossif describes the bitter struggle that was the Spanish Civil War. Fine editing and a poetic commentary by Madeleine Chapsal help re-create the anguished emnotions of 1936-39 and derive some significance from the tragic war

title: To Die of Love
synopsis: Fact-based French drama about a teacher (Annie Girardot) who falls in love with a 17-year-old student (Bruno Pradal) and wants to marry him but, harassed by officals, she commits suicide. Directed by Andre Cayatte, the movie is more concerned with the impersonal bureaucratic system responsible for the tragedy than it is with the two main characters. Those viewing it as nothing more than a love story will find it romanticizing a relationship that the movie does not even try to make dramatically credible

title: To Each His Own
synopsis: Slick tearjerker about a World War I unwed mother (Olivia de Havilland) who gives up her baby boy, then watches from afar as he grows into manhood (John Lund) until they meet by chance during World War II. Directed by Mitchell Leisen, the flashback form of the narrative is mightily contrived and emotionally manipulative, but de Havilland makes the mother's heartache seem real enough

title: To End All Wars
synopsis: Affecting World War II drama about prisoners of war (including Kiefer Sutherland, Robert Carlyle and Ciaran McMenamin) forced by the Japanese to build the "railway of death" between Burma and Thailand and, despite experiencing brutal conditions at the hands of their captors, discover within themselves the capacity for compassion, mercy and forgiveness. Edited to maximize the humanity of the characters without overlooking the cruelty of war, director David L. Cunningham's fact-based film grapples with the difficulties of comprehending justice and living a morally upright life in the face of degradation, humiliation and death. Several scenes of war violence including torture and intermittent rough language

title: To Find a Man
synopsis: Self-centered Catholic girl (Pamela Martin) finds herself pregnant and returns home for the Christmas holidays to find an abortionist with some help from the boy next door (Darren O'Connor). The trouble with director Buzz Kulik's mediocre effort is its shallow treatment of adolescent values and acceptance of abortion as natural in a society where everything, including morality, is disposable

title: Together
synopsis: Touching story about a young violin prodigy (Tang Yun) and his father (Liu Peiqi), who, having traveled from a rural Chinese town to big-city Beijing, find themselves torn between two violin instructors, one passionate about music, the other promising fame. Weaving larger cultural issues into the father-son plot, director Chen Kaige hits all the right notes in composing a modest yet eloquently poetic coming-of-age symphony. Subtitles. Emotionally complex relationships

title: Together
synopsis: Pseudo-documentary promotes a summertime romp at the estate of a self-proclaimed pioneer in sexual guidance. Filmmakers Roger Murphy and Sean C. Cunningham encounter uninhibited and unclad couples who explicate and demonstrate their host's theories of tactile therapy

title: Together Brothers
synopsis: Good action movie, filmed in steamy Galveston, Texas, with a cast largely of unknowns, it involves a black street gang tracking down the killer of a cop who treated them fairly. Director William A. Graham gets some extraordinarily sensitive character portrayals and conveys a feel for the ramshackle black ghettos of Galveston. Though there is a minimum of street language, the sudden, concluding violence is adult fare

title: To Gillian on Her 37th Birthday
synopsis: Soapy tale of a widower (Peter Gallagher) who can't get over the death of his wife (Michelle Pfeiffer) until he comes to realize his obsession with keeping her memory alive is harming his relationship with his teenage daughter (Claire Danes). Scripted by David E. Kelley and directed by Michael Pressman, the hokey proceedings are too thin to sustain emotional credibility in the characters and their problems, especially the husband's soppy conversations with his late wife's apparition. Morbid obsession, sexual innunedo, a teen's excessive drinking and some rough language

title: To Have and Have Not
synopsis: Lively adventure from Ernest Hemingway's novel set in the Caribbean where the American captain (Humphrey Bogart) of a charter fishing boat throws in with the Free French resistance after being pushed around by Vichy agents in 1940 Martinique, while managing to find romance along the way with a slim adventuress (Lauren Bacall). Directed by Howard Hawks from a script by Jules Furthman and William Faulkner, the melodramatic action is secondary to the romantic subplot and interesting cast of stereotypes, notably Walter Brennan's drink-addled seaman and his recurring question: "Was you ever bit by a dead bee?" Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: To Hell and Back
synopsis: Audie Murphy plays himself in the Hollywood version of how he came to be the most decorated U.S. soldier in World War II. Directed by Jesse Hibbs, Murphy seems less self-conscious on the battlefield than off in portraying himself as a soft-spoken, patriotic Texas boy who enlists at 16, then proceeds to win medals fighting through North Africa, Sicily, Italy and France. Wartime violence and heroics as well as several muted sexual references

title: To Kill a Mockingbird
synopsis: When a Southern lawyer (Gregory Peck) undertakes the defense of a black man (Brock Peters) accused of rape, he has to help his young children cope with the town's racial hostilities and their own fears of a retarded neighbor (Robert Duvall). In this fine adaptation of the Harper Lee novel, director Robert Mulligan evokes a nostalgic picture of small-town life as seen mostly through the eyes of a youngster whose father is a reassuring figure of integrity in the confusing world of adults. Excellent for discussions of racial prejudice

title: To Kill a Priest
synopsis: Uneven fictionalized drama based on actual events in 1984 Poland when Father Jerzy Popieluszko, a popular pro-Solidarity activist (Christopher Lambert), was murdered by state security police on the orders of a captain (Ed Harris) obsessed by his conviction that the priest is a dangerous subversive. Filmed in France in the English language by Polish director Agnieszka Holland, the movie contrasts the spiritual power and national appeal of the priest with the wavering Marxist dedication of the psychologically troubled officer. The work succeeds best in its depiction of the historical context -- an armed government at war with its own people and their faith. Some hard-edged violence, a bedroom scene and several instances of rough language

title: Tokoloshe
synopsis: Uneven South African production about a winsome Bantu youngster (Saul Pelle) who escapes the curse of the evil spirit of the title through his mother's intervention and reaches safety in Johannesburg. Directed by Peter Prowse, the sequences in the city unfortunately lack the narrative interest and sense of conviction found in the earlier portions of the movie

title: Tokyo Joe
synopsis: Returning to Japan where he had built a business before the war, a former Army officer (Humphrey Bogart) is blackmailed into helping a gang of war criminals in order to save his ex-wife (Florence Marley) and child. Directed by Stuart Heisler, the convoluted proceedings unfold awkwardly and never quite jell into a satisfying whole. Stylized violence and heavy romantic complications

title: Tokyo Story
synopsis: Elderly couple on their first visit to the Tokyo homes of their children meet only disguised rejection except, ironically, for the kindness of their dead son's wife. When the mother dies shortly upon returning to their country village, it is only the widowed daughter-in-law who shows any real feeling of loss. Director Yasujiro Ozu's eloquent treatment of old age makes it a uniquely moving hymn to life

title: To Live
synopsis: A Chinese couple (Ge You and Gong Li) struggle to raise two children while coping with tumultuous personal and political upheavals during the civil war of the 1940s through three decades of poverty under the repressive reign of Chairman Mao and the excesses of the Cultural Revolution. Director Zhang Yimou's rich tapestry of bittersweet family life affords heartfelt insights into the universal will to live and to nurture one's family. Subtitles. Some gory corpses and a young woman's death in childbirth

title: To Live and Die in L.A.
synopsis: Director William Friedkin attempts to make a Southern California version of the "French Connection" in this story of two Treasury agents (William Petersen and John Pankow) pursuing a vicious counterfeiter (Willem Dafoe). The result, however, has no more depth than an extended music video. Brutal and so amoral that it's hard to tell the good guys from the bad

title: Tomahawk
synopsis: Routine Western directed by George Sherman is set in 1866 Wyoming where frontiersman Jim Bridger (Van Heflin) saves an enterprising entertainer (Yvonne de Carlo) as well as an Army garrison (under Preston Foster) from Sioux warriors stirred up by a cowardly soldier (Alex Nicol). Frontier violence

title: Tomahawk and the Cross, The
synopsis: ( see: "Pillars of the Sky" )

title: Tomahawk Trail, The
synopsis: Low-budget Western follows the misfortunes of a U.S. cavalry patrol after its horses are stolen by hostile Apaches, its lieutenant goes balmy and a sergeant (Chuck Connors) leads the troopers on foot to Fort Bowie where they find the garrison massacred. Directed by Lesley Selander, the story of the hard-luck patrol is mostly about men in combat or preparing for it, though the outcome relies on the friendship between the daughter of the Apache chief and a white woman captive. Frontier violence including attempted assaults on both women

title: Tom and Huck
synopsis: Sluggish tale of Tom Sawyer (Jonathan Taylor Thomas) and Huckleberry Finn (Brad Renfro) out to rescue the town drunk from being wrongly hanged for murder while preventing the killer from absconding with stolen gold. Directed by Peter Hewitt, the weak script results in a colorless narrative with no surprises and little adventure. Some violence, frequent menace and a profanity

title: Tom and Jerry -- The Movie
synopsis: When their home is demolished, the mischievous cartoon cat-and-mouse duo must take to the mean streets where they rescue a poor little rich girl from the clutches of a greedy aunt who's after her trust fund. Producer-director Phil Roman's adventuresome animated tale of the scrappy twosome will hold the small fry, while some of the six musical numbers sprinkled throughout this amiable cartoon may entertain grown-ups as well

title: Tomb of Ligeia, The
synopsis: Moody chills from the Edgar Allan Poe story in which a morose widower (Vincent Price) in Victorian England leaves off mourning his late wife (Elizabeth Shepherd) to wed a bright young lady (also Shepherd) who soon fears the first wife's unearthly presence in the form of a black cat. Directed by Roger Corman, the eerie tale of hypnotism and the undead doesn't quite hold together but the nighttime antics in the widower's creepy old abbey certainly hold attention. Supernatural menace

title: Tomboy
synopsis: Minor rural romance directed by Robert McGowan in which a brassy Chicago girl (Marcia Mae Jones) is enrolled in a country school where she takes up the cause of a farmboy classmate (Jackie Moran) who's overworked by his mean-spirited uncle

title: Tom Brown's School Days
synopsis: Sturdy version of the Thomas Hughes novel about the troubles of a new boy (Jimmy Lydon) in 19th-century England's Rugby where he's tormented by the house bully (Billy Halop), then ostracized mistakenly as a tattle-tale by classmates, but makes it through thanks to the school's reformist headmaster (Cedric Hardwicke). Director Robert Stevenson provides a robust period picture of life in a boys' boarding school and the struggle to end the tyranny of the older students

title: Tombstone
synopsis: Bloody retelling of the legendary events of 1879 in the Arizona town where a gang of murderous outlaws (led by Michael Biehn and Powers Boothe) come up against the new sheriff Wyatt Earp (Kurt Russell), his brothers (Sam Elliott, Bill Paxton) and Doc Holliday (Val Kilmer) who have decided to wipe them out. George P. Cosmatos directs a glossy dud filled with shootouts between wooden characters mouthing cliches while attired in high-fashion Western duds. Excessive violence including numerous grisly murders, acceptance of cold-blooded murder, recurring substance abuse and an instance of rough language

title: Tomcats
synopsis: Crass comedy about a cartoonist (Jerry O'Connell) whose only way to clear hefty gambling debts is to win a pooled bet by being the last of his buddies to get hitched, but first he must quickly marry off his philandering friend and sole competition (Jake Busey). Barely worth the celluloid it's printed on, director Gregory Poirer's derivative film has a strained premise and calculated, repulsive gross-out humor. Many sexual situations and crude sexual references, fleeting nudity, some homosexual innuendo, brief violence and sporadic rough language with some profanity. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Tom, Dick and Harry
synopsis: Daffy comedy in which a telephone operator (Ginger Rogers) has strange dreams about her persistent suitors -- a rich socialite (Alan Marshal), a car salesman (George Murphy) and a genial dreamer (Burgess Meredith) -- with her choice coming as no surprise. Director Garson Kanin has a lot of fun with the attitudes of the time, especially in the wacky dream sequences, but the love story's sentimentality wears less well. Romantic complications

title: Tom Horn
synopsis: Frontier hero at the end of his career (Steve McQueen) is hired by a group of ranchers to stop some rustlers, a job he performs with such murderous zeal that they decide to get rid of him by framing him for murder. Though director William Wiard fails to provide much dramatic steam, McQueen's solid performance raises the material a notch above the standard Western. Some graphic violence

title: Tom Jones
synopsis: Zestful adaptation of Henry Fielding's classic novel about the misadventures, largely amorous, of a young man (Albert Finney) among the high-born and low of 18th-century England. Director Tony Richardson treats the melodramatic proceedings with a droll combination of mock heroics, antic slapstick, bawdy asides and much social satire. Though the humor is often coarse and the blood-lust of a deer hunt is brutally graphic, it succeeds largely as a period comedy of manners and morals

title: Tommy
synopsis: British adaptation of Peter Townshend's rock opera about a pinball wizard (Roger Daltrey) who becomes a religious guru and ends as a rejected mystic calling out for a new consciousness. Though the performances of Eric Clapton, Elton John and Tina Turner are excellent, director Ken Russell's treatment is ludicrously out of control, obscuring the sense of the opera by an undue emphasis on visual pyrotechnics that is not dramatic but destructive. Satiric jabs at religion are excessive if taken literally

title: Tommy Boy
synopsis: Derivative comedy in which a porky, likable dimwit (Chris Farley) battles the machinations of his late dad's scheming bride (Bo Derek) while trying to save the family business from a hostile takeover, getting grudging help from a clever employee (David Spade). Director Peter Segal's innocuous buddy movie offers only a few funny moments sandwiched between endless fat jokes. Some slapstick violence, minor sexual innuendo, a few crude remarks and minimal profanity

title: Tomorrow
synopsis: Winter watchman (Robert Duvall) for a backwoods Mississippi sawmill gives shelter to a pregnant woman (Olga Bellin) abandoned by her husband. As the winter passes, he falls in love with her, but she dies shortly after her child is born. Adapted from a William Faulkner story by Horton Foote and directed by Joseph Anthony, the material is sparse, even tedious, but the characters -- the taciturn man of the land and the wornout woman -- convey a genuine sense of the American rural ethic

title: Tomorrow Never Dies
synopsis: The 18th James Bond movie finds superagent 007 (Pierce Brosnan) out to prevent a maniacal missile-bearing media magnate (Jonathan Pryce) from instigating a war between England and China in order to boost ratings for his new global news network. Directed by Roger Spottiswoode, the explosive action is virtually non-stop, bypassing Bond's supposed suave sophistication in favor of numbingly mindless mayhem. Excessive violence, sexual innuendo and fleeting profanity

title: Tom Sawyer
synopsis: Reader's Digest musical adaptation of the Mark Twain classic with Johnny Whitaker as Tom, Jeff East as Huck, Jodie Foster as Becky and Celeste Holm as Aunt Polly. Directed by Don Taylor, the movie is a quite diverting though undistinguished bit of nostalgia that, if it misses the wit and cultural perceptions of the orginal, succeeds nonetheless in being continually engaging. Young viewers will be delighted

title: Tom Thumb
synopsis: Amiable retelling of the Brothers Grimm fairy tale about a woodsman and his wife (Bernard Miles and Jessie Matthews) whose thumb-sized son (Russ Tamblyn) thwarts the scheme of a comic pair of villains (Terry-Thomas and Peter Sellers) to rob the village treasury. Director George Pal mixes a variety of animation and special effects with occasional lyrics sung by Peggy Lee to fashion a pleasant fantasy that will amuse children and pacify parents, though of less appeal for more demanding viewers

title: Tom & Viv
synopsis: Literate portrait of the turbulent marriage of American-born, British-based poet T.S. Eliot (Willem Dafoe) to first wife Vivien Haigh-Wood (Miranda Richardson) from 1914 through Viv's growing mood swings which in 1936 cause Tom to have her committed to an institution where she remained until her death in 1947. Brian Gilbert directs this adaptation of Michael Hasting's controversial play portraying Vivien as a true collaborator on Eliot's poetry as well as a tragic victim of his social ambitions and inability to discuss intimate personal problems, notably her hormonal imbalance. Harrowing depiction of a troubled marital relationship and some sexual innuendo

title: Tonight and Every Night
synopsis: Wartime morale booster pays tribute to the brave cast and stagehands of a London music hall who put on five performances a day throughout the Blitz, even living in the theater during the worst of the bombing, though the revue's American star (Rita Hayworth) finds time for romance with an RAF pilot (Lee Bowman). Directed by Victor Saville, the musical numbers are bright but unmemorable and the cardboard romance becomes tiresome long before the bittersweet patriotic ending. Sexual situations and innunedo

title: Tonka the Comanche
synopsis: Director Lewis R. Foster's mildly entertaining Disney movie is set in the Old West where a young Indian (Sal Mineo) captures a wild stallion, loses him and then gets back again

title: Tony Rome
synopsis: Frank Sinatra stars as a Miami private eye who displays a nice sense of values and humor as his work takes him deeper and deeper into the corrupt layers of the resort town. Directed by Gordon Douglas, its sporadic gunplay and fist-fights are standard but some of the subject matter is sordid and some of the language is rough

title: Too Beautiful for You
synopsis: Wealthy Frenchman (Gerard Depardieu) shocks his beautiful wife (Carole Bouquet) and their friends by falling madly in love with a plain, plump woman (Josiane Balasko). Director Bertrand Blier twists the cliches of marital infidelity and French film convention with this serio-comic farce that mixes fantasy with reality and raises but does not answer philosophical questions about love, infidelity and the nature of sexual attraction. Subtitles. Some sexually explicit dialogue

title: Too Late Blues
synopsis: Ambitious jazz bandleader (Bobby Darrin) falls for a novice singer (Stella Stevens), goes haywire when they break up and leaves the band cold to go it alone, though his envious agent (Everett Chambers) sets him up for a fall. Directed by John Cassavetes, the cameraderie between the musicians and their circle makes a convincing background for a story which has many fine scenes but never quite jells as a dramatic whole. Some stylized violence, notably a drunken brawl, and sexual situations

title: Too Late the Hero
synopsis: Routine World War II movie set on a small Pacific island where an Allied patrol (notably Cliff Robertson and Michael Caine) makes its way through the jungle to blow up a Japanese radio transmitter, then returns back to base. Director Robert Aldrich offers the usual amount of bloody violence in glossy color but all except hardened action buffs will find it disappointing. Some hard-edged wartime violence

title: Too Many Girls
synopsis: Sappy Rodgers and Hart musical in which collegiate football stars (Richard Carlson, Eddie Bracken, Hal LeRoy and Desi Arnaz), hired as bodyguards for a millionaire's daughter (Lucille Ball) attending Pottawatomie College in New Mexico, transform the small school into a football powerhouse. Director George Abbott stages the sophomoric proceedings in stilted fashion, pausing occasionally for forgettable songs (Frances Langford) and dance numbers (Ann Miller) whose energy seems misplaced. Considerable emphasis on double entendres

title: Too Much Sun
synopsis: The fortune left in an old man's will galvanizes various money grabbers, including the man's gay son (Eric Idle), his lesbian daughter (Andrea Martin) and his unscrupulous parish priest (Jim Haynie). Director Robert Downey's sex farce mocks gays and religious in a lame attempt at outrageous humor that never gets beyond tasteless twaddle. Promiscuous encounters, heavy homosexual innuendo and much rough language

title: Too Much Too Soon
synopsis: In this account of the troubled life of Diana Barrymore (Dorothy Malone), she leaves her domineering mother, writer Michael Strange (Neva Patterson), for an acting career in Hollywood but fails badly, then sees her father, John Barrymore (Errol Flynn), die of alcoholism and becomes one herself. Directed by Art Napoleon, the glossy proceedings have little depth and are mostly unconvincing, except for Flynn's compelling performance as a gifted actor who's lost his bearings. Violence, sexual situations and alcoholic excess

title: Too Outrageous
synopsis: Low-budget Canadian production about a homosexual (Craig Russell) whose career as a female impersonator leads to a chance at television stardom if he will change his act, but he prefers to remain the way he is. Written and directed by Dick Benner, the movie condones but does not glamorize homosexual relationships

title: Tootsie
synopsis: Very funny movie about an unemployed actor (Dustin Hoffman) who dresses up as a woman to get a part in a TV soap opera, but his success in the role complicates matters when he falls in love with the show's beautiful co-star (Jessica Lange). Director Sydney Pollack's romantic comedy makes some witty points about being a woman in a man's world. Adult sexual humor

title: Topaz
synopsis: Alfred Hitchcock's adaptation of the pulpy Leon Uris novel about high-powered espionage and counterspying in a variety of exotic locales. The dialogue is mostly banal and the action largely unconvincing, but there are occasional glimmers of the Hitchcock touch in subtle plot twists here and blind alleys there. Diverting if ultimately disappointing. Some physical and psychological violence and a lot of confusing intrigue

title: Topaze
synopsis: Droll comedy from Marcel Pagnol's play in which a poor but honest Paris schoolteacher (John Barrymore) becomes a wealthy man after turning the tables on the baron (Reginald Mason) who duped him into promoting a shoddy product. Directed by Harry d'Abbadie d'Arrast, the story's humor stems from Barrymore's tongue-in-cheek portrayal of the meek academic who learns to enjoy the rewards of dishonesty. An unfaithful husband and sexual innuendo

title: Top Dog
synopsis: Dumb action-comedy in which a San Diego cop (Chuck Norris) investigating a blood-thirsty band of neo-Nazi terrorists is assigned a shaggy canine partner who sniffs out clues about the imminent bombing of a gathering of religious leaders. Director Aaron Norris does little but intercut cutesy, unrelated doggy tricks with standard martial arts violence and gunfights but this feeble attempt at humor does not make the results any less violent. Intermittent violence and an instance of profanity

title: Topeka Terror, The
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Howard Bretherton in which a cowboy (Allan Lane) takes a hand when he sees a group of settlers being swindled out of their land claims during the 1889 Oklahoma Land Rush. Frontier violence

title: Top Gun
synopsis: The bravado of a Navy hot-shot jet pilot (Tom Cruise) wins the grudging admiration of his comrades, the affection of his female flight instructor (Kelly McGillis) and audience commendation for his patriotic hip-shooting heroism. Director Tony Scott's high-flying celebration of peacetime military training is mostly a hollow exercise in macho derring-do. Fairly restrained bedroom scene, brief nudity and incidental profanity

title: Top Hat
synopsis: Stylish musical romance between a hoofer (Fred Astaire) and a socialite (Ginger Rogers) starts with comic misunderstandings in London, then go on to ever more zany encounters in Venice. Director Mark Sandrich keeps the lightweight proceedings on the boil, with only the dance routines and Irving Berlin songs providing any substance. Sexual innuendo and frivolous treatment of marriage

title: Topkapi
synopsis: Entertaining adaptation of Eric Ambler's comic thriller in which a bungling two-bit con man (Peter Ustinov) becomes part of a fantastic plot to steal a priceless jeweled dagger from the Istanbul Museum. Directed with gusto by Jules Dassin, the suspenseful caper is pulled off in sparkling style by a cast including Melina Mercouri, Maximillian Schell and Robert Morley, but they are all upstaged by a little bird. Some stylized violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Top of the Heap
synopsis: Black policeman in Washington, D.C., (Christopher St. John who also wrote, produced and directed) works with racist, bribe-taking fellow officers and off the job his wife browbeats him, his daughter experiments with sex and drugs and even his boozy mistress mocks him with abandon. He proves as nasty as anyone else in a movie that goes out of its way to alienate viewers with needless, salacious nudity and an endless barrage of gutter epithets

title: Topo Gigio
synopsis: Delightful little movie about a small talking mouse who outwits a wicked magician to save his friends. Young children will love it and the puppet characterization is droll enough to please their parents

title: Top o' the Morning
synopsis: Thin slice of stereotyped Irish whimsey as a Manhattan insurance investigator (Bing Crosby) comes to Cork to recover the stolen Blarney Stone, then falls for the daughter (Ann Blyth) of a cranky village policeman (Barry Fitzgerald) whose dim assistant (Hume Cronyn) keeps gumming up the works. Directed by David Miller, the lighthearted proceedings are darkened by the strange prophecies of a local wise woman (Eileen Crowe) and a heavy-handed conclusion involving murder, though there are enough Irish songs to keep a viewer's eyes shining

title: Topper
synopsis: Comic fantasy from the Thorne Smith novel in which a carefree couple (Cary Grant and Constance Bennett) die in a drunken car accident, then return as ghosts to do a good deed by helping the dull title banker (Roland Young) learn to enjoy life. Directed by Norman Z. McLeod, Topper's frantic reactions to the invisible pair's shenanigans are still quite funny, though the proceedings may be a bit slow-paced for present tastes. Sexual innuendo and comic inebriation

title: Topper Returns
synopsis: Zany sequel with Topper (Roland Young) reluctantly aiding a ghost (Joan Blondell) solve her own murder in the spooky mansion of her girlfriend (Carole Landis) whose ailing father (H.B. Warner) is in the care of a sinister doctor (George Zucco). Director Roy Del Ruth mixes perilous situations involving a cloaked mystery figure, sliding panels and hidden passages with the wacky goings-on of a very funny cast (Billie Burke, Eddie Rochester, Patsy Kelly, Donald McBride and Dennis O'Keefe). Comic menace

title: Top Secret
synopsis: Creators of "Airplane" (Jim Abrahams, David Zucker and Jerry Zucker) have set out to parody movies of international intrigue. But this time they haven't gotten it right and most of the jokes misfire. Some sexually oriented humor

title: Top Secret Affair
synopsis: Glossy romantic comedy in which a magazine publisher (Susan Hayward) sets out to trash the reputation of an Army general (Kirk Douglas) to keep him from getting a diplomatic post, then falls in love with him. Directed by H.C. Potter, the on-again, off-again romance becomes increasingly tiresome, though Hayward's bright performance almost makes it work. Sexual situations

title: Topsy-Turvy
synopsis: Sprightly dramatization follows the 1884 career slump of British light-opera mavens Gilbert and Sullivan (Jim Broadbent and Allan Corduner), followed by renewed vigor on their next, and best-remembered collaboration, ``The Mikado.'� Director Mike Leigh turns in a lengthy, bustling valentine to the creative process involved in musical theatre productions while wryly mocking the human frailties of the artistic temperament. Sexual situations with brief full nudity, references to abortion and occasional substance abuse

title: Tora! Tora! Tora!
synopsis: Huge, sprawling and occasionally unfocused wartime epic based on the events leading up to the surprise Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor. Director Richard Fleischer alternates American and Japanese points of view as the one side goes about its daily routines unsuspecting the deadly assault that the other side is preparing. The Japanese segments are the more interesting in showing less known aspects of a strategy that some realized would start an unwinnable war

title: Torchlight
synopsis: The destruction of a succcssful businessman and loving husband (Steve Railsback) by cocaine is a serious and important theme but director Tom Wright's treatment is so uninspired and at times ludicrous that the movie fails even as a cautionary tale. Explicit depiction of drug taking

title: Torch Song
synopsis: Slick romantic melodrama in which a tough-as-nails musical star (Joan Crawford) comes to realize that she's only human when she falls for a blind pianist (Michael Wilding) unintimidated by her success or tantrums. Directed by Charles Walters, the vehicle provides a chance for Crawford to strut in the musical routines (including a blackface number) while showing off her emotional range in the character's change of heart. For incurable romantics

title: Torch Song Trilogy
synopsis: Screen version of Harvey Fierstein's play about a homosexual (Fierstein) who works as a female impersonator in a drag revue and his unfulfilling love life and ongoing mother-son conflicts. Directed by Paul Bogart, the movie compassionately and often raucously shows the common threads that connect heterosexual and homosexual family relationships, courtship and love, but its validation of homosexuality and depiction of promiscuity in the 1970s is disturbing, especially in light of the AIDS epidemic. A few fleeting scenes of male kissing and discreet touching, a scene of a brutal beating, much rough language with homosexual innuendoes and a few bawdy musical drag numbers

title: Torn Apart
synopsis: Trite romance about an Israeli youth (Adrian Pasdar) and a Palestinian girl (Cecilia Peck) who defy the wishes of their families only to be sacrificed to the political conflict that engulfs them. Director Jack Fisher fails to develop the characters as individuals and the narrative never gets beyond a superficial examination of Mid-East tensions and the human realities behind them. Intermittent scenes of bloodshed and violence and a restrained scene of sexual passion

title: Torn Curtain
synopsis: Slack Alfred Hitchcock suspense thriller about an American physicist (Paul Newman) who pretends to defect to East Germany in order to get some secret information. The predictable plot is further marred by a detailed treatment of a realistically brutal killing

title: Torpedo Alley
synopsis: Routine service drama from director Lew Landers in which a guilt-ridden World War II Navy pilot (Mark Stevens) flops in civilian life, then tries to pull himself together by re-enlisting in the Navy and graduates from submarine school in time to become a hero in the Korean War. Wartime violence

title: Torpedo Run
synopsis: Turgid war actioner directed by Joseph Pevney with Glenn Ford as a troubled submarine skipper chasing a Japanese aircraft carrier across the Pacific, intent on sinking it to avenge the deaths of his wife and daughter. Standard wartime heroics and underwater dangers

title: Torque
synopsis: Sleek but vacuous action flick in which a heartthrob biker (Martin Henderson) is framed for murdering the brother of a motorcycle gang leader (Ice Cube) by a ruthless drug dealer (Matt Schulze) from whom he stole several motorcycles stuffed with drugs. Director Joseph Kahn�s tightly choreographed fight scenes and outrageous, far-fetched biker stunts are devoid of spontaneity, and only thinly veil a forced narrative bloated with artificial dialogue and good-looking actors who mainly pose and pout, but fail to convince on any level. Several scenes of stylized violence, some sexual references and sensuality, drug content, sporadic crass language and profanity

title: Torrent
synopsis: Creaky silent melodrama from the Blasco Ibanez novel about star-crossed lovers in Spain as a wealthy mama's boy (Ricardo Cortez) comes to regret breaking his vows of love to a poor country girl (Greta Garbo) after she goes to Paris and becomes a famous opera star. Directed by Monta Bell, the picture's highlight is a torrential flood but it's not enough to save this soggy tale of unrequited love between a weak hero and a strong heroine. Romantic complications

title: Torrents of Spring
synopsis: Visually lovely, emotionally bland version of Ivan Turgenev's novel about a 19th-century Russian nobleman (Timothy Hutton) traveling in Germany who becomes engaged to a sweet Italian immigrant (Valeria Golino) but then falls passionately in love with the wanton wife (Nastassja Kinski) of an old school chum. Director Jerzy Skolimowski fails to clearly delineate the time and place of this oddly cast, multi-national movie whose one-dimensional characters undercut its cautionary tale of misdirected love. Lengthy, clothed sexual liaison

title: Torrid Zone
synopsis: Tough-guy romantic comedy set in Latin America where the cynical manager (Pat O'Brien) of a banana export company uses a stranded night club entertainer (Ann Sheridan) to keep his top troubleshooter (James Cagney) from taking a job in Chicago. Directed by William Keighley, the shifting Cagney-Sheridan romance takes a backseat to the movie's he-man heroics and adolescent pranks that seem less amusing today than then. Stylized violence, ethnic stereotypes and sexual innuendo

title: Torso
synopsis: Low-budget European co-production is a heavy-breathing, sex-and-brutality melodrama directed by Sergio Martino and dubbed into a language at times reminiscent of idiomatic English

title: Tortilla Heaven
synopsis: Well-meaning misfire about wacky complications and a mysterious stranger in a devout Southwestern hamlet when the image of Jesus manifests itself on a tortilla. The ensemble comedy-drama by first-time feature director Judy Hecht Dumontet, who also co-wrote the script, finds curmudgeonly nonbeliever Isidor Navarro (Jose Zuniga), owner of the Tortilla Heaven restaurant in a tiny New Mexican town, caught between a miracle and Mammon as his friends, family, the mayor and the local priest (all played by a remarkably high-profile cast of Latino actors including George Lopez, Alexis Cruz, Elpidia Carrillo, Irene Bedard, Geno Silva, Marcelo Tubert and Anna Ortiz of TV's "Ugly Betty") try to cash in on pilgrimage tourism with the help of a shady dealmaker (an excellent Miguel Sandoval)

title: Torture Chamber of Baron Blood, The
synopsis: ( see: "Baron Blood" )

title: Torture Dungeon
synopsis: Bungled medieval tale about a duke's problems in ensuring an heir for his kingdom, preoccupied as he is in dispatching his peers of both sexes by prolonged torture or sudden death. Played apparently for laughs, the movie is far from funny in its own preoccupation with nudity and acts of swift, bloody violence

title: Torture Garden
synopsis: Five visitors to a carnival fright show run by Dr. Diablo (Burgess Meredith) are given warning visions of the inner evil within each. Written by Robert Bloch and directed by Freddie Francis, the omnibus is more hokey than scary, though the episode about a collector (Jack Palance) of Edgar Allen Poe memorabilia has at least a suitably sinister atmosphere. Fanciful but unconvincing scenes of violence

title: Tosca
synopsis: Filmed version of Puccini’s opera in which the passionate Tosca (Angela Gheorghiu) is tricked into betraying her lover (Roberto Alagna) by a lustful baron (Ruggero Raimondi) who gets his comeuppance from her before she joins her doomed beloved. While the music, voices, performances and costumes are grandly operatic, director BenoitJacquot’s techniques are choppy and his filming artlessly stagebound. Subtitles.Brief violence and an implied affair. A-III - - adults. (Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America) 2002 Full Review Opera lovers who can tolerate seeing a work not performed live before their eyes may enjoy director Benoit Jacquot's filmed adaptation of Giacomo Puccini's 1900 opera, "Tosca" (Avatar). Film has the advantage of allowing each viewer to see the facial close-ups, unlike an opera house where some individuals strain to see the performers from the nosebleed section. Jacquot uses this plus to good advantage, yet in other respects his technique is puzzling. Instead of opening up "Tosca" to the possibilities that film offers, he chooses to keep it stagebound. Each act, set in 1800, is confined to one set. On the other hand, he abruptly intercuts brief scenes of Antonio Pappano conducting the orchestra and of the actors recording in the studio, or grainy visuals of the countryside and an ornate church interior, none of which adds anything to the overall effect, except to distract. The production itself, however, has a lush look, especially the glorious costumes worn by Tosca (Angela Gheorghiu), and some shots of her in long view and from above are beautifully composed. She carries the film with her impassioned performance, emotional expressiveness and commanding vocal talent. Playing her lover Mario is her real-life husband, Roberto Alagna, who emotes less but still makes a strong impression. Bringing a steely ferocity to his villainous role is Ruggero Raimondi as the Baron Scarpia, who tricks Tosca into betraying her lover, thinking he will also seduce her, but she vents her rage on him and rushes out to rejoin her lover for the climactic finale. In a lesser role, David Cangelosi makes a truly repulsive toady to the arrogant Scarpia. While the look and tone of the movie are grandly operatic, the cutaways to the orchestra and performers in street clothes break the spell and give the impression of outtakes from a rehearsal. Nor does their singing always seem to be in sync. On other occasions the actors are seen murmuring their lines in Italian while their singing voices are heard in the background. Some may feel the movie offers an intimacy not found in a large opera house while others may simply leave the film disappointed with its less-than-cinematic treatment of Puccini's work. Subtitles. Because of brief violence and an implied affair, the U. S. Conference of Catholic Bishops

title: To Sir with Love
synopsis: Warm British melodrama about an American (Sidney Poitier) who takes a teaching job in London where he tries to turn teenage students from a Cockney slum into ladies and gentlemen. Though the story offers some pat solutions for real problems and the student transformations seem overswift, director James Clavell gets winning performances from Poitier and his fine supporting cast to show aspects of life, love and adolescence that American audiences will find familiar, despite the accent

title: To Sleep with Anger
synopsis: Tensions within a black middle-class family escalate when a boyhood pal from the Deep South (Danny Glover) shows up on the Los Angeles doorstep of the family patriarch (Paul Butler) and slyly insinuates himself into the family circle. Glover's multi-layered performance and a fine ensemble cast help director Charles Burnett meld comedy and drama into a cohesive whole contrasting the servile ways of the rural South with modern urban life. Mild violence and a few vulgarities

title: Total Recall
synopsis: Ultraviolent sci-fi thriller about a man (Arnold Schwarzenegger) who has to travel to Mars to discover why his wife (Sharon Stone), as well as total strangers, are trying to kill him. Director Paul Verhoeven's intricate plot exposes an ugly futuristic society where human life warrants no respect, women are manipulative sexual playthings and the only solution to injustice is massive bloodshed. Excessive violence, sexual exploitation, including nudity, and rough language

title: Toto le Heros
synopsis: Believing he was switched in the hospital nursery with a neighborhood boy who then led a privileged life, an embittered old man (Michel Bouquet) recalls his lifelong envy and fantasies about killing the man who ``stole'' his life. Using flashbacks and fantasies, Belgian writer-director Jaco Van Dormael imaginatievly captures an entire lifespan going from a child's innocence to a crusty old codger who finally learns to accept the mixed blessings of the life he has led. Subtitles. An implied affair, brief violence and momentary nudity

title: To Trap a Spy
synopsis: Movie version of the TV spy series, "The Man from U.N.C.L.E.," features Robert Vaughn going through his paces as a superagent with little help from the sets, the gimmicks or director Don Medford. Violence and sexual innuendo

title: Touch
synopsis: Botched satire from Elmore Leonard's novel about a Catholic stigmatic (Skeet Ulrich) whose healing powers attract the attention of a one-time bogus faith healer (Christopher Walken) but his plans to exploit those powers for profit go awry when the miracle worker falls in love with the con man's confederate (Bridget Fonda). Scripted and directed by Paul Schrader, the heavy-handed narrative drifts along, aimlessly following the eccentric types who make up the tiresome plot, but even worse is the movie's negative attitude to institutional religion. Due to jaundiced views of religion, sexual situations, rear nudity, coarse language and occasional profanity

title: Touchables, The
synopsis: Dull British sex fantasy ineptly directed by Robert Freeman in which four teenage girls kidnap a rock star and force him to make love to them

title: Touch and Go
synopsis: French World War II comedy about a French deserter (Michel Picoli), an inept British officer (Michael York) and the wife of the Swiss consul (Marlene Jobart) who find themselves fleeing for their lives from Nazis who are certain they are spies. Director Philippe de Broca's comedy is full of sight gags, absurd situations and broad humor that not everyone appreciates. His insistence upon the wartime vulnerability of his characters, however, makes the laughter at their ridiculous adventures somewhat uneasy

title: Touch and Go
