synopsis: Failed medieval romance about two young lovers (Anjelica Huston and Assaf Dayan) caught in the midst of a peasant's war and doomed to death either by knight's sword or serf's cudgel. Directed by John Huston, the dark atmosphere of feudalism is convincing but little else is, especially the acting of its two young principals. Mature theme and treatment

title: WALL-E
synopsis: Beautiful and deeply touching futuristic fable about a soulful-eyed waste removal robot (voice of Ben Burtt), the last on an abandoned, garbage-strewn earth, who falls in love with a visiting search robot (Elissa Knight) and follows her onto a spaceship manned by an ineffectual Captain (Jeff Garlin) and populated by earth's passively sedentary obese refugees. Using Pixar's breathtaking animation techniques, director and co-writer Andrew Stanton has concocted a canny mix of sharp humor, honest sentiment and surprisingly potent romance with (for those adults looking deeper) an underlying indictment of our consumer-oriented society and a timely environmental warning. An instant classic

title: Wall Street: Money Never Sleeps
synopsis: Uneven sequel in which, seven years after being released from prison, a disgraced financier-turned-author (Michael Douglas) convinces his estranged daughter's (Carey Mulligan) fiance (Shia LaBeouf) to help him reconcile with her. He offers in return to assist the young investment executive's business vendetta against a ruthless mogul (Josh Brolin) whose machinations ruined the lad's mentor (Frank Langella). Set against the backdrop of the economic crisis that began in 2007, and directed -- like its 1987 predecessor "Wall Street" -- by Oliver Stone, the high stakes drama benefits from Douglas' magnetic performance as a man compounded of charisma, corruption and a few remaining shards of human decency. Less appealing are the script's heavy-handed attempts at social comment and a central romantic relationship that puts the sexual cart before the marital horse. Cohabitation, brief sexual imagery and occasional sexual references, several uses of profanity, at least two instances of rough language, a few crude and some crass terms

title: Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit
synopsis: Frolicsome clay-animated adventure about a cheese-loving inventor (voiced by Peter Sallis) and his faithful pooch, who are hired by a batty blueblood (voiced by Helena Bonham Carter) to catch a monstrous rabbit terrorizing neighborhood gardens before it jeopardizes the town's annual vegetable competition. Co-directed by Nick Park and Steve Box (based on characters created by Park), the disarmingly whimsical and visually delightful film is an amusing family treat, despite a few "naughty" jokes that will go over the heads of most children. Some double entendres and a brief, mildly irreligious sight gag

title: Wall in Jerusalem, A
synopsis: Excellent documentary account of the birth of the state of Israel in 1948, and its struggle for survival ever since, limits itself chiefly to political history, detailing various major events and the leaders who participated in them. Director Frederic Rossif's compilation of archival footage makes a fascinating visual chronicle and Richard Burton's narration lets the images communicate the emotion while it understates the facts

title: Wall Street
synopsis: An earnest young stockbroker (Charlie Sheen) wnats to make an honest million but a financial wheeler-dealer (Michael Douglas) teaches him that there are easier ways to make money than working for it. Directed by Oliver Stone, the cautionary tale does a creditable job in showing how part of the financial community has made greed a way of life but is somewhat unconvincing in its dramatization of the corruption of an innocent and his ultimate redemption. Several scenes depicting sexual activity and some very rough language

title: Wanda
synopsis: Low-budget but impressive portrait of a woman, a nobody wandering through life conditioned to being badly used by others, who meets an insecure petty thief (Michael Higgins) and the two go off together, leaving viewers hoping this relationship will turn out better than her other experiences. Directed by and starring Barbara Loden, the movie succeeds in making an unvarnished plea for understanding the needs of isolated, impoverished human beings

title: Wanda Nevada
synopsis: Laid-back gambler (Peter Fonda who also directs) wins an orphan (Brooke Shields) in a poker game and then goes hunting for gold with her in the Grand Canyon. Indian ghosts and a couple of flesh and blood villains complicate matters, but not enough to make things interesting. Some violence and the unresolved nature of the relationship between the two principals make this aimless movie adult fare

title: Wanderers, The
synopsis: Screen version of the novel by Richard Price about a group of Italian teenagers growing up in the Bronx in 1963 has a lot of vitality and some good acting (Ken Wahl, John Friedrich, Karen Allen). Philip Kaufman's direction, however, is too pretentious to stir any real emotional response in a movie that lacks a significant context. Violence, sexual references and foul language. O (R) ( 1979 )

title: Wanderer, The
synopsis: French screen version of the Alain-Fournier novel about the romantic illusions of youth melting into the realities and responsibilities of adulthood in a story focusing on the one boy in the class who never quite matures and ultimately brings tragedy to those he loves most. Director Jean-Gabriel Albicocco has beautifully filmed the simple, turn-of-the-century narrative, conveying well the adult narrator's glow of nostalgia for those youthful years. Subtitles

title: Wannsee Conference, The
synopsis: German dramatization of the meeting held on January 20, 1942, at which the final decision was made by the Nazi leadership to exterminate all European Jews. Directed by Heinz Schirk, it is an historical document filled with anti-Semitic statements but the brutish manner of the participants shows them clearly as racists. Mature theme and treatment

title: Wanted
synopsis: Overheated action rampage in which a downtrodden, panic-prone accountant (James McAvoy) is recruited by the leader (Morgan Freeman) of a secret fraternity of assassins and trained by its members (Angelina Jolie, Marc Warren, Konstantin Khabensky and Dato Bakhtadze) to avenge the murder of his estranged father (David O'Hara), who was also their colleague. Spectacular special effects fail to camouflage the random violence and glamorization of killing that underpin Kazak director Timur Bekmambetov's slick comic-book adaptation. Bloody violence, graphic sexual activity, rear nudity, beatings, nonmarital cohabitation, pervasive rough and crude language, a few profanities and birth-control references

title: Wanted Dead or Alive
synopsis: Bounty hunter (Rutger Hauer) tracks down a ruthless international terrorist (Gene Simmons), but is then set up as bait, loses his best friend and his lover, which impels him to inflict a terrible vengeance on those responsible. Its rough language, bloodshed and brutality are not redeemed by director Gary Sherman's eye-for-an-eye brand of justice. O (R) ( 1987 )

title: War
synopsis: In this brutal police thriller, an FBI agent (Jason Statham) has his hands full when the legendary assassin (Jet Li) who murdered his partner (Terry Chen) returns to San Francisco and sparks a war between the absent leader of the Japanese Yakuza (Ryo Ishibashi), who is represented locally by his ruthless daughter (Devon Aoki), and the very present commander of the Chinese Triads in the city (John Lone). Philip G. Atwell's noisy, overblown film offers some interesting plot developments, but ultimately tries to substitute sound and fury for genuine drama. Extensive violence with gore, torture and mutilation, rear and upper female nudity, frequent rough and crude language, and occasional profanity

title: War and Peace
synopsis: Episodic Hollywood version of Leo Tolstoy's epic novel centers on Russian aristocrats (Mel Ferrer, Audrey Hepburn and Henry Fonda) caught up in the Napoleonic Wars. Directed by King Vidor, the U.S.-Italian co-production muddles through the human dimension of events but excels in its reenactment of military movements and historic battles, especially Napoleon's retreat from Moscow through the devastations of a Russian winter. Stylized violence and muted romance

title: War and Peace
synopsis: Massive Russian version of the Tolstoy novel, originally released in three parts, evokes both the feeling of an era (1805 Russia threatened by Napoleon's march East) and Tolstoy's vision of individuals and destiny. Directed by and starring Sergei Bondarchuk as the contemplative Pierre, the movie in its sweep and detail provides an absorbing visual rendition of a great classic

title: War Arrow
synopsis: Standard Western fare with a cavalry officer (Jeff Chandler) training a band of Seminole Indians to fight Kiowa hostiles in Texas, despite interference from his Indian-hating superior (John McIntire). Director George Sherman does better with the action scenes, including an all-out attack on the fort, than with a romantic subplot involving the hero with an apparent widow (Maureen O'Hara) and an Indian maid (Suzan Ball)

title: War at Home, The
synopsis: Sluggish story of a traumatized Vietnam vet (Emilio Estevez) returning to 1972 Texas as a psychological time bomb, increasingly consumed by inner rage that his parents (Kathy Bates and Martin Sheen) expect him to get on with life and stop thinking about those he unwillingly killed. Also directed by Estevez, the talky drama illustrates that war can destroy many more lives than those taken on the battlefield. Scenes of wartime violence and frequent profanity and rough language

title: War Between Men and Women, The
synopsis: Caustic cartoonist with failing eyesight (Jack Lemmon) hates women, children and dogs, and naturally succumbs to the charms of a divorcee (Barbara Harris) who has three children and a terrier. Losing his sight completely, he is overtaken by a bout of self-pity that cuts him off from wife and children. Written and directed by Melville Shavelson, it tries to wring humor and pathos out of a human tragedy by using casual profanity, misanthropic wit and finally cloying sentimentality

title: War Between the Planets
synopsis: Italian sci-fi programmer about the choleric commander (Jack Stuart) of a space expedition whose mission is to destroy a gaseous asteroid that is causing tidal waves and other catastrophic destruction on Earth. Director Anthony Dawson tries to compensate for his undernourished script by using low-budget special effects but they don't hide the fact that this is a colossal clunker

title: War Devils, The
synopsis: Routine Italian action movie with Guy Madison leading a squadron of U.S. paratroopers behind German lines in Tunisia but he turns the mission into a personal battle between himself and the German commander (Van Tenney). Director Bert Albertini serves up World War II according to the war-is-fun formula with a lot of special effects flourishes

title: Warehouse
synopsis: Strange Japanese story of a blind sculptor who kidnaps a beautiful model and imprisons her in his hidden studio where she becomes as obsessed as he with tactile sensations, leading to tragedy for both. As an allegory on the consequences of enslavement to the senses, director Yasuzo Masumura's treatment will please neither hedonist nor puritan, but its technical virtuosity in creating the intensely physical world of a mad artist does have some interest

title: WarGames
synopsis: Good teen suspense thriller about a high school computer-wizard (Matthew Broderick) who breaks into a government nuclear-strategy computer and starts playing a war game whose logical conclusion is nuclear Armageddon. Directed by John Badham, the story loses much of its momentum when the program's designer (John Wood) is tracked down and points out the just desserts of human folly just before the slack conclusion. A few vulgar expletives

title: War Game, The
synopsis: British docudrama about the effects of nuclear warfare on a civilian population features non-professionals in realistically simulated scenes. Produced, written and directed by Peter Watkins, the movie gets considerable shock value from its hypothetical events but in making the unthinkable appear possible, it raises important questions of public concern

title: War-Gods of the Deep
synopsis: Convoluted adventure fantasy set on the English seacost in the early 1900s when the search for a missing woman (Susan Hart) leads a scientist (Tab Hunter) to discover an ancient undersea city inhabited by gill-people and ruled by a smuggler (Vincent Price) who hasn't aged a day since his arrival in 1803. Directed by Jacques Tourneur from a poem by Edgar Allan Poe, the mystery of the city and its strange inhabitants is oversahdowed by a nearby underwater volcano which is about to explode. Stylized violence and menace

title: War Hunt
synopsis: Posted to a front-line infantry unit in 1953 Korea, a green recruit (Robert Redford) comes to fear for the safety of an orphaned Korean boy looked after by a combat-crazed veteran (John Saxon) who slips behind enemy lines on nightly killing sprees. Director Denis Sanders probes the psychological damage of war in this chilling portrait of a psychotic soldier whose dangerously bizarre behavior is considered commendable rather than abnormal by his superiors. Combat violence and perilous situations

title: Warlock
synopsis: Muddled Western in which the title town hires a paie of gunmen (Henry Fonda and Anthony Quinn) to enforce the law, then a former outlaw (Richard Widmark) takes the vacant job of sheriff and comes up against both the hired guns and his old gang. Director Edward Dmytryk's variation on law-and-order themes is tangled with complications that add nothing to the basic plot of justice prevailing at the end of a six-shooter. Stylized shootouts and some romantic complications

title: Warlock
synopsis: A time traveler (Richard E. Grant) from the 17th century enlists the aid of a spunky California girl (Lori Singer) to defeat a male witch (Julian Sands) on the verge of destroying humanity. Strong performances and a steady build-up of suspense bolster producer-director Steve Miner's preposterous tale of black magic mumbo-jumbo. Some stylized violence and minimal rough language

title: Warlords of Atlantis
synopsis: Innocuous British adventure with two young scientists (Doug McClure and Peter Gilmore) who find themselves in the power of the rulers of an undersea kingdom where they encounter a beautiful and apparently ageless princess (Cyd Charisse). Directed by Kevin Connor, there's plenty of paper-mache monsters, wooden dialogue and leaden comic relief

title: War Lord, The
synopsis: Muddled medieval tale in which a veteran knight (Charlton Heston) is made lord of a coastal area in Normandy, falls for a betrothed woman (Rosemary Forsyth) and exercises his right according to local custom for her to spend her wedding night with him, then refuses to give her up and faces considerable retribution. Directed by Franklin Schaffner, the period spectacle gets lost in a convoluted plot involving the local practice of the old Druid religion, raiding Norsemen and the lord's conniving brother (Guy Stockwell). Feudal battles, an implicit unwed relationship and sexual innuendo

title: Warm December, A
synopsis: Black doctor (Sidney Poitier) is racing motorcycles on a vacation in England when he runs across the gorgeous niece of an African ambassador (Ester Anderson), falls in love but then learns she is dying of sickle cell anemia. Also directed by Poitier, the romantic melodrama is laid on with a sledgehammer to the tune of "Love Story" and its entertainment appeal is limited to devotees of the TV soaps

title: Warning Shot
synopsis: Story begins interestingly as a social drama about a policeman (David Janssen) who kills a highly-regarded public figure. From there the movie turns into a routine detective thriller directed by Buzz Kulik with little suspense but more than a little violence

title: Warning Sign
synopsis: An accident in a genetic engineering lab where biological warfare experiments are being carried on causes those inside to be transformed into crazed zombies save for a lone security guard (Kathleen Quinlan). Written and directed by Hal Barwood, it is a run-of-the-mill exercise in gory violence. O (R) ( 1985 )

title: War of the Buttons
synopsis: Remake of the 1962 French movie is set in Ireland where the boys of a one village (led by Gregg Fitzgerald) battle those of a neighboring village (led by John Coffey), with each side trying to outdo the other in youthful bravado, including cutting the buttons off captives' clothing and once fighting in the buff. Directed by John Roberts and filmed entirely in West Cork, the picture captures the innocent seriousness of the rival bands, but the treatment falters in a mix of whimsey, social consciousness and youthful self-importance. Stylized violence, flashes of rear nudity and some coarse language

title: War of the Colossal Beast
synopsis: Director Bert I. Gordon's clunky sequel to his 1957 sci-fi monster entry, "The Amazing Colossal Man," has the presumed dead 60-foot radiation victim turn up in Mexico, then brought back to Los Angeles for treatment but instead goes beserk until tangling with high-voltage power lines. Stylized violence and life-menacing situations

title: War of the Gargantuas
synopsis: Below-average Japanese monster movie about a scientist (Russ Tamblyn) whose experiments on a baby ape go awry and it and a companion grow large enough to crush the city of Tokyo. Director Inoshiro Honda relies on nature and the special effects crew to resolve the difficulty, while leaving a few cardboard buildings standing for a sequel

title: War of the Planets
synopsis: Dubbed Italian sci-fi adventure directed by Anthony Dawson offers a muddled, lackluster story in which a space station captain (Tony Russell) saves Earth, along with his girlfriend (Lisa Gastoni), from a mass of extraterrestrial green vapor seeking to inhabit human bodies. Silly special effects violence

title: War of the Roses, The
synopsis: Black comedy on the battle of the sexes has a divorce lawyer (Danny DeVito) telling the story of a couple (Michael Douglas and Kathleen Turner) who go from happy penury to wealthy discontent and then divorce proceedings that turn into a horror show as they fight over house and possessions. As director, DeVito does a good job satirizing the anger and greed of divorce settlements but has little sensitivity to the problems underlying the break-up. Nasty cartoon-like marital violence, brief but explicit sexual encounters and some rough language

title: War of the Wildcats
synopsis: Boisterous Western romance directed by Albert S. Rogell is set in 1900 Oklahoma where an enterprising cowboy (John Wayne) goes into the oil business in order to compete with a local tycoon (Albert Dekker) for the affections of an ambitious woman author (Martha Scott). Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: War of the Worlds
synopsis: Impressive but distressingly violent updating of H.G. Wells' classic sci-fi story, about (in this version) a deadbeat dad (Tom Cruise) who is jolted into responsible parenthood when he must struggle to survive and keep his two children (Justin Chatwin and Dakota Fanning) safe amid a hostile invasion by space aliens bent on exterminating humanity. Directed by Steven Spielberg, the decidedly dark and scary thrill ride delivers edge-of-your-seat excitement and knockout action sequences, which though visually stunning never drown out the human drama at its core about a father trying to reconnect with his children. Intense sci-fi violence, including mass destruction and slaughter, disintegrated bodies, a murder with extenuating circumstances, child peril, as well as scattered crude language and profanity

title: War of the Worlds, The
synopsis: First-rate version of H.G. Wells' sci-fi classic about Martians invading Earth with deadly heat rays from whose destructive path through California flee nuclear physicist Gene Barry and companion Ann Robinson until the aliens meet with the unexpected. Produced by George Pal and directed by Byron Haskin, the apocalyptic tale is tautly told with often frightening effect, thanks to its superior model work and astonishing special effects. Some religious dimension, much menace and stylized violence

title: War Paint
synopsis: Trekking through the desert with a peace treaty promised to an Indian chief, a cavalry officer (Robert Stack) copes with all manner of problems as his small column of troopers is decimated from without and within. Directed by Lesley Selander, the deadly journey is outlandishly contrived, though gains some interest by being filmed appropriately in Death Valley. Stylized violence, including the attempted rape of a captured Indian woman

title: Warpath
synopsis: Civil War veteran (Edmond O'Brien) enlists in the Seventh Cavalry to track down his girlfriend's killers (Forrest Tucker and Dean Jagger), becomes an heroic Indian-fighter and warns Custer that the Sioux are massing for an attack before riding off with his new love (Polly Bergen). Director Byron Haskin's routine Western has an earnest cast and some mildly interesting plot twists. Frontier violence and Indian stereotypes

title: Warrior Empress, The
synopsis: Dubbed Italian clunker directed by Pietro Francisci is set in ancient Greece where a rebel (Kerwin Matthews) fights an unjust king while wooing his poetic niece, Sappho (Tina Louise). Stylized violence, sexual innuendo and bevies of scantily clad maidens

title: The Warrior's Way
synopsis: After refusing to kill the baby girl who is the lone survivor of a rival clan, the world's greatest samurai swordsman (Jang Dong-gun) turns his back on his murderous past and seeks a new start on the American frontier, befriending the circus folk (most prominently Geoffrey Rush and Tony Cox) who inhabit the ramshackle town in which he settles, bonding with a local lass (Kate Bosworth) and raising the infant he spared as his own. But his peaceable ways are tested when the demonic Army colonel (Danny Huston) who slaughtered his true love's family when she was a girl -- and nearly raped her -- returns in a bid to wreak fresh mayhem. The West was never wilder than in Korean writer-director Sngmoo Lee's U.S. feature debut. But this larger-than-life blend of martial arts, duels in the sun and operatic emotion winds up graphically celebrating the very violence its hero has ostensibly rejected and implicitly endorsing its heroine's quest for revenge against her inhuman persecutor. Excessive bloody violence, the attempted rape of a minor, a vendetta theme, about a half-dozen uses of profanity, a few crude and crass terms

title: Warriors of Virtue
synopsis: Martial arts fantasy in which an American teen-ager (Mario Yedidia) finds himself transported to a mythical kingdom of warring kung fu masters as a villainous warlord (Angus Macfadyen) tries to conquer a peaceable land led by the wise Master Chung (Chao-Li Chi). Directed by Ronny Yu, the good master's words of wisdom get lost in the fury of the fantasy action but the formula story doesn't measure up to the imaginative sets and costuming in a production filmed mainly in China's Beijing Film Studios. Some stylized violence, much menace and a vulgar expression

title: Warriors, The
synopsis: While leading the English forces defending Aquitaine during the 100 Years Wars, Edward Prince of Wales (Errol Flynn) takes time out to rescue a lady (Joanne Dru) abducted by a French nobleman (Peter Finch). Directed by Henry Levin, the colorful British production has a good cast and well-mounted action sequences though it takes itself more seriously than the story warrants. Much derring-do and stylized battle scenes

title: Warriors, The
synopsis: Screen version of Sol Yurick's novel about a youth gang trying to make their way back to their own neighborhood through a New York City in which every hand is turned against them. Directed by Walter Hill, the gang's sordid adventures are of even less interest than its one-dimensional characters and their stilted dialogue. Constant violence and glorification of vicious behavior. O (R) ( 1979 )

title: War Room, The
synopsis: Human interest documentary centers on the political strategies used by George Stephanopoulos and James Carville during the 1992 presidential campaign to get Bill Clinton elected. In low-key but entertaining fashion, directors D.A. Pennebaker and Chris Hegedus capture the very different styles of the two men in deflecting issues of the candidate's personal character to concentrate on a weak national economy as the reason to vote for change. Discreet sexual references and an off-screen instance of rough language

title: War, The
synopsis: Affecting anti-war parable set in 1970 rural Mississippi where a guilt-ridden Vietnam vet (Kevin Costner) encourages his young son and daughter (Elijah Wood and Lexi Randall) to befriend rather than fight neighborhood bullies bent on taking over their prized treehouse. Handsomely shot and delicately acted, director Jon Avnet connects the children's increasingly physical skirmishes with the wartime experiences of the emotionally scarred father but the movie suffers from the script's stridently preachy tone as the two children learn valuable life lessons from caring parents. Flashbacks of battlefield violence, escalating juvenile violence and menace as well as minimal profanity

title: War Wagon, The
synopsis: Familiar Western story about a supertough hombre (John Wayne) just out of jail and bent on robbing a gold shipment belonging to the villain (Bruce Cabot) who framed him and now has hired a gunman (Kirk Douglas) to kill him. Director Burt Kennedy mixes some comedy into the rough, he-man action but the resultis nothing out of the ordinary. Stylized violence

title: Wasabi
synopsis: Mildly engaging action-comedy in which a French cop (Jean Reno), called to Tokyo upon the death of his long-lost love, discovers she left him a free-spirited 19-year-old daughter (Ryoko Hirosue) and a fortune that Japanese gangsters intend to steal. As directed by Gerard Krawczyk, the melancholy cop and his exuberant daughter make an appealing odd couple, unlike the contrived mobsters they must contend with. Subtitles. Recurring stylized violence and an instance of rough language. A-III � adults. (R) 2002 Wasabi Called to Tokyo for the reading of his long-lost love's will, a French cop finds she has left him a fortune -- as well as a 19-year-old daughter being pursued by gangsters -- in the mildly engaging action-comedy "Wasabi" (Columbia). Sad-sack Hubert (Jean Reno) has been romantically uninvolved and overly aggressive as a policeman ever since the love of his life, Miko, mysteriously dumped him while he was on assignment in Japan 20 years earlier. Too quick to beat up on suspects, Hubert is told to take a vacation and chill out just as an extraordinary call comes from Tokyo. He must take the next plane from Paris as Miko has died and named him as her executor and heir. That's only the first shock. He finds he has a free-spirited 19-year-old daughter Yumi (Ryoko Hirosue), that they have been left a fortune, and that Japanese gangsters are on their tail, out to relieve them of the entire $200 million windfall. And he still doesn't know why his beloved so abruptly terminated their romance. Helping him determine if Miko died a natural death, and what she was up to the past two decades, is Hubert's former rookie partner, the clownish Momo (Michel Muller). But less easy to deal with is his exuberant daughter, whose grief vanishes at her mention of the magic words: "Let's go shopping!" Trigger-happy Hubert, however, is quick to shoot (apparently rubber bullets) at those pesky hoods in black suits and shades whenever they get close, but eventually father and daughter end up in the clutches of the Japanese mafia -- at least temporarily. As scripted by Luc Besson, there's a not inconsiderable amount of violence in the form of sluggings and shootouts, but they are stylized rather than realistic and often appear in an almost comic context. Underneath these action sequences is an almost-sweet film about a man who never forgot his first love and now has a daughter to love and protect. In this role, cop Reno is very adept at going from professional stoicism to emotionally involved father figure. The narrative is weak in sketching out the past relationship between mother and child, but Hirosue, as excitable Yumi, is winsome, the very picture of a bubble-headed teen, and she keeps the film light and goofily endearing. We eventually discover why her mom felt obliged to ditch the Frenchman she loved but the whole subplot about the Japanese gangsters looks thoroughly contrived just to give the picture its chase and action elements. Nonetheless, as directed by Gerard Krawczyk, the film has energy, a bright palette of vibrant colors and costumes and a sprinkling of frothy comic moments. Subtitles. Due to recurring stylized violence and an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops

title: Washington Heights
synopsis: Low-budget ethnic drama about an aspiring comic illustrator (Manny Perez) who must weigh ambition against responsibility when his bodega-owning father (Tomas Milian) is shot and paralyzed during a robbery. With a contrived plot not worth emotional investment, director Alfredo de Villa's cliched narrative is undermined by the protagonist's all-too-familiar dilemma: how to escape his dead-end existence while maintaining his cultural identity

title: Washington Square
synopsis: Sobering dramatization of Henry James' tale in which a plain young heiress (Jennifer Jason Leigh) is eager to marry an attentive suitor (Ben Chaplin) even though her brutally honest father (Albert Finney) denounces him as a golddigger and vows to disinherit her. Director Agnieszka Holland stresses the woman's hard-won sense of self-esteem despite male rejection, but the solemn pace and a clumsy attempt to make her aunt (Vanessa Redgrave) a comic figure diminish the story's emotional impact. A theme of false love as well as a brief scene of gore

title: Washington Story
synopsis: Assigned to do a hatchet job on novice Congressman Van Johnson, journalist Patricia Neal has a change of heart when he stands up for the national interest. Written and directed by Robert Pirosh, it's less a drama than a patriotic civics lesson, chiefly of interest for its picture of the relatively unsophisticated trappings of yesteryear's federal government

title: Wash, The
synopsis: Poignant chronicle of the end of a long-term Japanese-American marriage in which the wife (Nobu McCarthy) is quietly determined to forge a new, happy life for herself after years of being ignored and belittled by her husband (Mako). Director Michael Toshiyuki Uno does a wonderfully restrained job of exploring the fears that plague the couple and their grown children in coming to terms with the marriage's dissolution. Incidental rough language, a fairly explicit sexual encounter within marriage and implications of cohabitation outside marriage

title: Wasp Woman, The
synopsis: Flimsy horror quickie directed by Roger Corman has an aging cosmetics queen (Susan Cabot) seek youthful transformation from wasp enzymes processed by a quack doctor (Michael Mark), with predictable results. Mild stylized violence and silly wasp-woman mask

title: Watched!
synopsis: Interesting independent production about a drug case prosecutor (Stacy Keach) who is set up by his own agents after he begins to have second thoughts about the legality of their surveillance methods. Written and directed by John Parsons, the movie suggests that bugging has become a way of life in America, with some well-executed scenes of extra-legal surveillance techniques

title: Watcher in the Woods, The
synopsis: Mediocre Disney suspense thriller in which an American teenager (Lynn-Holly Johnson) staying in a gloomy English country house tries to solve the mystery of what happened to the teenage girl who disappeared from the house 30 years before. Directed by John Hough, the script and its mystery are rather banal but the movie does have its frightening moments. Though too scary for pre-teens, its primary appeal is to younger teenagers

title: Water
synopsis: Poignant drama set in 1938 India about the lives of women who, in accordance with Hindu tradition, are required -- following their husbands' deaths -- to live out their days as outcasts in a squalid widows' ashram; they include an 8-year-old child bride (Sarala); a young beauty (Lisa Ray) forced into prostitution by the camp's matriarch (Manorma) who falls for a progressive-minded law student (John Abraham); and a devout older woman (Seema Biswas), torn between conscience and her faith. Visually poetic with soulful performances, director Deepa Mehta's film is simple yet deeply moving, balancing heartbreak and hope as it explores the lives of the widows in whose humanity is reflected the dignity of all women. Implied prostitution, a suicide, brief drug usage, a transvestite character, some sexual references and a few mildly crude expressions. Subtitles

title: Water
synopsis: This adult comedy is funnier on paper as Michael Caine stars as the frustrated governor of an underdeveloped island nation in the Caribbean. Prosperity and independence are achieved only after diuretic mineral water and oil are discovered at a defunct U.S. drilling rig. Ethnic jokes, TV sitcom-style humor and sexual innueundo predominate as "Water" oozes rather than bubb1es

title: Waterboy, The
synopsis: Slack sports comedy in which a dimwitted waterboy (Adam Sandler) for a Southern college's losing football team becomes their star player despite the fierce objections of his wild-eyed Cajun mama (Kathy Bates). As directed by Frank Coraci, Sandler's sweetly stupid character is just one of many Southern stereotypes in a halting comedy where brute strength is valued above all. Bruising athletic competitions, brief alcohol abuse and sexual innuendo, fleeting nudity, crude expressions and an instance of rough language

title: Waterdance, The
synopsis: Insightful drama of a newly wheelchair-bound writer (Eric Stoltz) in a multiracial rehabilitation center where he must deal with two battling patients (Wesley Snipes and William Forsythe) and a decision regarding his married girlfriend (Helen Hunt). Co-directed by Neal Jimenez and Michael Steinberg and based on Jimenez' experiences, the movie is an emotionally honest and exceptionally well-acted look at four distinct personalities, each at a turning point in their lives. Some discreet bedroom encounters, brief nudity and occasional rough language

title: Water for Elephants
synopsis: Life under the big top is not all clowns and cotton candy in this lavish but morally flawed period drama, adapted from Sara Gruen's eponymous novel. In the depths of the Great Depression, a promising veterinary student (Robert Pattinson), whose dreams have been shattered by fate, jumps a train and inadvertently lands in the midst of a traveling circus. Though his knowledge of animals soon draws the attention of the enterprise's loathsome owner (Christoph Waltz), disaster looms when the newcomer falls for the star of the show (Reese Witherspoon) who turns out to be the boss' wife. From there, the operatic proceedings barrel along to a shocking climax. While artfully conceived and well acted, director Francis Lawrence's film accepts -- and even glamorizes -- adultery, albeit within the context of an extreme situation. Intense violence, including murder and animal abuse, nongraphic but implicitly condoned adultery, partial nudity, at least one use of profanity, two crude terms

title: Waterhole No. 3
synopsis: When the fastest con artist in the West (James Coburn) lifts a thief's wallet containing a map to a cache of stolen gold, he lights out for the loot with the robber in pursuit and the Army pursuing him. Directed by William Graham, the tone of the movie is coarse, bawdy and frequently just plain crude. O (br) ( 1967 )

title: The Water Horse: Legend of the Deep
synopsis: Engaging but, by the end, surprisingly intense fantasy adventure, set during World War II, in which a forlorn Scottish boy (Alex Etel), coping with the absence of his sailor father (Craig Hall), discovers an egg in the waters of the local loch that hatches a rapidly growing dinosaurlike creature which he eventually identifies as the "Water Horse" spoken of in Celtic legends and which he nurtures with the help of his sister (Priyanka Xi) and a war-veteran handyman (Ben Chaplin), while concealing its existence from his housekeeper mother (Emily Watson) and the strict Army officer (David Morrissey) whose soldiers are encamped on the estate she serves. Director Jay Russell's screen version of Dick King-Smith's 1990 children's book, like its title character, starts off unthreateningly, but gets steadily more ominous as it moves toward a turbulent climax that would likely frighten most young children. Fantasy violence, one crass expression and one profanity; acceptable for less sensitive younger viewers

title: Waterland
synopsis: A middle-aged history teacher (Jeremy Irons) recounts to his class his own troubled adolescent history and the resulting guilt that weighs so heavily on his rocky marriage to a woman (Sinead Cusack) who is suffering a nervous breakdown. Stephen Gyllenhaal directs a rambling, unwieldy story of dark sexual secrets, madness and murder whose tragic elements are dissipated by the jarring flashbacks. Much discussion of sexual matters, a discreet sexual encounter and some nudity

title: Waterloo
synopsis: Stately, grandiose set piece re-creates Napoleon's return from exile on Elba to his final defeat at Waterloo. Director Sergei Bondarchuk reduces the two principal opponents, Napoleon (Rod Steiger) and Wellington (Christopher Plummer), to little more than historical caricatures speaking the famous epigrams attributed to them. Yet the movie comes alive in the broad, colorful sweep of action sequences showing an epic moment in European history

title: Waterloo Bridge
synopsis: Soapy romantic tragedy of World War I as a Scottish captain (Robert Taylor) and a London ballet student (Vivien Leigh) fall in love but before they can wed, he's sent to the front, then reported dead and she turns to prostitution until he turns up at war's end and her shame drives her to suicide. Directed by Mervyn LeRoy from Robert E. Sherwood's play, the contrived proceedings haven't worn well, though the moody photography and a strong supporting cast (notably Lucile Watson and Virginia Field) at least make it watchable. Romantic complications, veiled treatment of prostitution and suicide in the plot resolution

title: Watermelon Man
synopsis: When a mindlessly bigoted white (Godfrey Cambridge) one night turns black, he undergoes the indignities and injustices of white America. Unfortunately, in dealing with all-too-familiar racial stereotypes (sexual, musical, commercial), director Melvin Van Peebles' satire is crude, embarrassing, and at times consciously offensive. Though terribly uneven, it at least attempts to deal with the festering ulcer of everyday racial prejudice

title: Watership Down
synopsis: British animated adaptation of Richard Adams' popular novel about a band of brave rabbits making a dangerous journey in search of a new home has been done with taste and intelligence under Martin Rosen's direction. Some of the voices belong to John Hurt, Ralph Richardson, Denholm Elliot and Harry Andrews, with Zero Mostel providing comic relief as a zany German seagull. Some scenes may be too intense for younger children

title: Waterworld
synopsis: In a waterlogged future where scattered bands of people subsist on man-made atolls, a mutant fish-man (Kevin Costner) reluctantly gives refuge aboard his uniquely rigged sailboat to a woman (Jeanne Tripplehorn) and a child with a mysterious tatoo sought by a murderous pirate gang (under Dennis Hopper) because it supposedly shows the location of a hidden patch of dry land. Aside from a visually bleak vision of humans struggling for survival in an aquatic world, director Kevin Reynolds' shallow action picture offers little more than formula chase fare with a decided mean streak and badly underwritten characters. Recurring violence, partial nudity, sexual innuendo, profanity and an instance of rough language

title: Wattstax
synopsis: Exciting documentary directed by Mel Stuart with rock, jazz, and general all-around soul performers (Issac Hayes, The Staple Singers, Bar-Kays), centering around the black experience and, in particular, the Los Angeles community of Watts. Giving it continuity is a funny but sad and, at times, raunchy commentary by Richard Pryor

title: Way Ahead, The
synopsis: World War II saga of British draftees (Stanley Holloway, James Donald, John Laurie and many others) grousing their way through boot camp while being gradually transformed under the guidance of a dedicated officer (David Niven) into a crack infantry unit sent to fight in North Africa. Directed by Carol Reed, the movie's patriotic intentions wear well, principally because its group portrait is grounded in convincing individual details, though the heroics in the concluding battle sequence seem today surprisingly hollow. Wartime violence

title: The Way Back
synopsis: Inspirational, partly fact-based portrayal of a 4,000-mile trek by escaped prisoners from a Russian gulag to political asylum in India. Director and co-writer Peter Weir's superbly made drama sees an ensemble of skilled actors (Jim Sturgess, Ed Harris, Colin Farrell, Saiorse Ronan) displaying deeply-felt emotions along with stunning courage, although "The Long Walk" -- the 1956 book on which the script is based -- has been shown to fall short of the truth. Probably acceptable for older teens. Fleeting rough language

title: Wayne's World
synopsis: Dopey comedy about two bumblers (Mike Myers and Dana Carvey) whose cable access talk show is threatened by a smarmy producer (Rob Lowe). Director Penelope Spheeris stretches what was originally a "Saturday Night Live" TV skit into 95 mindless minutes of numbing nonsense. Sexist attitudes, implied premarital encounter, some sexual innuendo and toilet humor

title: Wayne's World 2
synopsis: Inane comedy sequel in which overgrown adolescents Wayne and Garth (Mike Myers and Dana Carvey) juggle trouble with girlfriends (Tia Carrere and Kim Basinger) while throwing a Woodstock-like rock concert without performers or ticket sales. Director Stephen Surjik simply cranks up the sophomoric humor, adding spoofs of other movies to liven up the lads' lame repertoire of airhead asides. Frequent sexual innuendo, recurring rear nudity, minor violence and occasional profanity

title: Way Out West
synopsis: Entrusted with delivering the deed for a gold mine to a poor orphan, Stan Laurel and Oliver Hardy trace her to a frontier town where they run afoul an outrageously crooked innkeeper (James Finlayson). Directed by James Horne, the situation sets up some prime comedy routines as well as a couple of country tunes and a dance number by the boys that's truly elegant. Genial fun for all

title: Way to the Stars, The
synopsis: Fine World War II drama about(R) AF pilots who frequent a small hotel-bar near the airfield, with events centering on the death of a poetic pilot (Michael Redgrave) whose grief-stricken widow and child make a fellow aviator (John Mills) defer thoughts of marriage until war's end. Directed by Anthony Asquith, the narrative comes to include an American bomber unit as part of its picture of war's human cost for the pilots, their friends and loved ones, without any scenes of military heroics. Off-screen air battles and coping with troubled emotions

title: Way, Way Out!
synopsis: Jerry Lewis movie about a trip to the moon is preoccupied with sex in its dialogue, costuming and situations. O (br) ( 1966 )

title: Way We Live Now, The
synopsis: Advertising agency director (Nicholas Pryor), separated from his wife, has long conversations with himself and imaginary famous visitors but his time is mostly given to stalking and bedding women. Written, produced, directed and photographed by Barry Brown, the incessant talk is pretentious and the long string of sexual adventures tedious but exploitative. O (R) ( 1970 )

title: Way West, The
synopsis: Fairly good pioneer Western with Kirk Douglas as a harried wagonmaster trying to get a wagon train of Western settlers through the mountains and past Indian perils. Director Andrew V. McLaglen gets rugged acting support from Richard Widmark and Robert Mitchum, with Lola Albright on hand for the boys to fight over

title: Way We Were, The
synopsis: Robert Redford and Barbra Streisand as ill-matched lovers in a seriocomic story sweeping from Ivy League idylls in the late 1930s into World War II and on to Hollywood in the post-war era of blacklisting. There is just too much material here for anyone to put into a coherent shape, and director Sydney Pollack succumbs to the temptation of trivializing the period and their events in favor of the sheer glamour of it all. It's slick and shallow but romantics may find it diverting

title: W.C. Fields and Me
synopsis: Directed by Arthur Hiller, this story of the romance between the Hollywood comedian (Rod Steiger) and Carlotta Monti (Valerie Perrine) distorts the people and events of an era shamelessly and has a tone of leering vulgarity that destroys any pretense of serious intent. O (PG) WR -- Mysteries of the Organism (see: "Mysteries of the Organism'') ( 1976 )

title: We All Loved Each Other So Much
synopsis: Warm and moving Italian comedy about three men (Vittorio Gassman, Nino Manfredi and Stefano Satta Flores) who love the same woman (Stefania Sandrelli) at one time or another, with varying degrees of intensity, over the course of three decades. Directed by Ettore Scola, it is a rare, wise and entertaining movie on the theme of love and friendship

title: Weapons of the Spirit
synopsis: Pierre Sauvage is a Jew who survived the Holocaust only because he happened to be born in 1944 in Le Chambon-sur-Lignon, a French town which provided safe harbor for some 5,000 Jews during World War II. Returning to this largely Protestant community to make a documentary about those remaining strong-minded Christian farmers, educators and clergy who risked their lives as an act of faith against Nazi racism, Sauvage examines how and why they managed to get away with their massive unorganized opposition when other French resistance fighters faced reprisals. The result is a moving tribute to human solidarity and a reminder of the power of Christian teachings

title: We Are Marshall
synopsis: Moving true-life story about the aftermath of a 1970 plane crash in West Virginia that killed 70 players, coaches and fans of a college football team, and how the grieving university town came to recover its spirit by the formation of a largely new team galvanized by the leadership of a new coach (a dynamic Matthew McConaughey), working in tandem with the Marshall University president (David Strathairn) and the assistant coach of the former team (Matthew Fox). Director McG's (actually Joseph McGinty Nichol) film, though to some extent formulaic and predictable, is several notches above average, bolstered by solid performances including that of Ian McShane, and a script that mostly avoids cliche, with good messages about winning not being everything, accepting loss, and healing from it, with a good sense of this being a faith-based community. Several uses of the s-word as favored by the coach, a few other crass expressions and discreetly handled plane crash

title: Web, The
synopsis: Tricky crime story in which a brassy lawyer (Edmund O'Brien) is hired to protect a threatened industrialist (Vincent Price), then shoots an armed intruder in what a veteran cop (William Bendix) suspects is a case of murder linked to a million-dollar swindle. Directed by Michael Gordon, the plot takes some devious turns as the lawyer tries to clear himself of the murder rap with the help of the industrialist's secretary (Ella Raines). Stylized violence and callous deceptions

title: Wedding, A
synopsis: Some 20 major characters, and perhaps twice as many minor ones, assemble for a satiric assault on the extravagance of a wedding in a family recently risen to affluence. With no central plot worth mentioning, director Robert Altman lets the action go in every direction at once, much of it revolving around the many skeletons in the family closet. The actors (among them, Lillian Gish, John Cromwell, Vittorio Gassman, Dina Merrill, Howard Duff, Carol Burnett and Paul Dooley) are better than the material in this extremely uneven effort that is further marred by sexual goings on and gratuitous nudity. O (R) ( 1978 )

title: Wedding Banquet
synopsis: A gay couple in New York decides to help a Chinese friend (May Chin) get a green card by having one of them (Winston Chao) marry her in name only, but wind up living together when the groom's elderly parents (Sihung Lung and Ah-Leh Gua) arrive from Taiwan for a prolonged stay with the newlyweds. Director Ang Lee stresses the human side of the comic complications in a bittersweet comedy of manners. A sympathetic portrayal of a gay live-in relationship, fleeting nudity and occasional rough language

title: Wedding Bell Blues
synopsis: Weakly contrived tale of three single women (Illeana Douglas, Paulina Porizkova and Julie Warner) who impulsively decide to find husbands overnight in Las Vegas, then file for divorce the next day just so they can say they were married before age 30. Director Dana Lustig tries to make the instant romances seem comically poignant in what gradually ends up a mushy tale that affirms female friendship and marital commitment. Off-screen marital encounters, sexual references which include an abortion, and occasional profanity

title: Wedding Crashers
synopsis: Raunchy romantic comedy directed by David Dobkin about two lifelong friends (Owen Wilson and Vince Vaughn) who infiltrate weddings as a hobby and a way to seduce women, and who find themselves entangled in comic and romantic complications when they con their way into a high-profile D.C. wedding and wind up spending the weekend with the bride's dysfunctional family (headed by Christopher Walken). Despite considerable chemistry between Vaughn and Wilson, the farce makes light of casual sex and promiscuity, mucking up what could have been a smart screwball buddy film with lewd sight gags and foul-mouthed dialogue. Much crude sexual humor and situations, some involving partial nudity, a brief irreverent comment, as well as pervasive rough and vulgar language and profanity

title: Wedding Gift, The
synopsis: Maudlin British drama about a woman (Julie Walters) whose crippling disease completely baffles doctors as it progressively worsens until she finds her devoted husband (Jim Broadbent) a suitable replacement (Sian Thomas), then dies an apparent suicide. Directed by Richard Loncraine, the fact-based BBC production centers in the pathos of the wife's weakening condition and her determination, abetted by husband, to keep up flagging spirits by making jokes about it, then cops out in the end by sentimentalizing her terminal act of matchmaking. Ambiguity of the wife's death, a flash of nudity and occasional profanity

title: Wedding in Blood
synopsis: Disappointing French crime story about a couple (Stephane Audran and Michel Piccoli) who, drawn together by an almost incendiary passion, conspire to murder their spouses. Instead of trying to create a truly chilling horror movie out of this story of forbidden desire and desperate murder, director Claude Chabrol uses it to express his moralistic views on the middle class and their loss of values

title: Wedding in White
synopsis: Hard-edged but compassionate Canadian drama set in a small town during World War II tells the story of a father (Donald Pleasence) who, learning his teenage daughter (Carol Kane) is pregnant after an assault by a drunken soldier, persuades his best friend (Leo Phillips), a bachelor in his mid-fifties, to marry the girl, thereby saving the family reputation. Director William Fruet uses the situation to focus on the limited horizons and narrow attitudes of small-town life which proves just as much a closed society as the nearby prisoner-of-war camp where the father works

title: Wedding March, The
synopsis: Epic silent romance set in 1914 Vienna where a dissolute but bankrupt Hapsburg prince (Erich von Stroheim) falls in love with an innocent working-class beauty (Fay Wray), then breaks her heart by marrying a rich businessman's daughter (Zazu Pitts) for her wealth. Also directed by von Stroheim, the story is rooted in the historical period with its emotional pull coming from strikingly detailed scenes of aristocratic pomp, religious devotions, lower-class aspirations and the romantic yearnings of the principals. Originally released as a two-part picture, the second half no longer exists and what remains of the first part is visually uneven. Menacing situations, an implied sexual encounter and innuendo including a stylized orgy

title: Wedding Night
synopsis: Irish movie about a young Catholic woman (Tessa Wyatt) whose fears of sex and pregnancy make her unable to consummate her marriage. Directed by Piers Haggard, the story is told in strong and pointed discussions of the contraceptive pill, morality, the medical profession and an uncomprehending husband. Thoughtful drama about a deeply emotional subject, but offers no positive solutions

title: Wedding Party, The
synopsis: Unsure about marrying his fiancee (Jill Clayburgh), a prospective bridegroom (Charles Pfluger) tries a variety of ruses to call off the wedding. Directed by Cynthia Munroe, Brian De Palma and Wilford Leach, the low-budget black-and-white production tries all kinds of camera tricks but can't save its hodge-podge of comedy, satire and fantasy

title: Wedding Singer, The
synopsis: Sappy romantic comedy set in the suburbs of 1985 New York where a jilted fianc� (Adam Sandler) falls for a sweet waitress (Drew Barrymore), then discovers she is about to marry a crass playboy. Directed by Frank Coraci, the contrived comedy pokes heavy-handed fun at 1980's fads and fashions, but the bland proceedings remain largely lifeless. Implied affairs, fleeting violence, occasional profanity and an instance of rough language

title: We Dive at Dawn
synopsis: Taut World War II picture in which a British submarine tracks a German battleship into the enemy waters of the Baltic, then runs out of fuel after torpedoing it. Director Anthony Asquith turns the action story into a character study of men in war, focusing on the sub's capable captain (John Mills) and two seamen (Eric Portman and Niall MacGinnis) with very different marital problems. Wartime violence and domestic misunderstandings

title: Wednesday's Child
synopsis: British dramatization of the gradual psychic destruction of a young woman (Sandy Ratcliff) by her repressive working-class parents and by the behaviorist theories practiced on her in a government-run mental hospital. Written by David Mercer and directed by Kenneth Loach, the result is a plea for respect for the individuality of the person that is a powerfully moving, incontrovertible statement

title: Weekend
synopsis: Apocalyptic French vision of modern civilization's self-destruction is contructed out of a disjointed narrative of motorized mayhem, dehumanized people and mindless revolution. Directed by Jean-Luc Godard, the movie's attempts to shock and its static militant speeches become simplistic attacks on traditional morality and existing social values. O (nr) ( 1968 )

title: Weekend at Bernie's
synopsis: Silly, one-joke farce about two witless, low-level executives (Andrew McCarthy and Jonathan Silverman) who hide the fact that their boss (Terry Kiser) has been murdered so they can take advantage of his weekend beach house invitation. Director Ted Kotcheff knocks the conscienceless, self-absorbed hedonists who don't notice that their host is dead, but the main focus is on how easy it is to lie to get whatever you want in the way of materialistic ambitions. Alcohol and drug abuse, sexual innuendoes and implied necrophilia. O (PG-13) ( 1989 )

title: Weekend at Bernie's II
synopsis: Moronic sequel set in the Caribbean where two junior executives (Andrew McCarthy and Jonathan Silverman) pass off the corpse of their boss (Terry Kiser) as alive so they can get the funds he embezzled to clear their reputations. Writer-director Robert Klane's witless comedy resorts to a voodoo subplot in which the corpse becomes a dancing zombie, but nothing can save a script that was already dead on arrival. Disrespectful treatment of a dead person, some mild sexual innuendo and tasteless gallows humor

title: Weekend at Dunkirk
synopsis: French sergeant (Jean-Paul Belmondo), among the mass of troops trapped by the Germans in the Dunkirk pocket in June 1940, has to decide whether to try to escape with the British, desert and return home or stay and be captured. Directed by Henri Verneuil, the beaches of Dunkirk were a bitter French defeat and this movie is a grim picture of war without any of the usual movie heroics

title: Weekend in Havana
synopsis: Lightweight musical comedy in which a steamship official (John Payne) escorts a disgruntled passenger (Alice Faye) on a free trip to Cuba where she's romanced by a con man (Cesar Romero) whose girlfriend (Carmen Miranda) raises a storm before all ends happily. Directed by Walter Lang, the fluffy tale of a shopgirl's dream vacation has some amusing moments but not enough to make it memorable entertainment. Romantic complications

title: Weekend Murders
synopsis: Routine Italian mystery movie in which the relatives (among them, Anna Moffo) of a deceased British earl gather at his plush estate to learn of their legacies, fall prey to grisly pranks, sexual dalliances and ultimately five murders. The real villain of the piece is director Michele Lupo, who indulges in acute camera angles, and wears out his zoom lens in a supreme display of technique over talent

title: Weekend Pass
synopsis: Four sailors just out of boot camp hit Los Angeles on a weekend pass in this mediocre effort. Writer-director Lawrence Bassoff has put a variety of Los Angeles backgrounds to good use, but his script is thoroughly pedestrian. Although veering toward romantic wholesomeness, some graphic, utterly gratuitous nudity in an early cabaret sequence is highly offensive. O (R) ( 1984 )

title: Week-End with Father
synopsis: Sentimental family comedy in which a widower (Van Heflin) with two young girls courts a widow (Patricia Neal) with two young boys but their spoiled offspring do their best to break them up, then have a change of heart and conspire to bring them back together. Directed by Douglas Sirk, the formula proceedings are mired in contrived misunderstandings and slapstick situations, mostly in a summer camp setting which is as bogus as the story. Synthetic fare

title: Weekend with the Babysitter
synopsis: Low-budget exploitation movie about a suburban husband's marijuana smoking with the family's teen-age sitter while his wife shoots heroin with cutthroat drug smugglers. Sexual activity predominates in a ludicrous script with amateur actors. O (R) ( 1970 )

title: Wee Willie Winkie
synopsis: Unlikely but likeable Shirley Temple vehicle from a Rudyard Kipling story in which she stars as the American granddaughter of the crusty British commander (C. Aubrey Smith) in northern India where she has a glorious time playing a soldier of the Queen under the tutelage of a seasoned sergeant (Victor McLaglen), then stops a border uprising by befriending the local rebel chief (Cesar Romero). Director John Ford gets some lively humor from the ranks of the military post together with a few good battle scenes but does best with Shirley parading around in her kilted uniform and the byplay with the burly McLaglen. Colonial rhetoric doesn't impede the sentimental fun

title: Weight of Water
synopsis: Moody drama in which a contemporary photojournalist (Catherine McCormack) investigating a brutal 1873 double murder begins to suspect a sexual relationship between her poet husband (Sean Penn) and a seductive fan (Elizabeth Hurley) as they share a weekend boat near the century-old murder site. Kathryn Bigelow directs a murky tale of troubled romantic and familial relationships which constantly crosscuts from the present to the dark doings in the 19th-century bludgeoning but fails to gather emotional momentum. Recurring shadowy violence, a discreet sexual encounter and other sexual situations, brief nudity, minor profanity and an instance of rough language

title: Weird Science
synopsis: Two high school nerds conjure up their idea of the perfect woman (Kelly LeBrock) on a computer and have all their dreams of popularity and wild adventure fulfilled. Essentially a one-joke affair, written with an excess of rough language and directed with too many sexual inferences by John Hughes, it's a vulgar, mediocre effort which does a hard sell of promiscuity to teenagers. O (PG-13) ( 1985 )

title: Welcome Home Roscoe Jenkins
synopsis: Unruly family farce in which a successful TV talk-show host (Martin Lawrence), accompanied by his controlling fiancee (Joy Bryant), returns to his parents' (James Earl Jones and Margaret Avery) home in Georgia to attend their 50th wedding anniversary, only to encounter a host of eccentric relatives and resume the rivalry with his orphaned cousin (Cedric the Entertainer) that dominated his childhood. Writer-director Malcolm D. Lee's raucous film is often entertaining, but also at times crude and seemingly desperate for laughs. Nongraphic but aberrant premarital sexual encounter, partial frontal female nudity, one use of the f-word, much crude and pervasive crass language, some profanity, much sexual humor, drug references, a condom reference, gambling and dogs mating

title: Welcome Home
synopsis: Shot down over Cambodia in 1970, an Air Force flyer (Kris Kristofferson) is officially declared dead but 17 years later, when illness separates him from his new Cambodian family, he returns to the States to renew ties with the American family he left behind. As directed by Franklin J. Schaffner, this weepy melodrama fails to shed light on the very real problems facing Vietnam veterans and their kin. Some profanity and an adulterous sexual encounter

title: Welcome Home, Roxy Carmichael
synopsis: A small town anticipates the return of their one Hollywood celebrity, but none more eagerly than her former beau (Jeff Daniels), now a family man, and an alienated 15-year-old (Winona Ryder) who suspects Roxy may secretly be her mom. Director Jim Abrahams takes a basically frivolous story and, helped by Ryder's fine performance, develops it with charm, warmth and a small dose of insight about human relationships. References to a premarital relationship, minimal vulgar expressions and a flash of nudity

title: Welcome Home, Soldier Boys
synopsis: Four Vietnam vets (Joe Don Baker, Alan Vint, Paul Koslo and Elliott Street) pull into the sleepy hamlet of Hope, New Mexico, gang-rape a girl, kill everyone in town and then burn it to the ground. Directed by Richard Compton, the gruesome and ultimately cynical movie contributes nothing to understanding the problems of Vietnam veterans. O (R) ( 1972 )

title: Welcome Stranger
synopsis: Sentimental comedy about a likeable, good-natured doctor (Bing Crosby) arriving in Maine to fill in while a town's elderly physician (Barry Fitzgerald) takes a vacation, then has to win over the suspicious locals, a lovely schoolmarm (Joan Caulfield) and the cranky old doc himself. Director Elliott Nugent gets disappointing results from the artifical plot and setting, while the testy relationship between the two doctors grows maudlin rather than endearing. Romantic complications

title: Welcome to Collinwood
synopsis: Passable crime comedy set in a Cleveland working-class neighborhood where several petty crooks (including William H. Macy, Sam Rockwell and Michael Jeter) plot a big robbery that goes entirely awry. Written and directed by Joe and Anthony Russo, the film's clueless characters are mostly lovable losers but the jaunty tone can't fully compensate for the skimpy narrative. Brief violence, recurring profanity, minor sexual innuendo, fleeting rear nudity and much rough language

title: Welcome to L.A.
synopsis: Listless and pretentious account of the amorous adventures of a young song writer (Keith Carradine) whose charm is such that women jostle and trample one another in a mad rush to enjoy his favor. Writer-director Alan Rudolph's unsurprising message is that sex without love is unrewarding and that Los Angeles has some sort of monopoly on self-deception. Gratuitous nudity. O (R) ( 1977 )

title: Welcome to Mooseport
synopsis: Lukewarm comedy about a local handyman (Ray Romano) who, in an attempt to win back his girlfriend (Maura Tierney), decides to run against a former president (Gene Hackman) for mayor of his quaint New England town. Part triangular romance, part political satire, director Donald Petrie's flat farce pokes fun at the electoral process and media scrutiny of candidates' private lives while espousing a belief in the basic decency of Main Street America, but fails to make good on its campaign promises of comedy. Some sexual humor, instances of rear nudity and minimal crude language

title: Welcome to Sarajevo
synopsis: Fact-based story of a world-weary British TV journalist (Stephen Dillane) who grimly reports on civilian massacres in wartorn 1992 Sarajevo, then attempts to smuggle a 10-year-old girl back with him when he returns to London. By focusing on the touching story of one child's fate, director Michael Winterbottom's semidocumentary hits home emotionally in decrying the insanity of genocide. Some violence, numerous gory corpses, fleeting nudity and occasional rough language

title: Welcome to the Club
synopsis: Generally witless comedy about a naive Quaker morale officer (Brian Foley) who attempts to integrate a postwar Hiroshima officer's club, and comes off more as a fool than as a nice guy going through some sobering disillusionment. Directed by William Shenson, the result is rather depressing and, whatever its good intentions in trying to satirize both the military and bigotry, it contains considerable offensiveness, notably foul language. O (R) ( 1971 )

title: Welcome to the Dollhouse
synopsis: Painfully funny story of a geeky 11-year-old suburban girl (Heather Matarazzo) and her efforts to become popular which are continually undermined by her mom, siblings and taunting classmates. Writer-director Todd Solondz insightfully and unsentimentally captures the seventh grader's nightmare existence which just a little kindness from those around could dramatically change for the better. Fleeting violence, some sexual references and recurring rough language

title: We Live Again
synopsis: Hollywood version of Leo Tolstoy's novel, "Resurrection," about a Russian prince (Fredric March) who learns years later that he has ruined the life of a peasant girl (Anna Sten) on his aunt's estates by leaving her pregnant, then tries to atone by joining her when she is sent to Siberia for a crime of which she is innocent. Director Rouben Mamoulian evokes both the beauty of the Russian spirit and the injustices of the czarist regime but the characters and their emotions are melodramatically thin. Muddled treatment of an idealistic theme

title: Wells Fargo
synopsis: Interesting saga of the title overland express as portrayed in the exploits of its field agent (Joel McCrea) who forges the line from New York to St. Louis in the 1840s, establishes an office in 1850 San Francisco, then constructs a series of relay stations from Missouri to California on the eve of the Civil War. Directed by Frank Lloyd, the story is paced by frontier action and colorful pioneer lore, but the agent's marriage to a Southern belle (Frances Dee) adds some dark melodramatics that cloud the last portion of the picture. Stylized violence and domestic strife

title: We Own The Night
synopsis: Powerful character-driven drama set in 1980s New York about a drug-taking nightclub manager (a splendid Joaquin Phoenix) who changes his dissolute ways when his police-officer brother (Mark Wahlberg) is shot -- and their police-chief father's (Robert Duvall) life threatened -- by the Russian mobsters who control the venue. Writer-director James Gray sustains a taut, tragedy-drenched mood, the action secondary to the human drama; performances are fine, including Eva Mendes as Phoenix's girlfriend; and the narrative has an admirable gravitas, marred from a moral standpoint only by a revenge killing that is out of step with Catholic teaching. Sporadic but strong violence, rough language, some crude expressions and profanity, vigilante killing, some grisly crime images, drug use, sexual encounter and upper female nudity

title: We're Back! A Dinosaur's Story
synopsis: Magically transported to present-day New York City, four friendly dinos are saved by a gruff street urchin and a lonely little girl when an evil circus master changes them into snarling monsters. Steven Spielberg's animated production of Hudson Talbott's children's story sacrifices much of its charm and character appeal for an overabundance of busy and noisy misadventures that may delight children a lot more than their elders

title: We're No Angels
synopsis: Minor comedy in which bumbling convicts (Humphrey Bogart, Peter Ustinov and Aldo Ray) delay their escape from Devil's Island to save a kindly but inefficient French shopkeeper and his wife (Leo(G) . Carroll and Joan Bennett) from the machinations of a crafty relative (Basil Rathbone). Director Michael Curtiz gets some laughs from the unlikely antics of the good-hearted cons but the plot's intended whimsy falls flat. Devious deeds aplenty

title: We're No Angels
synopsis: Heavy-handed comic misadventure in which two escaped convicts (Robert De Niro and Sean Penn) hide out in a monastery pretending to be priests while they figure out a way to cross the border into Canada. David Mamet's script has plenty of comic possibilities in contrasting the spiritual impoverishment of the two earth-bound clods with the faith and innocence of the unworldly community of monks, but director Neil Jordan plays the piece so broadly that the result may appear to some as an irreverent farce, questionable in taste and treatment of religion. Some sexual references, several scenes of hard-edged violence and a bemused agnostic attitude toward religion

title: We're Rich Again
synopsis: Wacky Depression comedy in which a stock market casualty (Grant Mitchell) hopes to recoup his fortune after his daughter (Joan Marsh) marries a millionaire (Reginald Denny), but when her dizzy country cousin (Marian Nixon) arrives for the wedding, chaos follows. Directed by William A. Seiter, the zany proceedings feature running gags with a polo-playing grandmother (Edna May Oliver) and a frustrated process server (Edgar Kennedy), but the thin plot belabors the obvious. Light treatment of marriage and sexual innuendo

title: Werewolf of London
synopsis: Creaky but still effective monster tale in which a botanist (Henry Hull) is bitten by a werewolf while searching for a rare flower in Tibet, then returns to London with the plant only to learn too late its bloom is an antidote to becoming a wolfman. Directed by Stuart Walker, the twisty plot has the Tibetan werewolf (Warner Oland) turn up as a respected professor who steals the blooms for himself, leaving London to be terrorized by the botanist-wolfman during the four nights of the full moon. Stylized fantasy violence and menace

title: Werewolf, The
synopsis: Pedestrian monster fantasy directed by Fred F. Sears has a poor fellow (Steven Ritch) roaming the U.S. countryside after being turned into a wolfman by a botched radiation experiment. Stylized violence and unconvincing chills

title: Wes Craven Presents Dracula 2000
synopsis: Far-fetched thriller set in the present day, in which an antiques dealer (Christopher Plummer) travels from his home in London to America to save his daughter (Justine Waddell) from his life-long nemesis, Dracula (Gerard Butler). Despite a few frightening moments, director Wes Craven's sleek update has no bite with ordinary special effects and a convoluted narrative that ends with a cockamamie explanation of Dracula's origins. Intermittent violence with some gore, a few sexual references, fleeting partial nudity and sporadic rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference

title: Wes Craven's New Nightmare
synopsis: In the 7th of the "Nightmare on Elm Street" horror series, an actress (Heather Langenkamp) and her little boy (Miko Hughes) begin having violent nightmares which trigger the return of maniac Freddy Krueger (Robert Englund) who makes repeated attempts at killing them. Writer-director Wes Craven unreels a trite series of mother-and-child-in-peril situations in a suspenseless sequel featuring smug cameo appearances by the director and his studio boss. Some horror-fantasy violence, frequent menace to a child and a few instances of rough language

title: Westbound
synopsis: Standard Western about a Union officer (Randolph Scott) put in charge of a stagecoach line carrying California gold past Confederate sympathizers (led by Andrew Duggan). Directed by Budd Boetticher, it offers the usual brand of heroics and villainy but little else. Stylized violence

title: Westerner, The
synopsis: Cowboy Gary Cooper sides with the sodbusters against the cattlemen led by Roy Bean (Walter Brennan), the hanging judge of Vinegaroon, Texas. Directed by William Wellman, the situation is familiar but flavorsome and wryly fashioned, particularly Brennan's performance as the ornery judge whose ideal is the English singer, Lily Langtry. Periodic stylized violence

title: Western Union
synopsis: A reformed outlaw (Randolph Scott) and a rich tenderfoot (Robert Young) help a Western Union engineer (Dean Jagger) fight off Indians and Confederate raiders (headed by Barton MacLane) while stringing the last link in the telegraph line connecting the East and West coasts in 1861. The heroic theme is directed by Fritz Lang, with plenty of Western action and colorful characters galore, including Slim Summerville's comically fearful cook. Frontier violence and Indian stereotypes

title: West of the Badlands
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Joseph Kane in which a New York doctor (Roy Rogers) wrongly sought by the law shows up in 1875 Idaho where he's befriended by an old codger (George "Gabby" Hayes) and a pretty saloon owner (Maude Eburn), then joins a band of outlaws (led by Joe Sawyer) in order to stop their raids on his new friends. Mild violence

title: West of the Divide
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Robert N. Bradbury features John Wayne masquerading as an outlaw in order to get the man who killed his father 12 years before, during the course of which he saves a rancher's daughter (Virginia Faire Brown) and finds his longlost kid brother

title: West Point Story, The
synopsis: Strained musical romance in which a down-on-his-luck Broadway director (James Cagney) is required to live as a cadet while staging the military academy's annual revue (headed by Gordon MacRae), with some help from his devoted assistant (Virginia Mayo) and a friendly movie star (Doris Day). Directed by Roy Del Ruth, the dim plot's contrived romances are strictly formula fare, with only the academy setting and Cagney's energetic song-and-dance numbers to hold interest. Comic violence, romantic complications and much duplicity

title: West Side Story
synopsis: Rousing Broadway musical, with choreography by Jerome Robbins and music by Leonard Bernstein, is a contemporary, inner-city adaptation of the classic Romeo and Juliet theme, with Richard Beymer and Natalie Wood playing the star-crossed lovers set apart ethnically and by their opposing street gang backgrounds. Directed by Robert Wise, the picture captures the grit of life in the city's lower depths, with glimmers of hope and elements of tragedy in a delicate balance, carried along by song and the dance numbers that pulsate with energy and verve. Some of the social issues, relationships and street language, however, require a mature perspective

title: Westward Ho
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Robert Bradbury is set in 1866 when a California cowboy (John Wayne) organizes the Singing Riders, a vigilante band dedicated to ridding the West of outlaws, in particular, the gang who 16 years before had killed his parents and taken his baby brother. Frontier violence with vigilantes aiding outnumbered lawmen

title: Westward the Women
synopsis: Distaff Western chronicles the adventures of 140 women (Denise Darcel, Marilyn Erskine, Hope Emerson, et. al.) recruited in Chicago as prospective brides for California settlers, making their way cross-country in a wagon train led by a tough but increasingly bemused wagonmaster (Robert Taylor). Directed by William A. Wellman, there are plenty of dangers and some losses along the trail but the trek's sentimental ending is never in doubt. Stylized frontier violence and mild sexual references

title: Westworld
synopsis: James Brolin and Richard Benjamin vacation in a futuristic resort where, during the fun and games, a Western gunslinger robot (Yul Brynner) malfunctions, turns on the vacationers and starts to stalk them. Unfortunately, after about ten minutes, writer-director Michael Crichton has explored all the subtleties of the one-idea situation. Some ludicrous nonsense about "willing" female robots

title: Wetherby
synopsis: Vanessa Redgrave plays a schoolteacher in a small town who becomes the indirect victim of an act of violence that seems to be wholly unprovoked. But was it? This superbly acted but somewhat thin and contrived murder mystery, written and directed by playwright David Hare, explores the question of suicide in a careful, literate and sometimes compelling fashion. Good entertainment for mature viewers, although there is some violence and a few fairly restrained bedroom scenes

title: We Were Soldiers
synopsis: Powerful Vietnam War drama about the first battle between American troops, led by fatherly Lt. Col. Harold G. Moore (Mel Gibson), and the Viet Cong enemy. Despite slim characterizations and a few cliches, writer-director Randall Wallace's harrowing true story depicts war with raw, graphic imagery that underscores the wrenching loss of human life as it touches briefly upon the formidable struggle to reconcile Christianity and warfare. Constant war violence with many bloody, chilling images and some rough language with profanity

title: We Will All Meet in Paradise
synopsis: Thin French comedy about the life and times of four overaged, overindulged, middle-class Dead End Kids (Jean Rochfort, Claude Brasseur, Guy Bedos and Victor Lanoux) as they go through a round of sophomoric escapades. Directed by Yves Robert, the result is a tepid comedy of manners whose sole merit is the considerable charm of the performers. Adultery figures in the plot

title: Whale Rider
