synopsis: Evocative coming-of-age tale set among contemporary New Zealand Maoris where a 12-year-old girl (Keisha Castle-Hughes) secretly trains to become the warrior-like tribal leader against the fierce objections of her tradition-bound grandfather, the aging chief (Rawiri Paratene). Writer-director Niki Caro sensitively weds the ancient culture's rites to hardscrabble times, in the process dramatically exploring the role of community, change, and father figures in the formation of youngsters. Brief sexual and drug-related reference

title: Whales of August, The
synopsis: Two aged sisters (Bette Davis and Lillian Gish), sharing a cottage on an island off the coast of Maine, rely upon each other since one is blind but wealthy and the other is poor but kind. Director Lindsay Anderson's picture of old age and sibling rivalries is finely told through mood and characterization, and though sentimental, it is full of heart and small truths. Some incidental profanity

title: What Happens in Vegas
synopsis: An inebriated couple -- a commodities trader (Cameron Diaz), dumped by her longtime boyfriend, and a womanizing slacker (Ashton Kutcher), fired from his closet-building job -- get married in Las Vegas, much to their later regret, and must live with the consequences when they return to New York and a judge orders them to try to make the marriage work for six months, if they are to decide who keeps the $3 million jackpot they won at the slots. Director Tom Vaughan's romantic comedy is lame, tasteless and unfunny, despite a premise that could work in better hands, while the warm-if-predictable ending fails to erase the sophomoric ineptitude of what has come before it. Pervasive vulgar humor, implied premarital cohabitation, scatological elements, some skimpy costuming, much crude language and brief profanity

title: What a Girl Wants
synopsis: Contemporary fairytale about a spirited American teen-ager (Amanda Bynes) who travels to London in search of the father she has never known only to find out that she is the daughter of a blueblood politician (Colin Firth) running for Parliament. Directed by Dennie Gordon, this delightful modern Cinderella story celebrates the bonds between parents and children and the possibility of second chances that love affords. Instances of mildly offensive language and scattered sexual innuendoes

title: What a Way to Die
synopsis: ( see: "Beyond Control" )

title: What a Way to Go!
synopsis: Deadly one-joke comedy told in flashbacks as psychiatrist Bob Cummings listens to widow Shirley MacLaine explain how the untimely demise of husbands Dick Van Dyke, Paul Newman, Robert Mitchum and Gene Kelly left her enormously wealthy, but all she wants is penniless janitor Dean Martin. Directed by J. Lee Thompson, the lumbering production glitters with period costuming and decor but the witless plot and humor are painfully heavy-handed. Much sexual innuendo

title: What Dreams May Come
synopsis: Gooey afterlife fantasy in which a doctor (Robin Williams) killed in a car crash is reunited with his deceased children in the hereafter, then chooses to seek out his artist wife (Annabella Sciorra) in hell following her suicide. While director Vincent Ward's painterly visuals are exquisite, the incoherent treatment of afterlife reunions renders the movie largely unappealing. A suicide, theme of reincarnation and minimal profanity and rough language

title: Whatever
synopsis: Downbeat coming-of-age story of two high school seniors (Liza Weil and Chad Morgan) from dysfunctional families who sneak out to drug parties and try casual sex, but end up going in very different directions. Writer-director Susan Skoog captures the adolescent angst of rudderless girls lacking parental guidance, but the unsentimental narrative is flawed by one girl's sudden transformation. Brief violence, teen promiscuity, much substance abuse, frequent rough language, fleeting nudity and occasional profanity

title: Whatever Happened to Aunt Alice
synopsis: Suspense thriller with Geraldine Page as a widow, left without any observable means of income, who combines murder and gardening as profitable pastimes in bilking a series of housekeepers out of their life savings. Routine chiller directed by Lee H. Katzin. A-II (PG) (1969)

title: Whatever It Takes
synopsis: Forgettable romantic teen comedy in which a socially awkward boy and a popular high school jock hatch a plan to woo their respective dream girls, producing unexpected results. As directed by David Raynr, the "Cyrano de Bergerac" imitator lacks any original spark with its predictable plot and strained comedic efforts. Several sexual references, adolescent drinking and some rough language

title: Whatever Works
synopsis: A pessimistic New York grouch (Larry David) finds his life transformed when he reluctantly shelters a homeless but irrepressibly cheerful young Southerner (Evan Rachel Wood), and they fall for each other. Though undeniably clever at times, writer-director Woody Allen's comedy of manners mocks evangelical Christians through the waif's parents (Patricia Clarkson and Ed Begley Jr.) and heavy-handedly rams home the message that, in a meaningless universe, any path to temporary fulfillment, particularly that of unbridled sexuality, ought to be pursued. Adultery, implied group sex and homosexual activity, images of full nudity, a suicide theme, some sexual humor, at least one crude and one crass word, and about a dozen uses of profanity

title: What Every Woman Knows
synopsis: Droll adaptation of the James M. Barrie play about a bright but practical Scotswoman (Helen Hayes) who helps get her dashing but dim intended (Brian Aherne) elected to Parliament, then as his wife furthers his career while extricating him from a foolish infatuation with an English beauty (Madge Evans). Directed by Gregory La Cava, the proverbial tale of the woman behind any successful man is treated with disarming humor and convincing performances. Romantic complications and implied infidelity

title: What Happened Was...
synopsis: Unsettling two-person drama about a middle-aged paralegal (Tom Noonan) and a thirtyish secretary (Karen Sillas) in the same firm whose awkward first date begins with dinner in her Manhattan studio and ends up revealing both as very troubled adults, quite unlike the workaday personalities they project. Also written and directed by Noonan, the dramatic situation is intriguing as a reflection of the loneliness of urban life and the individual's need to have some sense of belonging. Concerns regarding emotional intimacy, some sex and drug references and occasional rough language

title: What Just Happened
synopsis: Perceptive, sporadically funny comedy as a beleaguered producer (Robert De Niro) tries to salvage his latest film starring Sean Penn (as himself), and convince star Bruce Willis (also as himself) to shave a bushy beard before filming another, and reconcile with his separated wife (Robin Wright Penn). Much of the humor of director Barry Levinson's satire strives for a trenchant insider look at Hollywood, though not all the jokes land, but there are good performances by John Turturro, Stanley Tucci, Catherine Keener and others, while De Niro manages to convey a sympathetic portrait of a man in the throes of midlife crisis. Much rough language and some profanity, crude expressions, brief violent images with gore, an implied nonmarital sexual encounter and a drug reference

title: What Lies Beneath
synopsis: Plodding ghost story in which a wife (Michelle Pfeiffer) feels haunted by a menacing spirit who turns out to have been involved with her geneticist husband (Harrison Ford). Director Robert Zemeckis attempts to generate Hitchcock-like suspense but falls far short with glaring plot holes and an abundance of thriller cliches. Some violence, sexual situations with implied adultery, occasional profanity and an instance of rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference

title: What Lola Wants
synopsis: ( see: "Damn Yankees" )

title: What Price Glory
synopsis: Stagey remake of the 1926 original with Captain James Cagney and Sergeant Dan Dailey as brawling Marines in World War I France where they battle over a barmaid (Corinne Calvet) before going back into the line. Director John Ford lets the romance slide in favor of manly horseplay and military heroics, with disappointing results. Wartime violence and romantic tomfoolery

title: What's Cooking
synopsis: Warmhearted comedy that follows the Thanksgiving dinners of four Los Angeles families (including Alfre Woodard, Maury Chaykin, Joan Chen and Kyra Sedgwick) as they cope with situations ranging from parental dismay over a daughter's gay lifestyle to teenage violence to infidelity. Highlighting the ethnically diverse aspects of Angelino families, director Gurinder Chadha's film contrasts dynamic families -- African-American, Latino, Jewish and Asian -- while connecting them through turkey and love in an often humorous and touching manner. Brief menace, a lesbian relationship, fleeting rear nudity and intermittent crass language with an instance of rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference

title: What's Eating Gilbert Grape
synopsis: A compassionate stranger (Juliette Lewis) helps a frustrated young man (Johnny Depp) deal with the burden of heading a dysfunctional household consisting of his mom (Darlene Cates), who's a 500-pound recluse, and his mentally disabled younger brother (Leonardo DiCaprio) who is often a danger to himself. Though the narrative sometimes ambles and rambles, director Lasse Hallstrom's offbeat, often downbeat drama features finely honed performances and a poignant script that never insults the emotional, mental or physical frailties of its characters. An implied affair and brief violence

title: What's Good for the Goose
synopsis: Failed British movie in which a glum bank manager (Norman Wisdom) is introduced to the psychedelic world of free love, loud music and general aimlessness by an uninhibited hitchhiker (Sally Geeson) who is always ready to disrobe and jump into bed. Directed by Menahem Golan, the movie's attempt to pass this off as social comment fails to overcome the exploitative elements that predominate. O (R) ( 1970 )

title: What's Love Got to Do with It
synopsis: Musical biography of rock singer Tina Turner (played by Angela Bassett) focusing on her rise to fame and troubled marriage to abusive husband Ike (Laurence Fishburne) until she left him and established a solo career. Director Brian Gibson serves up a spirited but ultimately superficial look at the entertainer, offsetting the ugly hysterics of a violent relationship with glossy musical set-pieces. A discreet bedroom scene, some intense domestic violence, occasional recreational drug use and recurring rough language

title: What's So Bad About Feeling Good
synopsis: Colorful tropical bird infects the rude, scowling citizens of New York City with a mysterious happiness virus and within hours everyone is smiling and polite to one another, including George Peppard and Mary Tyler Moore playing reformed hippies. But when New Yorkers also quit gambling, smoking and drinking, the government develops an antidote to protect their tax revenues. Produced and directed by George Seaton, it's an amusing little satire on urban life that some may find infectious. Romantic complications

title: What's the Worst That Can Happen
synopsis: Failed comedy about a billionaire tycoon (Danny DeVito) who snatches the lucky ring off a thief (Martin Lawrence) he catches robbing his house and triggers a battle of wills between the two men over the good-luck charm. Sluggish and dull-witted, director Sam Weisman's flimsy narrative is mostly a snore with a few cheap laughs. An implied sexual encounter, brief comically intended violence, sporadic profanity, some crass words and fleeting rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference

title: What the Bleep Do We Know
synopsis: Part documentary, part narrative film which uses a loose story line about an unfulfilled wedding photographer (Marlee Matlin) as a launching pad for discussions of quantum physics, the intersection of science and spirituality, and the underlying nature of reality. Directed by William Arntz, Betsy Chasse and Mark Vicente, the docudrama incorporates amusing animated segments and interviews with academics to explore its difficult subject matter in a lively and engaging manner. However, while the film raises some interesting questions, its arguments often become muddled by New Age mysticism which promotes private spirituality over traditional organized religion. Mild sexual content and a few crude expressions

title: What Women Want
synopsis: Leaden mix of fantasy and romantic comedy in which a womanizing advertising executive (Mel Gibson) who can read the minds of all the females around him steals the ideas of his new boss (Helen Hunt) to get her job even though they are becoming romantically involved. As directed by Nancy Meyers, the one-joke premise soon wears out its welcome in contrived and pathetically predictable situations. A sexual encounter, fleeting recreational drug use and sexist remarks. The U.S. Catholic Conference

title: Wheeler Dealers, The
synopsis: Romantic comedy about a cunning Texas high-roller (James Garner) who falls for a Wall Street broker (Lee Remick), then is indicted for helping her sell stock in a product that went out with high-button shoes. Director Arthur Hiller's comic treatment of stock market hijinks is no longer as wacky as it once seemed, though the characters still please. Romantic situations

title: Wheel of Fortune
synopsis: ( see: "A Man Betrayed" )

title: When in Rome
synopsis: Perky romantic comedy about a work-obsessed New York museum curator (Kristen Bell) who travels to Rome for her sister's (Alexis Dziena) wedding and falls for the best man (Josh Duhamel), but their path to bliss takes a detour when she defies local custom by removing several coins from the "Fountain of Love," causing the quartet of eccentric strangers who deposited the change (Danny DeVito, Will Arnett, Jon Heder and Dax Shepard) to become hopelessly infatuated with her. While the youthful, slightly pixilated priest (Keir O'Donnell) who performs the nuptials comes in for some gentle ribbing, director Mark Steven Johnson's pleasantly diverting, blithely illogical ensemble piece is mostly worry-free with only a fleeting scene of newlywed friskiness barring endorsement for teens. Brief nongraphic marital lovemaking with implied nudity, mildly irreverent portrayal of a clergyman and a few crass expressions

title: When a Man Loves a Woman
synopsis: After an airline pilot (Andy Garcia) discovers that his wife (Meg Ryan) has become a secret alcoholic, they get professional help but each must learn to change destructive behavior patterns in order to save their marriage and nurture their two small daughters. Despite its sometimes soggy treatment, director Luis Mandoki's inspirational drama is credible in its depiction of the tragic consequences of alcoholism on a family and its wrenching struggle for recovery. Scenes of drunkenness with fleeting nudity and minor violence as well as intermittent rough language

title: When a Stranger Calls
synopsis: Mediocre remake of the marginal 1978 psychological thriller about a high-school student (Camilla Belle) who, while baby-sitting at a secluded lakefront home, is terrorized by the phone threats of an unseen homicidal stalker, only to discover that the calls are coming from inside the house. Director Simon West forgoes plot and plausibility in favor of easy jolts, but does manage to create an unnerving atmosphere of isolation and suspense through suggestion, while keeping the violence relatively tame. Some violence, including a hand skewered by a fire poker, scenes of menace and child peril, implied murders, brief images of dead bodies and scattered crude language

title: When a Stranger Calls
synopsis: Homicidal maniac (Tony Beckley) stalks a babysitter (Carol Kane) in this plodding, mediocre thriller directed by Fred Walton. Some intense violence and the impending threat of violence are adult fare

title: When Dinosaurs Ruled the Earth
synopsis: British production directed by Val Guest is a few cuts above the average prehistoric monster movie which, aside from some Hollywood bikinis on the cavewomen, has some authentic-looking overgrown reptiles, birds, and dinosaurs. It's an enjoyable movie for the youngsters, not too scary and colorful enough to hold short attention spans

title: When Eight Bells Toll
synopsis: British adaptation of an Alistair MacLean novel about a Bond-type government agent (Anthony Hopkins) and his gentle partner (Corin Redgrave) who are dispatched to the Western Highland lochs to find out what lies behind the disappearance of several gold-carrying ships. Directed by Etienne Perier, the plot employs masterful twists and cross currents, but though handled with restraint, it is adult fare both in story and treatment

title: When Father Was Away on Business
synopsis: Yugoslavian production set in the time of Tito's break with the Soviet Union, has a plot following a philandering husband who is denounced by his mistress as a politica1 deviant and ends up in a labor camp. This warm human comedy by director Emir Kusturica ends in the resolution of personal problems and politica1 differences during a madcap wedding feast of family forgiveness. Some coarse language and partial nudity are treated with restraint

title: When Harry Met Sally...
synopsis: Story of the unlikely ways people connect with suitable marriage partners focuses on the comic and touching travails of one couple (Billy Crystal and Meg Ryan) over a dozen years as they wander in and out of each other's lives. Director Rob Reiner's comedy about love, commitment, sex and friendship intercuts distracting testimonials from elderly couples about how they met. Though there is much graphic talk about sex and love in Yuppieland and an indiscreet spoof of female orgasm, the movie demonstrates that true love and commitment are still here to stay. Implied sexual promiscuity

title: When Night Is Falling
synopsis: A solemn young woman (Pascale Bussieres) on the verge of marriage to a Protestant theology professor (Henry Czerny) chooses instead to join a traveling circus to be with her lesbian lover (Rachel Crawford). Writer-director Patricia Rozema's romanticized lesbian love story heavy-handedly presents the young teacher's crisis in faith, marriage and career as no match for the exotic creature who awakens latent homosexual desires. Positive portrayal of homosexuality, extended sex scenes with nudity and occasional rough language. O (nr) ( 1995 )

title: When Strangers Marry
synopsis: Twisty crime tale in which a bride (Kim Hunter) gets some help from a former beau (Robert Mitchum) when she comes to suspect her secretive husband (Dean Jagger) is a murderer. Directed by William Castle, the plot is overly contrived but the characters invite sympathy and most viewers will be unsurprised by the trick ending. Menacing situations and romantic complications

title: When the Cat's Away
synopsis: Serio-comic tale of a lonely Parisienne (Garance Clavel) who gets lots of help searching for her lost cat, particularly from older women, but others prove more interested in romance than locating the missing feline until the picture's sweetly hopeful ending. Writer-director Cedric Klapisch's wistful story of a single woman whose search for a pet turns into a quest for the right man to share her life is treated earnestly, yet with humor in an odd series of unsuitable encounters before a real prospect finally turns up. Subtitles. Several restrained sex scenes, sexual references, coarse expressions and occasional rough language

title: When the Daltons Rode
synopsis: Forced off their land by a crooked developer (George Bancroft), the Dalton Brothers (Broderick Crawford, Brian Donlevy and Stewart Irwin) become feared outlaws, though a steadfast friend (Randolph Scott) tries to clear their name. Directed by George Marshall, the old story is played for all its worth until the final demise of the Dalton Gang in a Kansas City shoot-out. Stylized violence

title: When the Legends Die
synopsis: Above average Western in which a sharp rodeo hustler (Richard Widmark) takes in an 18-year-old Ute Indian (Frederic Forrest) and teaches him the tricks of the trade but the youth does not see the value in taking money from suckers and returns to the reservation, sadder but wiser. Produced and directed by Stuart Millar, the fine character study of the two principals is chiefly what is of interest here, and not its commonplace message. Implied sexual affair

title: When the West Was Young
synopsis: Western programmer from a Zane Gray story about a bushwacked surveyor (Randolph Scott) who helps a horse rancher (J. Farrell McDonald) and his ward (Sally Blaine) fight off an outlaw gang. Director Henry Hathaway embellishes the simple action tale with colorful details and an appealing romantic subplot. Frontier violence

title: When the Whales Came
synopsis: Some 70 years after an 1844 legend about a curse befalling England's Scilly Isles for slaughtering a pack of beached whales, a deaf hermit (Paul Scofield) manages to successfully warn neighboring islanders to lay off some newly beached whales. In a tedious adaptation of Michael Morpurgo's children's book, director Clive Rees lets a lovely story with the gentle hermit, two island children and an ecological theme get bogged down in boring extraneous action and predictable period caricatures. Occasional menace involving parental abuse and minimal rough language

title: When Time Ran Out
synopsis: Paul Newman, Jacqueline Bisset, Burgess Meredith, Ernest Borgnine and other unfortunates are trapped on a Pacific island when the local volcano lets go. Directed by James Goldstone, the disaster epic is so dreadful that it could put an end to the disaster epic once and for all, though it probably won't

title: When Trumpets Fade
synopsis: World War II tale of an embittered private (Ron Eldard) who becomes a hero in spite of himself when his infantry unit is mauled by the German Wehrmacht during the 1944-45 Battle of the Hurtgen Forest along the Belgian-German border. Directed by John Irvin, the television production re-creates the inhuman carnage of the battlefield with special-effects realism but its anti-war story never gets beyond the usual movie stereotypes of men in war, especially the heroic anti-hero at its center. Gory battlefield violence, coarse humor, numerous sexual expletives and occasional profanity

title: When Worlds Collide
synopsis: With Earth doomed to destruction by an onrushing star, scientists build a rocket ship to serve as a new Noah's ark hoping to continue the human race on a new planet. Director Rudolph Mate's doomsday scenario is about as convincing as the wooden romance between Barbara Rush and Richard Derr, though the special effects by producer George Pal help build some interest in the desperate situation. Apocalyptic fantasy which may trouble young children

title: Where in the World Is Osama bin Laden?
synopsis: Genial but not particularly insightful documentary in which average citizen Morgan Spurlock's ostensible search for the titular terrorist takes him to North Africa and the Middle East, where he mingles with the mostly friendly locals and ponders the origins of Islamic extremism. Spurlock, who also directed, rehashes the familiar shortcomings of American policy in the area, and makes a vague plea for a more humane world, but suggests no specific reforms. Two gory scenes, three uses of the f-word, and occasional crude and crass language

title: Where Angels Fear to Tread
synopsis: Satiric comedy filters through tragedy in E.M. Forster's turn-of-the-century story of a wealthy English widow (Helen Mirren) who impulsively marries a penniless young Italian (Giovanni Guidelli) against the wishes of her in-laws. As directed by Charles Sturridge, the cultural clash between fiery Italian and straightlaced Britons affords several well-observed character studies. Brief violence

title: Where Angels Go...Trouble Follows!
synopsis: Weak sequel to "The Trouble with Angels" in which a liberal young nun (Stella Stevens) tries to update the convent boarding school under a traditionalist Mother Superior (Rosalind Russell) by leading a busload of nuns and students to a peace rally. Directed by James Neilson, the old pros in the cast (Binnie Barnes, Mary Wickes, Van Johnson, Robert Taylor and others) overcome the painfully contrived story and turn it into light, unsophisticated entertainment

title: Where Danger Lives
synopsis: Dark, muddled tale of a doctor (Robert Mitchum) on the run from the police with the wife (Faith Domergue) of the man (Claude Rains) he believes he killed. Directed by John Farrow, the tension is artificial in a situation that has little interest. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Where Eagles Dare
synopsis: A spy-counter-spy melodrama set in the Bavarian Alps during World War II pits Richard Burton, Clint Eastwood and Mary Ure against what must be half the German army ensconced in a castle literally inaccessible except by cable car. Brian Hutton directs the Alistair MacLean script which consists of an interminable, totally implausible series of killings, escapes and pyrotechnic displays

title: Where God Left His Shoes
synopsis: Somber but touching inner-city drama in which a down-on-his-luck professional boxer (John Leguizamo) and his 9-year-old stepson (David Castro) spend Christmas Eve crisscrossing New York in search of a job that will qualify him to move his family -- including his wife (Leonor Varela) and daughter (Samantha Rose) -- out of a homeless shelter and into a housing project. A brief but inappropriate sexual discussion aside, writer-director Salvatore Stabile's deeply felt but unsentimental portrait of life on the economic margins, with its social humiliations and bureaucratic stonewalling, quietly asserts the power of human dignity, marital fidelity and family solidarity in the face of challenging circumstances. Some instances of petty crime, one use of the F-word, some crude language, brief sexual references and a physical abuse theme

title: Where It's At
synopsis: Las Vegas casino owner (David Janssen) teaches his disinterested son (Robert Drivas) the tricks of exploiting the tourist trade but the lad beats his father at his own game, gains control of the casino and then hands it back, realizing it is his father's whole life but will never be his. Director Garson Kanin tries to gloss over a most implausible script by resorting to some sexual diversions. O (R) ( 1969 )

title: Where Love Has Gone
synopsis: Trashy sudser from Harold Robbins' novel about an artist (Susan Hayward) who divorces her war-hero husband (Michael Connors) after he's driven to drink by her domineering mom (Bette Davis), then takes a series of lovers until their 15-year-old daughter (Joey Heatherton) murders one of them. Directed by Edward Dmytryk, the soapy proceedings are dressed up in a glossy production whose shallow characters waste the talents of the cast. Stylized violence including a suicide and much sexual innuendo

title: Where the Boys Are '84
synopsis: Four women college students (Lisa Hartman, Lorna Luft, Wendy Schaal and Lynn-Holly Johnson) go to Fort Lauderdale for the spring break and carry on like amateur hookers, but viewers are supposed to believe its very wholesome and therapeutic. Director Hy Averback's updating of a silly 1960 movie contains nudity, sexually oriented humor and an appalling moral outlook. O (R) ( 1984 )

title: Where the Buffalo Roam
synopsis: Bill Murray portrays famed underground journalist Hunter S. Thompson, who seems to have derived much of his inspiration from drugs and alcohol. Director Art Linson tries to blend serious social concern with outrageous comedy but is only intermittently successful. Rough language and use of drugs

title: Where the Heart Is
synopsis: Because of some flippant attitudes towards sex and pregnancy, a few sexual encounters, brief subplot involving pedophilia, fleeting rough language and some profanity,

title: Where the Heart Is
synopsis: Pointless, humorless farce about a wealthy demolitions expert (Dabney Coleman) who attempts to teach his three grown but spoiled offspring a lesson in self-sufficiency by leaving them stranded in an abandoned Brooklyn tenement. Director John Boorman shows little sensitivity to family responsibilities and is offensively crass in dealing with minority issues and the reality of homelessness. Some nudity in the context of artwork, rough language and sexual innuendoes

title: Where the Lilies Bloom
synopsis: Four sturdy Appalachian children keep the death of their widowed father a secret so the state won't take them away to an orphan's home and provide for themselves out of the profits of "wildcrafting" (collecting and preparing certain herbs and wild flowers prized for their medicinal qualities). The Robert B. Radnitz production directed by William A. Graham tells its story of youngsters learning to care for themselves in the adult world with warm humor and genuine sensitivity for the conditions of life for the rural poor. A rare and satisfying entertainment for the entire family

title: Where The Money Is
synopsis: Because of a brief sexual encounter, some crass language and an instance of profanity,

title: Where There's Life
synopsis: Minor screwball comedy in which a New York radio announcer (Bob Hope) learns he's next in line to the throne of a small European country after a royal emissary (Signe Hasso) arrives to protect him from a band of rebels (led by George Zucco) sent to kill him. Directed by Sidney Lanfield, Hope is in good form as the frantic announcer whose pursuers include his hapless fiancee (Vera Marshe) and her irascible policeman brother (William Bendix). Comic menace and mild sexual innuendo

title: Where the Sidewalk Ends
synopsis: Quirky crime story of a hardened cop (Dana Andrews) who accidentally kills a suspect, then falls for the dead man's girlfriend (Gene Tierney) while trying to pin the murder on a slippery mobster (Gary Merrill). Director Otto Preminger diverts attention from the improbable plot twists by focusing on the gritty atmosphere and matching characterizations. Stylized violence and troubled relationships

title: Where the Truth Lies
synopsis: Stylish but unnecessarily salacious retronoir murder mystery based on the novel by Rupert Holmes. A young celebrity journalist (Alison Lohman), in researching a tell-all book on a Martin and Lewis-like comedy team (Colin Firth and Kevin Bacon), attempts to uncover the real story behind their breakup 15 years earlier and the true circumstances surrounding the death of a female fan (Rachel Blanchard) whose body was found in their hotel suite, the scandalous fallout of which tainted their showbiz careers and ruptured their friendship. Despite outstanding performances by Firth and Bacon, artful production design and a sensuous score, director Atom Egoyan's film makes pretensions about the nature of truth and celebrity, but is essentially a glossy whodunit wrapped up in nostalgia and glamour and spiced with soft-core sleaze and gratuitous nudity for titillating effect, and in the end doesn't even deliver much suspense. Several strong sex scenes, including an orgy, a lesbian encounter and a menage a trois, full-frontal nudity, homoerotic themes, a suicide, drug content, a brutal beating, and sporadic rough and crude language

title: Where The Wild Things Are
synopsis: Intriguing though melancholy fantasy in which a rambunctious young boy (Max Records) quarrels with his divorced mother (Catherine Keener) and runs away from home, eventually sailing to the island abode of the Wild Things, a close-knit but emotionally unstable community of giants (voiced, most prominently, by James Gandolfini and Lauren Ambrose) whose personalities reflect various aspects of the youth's real-life experiences and of his unsettled psychological state. While objectionable elements are minimal, director and co-writer Spike Jonze's subtle adaptation of Maurice Sendak's classic 1963 children's book -- which combines live action, puppetry and computer-generated animation -- far from being a film for kids, is instead a wistful adult meditation on the interior struggles of childhood. Also shown in Imax. Occasional menace and a few mild oaths

title: Whiffs
synopsis: Elliott Gould plays a medically discharged Army private whose use as a chemical warfare guinea pig has, among other ill effects, left him impotent. Gould gets his revenge, and cures his malady, by using stolen Army gas to disable an entire town and clean out its banks. Director Ted Post does nothing to redeem a singularly unfunny and tasteless screenplay, many of whose failed jokes have to do with the hero's sexual incapacity. O (PG) ( 1975 )

title: While You Were Sleeping
synopsis: Endearing screwball comedy in which the family of a comatose yuppie (Peter Gallagher) mistakenly believes he's engaged to a Chicago El token attendant (Sandra Bullock) who's actually attracted to the man's gentle brother (Bill Pullman), though neither will admit they're falling in love. Director Jon Turteltaub strengthens a predictable love story by fleshing it out with appealing characterizations of the brothers' big-hearted Catholic family and their wise Jewish neighbor (Jack Warden). Mild sexual innuendo and minimal profanity

title: Whip It
synopsis: Rough-and-tumble coming-of-age tale about a small-town Texas high school student (Ellen Page) who, with the help of her best friend (Alia Shawkat), defies her socially ambitious mother (Marcia Gay Harden) by secretly joining a hard-edged roller derby team (led by Kristen Wiig), eventually falling for a local rock singer (Landon Pigg) she meets at one of their matches. First-time director Drew Barrymore's adaptation of Shauna Cross' novel is buoyed by heartfelt performances from the principals, but the skimpy outfits and bruising smackdowns of the showcased competition come across as more exploitative than empowering, while Cross' script at least partially glamorizes irresponsible sexuality. Nongraphic nonmarital underage sexual activity, brief partial nudity, underage drinking, occasional irreverence, a few uses of profanity, some sexual humor and references, about a dozen crude terms and much crass language

title: Whirlpool
synopsis: Danish exploitation import about a wealthy woman (Pia Anderson), her psychopathic nephew (Karl Lanchbury) and a young model (Vivian Neves) lured into a sex triangle that ends with her rape-murder. Director J.R. Larrath, inept at fashioning suspense or terror, suffocates his English-speaking cast in a cesspool of stupefying dialogue, sex and blood. O (X) ( 1970 )

title: Whisperers, The
synopsis: Dame Edith Evans gives a brilliant performance as an impoverished old woman, beset by loneliness and physical infirmity, victimized and abandoned by an unfeeling husband and son, and finding her only comfort in the world of her imagination. Directed by Bryan Forbes, it is a compassionate examination of the struggles of old age and achieved without false sentimentality

title: Whispering Smith
synopsis: Off-beat Western in which a soft-spoken railroad troubleshooter (Alan Ladd) has to go after his best friend (Robert Preston) when he teams up with a crook (Donald Crisp). Directed by Leslie Fenton, the railroad setting has some interest as does the soured friendship, though the story's treatment is fairly routine. Frontier violence

title: Whispers in the Dark
synopsis: Lurid, violent melodrama has a psychiatrist (Annabella Sciorra) seeking help from her mentor (Alan Alda) after one of her patients (Deborah Unger) is murdered and her lover (Jamey Sheridan) and another patient (John Leguizamo) become prime suspects. Writer-director Christopher Crowe exploits sexual violence against women in a manipulative, tawdry potboiler. Recurring violence and nudity, graphic photos of tortured women, sexually explicit dialogue and situations and much rough language. O (R) ( 1992 )

title: Whistle Blower, The
synopsis: Veteran spy Michael Caine finds a way to avenge the death of his son, a British intelligence agent, without jeopardizing his position in the international club of spy organizations. British director Simon Langton's murder mystery has a plot device concerning infidelity and a far more subtle, pulpy and pernicious political bite which may confuse youngsters and certainly annoy sophisticated adults

title: Whistle Stop
synopsis: Unrewarding tale of a woman (Ava Gardner) who revisits the hick town in which she grew up, then finds herself caught between the surly loafer (George Raft) she was once sweet on and a smooth but hardened club owner (Tom Conway). Director Leonide Moguy focuses on the feuding males and their criminal pursuits, including attempted robbery and murder, leaving scant time for the story's romantic intentions. Stylized violence and sordid atmosphere

title: Whistling Bullets
synopsis: Western programmer directed by John W. English in which a Texas Ranger (Kermit Maynard) helps a bank robber escape prison hoping to find where he's hidden the loot, but the ruse is discovered and only the ranger's feisty girlfriend (Marlene Woods) can save the day. Frontier violence

title: Whistling in the Dark
synopsis: Dated but still amusing comedy in which a mild-mannered radio actor (Red Skelton) plays the role of a brilliant detective so well, he's kidnapped by the leader (Conrad Veidt) of a bogus cult who wants him to devise a fool-proof way to murder a wealthy cult member. Directed by Sylvan Simon, the silly radio-era proceedings provide a solid comedy vehicle for the bumbling, good-natured antics of Skelton in his first starring role. Mild comic menace

title: White
synopsis: Left penniless and homeless when divorced by his beautiful French bride (Julie Delpy) on the grounds of impotence, a Polish hairdresser (Zbigniew Zamachowski) amasses a fortune in Warsaw in hopes of luring her there for a devious reconciliation. Directed by Krzysztof Kieslowski, the murky and underdeveloped characterizations result in an ambiguous black comedy in which love is subjugated to power, greed and sexual prowess. Subtitles. Some violence, a few bedroom scenes and instances of rough language

title: White Balloon, The
synopsis: A seven-year-old girl living in Teheran goes to buy a plump goldfish for the Islamic New Year's celebration but loses the money down a streetside grate and enlists the aid of harried passersby to retrieve it before nightfall. Producer-director Jafar Panahi's Iranian production tells its simple tale in real time from the youngster's perspective with much of its appeal coming from the varied reactions of those called upon to help the child. Subtitles. Distraught youngster

title: White Buffalo, The
synopsis: Ponderous Western in which nightmares of a charging white buffalo bring Wild Bill Hickok (Charles Bronson) to the Black Hills in 1874 where, after a respite with an old friend (Kim Novak) and shootouts with old enemies, he teams with Sioux chief Crazy Horse (Will Sampson) in quest of a four-legged Moby Dick. Directed by J. Lee Thompson, the characters brood a good deal between vigorous spurts of action, with picturesque Dakota locales helping distract attention from the pretentious dialogue and phoney-looking beast. Stylized violence, a sexual encounter, course expressions and several profanities

title: White Chicks
synopsis: Painfully inept comedy in which two FBI agents (brothers Shawn and Marlon Wayans) go undercover to protect a pair of young white socialites at an exclusive summer resort from kidnappers by pretending to be the women. Director Keenen Ivory Wayans' preposterous premise quickly grows tiresome as do the unconvincing prosthetics and heavy makeup, while an actual story line is jettisoned in favor of flat jokes, well-worn gags and a handful of misogynistic jabs. A few sexual references, fleeting drug content, some scatological humor and fisticuffs, a few crass words and some profanity

title: White Christmas
synopsis: Cheerful but synthetic musical comedy about two World War II veterans (Bing Crosby and Danny Kaye) who use their popularity as entertainers to make a success out of the winter resort opened by their wartime commander (Dean Jagger). Directed by Michael Curtiz, the post-war feel-good plot is less memorable than Kaye's clowning and Crosby's crooning of the title song among other Irving Berlin numbers originally written for the earlier, better "Holiday Inn" (1942) pairing Crosby with Fred Astaire. While not a classic, it offers some good family entertainment

title: White Cliffs of Dover, The
synopsis: Dated patriotic sudser about an American tourist (Irene Dunne) whose whirlwind marriage to an English aristocrat (Alan Marshal) ends with his death in World War I but their child (Roddy McDowell) inherits the title and grows to become a military casualty (Peter Lawford) in World War II. Directed by Clarence Brown, it's an earnest, well-crafted sermon on Anglo-American relations with too little humor and too much bathos to be convincing. Of some interest as a period piece

title: White Comanche
synopsis: Dubbed European production directed by Gilbert Lee Kay has William Shatner playing twin brothers born of a captive white woman and a Comanche brave -- one raised by whites, the other by Indians -- until they meet on opposite sides in a range war that the local sheriff (Jospeh Cotton) has been unable to stop. Hokey plot and treatment paced with assorted stylized violence, including an off-screen rape

title: White Dawn, The
synopsis: Challenging fact-based story of three whalers (Warren Oates, Tomothy Bottoms and Lou Gossett) marooned in the 1890s on Baffin Island, 700 miles below the North Pole, are taken in by local Eskimos but their initial warm relationship degenerates into mistrust and finally vengeance as the two alien cultures threaten each other. Directed by Philip Kaufman, the corrupting influence of civilization on the savage innocence of the natives is depicted in realistic, often grisly, detail and Eskimo sexual customs are treated without sensation or exploitation

title: White Fang
synopsis: While hunting for gold with an older prospecter (Klaus Maria Brandauer) on the Alaskan frontier in 1898, a youth (Ethan Hawke) befriends a snarling, attack-trained wolf-dog that helps them fend off marauders. Director Randal Kleiser's version of the Jack London novel combines authentic Alaskan settings, untamed wildlife and a mildly suspenseful adventure to make diverting family fare for all but young children. Much simulated violence to animals and menace to humans

title: White Fang 2: Myth of the White Wolf
synopsis: Accompanied by his wolf-dog, a young goldminer (Scott Bairstow) in 1906 Alaska sets out to find food for a starving Native American tribe, falls in love with their princess (Charmaine Craig) and uncovers a dastardly plot against them. Director Ken Olin's scenic but uninspired sequel to Jack London's tale of a lad and his canine in the wilderness is a standard outdoors adventure with scenery-chewing stick villains and pat solutions involving aboriginal mysticism. Some stylized violence

title: White Hunter, Black Heart
synopsis: Egotistical director (Clint Eastwood) persuades a writer friend (Jeff Fahey) to collaborate on making a movie in Africa, but once there the director's obsession with killing a bull elephant puts the entire project in jeopardy. Eastwood also produced and directed this blandly uninvolving adaptation of a novel about director John Huston's experiences while filming "The African Queen," but the result is best enjoyed for its on-location cinematography. Minimal violence and vulgar expressions

title: White Lightning
synopsis: Routine country melodrama in which hard-driving Arkansas moonshiner (Burt Reynolds) is paroled from prison in order to get the goods on a county sheriff (Ned Beatty) who is not only taking graft but also murdered Reynolds' kid brother. Crisply directed by Joseph Sargent, the fragmented story of rough backwoods codes and justice is of less interest than the high-powered car chases that keep the dust swirling on those backcountry roads. Some romantic escapades

title: White Line Fever
synopsis: Young trucker Jan-Michael Vincent fights corruption in director Jonathan Kaplan's passably entertaining, though needlessly violent action movie. Benign attitude toward vigilantism

title: White Man's Burden
synopsis: Race-reversal story in which an unjustly fired white man (John Travolta) rashly kidnaps his company's African-American owner (Harry Belafonte), unsure what to do next as each begins to gradually open up to the other's different perceptions of life. Writer-director Desmond Nakano flips racial stereotypes in a heavy-handed yet thought-provoking narrative that has occasional insights on the irrationality of prejudice. Brief violence and much rough language

title: White Men Can't Jump
synopsis: While trying to hold onto his hot-tempered girlfriend (Rosie Perez) and elude loan sharks, a white basketball player and small-time con artist (Woody Harrelson) meets his match in a black street hustler (Wesley Snipes) who joins in on his scams. Writer-director Ron Shelton drops the ball early on in this shrill comedy of pointlessly tiresome macho posturing. Continual rough language, brief bedroom shots, much gambling and some nasty menace

title: White Mischief
synopsis: Fact-based story of the debauched lifestyles of wealthy British colonists living near Nairobi, Kenya, in 1940-41, and the doomed adulterous affair between a rogue earl (Charles Dance) and the beautiful young wife (Greta Scacchi) of an aged landowner (Joss Ackland). Director Michael Radford depicts an exotic, decadent society whose people exhibit few morals, little political or social conscience and no remorse. Treatment includes graphic sexual scenes, much explicit sexual language and some intense violence. O (R) ( 1988 )

title: White Nights
synopsis: Excellent dance sequences highlight this contrived story of a dissident American tap-dancer (Gregory Hines) and a Russian ballet star (Mikhail Baryshnikov) who join forces in escaping from the Soviet Union. Director Taylor Hackford gets little suspense from a muddled plot clogged with political posturing but Twyla Tharp's choreography generates some cultural excitement for those interested. Some romantic complications and coarse language

title: White Noise
synopsis: Schlocky supernatural thriller by director Geoffrey Sax about an architect (Michael Keaton) who, while mourning the tragic death of his wife, becomes obsessed with trying to contact her spirit through electronic means, resulting in unforeseen consequences from beyond the grave. Badly written, acted and directed, this paranormal potboiler makes almost no sense at all and with nary a ghost of a chance of a long screen life, should be haunting video store shelves soon. Some frightening episodes and grisly crime images, an attempted suicide, an instance of rough language and a few crass expressions

title: White Oleander
synopsis: Agonizing tale of a teen-age daughter (Alison Lohman) who is shuttled through a series of foster homes after her manipulative mother (Michelle Pfeiffer) is convicted of killing her lover. Directed by Peter Kominsky, fine performances bolster a harrowing coming-of-age drama exploring mother-daughter relationships, foster care and the role of art in coping with life experiences. Some violence including a suicide, one instance of rough language, brief substance abuse and implied sexual encounters. The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops

title: White Palace
synopsis: A 27-year-old yuppie (James Spader) is embarrassed by his affair with a common and much older waitress (Susan Sarandon) who insists on brutal honesty in their relationship. Luis Mandoki directs a moderately interesting story of a couple who find sex before love and then struggle to overcome age and class differences in hopes of surviving as a couple. Emphasis on an unmarried sexual relationship, some partial nudity and minimal rough language

title: White Sands
synopsis: Investigating a man's mysterious death by assuming his identity, a persistent New Mexico cop (Willem Dafoe) finds himself up against a slippery arms dealer (Mickey Rourke), a seductive heiress (Mary Elizabeth Mastrantonio) and a quicksilver FBI agent (Samuel L. Jackson). Roger Donaldson directs a well-acted thriller marred by a dense, confusing storyline. Recurring violence, a sexually suggestive scene with momentary nudity and frequent rough language

title: White Sister
synopsis: Uneven Italian melodrama about the Mother Superior (Sophia Loren) of a hospital in northern Italy whose confrontations with one of the male staff (Adriano Celentano), a lusty malingerer and a communist to boot, leads inevitably to a rather idealized romance, very platonic but serious enough to make both parties come to mature decisions about their lives. Director Alberto Lattuada plays it broadly, offering some pithy comic moments in the best tradition of Italian social comedy, but not enough to overcome the story's underlying sentimentality

title: White Squall
synopsis: Fact-based account of a 1961 voyage in which the skipper (Jeff Bridges) of a floating prep school takes a dozen adolescent lads on an around-the-world cruise until a freak storm drowns some of the students and crew, leading to a maritme inquiry into the skipper's culpability. Director Ridley Scott's sluggish character study finally gives way to harrowing scenes of the storm's violence, its tragic results and the sober reflections of the survivors. Some sexual innuendo and crude references, fleeting violence and intermittent profanity

title: White Squaw, The
synopsis: Low-budget Western directed by Ray Nazarro in which a mixed-blood Sioux woman (May Wynn) gets some help from a cowboy (David Brian) in trying to stop an Indian-hating rancher from driving her people off their lands on a Wyoming reservation. Stylized violence, including an attempted sexual assault

title: White Tower, The
synopsis: While vacationing in Switzerland, an American (Glenn Ford) joins a party of climbers (Alida Valli, Claude Rains, Oscar Homolka and Lloyd Bridges) trying to scale an unconquered peak. Directed by Ted Tetzlaff, the Alpine grandeur of the location climbing sequences far surpass the pretentious studio-bound character study of who will make it to the top. Much danger and some stylized violence

title: White Zombie, The
synopsis: Dated but still eerie tale of the living dead set in Haiti where a dissolute plantation owner (Robert Frazer) pays a voodoo master (Bela Lugosi) to turn a beautiful visitor (Madge Bellamy) into a zombie, and all seems lost until the power of love proves stronger than that of evil. Director Victor Halperin's nightmarish fantasy succeeds as an atmospheric chiller, despite the molodramatic treatment and technical limitation of early sound movies. Scary visuals, sexual situations and supernatural hooey

title: Who Framed Roger Rabbit
synopsis: Down-and-out 1940's Hollywood gumshoe (Bob Hoskins) attempts to clear the name of murder suspect Roger Rabbit, a cartoon stunt clown. Director Robert Zemeckis and animator Richard Williams achieve a seamless interaction of animated and human characters in this touching, hilarious movie. Some scary threats of violence and humorous sexual references

title: Who is Cletis Tout?t??
synopsis: Unusual romantic comedy in which an escaped convict (Christian Slater) assumes the identity of a marked man and must prove to a hit man (Tim Allen) that he's not the guy he's been sent to kill. Despite having an original love story and creative jewel heist, writer-director Chris Ver Weil's script, which is partly derived from other films, is hurt by disappointingly flat performances. An intense sexual situation, brief nudity, recurring violence, disturbing images of corpses, some homosexual references, and sporadic rough language

title: Whole Nine Yards, The
synopsis: A dark comedy set in Montreal about a mob hit man (Bruce Willis) hiding from a dangerous Chicago crime family who moves next door to a likeable but dopey dentist (Matthew Perry) who is unaware that his conniving wife (Rosanna Arquette) wants him dead to collect on his life insurance. Director Jonathan Lynn's often funny, cleverly plotted comedy shows off Perry's talent for physical comedy but is somewhat off-putting in its light take on killers and killing. Brief nudity, some stylized violence, a few sexual encounters, and some rough language

title: Whole Town's Talking, The
synopsis: Lively crime tale in which a timid accountant looks so much like a notorious gangster (Edward(G) . Robinson in a dual role) the police give him an ID pass which the criminal forces him to share, until the worm turns to free a feisty co-worker (Jean Arthur) taken hostage by the gangster. Directed by John Ford, the humorously contrived plot mixes the comic menace with occasional edgy violence, but the main attraction is Robinson's dual performance as tough guy and milksop, often in the same frame. Stylized violence, threatening situations and mild sexual innuendo

title: Whole Truth, The
synopsis: Boring, long-winded and utterly predictable account of two singles (Dyan Kane and Dan Cohen) who get together, break up and then reunite. Also written and co-directed by Cohen, the shallow vanity production lacks romantic credibility and comic sensibility. Superficial treatment of a serious subject and occasional profanity

title: Whole Wide World, The
synopsis: Fact-based story of a 1930's Texas schoolteacher (Renee Zellweger) whose aspirations to be a writer lead her to seek out a reclusive local author of pulp fantasy tales (Vincent D'Onofrio) and their mutual interests grow into an ill-fated romance due to the man's dependence on his mother. Director Dan Ireland evokes the period well and gets strong performances from the leads, but the picture fails to distinguish between creative genius and dysfunctional personality, leaving viewers unmoved by what is intended as a poignant conclusion. Off-screen suicide, unsettling romantic complications and occasional profanity

title: Wholly Moses
synopsis: Boring Biblical comedy in which the brother-in-law of Moses (Dudley Moore) believes he is the one entrusted with a mission from God. Directed by Gary Weis, its attempts at humor can best be described as tiresome, mirthless, and witless. Occasional vulgar jokes and some incidental irreverence

title: Whoopee!
synopsis: Primitive color version of the Ziegfeld stage musical with Eddie Cantor as a nervous wreck vacationing on a lazy Western dude ranch until finding himself pursued by a posse while helping the rancher's daughter reach her outcast boyfriend on an Indian reservation. Directed by Thornton Freeland, the hokey plot provides the comic context for Cantor's goofy clowning and corny one-liners, abetted by Gus Kahn's songs (notably "Making Whoopee") and Busby Berkeley's splashy production numbers. Some sexual innuendo and period comedy conventions that give offense today, including Native American stereotypes and a blackface routine

title: Whore
synopsis: A prostitute (Theresa Russell) provides those interested with a detailed account of the tricks of the trade and its degradations. Directed by Ken Russell, the low-budget production is tedious and unenlightening. Excessively graphic in its descriptions and simulations of sex acts as well as occasional violence and profanity. O (NC-17) ( 1991 )

title: Who's That Girl
synopsis: Dull and lifeless vanity production showcasing music idol Madonna as an ex-con trying to vindicate herself while ruining the marriage plans of her escort (Griffin Dunne). Director James Foley is unable to tone down the hard edge of the essentially irresponsible role model his star awkwardly creates in this failed action comedy of interest only to diehard fans

title: Who's Your Caddy?
synopsis: Witless attempt at a comedy about a rap mogul's (Antwan Patton, Big Boi of Outkast) entry to a South Carolina country club where his late father had been a caddy. Director Ron Paul, who co-wrote with Bradley Allenstein and Robert Henny, puts a competent cast through a series of uninspired sequences contrasting raucous hip-hop behavior and sedate, clueless white elites (for some unexplained reason, always male). Skimpy costuming in a brief filming of a hip-hop video, marijuana fed to a horse, some crude language, fleeting use of the n-word, partial female nudity, rear male nudity, and some mild sexual banter and frequent scatological humor

title: Why Did I Get Married?
synopsis: Raucous humor alternates with a serious examination of the challenges of married life as four couples gather in the Rockies for their annual vacation and retreat: a best-selling pop psychiatrist (Janet Jackson) resists her architect spouse�s (Malik Yoba) efforts to come to grips with a recent family tragedy; a successful lawyer (Sharon Leal) is too busy for her increasingly exasperated husband (Tyler Perry); a tough talking salon owner (Tasha Smith) tyrannizes her ex-NFL player husband (Michael Jai White); finally, an emotionally abusive husband (Richard T. Jones) heaps insults on his overweight wife (Jill Scott) while reserving his affection for her supposed friend, and his mistress (Denise Boutte). The film, as written, directed and produced by Tyler Perry features some very effective comedy and, though the dramatic elements are less successful, the script as a whole presents a resounding reaffirmation of the value of committed marital love. Some crass language, two uses of profanity, frank sexual discussions, including references to a character with venereal disease, one incident of domestic violence, domestic discord and divorce,

title: Why Do Fools Fall in Love
synopsis: Musical melodrama misfires in the story of a rock'n'roll singer (Larenz Tate) who dies of a drug overdose in 1985, leaving three wives (Vivica A. Fox, Halle Berry and Lela Rochon) to fight over a fortune in unpaid royalties. Directed by Gregory Nava, the result succeeds better in its re-creation of rock'n'roll's beginnings in the mid-1950s than in the flashbacks portraying the bickering widows' very different recollections of the same man who never becomes more than a cipher for viewers. Intense physical and psychological violence, explicit sexual situations, recurring rough language and some profanity

title: Why Not!
synopsis: Thin French comedy directed by Coline Serreau deals with the lives and domestic habits of a cozy trio (Sami Frey, Mario Gonzales and Christine Murillo) whose sleeping arrangements are quite complicated. Though the focus is not exclusively on sex, and there is an occasional droll sequence, its use of nudity and benign attitude towards moral anarchy are offensive. O (nr) ( 1979 )

title: Wichita
synopsis: Credible law-and-order Western directed by Jacques Tourneur portrays Wyatt Earp (Joel McCrea) as a mild-mannered frontiersman whose prowess with a gun leads him to reluctantly accept the job of keeping the peace in a booming cattle town. Anti-violence theme with considerable stylized violence

title: Wicked Dreams of Paula Schultz, The
synopsis: Low burlesque about an East German woman decathalon champ (Elke Sommer) who tries to defect to the West rather than be sent to work in a tractor factory. Directed by George Marshall, the feeble attempts at humor resort to some very crudely contrived calendar-art shots and sequences, a lesbian joke and other misguided attempts at humor. O (br) ( 1968 )

title: Wicked Lady, The
synopsis: Thoroughly inept remake of a 1945 British Restoration-era movie about a bored English noblewoman (Faye Dunaway) who turns to highway robbery for diversion. Under Michael Winner's aimless direction, not only does Dunaway give a poor performance but also cast adrift are Alan Bates, John Gielgud, Denholm Elliott and Prunella Scales. Abundant nudity and crass vulgarity. O (R) ( 1983 )

title: Wicked Stepmother
synopsis: Clunky horror spoof in which a modern-day witch (Bette Davis) and her equally diabolical confederate (Barbara Carraras) steal people's money after reducing them to the size of 6-inch dolls, until stymied by a dedicated policeman (Tom Bosley). With Davis having only a few scenes, writer-director Larry Cohen tries to pad out the time with a jokey script and ludicrous acting. Some sexual references and occasional profanity

title: Wicked, Wicked
synopsis: Clumsy thriller about the hunt for a psycho (Randolph Roberts) who murders blondes checking into an old seaside resort whose new singer (Tiffany Bolling) sports a blonde wig. Written, produced and directed by Richard L. Bare, the movie uses an ineffective split screen process. Restrained sex and violence

title: Wicker Man, The
synopsis: British melodrama in which a police sergeant (Edward Woodward) is called to a small island off the west coast of Scotland to investigate the disappearance of a child whom, he finds, has been made a human sacrifice in a pagan rite. Directed by Robin Hardy, the movie shows signs of intelligence and sophistication but its tragic ending is unprepared from what has gone before. Excessive nudity. O (R) ( 1980 )

title: Wicker Park
synopsis: Uneven drama set in Chicago about a lovelorn advertising executive (Josh Hartnett) who, after sighting someone he thinks is his former girlfriend (Diane Kruger), becomes obsessed with tracking her down and finding out the truth as to why she suddenly walked out of his life two years earlier. Director Doug McGuigan's remake of the French film "L'Appartement" awkwardly shifts gears between romantic melodrama and suspense, neither providing enough emotional torque to power the story beyond the overall lackluster material. Several sexual encounters, as well as sporadic crude language and humor

title: Wide Awake
synopsis: Disarming tale of a 9-year-old Catholic schoolboy (Joseph Cross) whose depression over the death of his grandpa (Robert Loggia) leads him to search for signs that God and heaven really exist. Writer-director M. Night Shyamalan deftly captures the child's sincerity and suggests the caring presence of God in the boy's daily life as he comes to terms with his loss. Vivid depiction of juvenile grief and a few crude words

title: Wide Sargasso Sea
synopsis: Passions cool between a proper 1840's English gentleman (Nathaniel Parker) and his sensuous Jamaican bride (Karina Lombard) when he suspects she is using voodoo to bewitch him. Director John Duigan's turgid romance rarely ventures beyond the couple's melodramatic bedroom hysterics which end unhappily. Some simulated sex and frequent nudity. O (NC-17) ( 1993 )

title: Widow Couderc, The
synopsis: Complex French melodrama set in the 1930s in which a killer (Alain Delon) hides out working on the farm of a widow (Simone Signoret) but life is so peaceful there that he begins thinking of it as home until someone in the small, inbred rural community calls the attention of the police to the outsider. Director Pierre Granier-Deferre's picture of country life contrasts human frailty with the beauty of the natural order, lust with love and death with life in a way which may discomfort some but evoke a sympathetic response in others

title: Widows' Peak
synopsis: Whimsical period piece set in a 1926 Irish village where scandal erupts when the arrival of a glamorous young widow (Natasha Richardson) upsets the delicate balance between an eccentric spinster (Mia Farrow) and the village's gossipy widows (led by Joan Plowright). Director John Irvin pours on the blarney in a fairly entertaining concoction that blends the hint of a murder mystery into a deftly acted comedy of manners. Some mild sexual references

title: Wifemistress
synopsis: Italian sex comedy in which a rich merchant (Marcello Mastroianni), implicated in a crime and forced into hiding in a building across the street from his home, observes the erotic as well as humanitarian activities of his formerly repressed wife (Laura Antonelli) who thinks he is dead. Directed by Marco Vicario, it is little more than a tepid and uninspired period comedy whose simplistic anti-religious views and frequent nudity are offensive. O (R) ( 1979 )

title: Wilby Conspiracy, The
synopsis: Sidney Poitier and Michael Caine star in a political chase melodrama set against the background of apartheid South Africa but Nicol Williamson steals the show as a cooly fanatic policeman. Director Ralph Nelson's movie is taut and well acted, but it is marred by some unnecessary sexual hijinks and a violent conclusion that sets up a moral problem beyond its depth. O (PG) ( 1975 )

title: Wild America
synopsis: Unaware their 12-year-old brother (Jonathan Taylor Thomas) has hidden himself in their station wagon, two Arkansas teens (Devon Sawa and Scott Bairstow) set out to cross the country filming wildlife footage of endangered predators as they go in hope of both adventure and fame as documentary filmmakers. Directed by William Dear, the fact-based tale of these high-spirited lads has several scary moments in the bush, but otherwise their tame adventures are less effectively staged. Scenes with menacing animals, mild sexual innuendo and a profanity

title: Wild and the Innocent, The
synopsis: Uneven Western in which a young trapper (Audie Murphy) picks up a runaway girl (Sandra Dee) on the trail to Casper, Wyoming, to sell his pelts, but there he falls for a fancy lady (Joanne Dru) whom he tries to reform, then has to rescue the runaway from the town's corrupt sheriff (Gilbert Roland). Directed by Jack Sher, the innocence of the two country bumpkins in the big bad city is depicted with some sympathetic amusement, though the plotting is contrived and the ending heavy-handed. Stylized violence and veiled sexual innuendo

title: Wild Angels, The
synopsis: Motorcycle gang movie with Peter Fonda and directed by Roger Corma is excessively violent and its theme of social protest is bogus. O (R) ( 1966 )

title: Wild at Heart
synopsis: Madly in love, a reckless couple (Nicolas Cage and Laura Dern) tear across the Deep South on the run from the law and killers hired by the girl's obsessive mother (Diane Ladd). Writer-director David Lynch captures the lovers' sensual passion but the movie's sluggish pace is accentuated by a tiresome parade of psychotic characters, revolting images and violent episodes that turn an upbeat ending into self-indulgent sham. Excessive violence, graphic sexual content and much rough language. O (R) ( 1990 )

title: Wild Bill
synopsis: Leaden Western depicting some of the shootouts which made Wild Bill Hickok (Jeff Bridges) a feared gunfighter until confronted in 1876 by an inept youth (David Arquette) determined to avenge his mother's mistreatment by Wild Bill. Writer-director Walter Hill whizzes through Hickok's early exploits, then bogs down in a prolonged series of bizarre events, including opium dreams, hired assassins and sex on a barroom table before he is finally gunned down in Deadwood Gulch. Much stylized violence, a constrained sex scene, sexual innuendo and coarse language

title: Wild Blue Yonder, The
synopsis: Routine World War II story directed by Allan Dwan centers on the camaraderie among the first group of pilots (Wendell Corey, Forrest Tucker, Phil Harris and others) assigned in 1943 to fly the new B-29 bomber aganinst Japanese targets in the Pacific. Wartime violence

title: Wild Bunch, The
synopsis: William Holden and Ernest Borgnine star in director Sam Peckinpah's violent and unglamorized account of the end of an outlaw band who had outlived the frontier era. Though its intentions are to show the ugly reality underlying the Western movie myth, the general viewer is apt to find the work's brutality and several sexual scenes quite excessive

title: Wildcats
synopsis: Goldie Hawn stars in this failed comedy about a woman coach of an inner-city high school football team. Excessive amounts of streetwise profanity, brief nudity and a scene invo1ving simulated fornication make this vanity production by director Michael Ritchie off limits for its intended youthful audience. O (R) ( 1986 )

title: Wild Child, The
synopsis: Exceptional French dramatization about a young boy who was found in 1798 living as an animal in a forest and the doctor who, rather than place in an asylum, took him into his own home for more intense care. Director Francois Truffaut (who also plays the doctor) creates an austerity of image, settings and music (Vivaldi) to mirror the child's alienation and gradual response to the doctor's openness. Most of all, the moving drama is an affirmation of the tireless efforts of educators to overcome environmental handicaps and an act of faith that humanity will survive in spite of itself

title: Wild Country, The
synopsis: Pittsburgh family (Steve Forrest, Vera Miles, Ron Howard and Clint Howard) arrives in the Wyoming territory of the 1880s full of hope and fervor of the early settlers but their farm is below expectations, their water supply jeopardized by cattlemen and a devastating cyclone nearly destroys their homestead. Above average Disney production directed by Robert Totten provides a wholesome, quality adventure story for solid family entertainment

title: Wild Duck, The
synopsis: Pallid German adaptation of the Ibsen classic, Director Hans W. Geissendorfer unwisely :2Oopens up:2O the play to the extent of showing Hedvig's cherished wild duck, but has made a much more critical mistake in casting a fat and clownish actor (Peter Kern) as the feckless but attractive Hjalmar

title: Wilder Napalm
synopsis: Seriocomic misfire about the showdown between two brothers, both born with telekinetic powers to make objects burst into flame, when the older (Arliss Howard) tries to keep the younger (Dennis Quaid) from exploiting this power to gain fame, fortune and his brother's free-spirited wife (Debra Winger). Directed by Glenn Gordon Caron, the movie generates little interest as the conflict between the brothers over whether their unique power is a gift or a curse is slowly dragged out until the climactic fiery confrontation, with only occasional comic diversions to pass the time. Some special-effects violence, sexual situations and coarse language

title: Wilderness Family, Part 2, The
synopsis: ( see: "The Further Adventures of the Wilderness Family" )

title: Wilderness Journey
synopsis: In the Far North, a 12-year-old Eskimo lad (Tony Tucker Williams) embarks on a courageous canoe journey to find his father (Richard Stitt), a hunting-party guide whose assistance is needed back home. The boy's adventure is made suspenseful and engrossing by Chuck D. Keen's superlative photography of the region and its wildlife and by the reverent narration explaining the tradition of the boy's ancestors. Directed by Ford Beebe, whose career in films dates back to 1914, the movie is splendid family entertainment

title: Wild Eye, The
synopsis: Italian story about a sleazy movie director (Philippe Leroy) who makes exploitation pseudo-documentaries by inventing what he thinks the public wants to believe is real. Director Paolo Cavara proceeds to demonstrate this sort of dishonesty by himself staging a number of sadomasochistic scenes. O (nr) ( 1968 )

title: Wild Geese, The
synopsis: Richard Burton, assisted by Roger Moore, Richard Harris and Hardy Kruger, lead a mercenary army to Africa to rescue a democratic African leader (Winston Ntshona). Although director Andrew V. McLaglen has a talented cast, a literate script and some well photographed action sequences, the complexity of its racial and political context are beyond the movie's capability to treat responsibly. The graphic nature of its brutal violence and accompanying rough language are excessive. O (R) ( 1978 )

title: Wild Hearts Can't Be Broken
synopsis: During the Great Depression, a blind 15-year-old orphan (Gabrielle Anwar) convinces a crusty stunt-show owner (Cliff Robertson) that she can ride a speeding stallion and leap into a pool of water as their new horse diver -- from 40 feet above Atlantic City's famed Steel Pier. Director Steve Miner's spunky heroine overcomes various obstacles and a harrowing tragedy in an inspiring, fact-based movie that shimmers in sun-drenched cinematography. Fine family fare

title: Wild Heart, The
synopsis: Dark tale of romance in 1897 Shropshire where a wild country girl (Jennifer Jones) marries the local minister (Cyril Cusack), then is seduced by a devil-may-care squire (David Farrar) but ultimately returns contritely to her husband for a tragic ending. Directed by Michael Powell and Emeric Pressberger, the story's strange nature girl is more than coy but less than convincing in her muddled ways, though the rustic setting of the Welsh-English border country is suitably moody and its local folkways hold interest. Sexual situations

title: Wild Heritage
synopsis: Mild frontier tale of two pioneer families headed by widows (Maureen O'Sullivan and Jeanette Nolan) who settle in a Western valley where they share a small herd of cattle, learn to fight rustlers and are befriended by a helpful lawyer (Will Rogers, Jr.). Directed by Charles Haas, the uneven narrative centers on fatherless teenagers having to shoulder adult responsibilities, in particular, learning to handle a gun for an inevitable shootout with a pair of local badmen. Stylized violence

title: Wild Hogs
synopsis: Four middle-age biker buddies from suburbia (Tim Allen, John Travolta, Martin Lawrence and William H. Macy) seize the day by taking a cross-country road trip and suffering various humiliating mishaps as they attempt to recapture their youthful vitality. The sputtering comedy of director Walt Becker ("National Lampoon's Van Wilder") subjects the audience to an exhausting barrage of crude humor and off-color banter. Pervasive crude language, much sexual innuendo, rear male nudity, fleeting images and sounds from Internet pornography sites, bathroom humor, a drug reference and some violence

title: Wild Horse Ambush
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Fred C. Brannon in which a young Texas buckaroo (Michael Chapin) enlists the aid of the Mexican border patrol in nabbing a group of counterfeiters using a herd of wild horses to transport bogus bills across the border. Stylized violence

title: Wild Horse Stampede
synopsis: Low-budget cowboy stars Ken Maynard and Hoot Gibson tangle with a band of renegades hired to halt the construction of a railroad. Directed by Alan James, it's strictly formula fare for undemanding Western fans. Stylized violence

title: Wild in the Country
synopsis: Soapy melodrama in which a troubled country youth (Elvis Presley) courts a nice girl (Millie Perkins) while pursued by a single mom (Tuesday Weld), then falls in love with an older woman (Hope Lange) who encourages him to become a writer. Directed by Philip Dunne from a script by Clifford Odets, the story is little more than glossy trash, though the cast is better than the roles and the sentimental ending is classic hokum. Stylized violence, including a suicide attempt, romantic complications and sexual innuendo

title: Wild in the Sky
synopsis: Brandon de Wilde and two fellow draft-dodgers escape jail by commandeering a SAC bomber captained by Robert Lansing and try to make it to Cuba as General Keenan Wynn back at SAC headquarters issues insane orders to stop them. Directed by William T. Naud, this low-budget flying Ship of Fools tries to work both the hijack and anti-war angles but is consistent only in its cheap vulgarities and exploitation of serious themes. O (GP) ( 1972 )

title: Wild in the Streets
synopsis: Young pop singer (Chris Jones) mobilizes America's youth, gets elected President and puts everyone over 30 into concentration camps. Director Barry Shear tries to satirize the youth culture of the 1960s while exploiting it as well but it is the kind of free-from-responsibility fantasy that is not good for adolescents

title: Wild Is the Wind
synopsis: Tangled romantic melodrama in which a prosperous Nevada sheep rancher (Anthony Quinn) marries his dead wife's sister (Anna Magnani) but she rebels at his expectations of her being like her sister rather than being herself and turns for affection to the rancher's adopted son (Tony Franciosa). Directed by George Cukor, there are some high-powered naturalistic performances but the contrived proceedings lessen their emotional impact and the story's credibility. Sexual situations and an extended sequence of a lamb's birth

title: Wild Life, The
synopsis: Dreary sequel to "Fast Times At Ridgemont High" shows what happens to Eric Stoltz after he graduates and moves into a swinging singles apartment complex. Directed by Art Linson, the proceedings feature the same sort of benignly viewed sexual amorality which permeated the first movie. Nudity and rough language. O (R) ( 1984 )

title: Wild North, The
synopsis: Rugged outdoor adventure in Canada's frozen backcountry where a Mountie (Wendell Corey) gets his man -- a French-Canadian hunter (Stewart Granger) accused of murder -- then needs his help to survive a series of disasters on the trail back. Directed by Andrew Marton, the plot is more than a little contrived but the vigorous action is in keeping with the remote setting and the shifting relationship between captor and captive has a satisfying human dimension. Much menace and some brutal violence, notably an attack by starving wolves

title: Wild One, The
synopsis: Motorcycle gang (headed by Marlon Brando) stops off in a small California town and, after being joined by a rival gang (led by Lee Marvin), the bikers go on a rampage trashing the town and terrorizing its inhabitants. Directed by Laslo Benedek, the work has dated badly in subject and style, especially the romantic subplot with Mary Murphy, but there is still some edge in its early look at the violence in American counter-cultures. Much menace and stylized violence, including vigilante action

title: Wild Orchid
synopsis: Boring voyeuristic exercise in titillation over the sexual awakening of an innocent young woman (Carre Otis) by a sleazy international operator (Mickey Rourke). Director Zalman King's hothouse fantasy about unappealing characters offers unrelieved tedium except for travelogue views of Rio de Janeiro and its environs. Several simulated sex acts. O (R) ( 1990 )

title: Wild Orchid 2: Two Shades of Blue
synopsis: Dreary sex drama about a teen-ager (Nina Siemaszko) lured into very lucrative prostitution after the death of her addict father (Tom Skeritt). Writer-director Zalman King can't imbue this soft-core peep show with any redeeming qualities. Prostitution glamorized, much nudity, brief violence, drug abuse and some rough language. O (R) ( 1992 )

title: Wild Pack, The
synopsis: Produced, directed and written by Hall Bartlett from a novel by Jorge Amado, the movie follows the fates of a gang of homeless children in Bahia, Brazil, as they struggle to survive on the fringes and in the slums of an indifferent South American society. It unfortunately clutters its statement of revolutionary protest with a romantic subplot and a graphic rape sequence. O (nr) ( 1972 )

title: Wild Party, The
synopsis: Part musical, part study of late 1920's Hollywood decadence and part compassionate character study of a silent film comedian (James Coco) ruined by the coming of sound pictures.
