Directed by James Ivory, these diverse elements fail to fuse and the result is an aimless, repetitious and more than a little distasteful melodrama. Excessive sexual display. O (R) ( 1975 )

title: Wild Racers, The
synopsis: American race car driver (Fabian) gets a shot at the Grand Prix circuit and leaves behind a trail of a compliant women. Director Dan Haller intercuts stock racing footage with numerous suggestive situations in the story of a man who values machines more than human beings. O (br) ( 1968 )

title: Wild Reeds
synopsis: Coming-of-age tale set in 1962 rural France at the end of the Algerian war when two boys and a girl confront issues of sex, class and politics after a French-Algerian youth is placed in their high school senior class. Andre Techine directs a slow yet sensitive story of youths facing adult realities during a turbulent period in French politics and society. Subtitles. Restrained portrayal of sexual encounters, brief nudity, sexual references and an instance of rough language

title: Wild River
synopsis: Uneven 1930's story about an official (Montgomery Clift) from the Tennessee Valley Authority who tries to get an old woman (Jo Van Fleet) to leave her island home before it's flooded by a new dam, but falls for the woman's granddaughter (Lee Remick) in the process. Director Elia Kazan evokes the hard times of the Depression era and racial inequalites in the rural South, but the contrived love story only weakens the movie's theme of individual rights in conflict with the common good. Some stylized violence and an implied sexual relationship

title: Wild Rovers
synopsis: William Holden and Ryan O'Neal are quite effective in this flawed but engagingly bittersweet study of ordinary cowpokes who dream of owning a little ranchero down in Mexico, rob a Montana bank and head toward the distant border. Written and directed by Blake Edwards, the characterizations are its strong point, the plot rather shaky and slow-moving and the resolution is a downer. Some brutal violence and a gratuitous bordello scene

title: Wild Season
synopsis: Belgian movie about the life of North Sea fishermen centers around a young boy who tries to prove to his father that he can be just as good a man as was the son lost at sea. Directed by Emil Nofal, the natural elements surpass the labored efforts of the actors but younger audiences will enjoy the outdoor adventure aspects of the story without much concern about character motivations

title: Wild Seed, The
synopsis: A drifter (Michael Parks) reluctantly helps a young runaway (Celia Kaye) cross the country to find her father but she gives up the search when they decide to get married. Directed by Brian Hutton, the contrived situation of the journey yields little interior growth in the two young people and the conclusion is not promising. Mature theme

title: Wild Strawberries
synopsis: During the day on which he is to be awarded an honorary degree from a nearby university, a 78-year-old retired scholar (Victor Sjostrom in a masterful performance) is visited with dreams and reveries about his past life, especially his failures and disappointments in personal relationships. Swedish director Ingmar Bergman brilliantly develops the man's interior journey from pangs of regret and anxiety to a refreshing sense of peace and reconciliation summed up in blissful images of his happy youth. One of the great films about aging that touches universal chords in all viewers. English subtitles

title: Wild Thing
synopsis: Orphaned child (Rob Knepper) grows up essentially on his own in the bowels of a deserted inner-city hovel and one day avenges his parents' death at the hands of ruthless drug dealers while saving a young social worker (Kathleen Quinlan). Director Mac Reid uses the thematic razor's edge of revenge to mutilate scriptwriter John Sayles' childlike fable. Restrained violence and a scene of implied sex lessen the urban Tarzan yarn's suitability for youngsters

title: Wild Things
synopsis: Trashy potboiler in which a police detective (Kevin Bacon) investigates the rape accusations of two high school seniors (Denise Richards and Neve Campbell) against their guidance counselor (Matt Dillon), then suspects all three are in cahoots to split the civil suit settlement once the counselor is exonerated. Director John McNaughton's steamy soap opera twists into ludicrous triple crosses before smugly rewarding the most vile of the conspirators. Sporadic violence, various sexual encounters, full nudity, substance abuse, recurring profanity and much rough language. O (R) ( 1998 )

title: Wild Westerners, The
synopsis: Low-budget oater directed by Oscar Rudolph is set in 1864 Montana where a U.S. marshal (James Philbrook) is tricked into marrying a stranded showgirl (Nancy Kovack), then falls in love with her while rounding up a gang of gold thieves. Frontier violence and romantic comlications

title: Wild Wild West
synopsis: Glossy adaptation of the 1960's TV series in which two post-Civil War government agents -- one trigger-happy (Will Smith) the other skilled at disguises and inventions (Kevin Kline) -- must disable a behemoth killing machine operated by a wheelchair-bound madman (Kenneth Branagh) bent on bringing down the Republic. Director Barry Sonnenfeld blends sci-fi contraptions, a comic tone and the Old West setting for a hallow, gimmick-driven plot with impossible stunts and decorative femme fatales for giddy escapist entertainment. Intermittent explosions and stylized violence, some sexual innuendo and double entendres, and fleeting rear nudity

title: Willard
synopsis: Grisly horror-comedy about a misfit (Crispin Glover), oppressed by a harridan mother and overbearing boss, who befriends an ever-growing army of rats in his basement. Glen Morgan's remake of the 1971 B-movie camps it up with over-the-top performances from Glover and his oppressors; the result, though decidedly not for all tastes, effectively works on the audiences' nerves where so many horror films deliver only gross-outs. Some grisly violence and menace, a depiction of a character viewing online pornography, an allusion to autoeroticism, occasional profanity and an instance of rough language

title: Willard
synopsis: Horror fantasy about a psychotic young man (Bruce Davidson) who, after the death of his mother (Elsa Lanchester), trains an army of rats to exact revenge for the injustices heaped upon him and his family by a businessman (Ernest Borgnine), but alas, he trains the little beasties all too well. Tighter editing and pacing might have given director Daniel Mann a first-class horror movie but, as it is, animal trainer Moe Di Sesso runs away with the prize for his direction of the rats

title: William Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream
synopsis: Fanciful adaptation of the Bard's comedy is updated to 1900 Tuscany in a magical forest where the fairy Puck (Stanley Tucci) causes all manner of romantic mix-ups overnight casting spells on mismatched young lovers (including Christian Bale and Calista Flockhart), an aspiring actor (Kevin Kline) and the fairy queen (Michelle Pfeiffer). Some cast members excel, others do not in articulating Shakespearean dialogue in writer-director Michael Hoffman's whimsical adaptation whose luminous visuals look sprinkled with fairy dust. Romantic complications and fleeting nudity

title: William Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet
synopsis: Ambitious adaptation of the classic tale of star-crossed lovers (Leonardo Di Caprio and Claire Danes) remains literally faithful to the original while updating the story to a contemporary U.S. urban setting. Director Baz Luhrmann's flawed but never dull adaptation is visually operatic, highly stylized -- and jarringly wedded to Shakespeare's Elizabethan language. Several violent deaths and romanticized suicides

title: Willie and Joe Back at the Front
synopsis: ( see: "Back at the Front" )

title: Willie Dynamite
synopsis: Big city's most successful pimp (Roscoe Orman) vies with a reformed-hooker-turned-social-worker (Diana Sands) over the girls he tries to keep on the street while she tries to get them off. Directed by Gilbert Moses, it is a lifeless, aimless and meaningless attempt to blend outright black exploitation material with a sober examination of the psychology of the pimp and his women. The result is largely a waste of time. O (R) ( 1974 )

title: Willie & Phil
synopsis: Writer-director Paul Mazursky's tale of a three-sided friendship begins with the 1970 meeting of Willie (Michael Ontkean) and Phil (Ray Sharkey) as they come out of a screening of Truffaut's triangle movie, "Jules and Jim," the inspiration for Mazursky's work. The trio is completed a few days later when they meet free-spirited Jeannette (Margot Kidder) and the movie follows their shifting relationships over the entire decade of the 1970s. Mazursky has created three charming characters and places their quest for meaning and fulfillment within the context of the ethnic, moral and religious traditions each represents. However, the nature and treatment of the theme makes this strictly mature viewing

title: Willow
synopsis: Fantasy adventure in which the tiny hero of the title (Warwick Davis) attempts at all odds to protect the baby girl prophesized to bring the downfall of the wicked sorceress (Jean Marsh) who rules the land. Directed by Ron Howard from a story by George Lucas, the tale is jampacked with strangely shaped and oddly sized characters, forbidding medieval sets and a complex plot. Breathtaking chases, dramatic sword fights and fearsome creatures may rattle the small fry

title: Will Penny
synopsis: Fine Western about an illiterate, aging but still capable cowhand (Charlton Heston) who after the fall roundup is sent to tend the cattle wintering in the hills where he gives shelter to a lost pioneer woman (Joan Hackett) and her son until the spring thaw. Director Tom Gries has achieved a realistic portrait of a cowboy whose code of morality reflects the rigors of frontier life, the shortage of marriageable women and the rudimentary nature of early Western justice. Some sadistic violence

title: Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory
synopsis: Screen version of Roald Dahl's children's story about a candy manufacturer (Gene Wilder) who conducts an electrifying tour of his factory for the five lucky children who learn that greed and selfishness can be their own reward. Even the punishments, occasionally a bit gruesome for younger children, are in good fun. Director Mel Stuart manages to avoid the cloying sentimentality of similar children's movies, though it's never quite as magical as one would have hoped

title: Wilson
synopsis: Historical dramatization follows the career of Woodrow E. Wilson (Alexander Knox) from New Jersey college president to U.S. President during World War I and his tragic final years rallying support for the League of Nations. Directed by Henry King, the picture succeeds best as an elaborate, convincingly detailed re-creation of the period but, with political events taking precedence over the human drama, the result is rather lifeless despite a fine cast including Charles Coburn, Cedric Hardwicke, Geraldine Fitzgerald and Thomas Mitchell

title: Wimbledon
synopsis: Appealing love story about retiring thirtyish British tennis pro (Paul Bettany) who, frustrated by his losing streak and encroachment by the younger set, is about to play his final Wimbledon tournament. But when he meets a rising American star (Kirsten Dunst), and they begin an affair under the disapproving eye of her father (Sam O'Neill), his luck miraculously improves. Director Richard Loncraine's film, though basically lightweight, has a good moral at heart, as it pits true love against the competitive rat race of the game. Implied sexual situations and innuendo, fleeting rear nudity, some crude language and a brief violent incident

title: Win a Date with Tad Hamilton!
synopsis: Breezy but slight teen romantic comedy about a small-town grocery clerk (Kate Bosworth) who enters a fan contest and wins a date with her idol (Josh Duhamel), a Hollywood heartthrob who warms up to her homespun charm, and, pledging to clean up his act, decides to follow her back home to rural West Virginia, much to the dismay of her best friend (Topher Grace) who happens to be hopelessly, though secretly, in love with her. Despite its formulaic script and flat characters, director Robert Luketic keeps his adolescent soap opera relatively well scrubbed, avoiding for the most part, the gross-out potty jokes and stock sexuality rampant in many teen films. Some crass humor and innuendo, as well as sporadic crude language and a few instances of alcohol abuse

title: Winchester '73
synopsis: After his prize rifle is stolen, a determined cowboy (James Stewart) sets out to find it and the man (Stephen McNally) who took it. Director Anthony Mann's meandering but energetic Western follows the trail through chance encounters with homesteaders, Indians and outlaws before the final showdown reveals the personal nature of the cowboy's persistent quest. Stylized violence

title: Wind
synopsis: After losing the America's Cup to Australia, a young sailboat skipper (Matthew Modine) teams with his ex-fiancee (Jennifer Grey) and her boyfriend (Stellan Skarsgard) to build a new boat for the rematch Down Under. Carroll Ballard directs a splendidly photographed but otherwise ordinary root-for-the-underdog picture that works best in the racing sequences. Implied premarital affairs

title: Wind and the Lion, The
synopsis: Writer-director John Milius takes some liberties with the 1904 incident in which Teddy Roosevelt (Brian Keith) thundered against a Moroccan brigand (Sean Connery) for kidnapping an American citizen (Candice Bergen). The historical facts are more interesting than this artificial romance, bogus adventure movie that glamorizes weapons and their use. Violence

title: Winded Migration
synopsis: Spectacular documentary that follows the annual journey of various birds as they often travel more than 10,000 miles between the tropics and the Arctic to ensure their survival. With minimal dialogue and exhilarating cinematography, director and narrator Jacques Perrin's quietly thrilling film provides a heady vicarious experience as it captures the migratory patterns of birds, uplifting the spirit and eliciting awe at God's perfection in creating such wondrous creatures

title: Wind from the East
synopsis: French director Jean-Luc Godard's first directly political work, this 1969 effort fails both as a movie and as Maoist propaganda. Basically a film of ideas, its dialectical progress fitfully winds down to a final call for total revolution, but it is unlikely to persuade viewers to accept its convictions

title: Wind in the Willows, The
synopsis: Charming live-action tale set in an English meadow where timid Mole (Steve Coogan), kindly Rat (Eric Idle) and bold Badger (Nicol Williamson) must save reckless Toad (Terry Jones) from losing his country estate to evil Weasels. Also written and directed by Jones, this adaptation of Kenneth Grahame's 1908 children's classic is enhanced by an endearing cast, sprightly songs, lovely visuals and a delightful sense of whimsy, which despite moments of menace translates into appealing family entertainment

title: Windows
synopsis: Failed thriller about a psychotic, homicidal lesbian (Elizabeth Ashley) who cherishes an unholy and, at times, quite noisy passion for a mousy friend (Talia Shire). Director Gordon Willis leaves his actresses to their own devices in the heavy-breathing and crying department while he devotes his energies to getting some exquisite views of the Manhattan skyline and landmarks. A brutal scene involving sexual assault is needlessly graphic. O (R) ( 1980 )

title: Window, The
synopsis: Gritty thriller in which a young lad (Bobby Driscoll) witnesses a murder but his parents (Arthur Kennedy and Barbara Hale) refuse to believe their highly imaginative son until the murderer (Paul Stewart) corners him in an abandoned building. Director Ted Tetzlaff's minor suspense classic about the boy who cried wolf once too often gains considerable credibility from its working-class setting and creditable characters. Mounting tension and life-threatening situations

title: Window to Paris
synopsis: Chaotic Russian fantasy in which the residents of a St. Petersburg apartment building discover a magical window through which they step daily into Paris amassing consumer goods to take home, though a music teacher (Sergei Dontsov) dallies with an eccentric Parisienne (Agnes Soral) and his young students refuse to return to their dreary city. Director Yuri Mamin carries the whimsical elements of the time-space warp to belabored extremes in a clash-of-cultures comedy haphazardly combining romance and political satire. Subtitles. Fleeting full nudity, occasional drunkeness, minor violence and a few instances of rough language

title: Winds of the Wasteland
synopsis: Low-budget Western directed by Mack V. Wright tells of former Pony Express riders (John Wayne and Lane Chandler) who turn a ghost town into a growing community by bringing in a telegraph line and winning the area's mail contract from a dishonest competitor (Douglas Cosgrave) in an exciting stagecoach race. Frontier violence

title: Windtalker
synopsis: Monotonous World War II drama in which the United States military recruits Navajos (Adam Beach, Roger Willie) to communicate the secret battle positions of U.S. troops in the Navajo language without the Japanese understanding, but the Marines (Nicolas Cage, Christian Slater) assigned to protect them must also be prepared to kill them if capture is imminent. Inspired by true events, the premise(s potential is never tapped in director John Woo(s ultra-bloody epic with the horrific battle scenes punctuated by dry storytelling that fails to flesh out the moral quandary faced by the Marines or the bonds forged among the men. Much graphic war violence with sporadic rough language and profanity

title: Windwalker
synopsis: A dying Cheyenne patriarch (Trevor Howard) yearns to see once again the son who was kidnapped by hostile Crows when he was an infant. Aside from the miscasting of Howard, director Keith Merrill has created an extremely authentic picture of Indian life told in an unusally absorbing story. Because of the violence and conflict essential to the plot, it is not suited to very young children, but for older ones, the dignity with which it portrays Indians and their culture recommends it highly

title: Windy City
synopsis: Written and directed by Armyan Bernstein, this story of young men growing up on the North Side of Chicago with their dreams unrealized has some good acting (John Shea, Kate Capshaw, Josh Mostel and Jim Borrelli) but can't overcome the handicaps of banal dialogue and sketchy characterizations. Considerable violence and gore

title: Wing and a Prayer
synopsis: Dated World War II morale booster directed by Henry Hathaway pays tribute to the officers (Charles Bickford and Don Ameche) and pilots (Dana Andrews, William Eythe, Henry Morgan and others) of an aircraft carrier during the Battle of Midway. Wartime violence and patriotic heroics

title: Wing Commander
synopsis: Uninvolving space adventure set 600 years in the future as a handful of interplanetary pilots (including Freddie Prinze Jr. and Saffron Burrows) attempt to short curcuit an invasion of Earth by a malevolent alien species. Director Chris Roberts' adapts his line of Wing Commander computer games to the big screen with routine special effects, standard spaceship shootouts and corny dialogue that add up to a sci-fi cipher. Frequent stylized fantasy violence, an implied sexual encounter and a few crude references

title: Winged Migration
synopsis: Spectacular documentary that follows the annual journey of various birds as they often travel more than 10,000 miles between the tropics and the Arctic to ensure their survival. With minimal dialogue and exhilarating cinematography, director and narrator Jacques Perrin's quietly thrilling film provides a heady vicarious experience as it captures the migratory patterns of birds, uplifting the spirit and eliciting awe at God's perfection in creating such wondrous creatures

title: Wings
synopsis: Silent screen epic about two young men (Buddy Rogers and Richard Allen), in love with the same girl (Jobyna Ralston), who wind up in the same flying squadron during World War I where their rivalry turns to friendship until one of them is accidentally killed by the other. Clara Bow is the girl-next-door who follows Rogers to France as a nurse. Directed by William Wellman, it's a classic adventure film with a refreshing sense of innocence unembarrassed by any doubts about the justice of the actions of the principals. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Wings and the Woman
synopsis: British wartime morale booster about 1930's record-setting aviatrix Amy Johnson (Anna Neagle) and her aviator husband Jim Mollison (Robert Newton). Produced and directed by Herbert Wilcox, the fact-based story treats the dangers facing the era's pilots in proper stiff-upper-lip fashion, ending in a patriotic flourish lauding the role of women in the war effort

title: Wings of Desire
synopsis: Arthouse film follows the lonely work of two angels (Bruno Ganz and Otto Sander) who wander about and above Berlin listening to the joys and travails of people in libraries, a circus and even on an American movie set (starring Peter Falk as himself). One angel chooses to shed his wings for the chance of expressing human emotions and love for a woman. German director Wim Wenders is by turns ponderous, playful, reflective and philosophic. Subtitles. Some sexually suggestive material, fleeting nudity and some profanity

title: Wings of Eagles, The
synopsis: Uneven but colorful bio of Frank "Spig" Wead (John Wayne), a pioneering naval aviator in the 1920s who became a writer after a spine injury in the 1930s. Director John Ford's sentimental tribute to the Navy has plenty of romanticized action and broad humor, with a solid cast including Maureen O'Hara as Wead's wife, Dan Dailey as his orderly and Ward Bond as a Ford-like movie director. Much drinking and brawling as well as some domestic strife

title: Wings of the Dove, The
synopsis: Lovely rendering of Henry James' 1902 novel in which a young Englishwoman (Helena Bonham Carter) urges her impoverished lover (Linus Roache) to court the dying American heiress (Alison Elliott) they have befriended in hopes she will leave him her fortune. Under Iain Softley's astute direction, the myriad ways of the human heart delicately unfold in this fine character study. A few sexual encounters and brief nudity

title: Wings of the Hawk
synopsis: Routine adventure in 1911 Mexico where an American mining engineer (Van Heflin) tries to protect his gold strike by siding with the rebels against corrupt government forces (led by George Dolenz). Directed by Budd Boetticher, the story bogs down in the bickering among the rebels until they unite in the final showdown with the local military. Stylized violence

title: Winners, The
synopsis: ( see: "My Way" )

title: Winner, The
synopsis: Uninvolving crime tale of a naive do-gooder (Vincent D'Onofrio) on a weekly winning streak in Las Vegas and how a manipulative lounge singer (Rebecca DeMornay), his estranged brother (Michael Madsen) and other lowlifes attempt to separate him from his winnings. Director Alex Cox trots out a half dozen quirky, one-dimensional characters in a failed attempt to mix film noir with hip comedy. Some murderous violence, a fleeting sexual encounter and frequent profanity as well as rough language

title: Winning
synopsis: Paul Newman is ruggedly impressive as a race-car driver whose obsession with the track leads his neglected wife (Joanne Woodward) to dally with his chief competitor (Robert Wagner). Directed by James Goldstone, the movie is as slick and quick as the race cars that provide its action thrills, and its message boils down to the fact that sometimes winning is really losing

title: Winning Team, The
synopsis: Dramatized story of baseball pitcher Grover Cleveland Alexander (Ronald Reagan), a Nebraska farmer whose major league career begins in 1911, then collapses in 1925 due to medical problems complicated by drinking binges, until given the chance to help the St. Louis Cardinals win the 1926 World Series. Directed by Lewis Seiler, the story holds interest though the human drama is surprisingly flat, despite the emotional support given Alexander by his wife (Doris Day) and loyal friend, Cardinal player-manager Roger Hornsby (Frank Lovejoy)

title: Winning Way, The
synopsis: ( see: "The All-American" )

title: Winslow Boy, The
synopsis: Eloquent adaptation of Terence Rattigan's stage play in which a father (Nigel Hawthorne) in 1910 London believes the naval academy has wrongly expelled his 14-year-old son for stealing a five-shilling postal order and at great cost, especially to his daughter (Rebecca Pidgeon), engages a prominent lawyer (Jeremy Northam) to prove the lad's innocence. Writer-director David Mamet unfolds the story through elegant dialogue and a marvelous cast of characters, honing and sharpening but not changing Rattigan's period piece about British justice upholding the rights of a citizen against the power of the state. Heavy sledding for pre-schoolers

title: Winter Guest, The
synopsis: Talky drama set on a bitterly cold day in a Scottish seaside town explores relationships between an elderly mother (Phyllida Law) and her widowed daughter (Emma Thompson), a pair of amorous teenagers, a couple of funeral-loving spinsters and two boys playing hookey. Writer-director Alan Rickman's moody set piece deals with themes of grief, friendship and coming of age in lyrical but lethargic fashion. Sexual references and situations, brief nudity, frequent profanity and much rough language

title: Winter Kills
synopsis: Failed screen version of Richard Condon's novel about the brother (Jeff Bridges) of an assassinated U.S. President who years later discovers that the actual assassin was not the man accused but another who was the agent of a vast and intricate conspiracy. Directed by William Richert, nothing makes much sense in this ill-conceived and badly executed melodrama which exploits memories of a tragic moment in American history. Some scenes of graphic sex. O (R) ( 1979 )

title: Winter People
synopsis: Melodramatic tale of love and revenge unfolds in the snowy hills of North Carolina during the Depression when an honorable city man (Kurt Russell) tries to protect an unfortunate country woman (Kelly McGillis) from the wild mountain man who fathered her illegitimate child. Directed by Ted Kotcheff, its family feud subplot, while key to the suspense, is poorly realized and its lush rural landscapes are wasted in an implausible period plot. Some rough language, a grisly bear hunt and several scenes of sadistic violence

title: Winterset
synopsis: Depression-era drama from Maxwell Anderson's play in which a young drifter (Burgess Meredith) finds the gangster (Eduardo Ciannelli) who years before had committed the crime for which the youth's anarchist father (John Carradine) was executed. Directed by Alfred Santell, the theatrical style of the adaptation fairly creaks, but the justice theme and characterizations of good people in hard times still hold interest. Some stylized violence

title: Winter Soldier
synopsis: During the winter of 1971, 200 men calling themselves Vietnam Veterans Against the War, sat before members of the press in Detroit and ruefully related their military experiences. The Pentagon refuted none of their testimony which found its way into the Congressional Record. Eighteen anonymous friends of the veterans preserved the recollections of some of these men in a documentary which eminently deserves to be seen as part of the record of a very troubled time in the history of our nation

title: Winter Solstice
synopsis: Engrossing domestic drama about a blue-collar widower (Anthony LaPaglia) coping with his two teenage boys -- one who announces he's leaving home (Aaron Stanford), and the other a troublesome, moody student (Mark Webber) -- and the compassionate woman (Allison Janney) who moves into a nearby house and reaches out to them. Writer-director Josh Sternfeld, in his feature-film debut, has crafted a sensitive slice-of-life story that rings absolutely true. The performances, especially LaPaglia's, are extraordinary, and a good pro-family message and a hopeful ending give a somber story a positive uplift. Rough and crude language, a couple of brief violent episodes, tobacco use

title: Winter Wind
synopsis: Hungarian director Miklos Jancso relates an incident about a Croatian anarchist in the 1930s who is considered a hero by his followers but only after they have destroyed him. The film is not for casual viewers but those interested in foreign films or European politics will find it worth seeing

title: Wired
synopsis: Muddled movie about the self-destruction of media personality John Belushi (Michael Chiklis) who died of a drug overdose in 1982. Director Larry Peerce fails to mesh diverse and contradictory elements of a narrative told largely in flashbacks, but the movie's anti-drug stance is clearly unambiguous. Graphic depictions of substance abuse and much foul language

title: Wisdom
synopsis: Ridiculous teenage Bonnie-and-Clyde team (Emilio Estevez and Demi Moore) show their defiance of adult authority and social injustice by destroying mortgage records. The vanity production, written and directed by Estevez, centers on an unhealthy preoccupation with guns and violence along with profanity and casual sex. O (R) ( 1986 )

title: Wise Blood
synopsis: Screen version of Flannery O'Connor's novel about a God-haunted young man (Brad Dourif) who on his way to Taulkinham, Tenn., to preach a new religion, meets such bizarre characters as a failed preacher pretending he is blind (Harry Dean Stanton), his mildly depraved daughter (Amy Wright) and a jovial evangelist (Ned Beatty). Director John Huston has made a powerful and provocative movie whose spiritual implications are as compelling as its artistic excellence. The incidental violence and moral complexity are more appropriate for adult viewers

title: Wise Guys
synopsis: Brian De Palma's brash and audacious parody of the gangster film relies too heavi1y upon profanity and violence as source of humor. Although Danny De Vito and Joe Piscopo create frantically likab1e but bungling small-time hoods, their stereotyped characterizations, along with others in the film, are likely to give offense to some Italian and Jewish viewers. O (R) ( 1986 )

title: Wishing Machine, The
synopsis: Czechoslovakian children's story about two boys whose visit to an industrial fair leads them to imagine they can make a trip to the moon. Written and directed by Josef Pinkava, the movie (dubbed into English) has imaginative visuals and a pleasant story that small children will enjoy because it is, from beginning to end, entirely made for them

title: Wishmaster
synopsis: Monster movie in which a powerful evil spirit can conquer the world if, after taking human form (Andrew Divoff), it's able to persuade a vulnerable young woman (Tammy Lauren) to make three wishes. Director Robert Kurtzman uses some imaginative visuals and special effects to enliven an otherwise routine horror film. Much fantasy violence, some of it gory, recurring rough language and a few instances of profanity

title: Wish You Were Here
synopsis: British director David Leland's sensitive, bittersweet evocation of a youngster's coming of age in a 1950's English coastal town focuses upon her sexual initation, disappointments with her father and encounters with the male-dominated working-class society of the period. The sexually explicit but emotionally accurate portrait of a young woman's discovery of self-worth and meaning deals responsibly with the issue of abortion, though takes a benign attitude toward birth control. Brief nudity and some vulgar language

title: Witchboard
synopsis: The bloody consequences of fooling around with a Quija board are demonstrated in this horror tale of a young woman (Tawny Kitaen) whose jousts with an evil spirit manage to get her former boyfriend killed and her current lover nearly dismembered. Writer-director Kevin Tenney's story of the supernatural presents all its gory excesses and vulgarities in broad daylight. O (R) ( 1987 )

title: Witchcraft '70
synopsis: Self-described as a serious documentary study of contemporary witchcraft throughout the world, it is anything but a documentary, though it does flit from place to place, seeking out what, apparently, is the main ingredient for any occult ceremony, namely that the participants be as naked as possible. Few will be bewitched, many will be bothered, and almost all will be bewildered. O (X/R) ( 1970 )

title: Witches' Brew
synopsis: Jokey horror story about a college psychology professor (Richard Benjamin) who laughs at his wife (Teri Garr) for dabbling in witchcraft, then is terrified when a dying witch (Lana Turner) tries to switch places with her. Directed by Richard Shorr and Herbert L. Strock, the comic menace is too fitful to be funny and too contrived to be frightening. Eerie witchcraft rituals, a hokey supernatural monster and sexual situations

title: Witches of Eastwick, The
synopsis: Jack Nicholson plays a devil summoned via the wishful thinking of three lonely, frustrated women (Cher, Susan Sarandon and Michelle Pfeiffer) who allow themselves to be seduced and impregnated while living a life of reckless abandon at the demon's mansion. In director George Miller's version of John Updike's sardonic, allegorical novel about the battle of the sexes, the action is entirely on the sexual level obscuring other dimensions of its theme while trying to find humor in vulgar excesses, promiscuous behavior and sexually derived profanity. O (R) ( 1987 )

title: Witches, The
synopsis: Uneven adaptation of Roald Dahl's contemporary fairy tale in which a grandmother (Mai Zetterling) helps her 9-year-old grandson (Jasen Fisher) thwart the plans of the Grand High Witch (Anjelica Huston) to turn all of Britain's children into mice. Produced by Jim Henson and directed by Nicolas Roeg, the fantasy starts well and has some cute mice puppetry but bogs down in the frenetic flamboyance of a witches' convention in a posh British spa. Some intense menace, several discreet sexual references and an instance of profanity

title: Witchmaker, The
synopsis: Psychology professor (Alvy Moore) stupidly leads his students into the Louisiana swamplands to investigate a series of occult-oriented murders where they succumb to spells cast by a maniacal fiend (John Lodge) who drains his victims' blood for use in satanic orgies. Written, produced and directed by William O. Brown, the feeble horror concoction keeps the camera at a distance from the mayhem

title: With a Song in My Heart
synopsis: Glossy screen biography of singer Jane Froman (Susan Hayward) and her successful struggle to make a comeback after being crippled in a plane crash during World War II. Despite director Walter Lang's sudsy treatment of marital woes (hubby David Wayne supplanted by true love Rory Calhoun) and extensive hospital stays (made bearable by wisecracking nurse Thelma Ritter), the movie's main appeal is its large offering of period songs with Froman's voice on the soundtrack. Marital misunderstandings and divorce

title: With Honors
synopsis: When a self-involved Harvard senior (Brendan Fraser) accidentally loses a crucial term paper, he gets it back from a cantakerous homeless man (Joe Pesci) by providing him with a place to sleep during the frigid winter nights, out of which develops an unlikely bond between privileged student and witty indigent. Director Alek Keshishian's poignant story unreels in earnest if methodical fashion as the student and his three roommates admirably -- and predictably-- come to care for the unfortunate stranger who in turn has some wisdom to share from the school of hard knocks. Fleeting bedroom scene, occasional sexual references and a few instances of profanity

title: Withnail and I
synopsis: British drama about two struggling young actors (Richard E. Grant and Paul McGann) who, at the end of the 1960's hippie era, spend a weekend on the country estate of the wealthy uncle of one of them. Their friendship dissolves in remorseful recognition of the hurt they cause their host (Richard Griffiths) by preying upon his homosexual tendencies. Director Bruce Robinson's movie is spotted with harsh language and some drug and sexual references but manages to convey a kind of elegaic farewell to the excesses of the times

title: Without a Clue
synopsis: This bit of British comic fluff reverses the roles of Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson by having Watson (Ben Kingsley) be secretly the supersleuth who writes stories about the fictional Holmes. To cover his tracks, Watson hires a third-rate actor (Michael Caine) to impersonate Holmes, but the actor's ineptitude and liberties with wine, women and song drive Watson to distraction. As directed by Thom Eberhardt, their comic relationship wears thin, but there are some hilarious moments. Fleeting violence with humorous undertones and mild sexual innuendo

title: Without a Paddle
synopsis: Fitfully funny comedy about three lifelong friends (Seth Green, Matthew Lillard and Dax Shepard), inspired by the untimely death of the clique's fourth amigo, who impulsively set out to make good on a childhood pact and search for a hidden treasure in the Pacific Northwest wilderness. But their canoe trip downriver hits some comical rapids -- including run-ins with a grizzly and a pair of heavily armed backwoods marijuana farmers. As directed by Steven Brill, the film is full of forced frat-house humor and gross-out sight gags, which, while balanced by a positive though schmaltzy message about friendship, leaves the story up the creek. A few sexual encounters, drug content and some violence as well as recurring coarse language and crude humor

title: Without Apparent Motive
synopsis: Tough, ruthless detective (Jean-Louis Trintignant) must flush out a madman who has been going about the picturesque city of Nice popping off one victim after another with his sniper's rifle. Nearly every encounter in director Philippe Labro's movie has sex simmering just below the surface and, as the story builds towards climax and resolution, twisted sexual relations not surprisingly provide all the keys

title: Without a Stitch
synopsis: To cure the frigidity of a young girl who is introduced to a life of sex and perversion, she is taught that anything is permissible as long as it does not hurt anybody. What is particularly insidious about this exploitation movie is that it not only portrays and exploits nudity and immorality, but makes a clear effort to win its viewers to accept a similar mode of thinking and living. O (R) ( 1970 )

title: Without a Trace
synopsis: Fact-based story of a six-year-old boy who is kidnapped on the way to school in New York City and his mother (Kate Nelligan) who convinces a police detective (Judd Hirsch) to stay on the case even when it looks as if there is no hope. Thanks largely to the performances of Hirsh and Nelligan, there are some good moments, but for the rest director Stanley Jaffe's effort remains a flat and uninspired story, sorely lacking any real dramatic development and with a ludicrous sentimental ending. Some strong language

title: Without Limits
synopsis: Uneven dramatization based on the life of track star Steve Prefontaine (Billy Crudup) and his University of Oregon coach, Bill Bowerman (Donald Sutherland), as the young athlete breaks records in collegiate meets but breaks his heart losing in the 1972 Munich Olympics, then after refocusing his efforts to compete in the 1976 Olympics, dies in a tragic auto accident. Directed by Richard Towne, the story of a talented athlete who insisted on winning his way will interest sports fans, but the human character portrayed on the screen is a quirky, self-centered rebel with a cause few non-fans are likely to find appealing. Explicit sexual situations, brief rear nudity. rough language and profanity

title: Without Love
synopsis: > The third pairing of Hepburn and Spencer Tracy, this is adapted from a Philip Barry comedy, and features a particularly good supporting cast which includes Lucille Ball, Keenan Wynn, and Gloria Grahame. Directed by Bucquet

title: Without Reservations
synopsis: Slight but amusing romantic comedy in which a novelist (Claudette Colbert) meets a Marine pilot (John Wayne) on a cross-country train journey, decides he'd be perfect as the hero in the movie version of her best-seller but hides her identity because he hated the book. Director Mervyn LeRoy gets the story off to a bright start but has trouble sustaining the contrived plot to its predictable conclusion, though the travelers' silly misadventures provide laughs along the way and there are some droll jabs directed at Hollywood. Romantic situations

title: Without You I'm Nothing
synopsis: Loosely structured version of Sandra Bernhard's one-woman show allows the comedienne to badmouth current pop idols, the political scene, commercial products and anything resembling conventional behavior. Directed by John Boskovich, the result is emotionally uninvolving with drawn-out musical numbers and sketches whose barbed humor and cold delivery accomplish little more than alienating the audience. Scenes of sexual exploitation with nudity, much rough language and a positive portrayal of drug use. O (R) ( 1990 )

title: With Six You Get Egg Roll
synopsis: Doris Day plays a widow in coveralls with three sons and Brian Keith is a widower with one daughter who try to keep their courtship a secret from the children and then get them to all act in harmony as part of the new family. Director Howard Morris is not only stuck with a contrived and saccharine situation, with four over-cute children, but the movie gags on attempts at slapstick humor. The result is the kind of entertainment film that gives family pictures a bad name

title: Witless Protection
synopsis: Generally crude and lowbrow comedy in which a headstrong rural sheriff's deputy (Larry the Cable Guy) kidnaps an elegant heiress (Ivana Milicevic) from the custody of an FBI special agent (Yaphet Kotto) he believes to be corrupt, and drives her to Chicago to testify against her former boss (Peter Stormare), who has hired a shady security guard (Eric Roberts) to bring her back. The film, as directed by Charles Robert Carner, succeeds in being funny about once every 15 minutes, making this journey to Chi-town one long, tedious trek. Much crass and crude language, three uses of profanity, frequent sexual and scatological humor, partial male nudity, ethnic stereotyping and an obscene gesture

title: Witness
synopsis: Tough Philadelphia police detective (Harrison Ford) hides out among the Amish to protect his life and that of a young boy who witnessed a murder committed by a corrupt fellow detective. He and the boy's widowed mother (Kelly McGillis) are drawn to each other despite their different worlds. Director Peter Weir gets excellent performances in a good romantic melodrama that also offers some relatively thoughtful reflections on violence and non-violence. Some graphic violence and brief nudity are handled as restrained but essential plot devices

title: Witness for the Prosecution
synopsis: Twisty Agatha Christie courtroom puzzler in which British barrister Charles Laughton defends accused lady killer Tyrone Power in a murder trial complicated by mysterious title character Marlene Dietrich and a double surprise ending. Director Billy Wilder plays the case's red herrings for all they're worth, helped by solid comic relief from the on-going feud between ailing lawyer Laughton and dictatorial nurse Elsa Lanchester. Implications of marital infidelity and stylized violence

title: Witness to Hope: The Life of John Paul II
synopsis: > Based on George Weigel's 1999 biography, this beautiful and rewarding documentary provides an intimate and nuanced portrait of Karol Wojtyla, from the tragedies of his childhood in Poland to his historic papacy. Less a chronology of events than an attempt to understand the man behind the globetrotting religious icon, the film examines how his experiences under Nazi and communist oppression influenced his lifelong commitment to religious freedom and human rights; how the early loss of his mother, older brother and, later, father, impacted his spiritual insights into suffering; how his love of drama and poetry enkindled a deep respect for culture and the power of the written word to express truth; and how interaction with students as a young priest contributed to shaping his views on human sexuality. Resisting categorization, the image of Pope John Paul that emerges is full of humanity, complexity and contradiction: priest, poet, playwright, actor, mystic, philosopher, pastor, intellectual, a revolutionary who championed tradition. Directed by Judith Dwan Hallet and narrated by Rene Auberjonois, the program incorporates archival photos and footage interspersed with re-creations and glossy location footage taken in Rome and Poland. Friends, colleagues and scholars -- including Weigel and former U.S. national security adviser Zbignew Brzezinski -- provide illuminating commentary. One of the better documentaries about John Paul II, the film is essential viewing for anyone interested in this towering figure, who, though acknowledging the 20th century as "the century of fear," challenged us to "be not afraid."

title: Wives and Lovers
synopsis: Flat satire of marital woes caused by the sudden success of a struggling writer (Van Johnson) whose wife (Janet Leigh) has a fling with an actor (Jeremy Slate) when she suspects her husband of having an affair with his agent (Martha Hyer). Director John Rich wrings little humor out of a contrived situation that grows tiresome as the bogus misunderstandings escalate until the counterfeit sentimental ending. Sexual situations

title: Wizard of Loneliness, The
synopsis: Bitter, precocious 12-year-old (Lukas Haas), forced to live with his grandparents in Vermont after his mother's death while his father's off fighting World War II, finally overcomes his resentment and accepts the unconditional love offered by an uncritical grandfather (John Randolph), gently seductive aunt (Lea Thompson) and tiny cousin (Jeremiah Warner). Director Jenny Bowen gets some fine acting in a richly detailed family drama based on a semi-autobiographical novel by John Nichols. Much rough language from the youthful protagonist, a clothed but intense sexual encounter, an assault on a child and a graphic murder scene

title: Wizard of Oz, The
synopsis: Dorothy rides her tornado to the magic land over the rainbow in director Victor Fleming's classic that skyrocketed Judy Garland's career and has given generations of families prime entertainment again and again. The 50th anniversary edition has 17 minutes of material not included in the original release

title: Wizard of Speed and Time, The
synopsis: A special effects artist (Mike Jittlov) tries to crack the big time in Hollywood only to come up against some sleazy TV producers who take advantage of him. Also written and directed by Jittlov, this amateurish bit of self-promotion is badly written and acted, though youngsters may enjoy the zany special effects. Some sexual innuendoes

title: Wizards
synopsis: Animated feature starts with a thermonuclear destruction of human life on earth, then jumps to the far distant future in which mutants inhabit radioactive lands and elves and fairies live in the uncontaminated area where are born twin wizards who battle for the future of the planet. It is animator Ralph Bakshi's most polished effort with bold, imaginative graphics and effective integration of live action footage. A number of violent visuals

title: Wizard, The
synopsis: Small-fry version of "Rain Man" tracks the exploits of a 13-year-old (Fred Savage) who kidnaps his emotionally disturbed 9-year-old brother (Luke Edwards) from an institution to enter him in a video game championship for a crass feel-good ending. Directed by Todd Holland, the sentimental, far-fetched plot plugs everything from Nintendo games to the Universal City Studios tour. Some rough language and an unfortunate gag about child molestation

title: Wiz, The
synopsis: Diana Ross stars as Dorothy, the girl who flies over the rainbow in a black musical version of "The Wizard of Oz." Chasing Toto into a snowstorm in Harlem, she winds up on the yellow brick road with the Scarecrow (Michael Jackson), the Tinman (Nipsey Russell) and the Cowardly Lion (Ted Ross) on their way to meet the Wiz (Richard Pryor). Directed by Sidney Lumet, it has lavishly staged musical numbers, opulent costumes and colorful settings, but is overlong and its humor seems addressed more to adults and teenagers than younger viewers

title: Wolf
synopsis: Bitten by a dying wolf he's accidentally run over, a Manhattan book editor (Jack Nicholson) fears he is turning into a fanged beast capable of attacking his estranged wife (Kate Nelligan), traitorous colleague (James Spader) or new love interest (Michelle Pfeiffer). Director Mike Nichols' elegant take on a classic monster myth may not scare anyone but will engross viewers in Nicholson's performance as the anguished wolfman trying to cling to his diminishing humanity. Brief but intense violence, implied affairs and intermittent rough language

title: Wolf Call
synopsis: Low-budget adventure directed by George Waggner in which a playboy (John Carroll) is sent by his father to look over an Alaskan radium mine, routs the crooks running the place, hires a backwoods chemist to refine the ore at low cost and stays on to sing duets with a local Indian maid (Movita). Mild menace

title: Wolf Creek
synopsis: Repulsive thriller inspired by true events about a trio of hikers (Cassandra Magrath, Nathan Phillips and Kestie Morassi) who, stranded in a remote region of the Australian Outback, find themselves in a nightmarish ordeal when they are "rescued" by a neighborly bushman (John Jarratt) who turns out to be a sadistic killer. Eliciting convincing performances out of his Aussie cast, director Greg McLean chillingly creates an unsettling sense of isolation, building suspense before detouring into dehumanizing and bloody depravity. Gratuitous realistic violence and gore, including vile scenes of mutilation and torture, sexual degradation, as well as recurring rough and sexually raw language

title: Wolfen
synopsis: Murky thriller in which a hard-boiled, nearly burnt-out detective (Albert Finney) investigating three brutal murders links them to some menacing wolflike creatures seen roaming the streets of New York. Directed by Michael Wadleigh with some spectacular camera effects, the story suggests that these preternatural creatures are punishment for the sins of a rapacious society, but its sense of moral indignation doesn't justify the violence and graphic depiction of blood and gore

title: The Wolfman
synopsis: Alternately spooky, savage and silly, this remake of the 1941 monster classic starring Lon Chaney Jr. tells of a decent if troubled man (Benicio Del Toro) periodically transformed into a hirsute beast after returning to his ancestral estate in England following the brutal murder of his brother in 1891. Striking a tone that might be described as "visceral camp," director Joe Johnston entertains by rendering the trappings of lycanthrope lore with first-rate special effects and actors -- Anthony Hopkins, Emily Blunt and Hugo Weaving -- willing to feast on the material. Frequent episodes of moderately graphic violence including fleeting images of human entrails, decapitations and severed limbs; an instance of partial upper female nudity; several references to prostitution; one use of profane language

title: Wolf Man, The
synopsis: Creaky screen-monster classic in which the son (Lon Chaney, Jr.) of an English lord (Claude Rains) is bitten by a werewolf (Bela Lugosi) but only realizes his fate when transformed into a human beast at the next full moon. Director George Waggner excels in creating a fearful atmosphere out of nighttime shadows and misty moors, with Chaney winning sympathy as the man who loathes what he becomes and the venerable Maria Ouspenskaya adding some dignity to the proceedings as the wise Gypsy matriarch who tries to help the tormented victim. Menacing situation and stylized violence

title: Woman Alone, A
synopsis: ( see: "Sabotage" )

title: Woman at Her Window, A
synopsis: Slack French 1930s political drama in which an Austrian woman (Romy Schneider) tries to help a Communist fugitive (Victor Lanoux) escape the secret police in Athens by involving her husband (Umberto Orsini) and a wealthy friend (Philippe Noiret). Director Pierre Granier-Deferre's narrative is needlessly complex and muddled, though it has compelling acting and some philosophical depth. Several scenes of police brutality

title: Woman Destroyed, A
synopsis: ( see: "Smash-Up: The Story of a Woman" )

title: Woman in Green, The
synopsis: Convoluted mystery with Sherlock Holmes (Basil Rathbone) and Dr. Watson (Nigel Bruce) on the trail of the trail of the nefarious master criminal, Professor Moriarty (Henry Daniell), who this time heads a blackmail scheme employing hypnosis and murder. Under Roy William O'Neill's direction, Holmes faces death by auto fumes, an assassin's bullet and a walk off a ledge high above the street before the case is closed. Some fairly effective menace and minimal stylized violence

title: Woman in Hiding
synopsis: Minor thriller in which a wealthy bride (Ida Lupino) flees her murderous husband (Stephen McNally), then seeks help from a friendly war vet (Howard Duff) and her husband's ex-flame (Peggy Dow). Directed by Michael Gordon, the cat-and-mouse game is too contrived to build much suspense, though there are some good bits, notably a raucous hotel convention. Stylized violence and menace

title: Woman in Red, The
synopsis: Gene Wilder directs and also stars as a philandering advertising manager who pursues a beautiful model (Kelly Le Brock) while keeping his wife (Judith Ivy) in the dark. It is an ill-conceived and clumsily-executed attempt to recast a French farce about adultery ("Pardon Mon Affaire") in an American mold. Nudity and a benign attitude toward illicit sex. O (PG-13) ( 1984 )

title: Woman Next Door, The
synopsis: Weak French romantic melodrama about a happily married couple who move next door to another happily married couple but, as it happens, the wife who has just moved in (Fanny Ardant) and the husband next door (Gerald Depardieu) had had a stormy love affair seven years before and soon the two are off and running again. Director Francois Truffaut handles this material with his usual adroitness, but to little purpose in a story that proves banal and unmoving, with some questionable amorous sequences

title: Woman Obsessed
synopsis: Turgid sudser from the Canadian northwest where a farmer's widow (Susan Hayward) marries her brawny, inarticulate hired man (Stephen Boyd) but comes to regret it. Directed by Henry Hathaway, the picturesque locales of the setting are a lot easier to watch than the cliched story of a woman's soured romance. Domestic misunderstandings and natural catastrophes

title: Woman of Dolwyn
synopsis: ( see: "The Last Days of Dolwyn" )

title: Woman of Straw
synopsis: Intriguing British mystery in which the cunning nephew (Sean Connery) of an aged, irascible millionaire (Ralph Richardson) convinces a beguiling nurse (Gina Lollobrigida) to marry the old man in order to get a share of his wealth. Director Basil Dearden sets up the mercenary situation convincingly, then bogs down in some improbable plot twists for a disappointing ending, though Richardson's rougish performance is worth catching. Some grisly situations, amoral characters and sexual innuendo

title: Woman of the Ganges
synopsis: French writer Marguerite Duras' story of a man at a resort during its winter off-season where he meets, or perhaps imagines that he meets, the woman of the title whom he had loved in India long ago. Also directed by Duras, the highly verbal movie takes place not on the screen, but in the mind of the beholder willing to plumb its blend of time, memory and illusion

title: Woman of the Town, The
synopsis: Intelligent Western opens in 1919 with Bat Masterson (Albert Dekker) working as a reporter for a New York paper, then flashes back 50 years to Dodge City where he takes the job of marshal, comes to admire a high-minded dance-hall belle (Claire Trevor) and stops her dangerous ex-suitor (Barry Sullivan), with tragic results. Directed by George Archainbaud, the melodrama follows the sterling lawman as he learns the futility of violence from the "painted angel" of the title, despite shootouts along the way. Frontier violence and romantic complications

title: Woman of the Year
synopsis: Robust romantic comedy in which a good-natured sportswriter (Spencer Tracy) romances a high-powered political commentator (Katharine Hepburn), then has his hands full trying to get her to fit into his schedule after they wed. Director George Stevens paces the opposites-attract premise with some hilarious funny business but what succeeds best are the performances of the two principals who prove entirely likeable in this wry battle-of-the-sexes comedy. Veiled sexual references and innuendo

title: Woman on Top
synopsis: Escapist comedy about a sizzling chef (Penelope Cruz), who leaves her native Brazil and stifling macho husband (Murilo Ben�cio) for San Francisco, where she lands a television cooking show that is an instant hit. Whimsical visual effects and exotic locations notwithstanding, director Fina Torres' dull film capitalizes on the aesthetic pleasures but lags behind in engaging narrative content. Includes mysticism, a few sexual encounters with nudity, minor homosexual innuendo and brief crass language with fleeting profanity. The U.S. Catholic Conference

title: Woman Rebels, A
synopsis: Creaky melodrama set in Victorian England where a young lady (Katharine Hepburn) falls for a scoundrel (Van Heflin), raises her illegitimate child as her niece while working for a woman's magazine, then uses it as a vehicle to crusade for women's rights. Directed by Mark Sandrich, the contrived storyline may not be very convincing today but the picture still holds interest as an early attempt to deal sympathetically with the theme of women's equality. Veiled sexual references

title: Woman's Decision, A
synopsis: Sensitive, extremely well-acted Polish triangle story whose heroine (Maya Komorowska) is married to a wonderful husband (Piotr Franczewski), has an affectionate son and a modern apartment in Warsaw but finds herself wanting to give it all up for the company of a footloose man (Marek Piwowski). Directed by Krzystof Zanussi, it is a perceptive study of the interior struggle each of the characters undergoes during the course of the narrative

title: Woman's Secret, A
synopsis: Transparent sudser in which a radio singer (Gloria Graham) is shot and her dour manager (Maureen O'Hara) arrested for the deed while their mutual friend, a debonair songwriter (Melvyn Douglas), seeks the truth along with a cop (Jay C. Flippen) whose wife (Mary Philips) knows a romantic triangle when she sees one. Despite the capable cast, director Nicholas Ray makes matters seem even duller than they actually are in numerous flashbacks slowly explaining the obvious. Brief violence and romantic complications

title: Woman's Tale, A
synopsis: Somber drama about an elderly, cancer-ridden woman (Sheila Florance) who, with her devoted young nurse (Gosia Dobrowolska) at her side, grittily determines to extract all the enjoyment she can from her final days. Though director Paul Cox elicits moving performances from both women, the life-affirming theme is delivered with belabored heavy-handedness. Uncritical attitude toward the nurse's extramarital affair and brief nudity

title: Woman's Vengeance, A
synopsis: When a rich Englishwoman is poisoned, her unfaithful husband (Charles Boyer) is convicted and sentenced to death, though a physician (Cedric Hardwicke) suspects the wife's best friend (Jessica Tandy) is guilty. Directed by Zoltan Korda, the murky plot gains interest from solid performances by the cast and moody period photography. Romantic complications

title: Woman, Thou Art Loosed
synopsis: Soul-inspiring drama about a young woman (Kimberly Elise) who, with the help of a compassionate evangelical minister (T.D. Jakes), struggles to come to terms with her troubled past and find redemption, while awaiting execution for murder. Based on the best-selling novel by Jakes, the hope-filled film deals with difficult subjects -- including sexual abuse, addiction and murder -- though in a way which challenges viewers of faith to take seriously the Christian imperatives of love and reconciliation. Several instances of violence, including the implied rape of a young girl, a sexual encounter with blurred nudity, recurring drug content and some crude language

title: Woman Times Seven
synopsis: Italian potpourri of comedy, farce and pathos is directed by Vittorio De Sica with Shirley MacLaine as the heroine of each episode. It is needlessly marred by one tasteless and provocative sequence. O (br) ( 1967 )

title: Woman Under the Influence, A
synopsis: The woman of the title (Gena Rowlands) is a mother of three small children in the middle of a nervous breakdown while her husband (Peter Falk), a rough, callous but loving man, is totally unable to cope with the situation. Directed by John Cassavetes in his characteristic improvisational style, the result is full of the small realities and individual details that make up ordinary human experience but it is short on the sort of heightened drama one expects from a conventional movie narrative

title: Women
synopsis: Sensitive Hungarian character study of an unlikely and slowly developing friendship between the wife of a successful engineer (Marina Vlady) and a factory worker (Lili Monori) whose husband is an alcoholic. The melodramatic plot and its soap opera problems simply provide the background against which director Marta Meszaros explores the human needs that draw these two women together despite their differences in character, education and social position. Mature themes

title: Women in Cages
synopsis: Philippine exploitation movie directed by Gerry De Leon about a group of women prisoners who use their sadistic lesbian matron as a hostage to escape into the jungle where they fall prey to bounty hunters and flesh-peddlers. Heavy-duty debasement. O (R) ( 1971 )

title: Women in Cellblock 7
synopsis: Inanely plotted, badly acted and atrociously dubbed Italian exploitation movie about a woman who goes to prison to get evidence to save her father. Abundant nudity. O (R) ( 1977 )

title: Women in Love
synopsis: British adaptation of the D.H. Lawrence novel about the gradual involvement of two couples, one (Alan Bates and Glenda Jackson) having a rather healthy though incomplete relationship while the other (Oliver Reed and Jennie Linden) tragically ends in suicide. Directed by Ken Russell, the acting is first-rate, the photography almost too beautiful and the treatment of the convoluted relationships remains on the superficial level of the physical. Lengthy naked wrestling match between the men is more symbolic than erotic. O (R) ( 1970 )

title: Women in Revolt
synopsis: Three women from different social levels (female impersonators Candy Darling, Holly Woodlawn and Jackie Curtis) get caught up in the Women's Liberation Movement. Typical of the poor film quality and sexual explicitness of Andy Warhol's efforts in the past, it makes men, women and sex look ridiculous, ugly and perverted. O (nr) ( 1972 )

title: Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown
synopsis: After an actress (Carmen Maura) is deserted by her live-in lover (Fernando Guillen), she attempts to face down the coward before he leaves town with another woman. Written and directed by Pedro Almodovar, this Spanish farce explores without exploitation the comic vicissitudes of male-female relationships. Subtitles. Some rough language and a benign attitude toward sex and pregnancy outside of marriage

title: Women's Prison
synopsis: Tawdry programmer directed by Lewis Seiler in which the warden (Ida Lupino) of the women's division in a prison also housing male inmates is a sadist who is finally put in a straightjacket by the prison doctor (Howard Duff) after her brutality causes a riot. Much stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Women, The
synopsis: Lavish screen version of Clare Boothe's satiric play in which a New York socialite (Norma Shearer) whose husband has fallen for a calculating gold digger (Joan Crawford) goes to Reno for a divorce, then returns home to pick up the pieces. Directed by George Cukor, the all-female cast (Rosalind Russell, Paulette Goddard, Mary Boland and many others) provides a comic compendium of feminine stereotypes and caustic comments on the battle of the sexes, much of which is unflattering to women but it is the unseen males who get the worst of it. Comic treatment of sex and marriage

title: Wonder Boys
synopsis: Fitfully amusing comedy about a grouchy, pot-smoking English professor (Michael Douglas) who, daunted by the success of his first novel, is laboring to finish his second and in the process unwittingly takes an odd but gifted writing student (Tobey Maguire) under his shaky wing. Skillful performances and the picturesque campus setting enhance director Curtis Hanson's character-driven movie but they aren't enough to sustain interest in the sluggish and insubstantial narrative. Recurring recreational drug abuse, implied homosexual encounter, an extra-marital affair and some rough language

title: Wonderful Country, The
synopsis: Convoluted Western directed by Robert Parrish centers on an American (Robert Mitchum) who's made a career as a gunslinger in 1880's Mexico, but the love of a good woman (Julie London) and the assassination of his boss (Pedro Armendariz) lead him back to the States to join the Texas Rangers. Stylized violence and sexual references

title: Wonderful Crook, The
synopsis: Off-beat French comedy about a good-natured, but inept young man (Gerald Depardieu) who, in order to pay the employee's wages of his family's furniture business, undertakes a series of holdups and falls in love with one of his victims (Marlene Jobert). Neither his wife (Dominique Labourier) nor his employees suspect his double life until the police arrive to arrest him. Directed by Claude Goretta, the movie details in a warmly humorous manner the complications that can arise from a simplistic notion of "doing good." Brief nudity and vulgar language

title: Wonderful, Horrible Life of Leni Riefenstahl, The
synopsis: Absorbing account of how German movie director Riefenstahl came to make "The Triumph of the Will" (1934), the powerful Nazi propaganda film which made her unemployable after World War II, though she never joined the Nazi Party nor was ever accused of being anti-Semitic. Written and directed by Ray Mueller, the subtitled German production also interviews the 90-year-old Riefenstahl about her subsequent career as a photographer, yet keeps returning to the question of how an artist, no matter how disinterested in politics, could have been so blind to the evils of a repressive regime. The subject of a movie-maker's social responsibility has importance for more than film students

title: Wonderful World of the Brothers Grimm, The
synopsis: Lavish but plodding Cinerama production interweaving the story of the 19th-century German brothers (Laurence Harvey and Karl Boehm) with dramatizations of three of the many folk tales they popularized despite personal adversities. Co-directed by George Pal and Henry Levin, the Rhineland locales and period settings are better realized than either the biographical material or the special effects used in the fairy tales. Intermittently diverting for youngsters, though a long sit for their elders

title: Wonderland
synopsis: Fact-based story of porn-movie king John Holmes' involvement in a grisly quadruple homicide which took place in the Laurel Canyon neighborhood of Los Angeles in 1981. Full of graphically disturbing violence, director James Cox sets out to explore a morally bleak landscape so devoid of redeemable features that it is nearly impossible for viewers to invest any emotional interest, let alone sympathy, in the film's mostly repellent characters. Excessive graphic violence, sexual encounters with partial nudity, recurring drug abuse, much rough and crude language, as well as profanity

title: Wonder Man
synopsis: Sappy Danny Kaye vehicle in which he doubles as a murdered nightclub comic whose spirit inhabits the body of his scholarly twin brother, thereby confounding police, gangsters and the brothers' girlfriends (Virginia Mayo and Vera-Ellen). Directed by Bruce Humberstone, there are a couple of good song-and-dance numbers and some funny routines but the phantom-brother gimmick wears thin. Minimal stylized violence

title: Wonders of Aladdin, The
synopsis: Embarrassingly inept comic adventure with Donald O'Connor as an over-aged Aladdin and Vittorio de Sica as a cut-rate genie all mixed up in the old story of a magic lamp. Directed by Mario Bava and Henry Levin, this dubbed Italian misfire suffers from an impoverished script and threadbare fantasy effects. Much sexual innuendo and comic violence, including a sadistic torture scene

title: Won Ton Ton, the Dog Who Saved Hollywood
synopsis: Director Michael Winner's wretchedly thrown-together slapstick comedy about a wonder dog of the old silent movie era is made all the more tasteless by seeing performers one once admired in a series of painfully inane cameos. It is definitely not for young viewers. O (PG) ( 1976 )

title: Woo
synopsis: Dopey comedy crudely chronicles a madcap blind date between a cautious law student (Tommy Davidson) and an impetuous beauty (Jada Pinkett Smith) who attracts trouble wherever they go. Director Daisy Von Scherler Mayer's lame battle-of-the-sexes comedy is a tiresome collection of witless pranks and dumb jokes. Brief violence, much sexist humor, racial slurs, sexual innuendo, fleeting nudity, occasional profanity and frequent rough language

title: Wooden Man's Bride, The
synopsis: In 1920's China, a woman (Wang Lan) whose groom is accidentally killed on their wedding day is forced by her mother-in-law (Wang Yumei) to live as a married woman with a wooden statue of her dead spouse until the kindly servant (Chang Shih) she comes to love resorts to desperate means to free her. Director Huang Jianxin's visually haunting melodrama explores a harsh feudal society in which the honor-bound but inwardly seething characters eventually rebel against the old lady in order to marry. Subtitles. Some gory violence, fleeting nudity and an instance of rough language

title: Wooden Soldiers
synopsis: ( see: "March of the Wooden Soldiers" )

title: Woodstock
synopsis: Documentary about the landmark musical event that brought together a half million young people to hear a parade of such talented performers as Richie Havens, Joan Baez, Country Joe and the Fish, The Who, Sha-na-na, Arlo Guthrie, Crosby Stills and Nash, Joe Cocker and so on. Directed by Michael Wadleigh, it is dazzling in image and sound but as a record of this particular music festival, it concentrates on the positive themes of love and peace, giving scant attention to the drugs and commercialism that for many marred the event. Brief nudity and some rough language and lyrics

title: Wood, The
synopsis: Drawn-out but warm-hearted tale of three African-American buddies, one of whom (Taye Diggs) vacillates about taking his vows hours before his wedding while another (Omar Epps) recalls in flashback their awkward teenage fumblings with the opposite sex. Essentially a coming-of-age tale, director Rick Famuyiwa presents overly familiar macho posturings to limited comic effect before the three are prepared to accept marital commitment. Sexual situations, brief violence, fleeting rear nudity, minimal profanity and much rough language

title: Working Girl
synopsis: A 30-year-old secretary (Melanie Griffith) with the training and dreams to make it big as a Wall Street stockbroker is held back by sexist male boses and a treacherous female boss (Sigourney Weaver) but when she transforms herself into a polished professional, her appealing vulnerability attracts the right boss (Philip Bosco) and suitor (Harrison Ford). Directed by Mike Nichols, the upbeat story balances its women-in-the-workplace concerns with a delightful Cinderella story that will entertain and enlighten even diehard anti-feminists. Much rough language laced with sexual innuendo and some frontal nudity within brief graphic sexual situations

title: Work Is a Four Letter Word
synopsis: British comedy about a man (David Warner) who grows mushrooms that have a narcotic effect. Directed by Peter Hall, its premise is better than the results

title: World According to Garp, The
synopsis: Uneven screen version of John Irving's novel about a fragile writer (Robin Williams) overwhelmed by catastrophes, bizarre events and his indomitable mother (Glenn Close). Under George Roy Hill's direction, Williams by going all out to turn the character into a lovable schnook makes his problems seem even crueler and more arbitrary than they might have been. Some nudity and graphic sexual references

title: World Apart, A
synopsis: Fact-based drama set in 1963 South Africa concerns an anti-apartheid white journalist (Barbara Hershey) and her inability to give her three young daughters the same love and devotion she channels into the political arena. British director Chris Menges skirts over the political and social issues to focus on the mother-daughter conflict. Some emotional and physical political violence, an off-camera suicide attempt and the suffering caused one of the daughters because of her parents' political activities

title: World for Ransom
synopsis: Low-budget espionage caper directed by Robert Aldrich is set in Singapore where an American undercover agent (Dan Duryea) rescues a nuclear physicist (Arthur Shields) from a kidnap gang (led by Gene Lockhart). Stylized violence, menacing situations and sexual innuendo

title: World in His Arms, The
synopsis: Romantic adventure with a Yankee sea captain (Gregory Peck) who's grown so rich poaching seals in Russian-owned Alaska that he decides to buy it from the Czar, but along the way falls for a Russian countess (Ann Blyth), battles a Portuguese freebooter (Anthony Quinn) and is captured by a Russian gunboat. Director Raoul Walsh submerges the 19th-century romance in high-seas derring-do and imperial despotism with the action sputtering to a bogus ending. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: World Is Not Enough, The
synopsis: Typical breathless Bond fare in which 007 (Pierce Brosnan), sent to protect a murder target (Sophie Marceau), finds she has joined forces with a sinister psychopath (Robert Carlyle) in a plot to seize control of the world's oil supply. As directed by Michael Apted, the fast and furious action eventually wears itself out in an overlong, overly elaborate by-the-numbers plot. Much stylized violence and a few discreet bedroom scenes

title: World of Buckminster Fuller, The
synopsis: Educational documentary directed by Robert Snyder provides a coherent outline of Fuller's basic concepts as well as a personal portrait of a humanist who put his scientific knowlege to the task of considering the present under the aspects of the future rather than from the conventional wisdom of the past

title: World of Hans Christian Andersen, The
synopsis: Feature-length cartoon about the childhood of young Hans and where he got some of the ideas for his highly imaginative fairy tales. The animation is colorful and creative, though stylistically comparable to Saturday morning TV shows. It provides a wonderful world of fantasy to absorb the small fry at a matinee

title: World of Henry Orient, The
synopsis: Peter Sellers stars in a wacky comedy about a fair-to-middling concert pianist whose pursuit of extra-curricular love (Paula Prentiss) is foiled by the unwitting but persistent efforts of two teenage girls who just may be his only fans in all the world. Directed by George Roy Hill, the acting is very good, the comedy nicely paced and the romantic element only in the background

title: World of Susie Wong, The
synopsis: Exotic but unappetizing tale of the rough life and times of a Hong Kong lady of the night, toned down from Paul Osborn's play in the Hollywood version starring Nancy Kwan as Susie and William Holden as her American love interest. Directed by Richard Quine, its plush production of a sentimental romance may have some interest for hardy adults, but not for youngsters or those with reservations about a drama which unfolds, for the most part, in a seamy brothel. O (br) ( 1961 )

title: World's Greatest Athlete, The
synopsis: Frustrated coach (John Amos) vacationing in Africa discovers a Tarzan-like jungle youth (Jan-Michael Vincent) and brings him to his sunny California campus where he starts making a shambles of the record books. Directed by Robert Scheerer, it is the Disney studio's special-effects men who save the day for sports as well as for parents who with their children will have to take the yawns along with the laughs in this matinee special

title: World's Greatest Lover, The
synopsis: Failed comedy written and directed by Gene Wilder who also stars as a hapless oaf who goes to Hollywood in the 1920s hoping to win a studio-sponsored world's greatest lover contest. The direction is inept, the writing shows no vestige of wit or originality and Wilder's performance is loud, vulgar and supremely unfunny. Boring but its low level of humor is not for young viewers

title: World Trade Center
synopsis: Two police officers (Nicolas Cage and Michael Pena) wait to be found after being crushed in the rubble of the World Trade Center terror attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, while their frantic wives (Maggie Gyllenhaal and Maria Bello) wonder if they've survived, and intrepid good Samaritans (Michael Shannon and Stephen Dorff among them) search the rubble for signs of life. Some may be disappointed that director Oliver Stone eschews an epic approach by focusing on this relatively small, true-life story which nonetheless paints an inspiring picture of bravery, fortitude and sacrifice in the face of enormous adversity. Some intense scenes of peril and suffering, a few profane and crude words uttered under extreme circumstances, injured victims, some bleeding and a brief but disturbing image of the towers with a long shot of a falling body may preclude viewing by younger adolescents

title: World Without End
synopsis: Fanciful sci-fi adventure as the first manned space flight speeds out of control through time, returning to Earth in the year 2508 A.D. to find the survivors of a nuclear holocaust living underground, while human mutants rule the planet's radioactive surface.
