Writer-director Edward Bernds focuses on the efforts of the spaceship's crew (notably Hugh Marlowe and Rod Taylor) to get the survivors to quit their unhealthy subterranean city and retake the now radiation-free surface from the mutants. Fantasy violence

title: World Without Sun
synopsis: Documentary made by oceanaut Jacques-Yves Cousteau details the human conquest of underwater space. It is an opportunity to see and experience an incredibly beautiful part of creation, till now hidden from human eyes

title: Worth Winning
synopsis: Adolescent male fantasy about a shallow Philadelphia TV weatherman (Mark Harmon) who bets a friend (Mark Blum) that he can propose marriage to three women (chosen by the friend) in three months and be accepted by each. The heel gets his comeuppance, but director Will Mackenzie treats him more sympathetically than the three female guinea pigs (Maria Holvoe, Madeleine Stowe and Lesley Ann Warren) in a sexist exercise demeaning to women. Sexual promiscuity including adultery and some profanity laced with sexual vulgarities. O (PG-13) ( 1989 )

title: Woyzeck
synopsis: Stark German adaptation of Georg Buchner's 19-century play about a much-abused soldier (Klaus Kinski) in a small garrison town who goes mad and brutally murders the woman (Eva Mattes) he has been too poor to marry. Directed by Werner Herzog, the story of a man's alienation and descent into irrationality is powerfully acted and its dark mood unrelieved

title: Wraith, The
synopsis: A brutally murdered teenager (Charlie Sheen) returns as an avenging angel to race to their deaths the depraved auto gang that had killed him. A deadly supernatural demolition derby filmed on the picturesque highways of Arizona sells violence, vengeance and a few sexual inferences with foul language to a youth market already overburdened with negative role models

title: Wrath of God, The
synopsis: Hard-drinking, gun-toting renegade priest (Robert Mitchum) joins forces with two other fugitive misfits to erase a fanatical madman-rancher in Central America during the revolutionary 1920s. Directed by Ralph Nelson, the result is downright painful in some sections, embarrassing and simply ludicrous in others. Some heavy violence

title: Wrecking Crew, The
synopsis: The only funny aspect of this limp spy spoof is watching Dean Martin lumber through it as super-agent Matt Helm entrusted to guard a gold shipment from Denmark to London, giving rise to jokes about Danish pastries (one of whom is Elke Sommer). Directed by Phil Karlson, the level of crude sexual humor is beneath adolescent interest. O (PG) ( 1968 )

title: Wreck of the Mary Deare, The
synopsis: What starts as a dandy mystery goes sour after a salvager (Charlton Heston) boards a floundering, storm-tossed freighter and discovers it abandoned by all but the captain (Gary Cooper) who insists he is still in command of the vessel. From there on, matters pale considerably as director Michael Anderson plods through the captain's trial by a maritime court, with entirely predictable results. Some stylized violence

title: The Wrestler
synopsis: Seamy but powerful character portrait of an aging professional wrestler (a superb Mickey Rourke) whose marginal career is threatened by a heart attack, as he initiates a tentative romance with a stripper (Marisa Tomei) and makes fumbling efforts to reconnect with his estranged daughter (Evan Rachel Wood). Director Darren Aronofsky's study of loneliness, set in a landscape of trailer parks and strip malls, is unsparing in its portrayal of the titular sport, the sadistic impulses of its fans, and the demeaning sexuality of the strip club where the protagonist unwinds, but the drama's artistic intent and achievement are clear, as are the fundamentally decent aspirations of the troubled man at its core. Strong sexual content, including graphic nonmarital sexual activity, some nudity, brutal wrestling scenes, drug abuse, pervasive rough and much crude language, and some uses of profanity

title: Wrestling Ernest Hemingway
synopsis: Slow-moving, sentimental portrait of the unlikely friendship that developes between two lonely old men -- a foul-mouthed, lecherous former sea captain (Richard Harris) and an introverted retired barber from Cuba (Robert Duvall). Directed by Randa Haines, it's an actor's feast with Harris chewing up whatever scenery he can find while Duvall concentrates on being slow and deliberate in everything, including his Hispanic accent, though Sandra Bullock's performance as a friendly waitress is brightly refreshing. Some lengthy discussions of love and sex, flashes of rear nudity and occasional rough language

title: Wristcutters: A Love Story
synopsis: Gritty, downbeat drama set in a purgatorial afterlife for suicides, three of whom -- a young slacker (Patrick Fugit) in search of the girlfriend (Leslie Bibb) for whose sake he killed himself, a young woman (Shannyn Sossamon) who insists she is there by mistake, and a Russian musician (Shea Whigham) whose entire family took their own lives -- become friends on a road trip during which they encounter the leader of a commune (Tom Waits) and a self-proclaimed messiah (Will Arnett). Writer-director Goran Dukic's film is engaging for the first 15 minutes or so, after which, despite its welcome stance against suicide, it becomes random, visually uncomfortable and ultimately stupefying. Brief upper female nudity, much rough and crude language, some crass language, four uses of profanity, graphic wounds, blood and a suicide theme

title: Written on the Wind
synopsis: Soapy sudser about the troubled life and death of a weak-willed Texas oil tycoon (Robert Stack), the strong wife (Lauren Bacall) who tries to reform him and his best friend (Rock Hudson) who secretly loves her while disdaining the love offered him by the oil man's dissolute sister (Dorothy Malone). Director Douglas Sirk's trashy exercise in sentimental melodrama is slickly contrived and mindlessly boring. Much alcohol abuse, some stylized violence and veiled sexual references

title: Wrong Arm of the Law, The
synopsis: Comic caper in which the London underworld (headed by Peter Sellers and Bernard Cribbens) join forces with the police (notably Lionel Jeffries) to nab an Australian gang masquerading as city policemen. Directed by Cliff Owen, the droll proceedings feature a cast of top British comedians who prove a lot funnier than the often cumbersome plot. Stylized violence, sexual innuendo and a comic view of criminal activities

title: Wrong Box, The
synopsis: British black comedy revolves around the bumbling attempts of someone to kill off members of a family in order to obtain a large inheritance. Directed by Bryan Forbes, the script is not very sharp but the acting of John Mills, Ralph Richardson, Michael Caine and Peter Sellers is first rate. The most hilarious performance, a classic of its kind, belongs to Wilfred Lawson as the old family retainer

title: Wrongfully Accused
synopsis: Uneven comedy in which a gullible violinist (Leslie Nielsen) becomes a fugitive from justice while hunting down the terrorists who got him framed for murder. Writer-director Pat Proft uses Nielsen's deadpan delivery to spoof up "The Fugitive" and other movies with goofy sight gags, comical props and silly situations that are fitfully funny. Slapstick violence, sexual situations and minimal profanity

title: Wrong Guys, The
synopsis: Often entertaining story about a wilderness reunion of a pack of onetime Cub Scouts who are threatened by their old neighborhood bullies and an escaped con who wields a mighty range of weaponry. Directed Danny Bilson is aided by a cast of young, stand-up comics (Louie Anderson, Richard Lewis, Richard Belzer, Franklyn Ajay and Tim Thomerson) who have their own particular comic shticks. Mild profanity

title: Wrong Is Right
synopsis: Failed black comedy in which Sean Connery plays a television news commentator who finds himself in the middle of a struggle between an American President (George Grizzard), his political rival (Leslie Nielsen), Arab terrorists and assorted villains to gain possession of two suitcases containing nuclear bombs. Writer-director Richard Brooks tries to satirize amorality in high places but the humor is flat and the story terribly jumbled. Graphic violence

title: Wrong Move, The
synopsis: Tedious, empty German drama in which a moody would-be writer (Rudiger Vogler), who doesn't like people and has no interest in politics, takes a rambling journey through West Germany. Written by Peter Hanke and directed by Wim Wenders, the random incidents and various characters met along the way occasion little interest for the young man and less for the viewer. Mature themes

title: Wrong Turn
synopsis: Schlocky slasher flick about a foursome of oversexed twentysomethings (including Desmond Harrington, Eliza Dushku and Jeremy Sisto) lost in the West Virginia wilderness and hunted by a trio of flesh.hungry, homicidal hillbillies. Buckets of blood flow in this clunky formulaic gorefest directed by Rob Schmidt, who leaves no cliche unturned and succeeds in killing off viewers' interest as quickly as he kills his cardboard cast members. Much graphic violence, recurring rough language, an implied sexual encounter, lewd humor and drug abuse

title: WUSA
synopsis: Confused political melodrama about the right-wing owner (Pat Hingle) of a New Orleans radio station, its liberal disc jockey (Paul Newman), his waitress girl friend (Joanne Woodward) and a manic social worker (Tony Perkins). Director Stuart Rosenberg toys with ill-formed notions of political polarization and reduces them to cliches in a nearly incoherent plot

title: Wuthering Heights
synopsis: Classic romantic melodrama from the Emily Bronte novel about the doomed love between Cathy (Merle Oberon), a Yorkshire doctor's daughter, and Heathcliff (Laurence Olivier), the downtrodden orphan who grows up with her, then runs away to make his fortune only to return to find Cathy wed to another (David Niven) and his riches meaningless without her. Directed by William Wyler, the well-crafted melodrama succeeds in evoking the fierce passion of Heathcliff's tormented yearnings for his lost love which allow him no peace until their spirits are united after death. Physical and mental cruelties, romantic obsessions and a spite marriage

title: Wuthering Heights
synopsis: Good British version of the Emily Bronte romantic classic of tragic love on the moors stars Anna Calder-Marshall as Cathy and Timothy Dalton as Heathcliff. Director Robert Fuest has made a conscious effort to enable young viewers to identify with the doomed pair but in doing so, he has softened the rough edges of the characters and the malevolent nature of their relationship. Good cast and fine creation of mood and period

title: W.W. and the Dixie Dancekings
synopsis: Burt Reynolds plays a professional con man who takes in hand a hapless group of country musicians. Director John(G) . Avildsen's comedy is often hilarious and is marked by fine acting. One scene at a drive-in is adult fare

title: WXIII: Patlabor the Movie 3
synopsis: Third in an animated Japanese movie series in which two police detectives investigating suspicious deaths on the waterfront discover the perpetrator is a bioengineered monster lurking in Tokyo Bay. Director Takayama Fumihiko's animation is well done but the jumbled narrative is a mishmash of sci-fi Japanese monster movie and plodding police procedural. Some fantasy violence, a suicide and several instances of rough language. Subtitles

title: Wyatt Earp
synopsis: Violent, over-long, revenge-themed Western in which reluctant lawmen Wyatt Earp (Kevin Costner) and two of his brothers (Linden Ashby and Michael Madsen) dole out six-shooter justice in lawless towns of the Old West, until, joined by buddy Doc Holliday (Dennis Quaid), they track down and willfully execute the Clanton-McLaury gang who dared defy them. Though visually impressive, director Lawrence Kasdan's shallow treatment of the characters centers in the depiction of Earp as a remorsely cold-blooded figure who is ultimately elevated to heroically triumphant stature. Much gory violence, justification of murders, discreet bedroom scene, fleeting nude photo and an instance of rough language. O (PG-13) ( 1994 )

title: Wyoming
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Joe Kane in which a pioneer ranching family (William Elliott and Vera Ralston) build a large spread after the Civil War, then get involved in a range war when homesteaders start moving into the area. Frontier violence

title: Wyoming Kid, The
synopsis: ( see: "Cheyenne" )

title: Wyoming Mail
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Reginald LeBorg in which an undercover government agent (Stephen McNally) passes himself off as an escaped convict in order to join a gang of mail train robbers (notably Ed Begley, Howard da Silva, James Arness and Richard Jaeckel), then bring them to justice. Stylized violence

title: Wyoming Outlaw
synopsis: Western programmer directed by George Sherman in which the Three Mesquiteers (John Wayne, Ray Corrigan and Raymond Hatton) help a starving Dust Bowl family by getting the goods on a corrupt political ring selling county jobs and pocketing relief funds. Stylized violence

title: Wyoming Renegades
synopsis: Murky tale of an ex-outlaw (Phil Carey) who tries to go straight but has to shoot it out with Butch Cassidy's Wild Bunch before his reformation is accepted by his neighbors. Directed by Fred F. Sears, it's a tired exercise in overly familiar territory. Stylized violence

title: Wyoming Roundup
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Thomas Carr in which a straight-shooting cowboy (Whip Wilson) stops off in a cattle town, replaces its late sheriff and averts a range war. Frontier violence

title: Wyoming Wildcat
synopsis: Western programmer directed by George Sherman in which a cowboy (Don "Red" Barry) returns from the Spanish-American War to find his rancher father heading an outlaw gang, then is suspected of complicity until his dad painfully squares matters. Frontier violence and a good badman

title: X-15
synopsis: Routine service melodrama directed by Richard D. Donner in which an Air Force pilot (Charles Bronson) breaks a speed record, then joins the program testing the experimental craft of the title which is being developed for manned space flights. Tense moments for test pilots and their families

title: X2: X-Men United
synopsis: Entertaining sci-fi actioner about outcast humans whose mutated genetics endow them with superpowers with which they battle evil counterparts bent on world domination. Directed by Bryan Singer and based on the enormously successful Marvel Comics series, the sequel, while continuing the original's positive message of tolerance, relies too heavily on imaginative special effects and action sequences at the expense of character and narrative development. Recurring comic book-style violence and some crass language

title: Xala
synopsis: Black African satire, filmed in Senegal, about a prosperous businessman who takes a third wife but, unable to consummate the marriage, is convinced someone has cursed him with a spell of impotence and spends all his money seeking the help of witch doctors. Director Ousmane Sembene's metaphor of impotence is vividly applied to the neo-colonialist values of the African middle class that is the movie's main target

title: Xanadu
synopsis: Olivia Newton-John sings her way through her role as a materialized Greek muse who inspires a middle-aged musician (Gene Kelly) and a young artist (Michael Beck) to become partners in a nightclub. Directed by Robert Greenwald, the movie offers little but special effects, optical devices and a few vulgar dance numbers in what is essentially an illustrated sound-track album

title: The X-Files: I Want to Believe
synopsis: Second big-screen version of the long-running TV series in which two former FBI agents, one now a full-time doctor (Gillian Anderson) and the other a fugitive (David Duchovny), are recruited by a current bureau official (Amanda Peet) to work with a purportedly psychic disgraced priest (Billy Connolly) to solve a kidnapping. Director and co-writer Chris Carter's rather ordinary film touches on issues of faith, forgiveness and medical ethics, but treats them only superficially as it pursues an unlikely, somewhat ghoulish plotline. Action violence, surgical gore including severed limbs and body parts, implied nonmarital relationship, sexual references, occasional crude and crass language and a profanity

title: X Files, The
synopsis: Meandering story based on the title TV series in which two stubborn FBI agents (Gillian Anderson and David Duchovny) stumble upon a global conspiracy involving frozen aliens, a mutating virus and the possible colonization of Earth by extraterrestrials. Directed by Rob Bowman, the result is little more than a two-hour series episode with the usual murky visuals of menacing aliens amidst elaborate theories of government and corporate conspiracies which are never resolved. Brief violence, menacing situations, occasional profanity and an instance of rough language

title: Xiu Xiu: The Sent-Down Girl
synopsis: In the waning days of China's Cultural Revolution a young girl (Lu Lu) sent by the government to learn horse herding techniques on the remote western plains alongside a stoic herder (Lopsang) eventually allows local officials to use her sexually in hopes of getting permission to return home. Director Joan Chen's bleakly poetic melodrama captures the desperate loss of innocence and ensuing tragedy as symbolic of so many lives disrupted or destroyed in that era. Subtitles. Brief violence including suicidal behavior, some sexual encounters with nudity and an instance of rough language

title: X-Men
synopsis: '' -- Entertaining sci-fi thriller that pits outcast humans whose genetic mutations give them super powers against evil mutants intent on ruling over humanity. Based on the Marvel comic book series, director Bryan Singer's live-action film has an absorbing, multi-layered narrative, sharp editing and imaginative special effects, but some sketchy characterizations. Some sci-fi violence and a few instances of crass language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: X-Men Origins: Wolverine
synopsis: Lavish and flashy action-packed prequel to the popular "X-Men" series exploring the origins of conflicted superhero Wolverine (Hugh Jackman), including his defining childhood, turbulent relationship with his brother, Victor Creed (Liev Schreiber), role in a team of fellow mutants (Ryan Reynolds, Will.i.Am, Kevin Durand, Dominic Monaghan) led by the duplicitous Col. Stryker (Danny Huston), and tragic romance with schoolteacher Kayla (Lynn Collins). Director Gavin Hood tries not to lose sight of the human elements with Wolverine generally demonstrating moral conscience, though the kinetic action and violence necessarily predominate. Intense action violence, killings, explosions, patricide, fleeting rear nudity, premarital habitation, some crude expletives, crass expressions and brief profanity, limiting its appropriateness to mature teens and up

title: X-Men: The Last Stand
synopsis: In this third film based on the popular Marvel comic-book series, the U.S. government develops a "cure" for the mutants' condition, sparking a revolution as the misanthropic Magneto (Ian McKellen) declares war on mankind, amassing an army of maddened mutants, while others like Wolverine (Hugh Jackman), Storm (Halle Berry) and a furry blue new ally (Kelsey Grammer) side with Professor Charles Xavier (Patrick Stewart) who advocates peaceful coexistence. Fans of the series won't be disappointed as director Brett Ratner, taking over the reins from Bryan Singer, injects a fair amount of human emotion into what is essentially one big special-effects X-travaganza, resulting in entertaining escapist fare. Much stylized action violence, a sexually suggestive encounter, brief suggested nudity, and a few instances of crude language, limiting its appropriateness to older adolescents and up

title: X--The Man with X-Ray Eyes
synopsis: Failed sci-fi chiller directed by Roger Corman in which a doctor (Ray Milland) developes a drug enabling the human eye to see through physical objects, but his obsession to perfect the drug leads to murder, flight and into hiding as a carnival mind reader, then a faith healer until the police chase him into a Christian revival tent for a gruesome "moral" ending. Stylized violence, menacing situations and occasional sexual innuendo

title: X the Unknown
synopsis: British sci-fi thriller pits a nuclear scientist (Dean Jagger) against a mysterious radioactive ooze which threatens a Scottish community after bursting from beneath the earth's crust in search of more radiation. Directed by Leslie Norman, the suspense mounts as the unseen deadly force takes its toll of victims, then deflates in a pat conclusion with disappointing visuals of the slimy blob. More menace than violence

title: XXX
synopsis: Chaotic action adventure in which an antisocial extreme-sports enthusiast (VinDiesel) is recruited by a veteran government agent (Samuel L. Jackson) to enter the shadowy world of espionage to fight a desperate and dangerous gang of anarchists in Prague. Director Rob Cohen's testosterone-revved flick follows a halfhearted narrative with time-worn undercover elements and features improbable, death-defying stunts which are used to diminishing effect. An implied sexual encounter, recurring violent action sequences, brief drug content, fleeting rear nudity and some crass language

title: XXX: State of the Union
synopsis: Odiously overwrought follow-up to the 2002 action film about an ex-Navy SEAL (Ice Cube, stepping in for Vin Diesel) serving time, who is recruited into a supersecret government agency by a former team member (Samuel L. Jackson) in order to prevent a rogue arm of the military -- headed by a hawkish secretary of defense (Willem Dafoe) -- from assassinating the president (Peter Strauss). Directed by Lee Tamahori, this tedious testosterone-revved sequel is twice as violent, twice as ridiculous and twice as pointless as the original. Excessive violence, sexual innuendo, an instance of rough language and recurring crude expressions and profanity

title: X, Y & Zee
synopsis: Shrill British sex melodrama involving a self-destructive, affluent, childless couple (Elizabeth Taylor and Michael Caine) and an attractive widow (Susannah York) with whom the husband falls in love and the wife tries to seduce in order to thwart the interest of her errant spouse. Directed by Brian G. Hutton, the perverse triangle is a vulgar, one-dimensional affair with brief nudity and considerable abusive language

title: The Yards
synopsis: Engrossing crime drama set amidst corruption in the New York City subway construction industry in which a newly released ex-con (Mark Walhberg) hides from a wrongful murder charge that would implicate a volatile friend (Joaquin Phoenix) and family member (James Caan). Director James Gray orchestrates a dark tale of moral dilemmas enhanced by muted performances but undermined by some glaring script implausibilities. Brief violence, much rough language, a sexual situation with fleeting nudity and occasional profanity. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: The Young Black Stallion
synopsis: Feel-good family adventure set in 1946 North Africa about a young Bedouin girl (Biana Tamimi) who befriends and tames a fiery wild stallion, which she eventually rides to victory in an important tribal horse race in order to restore her grandfather's reputation among the regional clansmen after losing all his wealth in the war. Based on the late Walter Farley's children's book series and shot in supersized Imax format; director Simon Wincer reins in character and narrative depth in favor of protracted, albeit stunning, panoramic desert vistas; nevertheless, despite a predictably sentimental payoff, the film still wins your heart -- if only by a nose

title: The Young Girl and the Monsoon
synopsis: Plodding drama about a divorced photojournalist (Terry Kinney) who unexpectedly gains custody of his 13-year-old daughter (Ellen Muth) just as his professional and personal life spins out of control. Bland performances, shallow characterizations, and strained dialogue undermine director James Ryan's well-intentioned debut feature. An implied sexual encounter, some rough language and brief profanity. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Yaaba
synopsis: Two youngsters befriend an old woman who lives as an outcast on the outskirts of their tiny village in the African country of Burkina Faso. Director Idrissa Ouedraogo's beautifully photographed movie shows the virtues as well as the foibles of the villagers in warmly human terms evoking a certain sense of kinship on the part of interested viewers, though those looking for casual entertainment are likely to be disappointed. English subtitles. Some youngsters may be confused or perplexed by aspects of this very different culture

title: Yakuza, The
synopsis: Robert Mitchum plays an American back in Japan, where he had served in the Occupation, to help get back a friend's kidnapped daughter (Keiko Kishi) by having a top gangster (Ken Takadura) repay the favor he owes the American. Though Mitchum is able to rise above the inane story with some dignity, director Sydney Pollack's Japanese gangster movie (which is what the title means) proves silly as well as repugnant in its exotic brutality and simple-minded concept of manhood

title: Yankee Buccaneer
synopsis: Historical hokum directed by Frederick de Cordova revolves around the captain (Jeff Chandler) of a U.S. Navy vessel ordered to masquerade as a pirate ship in order to locate a fleet of buccaneers plundering the Caribbean, with further complications stemming from his ornery second officer (Scott Brady), a Portuguese countess (Suzan Ball) and the area's Spanish governor (Howard da Silva). Stylized violence

title: Yankee Doodle Dandy
synopsis: Born on the Fourth of July, George M. Cohan melded patriotism with Irish charm in his rise from song-and-dance vaudevillian to leading Broadway songwriter and producer in a career celebrated by this nostalgic, flag-waving musical starring James Cagney as the feisty entertainer. Directed by Michael Curtiz, it features a grand collection of Cohan's best-remembered songs as well as Cagney at the top of his form singing and dancing his way to an Academy Award for the year's best performance. Fine family fare

title: Yankee Pasha
synopsis: Anemic romantic adventure directed by Joseph Pevney in which a sharpshooting American frontiersman (Jeff Chandler) pursues the kidnappers of his girlfriend (Rhonda Fleming) to Morocco, then rescues her from a dastardly Barbary pirate (Bart Roberts). Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Yank in the R.A.F., A
synopsis: Stale World War II tale of a hotshot American pilot (Tyrone Power) enlisting in the Royal Air Force only because a former girlfriend (Betty Grable) has taken a job in London, but he loses her to his squadron leader (John Sutton) until proving his heroism in the skies over Dunkirk. Directed by Henry King, what has dated badly is the romantic appeal of Power's character as a supposedly charming heel, but the wartime setting provides some agreeable humor and the scenes re-creating the desperate evacuation of Dunkirk are first-rate. Wartime violence and romantic complications

title: Yanks
synopsis: Overlong but beautifully photographed re-creation of a worn and ravaged England during World War II offers the thin story of two English women (Vanessa Redgrave and Lisa Eichhorn) and two American soldiers (William Devane and Richard Gere) told in terms of parallel romances. Directed by John Schlesinger, the story suffers from a slow-moving pace and lack of focus which leaves it without much dramatic force. Adultery figures in the plot, with some profane language and some bedroom scenes

title: Yearling, The
synopsis: A young boy's attachment to an orphaned fawn relieves the loneliness of life in the Florida wilderness but brings grief as the deer grows to threaten the family's crops in this classic version of the Marjorie Kinnon Rawlings story. With credible performances by Gregory Peck and Jane Wyman as the parents and Claude Jarman Jr. as the youth, director Clarence Brown has fashioned a genuine portrait of rural American life as well as a sincere celebration of family values

title: Year My Voice Broke, The
synopsis: Coming-of-age drama set in Australia in 1962 tells of a 15-year-old's (Noah Taylor) infatuation with his 16-year-old childhood friend (Loene Carmen) who has set her eyes on a wilder lad (Ben Mendelsohn) for her first sexual invovlement, forcing the younger boy to stand by and watch her ruin her life. Writer-director John Duigan's sensitive, non-exploitative handling of puberty results in a touching portrayal of boy-girl friendship and first love. Some rough language and the implications of sex and pregnancy outside marriage

title: Year of Living Dangerously, The
synopsis: Murky story set in 1965 Indonesia where a newly arrived Australian correspondent (Mel Gibson) comes to depend upon an Asian news photographer (Linda Hunt in a male role) for information about an impenmding revolution but along the way the Aussie's attention is distracted by a torrid love affair with a British intelligence agent (Sigourney Weaver). Director Peter Weir re-creates the place and chaotic period very effectively but characterizations are sketchy and the action lacks coherence. Though it has compassion for the poor and oppressed, the sexual relationship makes it mature fare

title: Year of the Comet
synopsis: Contrived chase story of a mismatched couple (Penelope Ann Miller and Tim Daly) on the run from assorted villains (led by Louis Jourdan) while trying to deliver a priceless bottle of Napoleonic wine to an auction. Producer-director Peter Yates' sprightly and visually delightful caper is all but ruined by its self-consciously precious tone. Occasional stylized violence and discreet sexual innuendo with a flash of nudity

title: Year of the Dog
synopsis: Quirky tale -- by turns, wryly amusing, sad and thought-provoking -- about a lonely office worker (Molly Shannon) whose beloved beagle dies suddenly, prompting her to reevaluate her priorities as she interacts with her hunting-obsessed neighbor (John C. Reilly), an animal rights activist (Peter Sarsgaard), her paranoid boss (Josh Pais), best friend-officemate (Regina King), and upscale brother (Tom McCarthy) and sister-in-law (Laura Dern). Writer-director Mike White's low-keyed comedy avoids the predictable as it explores the validity of its heroine's increasing obsession with dogs and animal rights; performances are finely etched and a compassionate worldview informs the whole film. Brief innuendo and sexual banter and mild profanity

title: Year of the Dragon
synopsis: A police captain and Vietnam veteran (Mickey Rourke) wages war against a dapper but ruthlessly deadly Chinatown gang lord (John Lone). Directed by Michael Cimino, and written by Oliver Stone, the film is muddled almost to the point of incoherence by extreme amounts of profanity and violence while being pointedly racist and sexist

title: Year of the Gun
synopsis: Standard political thriller set in 1978 terrorist-ravaged Rome where a naive American reporter (Andrew McCarthy) becomes involved with an Italian divorcee (Valeria Golino), a university professor (John Pankow) and an aggressive photojournalist (Sharon Stone) who is convinced the reporter is her ticket inside the Red Brigades terrorist organization. Routine performances dilute director John Frankenheimer's shadowy story of personal ambition and surprise betrayals, interestingly set against the political backdrop of President Aldo Moro's kidnapping and murder. A few bedroom scenes with nudity, sporadic brutal violence and some rough language

title: Year of the Quiet Sun, A
synopsis: An American soldier (Scott Wilson) and a Polish widow (Maja Komorowska) fall in love despite their lack of a common language in Russian-occupied Poland in the grim days following World War II. Under the masterful direction of Krzysztof Zanussi, the Polish production probes into the tragic complications arising from a relationship foundering over cu1tural differences. Sensitive treatment of serious matters

title: Year of the Woman
synopsis: Pretentious documentary on the politicization of women's rights adds, unfortunately, little enlightment about the subject. It suffers not only from missed opportunities to demonstrate systematic injustice, but from the misuse of interviews with articulate individuals, edited mainly to serve the needs of filmmaker Sandra Hochman

title: Year One
synopsis: Ramshackle road comedy in which two misfit hunter-gatherers (Jack Black and Michael Cera) set out from their prehistoric village and encounter a series of biblical figures, including Cain (David Cross), Abraham (Hank Azaria), Isaac (Christopher Mintz-Plasse) and the elite of Sodom (most prominently Oliver Platt). Director and co-writer Harold Ramis' lumbering journey is fuelled by sophomoric humor and smug irreverence. Profane treatment of scriptural figures and practices, pervasive sexual and some scatological humor, implied premarital sexual activity, at least one use of the F-word, much crude and crass language

title: Years of Lightning, Day of Drums
synopsis: Celebratory documentary about the promise of President Kennedy's years in office as seen from the perspective of his tragic assassination and burial. It recalls vividly the feeling of personal loss experienced by people around the world during that terrible November in 1963

title: Yellowbeard
synopsis: Several of the Monty Python troupe join forces with Cheech and Chong, Susannah York, James Mason, Peter Boyle, Madeline Kahn, and the late Marty Feldman in this leaden, stultifyingly unfunny pirate spoof directed by Mel Damski. Brief nudity and an abundance of coarse jokes

title: Yellow Cab Man, The
synopsis: Comedy of errors about an accident-prone inventor (Red Skelton) whose secret formula for unbreakable glass makes him the target of a crooked lawyer (Edward Arnold) and a bogus psychologist (Walter Slezak), until his girlfriend (Gloria de Haven) and a veteran cab driver (James Gleason) come to the rescue. Under Jack Donohue's direction, Skelton mugs his way through the comic complications, including dream sequences using Weegee's distorted urban images, and a big chase finish that turns a home furnishings exhibition into a shambles. Some comic violence and psychological duress

title: Yellow Rolls-Royce, The
synopsis: Slickly elegant romantic melodrama in which the automobile of the title passes from an English aristocrat (Rex Harrison) in Ascot to an American gangster (George C. Scott) in Florence and a Scandanavian heiress (Ingrid Bergman) in Yugoslavia. Directed by Anthony Asquith, the love interests are Jeanne Moreau, Shirley MacLaine and Omar Sharif respectively but only the third tale has any weight and that scarcely memorable. Sexual situations and some stylized violence

title: Yellow Sky
synopsis: When outlaws (Gregory Peck, Richard Widmark and Harry Morgan) come across an old sourdough (James Barton) and his granddaughter (Anne Baxter) living in a ghost town, they reason only a treasure could keep them there. Getting it from them, however, is what this Western is all about and director William A. Wellman makes it a hard, deadly business. Stylized violence and much menace, some of it quite nasty

title: Yellowstone Kelly
synopsis: Clumsy Western directed by Gordon Douglas places the title Montana trapper (Clint Walker) and his helper (Edd Byrnes) in the middle of a tribal dispute between the Sioux over a captured Arapaho woman, while an inexperienced Army major prepares to drive the Sioux back to the Dakotas. Frontier violence and romantic complications

title: Yellow Submarine
synopsis: Wonderful animated feature for young and old, with music from the Beatles' Sergeant Pepper album, follows the adventures of John, George, Paul and Ringo to the never-neverworld of Pepperland where they find the Blue Meanies overrunning its lovely terrain. Director George Dunning's animation is a wonder, the music a delight and, of course, Sgt. Pepper and his Lonelyhearts Club Marching Band get their peaceful land back at the end, and those Blue Meanies are not all that mean

title: Yellow Tomahawk, The
synopsis: Cliched Western directed by Lesley Selander is set in Wyoming where a former Army scout (Rory Calhoun) tries to save a cavalry outpost from Cheyenne warriors seeking revenge on its commander (Warner Anderson) for his part in the Sand Creek Massacre. Frontier violence and some unsavory characters

title: Yentl
synopsis: Barbra Streisand musical in which she stars in the title role as an intelligent Jewish woman living in Eastern Europe at the turn of the century who dresses as a man in order to study in a yeshiva (male religious school) and finds herself attracted to a student (Mandy Patinkin) already engaged to be married. When the engagement is called off, Yentl is persuaded to become the bridegroom instead, but all is resolved when she leaves handsome student and his beloved by emigrating to America and less restrictive educational prerequisites. Streisand, who also produced, directed and co-authored the script, is on center stage for almost the entire length of the movie, a bit much for all but her most avid fans. Yentl's mock marriage to another woman makes the movie inappropriate for young viewers

title: Yes, Giorgio
synopsis: Operatic tenor Luciano Pavarotti makes his film debut as a great opera star who, despite his wife in Italy, has a love affair with a beautiful American doctor (Kathryn Harrold) during a tour of the U.S. Pavarotti's singing would be enough to recommend it, except that director Franklin J. Schaffner's supremely silly movie takes a benign attitude toward the adulterous affair, which is not just incidental, but the main focus of the plot throughout

title: Yes Man
synopsis: Fitfully funny comedy in which a bored bank employee (Jim Carrey) attends a seminar run by a self-help guru (a comically intimidating Terence Stamp) and vows to say yes to every invitation or suggestion, leading to romance with a quirky singer (Zooey Deschanel), a renewed relationship with his best friend (Bradley Cooper) and greater respect from his nerdy boss (Rhys Darby, spot-on). Principally a vehicle for Carrey's facial and physical antics, director Peyton Reed's adaptation of Danny Wallace's best-selling memoir salutes openness to life and adventure and satirizes superstition, but also features considerable sexual humor, including a distasteful subplot involving Carrey's elderly but randy neighbor (Fionnula Flanagan). Nongrapic, nonmarital sexual activity, brief rear nudity, some sexual humor, one use of the F-word, much crude language and a few profanities

title: Yesterday's Enemy
synopsis: While sloughing through the Burmese jungle in 1942, a squad of British soldiers (led by Stanley Baker) execute some villagers to get information about the Japanese invaders, then ironically face the same treatment when captured by the Japanese. Directed by Val Guest, the tough-minded World War II drama effectively raises moral questions of military expediency and basic human rights. Much tension amid wartime violence

title: Yi Yi (A One and a Two)
synopsis: Absorbing domestic drama about the mid-life malaise of a Taiwanese businessman (Wu Nianzhen) who struggles to keep his family and computer company together while sorting out feelings for an old sweetheart (Ke Suyun) whom he unexpectedly bumps into after 20 years. Set in Taipei, director Edward Yang's three-hour film is a rich, funny and humane family portrait with keen observations, but the film's otherwise finely tuned pace lags somewhat in the final third. Subtitles. Mature themes, brief violence, fleeting nudity and some rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Yog -- Monster from Space
synopsis: Japanese monster moviemaker Ishiro Honda has picked the farthest recesses of his brain to create an elephantine octopus with a mitre-shaped head. The sight of this super squid might thrill moppets, but older kids may yawn and yearn for more imaginative stuff, and they are right

title: Yolanda and the Thief
synopsis: Odd musical romance set in a mythical South American country where an 18-year-old convent-raised heiress (Lucille Bremer) is duped by an American con man (Fred Astaire) posing as her guardian angel until his conscience gets in the way. Directed by Vicente Minnelli, the story's silly premise never gets off the ground, though the songs and dance numbers are fanciful enough and there's a bit of fantasy involving a real angel (Leon Ames). Romantic complications

title: Yoo-Hoo, Mrs. Goldberg
synopsis: Warmhearted documentary celebrating the life and career of Gertrude Berg, the creator, principal writer and star of "The Goldbergs," a popular radio series about a middle-class Jewish family that became one of TV's first sitcoms in 1949. Filmmaker Aviva Kempner's accomplished profile of this media pioneer, whose scripts promoted familial relationships over possessions, offers insights into the early history of broadcasting, the widespread anti-Semitism against which Berg courageously struggled, and the anti-communism crusade of the 1950s which temporarily drove the show off the air. Mature themes, including suicide, and incidental but negative treatment of Catholic historical figures

title: You Again
synopsis: Grown-ups find it hard to leave the dramas -- and traumas -- of their teen years behind in director Andy Fickman's entertaining multigenerational comedy about family, forgiveness, and second chances. A twenty-something ex-geek (Kristen Bell) who has evolved into a self-confident career woman is forced to relive her past horror when she returns home for her brother's (Jimmy Wolk) wedding, only to discover he is marrying her high school nemesis (Odette Yustman). Similarly, the groom's mother (Jamie Lee Curtis) has issues with the bride's aunt (Sigourney Weaver), a student-era best friend-turned-rival. Mild slapstick violence, some double-entendres

title: You Are What You Eat
synopsis: Pseudo-documentary about the youth counter-culture of the 1960s presents a montage of disjointed scenes of the so-called love generation engaged in various sexual activites, pot smoking, rock song gatherings and street happenings, sprinkled with scenes of the cult heroes of the period. Directed by Barry Feinstein, it tries to be outrageous but is mostly tasteless and vulgar. Some exploitative nudity

title: You Belong to My Heart
synopsis: ( see: "Mr. Imperium" )

title: You Came Along
synopsis: Three combat pilots (Robert Cummings, Don DeFore and Charles Drake) clown their way across the country on a World War II bond drive in a romantic comedy which turns serious when one of them (Cummings) determines to marry their tour guide (Lizabeth Scott) despite his terminal medical condition. Directed by John Farrow, there's plenty of fun along the way but what period audiences saw as an uplifting ending seems maudlin and heavy-handed today

title: You Can Count on Me
synopsis: Family drama in which a wayward drifter (Mark Ruffalo) returns to his small hometown to visit his loving sister (Laura Linney), the single mother of an 8-year-old son (Rory Culkin), but her brother's inappropriate behavior disrupts their peaceful existence. Although its slow rhythm takes some getting used to, writer-director Kenneth Lonergan's sensitive film skillfully explores the complex bond between adult siblings orphaned at a young age. An extramarital affair, several sexual encounters, sporadic marijuana use, brief fisticuffs and some profanity with intermittent rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: You Can't Beat Love
synopsis: Dated situation comedy about a wealthy playboy (Preston Foster) who runs for mayor on a bet, then falls for his opponent's daughter (Joan Fontaine). Directed by Christy Cabanne, the comedy gets heavy-handed on the issue of municipal corruption but Paul Hurst scores as a tough union leader aiming to become chief of police

title: You Can't Cheat an Honest Man
synopsis: Uneven comedy about a hard-up circus owner (W.C. Fields) whose constant flimflams keep him in trouble with the law until his daughter (Constance Moore) decides to marry a man wealthy enough to pay his debts. Directed by George Marshall, the comic proceedings include ventriloquist Edgar Bergen and his wooden pal, Charlie McCarthy, but the funniest scenes belong to Fields whose imaginative antics turn the circus into a fun house and transform a high society party into a chaotic shambles at picture's end. Slapstick humor and comic invective

title: You Can't Run Away from It
synopsis: Dim musical version of "It Happened One Night" with exasperated reporter Jack Lemmon helping spoiled heiress June Allyson elude domineering father Charles Bickford. Producer-director Dick Powell's mirthless remake of a classic romantic comedy has all the appeal of a flat tire. Sexual situations and innuendo

title: You Can't Sleep Here
synopsis: ( see: "I Was a Male War Bride" )

title: You Can't Steal Love
synopsis: ( see: "Live a Little, Steal a Lot" )

title: You Can't Take It with You
synopsis: Solid adaptation of the George Kaufman-Moss Hart screwball comedy about an impoverished family of eccentrics whose daughter (Jean Arthur) falls for a rich man's son (James Stewart). Directed by Frank Capra, the zany guests of the wacky household come and go as the family's head (Lionel Barrymore) tries to convince the rich man (Edward Arnold) that happiness has nothing to do with money. That sentiment may seem less convincing today than in the Depression but the cheerfully uninhibited antics of this house of sage fools are still very funny indeed

title: You Can't Win 'Em All
synopsis: Tony Curtis and Charles Bronson cavort through post-World War I Turkey as a pair of roguish mercenaries, periodically betraying each other for the least whiff of beauty or booty. Director Peter Collison's tired, formula adventure features Turkey's matinee idol, Fikret Hakan, but the real star of this turkey is a beautiful old steam-engine, lovingly photographed against a picturesque Turkish locations

title: You Got Served
synopsis: Slight hip-hop musical that follows a dancing crew led by two friends (Omari Grandberry and Marques Houston) who must put aside their recent feuding to triumph at the biggest dance competition of the year. High-energy, acrobatic dance scenes and all-the-rage pop singers may attract a young crowd, but the boilerplate script and the shoddy direction of Christopher B. Stokes misses a step and falls flat. A few crude dance moves, minor drug content, brief violence and some crass words

title: You Gotta Stay Happy
synopsis: Slack romantic comedy in which a mixed-up heiress (Joan Fontaine) runs out on her wedding night and falls for a diffident pilot (James Stewart) who lets her come along on a cross-country air cargo flight, with predictable results. Directed by H.C. Potter, the off-beat proceedings have some amusing moments but much of the humor is forced and the romance lacks the intended charm. Sexual situations and innuendo

title: You Light Up My Life
synopsis: Young singer-composer (Didi Conn) breaks away from the smothering influence of her comedian father and comes to New York determined to rely on no one but herself. Director Joseph Brooks neatly packaged bit of nothing fails to hold its thin story line together despite Conn's good performance. An incident of premarital sex is presented as a moral lapse which the heroine immediately regrets

title: You'll Find Out
synopsis: Creaky vehicle for radio personality Kay Kyser who takes his orchestra, including comic Ish Kabibble and vocalist Ginny Simms, to a debutante's isolated mansion where they spend a stormy night amidst sinister goings-on with ominous visitors (Boris Karloff, Peter Lorre and Bela Lugosi). Director David Butler's spooky comedy mixes silly period humor with tepid menace and hokey suspense. Unmemorable save for the period music

title: You'll Like My Mother
synopsis: When her husband is killed in Vietnam, the pregnant widow (Patty Duke) visits her mother-in-law but is met with unaccountable hostility, is troubled by a menacing man lurking in the shadows and gradually realizes she is being kept a prisoner in the creaky old mansion. Directed by Lamont Johnson, the twisting plot of this tight little mystery thriller offers a goodly number of chills and shocks

title: You, Me and Dupree
synopsis: After losing his job, home and car, the boorish best friend (Owen Wilson) of the groom moves in with the newlyweds (Matt Dillon and Kate Hudson) creating havoc until, midway through, he straightens himself out and proves himself useful. Directors Anthony and Joe Russo's uneven comedy starts out irritating and contrived, but improves as it goes along, while the leads are excellent. The vulgar comic elements (less pervasive than in most films of this type) are not entirely outweighed by the movie's humanistic tone, the characters' ultimately decent behavior, and feel-good affirmations of love, marriage and friendship. Some profanity, rough and crude language, sexual humor and innuendo, scatological humor, implied premarital kinky sex, brief rear and partial nudity, and a drug reference

title: You Never Can Tell
synopsis: Daffy off-beat comedy in which a dog, poisoned after inheriting a fortune, is sent back from "beastatory" in human form as a private investigator (Dick Powell) to find his poisoner (Charles Drake). Director Lou Breslow treats the fantasy premise in leaden fashion, though this doesn't impede the dizzy humor with the private eye's penchant for snacking on dog biscuits while his fellow "manimal" (Joyce Holden), a former horse, outraces automobiles on occasion. Those in the mood for silliness will not be disappointed

title: Young Americans
synopsis: Semi-documentary on a national tour of teenage singers presenting a program of show tunes, spirituals, folk songs and traditional melodies. Written and directed by Alex Grasshoff, the material is blended into a pleasant story of the personal interaction between the talented young musicians and the reaction of audiences to the troupe's humor and enthusiasm

title: Young and Innocent
synopsis: British mystery in which a jobless writer (Derrick de Marney) is arrested for the murder of a screen actress, then escapes to prove his innocence with the help of the local constable's daughter (Nova Pilbeam). Directed by Alfred Hitchcock, the couple's flight from the police is paced with grit and humor, eventually culminating in the capture of the killer who's playing the drums in a hotel dance band and whose blinking eyes give him away to the audience before the pursuers get wise. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Young Animals, The
synopsis: Crudely contrived story of Mexican-American teenagers trying to win acceptance and equal rights in a California small-town high school. Exploitative treatment of violence and teenage sexual relations

title: Young at Heart
synopsis: Often funny and ultimately moving documentary about a Northampton, Mass., senior citizens' chorus whose repertoire includes rock, R&B and punk selections as they rehearse over a two-month period for a hometown concert and cope with the death of one member and the ill health of others. Director-narrator Stephen Walker's film quickly engages viewers by introducing a winning array of real-life characters and charting their struggles to master the music and carry on with the show. Frank sexual discussion, innuendo, occasional crass language; possibly acceptable for older teens

title: Young at Heart
synopsis: Slick sudser in which the daughter (Doris Day) of a music teacher (Robert Keith) calls off her wedding to a promising composer (Gig Young) because she thinks her sister (Elizabeth Fraser) is in love with the guy, then marries an embittered musician (Frank Sinatra) who proves to be suicidal. Directed by Gordon Douglas, this musical version of Fannie Hurst's "Four Daughters" has some good songs, including the title number, but lays on the sentiment with a trowel and only Sinatra fans will appreciate the saccharine ending. Romantic complications and a suicide attempt

title: Young Billy Young
synopsis: Standard Western about the new marshall (Robert Mitchum) of a lawless town who takes the job in order to avenge the killing of his son while befriending a wild youth (Robert Walker) who reminds him of his dead boy. Directed by Burt Kennedy, the story is entirely predictable and the relationship between the older man and the youth is never explored with any depth. Some rather bloody shoot-outs

title: Youngblood
synopsis: Black youth (Bryan O'Dell) joins a street gang for self-protection and, when the gang takes on the local drug organization, he finds himself on a collision course with his older brother. It is an exxcessively violent movie whose morality is as muddled as its story line

title: Youngblood
synopsis: Rob Lowe stars as the young and talented amateur hockey player who must come to terms with the violence of his sport and his determination to be a winner. When turning the other cheek doesn't work, he learns how to be tough but still proves he can outclass the brutes. Nevertheless he can't resist a final display of macho combat to satisfy his critics. Brutality, an explicit nude sex scene and ambivalent values ruin a simple tale about sports ethics for youngsters

title: Young Cassidy
synopsis: Somewhat fictionalized biography of young Sean O'Casey (Rod Taylor) explores the background of poverty, ignorance, injustice and rebellion in Ireland that was to shape the playwright's dramatic vision. Directed by Jack Cardiff and John Ford, the British production is rich in period detail and attains some human dimension but is rather romanticized in its picture of Irish life. Some stylized violence and sexual references

title: Young Couple, A
synopsis: Familiar French tale of a young couple (Anna Gael and Alain Libolt) who marry, enjoy a rich party-going life but separate when the self-centered wife and the husband cannot reconcile their different visions of life. Directed by Rene Gainville, it is a well-made but somewhat fleeting portrait of early married life and the consequences of infidelity

title: Young Dillinger
synopsis: Clunky crime melodrama in which Dillinger (Nick Adams) is caught after robbing a safe with the help of his girlfriend (Mary Ann Mobley), then escapes custody to form his own gang and is hunted down by the FBI. Directed by Terry O. Moore, the Depression-era action is woefully unconvincing and the crime-does-not-pay ending is a bad joke. Nasty violence and common-law marriage

title: Young Doctors in Love
synopsis: Stupid spoof of doctor movies and soap operas intermixes sketches and sight gags with a narrative line about the adventures of first-year interns. Directed by Gary Marshall, there are a few good laughs along the way, but excessive vulgarity sours the humor. Some nudity

title: Young Einstein
synopsis: Wacky Australian comedy links the physicist who gave us the Theory of Relativity to the origins of rock 'n' roll music. Writer, director, editor, co-producer and star Yahoo Serious pratfalls his way through an eccentric interpretation of Einstein's youth, taking Monty Python-esque liberties and introducing a comedy persona rivaling that of Pee-wee Herman. Shower scene with rear male nudity and minimal sexual innuendo

title: Younger Brothers, The
synopsis: Routine Western in which paroled outlaw Cole Younger (Wayne Morris) and his three brothers try to go straight, despite an old friend (Janis Page) who wants them to join her gang and an ex-lawman (Fred Clark) who wants them dead. Director Edwin L. Marin's weak shoot-'em-up is filled with cliches, though the double-take bank robbery in the finale is one for the books. Stylized gunplay and fisticuffs

title: Younger Generation, The
synopsis: Sentimental tale from Fannie Hurst's novel about a Jewish family (headed by Jean Hersholt) moving from Manhattan's Lower East Side into a plush Fifth Avenue apartment after their son (Ricardo Cortez) becomes a wealthy antique dealer, but they move out again when he proves ashamed of them and his ethnic identity. Directed by Frank R. Capra, it's essentially a silent movie with a few dialogue sequences, but the result is eloquent enough in universalizing the pain of immigrant parents over offspring who reject their family heritage. Domestic strife

title: Young Frankenstein
synopsis: Director Mel Brooks' spoof of the venerable horror classic stars Gene Wilder as an American doctor who inherits the family's Transylvanian estate, with Peter Boyle as the monster whose prodigious sexual appetite provides the one-liner for the movie. Bright spots are Marty Feldman whose pop-eyes are upstaged by his shifting hump and Cloris Leachman as the housekeeper whose name causes horses to whinny. Though generally amusing, with some clever bits and occasionally hilarious moments, it features much vulgarity, verbal and otherwise

title: Young Girls of Rochefort, The
synopsis: French musical romance in which false values are nicely ribbed, star-crossed lovers are united and everyday dreams come true when a fair comes to town and two local girls (Catherine Deneuve and Francoise Dorleac) join in the fun. Directed by Jacques Demy, the production has some simple charm but suffers from a static setting, lack of continuity and a surfeit of non-professional singing

title: Young Guns
synopsis: The young Billy the Kid (Emilio Estevez) teams up with a group known as the Regulators to avenge the murder of his mentor, a good-guy cattle rancher (Terence Stamp). Director Christopher Cain depicts Billy and his buddies (Kiefer Sutherland, Charlie Sheen, Lou Diamond Phillips) cavorting like Robin Hood's merry band as they destroy a corrupt rancher and his murderous gang. Some intense violence and bloodshed, much profanity, a sequence glorifying drug use and implications of sexual impropriety

title: Young Guns II
synopsis: Claiming to be Billy the Kid, a grizzled old cowboy (Emilio Estevez) recounts in flashback what really happened after his one-time friend, Pat Garrett (William Petersen), put on a sheriff's badge and set out to kill the Kid and his gang. Director Geoff Murphy's spirited sequel has some good performances and eye-catching scenery but tends to idealize the outlaws as hip and funny true-blue buddies -- especially troubling as they introduce a young teen to their lusty, lawless way of life. Some gory violence, implied sexual liaisons, several shots of rear nudity and occasional profanity

title: Young Guns, The
synopsis: Formula Western set in 1897 Wyoming where the son (Russ Tamblyn) of an executed outlaw tires of being treated as an outcast and joins a wild bunch of young toughs, then has to decide whether to be their leader or go straight as urged by an outlaw's daughter (Gloria Talbott). Directed by Albert Band, there are no surprises here except for a pretentious foreword equating the story's young gunmen with the juvenile delinquents of its own day. Stylized violence, some of it quite nasty

title: Young Lions, The
synopsis: Flawed adaptation of Irwin Shaw's novel about three soldiers in World War II France -- a brash Broadway entertainer afraid he's a coward (Dean Martin), an American Jew plagued by home-grown anti-Semites (Montgomery Clift) and a German officer disillusioned by Nazi inhumanity (Marlon Brando). Director Edward Dmytryk plods through a fitfully interesting but overlong script whose good intentions are largely undone by Martin's inept performance and Clift's limp portrayal of victim-turned-hero, though Brando commands attention as an ambiguous idealist. Wartime violence and sexual situations

title: Young Man with a Horn
synopsis: Uneven melodrama of a poor but musically gifted youth (Kirk Douglas) who is taught to play the trumpet by a jazz master (Juan Hernandez), achieves success with a popular dance band, then falls for a rich, neurotic woman (Lauren Bacall) who takes the joy out of his life and music, leaving him a self-destructive has-been, except to his friends (Hoagy Carmichael and Doris Day). Directed by Michael Curtiz, the episodic story is musically effective with Harry James dubbing the horn work, but the character's personal lives are thinly written and dramatically unconvincing. Some stylized violence and emotional outbursts

title: Young Mr. Lincoln
synopsis: Henry Fonda gives a warm, ingratiating performance as the young country lawyer whose self-deprecating wit and common-sense intelligence are put to the test in defending an innocent youth charged with murder. Director John Ford is at his best in this leisurely slice of Americana that gains stature in credibly foreshadowing the homespun virtues which would soon propel young Abe into Illinois politics and the White House. Durable family fare that is as meaningful as it is entertaining

title: Young People
synopsis: Tired Shirley Temple vehicle in which the moppet actress plays an orphan whose vaudevillian foster parents (Jack Oakie and Charlotte Greenwood) retire to an unfriendly town. Despite some lively song-and-dance numbers, director Allan Dwan fails to find any fresh angles on the formula plot and stereotyped characters. Best for the young and undemanding

title: Young Philadelphians, The
synopsis: Slick melodrama in which a poor law student (Paul Newman) loses a rich girlfriend (Barbara Rush), then becomes a high-priced lawyer by cultivating the wife (Alexis Smith) of a partner (Otto Kruger) in a leading law firm, aquiring the account of a wealthy dowager (Billie Burke) and winning aquittal for a buddy (Robert Vaughn) in a murder trial. Directed by Vincent Sherman, the soapy story mixes the greed and sexual intrigues of the mainline set with the struggles of a young man to reach the top on his own terms. Sexual situations

title: Young Poisoner's Handbook, The
synopsis: Uneven black comedy in which a chemistry-obsessed London teen (Hugh O'Conor) spends 8 years in a mental asylum after poisoning his stepmother (Ruth Sheen), then is released only to resume experimenting with lethal poisons on unsuspecting co-workers. Directed by Benjamin Ross, the fact-based events are viewed mostly from the poisoner's warped perspective, resulting in some mean-spirited humor about the tragic loss of innocent lives caused by a lunatic would-be scientist. Stylized death scenes and some rough language

title: Young Rebel
synopsis: European co-production directed by Vincent Sherman in which the young Cervantes (Horst Buchholz) serves as secretary to the Cardinal (Louis Jourdan) negotiating a truce with a Turkish emissary (Jose Ferrer), then becomes a hero in the Battle of Lepanto but is later captured and held prisoner in Algiers until ransomed. The disjointed English-language version has much action but little insight into the character of the man who wrote "Don Quixote." Period violence and sexual innuendo

title: Young Runaways, The
synopsis: Contrived story of three teenagers who flee abusive home situations and find their fate on their own even worse. Director Arthur Dreifuss treats a significant social subject in a superificial manner, leaving viewers with no clear insight into the reasons or solutions of the problem. Mature themes

title: Young Sherlock Holmes
synopsis: A series of fatal accidents in Victorian London baffle the police but not a student named Sherlock Holmes (Nicolas Rowe) and his school chum John Watson (Alan Cox). Directed by Barry Levinson, Chris Columbus' script gives a convincing account of Holmes' early school days that is entirely in keeping with the character of the master sleuth found in the pages of Arthur Conan Doyle's classic stories. The specia1 effects are spectacular, but never gory or overdone, though some nightmare sequences may frighten young chi1dren

title: Young Tom Edison
synopsis: Hollywood version of the inventor's youth in a small Midwestern town features Mickey Rooney whose curiosity about how and why things work constantly get him in trouble until his ingenuity saves his mother's life and stops a train wreck. Directed by Norman Taurog, the script is emotionally manipulative but goes down easily enough thanks to a good cast and credible period production. While inspirational fare for youngsters, some of their elders may find the sentimental exercise rather cloying

title: Young Winston
synopsis: British dramatization of Churchill's memoir, "My Early Life," retells uncritically his own version of his formative years from war correspondent in the Boer War to Parliament, with Simon Ward in the title role. Directed by Richard Attenborough, it excells as a panorama of life in the Empire before World War I, through a succession of tableaux of balls and battles, of parliamentary debates and family discourses. Although not a perfect film, it is a film of idealism and very enjoyable on a number of levels

title: Young World
synopsis: French movie about the sexual excesses of contemporary youth indulges in needlessly detailed erotic treatment

title: You Only Live Once
synopsis: Depression-era melodrama in which an ex-con (Henry Fonda) tries to go straight after marrying a good woman (Sylvia Sidney) but gets framed for murder, then kills a priest (William Gargan) in a prison break and heads for the border with his pregnant wife at his side. Director Fritz Lang gives credibility to this picture of a marginalized victim of an uncaring society through convincing performances and realistic action scenes that temper the plot's sentimentality. Stylized violence and much menace

title: You Only Live Twice
synopsis: Sean Connery in his fifth appearance as James Bond goes through the motions of tracking down some mission space capsules amidst oriental intrigue in Japan and finally bests his arch foe Blofeld (Donald Pleasence). The agent 007 formula of impersonal sex and violence has worn thin with the result that director Lewis Gilbert's Bond movie is just another mediocre spy thriller

title: You Only Love Once
synopsis: Unpretentious French romance depicting the loving relationship of a couple (Karen Blanguernon and Frederic de Pasquale) from first fancy to marriage, parenthood, estrangement and reconciliation. Directed by Dirk Sanders, it is a gay, moody, colorful expression of the simple things in real life, often having the effect of a lilting visual ballet, and is well worth seeing for its vision of the constancy of love

title: You're a Big Boy Now
synopsis: Wacky comedy about young man (Peter Kaster) who, in trying to make the transition from adolescence to independence from overbearing father (Rip Torn) and clinging mother (Geraldine Page), gets his own apartment and becomes infatuated with an actress (Elizabeth Hartman). Directed by Francis Ford Coppola, its exaggerated comic style does not always succeed, especially with some of the erotic elements

title: You're Lying
synopsis: Powerful Swedish semi-documentary indictment of the inadequacies and outright injustices existing in a penal system that prides itself on being the best in the world. Directed by Vilgot Sjoman, it demonstrates the contradictions between official policy and the actual practice of using prisons to effect social rehabilitation as well as society's indifference to how its prisons actually operate. Excessively explicit treatment of sexual matters

title: You're My Everything
synopsis: Boston socialite (Anne Baxter) and vaudeville song-and-dance man (Dan Dailey) marry, make it big in early movies, then argue about whether to let their daughter (Shari Robinson) become a Shirley Temple-like child star. Director Walter Lang gets some brisk fun with old Hollywood nostalgia but the characters are superficial and the domestic situations syrupy. Few bright spots for youngsters

title: You're Never Too Young
synopsis: Silly comedy in which Jerry Lewis escapes a murderer by getting on a train dressed in an 11-year-old's sailor suit with a ticket bought a teacher (Dean Martin) returning to his post in a girl's academy. In a tiresome remake of "The Major and the Minor," director Norman Taurog drags out the mirthless proceedings in slack fashion, save for Lewis' frenetic mugging. Mild romantic complications and sexual innuendo

title: You're Only Young Once
synopsis: Judge Hardy (Lewis Stone) and family vacation at the seashore with romantic complications furnished by son Andy (Mickey Rooney) and daughter Marian (Cecilia Parker). Director George B. Seitz's pleasant but lightweight entry in the Hardy series is notable chiefly for its period picture of fun at a family resort

title: You're Telling Me!
synopsis: W.C. Fields comedy in which he plays a hard-drinking small-town inventor whose bad luck is changed by a chance encounter with a foreign princess (Adrienne Ames). Directed by Erle C. Kenton, the plot's not much but Fields makes what's there hilarious, especially a classic comic routine on the golf links. Intemperance and malicious gossip as sources of humor

title: Your Friends & Neighbors
synopsis: Sordid series of sketches involving six dim individuals whose unsatisfying sexual relationships have become the source of frustration, anger and resentment. Writer-director Neil LaBute puts his cast of self-centered characters through the torments of sexual disappointments and misalliances but the result becomes tediously monotonous and lacks any moral perspective. Numerous sexually explicit situations and dialogue, recurring rough language and occasional profanity

title: Your Highness
synopsis: This sophomoric send-up of medieval swashbucklers follows the quest of a gallant prince (James Franco) to rescue his bride-to-be (Zooey Deschanel) from the clutches of the evil wizard (Justin Theroux) who kidnapped her, an adventure which affords his ne'er-do-well younger brother (Danny McBride) a shot at bettering himself. The humor in director David Gordon Green's smirking spoof -- which also features Natalie Portman as a freebooting warrior with an agenda of her own -- relies heavily on the supposed joke of "olde tyme" characters inhaling pot and exhaling murky clouds of foul language. Strong sexual content, including full nudity and masturbation, drug use, pervasive sexual humor, a couple of uses of profanity, close to 50 instances of rough language, many crude and crass terms

title: Yours, Mine and Ours
synopsis: Fact-based story of a Navy widower (Henry Fonda) and a Navy widow (Lucille Ball) who fall in love, get married and merge their 18 children into one big, happy family. Director Melville Shavelson's comedy has predictable but genuinely funny complications such as an interrupted honeymoon, identity crises, bathroom lineups, troop-movement planning and economy-sized. Underneath all the broad humor is a gently moving story that manages to keep in touch with human reality. Truly a family picture

title: Yours, Mine & Ours
synopsis: Inferior remake of the 1968 Henry Fonda-Lucille Ball charmer about a widowed naval officer (Dennis Quaid) with eight children, and a free-spirited widow (Rene Russo) with 10, who marry years after being high school sweethearts, and the comic complications that arise from merging the families. Despite a heart-tugging ending, director Raja Gosnell relies on too much unrealistic slapstick and though Quaid gives an accomplished performance, Russo is utterly bland, making the original a far better bet all around. Some mild innuendo

title: Your Three Minutes Are Up
synopsis: Unemployed swinger (Ron Liebman) initiates his younger, hard-working buddy (Beau Bridges) into a series of con games that at first seem easy and fun but they threaten the young man's approaching marriage (to Janet Margolin) and in the end events take an ugly turn. Director Douglas Schwartz introduces some heavy-handed and explicit sex scenes which only compound the problem of its murky underlying morality

title: Your Turn, My Turn
synopsis: Unpleasant French comedy romance stars Marlene Jobert as the mother of an 8-year-old boy who meets Philip Leotard, the father of a 9-year-old girl, and though encumbered by their perceptive childen, they begin an adulterous affair. Directed by Francoise Leterrier, the movie's Gallic view of life is not especially amusing despite its frothy treatment. Benign attitude towards adu tery

title: You So Crazy
synopsis: Martin Lawrence demonstrates his limited talents as a stand-up comic in a series of rambling, very raunchy monologues devoted almost exclusively to sex in an unamusing, unenlightening and unimaginative performance recorded by director Thomas Schlamme. Trivialization of sexuality, explicit language and unrelenting use of sexual expletives

title: Youth in Revolt
synopsis: Sometimes witty but consistently sex-focused coming-of-age comedy about a lonely California teen (Michael Cera) whose sophisticated cultural tastes make him a fish out of water in his divorced parents' (Jean Smart and Steve Buscemi) lowbrow world, and his obsessive love for a like-minded girl (Portia Doubleday) he meets on vacation at a trailer park. Director Miguel Arteta's adaptation of "Youth in Revolt: The Journals of Nick Twisp" -- the first in C.D. Payne's series of novels about the titular adolescent -- sees Cera developing a suave but amoral alter ego willing to cause mayhem to help his timid original reunite with, and lose his burdensome virginity to, the object of his desire. Explicit animated images of intercourse, nongraphic premarital (and probably underage) sexual activity, masturbation, drug use, at least one profanity, much sexual humor and considerable rough and crude language

title: Youth Without Youth
synopsis: Visually rich but dramatically deficient fable in which a 70-year-old Romanian scholar (Tim Roth) regains his youth and acquires superhuman powers -- as well as a split personality -- after being struck by lightning, is protected and given a new identity by his doctor (Bruno Ganz), romances a Nazi spy (Alexandra Pirici) but evades her masters who want to study him, escaping to Switzerland, where he falls in love with a tourist (Alexandra Maria Lara), who looks exactly like the deceased woman he loved in his youth and who has also been struck by lightning with equally unusual effects. Writer-director Francis Ford Coppola's film captivates the eye but numbs the mind as it moves at a snail's pace through a series of surreal images and didactic conversations. Graphic nonmarital sexual activity; side, rear and upper female nudity; strong imagery of a burn victim; light sexual references; and suicide theme

title: You've Got Mail
synopsis: Breezy romantic comedy in which two rival Manhattan booksellers (Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan) trade barbs unaware they are falling in love with each other through anonymous e-mail messages. Director Nora Ephron turns in a romantic trifle made enjoyable by the winning chemistry between its appealing stars. Implied affairs and an instance of profanity

title: You've Got to Walk It Like You Talk It or You'll Lose That Beat
synopsis: Director Peter Locke's low-budget story of a confused young man in search of himself (Zalman King) is a witless attempt to satirize the Establishment but all that emerges is a stupefying amount of visual and verbal crudity

title: Yo Yo
synopsis: French comedy about a millionaire's son (Pierre Etaix) who, after his father is ruined in the Depression, becomes a renowned clown, makes a fortune in the novelty business but ultimately rejects the grand yet lonely style of life in which he had been raised. Also directed by Etaix, the episodic tale is told mainly through sight gags and visual humor that bears comparison with the antics of Keaton, Chaplin and Lloyd

title: Yukon Flight
synopsis: Adventure programmer directed by Ralph Staub in which singing Sgt. Renfrew (James Newill) of the Royal Mounted Police teams with a airplane pilot (Warren Hull) to stop a crooked air cargo service which is cheating gold miners of the true value of their ore shipments. Stylized violence

title: You Don't Mess With the Zohan
synopsis: Typically vulgar Adam Sandler comedy centers on Zohan Dvir, a lethal Israeli commando who abandons an illustrious army career in order to fulfill his dream of becoming a New York hairdresser. Perhaps the best that can be said about this inanity is that a message of intercultural harmony and understanding seeps through the sex-related raunchiness, rendering it less harsh and marginally less offensive than Sandler's last effort, "I Now Pronounce You Chuck & Larry," also directed by Dennis Dugan. Pervasive sexual content (much of it involving senior citizens), numerous sexual references (many spoken in Yiddish), countless obscene gestures, frequent crude and crass language, rear male and female nudity, some toilet humor, mildly disparaging racial and religious slurs, and a modicum of action violence

title: Z
synopsis: When a leftist minister (Yves Montand) in the Greek government is assassinated, the investigating magistrate (Jean-Louis Trintignant) tries to untangle the shadowy affair in order to find those responsible. The French dramatization directed by Costa-Gavras is a taut political thriller that goes beyond Greek politics and party labels because it is interested in justice and critical of any system of government that justifies criminal acts and violence in attaining its objectives

title: Zabriskie Point
synopsis: Taking its title from a promontory that overlooks Death Valley, director Michelangelo Antonioni's first movie about America is critical of its ill-treatment of youth and its self-cannibalism through violence and material excess, topped off in an explosive finale. Yet, because the message is expressed largely via cliches, all that it underscores is that perhaps middle-aged filmmakers should avoid making youth-oriented movies about other cultures. Some excessive sexual scenes

title: Zachariah
synopsis: Director George Englund updates the Western with rock music, hippie garb, the search for identity and a plea for peace, all laced together with self-parody and an incurable romanticism. The two heroes (Don Johnson and John Rubenstein) show the audience that peace, love and friendship are possible in a world of violence, hate and mistrust. Hokey as it sounds, the movie works if given a chance, and its overriding values and goals cannot be dismissed too lightly. Stylized violence, sexual innuendo, drug references and coarse language

title: Zack and Miri Make a Porno
synopsis: Wayward comedy in which two cash-strapped roommates (Seth Rogen and Elizabeth Banks) find their long-standing platonic friendship complicated when they star in their own improvised pornographic movie to pay the bills. Romantic aspirations are undercut, in writer-director Kevin Smith's film, by a frivolous approach to pornography which, instead of a profit-driven assault on human dignity, is portrayed as a lark and even as a means of self-fulfillment. Strong sexual content, including graphic nonmarital and aberrant sexual activity, adultery, frontal male and female, upper female and rear nudity, much sexual and some scatological humor, pervasive rough and crude language, a few uses of profanity

title: Zandy's Bride
